stem: A boy develops delayed motor development followed by spasticity, involuntary movements, compulsive biting, and gouty arthritis. Which substance accumulates in this disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has a classic case of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder due to near-complete deficiency of the purine salvage enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HPRT, or sometimes referred to as HGPRT). This enzyme recycles purine bases back into nucleotide synthesis and thereby prevents their degradation to uric acid. The deficiency of HPRT is associated with excessive de novo purine synthesis, hyperuricemia (elevated levels of uric acid in the blood), and the clinical signs and symptoms described in the question stem. The biochemical basis of the often striking self-mutilation, which may require restraints and even tooth extraction, has never been established. Treatment with allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase and its production of uric acid, and reduces the gouty arthritis, urate crystal formation, urate nephropathy, and subcutaneous deposits of urate crystals (tophi) associated with hyperuricemia. It does not, however, modify the neurologic/psychiatric presentation.

Galactosemia is an autosomal recessive trait that results from a defective gene encoding galactokinase, galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase, or galactose 6-phosphate epimerase. When galactose accumulates, it is metabolized by aldose reductase to galactitol (choice A) in the lens. Galactitol in the lens causes swelling and cataracts.

Glucocerebroside (choice B) is the sphingoglycolipid substrate accumulating in inclusion bodies of individuals with glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher disease). The disease is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, erosion and fractures of bones, thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia, and characteristic macrophages (crumpled-paper inclusions).

Orotic aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the pyrimidine synthesis pathway. Orotic acid (choice D) accumulates and spills into the urine, resulting in orotic acid crystals. Infants with some forms of this disorder can present with severe megaloblastic anemia that does not respond to supplementation with vitamin B12 or folic acid.

Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency results in phenylketonuria (PKU), in which accumulation of phenylalanine (choice E) results in slow development, severe intellectual disability, autistic symptoms, and loss of motor control. There is mandatory newborn screening for PKU in all states in the U.S. because early diagnosis and treatment (dietary restriction) prevent pathology.

ReKaps: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by near-complete HPRT deficiency. Characteristic features include intellectual disability, spastic cerebral palsy, compulsive self-mutilation (biting hands and lips), hyperuricemia leading to gouty arthritis, urate crystal formation, tophi and urate nephropathy, and early death. Allopurinol reduces uric-acid complications but does not modify the neurologic/psychiatric presentation.

stem: A 4-year-old girl with intellectual disability is brought to the physician because of poor vision. She is tall with long limbs, kyphosis, and bilateral lens dislocation. Which amino acid is most likely selectively elevated in her serum?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The child has cystathionine synthase deficiency, also known as homocystinuria. This enzyme occurs in the pathways involving the metabolism of sulfur-containing amino acids and normally catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine. When the enzyme is blocked, homocysteine (which is normally a degradation product of methionine) is remethylated by a salvage pathway, resulting in the resynthesis of methionine. Plasma methionine and homocysteine levels are elevated as a result. The clinical features illustrated in the question stem are typical and likely to be mistaken for Marfan syndrome. The history of mental retardation is not consistent with Marfan syndrome. Children with cystathionine synthase deficiency also have limited joint mobility, in contrast to the hyperextensible joints in Marfan syndrome. These patients are also vulnerable to potentially fatal thrombotic episodes, particularly in postoperative and postpartum periods. Note that mutations in the CBS (cystathionine beta-synthase) gene are the most common form of homocystinuria.

Cystathionine (choice A) and cysteine (choice B) occur in the pathway after the enzyme blockage and so are reduced. Associate abnormalities of phenylalanine (choice D) with phenylketonuria; associate abnormalities of tyrosine metabolism (choice E) with tyrosinemia, albinism, and alkaptonuria.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has fatigue and scleral pallor. Her sister and older brother have hemolytic anemia, while two younger brothers are unaffected. Her parents are second cousins. Which enzyme deficiency most likely explains this disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. In general, you should associate primary hemolytic anemia with defects in glycolysis or the hexose monophosphate shunt (pentose phosphate pathway) because those are pathways of energy generation and antioxidant defense in the red cell. A salient feature of the patient's presentation is that the disorder appears to be hereditary and that it is not X-linked, because there is not a male-bias in the inheritance. Only one enzyme of those listed in the answer choices specifically involves these pathways, causes hemolytic anemia when deficient, and is inherited in an autosomal fashion: pyruvate kinase (PK).

PK is a glycolytic enzyme; PK deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder, affecting males and females approximately equally. Consanguinity increases the incidence of any autosomal recessive condition. Deficiency of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH), which may be related to hemolytic anemia, is X-linked. A hemolytic anemia from inherited deficiency of G6PDH in a woman is expected to be very rare. If PK is deficient, red cells cannot produce sufficient ATP to maintain the Na+/K+ pump on the plasma membrane, secondarily causing swelling and lysis. Severe forms of PK deficiency are usually symptomatic in newborns and may be life-threatening. Milder cases are often missed earlier in life and may or may not produce symptoms later in life. Increased concentrations of glycolytic intermediates occur in red blood cells; 2 to 3 times the normal levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG or 2,3-DPG) are present, leading to a lower affinity of hemoglobin for O₂.

Debranching enzyme (alpha-1,4; alpha-1,6 transferase) (choice A) deficiency is characterized by mild fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly. Defects in glucose-6-phosphatase (choice B) produce profound fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperuricemia. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice C) deficiency decreases NADPH production in the red cell and decreases the red-cell antioxidant defense. G6PDH deficiency can produce a hemolytic anemia during oxidant stress or during infections. G6PDH is an X-linked gene, and hemolytic anemia in the woman's sister and herself makes that gene defect unlikely. Deficiency of muscle phosphorylase (myophosphorylase) (choice D) produces weakness and cramping during the initial phase of exercise, especially if strenuous. During this period, glycogen normally supplies much of the glucose used by muscle.

ReKaps: Consanguinity increases the incidence of any autosomal recessive condition. Pyruvate kinase deficiency is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, so both sexes are equally affected; severe forms are usually symptomatic in newborns and may be life-threatening, while milder cases may present later. Red cells have increased glycolytic intermediates and 2–3 times the normal 2,3-BPG, lowering hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen. G6PDH deficiency can also cause hemolytic anemia but is less likely here because the gene is X-linked.

stem: A 7-year-old boy develops severe abdominal cramps after high-fat meals. Genetic testing shows lipoprotein lipase deficiency. Which lipoprotein is most likely increased?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. After a person eats a high-fat meal, triglycerides are processed by the intestinal mucosal cells. They are assembled in chylomicrons and eventually sent into the circulation for delivery to adipocytes and other cells. Chylomicrons are too large to enter cells, but are degraded while in the circulation by lipoprotein lipase, an enzyme associated with the luminal surface of endothelial cell membranes. Lipoprotein lipase catalyzes the breakdown of triacylglycerides in chylomicrons to free fatty acids and glycerol. A defect in this enzyme results in the accumulation of chylomicrons in plasma, causing the plasma to appear milky (lactescence), even in a fasting blood sample.

Albumin-bound free fatty acids (choice A) is incorrect because fatty acids leave the intestine esterified as triglycerides in chylomicrons. Free fatty acids increase in plasma when they are released from adipose tissue.

HDL (choice C) is not a carrier of dietary fat from the intestine.

LDL (choice D) would not be elevated in this patient after a high-fat meal. However, VLDL would be elevated if the patient ate a high-carbohydrate meal. In this situation, the carbohydrate would be converted into fat in the liver and sent into the circulation as VLDL. VLDL would be unable to be degraded to LDL and therefore would accumulate.

Triglycerides are an example of esterified fatty acids. They are composed of three fatty acids linked to glycerol by ester bonds. Lipoprotein lipase catalyzes the hydrolysis of these ester bonds, releasing fatty acids for entry into adipose and other tissues. Thus, a defect in lipoprotein lipase would cause a decrease, not an elevation, of unesterified fatty acids (choice E).

ReKaps: Lipoprotein lipase is required to metabolize chylomicrons and VLDL; it converts their triacylglycerides to free fatty acids and glycerol. Its deficiency causes elevated chylomicrons and VLDL. Chylomicrons carry dietary fats, whereas VLDL carries predominantly fat synthesized in the liver. With symptoms after a fatty meal, chylomicrons are expected to be the major plasma carrier of fat.

stem: A 45-year-old man with poorly controlled insulin-requiring diabetes is hospitalized with severe hyperglycemia, dehydration, and metabolic acidosis. His breath smells of acetone. Which measurement is most likely decreased compared with normal?
explanation: The correct answer is E. This patient's blood gases reveal a metabolic acidosis (low pH, low HCO3−). The decrease in arterial CO2 resulting from the increased respiratory rate is an appropriate compensatory response to the acidosis. The smell of acetone (the primary solvent in nail-polish remover) on the breath of a diabetic suggests ketoacidosis. This occurs when uncontrolled diabetes mellitus leads to overproduction of ketoacids and high levels of plasma acetone. Together, these are referred to as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Because acetone is highly volatile, it is excreted mainly by the lungs and can be detected in the breath. Ketoacids, which include acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate, are normally produced in roughly equal amounts. However, in pathologic conditions such as poorly controlled diabetes and alcoholism, in which the concentration of NADH is high, the ratio shifts and 3-hydroxybutyrate predominates. Therefore, the ratio of acetoacetate to 3-hydroxybutyrate decreases, while the net amount of ketoacids increases. In diabetic ketoacidosis, the level of 3-hydroxybutyrate increases approximately five times the increase in acetoacetate. Plasma levels of acetone (choice A) are increased during ketoacidosis, which leads to the smell of nail-polish remover on the patient's breath. Plasma catecholamines (choice B) and glucagon (choice C) are increased during ketoacidosis due to a shift in metabolism to that resembling the starvation state as a result of insufficient insulin. Plasma 3-hydroxybutyrate (choice D) increases as a result of the increase in NADH, contributing to the decreased acetoacetate/3-hydroxybutyrate ratio. In diabetic ketosis, NADH increases as a result of increased fatty acid beta-oxidation, which supplies the acetyl-CoA for ketogenesis. In excessive alcohol consumption, NADH increases as a result of the NAD+-requiring alcohol dehydrogenase reaction. The source also notes that 3-hydroxybutyrate should be measured to more accurately assess the initial extent of ketosis and follow resolution during treatment, because bedside dipstick tests do not measure 3-hydroxybutyrate. DKA causes a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis because the ketoacids ionize and their anions are not measured in the clinical laboratory.

stem: A breast-fed 7-day-old newborn develops bruising and umbilical-stump bleeding after the mother takes a cephalosporin. Which biochemical process is impaired by the resulting deficiency?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Deficiency of vitamin K produces a clotting disorder characterized by an elevated prothrombin time and easy bleeding, particularly in neonates (hemorrhagic disease of the newborn). The biochemical basis for this hemorrhagic tendency is that glutamate residues on factors II (thrombin), VII, IX, and X must be converted to gamma-carboxyglutamate residues (in a vitamin K-requiring reaction) for optimal activity.

In breast-feeding mothers, certain antibiotics, e.g. cephalosporins, can interfere with the production of vitamin K in breast milk.

The conversion of homocysteine to methionine (choice A) requires vitamin B12.

Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA (choice B) requires vitamin B12.

Cystathionine synthase requires the coenzyme form of B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) to convert homocysteine to cystathionine. Cystathionine is further degraded (choice C) by other enzymes to products that can be oxidized in the TCA cycle.

Hydroxylation of proline (choice E) requires vitamin C. Vitamin C deficiency can cause easy bruising, but will not prolong the prothrombin time.

ReKaps: Vitamin K deficiency in a newborn results in defective gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues of factors II, VII, IX, and X.

This results in elevated PT, leading to bleeding diathesis (hemorrhagic disease of newborn).

Certain antibiotics, anticonvulsants and anti-tuberculosis drugs in nursing mothers can interfere with vitamin K in breast milk.

stem: An 8-month-old girl develops crying, sweating, and shaking after fruit is introduced. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Fructose-1-phosphate aldolase (aldolase B) deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder of fructose metabolism resulting in accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate because of the inability to cleave it to glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. The accumulated fructose-1-phosphate inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, causing severe hypoglycemia after ingestion of fructose. These processes are inhibited because free inorganic phosphate (Pi) levels are reduced. Pi is required for glycogen phosphorylase in glycogenolysis. Pi is also required for ATP production, and ATP is needed for gluconeogenesis. As ATP levels fall, AMP levels rise; AMP is degraded to uric acid, and hyperuricemia may be seen. Prolonged fructose ingestion in infants ultimately leads to hepatic failure and death. This condition is known as hereditary fructose intolerance. Treatment is removal of fructose (and sucrose, a disaccharide of glucose and fructose) from the diet. Free fructose is found in fruits, honey, and high-fructose corn syrup.

Aldose reductase (choice A) reduces glucose to sorbitol and galactose to galactitol. In patients with recurring hyperglycemia (as in diabetes) or galactosemia (as in galactokinase deficiency or UDP-galactosyltransferase deficiency), increased concentrations of sorbitol or galactitol in the lens of the eye lead to cataracts.

Essential fructosuria involves a defect in fructokinase (choice B) and is a benign, asymptomatic condition.

Hexokinase (choice D) catalyzes the first step in glycolysis.

Lactase (choice E) breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose. Primary or secondary intestinal lactase deficiency results in diarrhea, bloating, flatulence, and cramping after ingestion of lactose. The majority of the world's population is lactase deficient.

ReKaps: Aldolase B deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate. It inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, causing severe hypoglycemia after fructose ingestion. Hyperuricemia and lactic acidosis may be seen.

stem: A 3-month-old boy has recurrent seizures, hypotonia, psychomotor retardation, and developmental delay. Laboratory studies show hypoglycemia and elevated lactate, alanine, pyruvate, and ketoacids. Deficiency of an enzyme that catalyzes synthesis of which molecule best explains these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Pyruvate carboxylase is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the formation of oxaloacetate: pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP → oxaloacetate + ADP + Pi. This reaction serves to make the oxaloacetate used within the citric acid cycle. A deficiency of this enzyme has very broad metabolic consequences because the citric acid cycle is downregulated, with resultant downregulation of the cell's energy-producing capacity. In addition to a general loss of energy in the cell, pyruvate levels rise because pyruvate is not converted into oxaloacetate; alanine levels rise because the normal conversion to pyruvate is feedback-inhibited.

In hepatocytes, pyruvate carboxylase is also an essential enzyme in gluconeogenesis from the major gluconeogenic amino acid alanine. Thus, a defect in the enzyme results in hypoglycemia, as observed in the patient. The enzyme is also involved in converting lactate to glucose. Clinically, pyruvate carboxylase deficiency shows variable expression due to allelic heterogeneity. The North American type, a moderate phenotype, is associated with intellectual disability and lactic acidosis. Alanine and pyruvate levels are typically elevated. A more complex and life-threatening type is common in Great Britain and France; these children die before 3 months of age.

ReKaps: Pyruvate carboxylase is a mitochondrial enzyme requiring biotin. It is activated by acetyl-CoA (from beta-oxidation). During gluconeogenesis it produces oxaloacetate (OAA), which can ultimately be converted to glucose. A deficiency leads to accumulation of gluconeogenic precursors, alanine, pyruvate, and lactate. It is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by elevated alanine, pyruvate, lactate, and ketoacids.

stem: A woman has episodic headaches, palpitations, and severe hypertension with an adrenal mass. Which amino acid is the precursor of the hormone produced by this tumor?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The patient has an adrenal pheochromocytoma that is causing episodic hypertension (leading to headache) and arrhythmia (leading to palpitations). The tumor arises from the sympathetic chromaffin cells in the adrenal gland. Catecholamines secreted by the tumor include epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. All three of these are derived from tyrosine (which is, in turn, derived from phenylalanine). Catecholamine synthesis is shown below.

Tyrosine → 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) → dopamine → norepinephrine → epinephrine. The enzymes and cofactors shown are tyrosine hydroxylase with tetrahydrobiopterin (THB); DOPA decarboxylase with vitamin B₆; dopamine β-hydroxylase with vitamin C/Cu²⁺; and phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase with S-adenosylmethionine/S-adenosylhomocysteine.

Arginine (choice A) is the amino acid precursor of the biological messenger nitric oxide (NO). Arginine is also an intermediate in the urea cycle.

Glutamate (choice B) is the amino acid precursor of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA).

Glycine (choice C) is itself an amino acid and a neurotransmitter, not a precursor of hormones.

Tryptophan (choice D) is the amino acid precursor of 5-hydroxytryptophan, serotonin, and melatonin.

The source table lists amino acid products: arginine—nitric oxide (NO); glutamate—gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA); tryptophan—serotonin, NAD, and NADP; tyrosine—thyroid hormones (T₃ and T₄), melanin, and catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine).

ReKaps: Pheochromocytomas are tumors arising from the sympathetic chromaffin tissue in the adrenals. They are characterized by episodic release of catecholamines, which lead to a potentially life-threatening increase in blood pressure and heart rate. Catecholamines are synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine.

stem: A man with alcoholism presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion, and memory impairment. Which enzyme is impaired in this condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion, and a memory deficit, which he tries to cover by inventing bizarre explanations (confabulation). This constellation of neurologic symptoms is characteristic of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is caused by thiamine deficiency. In the United States, severe thiamine deficiency is seen most commonly in chronic alcoholics. Thiamine deficiency can also damage peripheral nerves (“dry” beriberi) and the heart (“wet” beriberi). Dietary deficiency is more common in countries in which “polished rice” (rice with hulls removed) is a dietary staple.

Pyruvate dehydrogenase is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. Cofactors and coenzymes used by pyruvate dehydrogenase include thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, from vitamin thiamine), lipoic acid, coenzyme A (from vitamin pantothenate), FADH₂ (from vitamin riboflavin), and NADH (from vitamin niacin). TPP is also a coenzyme for α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, and transketolase.

Treatment is with thiamine. Thiamine must be administered prior to glucose. Administration of glucose to malnourished patients can exhaust their thiamine supplies (because the complete oxidation of glucose is a thiamine-intensive process) and precipitate or worsen Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. If treated quickly and effectively, Wernicke encephalopathy can be reversible.

Deficiency of fructose 1-phosphate aldolase (also known as aldolase B; choice A) causes hereditary fructose intolerance, a disorder resulting in accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate in the liver and renal proximal tubules. Symptoms include lethargy, vomiting, hyperbilirubinemia, hypoglycemia, hyperuricemia, and renal proximal tubule defects (Fanconi syndrome).

Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice B) deficiency, an X-linked disorder, is the most common genetic deficiency that causes a hemolytic anemia. It is characterized either by episodes of hemolytic anemia (most common) induced by infections and drugs, or by chronic hemolysis with chronic granulomatous disease-like symptoms (very rare). Heinz bodies are characteristic.

Pyruvate carboxylase (choice C) is a mitochondrial enzyme activated by acetyl-CoA. It catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate during gluconeogenesis, and can increase the rate of the citric acid cycle caused by low levels of intermediates (anaplerosis). Pyruvate carboxylase requires the vitamin biotin as a coenzyme. Defects in the biotin cycle can cause multiple carboxylase deficiency, in which pyruvate carboxylase is one of the affected enzymes.

Pyruvate kinase (choice E) deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder, is the second most common genetic deficiency that causes a hemolytic anemia. Characteristics include chronic hemolysis, increased 2,3-BPG, and therefore a lower-than-normal oxygen affinity of HbA.

ReKaps: Thiamine is a coenzyme for pyruvate dehydrogenase. Deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, characterized by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion, severe memory deficit, and confabulation. Deficiency of this vitamin can also cause damage to peripheral nerves (“dry” beriberi) and the heart (“wet” beriberi). In the United States, thiamine deficiency is seen most commonly in chronic alcoholics.

stem: Muscle biopsies are obtained from a healthy volunteer at rest and after 30 minutes of aerobic exercise. Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity is higher in the post-exercise specimen. Which biochemical change most directly produces this effect?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. In most biochemical pathways, only a few enzymatic reactions are under regulatory control. These often occur either at the beginning of pathways or at pathway branch points. The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex controls the link between glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. It decarboxylates pyruvate (the end product of glycolysis) with production of NADH and acetyl-CoA (the substrate for the citric acid cycle).

The PDH complex decarboxylates pyruvate from glycolysis to CO₂ and acetyl-CoA as NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH. The PDH complex is active if dephosphorylated by PDH phosphatase and inactive if phosphorylated by PDH kinase. The kinase and phosphatase are regulated allosterically. The kinase is inhibited by pyruvate and ADP, and activated by acetyl-CoA, NADH, and ATP. The phosphatase is activated by calcium. Increased activity of PDH is necessary to break down the large amounts of pyruvate built up in the muscle from glycolysis, and to use the product of that breakdown (acetyl-CoA) in the citric acid cycle.

PDH in mitochondria is huge, visible as dots on electron microscopy, because it is composed of many copies of at least five separate enzymes. Three of these (pyruvate decarboxylase, dihydrolipoyl transacetylase, and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase) catalyze the actual biochemical reactions. The other two, PDH kinase and PDH phosphatase, covalently regulate the complex at pyruvate decarboxylase by adding or removing phosphate groups, respectively. The phosphorylated form of the complex is less active, whereas the dephosphorylated form is more active.

PDH kinase and PDH phosphatase are themselves regulated allosterically. In exercise, high ADP and pyruvate concentrations inhibit PDH kinase, while increased Ca²⁺ stimulates PDH phosphatase. Both effects produce more of the dephosphorylated, more active form of the PDH complex.

A higher, not decreased (choice A), concentration of ADP is seen with exercise and increases PDH activity by inhibiting PDH kinase.

Intracellular calcium is increased, not decreased (choice B), with exercise and increases PDH activity by activating PDH phosphatase.

Increased acetyl-CoA (choice C), a product of the PDH complex, decreases PDH activity by activating PDH kinase.

Increased NADH/NAD⁺ (choice D), as is seen when the cell's need for reduced NADH is already being adequately met, decreases PDH activity by activating PDH kinase.

ReKaps: The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex decarboxylates pyruvate from glycolysis to CO₂ and acetyl-CoA as NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.

PDH complex is active if dephosphorylated by PDH phosphatase and inactive if phosphorylated by PDH kinase.

The kinase and phosphatase are regulated allosterically. The kinase is inhibited by pyruvate and ADP, and activated by acetyl-CoA, NADH, and ATP. The phosphatase is activated by calcium.

Increased activity of PDH is necessary to break down the large amounts of pyruvate built up in the muscle from glycolysis, and to use the product of that breakdown (acetyl-CoA) in the citric acid cycle.

stem: A 5-day-old newborn develops poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, and then convulsions, coma, and apnea. Examination shows hypotonia; specialized testing reveals deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase. Which amino acid is most likely elevated?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The disease is maple-syrup urine disease, which is also known as branched-chain ketoaciduria. This is a rare autosomal recessive disease, with an incidence of 1 in 200,000 in most of the United States, although a Mennonite community in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, has been found with an incidence of 1 in 176.

The defective enzyme, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, normally is involved in the catabolism of branched-chain amino acids that have been previously transaminated to form their ketoacid derivatives. The branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, and valine) and their by-products build up in the organs and brain. Because they are toxic to these organs, the buildup leads to poor feeding, hypotonia, vomiting, and lethargy initially that progresses to seizures and death if not promptly recognized. Onset of the progressive neurologic decline is several days after birth. Because neonates do not normally produce acetoacetate, ketones detected on urinalysis should prompt consideration of an organic aciduria. Leucine, isoleucine, and valine should be minimized in the diet.

Abnormal histidine metabolism (choice A) is associated with histidinemia. This is a rare metabolic, autosomal recessive deficiency of the enzyme histidine deaminase, which leads to accumulation of histidine. Most individuals with this condition are asymptomatic.

For the USMLE, associate methioninemia (choice C) with homocystinuria. Classic homocystinuria is caused by deficiency of cystathionine β-synthase (the CBS enzyme). Homocystinuria is associated with an increased risk of atherosclerosis, stroke, deep vein thrombosis, Marfan-like habitus, mental retardation, and restricted joint mobility. Rare enzyme deficiencies resulting in hypermethioninemia include methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency (usually benign, although in severe cases neurologic symptoms may develop) and S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency (multiplicity of symptoms).

Associate abnormal phenylalanine metabolism (choice D) with phenylketonuria (PKU). Infants born with this condition are normal at birth. In contrast, infants born with maple-syrup urine disease show symptoms within a few days of birth. If untreated, persons with PKU will develop severe mental retardation, autistic behavior, and loss of motor control. These untreated patients have white-blond hair and fair skin related to a decrease in melanin synthesis. Treatment is dietary restriction of phenylalanine and supplementation with tyrosine. Untreated persons with either PKU or maple-syrup urine disease will show elevated urinary ketones. Pregnant women who are phenylketonuric must have their serum level controlled throughout the pregnancy for their infants to be born normal even if the fetus is heterozygous for the defective gene.

Associate abnormal tyrosine metabolism (choice E) with albinism, in which there is a congenital deficiency of tyrosinase or a tyrosine transporter. These deficiencies would both lead to reduced pigmentation of the skin, eyes, and hair (reduced melanin), which increases the risk of skin cancer. Also associate abnormal tyrosine metabolism with alkaptonuria, which is accumulation of homogentisic acid due to deficiency of homogentisate oxidase.

ReKaps: Branched-chain ketoaciduria: urine smells “sweet,” “like maple syrup,” or like “burnt sugar.” Onset of symptoms is 4 to 7 days after birth. If left untreated, a life-threatening metabolic, branched-chain ketoacidosis develops. Symptoms include lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting. There is a high prevalence in Old World Mennonites in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. Phenylketonuria (PKU) can be excluded in this scenario even though elevated urinary ketones are present in newborns with PKU. Infants with PKU will not show the clinical symptoms at birth or at an age of a few days, while infants born with maple-syrup urine disease will show clinically significant symptoms.

stem: An untrained man develops metabolic acidosis after running a marathon. Which pathway is most responsible for ATP production under these conditions?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Under normal conditions, when oxygen is readily available, pyruvate generated in glycolysis enters the mitochondria and is decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase. In severe exercise, particularly in individuals in poor physical condition, the oxygen demands of skeletal muscle may exceed the ability of the heart and lungs to provide oxygen. Consequently, oxidation of NADH by the electron-transport chain decreases, as does ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation. The muscles switch to anaerobic glycolysis, and pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase as NADH is oxidized. The NAD⁺ generated allows glycolysis to continue and ATP is generated by substrate-level phosphorylation. Much of the lactic acid is released into the bloodstream, where it causes a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

In addition to severe exercise, lactic acidosis can occur with tissue hypoxia (including seizures, cardiac failure, hypotension, carbon monoxide poisoning, and severe anemia), drug toxicity or toxins (including phenformin, catecholamines, salicylate, isoniazid, and cyanide), congenital defects in processes that use pyruvate such as gluconeogenesis, and many severe illnesses.

Beta-oxidation of fatty acids (choice B) can produce acetyl-CoA, which in liver mitochondria may be converted to ketone bodies such as acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate if it is not used in the citric acid cycle. When ketone-body production exceeds utilization, ketoacidosis, another type of high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, can result; this is not expected in this patient. The citric acid cycle (choice C) oxidizes acetyl-CoA from glucose, fatty acids, and some amino acids, producing CO₂, NADH, and FADH₂; increasing its activity would not cause metabolic acidosis. In mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (choice D), NADH and FADH₂ are oxidized by the electron-transport chain, whose electrons reduce oxygen to water; electron transport generates a proton gradient that drives ADP phosphorylation to ATP. The pentose phosphate shunt (choice E) produces NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate. NADPH supports reductive biosynthetic processes such as fatty-acid synthesis, and ribose-5-phosphate is used to make PRPP for de novo and salvage synthesis of purine and pyrimidine bases.

ReKaps: When skeletal-muscle oxygen demand exceeds the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen, muscle switches to anaerobic glycolysis. Pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase as NADH is oxidized; lactate enters the bloodstream and causes high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

stem: A malnourished man with alcoholism has multiple ecchymoses and perifollicular hemorrhages. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This alcoholic, malnourished patient suffers from scurvy due to a deficiency of dietary vitamin C. Absence of vitamin C leads to impaired hydroxylation of proline residues in nascent procollagen chains (see figure). The hydroxyl groups of hydroxyproline are involved in hydrogen bonding that stabilizes the triple helical procollagen. Its absence results in decreased tensile strength of the collagen, leading to weakness of blood vessel walls.

Clinically, the deficiency syndrome is characterized by perifollicular hemorrhages, fragmentation of hairs, purpura, ecchymoses, splinter hemorrhages, and hemorrhages into muscle. In patients with normal dentition, gum changes (swelling and bleeding of the gums and loosening of the teeth) are also noted. Without vitamin C supplementation, death may eventually occur. Bleeding in alcoholic patients may be of several etiologies. They could have a coagulopathy from failure to make clotting factors, if there is liver damage, or possibly a vitamin K deficiency. They may also have decreased platelets from hypersplenism. Of the choices listed, however, vitamin C is the only correct answer.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency (choice A) can cause Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff psychosis, peripheral neuropathy (“dry” beriberi), and congestive heart failure resulting from cardiomyopathy (“wet” beriberi).

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency (choice B) can cause microcytic sideroblastic anemia.

Cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency (choice C) can cause megaloblastic anemia and potentially a peripheral and progressive neuropathy.

Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) deficiencies (choice E), or the inability to activate D2 in an alcoholic liver, can result in osteoporosis and bone disease.

ReKaps: Alcoholism is associated with deficiencies of several nutrients and vitamins. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is necessary for the hydroxylation of proline residues in procollagen chains. Deficiency of vitamin C results in scurvy, which is characterized by perifollicular hemorrhages, fragmentation of hairs, purpura, ecchymoses, splinter hemorrhages, gum changes, and hemorrhages into muscle.

stem: A 3-month-old girl develops seizures several hours after feeding and has growth retardation and hepatomegaly. Which enzyme deficiency best explains the findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The demonstrably palpable liver indicates pronounced hepatomegaly. Hepatomegaly and hypoglycemic seizures strongly suggest a glycogen storage disease (GSD). Three listed enzymes are related to GSDs: glucose-6-phosphatase (choice C; deficiency produces von Gierke disease), acid maltase (choice A; lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase; deficiency causes Pompe disease), and muscle phosphorylase (choice E; deficiency causes McArdle disease).

Von Gierke disease is caused by deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase (GSD type Ia) or the glucose-6-phosphate translocase (GSD type Ib). It typically presents at 3–4 months of age with hypoglycemia, hyperlipidemia, and lactic acidosis. Failure to thrive is common early in life; convulsions may occur during episodes of profound hypoglycemia. Glycogen accumulation occurs primarily in the liver and kidneys, accounting for enlargement of these organs. Gout may develop later because of deranged glucose metabolism. Onset and severity vary because of allelic heterogeneity; it is inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder.

Pompe disease (choice A) is a muscle glycogenosis involving skeletal and cardiac muscle; severe cardiomegaly is the primary symptom. McArdle disease (choice E) is also a muscle glycogenosis, with relatively mild symptoms of muscle cramps and weakness on exercise and myoglobinuria; it causes muscle weakness beginning in the second or third decades and no hepatomegaly. Beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency (choice B) causes Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disease characterized by hepatosplenomegaly and glucocerebroside accumulation in phagocytic cells. Hexosaminidase A (choice D) deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, characterized by progressive neurologic deterioration; cherry-red spots in the macular region precede blindness, but are not pathognomonic and may also occur in Niemann-Pick disease.

The source table summarizes GSDs: type I (von Gierke), glucose-6-phosphatase, severe hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, short stature, doll-like facies, protruding abdomen, and emaciated extremities; type II (Pompe), lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase, cardiomegaly, muscle weakness, death by age 2, glycogen-like material in inclusion bodies; type III (Cori), glycogen debranching enzyme, mild hypoglycemia and liver enlargement, short outer branches with a single glucose residue at the outer branch; type IV (Andersen/amylopectinosis), branching enzyme, infantile hypotonia, cirrhosis, death by age 2, and very few glycogen branches especially toward the periphery; type V (McArdle), muscle glycogen phosphorylase, muscle cramps and weakness on exercise and myoglobinuria; type VI (Hers), hepatic glycogen phosphorylase, mild fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and cirrhosis.

stem: A 2-month-old boy has a generalized seizure and remains semicomatose. Laboratory testing shows elevated C8–C10 acylcarnitines. Which additional finding is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This infant most likely has medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency. MCAD is important in fatty-acid beta-oxidation after the initial cycles are carried out by long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCAD), yielding acetyl-CoA plus fragments 8 to 10 carbons in length. Without MCAD, these medium-chain fatty acids accumulate and eventually leave the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle. The resultant C8–C10 acylcarnitines are sufficiently amphipathic to exit cells and enter the bloodstream; blood levels are measured by mass spectrometry to diagnose MCAD deficiency.

Impaired fatty-acid beta-oxidation in the liver during fasting results in low ATP because less acetyl-CoA is produced. Decreased beta-oxidation during fasting increases reliance on proteolysis to supply glucose and ATP. Amino-acid degradation produces toxic ammonia, which is normally converted to nontoxic urea in the ATP-requiring urea cycle. When ATP is low, urea-cycle activity decreases and ammonia accumulates in blood. In the early neonatal period, frequent feedings may protect the newborn from fasting stress. As feeding frequency decreases, symptoms (often at night) may include irritability before meals, lethargy, jitteriness, sweating, and seizures. By about 3 months, a viral illness that decreases nutrient intake may trigger serious illness with hypoglycemia and hypoketonemia, lethargy, vomiting, and acidosis; an affected infant may die during a severe episode. Management ensures feedings at no more than 5-hour intervals. Hypoglycemia results from reduced gluconeogenesis (less NADH/ATP and less acetyl-CoA, an allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase) and reduced ketogenesis, increasing glucose dependence.

The source contrasts myopathic carnitine acyltransferase/CPT deficiency (muscle aches, weakness, myoglobinuria, prolonged exercise especially if fasting, elevated muscle triglyceride on biopsy; most common form autosomal recessive with late onset) with MCAD deficiency (fasting hypoglycemia, no ketone bodies/hypoketosis, C8–C10 acylcarnitines in blood, vomiting, coma/death; autosomal recessive with variable expression). Hypoglycemia increases glucagon secretion, eliminating choice A. Glucagon and catecholamines mobilize adipose triglycerides, so plasma free fatty acids increase rather than decrease (choice B). A hallmark is severe fasting hypoglycemia, eliminating hyperglycemia (choice D). Decreased fatty-acid oxidation decreases acetyl-CoA substrate for ketogenesis, causing hypoketosis rather than hyperketosis (choice E).

stem: A woman with acute intermittent porphyria develops abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypertension, and proximal weakness. Which laboratory finding is most likely?

options.text: Increased porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD) activity in erythrocytes
Increased urinary delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG)

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD), also known as hydroxymethylbilane synthase. In an acute attack, patients excrete delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG) in the urine; serum ALA and PBG also increase. Attacks may be triggered by drugs (especially barbiturates and alcohol that induce cytochrome P450), or changes in nutritional or hormonal state. Symptoms include acute abdominal pain, tachycardia, and neurologic effects; patients are not photosensitive. Urine may rarely turn port-wine color due to porphobilin, an oxidation product of PBG. Diagnosis is usually made by showing decreased PBGD activity in red blood cells, so choice B is incorrect. AIP is more common in women, but penetrance is only about 15%; affected individuals rarely have episodes before puberty.

Increased erythrocyte zinc-protoporphyrin (choice A) results when the last step in heme synthesis fails: ferrochelatase normally inserts ferrous iron into protoporphyrin to form heme. Lead poisoning, ferrochelatase defects, or severe iron deficiency can prevent this step, allowing zinc to be inserted instead. Increased serum porphyrins (choice C) is incorrect because partial PBGD deficiency reduces porphyrin synthesis. Decreased urinary coproporphyrins (choice D) are found in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency and congenital erythropoietic porphyria; hereditary coproporphyria causes increased urinary and fecal coproporphyrins. Many affected individuals are asymptomatic; attacks may be triggered by chemicals (including oral contraceptives) or fasting that boost heme synthesis. Coproporphyria can cause abdominal pain, neuropathies, constipation, and photosensitive skin changes.

ReKaps: AIP results from PBGD deficiency; during acute attacks patients excrete ALA and PBG in urine. Attacks feature abdominal pain, tachycardia, and neurologic effects, without photosensitivity.

stem: A physician treats a patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Which clinical presentation is most likely?

options.text: A child with short stature, radial abnormalities, absent thumbs, and café-au-lait spots develops severe anemia
A child develops myoglobinuria after vigorous exercise
A neonate has splenomegaly and severe anemia
An adult develops anemia after taking an antimalarial drug
An adult develops severe shortness of breath during an airplane ride

explanation:
The correct answer is D. There are several variants of G6PD deficiency (X-linked recessive) in Africa. The most common clinically significant variant is the so-called A-type, which produces an unstable G6PD enzyme. This variant is found in up to 11% of African-American males. In red cells, NADPH from the HMP shunt is essential for detoxifying reactive oxygen species that otherwise would damage proteins and lipids in the RBC. Glutathione reductase and glutathione peroxidase are involved in the normal detoxification process. The A-variant renders the individual's red cells susceptible to oxidative stresses, such as those that occur with administration of the antimalarial drug primaquine. Sulfonamides and dapsone are other agents that can trigger hemolytic episodes. Infections (bacterial or viral) are another important trigger for hemolysis in these individuals. Rarely, G6PD deficiency presents as neonatal jaundice or with chronic hemolysis. In Mediterranean populations, G6PD deficiency-associated hemolysis may occur in individuals who eat a meal of fava beans (Vicia fava) and several hours later develop hemoglobinuria and peripheral vascular collapse secondary to intravascular hemolysis as a result of the oxidant injury initiated by the fava beans.

Fanconi anemia (choice A) is caused by a mutation in one of several genes encoding a multiprotein nuclear complex that functions in the BRCA pathway, which repairs damage to DNA caused by cross-linking agents. All bone marrow elements are affected. In addition to the often-fatal leukemia, pigmentary changes in the skin and malformations of the heart, kidney, and limbs (aplasia of the radius, thumb deformity) are associated features.

Myoglobinuria following strenuous exercise, especially in the initial phase (choice B), is characteristic of myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease), a defect in muscle glycogenolysis.

A neonate with an enlarged spleen and chronic hemolysis (choice C) is consistent with pyruvate kinase deficiency, the neonatal form of which is often fatal. Transfusions coupled with splenectomy often lessen the symptoms.

An adult who suffers shortness of breath during an airplane ride (choice E) (or any activity at low pO2) is consistent with a person who is heterozygous or homozygous for the HbS allele of the hemoglobin beta-chain locus and is either a carrier (heterozygous) or a person with sickle cell anemia (homozygous).

stem: A 5-year-old girl has irritability, poor attention, lethargy, anorexia, abdominal pain, constipation, pallor, and reduced reflexes. She is treated with dimercaprol and EDTA for lead poisoning. Which enzyme inhibition causes her illness?
explanation: The correct answer is A. This child is presenting with typical signs and symptoms of lead poisoning. Lead affects enzymes in the heme biosynthetic pathway. Lead poisoning is a chronic disorder often seen in children exposed to environmental sources of lead, such as paint chips, putty, or plaster from old buildings, which a child may ingest. It can cause constitutional symptoms including lethargy, headache, memory loss, nausea, abdominal pain, and diarrhea or constipation. With high blood lead levels, lead lines may appear in the gums (usually seen in adults more than children) and in bones on x-ray as opaque metaphyseal bands in growing bone. Inhibition of aminolevulinate (ALA) dehydratase and ferrochelatase can result in microcytic, hypochromic anemia due to impaired heme synthesis. Ferrochelatase inhibition also results in accumulation of free erythrocyte protoporphyrin. Lead also inhibits 5′-nucleotidase, producing basophilic stippling of erythrocytes due to retained RNA. Lead competes with uric acid for reabsorption in the renal tubules, and hyperuricemia may be seen. Treatment with dimercaprol (BAL), which crosses the blood-brain barrier and is the drug of choice in lead encephalopathy, or chelation therapy with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) is indicated in cases with high blood lead levels. Succimer is an oral chelator that may also be given depending on lead levels; chelating agents enhance lead excretion in urine. Ceruloplasmin (choice B) catalyzes oxidation of ferrous to ferric iron. Ceruloplasmin deficiency produces low serum iron, high serum ferritin, and tissue iron deposition, with mild anemia; symptoms usually present later in life and may include retinal degeneration, CNS disorders, and diabetes. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (choice C), an X-linked disease affecting the pentose phosphate pathway, causes episodic hemolysis triggered by infections, certain drugs, or fava beans. Porphobilinogen deaminase (choice D) deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria, with increased urinary ALA and porphobilinogen and port-wine urine in some patients; patients are not photosensitive. Pyruvate kinase deficiency (choice E), an autosomal recessive disease affecting glycolysis primarily in red blood cells, produces chronic hemolytic anemia, decreased hemoglobin, increased reticulocytosis, and commonly jaundice.

stem: Exercise-induced endothelial release of a vasodilator relaxes vascular smooth muscle by increasing which intracellular signaling enzyme?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Nitric oxide (NO) is a short-acting (about 100 msec) physiologic messenger released from endothelial cells. NO diffuses to a nearby smooth muscle cell, enters the cell, and activates soluble (cytosolic) guanylate cyclase. Guanylate cyclase makes the second messenger cGMP, which triggers smooth-muscle relaxation by facilitating dephosphorylation of myosin light chains. This prevents interaction of myosin with actin. This is also the mechanism by which NO causes vasodilation in the corpus cavernosum of the penis, leading to penile erection.

Adenylate cyclase (choice A) is a plasma membrane-bound enzyme activated by ligand binding to a Gs protein-coupled receptor. It converts ATP into cAMP and pyrophosphate; cAMP, a second messenger, activates protein kinase A (PKA). Heme oxygenase (choice C) initiates conversion of heme to bilirubin. It cleaves cyclic heme to linear biliverdin, releasing free iron and carbon monoxide; biliverdin reductase converts biliverdin to bilirubin. Nitric oxide synthase (choice D) synthesizes NO from arginine. The reaction requires NADPH and oxygen and produces NO and citrulline. There are three NOS isoforms: endothelial (eNOS) and neuronal (nNOS), which are constitutively expressed and respond to a rise in calcium, and inducible (iNOS), which is independent of calcium levels and is induced in response to bacterial infection. In addition to its role in vasodilation, NO is a neurotransmitter. Phospholipase C (choice E) cleaves phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate (PIP2) into diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol trisphosphate (IP3). IP3 causes release of calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, and DAG activates protein kinase C (PKC). This cascade is initiated by ligand binding to a Gq protein-coupled receptor.

The source’s signal-transduction summary also lists: Gs → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → PKA (including glucagon, epinephrine at β1/β2, and vasopressin at V2); Gq → phospholipase C → DAG/IP3/Ca2+ → PKC (including vasopressin at V1/V3 and epinephrine at α1); and guanylate cyclase → cGMP → protein kinase G (including atrial natriuretic factor and NO). Insulin and related growth factors signal through receptor tyrosine kinase activity.

stem: A 10-year-old boy has recurrent shoulder dislocations, easy bruising, and hyperextensible joints. Which deficient enzyme is associated with this connective-tissue disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This boy presents with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), a collagen disorder, including hyperextensible joints, frequent joint dislocations, and easy bruising. Several EDS forms are due to mutations in collagen genes. EDS type VI is caused by a mutation in the gene encoding lysyl hydroxylase (step 3 in collagen synthesis). Lysyl hydroxylase hydroxylates lysine residues during collagen processing; absence of hydroxylated lysines leads to defective collagen-fiber synthesis and hyperextensible joints, easy bruising, and frequent dislocations. The source figure shows synthesis of the prepro-alpha chain with a hydrophobic signal sequence, signal-peptide removal, hydroxylation of selected proline and lysine residues (vitamin C-dependent), glycosylation of hydroxylysines, triple-helix formation, procollagen secretion, cleavage of propeptides to form tropocollagen, assembly into fibrils, and stabilization by lysyl oxidase cross-linking.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin (choice A) inhibits elastase. Inflammation causes neutrophils to release elastase, which degrades elastic fibers; alpha-1 antitrypsin regulates this process. Deficiency can cause emphysema and COPD from elastase-mediated lung destruction; this patient has no respiratory issues. Ascorbic acid deficiency (choice B) causes scurvy, with loose teeth, bleeding gums, poor wound healing, poor bone development, and petechiae (red or purple skin spots). Lysyl hydroxylase and prolyl hydroxylase require vitamin C, so deficiency also impairs collagen processing; this child lacks the typical scurvy findings.

Menkes disease is caused by ATP7A mutation and an ATP-dependent copper-transporter deficiency (choice C). Loss of copper distribution inactivates copper-dependent enzymes, including lysyl oxidase, which cross-links collagen triple helices to form functional fibers. This X-linked recessive disease is often severe, with sparse depigmented hair, seizures, failure to thrive, and neurodegeneration; affected individuals often die before age 10. Fibrillin (choice D) polymerizes into microfibrils that combine with elastin to form elastic fibers in blood vessels, lungs, and skin. Marfan syndrome results from a fibrillin-1 defect and features ectopia lentis, aortic defects with rupture risk, tall and slender build, elongated digits, and arm span greater than body height. This patient is short for age and has no reported vision problems, making Marfan syndrome unlikely.

The source table on collagen-biosynthesis disorders contrasts scurvy (vitamin-C-dependent deficient hydroxylation; petechiae/ecchymoses, loose teeth, bleeding gums, poor wound healing and bone development), osteogenesis imperfecta (collagen-gene mutations; skeletal deformities, fractures, blue sclera), Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (collagen and lysyl-hydroxylase mutations; hyperextensible/fragile skin, hypermobile joints, dislocations, varicose veins, ecchymoses, arterial and intestinal rupture), and Menkes disease (defective cross-linking from functional copper deficiency; depigmented/steely hair, arterial tortuosity or rupture, cerebral degeneration, osteoporosis, anemia).

stem: An enzyme assay contains sodium citrate and shows decreased activity of one intermediary-metabolism enzyme. Which enzyme is inhibited by citrate?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Citrate is produced by citrate synthase from acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. This is a reaction of the mitochondrial citric acid cycle, but citrate can move freely from the mitochondria into the cytosol using the citrate shuttle. When the citric acid cycle slows down, citrate accumulates and enters the cytosol. There it acts as a negative allosteric regulator of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1), the enzyme that catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis. This prevents excess substrate from entering the cycle. Citrate is a positive allosteric effector of cytosolic acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the rate-limiting and regulated enzyme of fatty-acid synthesis.

ReKaps: When the TCA cycle slows down, citrate leaves the mitochondria and enters the cytosol, where it acts as a negative allosteric regulator of phosphofructokinase-1, the rate-limiting enzyme and main control point in glycolysis. Cytosolic citrate is a positive allosteric regulator of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the rate-limiting and regulated enzyme in fatty-acid synthesis.

stem: A 9-year-old boy who recently emigrated from the Philippines is brought to the physician by his parents because he has trouble keeping up with his classmates on the playground. Physical examination shows mild pallor. and pulmonary rales are heard on auscultation of the chest. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is most likely responsible for this boy's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency is most frequently encountered in alcoholics and in developing countries where a major source of calories is white rice. Deficiency of this vitamin can take several forms: dilated cardiomyopathy (“wet” beriberi), polyneuropathy (“dry” beriberi), and mammillary body degeneration (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome). Thiamine is required for two enzymes in the TCA cycle, and a thiamine deficiency may impair energy generation in tissues with a high demand for oxidative metabolism, such as cardiac tissue.

Ascorbic acid (choice A) (vitamin C) deficiency causes scurvy, associated with capillary fragility, bony abnormalities, and poor wound healing.

Retinol (choice B) (vitamin A) deficiency causes blindness and impaired immune responses. It also manifests as poorly differentiated epithelium, including corneal ulceration, squamous cell metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium, and follicular hyperkeratosis.

Riboflavin (choice C) (vitamin B2) deficiency causes cheilosis, glossitis, red, irritated eyes, and dermatitis often involving the genital region.

Vitamin K (choice E) deficiency causes impaired blood clotting because of decreased production of factors II, VII, IX, and X and the control proteins C and S.

ReKaps: A diet containing milled rice is associated with thiamine deficiency, resulting in beriberi. There are two types of beriberi: (1) Dry beriberi causes progressive polyneuropathy with myelin degeneration, leading to foot drop and wrist drop. (2) Wet beriberi is associated with high-output cardiac failure. Thiamine is required for two TCA cycle enzymes, and a deficiency of thiamine may lead to a deficiency of energy metabolism from carbohydrate, fatty acid, or amino acid fuels.

stem: A 47-year-old man has a swollen, tender great toe and recurrent renal colic. Synovial fluid contains needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Which underlying metabolic disorder is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has gout, characterized by painful joints due to the precipitation of sodium urate crystals caused by either underexcretion (the majority) or excessive production of uric acid (the minority). Acute gouty arthritis is seen most commonly in males. The crystals, identified as negatively birefringent and needle-shaped, initiate neutrophil-mediated acute inflammation, often first affecting the big toe, although other joints such as the ankle, heel, and wrist can also be affected. Kidney disease is also seen due to accumulation of uric acid in the tubules, leading to repeated episodes of renal colic (severe flank pain radiating to the groin).

Acute attacks are treated with colchicine or indomethacin to reduce inflammation. Overproduction of uric acid and chronic gout are treated with allopurinol, which inhibits xanthine oxidase and can indirectly reduce purine synthesis through inhibition of PRPP-amidotransferase. Xanthine oxidase catalyzes the sequential oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine to uric acid.

ReKaps: Hyperuricemia may result from overproduction of uric acid (an abnormality of the purine pathway) or underexcretion of uric acid by the kidneys. Chronic gout and uric-acid overproduction are treated with allopurinol, an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, the enzyme of purine catabolism that produces uric acid from hypoxanthine and xanthine.

stem: At autopsy, a man has cocaine-associated contraction-band necrosis of the myocardium. Which enzyme's activity was most likely increased before death?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine, resulting in tachycardia as well as excessive vasoconstriction of coronary vessels, leading to ischemia and infarction of heart tissue known as contraction band necrosis. Under these pathologic conditions, myocardial cells switch to anaerobic metabolism, and glycolysis becomes the major source of ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase. Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, and its activity would therefore be increased.

Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice A) is an enzyme of glycolysis that produces 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, a substrate for the ATP-producing enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase. It is not a regulated enzyme of glycolysis and is not expected to increase in activity under hypoxic conditions or with a shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism.

Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (choice B) is a regulatory enzyme in gluconeogenesis, which is induced by cortisol, epinephrine, and glucagon. It functions in the hepatic synthesis of glucose when energy levels from beta-oxidation of fatty acids are adequate.

Pyruvate dehydrogenase (choice D) produces acetyl-CoA from pyruvate and coenzyme A, bridging glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. It requires five cofactors, including NAD and FAD, which would no longer be regenerated by the electron transport chain under hypoxic conditions, decreasing its activity.

Succinate dehydrogenase (choice E) is a key enzyme of the TCA cycle and produces a reduced equivalent of FAD to feed into the electron transport chain. It is also known as Complex II. The TCA cycle functions only if oxygen is present in appropriate concentrations, since NADH is consumed by the electron transport chain only when enough oxygen is available. In the absence of oxygen, NADH accumulates and TCA-cycle enzyme activities decrease.

ReKaps: Cocaine can cause cardiac ischemia, leading myocardial cells to switch to anaerobic (substrate-level phosphorylation) metabolism. The rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis is phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1), whose activity increases.

stem: A diagnostic test for fetal trisomy 21 is administered to 500 women at risk. The results are shown below. What is the positive predictive value of this test?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Positive predictive value (PPV) is the probability of disease in a person who receives a positive test result; it is the probability that a positive result is a true positive. PPV measures only the distribution of people who receive a positive result. The formula is PPV = TP/(TP + FP), or true positives divided by all positive test results. Here, 100 women have a fetus with trisomy 21 and a positive result (true positives), and 50 have a normal karyotype with a positive result (false positives). Thus, PPV = 100/(100 + 50) = 100/150 = 67%.

The 2 × 2 table is: positive screening—100 true positives and 50 false positives, total 150; negative screening—100 false negatives and 250 true negatives, total 350. There are 200 affected pregnancies, 300 unaffected pregnancies, and 500 participants overall.

Forty percent (choice A) is the prevalence of trisomy 21 in the tested population: (true positives + false negatives)/all participants = (100 + 100)/500 = 200/500. Fifty percent (choice B) is sensitivity: true positives divided by all affected pregnancies = 100/200. Seventy-one percent (choice D) is the negative predictive value: true negatives divided by all negative results = 250/350. Eighty-three percent (choice E) is specificity: true negatives divided by all unaffected pregnancies = 250/300.

ReKaps: PPV is the probability of disease in a person with a positive test result; it measures only people who tested positive. PPV = TP/(TP + FP) = true positives/(true positives + false positives).

A study is conducted to determine the relationship between the amount of time spent studying for the USMLE in weeks and the score that the person makes on the exam. Which of the following k methods will most likely be used to evaluate the findings of the study?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Pearson correlations are used to analyze data from a single study in which the design provides two interval variables. A positive value means that two variables go together in the same direction. If it is found that the more time one spends studying leads to higher USMLE scores, this would be a positive correlation. Pearson correlation coefficients (r) range from −1.0 (negative correlation) to +1.0 (positive correlation). Conversely, a negative value indicates that the presence of one variable is associated with the absence of another variable. For example, there is a negative correlation between age and quickness of reflexes. These correlations can be graphed and evaluated using scatterplots. A summary of various scatterplots is presented below.

Analysis of variance (choice A) is used to analyze data from a single study where the design provides one or more nominal variables and one interval variable. Chi-square analysis (choice B) is used to analyze data from a single study where the design provides two nominal variables. A meta-analysis (choice C) is a set of methods for conducting a mathematically based review of literature. Simply stated, the results of all studies are combined, weighted by such issues as sample size and design quality, and summarized to yield a single p-value. The results of a meta-analysis are based on the weight of existing data, what treatment among many works best, and the degree of benefit that treatment provides. A meta-analysis summarizes both statistical and clinical significance. Odds-ratio analysis (choice D) is used to analyze data from a single case-control study. Relative-risk analysis (choice F) is used to analyze data from a single cohort study.

stem: An investigator studies the incidence of ischemic heart disease (IHD) in relation to habitual physical activity (PA). The data are shown below. Based on the data, which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Adose-response relationship is evident, but sgnificance cannot be determined
Alllevels of PA appear to have a significant protective effect
High and moderate levels of PA appear to have a significant protective effect
Only high levels of PA appear to have a significant protective effect
The higher the level of PA, the higher the IHD risk

explanation:
The correct answer is D. A cohort study follows people over time and assesses disease incidence as an outcome. Here the incidence is presented as relative risk (RR), the incidence rate in one group divided by that in another. Sedentary activity is the reference group and therefore has RR 1.00. The reported RRs decrease with increasing activity: low 0.95, moderate 0.86, and high 0.64. A relative risk of 1.0 means the two incidence rates in the ratio are equal.

Statistical significance is assessed from the confidence interval (CI). If 1.0 falls within the interval, the relative risk is not statistically significant because equality of risk cannot be excluded. If 1.0 is outside the interval, the relative risk is significant. The low-activity CI (0.89–1.21) and moderate-activity CI (0.73–1.09) both include 1.0, so neither shows a statistically significant protective effect. The high-activity CI (0.49–0.87) lies entirely below 1.0, so only high activity shows a statistically significant protective association. Thus, only high levels of physical activity appear to have a significant protective effect.

A relative-risk confidence interval containing 1.0 indicates no statistically significant effect. If the interval excludes 1.0, the finding is statistically significant; an RR above 1.0 indicates increased risk, while an RR below 1.0 indicates decreased risk.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent bacterial infections. Genetic testing shows an inherited defect in a component of NADPH oxidase. Which leukocyte process is most directly impaired?

options.text: Transfer of lysosomal enzymes to phagosomes

explanation: The correct answer is C. Phagocytosis is followed by rapid activation of oxygen-dependent enzymatic reactions referred to as the oxidative burst, which leads to generation of reactive oxygen radicals capable of killing bacteria. NADPH oxidase plays a fundamental role in the oxidative burst. NADPH oxidase is a multiprotein complex that oxidizes NADPH, producing superoxide anions (O₂⁻) from molecular oxygen. Superoxide anions then convert to H₂O₂ by spontaneous dismutation. Hydrogen peroxide serves as the substrate for myeloperoxidase, which acts to produce toxic halide radicals. Mutations in one of the genes encoding NADPH oxidase proteins cause chronic granulomatous disease, a group of congenital disorders characterized by defective bacterial killing and chronic predisposition to infections with catalase-positive microbes. Patients with CGD are prone to persistent infections with catalase-positive bacteria and fungi because these organisms destroy the hydrogen peroxide that they produce metabolically, so neither of the oxygen-dependent mechanisms can function in intracellular killing during these infections.

choice_explanations.A: Leukocyte adhesion and transmigration depend on adhesion molecules, not NADPH oxidase.
choice_explanations.B: Chemotaxis is not the primary defect in chronic granulomatous disease.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. NADPH oxidase initiates the respiratory burst and generates superoxide, leading to H₂O₂.
choice_explanations.D: HOCl production by myeloperoxidase is reduced downstream because NADPH oxidase supplies H₂O₂; it is not the direct enzyme defect asked for.
choice_explanations.E: Lysosomal-enzyme trafficking to phagosomes is not the NADPH-oxidase function.

B.text: C5a is a potent chemotactic complement fragment.

C.text: The respiratory burst generates reactive oxygen species through NADPH oxidase.

D.text: Myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide to form hypochlorous acid.

stem: An investigator compares normally distributed systolic blood-pressure measurements among five independent age groups and wants to test whether their means are equal. Which statistical method is most appropriate?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The investigator is evaluating the means of five independent groups. For each member of the group, a single value is obtained, and the subjects are independent within each group (ie, their blood-pressure values will not influence those of any other participant in any group) and belong to only one group. A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares the means of two or more groups of a single nominal variable using an interval variable. When comparing the means of multiple groups for a continuous variable, the appropriate statistical test is analysis of variance (ANOVA).

Since the investigator is interested in determining whether the group means differ, the null hypothesis to be tested is that the group means are equal. Whenever multiple means are compared, the statistic must avoid excessive type I error, falsely rejecting the null hypothesis (ie, falsely concluding that group means were significantly different). Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is appropriate for this purpose. ANOVA requires that the data reasonably fit a normal distribution; this requirement was met, so ANOVA is a valid analysis to perform.

The odds ratio (choice B) is a descriptive statistic used to describe the strength of association between an exposure and an outcome, for example, exposure to cigarette smoke and lung cancer. The odds ratio is used for binary data sets, not continuous data; for example, it could be used if investigators were testing occurrence of hypertension versus non-hypertension in young versus old age groups. In this case there are more than two age groups, and blood pressure is measured as a continuous rather than a binary variable, so it is not appropriate for this experimental design. Chi-square (choice C) is used to compare estimated expected values of two categorical variables with observed values. For example, comparing the number of patients with hypertension versus the number without hypertension is a comparison of a categorical variable. The data collected in this experiment were not categorical; they were measured on a continuous scale (blood-pressure numerical values), so the Chi-square statistic is not appropriate. The Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (choice D), or Pearson’s r, measures the linearity of the relationship between two continuous variables; the investigators are not measuring a relationship between two continuous variables. Student’s t-tests are used to compare two different groups. Using t-tests to compare each group to every other group (choice E) is incorrect because performing multiple t-tests over the same data greatly increases the probability of a type I error. In this experiment there would be an unacceptably high risk of identifying a difference between age groups that is not real. The use of t-tests for multiple different data sets is acceptable; for example, comparing blood pressures in two age groups, then comparing weights in the same two age groups.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. ANOVA compares means across multiple independent groups.
choice_explanations.B: An odds ratio measures association between categorical exposure and outcome, not equality of continuous group means.
choice_explanations.C: Chi-square tests compare categorical counts or proportions.
choice_explanations.D: Pearson correlation measures linear association between two continuous variables.
choice_explanations.E: Repeated pairwise t tests inflate type I error when comparing five groups.

fa_summary: Use ANOVA to compare means among three or more groups; t tests compare two means.
