stem: A newborn has a large, irregular, red, flat facial lesion that does not cross the midline and persists into adulthood. Which disorder is most likely associated with this lesion?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is a rare congenital vascular disorder characterized by a facial capillary malformation (port-wine stain) and capillary-venous malformations that affect the brain and eye. The lesion described is a port-wine stain, a flat, vascular lesion that, unlike the more common strawberry nevus, does not usually regress with age. Facial port-wine stains can be a component of Sturge-Weber disease and typically occur in the ophthalmic and maxillary distributions of the trigeminal nerve (V1 and V2, respectively). Other features include similar vascular lesions of the meninges (leptomeningeal angiomatosis) ipsilateral to the port-wine stain. CT of the brain demonstrates hemispheric atrophy due to venous infarction of vessels associated with leptomeningeal angiomas, with tram-track calcification along the cortical ribbon. Neurologic sequelae include seizures, intellectual disability, and hemiparesis. Patients can also present with glaucoma and pheochromocytoma. Sturge-Weber occurs sporadically and is not inherited.

Arnold-Chiari malformations (choice A) are a cluster of related brain and spinal cord malformations in which there is downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils and vermis into the foramen magnum. Associated conditions include hydrocephalus, lumbar myelomeningocele, and syringomyelia. In myelomeningocele, a bony defect in the spine allows both the meninges and spinal cord to herniate into the sac. In syringomyelia, hydrocephalus of the central canal of the spine impinges on decussating C8–T1 spinothalamic tract fibers, producing a bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature sensation. Skin defects are not associated with this disorder.

Dandy-Walker malformation (choice B) includes a large, distended fourth ventricle with a hypoplastic (or absent) cerebellum. These patients may also have associated spina bifida (a bony defect in the spine without herniation). Though no skin findings are associated with spina bifida, there may be a tuft of hair overlying the site of the defect (spina bifida occulta).

Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1; choice C) is an inherited, autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome characterized by benign, subcutaneous neurofibromas arising from peripheral nerves. The involved NF1 gene is located on chromosome 17. Other findings can be encapsulated by the mnemonic CAF-SPOT: café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, eye Lisch nodules (hamartomas of the iris), scoliosis, pheochromocytoma, and optic tumors (usually optic glioma). The skin findings in NF1, namely café-au-lait spots, are usually brown and small, unlike the port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber.

Tuberous sclerosis (choice E) is also an inherited, autosomal dominant condition, characterized by renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, cortical tubers (malformed neural tissue), retinal hamartomas, lung cysts, seizures, and intellectual disability. Important cutaneous manifestations are ash-leaf spots (scattered hypopigmented macules) and adenoma sebaceum. Unlike port-wine stains, adenoma sebaceum, also known as a facial angiofibroma, appears like severe acne with raised red papules in a malar (butterfly) distribution across the nose and cheeks.

ReKaps: Characteristic findings of Sturge-Weber syndrome include a facial port-wine stain in the V1/V2 distribution that persists into adulthood; leptomeningeal angiomatosis resulting in hemispheric atrophy; nonspecific neurologic findings (hemiparesis, intellectual disability, seizures); and glaucoma.

choice_explanations.A: Arnold–Chiari malformations involve hindbrain displacement and do not cause a port-wine stain.
choice_explanations.B: Dandy–Walker malformation is a posterior-fossa/cerebellar developmental abnormality.
choice_explanations.C: NF1 causes café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, not a facial port-wine capillary malformation.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: Sturge–Weber syndrome is associated with a facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal vascular malformations.
choice_explanations.E: Tuberous sclerosis causes hypopigmented macules, angiofibromas, and other hamartomas.

stem: A 56-year-old woman with a 60-pack-year smoking history has proximal limb weakness that improves with activity. She has clubbing and decreased breath sounds over the left upper lung. Edrophonium produces slight improvement in strength. Dysfunction of which structure most likely causes her weakness?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a rare presynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission in which release of acetylcholine is impaired, resulting in proximal muscle weakness, particularly of the limbs (the patient has difficulty raising her arms and legs). Many cases of LEMS occur as part of a paraneoplastic syndrome, especially in small-cell lung cancer. In this patient, digital clubbing suggests hypoxemia from chronic tobacco smoking as well as obstruction of the bronchial airway. Decreased breath sounds identified on physical examination also confirm bronchial airway obstruction, in this case by a bronchogenic tumor.

During the course of the malignancy, autoantibodies are generated against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, inhibiting presynaptic release of acetylcholine. Patients present with weakness that is worse with inactivity and improves after exertion. On electromyography, contraction strength increases with repeated nerve fiber stimulation. Patients may also have autonomic abnormalities (orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, dry mouth, blurry vision, constipation), though the pathophysiologic mechanism is unclear. There is no sensory loss in these patients.

The patient also received an edrophonium (Tensilon) challenge test and demonstrated some mild reversal of symptoms. The application of edrophonium reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, thus increasing the amount of acetylcholine in synaptic clefts. In patients with myasthenia gravis, this causes immediate and profound clinical improvement. In LEMS, edrophonium may produce some improvement, but not to the same extent.

The most important disease in the differential diagnosis for LEMS is myasthenia gravis. In this disease, autoantibodies are directed against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (Nm) at the neuromuscular junction. These receptors are ligand-gated ion channels (choice B). Myasthenia gravis, like LEMS, also presents with muscle weakness without sensory findings. Important features of myasthenia gravis that distinguish it from LEMS include: no paraneoplastic association; prominent extraocular muscle involvement; weakness worsening with activity; no autonomic findings; and rapid and profound clinical improvement with edrophonium.

Disorders of extracellular matrix molecules (choice A), such as proteoglycans, can result in limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. This is an inherited condition characterized by proximal muscle weakness and wasting. It is not associated with malignancy, and muscle strength would not improve with edrophonium.

Myotonic dystrophy results from congenital defects in a dystrophic myotonia protein kinase (DMPK) (choice C). Patients present with muscle wasting, cataracts, and heart block. The disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and associated with the CTG trinucleotide repeat.

Autoantibodies are usually directed at extracellular and membrane-bound proteins. Transcription factors (choice D) are intracellular and rarely the target in autoimmune illnesses.

choice_explanations.A: Extracellular matrix defects do not explain use-dependent proximal weakness with a paraneoplastic pattern.
choice_explanations.B: Postsynaptic ligand-gated acetylcholine receptors are targeted in myasthenia gravis, which typically worsens with repeated use.
choice_explanations.C: A protein kinase abnormality is not the presynaptic defect in Lambert–Eaton syndrome.
choice_explanations.D: Transcription-factor dysfunction does not explain the characteristic presynaptic neuromuscular-junction syndrome.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels impair acetylcholine release.

stem: A 57-year-old man has a painless enlarged superficial inguinal lymph node. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. Metastasis from which site most likely occurred?

options.text: Anal canal below the dentate line

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The lymph nodes of the groin are divided into superficial and deep groups. Tumors from the penis, skin of the vagina, and anal canal below the dentate line drain to the superficial group of inguinal lymph nodes. Superficial inguinal lymph nodes also drain the lower extremity, gluteal region, and skin below the level of the umbilicus. The tumor is a squamous cell carcinoma, indicating that it arose from mucosa below the dentate (pectinate) line. The mucosa above the dentate line is simple columnar epithelium and would give rise to adenocarcinoma.

When the inguinal lymph nodes are involved, a search for the cause, focusing on the areas mentioned above, should be done immediately. A melanoma from under the toenail can manifest as far away as the inguinal lymph nodes.

Anal squamous cell carcinoma is associated with HPV infection, especially HPV 16 and 18, the same high-risk HPV types thought to predispose women to cervical cancer. Anal cancer risk is higher in men who have sex with men (MSM). Condylomas (anal warts) are also caused by HPV, specifically HPV 6 and 11. These sometimes progress to verrucous carcinoma and/or squamous cell carcinoma.

Tumors from the colon (choices B, C, and E) do not usually metastasize to easily palpable lymph nodes; they instead metastasize to mesenteric nodes.

Tumors from the rectum (choice D) do not usually metastasize to the inguinal lymph nodes. Rectal tumors tend to travel to perirectal, internal iliac, external iliac, and sacral lymph nodes. In addition, the most common colorectal cancers are adenocarcinomas, not squamous cell carcinomas.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: the anal canal below the dentate line drains to superficial inguinal nodes.
choice_explanations.B: The ascending colon drains to ileocolic/right colic nodes.
choice_explanations.C: The descending colon drains to left colic/inferior mesenteric nodes.
choice_explanations.D: The rectum primarily drains to mesorectal and internal iliac nodes.
choice_explanations.E: The transverse colon drains to middle colic/mesenteric nodes.

stem: A 76-year-old man dies suddenly after fatigue and dyspnea. Examination before death showed elevated jugular venous pressure and a positive Kussmaul sign. Cardiac tissue contains perivascular extracellular deposits that are Congo-red positive with apple-green birefringence. Which additional finding was most likely present?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The extracellular deposits with an apple-green hue under polarized light after staining with Congo red are suggestive of amyloid deposition. Amyloidosis is the accumulation of insoluble fibrillar material in tissues. Amyloidosis can be primary or secondary. Secondary amyloidosis is usually related to chronic inflammation (eg, rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis), while primary amyloidosis is often related to disorders of immune cells, such as multiple myeloma.

Cardiac amyloidosis is usually a primary amyloidosis and results from deposition of AL-type or ATTR-type amyloid. Cardiac amyloidosis causes restrictive cardiomyopathy, often known as “stiff heart syndrome.” It may manifest with symptoms of palpitations, leg swelling, shortness of breath, and/or fatigue. However, the diagnosis is difficult to make, since findings from examination are not specific. Nevertheless, the disease may be complicated by atrial fibrillation or ventricular arrhythmias, which in some cases may be fatal.

Apart from cardiac manifestations, amyloidosis is associated with a wide variety of systemic conditions resulting from extracellular deposition of amyloid fibrils. These include proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome (choice E), gastroparesis, peripheral neuropathy, various forms of organomegaly, and bleeding diathesis.

Pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles is more likely to be seen in amyloidosis than atrophy (choice A). This is a result of fluid or amyloid infiltration of the glenohumeral joint and surrounding structures.

Amyloidosis is more often associated with decreased functioning of coagulation factors rather than hypercoagulability (choice B). The bleeding tendency for these patients is thought to be due to a combination of vessel fragility (from amyloid infiltration in the vessel walls) and factor X deficiency.

Amyloidosis-induced cirrhosis (choice C) is extremely rare. More typically, amyloidosis will produce hepatomegaly due to infiltration, which may impair some of its synthetic function, but is unlikely to progress to cirrhosis.

Though amyloidosis does produce restrictive cardiomyopathy, it is unlikely to produce a pericardial knock (choice D), which is more related to constrictive pericarditis. The “knock” results from an expanding myocardium physically impinging on a fibrosed pericardium.

ReKaps: Primary amyloidosis is characterized by deposition of fibrillar immunoglobulin light chains (AL) systemically, or fibrillar TTR protein (ATTR) in the myocardium. Amyloid deposition in the myocardium typically presents as restrictive cardiomyopathy.

choice_explanations.A: Shoulder muscle atrophy is not a typical systemic amyloidosis manifestation.
choice_explanations.B: Amyloidosis does not characteristically cause a hypercoagulable state.
choice_explanations.C: Liver involvement may occur in systemic amyloidosis, but proteinuria is the expected renal manifestation among these choices.
choice_explanations.D: A pericardial knock suggests constrictive pericarditis, not myocardial amyloid deposition.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: systemic amyloidosis can involve the kidneys and cause proteinuria.

stem: A 58-year-old Japanese man has unintentional weight loss, persistent epigastric discomfort, guaiac-positive stool, and an ulcerated antral gastric mass. Which risk factor most likely predisposed him to this disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The Japanese, both in Japan and to a lesser extent in the United States, have an unusually high incidence of gastric adenocarcinoma. The Japanese diet, with its high concentration of polycyclic hydrocarbons present in smoked fish, has been strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of gastric adenocarcinoma. Nitrites are also potential carcinogens present in preserved foods, and have been shown to cause gastric cancer in laboratory animals.

The Japanese population is routinely screened for gastric adenocarcinoma (contrary to choice B), and as such is more frequently treated when the tumor is at an earlier stage. While screening can detect carcinoma at an earlier stage, it is not considered to alter the overall incidence of carcinoma, and so the lack of screening cannot be considered a risk factor. In the United States, such screening is not routinely performed because the incidence of gastric carcinoma is much lower than in Japan.

Helicobacter pylori in the antral mucosa is highly associated with peptic ulcer disease, gastric lymphoma, and gastric adenocarcinoma. The bacterium is just as prevalent in the Japanese population as in the American population. There is a decreasing incidence of gastric adenocarcinoma in the United States, probably related to identification of H. pylori and its treatment.

A low-fiber diet (choice C) is not associated with gastric adenocarcinoma. The role of fiber in cancer prevention is unclear, and the data on high-fiber diets reducing colon cancer risk is inconclusive. However, a healthy diet, including a diet high in fiber from fruits and vegetables, is probably protective against some forms of cancer. A high-fiber diet also protects against diverticulosis.

Ménétrier disease (or hypertrophic gastritis; choice D) is a very rare condition characterized by markedly thickened gastric rugal folds, accompanied by hyperplasia of mucous glands and protein-losing enteropathy. A few cases of gastric carcinoma arising in Ménétrier disease have been described, but this would not be the most likely scenario in an individual such as described in the question stem.

Schistosomiasis (choice E) may injure the liver, bladder, or intestines, depending upon the species, but it is not a risk factor for gastric carcinoma. Schistosoma haematobium infection is a risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: smoked and preserved foods can contain carcinogenic compounds associated with gastric adenocarcinoma.
choice_explanations.B: Inadequate screening is not the carcinogenic exposure described in the source.
choice_explanations.C: A low-fiber diet is not the risk factor highlighted for this gastric mass.
choice_explanations.D: Ménétrier disease is a protein-losing hypertrophic gastropathy, not the dietary exposure described.
choice_explanations.E: Schistosoma is associated with other malignancies, not this gastric adenocarcinoma risk pattern.

stem: A 53-year-old man with an ST-elevation myocardial infarction receives thrombolytic therapy. Blood flow is restored, but an echocardiogram 1 hour later still shows regional hypokinesis; wall motion returns 24 hours after reperfusion. Which mechanism most likely caused the transient dysfunction?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient presents with a severe myocardial infarction with classic symptoms of unrelenting chest pressure/pain and shortness of breath. ST elevation is suggestive of transmural infarction, and CK-MB is released into the circulation from dying myocytes within hours.

To re-establish blood flow to thrombosed coronary arteries, several approaches may be taken. Two common approaches are percutaneous coronary intervention, which uses a balloon catheter to physically stent open the artery, or thrombolytic agents, including alteplase (tissue plasminogen activator; tPA).

Unfortunately, rapid reperfusion of the coronary arteries can injure cells that otherwise would be able to recover. This is called reperfusion injury. During reperfusion of an ischemic environment, oxygen delivery may produce free radicals in several ways, including activation of neutrophils, leakage from ischemic mitochondria, cyclooxygenase enzymes, and catecholamine oxidation. These free radicals, including superoxide anion radical (O₂⁻), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and hydroxyl ions (OH⁻), are highly toxic to myocyte DNA, proteins, and plasma-membrane lipids.

This myocyte injury can manifest as arrhythmia, coronary microvascular dysfunction, myocardial death, or, as in this patient, myocardial stunning. Myocardial stunning is temporary dysfunction of the myocardium with subsequent recovery. Superoxide dismutase and other free-radical scavengers used with thrombolytics can help prevent reperfusion injury.

Arrhythmia (choice A) is a common cause of death in myocardial infarction, typically ventricular fibrillation. Arrhythmia can also be induced by reperfusion injury. However, this patient has wall hypokinesis on echocardiogram rather than electrocardiographic changes.

Cardiac tamponade (choice B) may occur in myocardial infarction complicated by left-ventricular free-wall rupture or hemorrhagic pericarditis. Thrombolytics can increase the risk of free-wall rupture; however, echocardiography would show evidence of pericardial effusion or diastolic ventricular collapse due to surrounding pressure. It is also unlikely that the patient would recover without intervention in this case.

The direct effect of thrombolytics (choice C) is primarily related to bleeding complications, which this patient does not exhibit. For this reason, thrombolytics are contraindicated in hemorrhagic stroke and during active bleeding.

Repeat coronary artery thrombosis (choice E) is possible, but typically occurs a few days after the initial event. It is also unlikely to occur immediately after the patient is given systemic thrombolytics.

choice_explanations.A: An arrhythmia does not explain persistent regional hypokinesis followed by recovery of the same segment.
choice_explanations.B: Tamponade would cause hemodynamic compromise and would not selectively cause transient regional wall-motion abnormality.
choice_explanations.C: The thrombolytic itself is not the usual cause of transient myocardial stunning after reperfusion.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: reperfusion-generated oxygen free radicals contribute to reversible myocardial stunning.
choice_explanations.E: Recurrent thrombosis would be expected to cause ongoing ischemia or infarction, not spontaneous recovery of wall motion.

stem: A 29-year-old woman at 11 weeks’ gestation has vaginal bleeding and premature contractions. Ultrasound shows a nonviable fetus, and dilation and curettage is performed. Which fetal karyotype is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Approximately half of all spontaneous abortions are of fetuses with major chromosomal defects, most commonly trisomy 16, triploidy (due to fertilization of an egg by two sperm), and 45,X (Turner syndrome). Trisomy 16 and triploidy do not produce viable offspring, unlike 45,X.

Klinefelter syndrome (choice A) is a common genetic abnormality involving aneuploidy of the X chromosome. Typically, the embryo implants and carries to term. Individuals with Klinefelter syndrome are male, but their sexual development is impaired. Their phenotypic features include small testes that are not able to produce sufficient amounts of testosterone, resulting in delayed or incomplete puberty, gynecomastia, undescended testes, micropenis, and infertility. As adults, they tend to be taller than their peers.

Trisomy 13 (choice B) is one of the more common live-birth trisomy syndromes (Patau syndrome). The major phenotypic features of trisomy 13 are the result of an early defect in development of the prechordal mesoderm, which is the origin of the midface, eye, and forebrain. These abnormalities include holoprosencephaly, absence of the olfactory nerve or bulb, sloping forehead, severe eye defects, deafness, and cleft lip and/or palate.

Trisomy 18 (choice D), also known as Edwards syndrome, is the second most common autosomal trisomy observed in live births (1 in 5,500 live births). Trisomy 18 may involve any organ system. The major phenotypic features include hypertonia, prominent occiput, small mouth, micrognathia, short sternum, horseshoe kidney, ectopic pancreatic tissue, small pelvis, and flexed fingers with overriding index fingers or third fingers. Congenital heart disease occurs in more than 50% of affected individuals.

Trisomy 21 (choice E), also known as Down syndrome, is the most common chromosomal abnormality among live births (1 in 730 live births) and the most frequent form of intellectual disability caused by a microscopically demonstrable chromosomal aberration.

ReKaps: Trisomy 16 is the most common trisomy among miscarriages and is never encountered in live births.

choice_explanations.B: Trisomy 13 can cause severe congenital anomalies but is less common than trisomy 16 in early pregnancy loss.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has progressive difficulty climbing stairs, calf pseudohypertrophy, a waddling gait, proximal weakness, a positive Gowers sign, and elevated creatine kinase. The inheritance pattern of his disease is most similar to which disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The young boy is presenting with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive genetic disease caused by a defective gene responsible for the production of dystrophin. Dystrophin is a protein involved in stabilizing membrane proteins on muscle fibers. Loss of these proteins initiates degeneration of muscle fibers, leading to weakness. Males usually present with proximal muscle weakness at age 2 to 3 years. Additional clinical features include dilated cardiomyopathy and scoliosis. Physical examination reveals pseudohypertrophy of the calf, a waddling gait, and hyporeflexia. Gowers sign, which is the use of a patient's hands/arms to push himself to an upright position, is usually present. Laboratory values show an increase in creatine kinase due to muscle-fiber degradation. Patients with DMD usually die in their late teens to twenties from respiratory insufficiency and/or dilated cardiomyopathy.

The mode of inheritance of DMD is similar to that of hemophilia A. Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive genetic disease characterized by a deficiency in factor VIII. Patients with hemophilia experience spontaneous bleeding, particularly into joint spaces and muscles, and bleeding that is out of proportion to the degree of trauma. Diagnostic testing reveals an elevation in the partial thromboplastin time (PTT).

Cystic fibrosis (choice A) is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by an abnormality in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein. The protein conducts chloride transportation in epithelial cells, especially those present in the lungs, pancreas, intestine, and reproductive tract. The consequence of abnormal chloride transport is viscous secretions in the lungs, pancreas, intestines, and reproductive tract. Patients present with recurrent, frequent respiratory infections, including pulmonary and sinus disease; failure to thrive; bulky, foul-smelling stools due to malabsorption secondary to pancreatic insufficiency; and infertility due to defective sperm transport.

Huntington disease (choice C) is an autosomal dominant inherited neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia and abnormal choreiform movements. The disease is caused by a trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene.

Fragile X syndrome (choice D) is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by an expansion of a trinucleotide CGG repeat in the 5′ untranslated region of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. The expansion causes a loss of function of the fragile X mental retardation protein. Males with this condition have characteristic physical features, particularly prominent in adolescence, including a long and narrow face with prominent forehead and chin, large ears, and testicular enlargement.

Neurofibromatosis type 1 (choice E) is an autosomal dominant disease characterized by multiple physical findings, including café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), and neurofibromas.

choice_explanations.B: Correct: hemophilia A and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are X-linked recessive.
choice_explanations.C: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant.
choice_explanations.D: Fragile X has atypical X-linked inheritance and is not the classic X-linked recessive pattern tested here.

stem: A newborn has hypotonia, microcephaly, widely spaced eyes with downward-slanting palpebral fissures, micrognathia, and a high-pitched cry. Karyotyping shows 46,XX with a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5. Which additional finding is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The presentation is classic for cri-du-chat syndrome, caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p−). Approximately one-quarter of such patients have a ventricular septal defect. Other features of the syndrome include short stature, distorted laryngeal anatomy, profound intellectual disability, microcephaly, micrognathia, a wide nasal bridge, widely spaced eyes, and downward-slanting eyes. The laryngeal malformation causes feeding and respiratory difficulties, as well as the cat-like cry, which typically disappears by age 1. Some patients survive to adulthood, but are usually institutionalized.

Duodenal atresia (choice A) is seen with Down syndrome, trisomy 21. Infants with Down syndrome can also have congenital heart anomalies (VSD, ASD, and AV canal defects), intellectual disability, upward-slanting palpebral eye folds, and Hirschsprung disease. They would not have the distinct cry seen with cri-du-chat. Mothers are usually older than 40 years of age (nondisjunction of chromosome 21), although Robertsonian translocations are seen in younger women who can have several children with Down syndrome.

Obesity (choice B) is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome, a deletion of the functional paternal gene present on the short arm of chromosome 15. This genetic abnormality is associated with genomic imprinting (silencing) of the maternal chromosome and lack of inheritance of the functional paternal gene. The inherited maternal Prader-Willi gene is silenced/unactivated and cannot be “turned on.” Obesity would not be seen at birth, but would develop as the child ages because of an urge to constantly eat. Children would also have intellectual disability and fair hair and skin. Note: the opposite condition is Angelman syndrome, in which the paternal Angelman gene is silenced with lack of inheritance of the maternal gene.

Renal cysts (choice C) are seen with childhood-type autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD). Usually both kidneys are enlarged with radially arranged cysts that do not distort the renal capsule surface (the adult type does). The condition is caused by a PKHD1 gene mutation associated with fibrocystin protein, which maintains the cilia of the renal tubules and hepatobiliary ducts, thus resulting in renal and hepatic cysts. Kidney enlargement and dysfunction may be present at birth, with associated oligohydramnios, Potter facies, and abnormally flexed extremities, but not with the findings seen in the question stem.

Wilms tumor (choice E), also known as nephroblastoma, is associated with the WT1 gene mutation, located on the short arm of chromosome 11. It is the most common childhood tumor, with peak age under 5 years. Wilms tumor is associated with WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformations, and intellectual disability), in which some of these are present at birth.

ReKaps: Cri-du-chat syndrome is due to a terminal deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5. Congenital abnormalities in this disorder include cat-like neonatal crying, microcephaly with dysmorphic facial features, cardiac defects (e.g., ventricular septal defects), hypotonia, and severe intellectual disability.

choice_explanations.B: Obesity is not a characteristic neonatal finding of cri-du-chat syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: Renal cysts are not the characteristic associated anomaly.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has progressive clumsiness, falls, difficulty running and climbing stairs, enlarged calves, thigh-muscle wasting, and a molecular test showing defective dystrophin. Which relative is most likely to also have this disease?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The disease is Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive muscular disease usually caused by a deletion involving the dystrophin gene. This defect produces accelerated muscle breakdown, leading initially to proximal muscle weakness and later to generalized weakness that typically begins before age 5.

A feature of X-linked recessive diseases is that carrier mothers pass the disease to half of their sons; affected fathers can pass the abnormal allele to their daughters but not their sons. Since the mother is presumably normal (because the disease is X-linked), she must be a carrier to have an affected son, and there is a good chance that the grandmother is a carrier. Therefore, the mother's brother (maternal uncle) may also have the disease.

choice_explanations.B: The father’s brother is not on the maternal X-linked branch.

choice_explanations.D: Correct: a maternal uncle is a male relative on the X-linked maternal side and is the most likely affected relative among these choices.

stem: A 12-year-old boy has recurrent fractures after minor trauma and blue sclerae. Which genetic concept best explains the multiple effects of his disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The clinical presentation strongly suggests osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), an autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder affecting type I collagen. The most common mutations in OI are in the gene for type I collagen and result in abnormal collagen conformation or post-translational modification. This patient's presentation is a classic example of pleiotropy, which refers to the multiple, often seemingly unrelated, physical effects caused by a single genotype. Clinical manifestations of osteogenesis imperfecta include excess or atypical fractures, scoliosis, basilar skull deformities, blue sclerae, opalescent teeth, and laxity of ligaments and skin. Children with OI are often misdiagnosed with child abuse before discovery of the disorder.

Allelic heterogeneity (choice A) refers to different alleles at the same gene locus resulting in a similar phenotype. This is observed in osteogenesis imperfecta, but this question asks about the findings of multiple unrelated phenotypes resulting from a gene lesion in an individual patient.

A gain-of-function mutation (choice B) is inconsistent with the observed pathology.

Locus heterogeneity (choice C) refers to mutations at different gene loci resulting in the same phenotype. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a good example of a disease in which locus heterogeneity is observed, because genes for type I procollagen are found on chromosome 7 and on chromosome 17. Mutations in either gene locus can result in imperfect formation of the trimeric collagen protein and OI. Though seen in OI, this principle does not explain the co-occurrence of fractures and blue sclerae asked about in this question.

A single mutation at either the chromosome 7 or chromosome 17 locus is sufficient to cause the disease, so multiple mutations (choice D) do not explain the pattern.

ReKaps: Pleiotropy refers to the multiple, often unrelated phenotypic effects from a mutation within a single gene. Blue sclerae and a history of multiple fractures, frequently observed in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta, are examples of pleiotropy. Osteogenesis imperfecta is most commonly associated with mutations in a gene for type I procollagen.

choice_explanations.A: Allelic heterogeneity means different mutations in the same gene cause the same disease.
choice_explanations.B: Gain of function describes a mutation’s effect on protein activity, not the multiple-organ pattern asked about.
choice_explanations.C: Locus heterogeneity means variants in different genes cause a similar disease phenotype.
choice_explanations.D: Multiple mutations is not the named concept for one defect producing several phenotypic effects.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: pleiotropy is one gene contributing to multiple phenotypic effects.

stem: A 26-month-old boy has poor eye contact, hand-flapping, self-biting, and delayed social, motor, and language skills. He has a long narrow face, large ears, and flat feet. Which genetic abnormality best explains these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The findings are typical of fragile X syndrome, the most common heritable cause of intellectual disability, affecting approximately 1 in 2,000 males. Clinical features can worsen in successive generations (anticipation), and males are usually more severely affected than females; nearly half of females with a full mutation demonstrate characteristic physical features and developmental delay.

Fragile X is caused by expansion of CGG tandem repeats in the 5′ untranslated region of FMR1 on the X chromosome. The normal gene contains about 6–54 repeats; carriers have a premutation that can contain up to about 200 repeats, while clinically affected individuals have a full mutation (about 200–4,000 repeats). Expansion methylates the 5′ promoter region, causing epigenetic gene silencing. Premutations are much more likely to expand to full mutations during oogenesis than during spermatogenesis; in contrast, paternal amplification is more prominent in Huntington disease.

Genomic imprinting (B) means gene expression differs depending on whether the gene was inherited from the mother or father; examples include Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes. A chromosome 22q11.2 microdeletion (C) causes DiGeorge syndrome, with cardiac abnormalities, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia/hypoparathyroidism. The t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation (D) fuses BCR and ABL, producing the BCR–ABL oncoprotein characteristic of Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia. Trisomy 21 (E) causes Down syndrome, associated with intellectual disability, congenital heart defects, increased leukemia risk, and characteristic facial features.

ReKaps: Fragile X is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and is due to CGG-repeat expansion, promoter methylation, and gene silencing. Females tend to have fewer and milder behavioral and cognitive manifestations.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: fragile X syndrome is caused by CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in FMR1.
choice_explanations.B: Genomic imprinting is associated with disorders such as Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes, which have different phenotypes.
choice_explanations.C: Robertsonian translocation can cause chromosomal imbalance such as Down syndrome.
choice_explanations.D: Trisomy 13 causes severe congenital anomalies including midline defects and polydactyly.
choice_explanations.E: Trisomy 18 causes growth restriction and clenched overlapping fingers.

B.text: Genomic imprinting underlies Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.

C.text: Robertsonian translocations can cause chromosomal imbalance.

D.text: Patau syndrome is trisomy 13.

E.text: Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has had four spontaneous abortions. Examination of the current aborted fetus shows mature tissue containing Barr bodies. Which description best fits the fetus?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The Barr body, or X chromatin body, is an inactivated X chromosome seen as a small, perinuclear, dark-staining dot in somatic cells with two or more X chromosomes. Barr bodies are seen in any individual born with at least two X chromosomes, including normal females. 47,XXY, the classic karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome, is defined as male hypogonadism due to the presence of a Y chromosome and two or more X chromosomes. As in normal females, one of the X chromosomes becomes a Barr body in Klinefelter syndrome.

Classic Turner syndrome females (choice A) and genotypically normal males (choice D) have only one X chromosome. Thus, no X chromosome is inactivated, and somatic cells do not show any Barr bodies.

47,XY,+18 is the karyotype of an Edwards syndrome male (choice B) fetus. Although this trisomic phenotype is associated with a characteristic syndrome of physical abnormalities, there is no programmed inactivation of the extra chromosome 18. Since the fetus is male, there is no Barr body formation from X-chromosome inactivation.

XYY syndrome (choice E) is not associated with inactivation of any X chromosome because there is only one X. Barr bodies are not present. Like a trisomy involving any of the non-sex-linked chromosomes, the duplicated Y chromosome is expressed in its entirety.

ReKaps: If the embryo contains two or more X chromosomes, the extra ones will be inactivated until only one X chromosome remains active in a given cell line. This leads to formation of a Barr body. X-chromosome inactivation and Barr body formation occur in normal females and in persons with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY). In normal males and in aneuploidies with one X chromosome, Barr bodies are not formed.

choice_explanations.B: Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18 and does not itself produce a Barr body.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY and contains one inactivated X chromosome (Barr body).
choice_explanations.D: A normal 46,XY male has no Barr body.
choice_explanations.E: XYY males have one X chromosome and ordinarily no Barr body.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with lifelong intellectual disability develops progressive memory loss. Neuropathology shows neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. Which genetic finding is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Features of Down syndrome (trisomy 21, 47,+21) in children include intellectual disability (formerly mental retardation), epicanthal folds, dysplastic ears, hypotonia, a horizontal palmar crease (simian crease), redundant neck skin, and a short trunk. Congenital heart disease is present in about one-third of liveborn Down syndrome (DS) infants. Additional malformations are more common in DS, including duodenal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula. There is a 15-fold increase in leukemia.

Individuals with Down syndrome develop a clinical dementia with clinical and pathologic characteristics that are virtually identical to Alzheimer disease (AD). Autopsy findings include intraneural neurofibrillary tangles, extracellular neuritic plaques, amyloid beta (Aβ) protein in senile plaques, and amyloid angiopathy. There are some differences because this neuropathology is superimposed on brain pathology unique to DS. One important clinical difference is the early age of onset of AD in patients with DS. There is no treatment and prognosis is poor. AD causes a sharp decline in survival in DS patients older than 45 years. Many genes coding for proteins likely involved in AD development, such as amyloid precursor protein (APP) and superoxide dismutase (SOD-1), are located on chromosome 21. The overexpression of these genes because of trisomy 21 is likely responsible for early AD.

ReKaps: Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal abnormality among live-born infants. Premature senility associated with neuropathologic findings characteristic of Alzheimer disease affects patients with Down syndrome several decades earlier than the typical age of onset in the general population.

Patients with the other listed conditions are not particularly prone to early AD. Common features of 45,XO (choice A), also known as Turner syndrome, include short stature, webbed neck, lymphedema in hands and feet, skeletal abnormalities, congenital heart defects, and infertility. Individuals show learning disabilities, though intelligence is usually normal.

47,+13 (choice B), also known as Patau syndrome or trisomy 13, is characterized by severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, microphthalmia, polydactyly, cleft lip and palate, renal defects, and cardiac abnormalities. Affected infants typically die before the age of 1 year.

Patients with 47,XXY, or Klinefelter syndrome (choice D), are male and have impaired sexual development. They typically have small testes that are not able to produce sufficient amounts of testosterone, resulting in delayed or incomplete puberty, gynecomastia, undescended testes, micropenis, and infertility. As adults, they tend to be taller than their peers.

Fragile X syndrome (choice E) can occur in males and females, although females often have milder symptoms than males. It is associated with enlarged testes after puberty (macroorchidism, in males) as well as intellectual disability, large ears, and prominent jaw and forehead. The condition is unusual in that it is related to expansion of a CGG repeat sequence located on the X chromosome. Fragile X syndrome is caused by mutation in the FMR1 gene.

choice_explanations.A: 45,X is Turner syndrome and does not explain lifelong intellectual disability with Alzheimer-like changes.
choice_explanations.B: Trisomy 13 causes a severe congenital syndrome that is rarely compatible with survival to adulthood.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: Down syndrome is trisomy 21 and is associated with early Alzheimer-like neuropathology.
choice_explanations.D: 47,XXY causes Klinefelter syndrome, not this phenotype.
choice_explanations.E: Fragile X causes intellectual disability but not the characteristic association of trisomy-21 Alzheimer-like changes.

B.text: Patau syndrome is trisomy 13.

C.text: Down syndrome is trisomy 21 and is associated with Alzheimer-like changes.

D.text: Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY.

E.text: Fragile X syndrome is a separate cause of intellectual disability.

fa_summary: The combination of lifelong intellectual disability and Alzheimer-like neuropathology in mid-adulthood is characteristic of Down syndrome. The expected karyotype is trisomy 21.

stem: A disease is caused by a small deletion on chromosome 15. Across families, the deletion is found only when inherited from the father. Which mechanism best explains this parent-of-origin effect?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Genomic imprinting refers to the differential expression of genes inherited from the father and the mother. Imprinting is a genomic “silencing” in which genes on the maternal chromosome are not expressed (maternal imprinting) or genes on the paternal chromosome are not expressed (paternal imprinting). If a defect occurs on the paternal chromosome in a gene that is maternally imprinted, then the offspring will express the defective gene and be at risk to show the disease. For example, Prader-Willi syndrome results from a deletion at a specific gene locus on the paternally derived chromosome 15 that is imprinted on the maternally derived chromosome 15. Interestingly, a deletion of a paternally imprinted gene in the same locus in the maternally derived chromosome 15 results in Angelman syndrome (“Happy Puppet syndrome”). This difference reflects the fact that the genes deleted in Prader-Willi syndrome are normally active only on the paternally transmitted chromosome, while the genes whose deletion causes Angelman syndrome are normally active only on the maternally transmitted chromosome.

In mitochondrial inheritance (choice B), only an affected mother can transmit the disease phenotype; the offspring of affected males are always unaffected.

ReKaps: Genomic imprinting means that the expression of a gene depends on the gender of the parent donating the gene. Prader-Willi syndrome usually arises due to loss of the paternal copy of a segment of chromosome 15 that is normally silenced in the homologous region on the maternal chromosome. Classic features include hyperphagia, obesity, and intellectual disability (formerly mental retardation). Angelman syndrome, historically referred to as “Happy Puppet syndrome,” is usually due to loss of a segment of a maternally transmitted chromosome 15 that is normally silenced in the homologous region on the paternal chromosome. Typical features include severe intellectual disability, happy disposition, and puppet-like posture of limbs.

The other modes of inheritance would influence the relative proportions of affected individuals who belong to one gender or the other. Sex-dependent penetrance (choice C) occurs when there is differential penetrance depending on sex. X-linked recessive inheritance (choice D) will show a disproportionate number of males affected irrespective of the father's genotype. Y-linked inheritance (choice E) would be expected to only affect males, with no transmission from father to daughters. Other examples of sex differences in genetic transmission are X-linked recessive or dominant, mitochondrial, or Y-linked inheritance.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: genomic imprinting creates parent-of-origin-specific expression.
choice_explanations.B: Mitochondrial traits are transmitted through the mother and involve mitochondrial DNA.
choice_explanations.C: Sex-dependent penetrance varies by sex, not by which parent transmitted a deletion.
choice_explanations.D: X-linked recessive inheritance involves genes on the X chromosome, not chromosome 15.
choice_explanations.E: Y-linked inheritance is transmitted father-to-son and cannot explain affected individuals of both sexes.
