stem: An 8-year-old boy has intellectual disability, hyperactivity, a long narrow face, prominent jaw, large ears, and macroorchidism. His mother has mild intellectual disability. Which genetic abnormality is diagnostic?

options.text: Loss of expression from the paternal chromosome 15q11–q13 region
CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the 5′ untranslated region of FMR1

explanation:
The correct answer is B. The patient is presenting with Fragile X syndrome, the most frequently inherited form of intellectual disability. Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked dominant genetic disorder caused by an expansion of trinucleotide CGG repeats in the 5′ untranslated region of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. The expansion causes a loss of function of the fragile X mental retardation protein. Males with this condition have characteristic physical features, particularly prominent in adolescence, including a long, narrow face with a prominent forehead and chin, large ears, and testicular enlargement. They also characteristically have problems with hyperactivity and hyperarousal. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is found in a majority of affected males. Females with the condition may present with normal intelligence or with the classic manifestations, but most are less severely affected than males due to the variability in X-inactivation.

Absence of expression from the paternal chromosome 15q11–13 (choice A) is the cause of Prader-Willi syndrome. Patients with Prader-Willi syndrome present with hypotonia and feeding difficulties as neonates that progress to hyperphagia and an insatiable appetite that may cause secondary comorbidities due to morbid obesity. Patients typically have intellectual disability. Physical characteristics include small hands and feet, short stature, and almond-shaped eyes.

A genetic defect in the gene responsible for production of dystrophin (choice C) is the cause of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Males usually present with proximal muscle weakness at age 2–3 years. Additional physical examination features include pseudohypertrophy of the calf, a waddling gait, and hyporeflexia.

Trisomy 21, or three copies of chromosome 21 (choice D), is the cause of Down syndrome. Patients typically have some component of intellectual disability, upslanting palpebral fissures, a flattened facial profile, hypotonia, short broad hands, a single palmar crease, and a gap between the first and second toes. Patients are at risk for congenital heart disease, hypothyroidism, and gastrointestinal issues.

A karyotype demonstrating XXY (choice E) is characteristic of Klinefelter syndrome. Patients have mild intellectual disability, tall stature, hypogonadism, and gynecomastia. Individuals demonstrate decreased serum testosterone and increased follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH).

choice_explanations.A: Paternal chromosome-15 loss of expression causes Prader-Willi syndrome, not macroorchidism and the fragile-X facies.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: fragile X syndrome results from a CGG repeat expansion in FMR1.
choice_explanations.C: Dystrophin defects cause Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy.
choice_explanations.D: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome.
choice_explanations.E: 47,XXY causes Klinefelter syndrome.

A.text: Paternal chromosome-15 deletion is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome.

B.text: Fragile X syndrome is due to CGG expansion in FMR1 with hypermethylation.

C.text: Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophies involve dystrophin.

D.text: Down syndrome is trisomy 21.

E.text: Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY.

fa_summary: The phenotype is fragile X syndrome. A CGG repeat expansion in the 5′ untranslated region of FMR1 leads to hypermethylation and reduced gene expression; a premutation in the mother can expand during oogenesis.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has developmental and behavioral difficulties, an elongated face, large protruding ears, flat feet, and hypotonia. His brother is similarly affected, but his three sisters are unaffected. Which genetic defect most likely causes this condition?

options.text: CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion on a sex chromosome

explanation:
The correct answer is A. This child has the traits associated with fragile X syndrome. This disorder is characterized by developmental delay and behavioral issues, as well as the physical features of an elongated face, large protruding ears, flat feet, and hypotonia. Fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the 5′ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome.

Genomic imprinting on chromosome 15 (choice B) is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome. This disorder is associated with intellectual delay, poor physical coordination, delayed puberty, and excessive weight gain. It is due to deletion of several genes on the paternal copy of chromosome 15. Angelman syndrome is associated with deletion of genes on the maternal copy of chromosome 15.

Microdeletion on chromosome 22 (choice C) causes DiGeorge syndrome, the most common microdeletion syndrome. A deletion of 22q11.2 results in cardiac abnormalities, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia/hypoparathyroidism.

A translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (choice D), t(9;22)(q34;q11), results in fusion of the genes encoding BCR and ABL kinase, creating the BCR-ABL oncoprotein. This translocation is characteristic of Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia.

Trisomy of chromosome 21 (choice E) results in Down syndrome. Individuals with this disorder are intellectually disabled, commonly have congenital heart defects, and are at increased risk of leukemia. They also have characteristic facial features, including a single palmar crease, slanted eyes, a large protruding tongue, and short stature, and are often obese.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: fragile X syndrome is an X-linked CGG-repeat expansion disorder.
choice_explanations.B: Chromosome-15 imprinting disorders include Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes, with different hallmark findings.
choice_explanations.C: A 22q11 deletion causes DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome.
choice_explanations.D: t(9;22) is the Philadelphia chromosome associated with CML and some ALL.
choice_explanations.E: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome; the described facies and sex-linked family pattern favor fragile X.

A.text: Fragile X is caused by CGG-repeat expansion in FMR1 on the X chromosome.

B.text: Chromosome-15 imprinting disorders include Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.

C.text: 22q11 deletion is associated with DiGeorge syndrome.

D.text: First Aid 2026未找到可直接支持该选项的独立知识点；不显示页码。

E.text: Down syndrome is trisomy 21.

fa_summary: The facies, hypotonia, developmental difficulties, and affected male siblings suggest fragile X syndrome, caused by CGG-repeat expansion in FMR1 on the X chromosome.

stem: A healthy 30-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish woman seeks genetic counseling. Two of her siblings died of Tay-Sachs disease; her parents may be first cousins. Assuming she is unaffected, what is her probability of being a carrier of the disease-causing variant?

options.text: No higher than the general-population risk

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Tay-Sachs disease (TSD) is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by a deficiency of hexosaminidase A. Clinically, patients are identified early in life and exhibit developmental delay, progressive neurodegeneration, and a cherry-red macula on retinal examination.

Because two of the woman's siblings had Tay-Sachs disease, her parents must both be carriers. This clearly elevates her risk above the general population and excludes choice E. Her risk of inheriting one copy of the disease gene at conception is 1/2 (choice B). However, the fact that she is phenotypically normal at age 30 means she cannot have inherited copies of the disease gene from both parents. Three possible scenarios are then possible: she inherited no copies of the mutation; she inherited a copy from her father; or she inherited a copy from her mother. Each of these three possibilities is equally likely, and two lead to heterozygosity. Thus, the risk that she is a carrier is 2/3. This is illustrated in the Punnett square below.

ReKaps: For an autosomal-recessive condition, if a phenotypically normal child is born to parents who are both heterozygous for the condition, the probability that the child is heterozygous for the condition is 2/3.

choice_explanations.A: 1/4 is the probability of an affected child when both parents are carriers, not the conditional carrier risk for an unaffected sibling.
choice_explanations.B: 1/2 is the probability of transmitting one allele from a carrier parent, not the conditional risk after excluding affected offspring.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: an unaffected sibling of an individual with an autosomal-recessive disease has a 2/3 carrier probability.
choice_explanations.D: 3/4 is the probability of being unaffected when both parents are carriers, not the conditional carrier probability.
choice_explanations.E: Two affected siblings establish that both parents are carriers, so her risk exceeds the population risk.

A.text: Two carrier parents have a 25% risk of an affected child.

B.text: Each carrier parent transmits the allele with probability 1/2.

C.text: An unaffected sibling of a patient with an autosomal-recessive disease has a 2/3 carrier probability; Tay-Sachs is a sphingolipidosis.

D.text: The 3/4 probability is unaffected genotype probability before conditioning on being unaffected.

E.text: Tay-Sachs is an autosomal-recessive sphingolipidosis.

fa_summary: Tay-Sachs disease is autosomal recessive. Because she has affected siblings, both parents are obligate carriers. Among their unaffected children, the possible genotypes are AA, Aa, and Aa; therefore the conditional probability that she is a carrier is 2/3.

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to a geneticist because of continued poor school performance. Two years earlier, a blood test for genetic abnormalities was reported as negative. Because his mother requests additional testing, a skin biopsy is obtained; his skin cells show trisomy 21. Which genetic mechanism best explains the discrepancy between the two test results?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Down syndrome is primarily caused by three genetic variants: full trisomy 21 (47,+21), most often due to maternal nondisjunction during meiosis I and accounting for about 95% of cases; a Robertsonian translocation that produces three copies of the critical Down-syndrome region (about 3–4%); and mosaicism (about 1–3%). Mosaicism occurs after fertilization and produces two cell lines, one with free trisomy 21 (47,+21) and one with a normal karyotype (46). Different tissues can contain different proportions of these cell lines. Thus, a blood sample can be normal if the trisomic line is absent or very low in blood, while testing another tissue can reveal trisomy 21 mosaicism.

This patient's earlier blood test was negative, but the continuing clinical concern supports testing another tissue to detect a postfertilization mitotic nondisjunction event. The key distinction is that meiotic nondisjunction produces full trisomy in the sampled line, whereas postzygotic mitotic nondisjunction can produce a mosaic mixture of normal and trisomic cells.

choice_explanations.A: A balanced translocation does not create separate normal and trisomy-21 cell populations.
choice_explanations.B: A postzygotic mitotic chromosome-segregation error can generate mosaic cell lines, but the condition described by different karyotypes across tissues is mosaicism.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: mosaicism is the presence of genetically distinct cell lines in one individual; the proportion of affected cells can differ by tissue.
choice_explanations.D: A reciprocal translocation exchanges material between nonhomologous chromosomes and does not explain normal blood cells with trisomic skin cells.
choice_explanations.E: A Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21 can cause translocation Down syndrome, but it would not account for the tissue-specific discordance described.

A.text: Balanced translocations generally do not cause an abnormal phenotype when no significant genetic material is gained or lost.

B.text: Somatic mosaicism can arise from mitotic errors after fertilization.

C.text: Mosaicism means genetically distinct cell lines are present in one individual; trisomy 21 is also summarized on p. 61.

D.text: First Aid 2026未找到可直接支持该选项的对应知识点；不显示页码。

E.text: Robertsonian translocations commonly involve acrocentric chromosomes, including 21, and can cause chromosomal imbalance.

fa_summary: The findings are consistent with trisomy 21 mosaicism: different tissues contain different cell lines, so a blood sample can be normal while skin cells contain trisomy 21. The supplied explanation attributes this to a postfertilization mitotic nondisjunction event.

stem: A male newborn born at 30 weeks’ gestation is small for gestational age. He has hypotonia, marked skeletal muscle and subcutaneous fat hypoplasia, a pinched face with hypoplastic orbital ridges, short palpebral fissures, a small mouth and jaw, a small head with a prominent occiput, and low-set malformed ears. His fists are clenched with overlapping third and fourth fingers. Which diagnosis is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This is trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome, the second most common autosomal trisomy observed in live births (1 in 6,000 live births) after trisomy 21. There is a relationship between meiotic nondisjunction and advanced maternal age, as with trisomy 21.

The phenotype described in the question stem is typical. Affected individuals often have intrauterine growth retardation and low birth weight. They have failure to thrive and feeding problems. These babies often have multiple congenital anomalies, including those involving the heart and kidneys. They have severe intellectual disability, micrognathia (small jaw), a prominent occiput, low-set ears, a short neck, rocker-bottom feet, and clenched hands with overlapping fingers. These babies have a very poor prognosis, and most die by 1 year. Very low beta hCG and very low PAPP-A (pregnancy-associated plasma protein A) are characteristic in the first trimester. Quad screening in the second trimester typically shows decreases in AFP (alpha-fetoprotein), uE3 (unconjugated estriol), inhibin A, and beta hCG.

47,XXY (choice A) is Klinefelter syndrome, which causes males to have tall stature, testicular atrophy, gynecomastia, eunuchoid body habitus, a high-pitched voice, and a female distribution of hair. It often goes unnoticed in early life and is usually diagnosed during workup for infertility.

Triple X (choice B) causes apparently phenotypically normal women; it is usually not diagnosed in newborns.

Trisomy 13 (choice C) is Patau syndrome. It produces many midline defects, including holoprosencephaly (embryologic failure of the brain to develop into two hemispheres) and cleft lip and palate. Microphthalmia (small eyes), microcephaly, cardiac and renal defects, polydactyly (six fingers), and severe intellectual disability also occur.

Trisomy 21 (choice E) is Down syndrome, the most common trisomy in live births. It is characterized by intellectual disability, a flat face, a low-bridged nose, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots (a speckled appearance) of the irises, palmar simian creases, and congenital heart defects. There is an increased risk of early Alzheimer disease (chromosome 21 contains the amyloid precursor protein gene), AML, ALL, Hirschsprung disease, and duodenal atresia (the “double-bubble” sign).

choice_explanations.A: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome and does not produce this neonatal pattern of severe growth restriction and overlapping fingers.
choice_explanations.B: Triple X is a sex-chromosome aneuploidy and does not match the Edwards phenotype.
choice_explanations.C: Trisomy 13 more characteristically causes midline defects, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, and holoprosencephaly.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: trisomy 18 classically causes growth restriction, prominent occiput, micrognathia, low-set ears, and clenched overlapping fingers.
choice_explanations.E: Trisomy 21 has a distinct phenotype and is associated with AV septal defects, hypotonia, and characteristic facies, not this combination.

A.text: Klinefelter syndrome is listed as 47,XXY.

B.text: First Aid 2026未找到可直接支持该选项的对应知识点；不显示页码。

C.text: Patau syndrome is trisomy 13; the page lists its distinguishing midline and limb findings.

D.text: Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18 and is associated with prominent occiput and clenched fists with overlapping fingers.

E.text: Down syndrome is trisomy 21; the page summarizes its common findings and complications.

fa_summary: This is Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18). The low birth weight, prominent occiput, micrognathia, low-set ears, and clenched fists with overlapping fingers are characteristic. The source explanation confirms the key as D.

stem: A 2-year-old boy with Down syndrome is studied to determine how the trisomy arose. A microsatellite marker near the centromere of chromosome 21 is used to track inheritance. The father has alleles A and C, the mother has alleles B and D, and the child has alleles A, B, and C. In which parent and meiotic division did nondisjunction most likely occur?

options.text: The child, during the first mitotic division

explanation:
The correct answer is B. The microsatellite marker detects a region near the centromere of chromosome 21. The region around the centromere exhibits a phenomenon called crossover suppression. Since genetic exchange cannot happen in this area, the probe is a reliable marker for the individual chromosomes.

During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes that form the tetrad should separate, leading to haploid daughter cells containing a single chromosome composed of two sister chromatids (which are two identical copies of the same chromosome). During meiosis II, the sister chromatids should separate. One can determine that the nondisjunction event occurred in the father because the progeny received only a single allele from the mother (B) and two alleles from the father (A and C). The nondisjunction event occurred during paternal meiosis I because the progeny received two different alleles/chromosomes (A and C) from the father. This implies that alleles from each of the homologous chromosome 21s were inherited. If the nondisjunction event occurred during paternal meiosis II, the progeny would have received two copies of either the A or the C allele.

Choice A (the child during the first mitotic division): If a nondisjunction event of chromosome 21 occurs early in development, a child who is likely to be mosaic for trisomy 21 results. In addition, the child should have only two different alleles at this marker, not three (ABC). Approximately 1% of children with trisomy 21 exhibit mosaicism. Since some of their cells are normal, these individuals, as a population, tend to have a milder trisomy 21 phenotype. It is important to remember that each individual's phenotype will depend on which cells actually have each genotype; therefore, their phenotype can range from mild to severe.

Choice C (the father during meiosis II): If the father had a failure in meiosis II, either an AA gamete or a CC gamete would be produced, and the mother would pass a B gamete or a D gamete. Various combinations could produce BAA, DAA, BCC, or DCC.

Choice D (the mother during meiosis I): If a BD woman had a failure in meiosis I, a BD gamete would be produced. When fertilized by the man's A or C sperm, a child that was ABD or BCD would result.

Choice E (the mother during meiosis II): If a BD woman's sister chromatids failed to disjoin during meiosis II, BB or DD gametes would result. When fertilized by the A or C male's sperm, a child that was BBA, BBC, DDA, or DDC would result.

ReKaps: Homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis I. Sister chromatids separate during meiosis II. Nondisjunction events during mitosis often result in mosaicism in the progeny.

choice_explanations.A: A postzygotic mitotic error can produce mosaicism, but the child’s genotype shows two paternal homologous alleles and one maternal allele.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: both paternal homologs (A and C) were transmitted, indicating failure of homologous chromosomes to separate in paternal meiosis I.
choice_explanations.C: Meiosis II nondisjunction would transmit two copies of one paternal homolog/sister-chromatid marker allele, not the distinct A and C alleles shown.
choice_explanations.D: The child received only one maternal allele, so maternal nondisjunction is not supported.
choice_explanations.E: The child received only one maternal allele, so maternal meiosis-II nondisjunction is not supported.

A.text: A postfertilization mitotic error can produce somatic mosaicism.

B.text: Autosomal trisomy most often results from nondisjunction during meiosis I; distinct paternal homolog marker alleles identify a meiosis-I error.

C.text: The nondisjunction diagram distinguishes meiosis-I homolog separation from meiosis-II sister-chromatid separation.

D.text: The page notes that trisomy 21 most commonly follows maternal meiosis-I nondisjunction; this case’s inherited alleles instead identify the father.

E.text: The nondisjunction diagram distinguishes meiosis-II errors; the inherited marker pattern does not fit a maternal event.

fa_summary: The child inherited one maternal allele (B) and both paternal alleles (A and C). Because the marker is near the centromere, the two paternal alleles identify the two homologous chromosome-21 copies; their failure to separate indicates paternal meiosis-I nondisjunction. Meiosis-II nondisjunction would duplicate one sister-chromatid allele at this marker.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 8 weeks’ gestation comes for prenatal care. Her husband is affected by an inherited disease. His father is affected, as are his paternal aunt and her son, and affected individuals appear in several generations. What is the most appropriate counseling statement about the risk to their child?

options.text: The child will not be affected
The risk cannot be determined until the child’s sex is known
There is a 25% chance the child will have the disease
There is a 50% chance the child will have the disease

explanation:
The correct answer is E. The question uses family history to determine the mode of inheritance. Because there is female-to-male transmission (the paternal aunt to her son), the disease could be X-linked or autosomal. Because there is also male-to-male transmission (the patient's father to the patient), it cannot be X-linked; the disease gene must be autosomal. When affected individuals appear in multiple successive generations, the disease is most likely autosomal dominant, giving an average 50% recurrence risk for each child when one parent is affected. If affected individuals do not appear in multiple generations, autosomal recessive inheritance is more likely, with a 25% recurrence risk when both parents are carriers.

An affected parent does not mean the child will certainly be affected (A), nor that the child will certainly be unaffected (B). The child's sex is not needed because autosomal transmission is independent of sex (C). With one affected heterozygous parent, the risk is 50%, not 25% (D).

ReKaps: Male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked inheritance. In autosomal dominant inheritance, affected individuals usually occur in successive generations, except with incomplete penetrance. Each child of an affected heterozygous parent has a 50% risk.

choice_explanations.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance gives a probability, not certainty, when one heterozygous parent is affected.
choice_explanations.B: The child has a 50% risk, so the disease cannot be ruled out.
choice_explanations.C: Male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked inheritance; autosomal dominant risk does not depend on the child’s sex.
choice_explanations.D: A 25% risk is typical when both parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive condition, not the pedigree shown.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: each child of an affected heterozygous parent with an autosomal dominant disorder has a 50% risk.

A.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance is seen across generations; each child of an affected heterozygous parent has a 50% risk.

B.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance gives each child a 50% risk, not zero risk.

C.text: No male-to-male transmission is expected with X-linked inheritance; autosomal dominant transmission is not sex-dependent.

D.text: A 25% affected risk is described for two heterozygous autosomal-recessive parents.

E.text: Each child of an affected heterozygous parent has a 50% risk in autosomal dominant inheritance.

fa_summary: The husband’s affected father demonstrates male-to-male transmission, excluding X-linked inheritance. The repeated appearance in successive generations is most consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. An affected heterozygous parent has a 50% risk of transmitting the condition to each child, regardless of sex.

stem: A 42-year-old pregnant woman returns to receive the results of amniocentesis. She is told that her fetus has a chromosomal abnormality associated with intellectual disability and increased risks of congenital heart defects and acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Which abnormality is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. In addition to the well-known intellectual disabilities associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21), affected individuals have an increased incidence of a variety of medical problems. Acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML) is seen in newborns and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is seen in older children. Congenital malformations of the cardiac system are common (40–50% of cases) and include atrial and ventricular septal defects, tetralogy of Fallot, and patent ductus arteriosus. Development of the hypopharynx is often poor, predisposing to both aspiration pneumonia and obstruction by enlarged adenoids. Nearly all boys are infertile; girls are subfertile but can become pregnant. Epilepsy affects up to 10% of children with Down syndrome. On occasion, the malformed head and neck region can undergo atlantoaxial dislocation, causing sudden or progressive quadriparesis. Other malformations that occur with lower frequency include duodenal atresia and imperforate anus. Acquired autoimmune hypothyroidism is frequent. Alzheimer-like changes develop in mid-adulthood. Visual problems related to strabismus, nystagmus, or myopia are common.

ReKaps: Aside from intellectual disability, trisomy 21 is associated with numerous other medical issues. Examples include acute lymphoblastic leukemia, cardiac malformations, quadriparesis, Alzheimer-like changes, epilepsy, duodenal atresia, and visual problems.

Trisomy 13 (choice A) and trisomy 18 (choice B) arise from nondisjunction of an autosome, resulting in an individual in which all cells have three copies of chromosome 13 or 18, respectively, instead of the normal two copies. Both conditions are associated with severe intellectual disability and congenital heart defects. Both conditions are usually fatal within the first few weeks of life. Trisomy 13, also known as Patau syndrome, is associated with rocker-bottom feet, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly (extra fingers or toes), and cardiac and renal defects. Trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome, is characterized by rocker-bottom feet, low birth weight, low-set ears, micrognathia (small lower jaw), clenched fists with overlapping fingers, and congenital heart defects. Although heart defects are common with both trisomy 13 and 18, neither is associated with an increased risk of ALL.

Genotypes 45,XO (choice D) and 47,XXY (choice E) arise from nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes, resulting in either the absence of one X chromosome (45,XO) or the presence of an additional X chromosome (47,XXY). An individual with a 45,XO genotype has Turner syndrome, whereas an individual with 47,XXY has Klinefelter syndrome. Individuals with Turner syndrome are female, but the loss of the second X chromosome affects several aspects of development both before and after birth. Common features of Turner syndrome include short stature, webbed neck, lymphedema in the hands and feet, skeletal abnormalities, and congenital heart defects. In addition, they have nonfunctioning ovaries due to ovarian tissue degeneration before birth and are infertile. Individuals with Klinefelter syndrome are male, but their sexual development is impaired. They typically have small testes that are not able to produce sufficient amounts of testosterone, resulting in delayed or incomplete puberty, gynecomastia, undescended testes, micropenis, and infertility. As adults, they tend to be taller than their peers. Neither Turner syndrome nor Klinefelter syndrome is associated with an increased risk of ALL.

choice_explanations.A: Trisomy 13 is associated with severe midline defects such as holoprosencephaly and cleft lip/palate.
choice_explanations.B: Trisomy 18 is associated with prominent occiput, rocker-bottom feet, and clenched overlapping fingers.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: trisomy 21 is associated with congenital heart disease and increased leukemia risk, including ALL in older children.
choice_explanations.D: 45,X causes Turner syndrome, characterized by short stature and gonadal dysgenesis.
choice_explanations.E: 47,XXY causes Klinefelter syndrome with small firm testes, infertility, and gynecomastia.

A.text: Patau syndrome is trisomy 13 and is summarized with its distinguishing midline findings.

B.text: Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18 and is summarized with its distinguishing phenotype.

C.text: Down syndrome is trisomy 21; First Aid lists cardiac defects and age-related AML/ALL risk.

D.text: Turner syndrome is 45,XO.

E.text: Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY.

fa_summary: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is associated with congenital heart defects and increased leukemia risk, including ALL in older children. The supplied explanation explicitly confirms answer C.

stem: A 38-year-old man with autosomal recessive albinism marries a 34-year-old woman who also has autosomal recessive albinism. Genetic testing shows that his condition is caused by mutations in TYR on chromosome 11, whereas hers is caused by mutations in OCA2 on chromosome 15. What is the probability that their first child will have albinism?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The key is that the parents have albinism due to two independent genes, TYR and OCA2. This situation, when a similar phenotype is caused by mutations in two or more different genes or loci, is referred to as locus heterogeneity.

Since each parent is homozygous for their respective disease, all of the offspring will be heterozygous carriers of both mutations, but none (0%) will be affected because homozygosity for the disease-causing mutation would be required to produce a recessive disease. In other words, each parent is homozygous for their respective disease and there is no possibility that an offspring will be homozygous at the disease locus (the other parent has two good copies of the other gene). None of the children will be affected by albinism.

ReKaps: If two different autosomal recessive loci are causing the phenotype of a disease in the parents, the children will be heterozygous at both loci and hence normal.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: the parents’ variants affect different genes, so the child receives a normal allele at each locus and is not affected.
choice_explanations.B: A 25% risk would apply if both parents carried pathogenic variants in the same autosomal-recessive gene.
choice_explanations.C: A 50% risk does not follow from the two distinct loci described.
choice_explanations.D: A 75% affected risk is not supported by the genotype pattern.
choice_explanations.E: A 100% risk would require both parents to transmit disease-causing alleles at the same relevant locus.

A.text: Locus heterogeneity means mutations at different loci can cause the same disease; albinism is an example.

B.text: The same phenotype can result from different loci; recessive risk is not 25% when parental defects are in different genes.

C.text: Locus heterogeneity explains why two affected parents with different causal genes can have unaffected children.

D.text: First Aid 2026未找到可直接支持该选项的对应知识点；不显示页码。

E.text: First Aid 2026未找到可直接支持该选项的对应知识点；不显示页码。

fa_summary: The parents’ similar phenotype is caused by pathogenic variants in different genes (locus heterogeneity). Each parent is homozygous for a defect at a different locus; their child receives a functioning allele at TYR from the mother and at OCA2 from the father. The child may be a carrier at both loci but is not expected to be affected, so the risk is 0%.

stem: A 23-year-old pregnant woman has had an uncomplicated pregnancy. She is offered cystic fibrosis carrier screening because the frequency of the mutant allele in her population is 1 in 10. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what is the likelihood that she is a carrier?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disease caused by a mutation in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene located on chromosome 7. The gene encodes a chloride channel which, if defective, leads to secretion of thick mucus and high sodium/chloride levels in sweat and mucus. Fifteen percent of these patients present with meconium ileus at birth, and many also have recurrent pulmonary infections, infertility, pancreatitis, and malabsorption. CF is the most common lethal inherited disease in Caucasian people.

The equations of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) can be used to find the estimated incidence of cystic fibrosis in this population. The allele (gene) frequencies at that locus can be expressed as p + q = 1. The genotypic frequencies can be expressed as p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Here, p is the frequency of the normal A allele and q is the frequency of the recessive a allele. The frequency of individuals with genotype AA is p², with genotype Aa is 2pq, and with genotype aa is q².

In the present problem, the frequency of the cystic fibrosis allele is 1/10. This number is equal to q. The frequency of the normal allele, p, is 9/10, since 1 − q = p. Thus, the frequency of those who are affected is q² and equals 0.01 (choice A).

To determine the likelihood that our patient is a carrier, we must first exclude the chance that she is affected, since we know that she has no medical problems and it would be unusual for a patient to be asymptomatic at age 23 with cystic fibrosis. The Hardy-Weinberg equation is p² + 2pq + q² = 1; in this case, (0.9)² + 2(0.9)(0.1) + (0.1)² = 1. We can calculate the likelihood that she is a carrier (2pq) as 2(0.9)(0.1) = 0.18, which is the correct answer.

The frequency of the diseased allele q, 0.10, is choice B. The frequency of the homozygous normal genotype p², 0.81, is choice D. The frequency of unaffected individuals (p² + 2pq), 0.99, is choice E.

choice_explanations.A: 0.01 is q², the expected frequency of affected homozygotes, not carriers.
choice_explanations.B: 0.10 is the mutant-allele frequency q, not the heterozygous genotype frequency.
choice_explanations.D: 0.81 is p², the expected frequency of homozygous individuals with the common allele.
choice_explanations.E: 0.99 is not a Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequency for the stated q = 0.1.

A.text: Hardy-Weinberg gives q² for homozygosity for the recessive allele; with q = 0.1, q² = 0.01.

B.text: q is the recessive-allele frequency (0.10); carrier frequency is 2pq.

C.text: Carrier frequency for an autosomal-recessive disease is 2pq; here it equals 0.18.

D.text: p² is homozygosity for the common allele; here p² = 0.81.

E.text: Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies are p², 2pq, and q² and must sum to 1; 0.99 is not one of them here.

fa_summary: The mutant-allele frequency is q = 0.10, so p = 0.90. Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the heterozygous carrier frequency is 2pq = 2(0.90)(0.10) = 0.18. The correct choice is C.

stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he has not developed normal male secondary sexual characteristics. He is taller than average and has small testes, a small penis, and gynecomastia. He has repeated two school grades and continues to struggle academically. Which mechanism most likely caused his condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The boy probably has Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), which has the typical presentation described in the question. Klinefelter syndrome is the most common congenital abnormality causing primary hypogonadism and occurs in approximately 1 in 1,000 live births. The diagnosis is commonly made during adolescence or adulthood in males who have small testes with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and gynecomastia. The condition arises as a result of failure of separation (nondisjunction) of the sex chromosomes during meiotic division and can be related to either paternal nondisjunction (slightly more common) or maternal nondisjunction. Two common symptoms leading to diagnosis include infertility and gynecomastia. Other symptoms include fatigue, erectile dysfunction, language impairment, academic difficulty, subnormal libido, osteoporosis, and behavioral problems.

Examples of nondisjunction of autosomes (choice B) include trisomies such as most cases of Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18), and Patau syndrome (trisomy 13).

There are two types of translocations: non-Robertsonian (choice D) and Robertsonian (choice E). Non-Robertsonian (reciprocal) translocations result when two nonhomologous chromosomes exchange genetic material. Robertsonian translocations are a special type of translocation that involves exchange of genetic material from the long arms of one acrocentric chromosome to the long arms of another acrocentric chromosome, with fusion of the centromeres. Four percent of cases of Down syndrome are caused by this mechanism.

ReKaps: Klinefelter syndrome is the most common congenital abnormality causing primary hypogonadism. The most common genotype is 47,XXY, resulting from nondisjunction of sex chromosomes of either parent's germ cells during meiotic division.

choice_explanations.A: A deletion is loss of a chromosome segment and does not explain the classic 47,XXY phenotype.
choice_explanations.B: Autosomal nondisjunction produces an autosomal aneuploidy rather than an extra X chromosome.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: sex-chromosome nondisjunction can produce 47,XXY Klinefelter syndrome.
choice_explanations.D: A non-Robertsonian translocation exchanges material between nonhomologous chromosomes; it does not produce XXY.
choice_explanations.E: A Robertsonian translocation involves fusion of acrocentric chromosome long arms and is not the cause of Klinefelter syndrome.

stem: A 14-year-old boy has painful yellow nodules over his calves and knees, total cholesterol 690 mg/dL, LDL 593 mg/dL, and a father who died of myocardial infarction at age 40. Which cellular process is most likely impaired?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The patient has the hallmarks of familial hypercholesterolemia, including xanthomas on his knees, described as nodules, and a very high serum cholesterol level. Familial hypercholesterolemia is due to a mutation in the LDL receptor, a membrane protein on the cell surface that allows cholesterol uptake. Normally, binding of cholesterol molecules to the LDL receptor is followed by receptor-mediated endocytosis and internalization of the receptor–cholesterol complexes. Inside the cell, these complexes are sent to the lysosome, where the acidic environment releases cholesterol from the receptors, making free cholesterol available to the cell. In this disease, mutation of the LDL-receptor gene results in loss of functional receptors on the cell surface. The inability of cells to absorb cholesterol results in a dramatic accumulation of cholesterol in the blood, where it is deposited in certain areas of the body, most commonly on the knees as xanthomas. Cholesterol may also deposit in arteries, leading to atherosclerosis and premature cardiovascular disease, as seen in this patient's father. The typical laboratory pattern is elevated total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol, with normal HDL and triglyceride levels.

HMG-CoA reductase (choice A) converts HMG-CoA to mevalonic acid, a key step in cholesterol biosynthesis. Loss of HMG-CoA reductase activity would lower cholesterol levels, the opposite of what is seen here. Statins lower serum cholesterol by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase.

Lysosome-mediated proteolysis (choice B) is not affected in familial hypercholesterolemia. Loss of lysosomal function causes lysosomal storage diseases, including Tay-Sachs and Gaucher disease, characterized by accumulation of cellular components that would normally be degraded by lysosomes.

N-linked glycosylation (choice C) is a post-translational protein modification performed by enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum and can help determine a protein's destination. I-cell disease is caused by deficiency of GlcNAc phosphotransferase, which phosphorylates mannose residues to mannose-6-phosphate on N-linked glycoproteins such as lysosomal enzymes. These modifications are needed to send enzymes to lysosomes; affected individuals lack lysosomal function and have symptoms resembling other lysosomal storage diseases.

Loss of proteasome activity (choice D) would cause accumulation of proteins marked for degradation. In familial hypercholesterolemia, the LDL receptor is not folded properly and is marked for degradation in the proteasome. Therefore, loss of proteasome activity would cause accumulation of misfolded LDL-receptor protein, which is not seen in familial hypercholesterolemia.

choice_explanations.A: HMG-CoA reductase synthesizes cholesterol; the classic familial disorder is impaired LDL clearance, not excess enzyme activity.
choice_explanations.B: Lysosomal degradation occurs after LDL-receptor internalization and is not the primary defect.
choice_explanations.C: N-linked glycosylation is not the characteristic process disrupted in familial hypercholesterolemia.
choice_explanations.D: Proteasomes degrade cytosolic proteins and do not mediate LDL uptake.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Defective LDL-receptor-mediated endocytosis reduces cellular LDL clearance.

stem: A 7-year-old boy has a week of coryza followed by severe paroxysmal coughing with posttussive vomiting. Nasopharyngeal culture grows a gram-negative aerobic coccobacillus. Which cellular effect is caused by its toxin?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has the classic clinical signs of a Bordetella pertussis infection, commonly referred to as whooping cough. Early symptoms of this illness are similar to those of the common cold, including mild cough, runny nose, and sneezing. However, approximately two weeks following initial infection, frequent, violent coughing spells develop, which may be followed by fainting or vomiting. Bordetella pertussis releases an AB-type exotoxin known as pertussis toxin (PT). Inside the cell, this toxin is responsible for the ADP-ribosylation of the Gαi subunit of the heterotrimeric G-protein complex. The ADP-ribosylation prevents Gαi from inhibiting adenylyl cyclase, thus resulting in increased levels of cAMP in the cell.

PI3 kinase (choice A) is an enzyme that is responsible for the phosphorylation and conversion of the phosphatidylinositol PIP2 to PIP3. Through activation of the downstream components AKT and mTOR, this enzyme is a key modulator of cellular proliferation and survival. PI3 kinase is not a target of the pertussis toxin.

A decrease in the activity of adenylyl cyclase (choice B) would occur as a result of the activation of the Gαi subunit. Active Gαi normally functions to inhibit adenylyl cyclase activity, preventing the production of cAMP. Since pertussis toxin inhibits Gαi activity, there would not be a decrease in cAMP, but rather an increase in cAMP.

Decreased activity of protein kinase A (PKA) (choice C) would not be expected in this patient because PKA is activated by cAMP, so a decrease in this enzyme's activity would be associated with inhibition of adenylyl cyclase. Since pertussis toxin prevents the inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, resulting in an increase in cAMP, higher activity of PKA would be expected.

An increase in IP₃ levels (choice E) is associated with the activity of the Gαq-subunit-associated heterotrimeric G-protein complex. When active, the Gαq subunit activates phospholipase C. Phospholipase C then cleaves phosphatidylinositol PIP2 to form IP₃ and diacylglycerol (DAG), two second messengers that are responsible for release of calcium from intracellular stores and activating protein kinase C (PKC) as well as other intracellular kinases, respectively. This pathway is not affected by pertussis toxin.

ReKaps: Bordetella pertussis infection, commonly referred to as whooping cough, may be mistaken for the common cold early in the infection. Eventually, it develops into frequent, violent coughing spells, which may be followed by fainting or vomiting. The responsible agent is an exotoxin called pertussis toxin, which ADP-ribosylates the Gαi subunit of the heterotrimeric G-protein complex, resulting in an increase in cAMP levels inside the cell.

choice_explanations.A: PI3-kinase activation is not the characteristic pertussis-toxin effect.
choice_explanations.B: Pertussis toxin disables inhibitory Gi, so adenylyl cyclase activity rises rather than falls.
choice_explanations.C: Increased cAMP activates PKA signaling rather than decreasing PKA activity.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Loss of Gi inhibition increases cAMP.
choice_explanations.E: IP₃ is generated through phospholipase C signaling, not the pertussis-toxin mechanism.

stem: A 56-year-old woman has painful oral erosions, a positive Nikolsky sign, and acantholysis on biopsy. Which antigen is targeted by the pathogenic antibodies?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. These symptoms are typical of pemphigus vulgaris, an autoimmune disease in which antibodies attack desmoglein 3. Desmoglein is the transmembrane cadherin that forms the intercellular linkages at desmosomes. Desmosomes provide the strongest attachments between neighboring epithelial cells, and interference with desmosome structure is the cause of this type of blistering. Lesions exhibit a positive Nikolsky sign (pressure to the skin separates epidermal layers). Source ReKaps: lesions begin in the oral mucosa; acantholysis with intradermal blisters is seen; IgG antibodies are directed against desmoglein, which forms the specialized cell-cell adhesion.

Interfering with collagen (choice A), such as the type IV collagen present in basement membranes, will not specifically cause the inability of epithelial cells to interact with their neighboring cells. Antibodies against collagen type IV are seen with Goodpasture syndrome, which would affect the glomeruli and lungs but not the skin. Gap junctions (choice C) allow communication between cells but do not contribute to desmosomes or provide substantial binding between epithelial cells. Keratinocytes are attached to the basement membrane via hemidesmosomes (choice D), and disruption by antibodies is seen with bullous pemphigoid. The specific antigens are called BPAg1 and BPAg2. Antibodies against transglutaminase (choice E) are associated with dermatitis herpetiformis and celiac disease. In celiac disease, antibodies cross-react with epidermal transglutaminase and deposit within the dermal papillae to cause the lesions of dermatitis herpetiformis.

choice_explanations.A: Basement-membrane collagen antibodies suggest anti-GBM disease or other subepidermal disorders, not pemphigus vulgaris.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Anti-desmoglein antibodies disrupt desmosomes and produce acantholysis.
choice_explanations.C: Gap-junction proteins permit intercellular communication; they are not the pemphigus target.
choice_explanations.D: Hemidesmosomes anchor basal cells to basement membrane and are targeted in bullous pemphigoid.
choice_explanations.E: Anti-transglutaminase antibodies are associated with celiac disease.

D.text: Hemidesmosomes anchor basal keratinocytes to basement membrane; bullous pemphigoid is on p. 489.

E.text: Anti-tissue-transglutaminase antibodies are associated with celiac disease.

fa_summary: Pemphigus vulgaris is a type II hypersensitivity against desmoglein in desmosomes, causing acantholysis and a positive Nikolsky sign.

stem: A 63-year-old man has pruritic, tense blisters on the lower abdomen and thighs, with normal oral mucosa and a negative Nikolsky sign. Biopsy shows separation of epidermis from basal lamina; antibodies target dystonin. Which structure is disrupted?
explanation: The correct answer is D. Hemidesmosomes (see figure) are a type of membrane junction found on the basal surface of epithelial cells that connects the cells to the underlying basal lamina. They consist of the proteins dystonin and plectin, which form a plaque on the intracellular side of the plasma membrane. This plaque binds to the keratin filaments inside the cell and connects these cytoskeletal components to the extracellular matrix of the basal lamina via integrin molecules. In individuals with the autoimmune disease bullous pemphigoid, such as this patient, antibodies are made that bind to dystonin (bullous pemphigoid antigen) and disrupt the hemidesmosome structure. As a result, the epithelial sheet of skin separates from the basal lamina, allowing for accumulation of fluid in this space and resulting in the formation of tense subepidermal blisters. Nikolsky sign is negative.

choice_explanations.A: Adherens junctions connect actin cytoskeletons between adjacent cells.
choice_explanations.B: Desmosomes connect neighboring keratinocytes; desmoglein antibodies cause pemphigus vulgaris and acantholysis.
choice_explanations.C: Gap junctions form intercellular communication channels.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Hemidesmosomes anchor basal epithelial cells to the basal lamina.
choice_explanations.E: Tight junctions seal adjacent epithelial cells and are not the anchoring structure involved.

stem: A 25-year-old man has recurrent pulmonary infections, bronchiectasis, situs inversus, and infertility with markedly impaired sperm motility. Which cellular process is affected?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The presentation described is typical of Kartagener syndrome, a subset of primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by congenital impairment of mucociliary clearance due to defective cilia. Bronchiectasis and chronic sinusitis are features; when a patient also has situs inversus totalis, it is called Kartagener syndrome. It is a rare autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations of the gene encoding the protein dynein. Dynein is a motor protein that forms the side arms of microtubule doublets in axonemes, allowing for motility of cilia and flagella. A defect in this protein would affect the cilia of respiratory epithelial cells as well as the flagella of spermatozoa. Consequently, poor sperm motility results in infertility, whereas deficient mucociliary function in the respiratory system leads to defective bacterial clearance and recurrent pulmonary infections. Bronchiectasis is an abnormal and permanent dilation of the bronchi that can be focal or diffuse in nature. Bronchiectasis is a frequent complication of primary ciliary dyskinesia because recurrent bouts of lung infections cause destruction and subsequent dilation of the bronchial walls. Another key feature of Kartagener syndrome is situs inversus, a condition in which the organs of the body lie on the opposite side from usual. In addition to mediating ciliary motility, dynein is also involved in transport of vesicles within the cell.

Chloride transport (choice A) is defective in cystic fibrosis, an inherited autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in the gene coding for a chloride-channel protein, CFTR. Respiratory pathology is frequent and usually severe in cystic fibrosis, consisting of recurrent infections and, consequently, bronchiectasis. Also, 95% of male patients are infertile because of obstruction of the vas deferens and resultant azoospermia. Cystic fibrosis and Kartagener syndrome have clinical similarities but entirely different etiologies. Because CFTR mutations do not affect axoneme structure or ciliary function, this individual must have Kartagener syndrome.

Although defects in cytokine signaling (choice B) can result in immunodeficiency, leading to recurrent infections, they are not associated with situs inversus and they do not directly cause infertility. Therefore, it is not likely that this patient's condition is due to cytokine-signaling defects.

Synthesis of IgA (choice C) is essential in immunologic defense at mucosal barriers, such as in respiratory, gastrointestinal, and urogenital tracts. Defective IgA synthesis occurs in isolated IgA deficiency, a common disorder that renders patients susceptible to sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections, but it is not associated with situs inversus.

The oxidative burst (choice E) refers to the production of reactive oxygen species after rapid activation of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase. NADPH is oxidized, and oxygen is reduced to superoxide anion in the process. Superoxide is then converted into H2O2, which is involved in bacterial killing. A defect in the oxidative burst causes chronic granulomatous disease, characterized by susceptibility to recurrent bacterial infections, but it is not associated with situs inversus.

ReKaps: In Kartagener syndrome, the dynein motor that facilitates ciliary movement is nonfunctional because of an inherited gene mutation. Ciliary dysfunction inhibits respiratory clearance of debris, leading to bronchiectasis. Sperm motility is inhibited because of flagellar dysfunction, although the sperm count is normal. Situs inversus and bronchiectasis are commonly found in individuals with Kartagener syndrome. Intracellular transport of vesicles is also affected in Kartagener syndrome.

choice_explanations.A: Chloride-channel defects cause cystic fibrosis, which does not explain situs inversus with sperm immotility in this pattern.
choice_explanations.B: Cytokine signaling is not the structural defect in primary ciliary dyskinesia.
choice_explanations.C: IgA deficiency can cause recurrent infections but not situs inversus or impaired sperm motility.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Dynein-dependent ciliary and flagellar motility is impaired.
choice_explanations.E: An oxidative-burst defect causes chronic granulomatous disease, not situs inversus and sperm immotility.

stem: A couple is evaluated for infertility; the husband has recurrent sinus and ear infections and severely impaired sperm motility. Which cardiac anomaly may also be present?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The man has Kartagener syndrome, which is characterized by an inherited defect in dynein protein. Cilia and flagella contain 9 peripheral pairs of microtubules and 2 central microtubules. The microtubules convey motility to cilia through the ATPase dynein. Dynein is a cellular motor that travels along microtubules, typically toward the minus end, which is anchored to the basal bodies in the axonemes of cilia or flagella. Ciliary or flagellar movement occurs when the dynein arms attached to an outer microtubule doublet move along the adjacent doublet's microtubules. The coordinated movement of the dynein arms attached to the nine outer microtubule doublets in an axoneme creates normal ciliary or flagellar motion. Patients lacking axoneme structures due to defects in dynein or radial spoke proteins display symptoms associated with loss of ciliary and flagellar function. Sperm motility is reduced or absent, and respiratory and ear infections are common due to lack of respiratory epithelial cilia. The structure of the axoneme of a cilium is shown below.

ReKaps: In Kartagener disease, the dynein motor that facilitates ciliary movement is nonfunctional through an inherited gene mutation. As a result, respiratory clearance of debris is inhibited. Additionally, sperm movement is inhibited due to dysfunction of the dynein motor, while sperm count is unaffected. Situs inversus, which can cause dextrocardia, can be seen in Kartagener disease.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Kartagener syndrome may include situs inversus and dextrocardia.
choice_explanations.B: Ostium primum defects are endocardial-cushion defects, not a consequence of ciliary dyskinesia.
choice_explanations.C: A patent foramen ovale is common and unrelated to dynein dysfunction.
choice_explanations.D: Tetralogy of Fallot is a conotruncal defect unrelated to this ciliary syndrome.
choice_explanations.E: Great-artery transposition is a conotruncal defect, not the expected laterality abnormality.

B.text: Ostium primum defects arise from endocardial-cushion development.

D.text: Tetralogy of Fallot is a conotruncal congenital heart defect.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a family history of gastric adenocarcinoma and infiltrating lobular breast carcinoma. The mutated gene in this patient most likely encodes a component of which structure?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Adherens junctions are protein complexes on the lateral surface of an epithelial cell that allow cell–cell adhesion by linking the actin microfilaments of two adjacent cells. This adhesion is mediated by homotypic interaction between E-cadherin proteins on adjacent cells. Individuals who inherit a mutation in the gene encoding E-cadherin (CDH1) are at high risk of developing gastric adenocarcinoma and infiltrating lobular carcinoma.

Desmosomes (choice B) are protein complexes on the lateral surface of epithelial cells that link the keratin filaments of two adjacent cells. The intercellular linkage is mediated by desmoglein and desmoplakin. Pemphigus foliaceus and pemphigus vulgaris are autoimmune blistering skin diseases that lead to loss of desmosome function.

Gap junctions (choice C) are intercellular channels connecting the cytoplasm of two adjacent cells and allow the passage of ions and small molecules. These channels are composed of protein subunits called connexins. Although mutations in connexin genes are associated with some forms of congenital heart defects, there is no link between these mutations and gastric cancer.

Hemidesmosomes (choice D) are adhesion complexes on the basal surface of epithelial cells that connect the cell to the basal lamina. Bullous pemphigoid is caused by antibodies against a hemidesmosome component, dystonin, inhibiting its function.

Tight junctions (choice E) are areas along the lateral surface of adjacent epithelial cells where the plasma membranes join tightly to form a barrier impermeable to fluid, preventing molecules from passing between the cells. Tight junctions are composed of occludins and claudins. Defects in tight junctions are not specifically associated with gastric adenocarcinoma.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. E-cadherin is a component of adherens junctions and is linked to diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancers.
choice_explanations.B: Desmosomes use desmogleins/desmocollins and provide strong intercellular mechanical adhesion.
choice_explanations.C: Gap junctions use connexins for intercellular communication.
choice_explanations.D: Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to basement membrane.
choice_explanations.E: Tight junctions create paracellular seals.

B.text: Desmosomes link intermediate filaments between neighboring cells.

C.text: Gap junctions are connexon channels.

D.text: Hemidesmosomes link basal epithelial cells to basement membrane.

E.text: Tight junctions seal the paracellular space.

fa_summary: E-cadherin in adherens junctions supports cell–cell adhesion; loss is associated with diffuse gastric and lobular breast carcinoma.

stem: A 2-day-old newborn has severe diarrhea. Duodenal biopsy shows enterocytes with sparse, short, disorganized microvilli; genetic testing identifies a MYO5B mutation. Which cytoskeletal component is most directly involved?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The take-home point in this question is that microvilli contain a core of actin microfilaments and increase the absorptive surface area of epithelial cells. Myosin, including nonmuscle myosin in epithelial cells, is associated with actin microfilaments and thus contributes to the function of microvilli. Microvillus atrophy is the leading cause of secretory diarrhea in the first few weeks of life. Brush-border microvilli are disorganized, short, and scanty. As a result, enterocytes cannot efficiently absorb ions and nutrients, causing a malabsorption syndrome. The diarrhea is primarily a result of active water and electrolyte secretion in the intestinal lumen. Mutations in MYO5B, the gene encoding myosin Vb, are commonly found in individuals with microvillus atrophy.

The centrosome (choice B) is the microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) in animal cells. Its function is to nucleate, anchor, and organize the microtubules in interphase cells as well as the mitotic spindle apparatus during mitosis. Microvilli are composed of actin microfilaments, not microtubules (choice E); myosin does not associate with microtubules.

Although keratin (choice C) is a type of intermediate filament that is abundant in epithelial cells, it does not contribute to microvillus structure or function.

Laminin (choice D) is a component of the basal lamina that underlies epithelial sheets. As a component of the extracellular matrix, it does not function in maintaining microvillus structure or function.

ReKaps: Congenital microvillus atrophy is the leading cause of secretory diarrhea in the first few weeks of life and is associated with mutations in MYO5B. Biopsy of the small intestine in a neonate with congenital microvillus atrophy reveals scanty and disorganized microvilli. Microvilli are composed of actin microfilaments. Abnormal binding of myosin to actin microfilaments contributes to microvillus dysfunction.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Actin microfilaments form the structural core of microvilli and interact with myosin Vb.
choice_explanations.B: The centrosome organizes microtubules and is not the microvillar core.
choice_explanations.C: Keratin is an intermediate filament supporting epithelial structure.
choice_explanations.D: Laminin is an extracellular-matrix basement-membrane protein.
choice_explanations.E: Microtubules support intracellular transport and cilia but do not form the microvillus core.

C.text: Keratin is an intermediate filament that maintains epithelial structure.

D.text: 已核对 First Aid 2026 相关章节，未找到可直接支持该选项的独立知识点。

fa_summary: Microfilaments are actin-based; microvilli increase absorptive surface area and have an actin core.

stem: A 6-month-old boy has failure to thrive, skeletal abnormalities, restricted joints, corneal clouding, gingival hyperplasia, and elevated serum lysosomal hydrolases. Which metabolic step is defective?

options.text: Degradation of dermatan and heparan sulfate

explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient has I-cell disease, also known as mucolipidosis II, which is caused by a defective UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, the enzyme that phosphorylates mannose on enzymes destined for lysosomes. Proteins coded by nuclear DNA are synthesized on cytoplasmic ribosomes, which may be either free or associated with the endoplasmic reticulum to form the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER). Proteins synthesized in the RER are transferred into the Golgi apparatus, where they undergo further modifications that determine whether they remain part of the Golgi apparatus, become part of the plasma membrane, or are shipped to lysosomes or other locations. Proteins not marked for transport to a specific intracellular site follow the default pathway and are exported into the extracellular compartment. The signal for transport of acid hydrolases and other enzymes to lysosomes is phosphorylation of a terminal mannose moiety on an N-linked oligosaccharide to form mannose 6-phosphate.

In I-cell disease, this terminal mannose moiety is not phosphorylated, and the acid hydrolases follow the default pathway and are secreted. Like many lysosomal storage diseases, the lack of lysosomal enzymes causes structural defects in the cells. One characteristic of I-cell disease is abnormal vacuolization and inclusion bodies in the cytoplasm. By 6 months of age, there is failure to thrive and other developmental delays, as well as abnormal skeletal development, coarse facial features, and restricted joint movement.

Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs disease; choice A) is one example of a condition in which ganglioside accumulation occurs.

Deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase results in lysosomal accumulation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate (choice B) in several conditions, such as mucopolysaccharidosis I, Hurler disease, and Hurler-Scheie syndrome.

There are several diseases in which glycogen degradation (choice C) is defective. These are collectively termed glycogen storage diseases because they result in abnormal cellular accumulation of glycogen. In Pompe disease, or type II glycogen storage disease, a lysosomal glucosidase is deficient, resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation.

Deficiency of sphingomyelinase (choice D), an enzyme involved in degradation of sphingomyelin, results in Niemann-Pick disease.

Phosphorylation of tyrosine moieties (choice F) is unrelated to lysosomes or lysosomal enzymes; however, decreased ability to phosphorylate tyrosine moieties might be associated with diabetes or dwarfism.

ReKaps: I-cell disease results from defective phosphotransferase activity in the Golgi apparatus. Tay-Sachs disease results from deficient hexosaminidase A activity in the lysosome. Niemann-Pick disease results from deficient sphingomyelinase activity in the lysosome. Hurler disease results from deficient iduronidase activity in the lysosome.

choice_explanations.B: Dermatan/heparan sulfate accumulation occurs in mucopolysaccharidoses.
choice_explanations.C: Glycogen accumulation occurs in glycogen-storage disorders such as Pompe disease.
choice_explanations.D: Sphingomyelin accumulation occurs in Niemann-Pick disease.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Failure to phosphorylate mannose prevents lysosomal targeting of hydrolases.

stem: A neonate born to a mother with gestational diabetes is cyanotic and responds minimally to 100% oxygen. Which congenital lesion is most likely responsible for the fatal course?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Maternal diabetes is associated with a number of neonatal complications and congenital anomalies. Perhaps one of the most well-known complications is neonatal macrosomia (large for gestational age), which may produce a number of issues during delivery. Macrosomia, as seen in this patient, results from hyperinsulinemia (insulin has anabolic functions) secondary to excessive glucose in the baby's circulation. Another complication is respiratory distress syndrome, which is thought to occur as a result of insulin's inhibition of surfactant production. Although this is entirely possible in this patient, it is not one of the answer choices.

An important congenital anomaly associated with maternal diabetes is transposition of the great arteries (TGA). In TGA, the aorta takes off from the anterior part of the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk takes off from the posterior part of the left ventricle. This produces a complete separation of the systemic and pulmonary circulations. A shunt of some sort (patent ductus arteriosus, atrial septal defect, or ventricular septal defect) is required for viability, since without such a defect, blood cannot be oxygenated after returning from the systemic circulation. The cyanosis results because of a right-to-left shunt in which venous blood directly mixes with freshly oxygenated blood. This shunt physiology results in a lack of improvement in oxygenation even after providing 100% oxygen. Surgical correction is required. Without surgical correction, most affected infants die within the first months of life. The chest x-ray may appear normal in newborns with TGA if there is no associated ventricular septal defect, but may show the classic "egg on a string" appearance (cardiomegaly with narrowed superior mediastinum) in about one-third of cases. Transposition of the great arteries is the most common cyanotic congenital heart defect presenting in the neonatal period, particularly in diabetic mothers, but truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia/stenosis, tetralogy of Fallot, and total anomalous venous return (the 5 T's) are also causes of cyanotic congenital heart disease.

Atrioventricular septal defect (choice A), also called AV canal defect or endocardial cushion defect, involves maldevelopment of the septum at both the atrial and ventricular levels as well as the tricuspid and mitral valves. It typically does not cause significant problems until 6 to 8 weeks of age, when congestive heart failure can develop. This is commonly seen in Down syndrome. Reparative surgery is typically done at 4 to 6 months of age.

Coarctation of the aorta (choice B) involves stenosis of a segment of the aorta and occurs in two patterns, adult and infantile. In the infantile type, the stenosis is proximal to the insertion of the ductus arteriosus (preductal); this pattern is associated with Turner syndrome. These patients may present with heart failure (if severe) and weak distal pulses but are unlikely to present with cyanosis, as in this patient. In the adult type, the stenosis is distal to the ductus arteriosus (postductal), and patients develop collateral circulation of the intercostal arteries. Notching of the ribs can be seen on chest radiographs.

Eisenmenger syndrome (choice C) results when an initially noncyanotic left-to-right shunt (such as an atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, or patent ductus arteriosus) is allowed to persist. The overload of fluid into the pulmonary circulation results in pulmonary hypertension, which gradually over time produces a right-to-left shunt. This may then lead to cyanosis since freshly oxygenated blood is mixing with deoxygenated blood prior to entry into the systemic circulation. This commonly presents months or years later in life.

Tetralogy of Fallot (choice D) consists of a ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, pulmonic stenosis, and right ventricular hypertrophy. It causes cyanosis and is usually diagnosed in infancy. Tetralogy of Fallot is more commonly associated with DiGeorge syndrome and is not classic for an infant of a diabetic mother.

choice_explanations.A: An AV septal defect causes a left-to-right shunt and is not the classic cyanotic lesion linked to maternal diabetes.
choice_explanations.B: Coarctation causes upper–lower extremity pressure/pulse differences rather than this parallel-circulation physiology.
choice_explanations.C: Eisenmenger syndrome is acquired pulmonary vascular disease after a longstanding shunt.
choice_explanations.D: Tetralogy can cause cyanosis, but TGA is the congenital lesion specifically associated with maternal diabetes here.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. TGA creates parallel systemic and pulmonary circuits and is associated with maternal diabetes.

B.text: Coarctation is an aortic narrowing with upper–lower pulse/pressure differences.

stem: An 80-year-old woman becomes bedridden after hip-fracture repair. On day 5 she develops sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypotension, hypoxemia, a parasternal heave, and loud P2, then dies. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Pulmonary emboli from a right common femoral vein thrombus

explanation:
The correct answer is A. Ninety percent of deep vein thrombi are formed in the lower extremities. These thrombi may dislodge and travel to distant sites, most importantly to the lungs, forming pulmonary emboli. The most frequent cause of pulmonary thromboembolism is deep venous thrombosis of the legs. Pulmonary embolism is estimated to be responsible for 15% of all cases of sudden death. In this case, the patient's prolonged bed rest predisposed her to deep venous thrombosis. Other factors that predispose to clot formation include pregnancy, cancer, or other hypercoagulable states. Some emboli are clinically silent; others affect only those with preexisting cardiac compromise. However, if the clot is large enough, it will cause nearly instantaneous death.

A postoperative patient is at risk of a myocardial infarction (choice B); however, in this case this is not the most likely scenario. The physical examination and the character of the pain more strongly support pulmonary embolism. A pulmonary embolus can cause heart failure, but this is not the primary etiologic event.

Fat emboli (choice C) can occur after a fracture of long bones that releases material from the bone marrow; this is also much less likely than a thromboembolus. The fat particles cause a systemic inflammatory response.

Veins in the upper limbs (choice D) rarely develop thrombosis. This occurs only in disorders leading to a marked thrombotic propensity, such as carcinoma-associated migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome), antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, protein C deficiency, and inherited mutations of the factor V gene.

An embolus to the pulmonary artery is the typical sequela of deep venous thrombosis, rather than clot formation in the pulmonary vein (choice E).

ReKaps: Suspect pulmonary embolus arising from a femoral vein thrombosis in a bedridden patient who develops sudden-onset chest pain and dyspnea.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. A proximal leg DVT can embolize to the pulmonary arteries and cause obstructive shock.
choice_explanations.B: MI may cause shock, but the sudden pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, and acute right-sided pressure findings support PE.
choice_explanations.C: Fat embolism may follow long-bone trauma, but this delayed event after immobility with signs of acute pulmonary vascular obstruction favors thromboembolism.
choice_explanations.D: Upper-extremity thrombi are less likely and do not fit the prolonged lower-limb immobility risk.
choice_explanations.E: Pulmonary-vein thrombi do not embolize into the pulmonary arterial circulation as described.

A.text: Deep venous thrombosis is associated with stasis and can embolize.

B.text: Myocardial infarction causes myocardial ischemic necrosis.

C.text: Fat embolism may follow trauma/fracture; this case instead favors thrombotic PE.

D.text: DVT can occur in veins, but the source risk is lower-extremity stasis.

fa_summary: Virchow triad and immobility predispose to DVT; proximal lower-extremity thrombi may cause massive pulmonary embolism.

stem: A healthy man has resting cardiac output of 5 L/min and heart rate of 50/min. What is his stroke volume?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Cardiac output (CO) is equal to the volume of blood ejected from the heart during each systole (i.e., the stroke volume; SV) multiplied by the number of times the heart beats each minute (heart rate; HR). In other words, CO = SV × HR. Therefore, SV = CO/HR, and since CO = 5,000 mL/min and HR = 50/min, SV = 5,000/50 = 100 mL.

ReKaps: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. Stroke volume is determined by preload, afterload, and contractility of the heart. Stroke volume is a key measure of cardiac function. Heart rate is mediated by parasympathetic and sympathetic neural input to cardiac pacemakers. Measurement of stroke volume is one of the initial steps in evaluating cardiac function.

choice_explanations.A: Would imply cardiac output of only 0.5 L/min at this heart rate.
choice_explanations.B: Would imply cardiac output of 2.5 L/min.
choice_explanations.C: Would imply cardiac output of 3.75 L/min.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: 5,000/50 = 100 mL/beat.
choice_explanations.E: Would imply cardiac output of 6.25 L/min.

A.text: Cardiac-output equations relate SV, HR, and CO.

B.text: Stroke volume is calculated from cardiac output and heart rate.

C.text: Stroke volume is calculated from cardiac output and heart rate.

D.text: CO = SV × HR; SV = 5,000/50 = 100 mL/beat.

E.text: Stroke volume is calculated from cardiac output and heart rate.

fa_summary: Stroke volume = cardiac output ÷ heart rate; cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate.

stem: A male newborn has a holosystolic murmur and an ostium primum atrial septal defect with adjacent atrioventricular-valve defects. Which condition is most strongly associated?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient presents with an atrioventricular septal defect, also called an endocardial cushion defect, which is most commonly associated with Down syndrome. About 50% of infants with Down syndrome have heart defects. The endocardial cushions, also known as atrioventricular cushions, are cells within the primordial heart responsible for septation and development of the atrioventricular canals. In Down syndrome, the superior and inferior cushions often fail to fuse, resulting in tricuspid and mitral valvular abnormalities, along with an ostium primum atrial septal defect (inferior atrial septal defect). The murmur is caused by turbulent flow through the defects during systole. In contrast, most atrial septal defects not associated with Down syndrome are ostium secundum defects, located more superiorly. Primum and secundum atrial septal defects are shown below.

ReKaps: About 50% of infants with Down syndrome have heart defects.

choice_explanations.A: 22q11 deletion is associated with conotruncal defects, not the classic primum/AV-cushion pattern.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Down syndrome is associated with endocardial-cushion defects and AV septal defects.
choice_explanations.C: Maternal diabetes is associated with several defects including TGA, not specifically primum ASD.
choice_explanations.D: Marfan syndrome affects connective tissue and the aortic root/valves, not endocardial cushions.
choice_explanations.E: Turner syndrome is associated with coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve.

A.text: 22q11 deletion is associated with selected congenital cardiac outflow defects.

B.text: Endocardial-cushion defects include ostium primum ASD and are associated with Down syndrome.

C.text: Maternal diabetes is associated with congenital anomalies such as TGA.
