choice_explanations.C: Duct ectasia causes dilated ducts with inflammation and fibrosis; it can mimic cancer clinically but does not increase malignancy risk.
choice_explanations.D: Fibroadenoma is a benign proliferation of fibrous and glandular tissue without atypia; it is not the proliferative lesion identified as increasing risk here.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Sclerosing adenosis with ductal hyperplasia is a proliferative fibrocystic lesion associated with increased risk of subsequent invasive carcinoma.

A.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss apocrine metaplasia as a benign breast-biopsy finding.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss blue-domed breast cysts.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss mammary duct ectasia or its benign biopsy pattern.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss fibroadenoma histology in the breast-cancer section.

E.text: First Aid 2026 p. 668 discusses breast carcinoma and risk context, but does not directly identify sclerosing adenosis with ductal hyperplasia or its risk. No direct FA match for this option.

stem: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 0, at 10 weeks’ gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal examination. Her pregnancy has been uneventful, but she has a history of 3 clinical spontaneous abortions. Serum progesterone is substantially below the usual range for this stage of pregnancy. Deficiency of which of the following most likely is responsible for the low progesterone production?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. One of the most common causes of first trimester spontaneous abortion is human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) deficiency. The corpus luteum secretes estrogens, progesterone, and relaxin. hCG, secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast lining the placental villi, maintains the corpus luteum during the first trimester of pregnancy. Deficiency of hCG would allow progesterone to drop, leading potentially to increased risk of miscarriage.

Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin; choice A) does not play a significant role during pregnancy. FSH (choice B) acts on granulosa cells to promote the conversion of androstenedione to estradiol. LH (choice D) acts on theca cells to promote androstenedione secretion. Progesterone (choice E) is important for maintaining the pregnancy; however, it does not act to maintain the corpus luteum.

choice_explanations.A: ADH regulates water balance and does not maintain the corpus luteum or drive progesterone production in early pregnancy.
choice_explanations.B: FSH stimulates granulosa-cell development and estrogen production; it is not the signal that rescues the corpus luteum in the first trimester.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Syncytiotrophoblast-derived hCG maintains the corpus luteum, preserving early-pregnancy progesterone secretion.
choice_explanations.D: LH supports theca-cell steroid production and is not the placental luteotropic signal responsible for corpus-luteum maintenance in early pregnancy.
choice_explanations.E: Progesterone is the deficient product, not the upstream hormone whose deficiency explains reduced luteal progesterone output.

A.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly connect ADH with corpus-luteum function or early-pregnancy progesterone.

B.text: FSH supports follicular/granulosa-cell function; it is distinct from hCG's first-trimester rescue of the corpus luteum.

C.text: hCG is secreted by syncytiotrophoblast and maintains the corpus luteum, increasing progesterone during the first trimester.

D.text: LH participates in the ovarian cycle and acts on theca cells; First Aid distinguishes this from hCG maintenance of the corpus luteum in early pregnancy.

E.text: Progesterone is mainly secreted by the corpus luteum during the first 10 weeks and later by the placenta; it is the product, not the deficient regulatory hormone.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is being evaluated for infertility. She has had four spontaneous abortions and chronic pelvic pain. Ultrasound shows a smoothly marginated, rounded 5-cm submucosal mass in the uterine fundus and several smaller, well-circumscribed subserosal and submucosal masses measuring 2–4 cm. Hysterosalpingography shows patent fallopian tubes but an irregular endometrial cavity. Which finding is most likely on microscopic examination of the uterine masses?

options.text: Heterogeneous cells with components of endoderm and ectoderm
Increased number of columnar cells with preservation of the basement membrane
Moderately differentiated cells with a striated pattern
Poorly differentiated cells with abundant atypical mitoses

explanation:
The correct answer is E. The lesions are the very common leiomyomas (fibroids) of the uterus, which are well-circumscribed, rubbery, white-tan masses. Leiomyomas, if numerous or large, may cause chronic pelvic pain and infertility or pregnancy complications (if they intrude on the uterine cavity). Histologically, they are characterized by whorls of spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells. There is continued debate over whether there is malignant potential associated with fibroids or whether leiomyosarcomas arise de novo.

Heterogeneous cells with components of endoderm and ectoderm (choice A) describes a teratoma, which is unlikely to be multiple or intrauterine. They tend to arise in the ovary. Increased number of columnar cells with preservation of the basement membrane (choice B) describes endometrial hyperplasia, which would not present with subserosal masses. Moderately differentiated cells with a striated pattern (choice C) describes rhabdomyomas, which are benign tumors of skeletal muscle and would not arise in the uterus. Poorly differentiated cells with abundant atypical mitoses (choice D) describes a malignant neoplasm, which would not be so well defined in its borders.

choice_explanations.A: Heterogeneous derivatives of endoderm and ectoderm suggest a teratoma, which is generally ovarian rather than a set of uterine masses.
choice_explanations.B: Increased endometrial glands with preserved basement membrane describes endometrial hyperplasia, not smooth-muscle uterine masses.
choice_explanations.C: A striated pattern suggests skeletal-muscle differentiation such as rhabdomyosarcoma, not a benign myometrial tumor.
choice_explanations.D: Poor differentiation and abundant atypical mitoses suggest malignancy; these well-circumscribed masses are characteristic of benign leiomyomas.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Leiomyomas show whorled bundles of well-differentiated smooth-muscle cells.

A.text: Ovarian mature cystic teratomas contain tissues derived from all three germ layers; this is a distinct ovarian germ-cell tumor, not a uterine mass.

B.text: Endometrial hyperplasia is abnormal endometrial-gland proliferation, distinct from a myometrial smooth-muscle tumor.

C.text: Sarcoma botryoides is an embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma variant; it presents as a vaginal grapelike mass in young children, not as uterine fibroids.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe leiomyosarcoma histology or atypical mitoses for this differential.

E.text: Leiomyomas are benign myometrial tumors, commonly multiple and submucosal/intramural/subserosal; histology shows whorled smooth-muscle bundles.

stem: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician because of sexual dysfunction for the last 7 years. He has sexual desire and can achieve an erection but cannot maintain it long enough to ejaculate. He recently began a sexual relationship with a new girlfriend; before this relationship, he had not been sexually active for about 7 years. He has non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and hypertension and takes an oral hypoglycemic agent and a calcium-channel blocker. His 60-year-old girlfriend is sexually healthy but has mild postmenopausal vaginal dryness. They have attempted intercourse four times in the past week without success. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's disorder?

options.text: Increased blood flow into the corpora cavernosa
Increased guanylate cyclase activity in penile smooth muscle

explanation:
The correct answer is A. Erectile dysfunction (ED) is diagnosed in men who cannot achieve or maintain an erection. It is estimated that 70% of men age 70 and above experience some degree of ED. Because erection is complex and involves psychologic and physiologic systems, the potential causes are numerous. This patient is experiencing ED due to a physiologic disorder. Sexually related psychic and/or physical stimuli are integrated in the limbic system and stimulate motor impulses in the spinal cord. The parasympathetic nervous system is responsible for impulses that enter the sacral region of the spinal cord before entering the penis. These impulses cause the vasodilation of the arterioles and corpora cavernosa. Nitric oxide is released from nonadrenergic, noncholinergic nerves and endothelial cells and stimulates guanylate cyclase in penile smooth muscle. This stimulation results in increased levels of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) and ultimately in smooth muscle relaxation, which allows engorgement of the blood vessels. Once the vessels are engorged, the penis is erect and the blood-filled arterioles and cavernosa occlude the veins. This occlusion restricts blood flow, trapping blood in the erectile tissue and reducing blood outflow. A decrease in nitric oxide release would prevent smooth muscle relaxation, thus preventing engorgement.

Increased blood flow to the cavernosum is required for erection and would not result in ED. When penile smooth muscle relaxes, the penile arteries dilate, allowing blood to flow into the corpora cavernosum. The cavernosum becomes engorged with blood, expanding and lengthening the penis. The expanding tissue compresses the veins that normally empty the blood from the penis, thereby maintaining the blood in the penile tissue. Therefore, choice B is incorrect. Increased guanylate cyclase in penile smooth muscle (choice C) would not cause ED, but would increase smooth muscle relaxation to facilitate blood flow into the penis. Increased parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) action (choice D) is incorrect because parasympathetic activity is responsible for vasodilation of vessels in the penis. This action is essential for increased penile blood flow. Penile smooth muscle relaxation (choice E) is required for erection and would not result in ED. Smooth muscle of the cavernosa must relax to facilitate penile engorgement. Once the penile arterioles have engorged, the swelling causes the occlusion of veins that prevents blood outflow. This blood trapping is required to maintain rigidity.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Less nitric oxide means less cGMP-mediated cavernosal smooth-muscle relaxation and reduced arterial engorgement.
choice_explanations.B: Increased cavernosal blood flow supports erection; it does not explain erectile failure.
choice_explanations.C: Increased guanylate-cyclase activity raises cGMP and promotes smooth-muscle relaxation, favoring erection rather than causing dysfunction.
choice_explanations.D: Parasympathetic activity mediates erection through nitric oxide and vasodilation; increased activity is not the cause described.
choice_explanations.E: Cavernosal smooth-muscle relaxation is required for erection, so increased relaxation would not cause this disorder.

A.text: Erection depends on parasympathetic NO release, increased cGMP, and cavernosal smooth-muscle relaxation; reduced NO interrupts this proerectile sequence.

B.text: NO/cGMP-mediated relaxation causes vasodilation and increased blood inflow during erection.

C.text: First Aid links NO to increased cGMP and smooth-muscle relaxation, which promotes erection.

D.text: Erection is mediated by parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4).

E.text: Penile smooth-muscle relaxation is part of the NO/cGMP proerectile pathway.

stem: A 25-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician for a routine prenatal examination. She is in the second trimester and has had no complications. Urinalysis shows glucose, and her blood glucose is 210 mg/dL. She has no history of diabetes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Growth hormone (GH) and its variants reduce insulin sensitivity. During pregnancy, the placenta produces a GH variant called placental GH (PGH), which is the product of the hGH-V gene. PGH differs from pituitary GH (encoded by the hGH-N gene) by 13 amino acids but is structurally and functionally similar. PGH gradually replaces maternal GH during pregnancy. PGH is present in only small amounts in the fetal circulation, and its influence on fetal growth is limited, although it may aid in maturation of the placenta. Because PGH/GH has anti-insulin effects, excess production of this hormone could increase circulating glucose levels in the mother. Therefore, decreased PGH (choice C) is incorrect. Other factors implicated in insulin insensitivity in gestational diabetes include adiponectin, TNF-α, leptin, and other adipokines.

Decreased human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG; choice A) and increased hCG (choice D) are incorrect because hCG functions to maintain the corpus luteum, and a reduction in this hormone would lead to termination of pregnancy during the first trimester. hCG is detected in serum about 6–8 days following implantation and peaks at days 60–90 of gestation. At this point, placental progesterone is the primary hormone for maintaining pregnancy. Therefore, hCG levels decrease during the second trimester, but this reduction is normal and would not alter serum glucose levels. Since hCG levels peak at about 10 weeks and then decline, hCG is unlikely to be causing her insulin resistance in the second trimester.

Decreased human placental lactogen (hPL; choice B) is incorrect because hPL also helps regulate intermediary metabolism, beginning about the sixth week of pregnancy. In the fetus, hPL modulates fetal development and regulates intermediary metabolism. Decreased hPL would not result in an increase in circulating glucose. Increased hPL is implicated in gestational diabetes, rather than decreased hPL.

choice_explanations.A: Reduced hCG would threaten early corpus-luteum support and does not cause second-trimester maternal hyperglycemia.
choice_explanations.B: hPL promotes maternal insulin resistance; a decrease would not explain hyperglycemia.
choice_explanations.C: PGH has anti-insulin activity, so decreased rather than increased PGH would not cause this glucose elevation.
choice_explanations.D: hCG supports the corpus luteum in early pregnancy; increased hCG is not the source's explanation for gestational diabetes in the second trimester.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Placental GH is anti-insulin and can reduce maternal insulin sensitivity, raising glucose.

A.text: hCG maintains the corpus luteum and increases progesterone in the first trimester; it is not the source of second-trimester insulin resistance.

B.text: Human placental lactogen is GH/PRL-like and increases maternal insulin resistance; the decrease in this option points away from hyperglycemia.

C.text: First Aid 2026 describes hPL-related maternal insulin resistance but does not directly discuss placental growth hormone (PGH).

D.text: hCG supports the corpus luteum and progesterone production; First Aid does not associate increased hCG with gestational hyperglycemia.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly identify placental growth hormone as a cause of gestational diabetes; the related hPL insulin-resistance concept is on p. 651.

stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of heavy menstrual bleeding and recurrent spotting between periods. She has regular menstrual cycles and takes no medications. Vital signs are normal. Pelvic examination shows an enlarged, nontender uterus. Ultrasound shows a large, round, well-circumscribed 4-cm submucosal mass on the anterior uterine wall. A day-14 endometrial biopsy shows normal secretory endometrium without inflammation. Which is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The differential diagnosis for vaginal bleeding includes uterine leiomyoma, uterine hyperplasia or carcinoma, other uterine malignancies, inflammation (acute or chronic endometritis), and dyssynchronous endometrium due to hormonal imbalance. This patient most likely has a uterine leiomyoma. Leiomyomas are common, benign smooth-muscle tumors of the myometrium with very low malignant potential. They are generally well-circumscribed, round masses and may be submucosal, intramural, or subserosal. Clinical presentation may include anemia, heavy menstrual periods (menorrhagia), bleeding between periods (menometrorrhagia), pelvic pain, and/or a pelvic mass. Submucosal and intramural tumors can also cause infertility by prohibiting implantation.

Endometrial adenocarcinoma (choice A) most commonly affects postmenopausal women and generally presents with postmenopausal bleeding. It is less likely here because the patient still has regular menstrual cycles and a normal endometrial biopsy. Endometrial hyperplasia (choice B) generally presents with irregular bleeding between menses. Causes include unopposed estrogen (exogenous hormone therapy or obesity with extra fat depots) and estrogen-secreting ovarian granulosa-cell tumors. The patient has none of these causes and has normal secretory endometrium without histologic confirmation of hyperplasia. If untreated, endometrial hyperplasia can progress to adenocarcinoma. Uterine leiomyosarcoma (choice D) is a rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor, commonly seen in older patients (over 60 years). It arises from the myometrium and is generally aggressive; imaging may show a large, irregular, hemorrhagic mass with necrotic foci. Although possible, this patient's well-circumscribed, round ultrasound mass makes it less likely. Pelvic inflammatory disease (choice E) results from ascending genital-tract infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and/or Chlamydia trachomatis. Patients generally have vaginal discharge, spotting or bleeding, and abdominal/pelvic pain with or without fever. Chlamydia may be asymptomatic; gonorrhea causes acute endometritis, whereas chlamydia causes chronic endometritis, which would be present on biopsy. PID may scar the fallopian tubes, causing infertility and increased ectopic-pregnancy risk. PID is unlikely to explain this patient's irregular bleeding.

choice_explanations.A: Endometrial carcinoma is not supported by the benign, well-circumscribed uterine mass and normal secretory endometrial biopsy.
choice_explanations.B: Endometrial hyperplasia is an endometrial gland-proliferation disorder; the biopsy is normal and the discrete mass is myometrial.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. A round, well-circumscribed submucosal myometrial mass with abnormal uterine bleeding is characteristic of leiomyoma.
choice_explanations.D: Leiomyosarcoma is malignant and is not the typical explanation for a well-circumscribed uterine mass with this presentation; the source identifies the lesion as benign leiomyoma.
choice_explanations.E: PID causes pelvic infection/inflammation, not an isolated well-circumscribed submucosal uterine mass; the endometrial biopsy shows no inflammation.

A.text: Endometrial carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the endometrium, distinct from the myometrial fibroid described.

B.text: Endometrial hyperplasia is abnormal gland proliferation, usually from excess estrogen unopposed by progesterone.

C.text: Leiomyoma is a benign, often multiple myometrial tumor that may be submucosal and cause bleeding, pelvic pain, or reproductive dysfunction; histology is whorled smooth muscle.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe leiomyosarcoma in this uterine-conditions section.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss PID as a differential for a discrete submucosal uterine mass.

stem: A 29-year-old primigravid woman is brought to the emergency department because of headache and dizziness at 34 weeks’ gestation. Prenatal care has been up to date. Her blood pressure has ranged from 140–170/90–105 mm Hg since 30 weeks. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein. Examination shows edema of the lower extremities. AST is 40 U/L and ALT is 45 U/L. Which is the most appropriate definitive therapy?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The woman has preeclampsia, the features of which include proteinuria and sustained elevation of blood pressure in pregnancy after 20 weeks of gestation (usually in the third trimester) in the absence of preexisting hypertension. A wide variety of other features of preeclampsia can also be seen, including excessive weight gain, generalized edema, ascites, hyperuricemia, hypocalciuria, increased plasma concentration of von Willebrand factor and cellular fibronectin, reduced plasma concentration of antithrombin III, thrombocytopenia, increased hematocrit, increased liver enzymes (as seen in our patient), intrauterine growth retardation, and intrauterine hypoxia. Modern theories suggest that the true primary lesion may involve the endothelium, and that medical control of hypertension (choice A) actually only treats a small part of the syndrome. At present, the only definitive therapy is delivery of the baby, and obstetricians often play a delicate game trying to delay delivery for a premature baby's sake as long as possible while judging the severity of the preeclampsia and its immediate risks to mother and fetus.

Low-dose aspirin (choice C) may have a modest effect in preventing preeclampsia, but this is not yet well established.

Oxygen supplementation (choice D) is used in some cases of cerebral hemorrhage secondary to preeclampsia, but does not constitute definitive therapy.

Renal dialysis (choice E) is usually not necessary in preeclampsia, although both renal cortical necrosis and renal tubular necrosis can occasionally occur in this disorder.

choice_explanations.A: Antihypertensives control blood pressure and reduce complications but do not remove the placental cause; they are not definitive treatment.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Delivery is definitive therapy for preeclampsia, particularly with severe features at 34 weeks.
choice_explanations.C: Low-dose aspirin is used for prophylaxis in patients at risk, not as treatment for established severe preeclampsia.
choice_explanations.D: Oxygen does not treat the underlying preeclampsia or resolve its maternal-fetal risks.
choice_explanations.E: Renal dialysis is not indicated by the presented findings and does not treat the pregnancy-related cause.

A.text: First Aid lists antihypertensives for blood-pressure control in preeclampsia, but delivery is definitive.

B.text: Preeclampsia treatment includes antihypertensives and IV magnesium; delivery is definitive. At 34 weeks, the question's timing supports delivery.

C.text: Aspirin is prophylaxis for preeclampsia, not definitive therapy after disease is established.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not recommend oxygen supplementation as preeclampsia therapy.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not identify dialysis as treatment for preeclampsia.

stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because she has not yet begun menstruating. Examination shows a very shallow vagina without a palpable uterus and palpable masses in the labia majora. Karyotype is 46,XY. Which of the following was most likely present during early fetal life?
explanation: The correct answer is D. Androgen insensitivity syndrome (testicular feminization; male pseudohermaphroditism) is a disorder of the androgen receptor. Phenotypically, the patient appears female but has a blind-ending vagina and lacks a uterus or other female internal reproductive organs. The patient has an XY genotype. Since the gene for testis-determining factor (TDF) is on the Y chromosome, TDF causes the indifferent gonad to develop into a testis containing Sertoli cells. Sertoli cells at this stage secrete Müllerian inhibitory factor (MIF), which suppresses the paramesonephric ducts and prevents formation of female internal reproductive organs. This patient would not possess a uterus (choice A) or an oviduct (choice B); both structures are derived from the paramesonephric duct, which is suppressed by MIF. Decreased androgen levels (choice C) would not occur. In fact, individuals with testicular feminization syndrome have normal or even slightly elevated testosterone levels. Development of female external genitalia results from defective androgen receptors, not depressed testosterone. The patient would not have streak ovaries (choice E), a finding in Turner syndrome associated with a 45,XO genotype. In fact, the patient has testes (the labial masses), since the genetic complement contains a Y chromosome. The testes in individuals with testicular feminization syndrome are often undescended and are usually removed surgically.

choice_explanations.A: A uterus is absent in androgen insensitivity because anti-Müllerian hormone causes regression of the Müllerian ducts.
choice_explanations.B: Oviducts derive from Müllerian ducts and are likewise absent after anti-Müllerian hormone exposure.
choice_explanations.C: Androgen levels are not decreased; the disorder is impaired androgen-receptor response despite testicular androgen production.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Sertoli-cell anti-Müllerian hormone (Müllerian inhibitory factor) is present and causes Müllerian-duct regression.
choice_explanations.E: Streak ovaries occur in other disorders of sexual development; this patient has testes, suggested by palpable labial masses and AMH exposure.

A.text: Androgen insensitivity syndrome has absent uterus and fallopian tubes because anti-Müllerian hormone persists from the testes.

B.text: Müllerian structures, including fallopian tubes, regress in androgen insensitivity syndrome due to anti-Müllerian hormone.

C.text: Androgen insensitivity is associated with increased testosterone, estrogen, and LH; the problem is receptor resistance, not low androgen production.

D.text: Anti-Müllerian hormone from testes causes absence of uterus and fallopian tubes in androgen insensitivity syndrome.

E.text: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is a genotypic male condition with testes; First Aid contrasts it with disorders involving streak gonads.

stem: Diagrams A–E show the relative osmolarity (y-axis) and volume (x-axis) of the intracellular and extracellular fluid compartments during normal conditions (solid lines) and after various disturbances in body fluids (shaded areas). Which diagram best depicts an individual who runs a marathon on a hot summer day and replaces all volume lost in sweat by drinking pure (solute-free) water during the race?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The patient lost hypotonic fluid as sweat and replaced it with solute-free water. This produces a hypotonic contraction of the extracellular fluid (ECF): body osmolarity decreases, water shifts into the intracellular fluid (ICF), ECF volume decreases, and ICF volume increases. Total body water is unchanged because the volume lost in sweat was replaced with an equal volume of water. Choice A depicts an isosmotic contraction; choices B and D depict changes in the wrong direction for the osmolarity/volume changes caused by replacing sweat with pure water.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Isotonic contraction occurs when isotonic fluid is lost, as in diarrhea; water and solute decrease proportionally, with little change in osmolarity or cell volume.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Hypertonic expansion follows net gain or retention of sodium chloride relative to water; extracellular osmolarity and volume rise and water shifts out of cells.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Sodium chloride lost in sweat is replaced by water alone, lowering extracellular osmolarity and volume while water shifts into and expands cells; total body water is restored.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypertonic contraction occurs when hypotonic fluid is lost without adequate water replacement; both compartments contract and osmolarity rises.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Hypotonic expansion follows excess free-water retention or intake; extracellular osmolarity falls while extracellular volume expands.

A.text: No direct First Aid 2026 match for isotonic contraction/Darrow–Yannet diagram A was identified in the reviewed fluid-compartment material.

B.text: Primary hyperaldosteronism is listed with Conn syndrome; the source explanation also notes mineralocorticoid excess as a possible cause of hypertonic expansion. The diagram label itself is not shown.

C.text: First Aid reviews total-body-water, intracellular-fluid, and extracellular-fluid compartments; it does not directly depict hypotonic contraction or sweat replacement.

D.text: No direct First Aid 2026 match for hypertonic contraction after hypotonic sweat loss without water replacement was identified in the reviewed fluid-compartment material.

E.text: SIADH causes free-water retention with euvolemic hyponatremia, a related source example of hypotonic water retention; the Darrow–Yannet label is not shown.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 p.599 gives the 60–40–20 total-body-water distribution, relative intracellular and extracellular compartments, and normal serum osmolality. It does not include the Darrow–Yannet labels or the specific sweat-replacement shift. Related alternative mechanisms appear separately: SIADH/free-water retention on p.342 and hyperaldosteronism on p.354.
question_figure_description: 仅含A–E流体隔室示意图与重新标注字母，不含原始radio控件、选中状态、正确答案标记、题干或解析。

stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menstrual cycles. She menstruates each month but cannot predict when. Review of her last 5 cycle dates shows a regular 35-day cycle. She wants to become pregnant but cannot predict when ovulation occurs. On which day of the cycle is ovulation most likely to occur?
explanation: The correct answer is D. Ovulation occurs at the same point in the cycle regardless of total cycle length. The interval between ovulation and onset of menstruation is relatively constant at 14 days because it is related to the lifespan of the corpus luteum. The beginning of the cycle, during the follicular phase, is the variable interval. Once ovulation occurs, LH and FSH levels fall because of negative feedback from estrogen and progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum. If fertilization does not occur and the corpus luteum is not rescued by hCG from an implanting fetal trophoblast, estradiol and progesterone levels fall severely, triggering menstruation within 2–3 days.

choice_explanations.A: Day 10 would be too early for a 35-day cycle; the follicular phase is longer than in a 28-day cycle.
choice_explanations.B: Day 17 is earlier than expected because ovulation is timed about 14 days before the next period.
choice_explanations.C: Day 20 is close but does not match the source's 14-day luteal-phase calculation for a 35-day cycle.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. A 35-day cycle minus the approximately 14-day luteal phase gives ovulation around day 21.
choice_explanations.E: Day 25 would leave only about 10 days before the next period, shorter than the usual luteal phase.

A.text: The menstrual-cycle diagram shows ovulation near midcycle in a typical 28-day cycle; a longer cycle mainly lengthens the follicular phase.

B.text: The luteal phase after ovulation lasts a fixed 14 days, so this timing is early for a 35-day cycle.

C.text: A 35-day cycle with a fixed 14-day luteal phase places ovulation around day 21, not day 20.

D.text: The luteal phase lasts a fixed 14 days; in a 35-day cycle, ovulation is approximately day 21.

E.text: The fixed 14-day luteal phase means ovulation is earlier than day 25 in this 35-day cycle.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has not begun menstruating. Examination shows Tanner stage I breasts and genitalia with sparse pubic hair. Further evaluation shows weak pulses in the lower extremities, markedly elevated LH and FSH, and decreased free T3 and T4. Which is the best explanation for her abnormal sexual development?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This is the classic presentation of Turner syndrome, which is the most common sex chromosome abnormality in females. It is due to complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome (45,XO). More than half of cases are due to the complete loss of the X chromosome (no Barr body is present in the karyotype), whereas the remaining cases are mostly due to mosaicism. Patients with 46,XY mosaicism are at increased risk for gonadoblastoma.

Turner syndrome is the most important cause of primary amenorrhea. Of cases, 90% include dysgenesis of the ovaries with atrophic or ‘streak’ ovaries. These patients lack the steroids required for breast development and cyclic function of the hypothalamus, pituitary, ovaries, and uterus. Patients with Turner syndrome have a characteristic appearance: They are short, have widely spaced nipples, have webbing of the neck, and have a cystic hygroma (cystic lymphangioma). Turner syndrome is frequently associated with congenital cardiac anomalies (aortic coarctation or bicuspid aortic valve), hypothyroidism (about one-third of patients), and diabetes. About 50% of Turner syndrome cases have thyroid autoantibodies; the mechanism is not well understood. The most common type of coarctation of the aorta associated with this disorder is the preductal type. The narrowing is proximal to the ductus arteriosus, and patients present with weak pulses, hypotension, and cyanosis of the lower extremities. Chest x-ray in patients with coarctation may show rib notching (erosion of the lower border of the ribs from enlargement of the intercostals providing collateral blood flow) and right ventricular hypertrophy with increased pulmonary markings.

Thyrotropin-releasing hormone in excess (choice A) increases prolactin sufficiently to suppress ovarian cycling, but it also tends to cause galactorrhea. It is not associated with Turner syndrome. Progesterone (choice B), which is produced by the ovary, is decreased in Turner syndrome because of ovarian dysgenesis. Hypothalamic disorders, such as deficient secretion of GnRH (choice D), are not the principal feature responsible for failure of menarche in Turner syndrome. Primary pituitary insufficiency (choice E) is not the typical cause of amenorrhea in Turner syndrome; failure of the gonads to develop is the key element of the amenorrhea. Elevated LH and FSH (to post-menopausal levels) commonly occurs after age 10 years. This occurs because of lack of the estrogen and progesterone feedback that inhibit gonadotropin secretion. The finding of elevated LH and FSH excludes primary pituitary hypofunction.

choice_explanations.A: Excess TRH can affect prolactin and ovarian cycling but does not explain the Turner phenotype, coarctation clue, and markedly elevated gonadotropins.
choice_explanations.B: Progesterone is reduced, not excessive, when ovarian dysgenesis prevents normal ovarian steroid production.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Streak ovaries in Turner syndrome cause ovarian dysgenesis, low sex steroids, and elevated LH/FSH.
choice_explanations.D: GnRH deficiency causes low or inappropriately normal LH/FSH, not the markedly elevated gonadotropins in this patient.
choice_explanations.E: Primary pituitary failure would not produce postmenopausal-range gonadotropins; elevated LH/FSH indicate primary gonadal failure.

A.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive pages do not directly link elevated TRH to this Turner-syndrome presentation.

B.text: Turner syndrome causes ovarian dysgenesis and loss of normal ovarian sex-steroid production; excess progesterone is not expected.

C.text: Turner syndrome is associated with ovarian dysgenesis (streak ovaries) and is a common cause of primary amenorrhea.

D.text: First Aid distinguishes hypergonadotropic primary gonadal failure from hypogonadotropic disorders; Turner syndrome is the former.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly identify primary hypopituitarism as a cause in this Turner-syndrome differential.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a congenital abnormality of her reproductive system undergoes hysterectomy. The surgical specimen is shown. Which is the most likely complication of this condition?
explanation: The correct answer is E. A bicornuate uterus is associated with recurrent pregnancy loss, particularly habitual second-trimester abortion, but is not associated with endometrial carcinoma. Dyspareunia (choice A) is pain during intercourse and may result from endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease. Endometrial carcinoma (choice B) usually develops on a background of unopposed estrogenic stimulation, leading to malignant transformation through increasing degrees of endometrial hyperplasia and atypia. In postmenopausal females, it can present with vaginal bleeding. Predisposing risk factors include exogenous estrogen hormone therapy and obesity (estrogen depot in fat). Bicornuate uterus is not a predisposing condition. Endometriosis (choice C) is characterized by endometrial tissue located outside the uterus and commonly causes dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility. Pelvic inflammatory disease (choice D) is an ascending infection that may cause pelvic pain, fever, cervical motion tenderness, and infertility from tubal scarring.

choice_explanations.A: Dyspareunia is pain with intercourse and can have many causes, but it is not the characteristic complication of a bicornuate uterus.
choice_explanations.B: A bicornuate uterus is not a recognized predisposing condition for endometrial carcinoma.
choice_explanations.C: Endometriosis involves ectopic endometrial tissue and is not the characteristic complication of incomplete Müllerian-duct fusion.
choice_explanations.D: Pelvic inflammatory disease is an ascending infection, not a congenital consequence of a bicornuate uterus.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. A bicornuate uterine cavity can impair implantation and is associated with recurrent spontaneous abortion and other obstetric complications.

A.text: First Aid 2026 p. 640 does not identify dyspareunia as a direct complication of bicornuate uterus.

B.text: Endometrial carcinoma is described as a separate endometrial malignancy; uterine anomalies are not identified as its risk factor.

C.text: Endometriosis is ectopic endometrial tissue and has a separate pathophysiology from Müllerian-duct fusion anomalies.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly link PID to bicornuate uterus.

E.text: Müllerian uterine anomalies decrease fertility and increase risk of complicated pregnancy, including spontaneous abortion.

question_figure_description: Tight crop of the bicornuate uterine specimen only, retaining its photographic background and excluding all interface, question, options, and key.

stem: A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician for follow-up because she has never menstruated. She has sparse downy hair in the axillae and pubic region. Pelvic examination shows a vagina but no palpable uterus. Karyotype is 46,XY, and laboratory studies show elevated testosterone and LH. Which is the most likely underlying condition?

options.text: Ovotesticular disorder of sex development (true hermaphroditism)

explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient presents with a medical history and physical examination typical for male pseudohermaphroditism. These patients are genetically XY with the presence of testes; however, their external and internal genitalia are ambiguous or primarily female. Cases may be picked up either at birth (because of ambiguous genitalia) or at puberty (because of irregular amenorrhea and failure to develop secondary sexual characteristics).

Many of the cases are due to testicular feminization, also known as androgen insensitivity syndrome. In this condition, testosterone is produced normally by Leydig cells in the testes, but there is a defect in the androgen receptor. Wolffian duct maturation depends on androgen stimulation, and absence of this stimulation results in small or nonexistent male internal genitalia (including the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate). Female internal genitalia (uterus, fallopian tubes, cervix, and upper third of the vagina) are also absent due to normal production of Müllerian inhibitory hormone (MIH) by the testes, which involutes the Müllerian duct.

External genitalia are primarily female due to inadequate dihydrotestosterone (DHT) effect. DHT requires a functional androgen receptor; thus, patients with androgen insensitivity cannot develop male genitalia. Lack of androgen receptors also results in the absence of genital or axillary hair during puberty. Laboratory studies in these patients show increased testosterone and luteinizing hormone, because there is no negative feedback during production of these hormones. Inhibitory feedback relies on a functional androgen receptor.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (choice B) can produce female pseudohermaphrodites, who are genotypically XX but phenotypically male. In this disease, absence of certain adrenal enzymes (particularly 21-hydroxylase deficiency) results in shunting of precursors toward androgen production. Increased androgens result in maturation of internal and external male genitalia. These patients may also have salt-wasting or hypoglycemia because of insufficient mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid production.

Klinefelter syndrome (choice C) occurs in patients with 47,XXY. They have atrophied testes, gynecomastia, a tall, thin body shape, and developmental delay. These patients have dysfunction of both seminiferous tubules and Leydig cells. True hermaphrodites (choice D) are very rare and have both ovarian and testicular tissue.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Androgen-receptor resistance in a 46,XY patient explains the female phenotype despite high testosterone; anti-Müllerian hormone explains absent Müllerian organs.
choice_explanations.B: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically causes androgen excess with virilization in a 46,XX patient and does not explain the 46,XY phenotype with absent uterus and elevated LH/testosterone.
choice_explanations.C: Klinefelter syndrome is typically 47,XXY with testicular failure and low testosterone, not this phenotype.
choice_explanations.D: Ovotesticular DSD is not supported by the characteristic 46,XY androgen-receptor resistance pattern and elevated testosterone/LH.
choice_explanations.E: Turner syndrome is 45,X with ovarian dysgenesis and low sex steroids, unlike this 46,XY patient.

A.text: Androgen insensitivity is a defect in the androgen receptor causing a female-appearing 46,XY individual with absent uterus/fallopian tubes and increased testosterone, estrogen, and LH.

B.text: First Aid 2026 p. 656 does not directly cover congenital adrenal hyperplasia in this androgen-insensitivity comparison.

C.text: Klinefelter syndrome is a sex-chromosome disorder with seminiferous-tubule dysgenesis and low testosterone, distinct from 46,XY androgen insensitivity.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe ovotesticular DSD in this differential.

E.text: Turner syndrome is 45,X and associated with ovarian dysgenesis and primary amenorrhea, unlike this 46,XY presentation.

stem: A 15-month-old boy develops a testicular mass. Examination shows a 5-cm nontender, firm left testicular mass that does not transilluminate. After orchiectomy, the cut surface has a heterogeneous appearance. Histology shows cartilage, thyroid tissue, and neural tissue, as well as a small focus of squamous cell carcinoma. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This is a teratoma with malignant transformation, as evidenced by the focus of squamous cell carcinoma. Mature teratomas with very well-differentiated tissues should be completely excised because there is a possibility of malignancy. There is a bimodal age distribution of testicular teratoma: 0–4 years and 20–40 years. Malignant transformation is more common in testicular than ovarian teratomas. Squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma are the most common malignancies.

Dermoid cyst (choice A) is a cystic form of mature teratoma, usually found in the ovaries. Embryonal carcinoma (choice B) is a type of adenocarcinoma rather than squamous cell carcinoma. Immature teratoma (choice C), while clinically malignant, shows immature embryonal tissues and often displays no clear-cut differentiation. Solid mature teratoma (choice D), without the added descriptor “with malignant transformation,” is by definition a benign tumor in females and prepubertal males; teratomas are considered to have malignant potential in postpubertal males. Careful, extensive sampling is required to exclude minute foci of cancerous transformation.

ReKaps: Solid mature teratoma with malignant transformation is development of carcinoma in a mature teratoma. Dermoid cyst is an almost always benign, cystic mature teratoma usually found in ovaries. Solid mature teratoma is benign in females (all ages) and in testes of prepubertal males; all teratomas in postpubertal males are considered to have malignant potential. Immature teratoma contains tissues resembling embryonal tissues and is considered potentially clinically malignant.

choice_explanations.A: A dermoid cyst is a mature cystic teratoma, but the carcinoma focus means this lesion has undergone malignant transformation.
choice_explanations.B: Embryonal carcinoma is a separate malignant germ-cell tumor; it does not account for the multiple differentiated tissues and squamous carcinoma arising within them.
choice_explanations.C: An immature teratoma contains immature/fetal tissue, especially immature neuroectoderm; the decisive finding here is a distinct squamous carcinoma focus.
choice_explanations.D: A mature teratoma alone does not account for the malignant squamous-cell component.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. A teratoma containing a focus of squamous cell carcinoma is a teratoma with malignant transformation.

A.text: Ovarian mature cystic teratoma is also called a dermoid cyst and contains tissues from all three germ layers; this is a related germ-cell-tumor concept.

B.text: Embryonal carcinoma is a distinct malignant testicular germ-cell tumor and may be associated with hCG; it is separate from teratoma with somatic tissue.

C.text: First Aid describes immature teratoma as malignant/aggressive and containing fetal or neuroectodermal tissue; it does not match the squamous carcinoma focus as directly as malignant transformation.

D.text: First Aid notes testicular teratoma may be malignant in adult males but is benign in children; the infant's carcinoma focus requires malignant transformation rather than mature teratoma alone.

E.text: First Aid notes malignant transformation of mature ovarian teratoma is rare and usually to squamous cell carcinoma; it does not directly state the same behavior for pediatric testicular teratoma, so this is a related rather than exact match.

stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician with a 3-month sensation of heaviness in his right scrotum. Examination shows painless testicular enlargement. Serum human chorionic gonadotropin and alpha-fetoprotein levels are normal, but placental alkaline phosphatase is elevated. The cut surface of the orchiectomy specimen is shown. Histology shows lobules and nests of large malignant cells with prominent nucleoli surrounded by abundant lymphocytes. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Testicular cancer is a common cancer in adult males age 20–35 years. The picture shows a seminoma, composed of a solid, fleshy testicular tumor surrounded by compressed normal testicular tissue. Microscopically, the tumor would show lobules or nests of large cells with prominent nucleoli, surrounded by abundant lymphocytic infiltrate. Seminoma is radiosensitive and has a favorable prognosis. Placental alkaline phosphatase is elevated in these tumors. A small percentage of seminomas can have elevated hCG or AFP if the tumor is mixed with other components, e.g., embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, or yolk sac tumors.

Choriocarcinoma (choice A) may be nonpalpable on examination. In spite of its small size, early and widespread metastases can occur. The cut surface of the tumor shows hemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopically, there is commonly a biphasic pattern of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) is the tumor marker for choriocarcinoma. Pure choriocarcinoma has a poor prognosis; when admixed with other subtypes, the prognosis is more favorable.

Embryonal carcinoma (choice B) presents as a bulky mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopically, tumor cells can vary considerably but they are distinctly malignant. Undifferentiated cells may be arranged in sheets or may form acinar, tubular, or papillary structures. Areas of hemorrhage and necrosis are also seen microscopically. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and beta-hCG may be elevated in embryonal carcinomas when admixed with other subtypes.

Teratoma (choice D) presents as a cystic mass derived from all three germ layers (often containing hair, cartilage, teeth, and bone). In mature teratomas, adult somatic tissue is seen microscopically; in immature teratoma, elements of a mature teratoma are often seen with tissues seen in embryonic and fetal development. There is no specific tumor marker for teratomas. Testicular teratomas tend to be immature and may have malignant transformation. The most common type of malignant transformation is squamous cell carcinoma.

Yolk sac tumor (choice E), also known as endodermal sinus tumors, is the most common germ cell tumor in children. Adults can have mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumors, which can include a yolk sac component. The tumor is unencapsulated with a gray-to-tan-to-yellow cut surface with hemorrhage and necrosis. The histology is polymorphous, with many microscopic patterns. One histologic feature is the Schiller-Duval body, which resembles immature glomerular structures. Eosinophilic hyaline globules are not specific, but if present, can be a helpful diagnostic clue since they are comprised of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). AFP is usually elevated in yolk sac tumor.

choice_explanations.A: Choriocarcinoma typically has markedly elevated β-hCG, hemorrhage/necrosis, and early hematogenous spread; it does not fit the PLAP-positive, AFP-normal pattern.
choice_explanations.B: Embryonal carcinoma is usually an aggressive, hemorrhagic and necrotic mass; AFP and/or β-hCG may rise, especially in mixed tumors.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Painless homogeneous enlargement, PLAP elevation, and large cells in lobules with lymphocytes are characteristic of seminoma.
choice_explanations.D: Teratomas contain tissues derived from multiple germ layers and have no characteristic PLAP elevation.
choice_explanations.E: Yolk sac tumors characteristically elevate AFP and may show Schiller-Duval bodies; this patient's AFP is normal.

A.text: Choriocarcinoma is a distinct testicular germ-cell tumor associated with elevated hCG and hematogenous metastases.

B.text: Embryonal carcinoma is typically hemorrhagic/necrotic and may be associated with elevated hCG or AFP when mixed.

C.text: Seminoma causes painless homogeneous enlargement, lobulated large cells, and increased PLAP.

D.text: Mature teratoma can be malignant in adult males; it is not the PLAP-associated tumor described here.

E.text: Yolk sac tumor is associated with elevated AFP and Schiller-Duval bodies.
