B.text: Anemia of chronic disease: low serum iron and transferrin/TIBC, high ferritin, and low or decreased transferrin saturation.

C.text: Pregnancy/OCP use: increased transferrin/TIBC with no direct change in iron stores; percent saturation decreases.

D.text: No First Aid iron-study pattern matches this combination. First Aid p.423 shows that hemochromatosis instead has high ferritin, low transferrin/TIBC, and high transferrin saturation.

E.text: Hemochromatosis: increased serum iron, low transferrin/TIBC, increased ferritin, and markedly increased transferrin saturation.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.423 directly compares iron-study patterns. Hemochromatosis is the column with increased serum iron, decreased transferrin/TIBC, increased ferritin, and increased transferrin saturation. This matches the clinical iron-overload syndrome in the stem.
question_figure_description: Liver-biopsy photomicrograph with coarse golden-brown iron pigment in hepatocytes, consistent with iron deposition.

stem: An autopsy is performed on a 12-year-old boy who died of multi-organ failure. He had a history of chronic anemia and required frequent hospitalizations and transfusions. On autopsy, he is found to have short stature, hepatosplenomegaly, and expansion of the calvarium. Histologic examination shows the presence of abundant pigment in macrophages of the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes, as well as in parenchymal cells of the heart, liver, endocrine organs, and kidney. The photomicrograph shows a section of kidney. The pigment seen histologically in this patient is most likely which of the following?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Any prolonged systemic overload of iron results in a condition called hemosiderosis. This may result from hemolytic anemias (intracellular release of iron), repeated blood transfusions as with our patient, or increased iron absorption in conditions such as congenital hemochromatosis. Due to elevated serum iron (along with increased ferritin, decreased TIBC, and increased transferrin saturation), hemosiderin accumulates within macrophages of the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, lung, and kidneys. The pigment appears as coarse, golden-brown granules within the cytoplasm, which can be identified with Prussian blue stain.

Patients with severe forms of sickle-cell anemia or thalassemia are especially prone to this complication. In these diseases, anemia results from mutated hemoglobin chains rather than a deficiency of iron. Providing iron transfusions to these patients temporarily relieves their anemia, but precipitates iron overload. Each unit of packed red blood cells contains 250 mg of iron. Signs of extramedullary hematopoiesis, including calvarial expansion and splenomegaly, suggest that our patient likely presents with one of the hereditary hemoglobinopathies described above.

With sufficient iron overload, patients may have symptoms of hemochromatosis. Features of this disease include restrictive cardiomyopathy, hepatic disease, diabetes mellitus (due to pancreatic involvement), and skin pigmentation (“bronze-diabetes”). Treatments include deferoxamine (iron chelator) and phlebotomy.

Bilirubin (choice A) is the normal pigment of bile. Bilirubin is responsible for coloration of stool and urine. In cases of obstructive jaundice or liver disease, excess serum conjugated bilirubin accumulates as yellow-green pigment within Kupffer cells and bile ducts, and can produce darker urine, while lack of excretion in the intestines results in pale stools.

Inhalation of carbon particles (choice B) is an inevitable consequence of living in polluted urban areas and of cigarette smoking. Carbon particles are taken up by alveolar macrophages and transported to the regional lymph nodes, causing a dark discoloration of hilar lymph nodes and lung interstitium known as anthracosis.

Homogentisic acid (choice D) is a black pigment occurring in alkaptonuria. It is an autosomal recessive deficiency in homogentisic acid oxidase, an enzyme in the tyrosine metabolism pathway. Findings include dark connective tissue, pigmented sclera, and dark urine. Sequelae include arthritis and kidney stones.

Lipofuscin (choice E) is a golden-brown pigment that accumulates in aging postmitotic cells such as cardiac myocytes, hepatocytes, skin, and neurons. It represents an epiphenomenon of free-radical injury, but as far as we know, lipofuscin is harmless.

Melanin (choice F) may appear remarkably similar to hemosiderin on H&E tissue sections. It is the brown pigment synthesized by melanocytes from the tyrosinase-catalyzed oxidation of tyrosine to melanin. Metastatic melanoma cells can be present in the brain and liver; some cells will retain their pigmentation.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Bilirubin is a bile pigment that accumulates particularly in hepatocytes/Kupffer cells and bile ducts in cholestasis or jaundice; it does not explain widespread iron-overload pigment after repeated transfusions.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Carbon particles are inhaled and accumulate in pulmonary macrophages and hilar lymph nodes (anthracosis), not throughout the reticuloendothelial system and parenchymal organs in this transfused patient.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Hemosiderin is an intracellular iron-storage pigment. Repeated transfusions and hemolysis can cause systemic iron overload, with deposits in macrophages and, when severe, parenchymal organs.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Homogentisic acid pigment occurs in alkaptonuria, causing dark connective tissue, sclera, and urine with ochronosis/arthritis; it is not caused by transfusional iron overload.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown wear-and-tear pigment that accumulates in aging or chronically stressed postmitotic cells; it does not cause this systemic iron-deposition pattern.
choice_explanations.F: Incorrect. Melanin is synthesized by melanocytes and may be present in melanocytic lesions or metastases; it does not explain iron-loading distribution or the transfusion history.

A.text: No directly matching First Aid passage was verified for bilirubin as a tissue-pigment distractor in this context.

B.text: No directly matching First Aid passage was verified for anthracotic carbon pigment as a distractor in this context.

C.text: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages are identified on First Aid p.316; the iron-overload pattern and hemochromatosis iron studies are summarized on p.423.

D.text: No direct First Aid printed-page match for homogentisic-acid pigment as a tissue differential was verified in this audit.

E.text: No direct First Aid printed-page match for lipofuscin as a tissue-pigment differential was verified in this audit.

F.text: No direct First Aid printed-page match for melanin as a tissue-pigment differential was verified in this audit.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.316 identifies hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Printed p.423 covers ferritin/iron storage and hemochromatosis iron-study patterns. Together these pages support hemosiderin as an iron-storage pigment, although the exact renal photomicrograph and transfusion-associated distribution are not reproduced in First Aid.
question_figure_description: Kidney histology photomicrograph showing coarse golden-brown cytoplasmic pigment granules in renal tissue.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of severe acid reflux is admitted to the hospital for biopsies of the antral and duodenal mucosa. Samples are prepared for light microscopy as well as fluorescence immunohistochemistry. Which of the following hormones is most likely to be detected in tissue from both biopsy samples?
explanation: The correct answer is C. Gastrointestinal hormones are secreted by different types of endocrine cells scattered throughout the mucosa from the stomach to the colon. The endocrine cells are not clumped together but are dispersed among epithelial cells, making it impossible to surgically remove the source of any one gastrointestinal hormone. Gastrin is a peptide hormone secreted by G cells and is the only one of the five hormones listed above to be secreted by the gastric antrum. G cells are also located in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa. Gastrin is normally released in response to stomach distension and by the presence of peptides and amino acids in the stomach and duodenum. Its physiologic role is to stimulate acid secretion from gastric parietal cells. The patient has a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), which can be associated with peptic ulcer disease (ulcers located in the stomach and duodenum). The most common cause of peptic ulcers is Helicobacter pylori, which infects and weakens the gastric acid barrier, resulting in acid damage to the mucosa.

choice_explanations.A: Cholecystokinin is produced by I cells in the duodenum and jejunum, not by the gastric antrum; it therefore would not be present in both sampled tissues.
choice_explanations.B: GIP is produced by K cells in the duodenum and jejunum, not the gastric antrum.
choice_explanations.C: Gastrin is produced by G cells in the gastric antrum and duodenum, matching both biopsy sites.
choice_explanations.D: Motilin is produced in the small intestine; it is not a hormone of both the gastric antrum and duodenum.
choice_explanations.E: Secretin is produced by S cells in the duodenum, not the gastric antrum.

A.text: Cholecystokinin is produced by I cells in the duodenum and jejunum.

B.text: GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) is produced by K cells in the duodenum and jejunum.

C.text: Gastrin is produced by G cells in the gastric antrum and duodenum; it increases gastric acid secretion.

D.text: Motilin is produced in the small intestine and stimulates migrating motor complexes.

E.text: Secretin is produced by S cells in the duodenum.

fa_summary: Gastrointestinal regulatory hormones are produced by region-specific enteroendocrine cells. Gastrin is the listed hormone found in both gastric antrum and duodenum.

stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child checkup. A large, palpable, nontender, right intra-abdominal mass that crosses the midline is found on physical examination. CT shows a mass in the right retroperitoneum and abdominal cavity. The tumor is resected. Microscopic examination shows ganglion cells and primitive small, round cells, occasionally organized in rosettes and embedded in a fibrillary pink matrix. Which of the following features is most likely associated with this tumor?
explanation:
The correct answer is B in this live option order: amplification of the N-MYC gene (the matching source option is labeled A). Neuroblastoma is a common childhood tumor derived from the neural crest and most commonly arises from the paravertebral sympathetic chain or adrenal medulla. Children most often present with a palpable, asymptomatic abdominal mass that crosses the midline. Occasionally, they may develop hypertension. Histopathology shows small, round, blue cells of varying degrees of differentiation, occasionally arranged in rosettes and admixed with pink neurofibrillary matrix. Neuroblastoma is associated with amplification of the N-MYC oncogene; this genetic event is associated with a poorer prognosis. Patients may also have elevated serum homovanillic acid (HVA), a breakdown product of dopamine.

It is important to distinguish between the two most common causes of childhood neoplastic abdominal masses: Wilms tumor and neuroblastoma. Wilms tumor derives from kidney nephroblasts (choice E in the live list) and is also called nephroblastoma. Patients present with an abdominal or flank mass that does not cross the midline, hematuria, and hypertension. Wilms tumor is associated with deletion of the WT1 gene (choice C in the live list), located on chromosome 11. Patients may develop Wilms tumor as part of the WAGR complex: Wilms tumor, aniridia (absence of the iris), genitourinary malformation, and retardation (mental/motor).

Multiple renal cysts (choice D) can occur in polycystic kidney disease. In this patient's age group, it would most likely be the autosomal recessive form. Patients present with hypertension, renal cysts, and hematuria. This is unlikely in a patient with a single mass and primitive small, round cells on pathology.

Translocation of the C-MYC gene (choice A in the live list) occurs in Burkitt lymphoma. C-MYC is located on chromosome 8. It is associated with t(8;14) and Epstein-Barr virus infection. Other translocations include t(2;8) and t(8;22), involving the lambda and kappa light-chain genes. Patients may occasionally present with an abdominal mass, more commonly in endemic Burkitt lymphoma. Histopathology demonstrates sheets of neoplastic B lymphocytes interspersed with tingible-body macrophages (a “starry-sky” pattern).

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. C-MYC amplification/translocation is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, not neuroblastoma.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. N-MYC (MYCN) amplification is associated with neuroblastoma and a poorer prognosis.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. WT1 loss is associated with Wilms tumor, a renal nephroblastoma; it does not explain this neural-crest tumor's histology.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Multiple renal cysts suggest polycystic kidney disease, not a solid tumor composed of ganglion cells and primitive neuroblastic cells.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Nephroblasts are the cells of origin of Wilms tumor. Neuroblastoma arises from neural-crest-derived sympathetic tissue.

A.text: MYCC (C-MYC) is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, not neuroblastoma.

B.text: MYCN (N-MYC) amplification is associated with neuroblastoma.

C.text: No direct First Aid p.220 pairing of WT1 deletion with this tumor is given; WT1 loss is a Wilms tumor association, unlike the neuroblastoma association tested here.

D.text: No direct First Aid p.220 association for renal cysts; this option points to polycystic kidney disease, not neuroblastoma.

E.text: No direct First Aid p.220 association for nephroblasts; nephroblasts are the contrasting cell of origin in Wilms tumor.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.220 lists MYCN (N-MYC) amplification as associated with neuroblastoma and MYCC (C-MYC) with Burkitt lymphoma. It also identifies WT1 as a tumor-suppressor gene; this supports the keyed distinction from Wilms tumor.

stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of abdominal fullness and pain. She reports early satiety and fewer bowel movements than usual, and has noticed decreased stool caliber. A radiographic bowel series shows a circumferential lesion narrowing the sigmoid-colon lumen and more than 100 polyps. Her carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level is 100 times the upper limit of normal. Further investigation reveals a genetic disease that predisposes her to this condition. The genetic defect most likely involves which chromosome site?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient has familial adenomatous polyposis syndrome (FAP), which is characterized by formation of large numbers of adenomatous polyps (>100). 5q21 is the location of the APC gene, and germline mutations of the APC gene cause FAP. The APC gene is a tumor-suppressor gene. Noninherited, spontaneous mutations of the APC gene also predispose to colon cancer. Spontaneous colon cancers are much more common than familial cancer syndromes.

By age 40, nearly all patients with FAP will develop invasive colon cancer. This patient's circumferential tumor is causing a partial bowel obstruction. Patients may complain of constipation, abdominal distension, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Obstipation (passing neither feces nor flatus) indicates complete obstruction. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is often elevated in advanced colon cancer. CEA is not used for routine screening but can be used to monitor for recurrence and track response to treatment. Elevated CEA is also associated with other cancers, especially pancreatic cancer, and other conditions such as pancreatitis.

11p13 (choice B) is the site of the WT1 Wilms tumor gene. 13q14 (choice C) is the site of the RB retinoblastoma gene. 17p13 (choice D) is the site of the p53 tumor-suppressor gene, associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome (sarcoma, breast, and adrenal cortical cancers, among others). 22q12 (choice E) is the site of the NF2 neurofibromatosis gene.

The source's clinically important tumor-suppressor table lists: 3p25, VHL—von Hippel-Lindau disease and renal cell carcinoma; 11p13, WT1—Wilms tumor; 11p15, WT2—Wilms tumor; 13q14, RB—retinoblastoma; 17p13, p53—lung, breast, colon, and other cancers; 17q12–21, BRCA1—hereditary breast and ovarian cancer; 13q12–13, BRCA2—hereditary breast cancer; 5q21, APC—adenomatous polyps and colon cancer; 18q21, DCC—colon cancer; 17q11.2, NF1—neurofibromas; and 22q12, NF2—acoustic neuromas and meningiomas.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. APC on chromosome 5q21–q22 is mutated in FAP, which causes numerous adenomatous colorectal polyps and a very high risk of colorectal cancer.
choice_explanations.B: 11p13 contains WT1; loss-of-function is associated with Wilms tumor, not FAP.
choice_explanations.C: 13q14 contains RB1; loss of both RB1 alleles causes retinoblastoma and is not the FAP locus.
choice_explanations.D: 17p13 contains TP53; germline TP53 variants cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, whereas APC is the classic polyposis gene.
choice_explanations.E: 22q12 contains NF2 (merlin); NF2 loss causes neurofibromatosis type 2, not FAP.

A.text: First Aid lists familial adenomatous polyposis under chromosome 5 (p. 62) and specifies an autosomal-dominant APC tumor-suppressor mutation at 5q21–q22 with thousands of adenomatous polyps (p. 394).

B.text: First Aid associates chromosome 11 and WT1 with Wilms tumor. The precise 11p13 band is not printed in these entries; this is the relevant competing chromosome/gene association, not FAP.

C.text: First Aid associates chromosome 13 and RB1 with retinoblastoma; the exact 13q14 band is not printed in these entries.

D.text: First Aid lists TP53 with chromosome 17 and Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and describes p53 as a tumor suppressor; the exact 17p13 band is not printed in these entries.

E.text: First Aid associates chromosome 22/NF2 (merlin) with neurofibromatosis type 2; the exact 22q12 band is not printed in these entries.

fa_summary: FAP is an autosomal-dominant APC tumor-suppressor disorder at 5q21–q22, characterized by numerous adenomatous polyps and near-certain progression to colorectal cancer without prophylactic treatment. Left-sided tumors may cause obstruction and decreased stool caliber; CEA is useful for monitoring, not screening.

fa_subchapter: Gastrointestinal regulatory substances / small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother after she saw him swallow a dime 30–45 minutes earlier. He has no choking or pain. His mother is told that the coin will most likely pass through the gastrointestinal tract and be evacuated within 24–48 hours by periodic contractile waves that clear foreign bodies from the stomach. An absence of these waves most likely causes an increase in which of the following?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Foreign bodies such as coins and toys are cleared from the stomach by periodic peristaltic waves called migrating motor complexes (MMCs, also known as migrating myoelectric complexes). MMCs are initiated every 90–120 minutes between meals, beginning in the stomach and migrating to the ileum, where they die out. MMCs have a general cleansing function, sweeping undigested food residues, inorganic materials, cellular debris, and bacteria through the intestine in preparation for the next meal. Eating a meal interrupts MMC activity. In the absence of MMCs, bacterial overgrowth syndrome can occur when the normally low bacterial colonization in the upper gastrointestinal tract increases significantly.

MMCs involve the duodenum, so their absence would decrease duodenal motility (choice A).

Gastric emptying (choice B) is regulated by the pyloric sphincter, which normally restricts passage to particles <2 mm in size. During passage of an MMC, the pyloric sphincter dilates and allows anything larger than 2 mm to be eliminated. An absence of MMCs would reduce emptying.

Colonic mass movements (choice D) and swallowing (choice E) are both independent of MMCs.

ReKaps: Migrating motility complexes (MMCs) are peristaltic waves of contraction that begin in the stomach and slowly migrate along the GI tract. Their absence can lead to bacterial overgrowth in the upper intestine.

choice_explanations.A: Not increased: MMCs involve the duodenum, so their absence decreases duodenal motility.
choice_explanations.B: Not increased: during an MMC the pyloric sphincter opens to pass larger particles; without MMCs gastric emptying is reduced.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Loss of MMC cleansing permits bacterial overgrowth in the proximal small intestine, where bacterial counts are normally low.
choice_explanations.D: Colonic mass movements are independent of MMC activity.
choice_explanations.E: Swallowing is independent of MMC activity.

A.text: First Aid p.378 links motilin to MMC production but does not directly describe the effect of MMC loss on duodenal motility. Word explanation confirms absent MMCs decrease it.

B.text: First Aid p.378 links motilin to MMC production but does not directly describe the effect of MMC loss on gastric emptying. Word explanation confirms absent MMCs reduce emptying.

C.text: Motilin produces MMCs (p. 378). First Aid describes small intestinal bacterial overgrowth as abnormal bacterial accumulation associated with dysmotility (p. 393); this supports the consequence of losing the MMC cleansing pattern.

D.text: First Aid p.378 identifies motilin/MMCs but does not discuss colonic mass movements as an MMC effect; Word explanation states they are independent.

E.text: First Aid p.378 identifies motilin/MMCs but does not discuss swallowing as an MMC effect; Word explanation states swallowing is independent.

fa_summary: Motilin from the small intestine produces fasting migrating motor complexes. MMC activity sweeps residual matter and helps maintain low bacterial counts in the upper small intestine; dysmotility is a risk factor for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease is participating in a clinical study of a new therapy that alters fluid distribution between plasma and interstitial fluid. The table gives the volume of distribution (VOD) of radioactive sodium (extracellular fluid marker), radioiodinated serum albumin (RISA; plasma marker), and deuterium-labeled water (D₂O; total-body-water marker) before and after therapy.

Which of the following best characterizes the effect of therapy on plasma volume and interstitial fluid volume, respectively?

options.text: Plasma volume increases; interstitial fluid volume increases
Plasma volume increases; interstitial fluid volume decreases
Plasma volume increases; interstitial fluid volume is unchanged
Plasma volume decreases; interstitial fluid volume decreases
Plasma volume decreases; interstitial fluid volume increases
Plasma volume decreases; interstitial fluid volume is unchanged

explanation:
The correct answer is B. Fluid volumes in the body are measured by injecting a test substance of known properties and calculating its volume of distribution (VOD) from its concentration in a plasma sample. Once you know how to measure each compartment, this should be relatively simple. The table below shows body compartments used in this question.

| Body compartment | Percent of body weight | Fraction of TBW | Measurement | Substances |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| Total body water | 60% | 1.0 | Measured with a substance that passively diffuses into all compartments | Tritiated water, D₂O, antipyrine |
| Intracellular fluid | 40% | 2/3 | TBW − ECFV | — |
| Extracellular fluid volume (ECFV) | 20% | 1/3 | Measured with substances that rapidly diffuse through capillary walls and do not readily enter cells | Inulin, mannitol, sucrose, radioactive sodium |
| Interstitial fluid volume (ISFV) | 16% | 1/4 (3/4 of ECF) | ECF − plasma volume | — |
| Plasma volume (PV) | 4% | 1/12 (1/4 of ECF) | Measured with a substance that binds plasma proteins or is too large to cross capillary walls | Radio-iodinated serum albumin (RISA), Evan's blue |

In this patient, her initial plasma volume (RISA) was 6 L and her ECFV (radioactive Na⁺) was 23 L, so her ISFV was 23 L − 6 L = 17 L. After therapy, her plasma volume increased to 8 L and her ECFV decreased to 19 L. Her new ISFV = 19 − 8 = 11 L. So, her ISFV decreased from 17 L to 11 L and her plasma volume increased from 6 to 8 L. Her total body water also decreased by 4 L, so the therapy apparently was effective in promoting loss of excessive water from her body.

Choice A would be correct if the VOD of radioactive sodium and RISA both increased, although the increase in RISA would have to be less than the sodium increase or ISFV would fall. Choice C would be correct if the VOD of RISA and radioactive sodium increased by the same amount. Choices D, E, and F are incorrect because the measure of plasma volume, VOD of RISA, increased after therapy.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Plasma volume does increase, but ISFV falls from 17 L (23 − 6) to 11 L (19 − 8), rather than increasing.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. RISA-measured plasma volume increases from 6 L to 8 L; calculated ISFV decreases from 17 L to 11 L.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. ISFV is not unchanged: ECFV − PV changes from 23 − 6 = 17 L to 19 − 8 = 11 L.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. ECFV falls, but RISA-measured plasma volume rises from 6 L to 8 L.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Plasma volume rises, not falls; ISFV decreases rather than increases.
choice_explanations.F: Incorrect. Plasma volume rises rather than falls, and ISFV decreases rather than remaining unchanged.

A.text: First Aid p.599 distinguishes interstitial fluid and plasma as portions of extracellular fluid and provides their usual relative proportions; these measured values do not show both compartments increasing.

B.text: First Aid p.599 shows plasma and interstitial fluid are distinct ECF compartments and that plasma volume is measured with radiolabeled albumin. Applying the question's marker values gives PV 6→8 L and ISFV (ECFV−PV) 17→11 L.

C.text: First Aid p.599 identifies plasma and interstitial fluid as separate ECF compartments; the given tracer values show ISFV changes rather than remaining constant.

D.text: First Aid p.599 describes the ECF compartments and radiolabeled-albumin measurement of plasma volume; here RISA rises from 6 L to 8 L, contradicting a plasma-volume decrease.

E.text: First Aid p.599 distinguishes plasma from interstitial ECF; the supplied values show plasma rises and ISFV decreases, the reverse of this pairing.

F.text: First Aid p.599 identifies the plasma/interstitial compartments; tracer subtraction shows ISFV decreases, while RISA shows plasma volume increases.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.599 shows fluid compartments: ECF is divided into interstitial fluid and plasma, with interstitial fluid comprising about 75% of ECF and plasma about 25%. It states plasma volume can be measured with radiolabeled albumin and extracellular volume with inulin or mannitol. The question's radioactive-sodium marker for ECFV and subtraction (ISFV = ECFV − PV) are supplied by the question's measurement framework; the numerical calculation is shown explicitly in the explanation.
question_figure_description: 治疗前后各体液标记物分布容积(VOD)表。

stem: A 55-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of hematemesis. His fasting serum gastrin level is 8 times normal, and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy shows multiple duodenal ulcers. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is suspected. Administration of which substance is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The patient has Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES), which is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) typically located in the pancreas or duodenal wall. Gastrinomas are multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) tumors that secrete the GI hormone gastrin in an unregulated manner. Gastrin is normally produced by G cells located in the gastric antrum or duodenum; its physiologic role is to stimulate gastric acid production by parietal cells. Gastrin production is normally subject to negative feedback regulation by two other GI hormones, somatostatin and secretin. Because gastrinomas are not subject to this feedback regulation, fasting gastrin levels and gastric acid production in patients with ZES are typically elevated, resulting in peptic ulcers and diarrhea. While ZES is strongly suspected in patients with elevated gastrin levels, the test is not diagnostic. The secretin stimulation test is used to differentiate ZES from other causes of hypergastrinemia. Whereas secretin injection inhibits gastrin production in a healthy individual, it causes a marked increase in serum gastrin in patients with ZES. The physiologic mechanism remains unclear. A secretin stimulation test involves rapid (over approximately 1 minute) intravenous infusion of 2 units/kg secretin. Serum gastrin levels are measured at various times for 30 minutes after injection. An increase in serum gastrin of more than 200 ng/mL is diagnostic for ZES.

Cholecystokinin (CCK, choice A) is a peptide hormone secreted by I cells in the small intestine. It normally stimulates gallbladder contraction, facilitates bile secretion, and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion.

Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP, also known as glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide, choice B) is released by K cells in the duodenum and jejunum. It stimulates insulin release from the endocrine pancreas, although it can also decrease gastric acid secretion at sufficiently high levels.

Motilin (choice C) is a hormone secreted by M cells that enhances peristalsis in the small intestine. It has an important role in facilitating migrating myoelectric complexes, which begin in the stomach during the fasting state and drive a peristaltic wave that clears residual intestinal contents (indigestible particles, bacteria, cells that have been shed from the mucosa) from the GI tract in preparation for the next meal.

Pentagastrin (choice D) is a synthetic peptide that stimulates gastric acid production by binding to the gastrin-CCK-B receptor on parietal cells. Although up to 40% of pancreatic gastrinoma cells contain CCK-B receptors and therefore can respond to either CCK or gastrin itself, pentagastrin has minimal effects on gastrin secretion and response to its infusion is not reliable as a clinical test.

choice_explanations.A: CCK stimulates pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction; it is not the diagnostic stimulation test for gastrinoma.
choice_explanations.B: GIP is an incretin from K cells that increases insulin release and suppresses gastric acid secretion; it does not confirm ZES.
choice_explanations.C: Motilin stimulates migrating motor complexes during fasting; it is unrelated to the diagnostic test for a gastrinoma.
choice_explanations.D: Pentagastrin is a gastrin-like secretagogue, not the confirmatory test for ZES; the diagnostic response is measured after secretin.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Secretin usually inhibits gastrin release, but gastrinoma cells produce a paradoxical increase in serum gastrin after secretin administration.

A.text: CCK is produced by I cells and stimulates pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction; it is not the ZES test.

B.text: GIP is produced by K cells and increases insulin release; it also suppresses gastric H+ secretion.

C.text: Motilin from the small intestine produces migrating motor complexes.

D.text: No direct First Aid 2026 entry for pentagastrin or its diagnostic use was found; it is not the ZES confirmatory stimulus.

E.text: First Aid identifies a positive secretin stimulation test in ZES: gastrin rises after secretin administration, which normally inhibits gastrin release.

fa_summary: MEN1 includes pancreatic endocrine tumors such as gastrinomas. In Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, a positive secretin stimulation test produces increased gastrin after secretin administration, unlike the normal inhibitory response.

fa_subchapter: Colorectal cancer risk / Lynch syndrome / FAP
stem: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician for health maintenance. He has no complaints, drinks no more than one alcoholic drink per day, and does not smoke. He has not previously undergone screening colonoscopy and is scheduled for one. The pedigree summarizes his immediate family history and the ages at diagnosis for each illness. Which is his strongest risk factor for colon cancer?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Patients over 50 years old are at increased risk for colon cancer. Other risk factors are listed below: obesity; low-fiber, low fruit/vegetable, high red-meat, and high animal-fat diets; familial cancer syndromes; inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis more than Crohn disease); and a first-degree relative with colon cancer.

Alcohol use (choice B) is associated with oropharyngeal, laryngeal, esophageal, and pancreatic cancer. Heavy alcohol use may increase the risk of colon cancer, but this patient does not have this pattern of use.

Endometrial carcinoma (choice C) in the mother (family history), if this was an isolated (nonhereditary) condition, would not predispose the patient to colon carcinoma. The hereditary association of endometrial carcinoma before age 50 and increased risk of colon cancer reflects Lynch syndrome [hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), choice E] in a family. However, the patient's mother was diagnosed much later than 50. Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant cancer syndrome which, like familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), predisposes patients to colon cancer. The defect is in DNA repair enzymes. As an aside, no autosomal dominant conditions can be proven with a genogram or family tree. A genetic test would be required. Only recessive conditions can be proven with at least three generations of a family tree, if the condition skips a generation. Variable penetrance complicates this relationship even further.

Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP, choice D) is an autosomal dominant cancer syndrome. Patients have a congenital defect in the APC gene. FAP patients have a strong family history of colon cancer, especially at a young age (under 40). Many hundreds or thousands of polyps are seen on colonoscopy.

Lack of screening (choice F) is not a risk factor for colon cancer. Screening by itself does not increase or decrease one's chances of disease, though it may decrease one's chances of dying from the disease. The main goal of screening is to catch diseases early so that intervention can occur early. Currently, screening either with colonoscopy, high-sensitivity fecal occult blood testing, or sigmoidoscopy is recommended per the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines. Colon cancer screening is recommended to start at age 50 and continue until age 75. Screening at earlier ages is recommended if there is a previous diagnosis of colon cancer, a strong family history, or diagnosis of FAP, HNPCC, or inflammatory bowel disease.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Colorectal cancer risk rises with age; most cases occur after age 50, and age is the strongest risk factor among the choices for this patient.
choice_explanations.B: The patient reports only occasional/light alcohol use. The source explanation notes that heavy alcohol use may contribute to colorectal cancer risk, but this history does not fit that pattern.
choice_explanations.C: Endometrial cancer can be associated with Lynch syndrome, especially when it occurs at a younger age. His mother's diagnosis at 72, without a family history of colorectal cancer, is less suggestive of Lynch syndrome.
choice_explanations.D: FAP is an autosomal-dominant APC syndrome characterized by hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas and often early colorectal cancer; the pedigree does not show that pattern.
choice_explanations.E: Lynch syndrome is an autosomal-dominant mismatch-repair syndrome associated with colorectal and endometrial cancers. The family history here lacks colorectal cancer and the mother's endometrial cancer was late-onset.
choice_explanations.F: Not a biological risk factor for developing cancer. Screening helps detect precancerous polyps/cancer and can lower mortality, but absence of prior screening does not itself cause colorectal cancer.

A.text: First Aid states most colorectal cancers occur in patients over 50; age is the strongest supported listed risk in this case.

B.text: No direct First Aid 2026 entry for this patient's light alcohol exposure as a colorectal-cancer risk factor was found; the First Aid CRC risk list emphasizes adenomatous/serrated polyps, familial syndromes, IBD, tobacco, and processed meat/low fiber.

C.text: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is associated with endometrial cancer; the question's late-onset family history is interpreted with the Word explanation, not as a direct FA age threshold.

D.text: FAP is an autosomal-dominant APC tumor-suppressor syndrome with thousands of colorectal polyps and very high CRC risk.

E.text: Lynch syndrome is hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer caused by mismatch-repair gene mutations and is associated with endometrial, ovarian, stomach, and skin cancers.

F.text: No direct First Aid entry frames lack of screening as a cause/risk factor. Printed p. 395 describes screening recommendations and states CEA is for monitoring rather than screening; the distinction that screening changes detection/mortality rather than incidence is from the verified Word explanation.

fa_summary: Colorectal cancer risk increases with age; most patients are over 50. Distinguish common sporadic risk from hereditary syndromes: FAP (APC; numerous polyps) and Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair; colorectal and endometrial cancers).
question_figure_description: Only the family pedigree and family-history labels are included; the full source screenshot, stem, answer choices, answer, and interface are excluded.

stem: A 46-year-old woman returns to her physician because of progressive fatigue and decreased urine output. She has chronic stiffness in her hands and knees that is worse in the morning and improves with activity. Physical examination shows mild periorbital and ankle edema, ulnar deviation of both wrists, and deformity of the proximal interphalangeal joints. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, leukocytes 5.0 × 10³/mm³, erythrocytes 3.0 × 10⁶/mm³, reticulocytes 3.0%, ESR 30 mm/h, platelets 250 × 10³/mm³, and MCV 90 μm³. Two-hour postprandial glucose is 115 mg/dL. Serum studies show Na⁺ 156 mEq/L, K⁺ 5.2 mEq/L, calcium 9.0 mg/dL, BUN 20 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.2 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and 1+ blood, with no crystals or casts; 24-hour urine protein is 3.8 g. Renal biopsy shows mesangial matrix thickening and amorphous eosinophilic material with apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining. In which location is this material most likely synthesized?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient most likely presents with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), complicated by amyloidosis. RA is a chronic inflammatory joint disease characterized by morning stiffness improving with activity, ulnar deviation, subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules, constitutional symptoms, and inflammatory pannus formation. RA can involve a number of joints, but in the hand it characteristically affects the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, while sparing the distal interphalangeal joints (DIP).

As with other systemic inflammatory conditions, RA can also result in amyloidosis. The liver produces serum amyloid-associated (SAA) protein in response to systemic inflammation (cytokine-mediated). SAA can degrade to form amyloid-associated (AA) protein, which can distribute in the kidneys, heart, and gastrointestinal tract. In our patient, deposition of amyloid in the kidneys results in glomerular disease. Amyloid stains red with Congo Red stain and exhibits apple-green birefringence upon polarization. Other chronic inflammatory conditions associated with AA amyloid deposition include chronic tuberculosis and SLE.

This patient has an elevated ESR and normocytic anemia (low RBC count and Hb, normal MCV) associated with chronic inflammation. An elevated reticulocyte count reflects normal bone marrow response to anemia. Elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen support renal dysfunction due to amyloid deposition within the kidney. Proteinuria is characteristic of amyloidosis. A normal calcium level rules out multiple myeloma-associated amyloid. A normal postprandial glucose rules out diabetes mellitus.

Bone marrow (choice A) and lymph nodes are the source of amyloid light-chain proteins, which cause amyloidosis in plasma-cell proliferations (e.g., multiple myeloma). Symptoms include hypercalcemia, renal disease, anemia (hemolytic), and lytic bone lesions (CRAB mnemonic), which is mostly inconsistent with our patient's presentation. This is the most common form of amyloidosis in the United States today. Beta-amyloid protein is found in the brain (choice B) and forms the core of the plaques in Alzheimer disease. The synovium (choice D) may be the site of chronic inflammation and pannus formation in RA, but is not the site of amyloid synthesis. In medullary thyroid carcinoma, excess calcitonin production by neoplastic parafollicular C cells leads to heavy amyloid deposition within the thyroid gland (choice E). Symptoms of this disease include an enlarging neck mass and diarrhea, which is not consistent with our patient's presentation.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Bone marrow plasma cells produce immunoglobulin light chains that form AL amyloid in plasma-cell dyscrasias; the chronic rheumatoid inflammation here points to AA amyloid instead.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. β-amyloid is generated in the brain from amyloid precursor protein and is associated with Alzheimer disease; it does not explain renal AA amyloid in chronic inflammatory arthritis.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Hepatocytes synthesize serum amyloid A, the precursor of secondary AA amyloid associated with chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Synovium is inflamed in rheumatoid arthritis, but it is not the source of circulating serum amyloid A.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Thyroid C cells produce calcitonin; calcitonin-derived amyloid can deposit locally in medullary thyroid carcinoma, not cause systemic renal AA amyloidosis.

A.text: First Aid associates AL amyloid from immunoglobulin light chains with plasma-cell dyscrasias, a distinct amyloid precursor from AA.

B.text: First Aid identifies β-amyloid in Alzheimer disease as a distinct amyloid type.

C.text: First Aid identifies AA as serum amyloid A and associates it with chronic inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis; the source explanation identifies the liver as the synthesis site.

D.text: No direct First Aid page match was identified for synovium as the synthesis site of systemic AA amyloid.

E.text: First Aid associates calcitonin-derived amyloid with medullary thyroid carcinoma, a localized deposit rather than systemic AA amyloidosis.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.208 distinguishes systemic amyloid types: secondary AA (serum amyloid A) occurs with chronic inflammatory conditions including rheumatoid arthritis; AL derives from immunoglobulin light chains in plasma-cell disorders; β-amyloid is associated with Alzheimer disease; and calcitonin amyloid with medullary thyroid cancer. Printed p.472 discusses rheumatoid arthritis. The source explanation supplies the specific synthesis site—liver; a primary study confirms hepatocyte synthesis of serum amyloid A.

stem: In an experiment, 20 male animals undergo orchiectomy. After 2 weeks of recovery, the effects of castration on hormone secretion are evaluated. The animals are otherwise normal. Which change in hormone secretion is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This question tests the concept of surgical castration. Through orchiectomy, the testicle is unable to respond to LH secretion by the pituitary to produce testosterone, and levels of LH will increase. This is actually a treatment for advanced prostate cancer. By surgically removing the testicles, the production of testosterone is inhibited, which will cause regression of hormone-sensitive prostate cancer. In such patients, a successful response to treatment is achieved by having castrate levels of testosterone in the blood (less than 50 mg/dL) and high levels of LH. The same effect can be achieved with LHRH agonist-antagonist agents such as leuprolide.

Consequently, GnRH and pituitary LH and FSH levels will increase.

Decreased prolactin (choice B) would not be an effect of decreased testosterone. The effect of prolactin on male reproduction is not well understood, but it is well known that hyperprolactinemia inhibits gonadotropin secretion and action. Therefore, elevated prolactin acts to decrease testicular steroidogenesis and spermatogenesis, and results in infertility and impotence.

Increased activin (choice C) and increased inhibin (choice D) are incorrect, because both of these hormones are made in the testes. Therefore, castration would decrease these hormones.

ReKaps: Castration drastically decreases testosterone levels, removing the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary. Consequently, GnRH and pituitary LH and FSH levels increase.

choice_explanations.A: Without testicular testosterone, negative feedback on the hypothalamus is reduced, so GnRH rises rather than falls.
choice_explanations.B: Prolactin is not directly lowered by orchiectomy; elevated prolactin can suppress gonadotropin secretion, but it is not the predicted response here.
choice_explanations.C: Activin is produced in the testes and falls after orchiectomy rather than increasing.
choice_explanations.D: Inhibin is produced by Sertoli cells in the testes and falls after orchiectomy.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Loss of testosterone feedback increases pituitary LH secretion.

A.text: The reproductive axis diagram shows testosterone feedback to hypothalamus/pituitary; removing testes removes this feedback, so GnRH rises rather than decreases.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly state that orchiectomy lowers prolactin.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss activin response to orchiectomy.

D.text: Sertoli cells produce inhibin B, which inhibits FSH; orchiectomy removes this source, so inhibin does not rise.

E.text: Leydig cells produce testosterone in response to LH; removal of testicular testosterone feedback raises pituitary gonadotropin drive.

stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of vaginal bleeding, nausea, and vomiting. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago, and a home pregnancy test was positive. The uterus is enlarged. Ultrasound shows a multiloculated cystic structure within the uterine cavity but no clearly defined embryo. Serum hCG is markedly elevated (>100,000 mIU/mL). Dilation and curettage yields placental-like tissue without fetal tissue. Which karyotype is most likely in the specimen?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The lesion described is a hydatidiform mole, of which two forms exist: complete and partial. In a complete mole, the karyotype is 46,XX (or, in a few cases, 46,XY). The most common presenting symptom is vaginal bleeding. Serum hCG levels are dramatically increased and the uterus is enlarged (greater than gestational age). Hyperemesis can occur in patients with complete moles, probably due to the extremely high hCG levels, but is rare in patients with partial moles. The chorionic villi are edematous and have a characteristic grape-like, multicystic appearance. In this form, fetal tissue is absent. Ultrasound reveals a snowstorm appearance. It is important to note that, unlike the partial mole, which very rarely develops into choriocarcinoma, complete moles carry a 2% increased risk for development of choriocarcinoma. This represents fertilization of an empty ovum with a diploid sperm rather than a haploid genotype (23,X; choice A). The disease is unrelated to Turner syndrome, 45,XO (choice B). A complete mole contains the normal number of chromosomes and does not contain an additional single Y chromosome (choice D); this karyotype is seen with Klinefelter syndrome. In a partial hydatidiform mole, fetal tissue is often evident. The conceptus is triploid, with a 69,XXX or 69,XXY karyotype (choice E), arising from one ovum and two sperm. Both enlarged and normal villi are present. Ultrasound reveals a mixed snowstorm appearance with fetal parts.

choice_explanations.A: 23,X is a haploid gametic complement, not the usual diploid karyotype of a complete mole.
choice_explanations.B: 45,XO is the karyotype of Turner syndrome, not a molar gestation.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Complete hydatidiform moles most commonly have a 46,XX karyotype and lack fetal parts.
choice_explanations.D: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, not a complete mole.
choice_explanations.E: 69,XXY is a triploid karyotype characteristic of a partial mole, which often has fetal parts.

A.text: First Aid 2026 lists complete-mole diploid and partial-mole triploid karyotypes, but does not directly discuss a haploid 23,X mole.

B.text: 45,XO is Turner syndrome, a sex-chromosome disorder rather than a molar karyotype.

C.text: Complete mole is most commonly 46,XX, with no fetal parts.

D.text: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome; it is distinct from molar pregnancy.

E.text: Partial mole can be triploid, including 69,XXY, and may contain fetal parts.

stem: A 38-year-old primigravid woman at 34 weeks’ gestation comes to the physician because of swelling of her hands and feet. Her blood pressure is 158/100 mm Hg; prior readings were normal. Urinalysis shows moderate proteinuria. Serum AST and ALT are elevated, and the platelet count is slightly decreased. Which event is believed to initiate the pathogenesis of this condition?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Preeclampsia is new-onset hypertension with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks of gestation. Severe disease may involve the liver, kidneys, and central nervous system; HELLP syndrome is a severe complication. The initiating event is placental ischemia due to abnormal trophoblast invasion of the spiral arteries. The resulting placental and vascular changes lead to maternal endothelial dysfunction and injury to organs including the liver, kidneys, and brain. Chorioamnionitis (choice A) is an infection and is not the initiating cause of preeclampsia. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (choice B) may complicate severe disease but is not the initiating event. Maternal hypertension (choice C) is a consequence of the placental process, not its cause. Ischemic injury to maternal organs (choice D) is likewise a downstream consequence.

choice_explanations.A: Chorioamnionitis is an ascending intra-amniotic infection and does not initiate the placental vascular pathology of preeclampsia.
choice_explanations.B: DIC may complicate severe preeclampsia/HELLP but is downstream, not the initial event.
choice_explanations.C: Maternal hypertension is a manifestation of the disease process after abnormal placentation and placental ischemia.
choice_explanations.D: Renal ischemia or injury can occur as maternal end-organ damage, but it is not the initiating event.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Abnormal placentation leads to placental ischemia, which initiates the maternal syndrome.

A.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss chorioamnionitis as a preeclampsia mechanism.

B.text: DIC is a possible complication of HELLP/preeclampsia, not the initiating event.

C.text: Preeclampsia is defined by new hypertension after 20 weeks, but hypertension follows the placental mechanism.

D.text: Renal dysfunction is an end-organ complication of preeclampsia, downstream from placental ischemia.

E.text: Abnormal placental spiral arteries cause ischemia and endothelial dysfunction in preeclampsia.

stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of abdominal pain and nausea. Her last menstrual period began 7 days ago, and she reports unprotected sexual intercourse. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). Examination shows lower abdominal tenderness; pelvic examination shows mucopurulent discharge, adnexal tenderness, and cervical motion tenderness. Pregnancy testing is negative, and the leukocyte count is 14,000/mm³. Which complication is most likely associated with this disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This young woman has pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which can involve the uterus, oviducts, and ovaries; it can often also involve neighboring pelvic organs. This disorder is classically caused by ascending infection with sexually transmitted agents such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis. Symptoms include a mucopurulent cervicitis (often producing a vaginal discharge), abdominal pain, or abnormal vaginal bleeding. Fever, an elevated white count, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate may also be seen. Therapy consists of antibiotics with activity against N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, vaginal anaerobes, and facultative gram-negative rods (e.g., ceftriaxone plus doxycycline with or without metronidazole). Infertility is a feared complication of tubal scarring and adhesions following salpingitis in PID. Another complication from tubal scarring is ectopic tubal pregnancy. Bacteremia, peritonitis (because the fallopian tubes open into the pelvic cavity), and intestinal obstruction (secondary to peritonitis, inflammation, and adhesion formation in bowel loops near the adnexae) may also complicate this disorder.

Abdominal enlargement due to ascites (choice A) is observed in advanced cases of ovarian carcinoma. Cervical carcinoma (choice B) is related to infection with certain high-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), e.g., strains 16, 18, and 31. Cervical carcinoma can present with intermittent vaginal bleeding. Pap smears are mainly used for screening of cervical dysplasia and carcinoma. Although this patient has unprotected sexual intercourse and is at increased risk for acquiring HPV infection, HPV is not the cause of her symptoms. Exsanguination (choice C) is a feared complication of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Pseudomyxoma peritonei (choice E) is a very serious complication of mucinous tumors of the ovary or appendix.

choice_explanations.A: Ascites can occur with advanced ovarian carcinoma, not as the typical complication of acute PID.
choice_explanations.B: Cervical carcinoma is associated with persistent high-risk HPV infection, not a direct complication of this acute PID presentation.
choice_explanations.C: Exsanguination is a feared complication of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; this patient's pregnancy test is negative.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Tubal scarring and adhesions after salpingitis can impair gamete transport and cause infertility.
choice_explanations.E: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is associated with mucinous ovarian or appendiceal tumors, not PID.

A.text: Advanced ovarian tumors may present with abdominal distention and ascites; this is separate from PID.

B.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive pages do not directly map acute PID to cervical carcinoma in this differential.

C.text: Ectopic pregnancy can cause first-trimester bleeding and pain and may require urgent treatment; tubal rupture is a potential emergency.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly state infertility as a PID complication; the source explanation identifies tubal scarring/adhesions as the mechanism.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss pseudomyxoma peritonei on its reproductive pages.

stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressive weakness, fatigue, and abnormal uterine bleeding. Examination shows pallor, a suprapubic mass, and an enlarged uterus with a normal cervix. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume of 68 μm³, and platelet count of 300,000/mm³. Hysterectomy reveals an 8-cm, well-demarcated submucosal uterine tumor with a whorled cut surface. Which histologic finding is most likely?

options.text: Hyperchromatic glandular cells invading the myometrium
Nests of typical endometrial glands within the myometrium
Pedunculated masses with closely packed benign endometrial glands
Pedunculated masses with cystically dilated benign endometrial glands
Whorled bundles of typical smooth muscle cells

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Abnormal uterine bleeding is commonly caused by polyps, hyperplasia, carcinoma, endometritis, and leiomyomas. The macroscopic features of leiomyomas are very characteristic. The most important clues to consider include well-demarcated borders and a whorled pattern on cut surface. Leiomyomas are the most common tumors in women. These benign neoplasms develop from smooth muscle cells of the myometrium and are estrogen dependent, so they may grow rapidly during pregnancy and undergo regression after menopause. Leiomyomas are asymptomatic in most cases, but those of large size, especially if in a submucosal location, may cause several gynecologic/obstetric complications, including abnormal uterine bleeding and recurrent spontaneous abortion. Such complications justify surgical treatment by hysterectomy. The smooth muscle origin of leiomyoma is evident on H&E-stained sections: neoplastic cells appear indistinguishable from normal smooth muscle cells of the myometrium. These cells express smooth muscle actin.

Hyperchromatic glandular cells invading the myometrium (choice A) would be seen in endometrial carcinoma. In the United States, endometrial carcinoma is the most common cancer of the female genital tract. It more commonly occurs in women between the ages of 55 and 65. Grossly, endometrial carcinoma may fill the uterine cavity, but the tumor mass tends to be fungating and can be necrotic. Carcinoma would have ill-defined invasive borders, and would not be circumscribed like a leiomyoma. Nests of typical endometrial glands within the myometrium (choice B) is the microscopic description of adenomyosis, which is another cause of abnormal uterine bleeding. It is most commonly seen in women before menopause. Adenomyosis is a nonneoplastic condition that causes diffuse enlargement of the uterus; although it can also focally thicken the myometrium, it does not present as a well-demarcated tumor like a leiomyoma. Pedunculated masses with closely packed benign endometrial glands (choice C) describes hyperplastic endometrial polyps. Hyperplasia and even carcinoma can arise inside an endometrial polyp. Polyps tend to be reddish brown in color and do not have a white, whorled cut surface. Pedunculated masses with cystically dilated endometrial glands (choice D) describes atrophic endometrial polyps. Endometrial polyps also give rise to uterine bleeding, more commonly close to menopause. Polyps tend to be reddish brown in color and do not have a white, whorled cut surface.

choice_explanations.A: Hyperchromatic glands invading myometrium indicate endometrial carcinoma, which is typically invasive and not a sharply demarcated whorled smooth-muscle mass.
choice_explanations.B: Endometrial glands within the myometrium describe adenomyosis, which usually causes diffuse, boggy uterine enlargement rather than a well-circumscribed tumor.
choice_explanations.C: Closely packed benign glands describe a hyperplastic endometrial polyp, not a whorled myometrial smooth-muscle tumor.
choice_explanations.D: Cystically dilated benign glands describe an atrophic endometrial polyp, not a leiomyoma.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Leiomyoma histology consists of well-demarcated whorled bundles of bland smooth-muscle cells.

A.text: Endometrial carcinoma is a separate uterine neoplasm; the well-demarcated whorled tumor instead matches myometrial leiomyoma.

B.text: Adenomyosis is endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, usually with diffuse boggy uterine enlargement.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe histology of hyperplastic endometrial polyps in this comparison.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe cystically dilated endometrial polyp glands in this comparison.

E.text: Leiomyoma is a benign myometrial tumor with a gross whorled pattern of smooth-muscle bundles and well-demarcated borders.

stem: A 35-year-old woman sustains head trauma in a motor vehicle collision. She was an unrestrained passenger and hit her head on the windshield. Upon arrival in the emergency department, she is unresponsive. Respirations are 6/minute and pulse oximetry is 85% on facemask. Her pulse is 125/min and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. She is intubated for airway protection and admitted to the intensive care unit. One week later, her hemoglobin decreases from 12 g/dL to 9 g/dL. An upper endoscopy shows several gastric ulcers and diffuse gastritis. An increase in which of the following is the most likely explanation for her gastric lesions?
explanation:
The correct answer is G. Pepsin production is a normal physiologic activity of the stomach that, in conditions of stress, may overwhelm the stomach’s weakened defenses. The result is gastric ulcers known as stress ulcers. These stress ulcers can be precipitated by severe stress, sepsis, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use, shock, severe burn or trauma, and/or elevated intracranial pressure. Gastric acid production may also increase and cause acute ulceration. Furthermore, pepsin and gastric acid production may remain unchanged and still result in gastric ulcers if the gastric defenses are weakened by stress. This patient has suffered significant physiologic stress from the accident, resultant head trauma, and shock. All of the other answer choices represent normal defensive forces in the stomach.

Hydrochloric acid absorption (choice A) does not occur in the stomach. Acid is neutralized by the alkaline small-bowel secretions before it reaches the colon. Increased bicarbonate transport (choice B) would protect the gastric epithelium from the potentially harmful acidity of the gastric contents. The adherent mucus is relatively alkaline, providing local protection to the superficial mucosa. Cholecystokinin (CCK; choice C) causes the gallbladder to contract in response to a fatty meal. CCK production falls dramatically in intensive care unit patients (mostly because they are not consuming large meals), and these patients are prone to developing gallstones due to bile stasis. There is no association between CCK and peptic ulcers.

Gastric epithelial cells can normally replicate rapidly, allowing mucosal defects to be repaired quickly. Increasing the regenerative capacity of the epithelium (choice D) would have a protective effect against ulceration. The gastric mucosa is richly supplied with blood, providing the epithelial cells with an ample supply of nutrients, oxygen, and bicarbonate to contend with the harsh gastric microenvironment. Stress ulcers are associated with compromised gastric blood flow, not increased flow (choice E). Mucus protects the gastric epithelium by virtue of being water-insoluble, impermeable to pepsin, and slowly permeated by acid (H⁺). Increasing mucus production (choice F) has a protective effect for the gastric mucosa.

ReKaps: Gastric stress ulcers are multiple small, superficial ulcers of the stomach and duodenum that generally present under severe stress. The increased production of pepsin and acid, along with the imbalance of the protective mechanisms of the stomach, accounts for the pathogenesis of this type of ulcer.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. The stomach does not absorb acid in the way implied; acid is neutralized in the small intestine. Increased acid secretion, not absorption, may contribute to acute ulceration.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Bicarbonate neutralizes acid at the mucosal surface and is protective; increasing its transport would oppose injury.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic secretion and slows gastric emptying; it is not the cause of stress ulcers. CCK levels may fall in critically ill patients with reduced food intake.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Faster epithelial regeneration repairs mucosal defects and is protective against ulceration.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Gastric perfusion supports mucosal defenses. Stress-related ischemia/compromised blood flow promotes injury; increased flow would be protective.
choice_explanations.F: Incorrect. Mucus forms a protective barrier over the epithelium and limits exposure to acid and pepsin; increased secretion would be protective.
choice_explanations.G: Correct. In severe stress, pepsin production can overwhelm weakened gastric defenses and contribute to stress-ulcer formation.

A.text: No direct First Aid 2026 match for gastric acid absorption; the source explanation distinguishes absorption from acid production.

B.text: Bicarbonate from gastric and other mucosal cells neutralizes acid and is trapped in mucus covering the gastric epithelium; it is protective.

C.text: CCK is produced by duodenal/jejunal I cells and stimulates pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction; no direct ulcer-causing role is listed.

D.text: No direct First Aid 2026 entry was found for increased gastric epithelial regenerative capacity as a named ulcer mechanism; the protective interpretation follows the source explanation.

E.text: First Aid links burn-associated Curling ulcers to hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia, supporting impaired—not increased—mucosal perfusion as injurious.

F.text: No direct First Aid 2026 statement was found that increased mucus secretion prevents stress ulcers. The page 379 figure labels gastric mucus-related cells, but does not state the protective rationale in this choice.

G.text: Pepsin is produced by chief cells and digests protein; local acid and vagal stimulation increase secretion, and acid converts pepsinogen to active pepsin. Page 386 separately links brain injury to acute Cushing ulcers through increased vagal stimulation and gastric H+ production.

fa_summary: Acute gastritis/erosions can follow brain injury (Cushing ulcer) through increased vagal stimulation → increased ACh → increased gastric H+ production. First Aid also identifies pepsin as a chief-cell protein-digesting secretion increased by vagal stimulation/local acid, and bicarbonate as an acid-neutralizing mucosal defense.

stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of dark urine and grayish stools. Physical examination shows mild scleral icterus and right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies show a total bilirubin of 3.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 2.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase of 150 U/L, AST of 9 U/L, and ALT of 10 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Blockage of the common bile duct by a gallstone (choledocholithiasis) causes a reflux of conjugated bilirubin back into the blood, resulting in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (‘direct’ bilirubin). Dark urine and pale stool color are pathognomonic for biliary tract obstruction. A fraction of conjugated bilirubin can be filtered into renal tubules as urine bilirubin, resulting in dark urine. Grayish, pale stools indicate a lack of stercobilins, indicating that the conjugated bilirubin never reached the intestine.

Complete blockage of the duct is usually severely painful. The right upper quadrant tenderness on palpation suggests that the duct is not completely obstructed; this would also account for the absence of grossly elevated alkaline phosphatase. Biliary duct inflammation typically increases alkaline phosphatase, but the normal transaminases indicate an absence of hepatocyte damage.

Autoimmune hemolysis (choice A) can cause red to red-brown urine if hemoglobinuria occurs, but would not cause gray stools. Autoimmune hemolysis along with Crigler-Najjar syndrome (choice C) and Gilbert syndrome (choice D) would result in indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia. The predominance of unconjugated bilirubinemia overwhelms bilirubin synthesis beyond maximum hepatocyte uptake. Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I is due to an absence of UDP glucuronyl transferase, which prevents the glucuronide conjugation of bilirubin by hepatocytes, resulting in severe unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia. Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II has markedly reduced UDP glucuronyl transferase activity, while Gilbert syndrome has mildly decreased bilirubin glucuronidation. Gilbert syndrome presents in young adulthood with intermittent jaundice during periods of fasting, stress, or use of alcohol or medications.

Viral hepatitis (choice E) causes marked increases in hepatic transaminases, AST and ALT, and mild increases in alkaline phosphatase. Patients would have a mixed pattern of elevated unconjugated and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, but would not have dark urine and gray stools. Additionally, viral hepatitis is frequently accompanied by fever.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Hemolysis causes predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and may cause hemoglobinuria, but does not explain pale stools from absent intestinal bilirubin delivery.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. A common bile duct stone obstructs bile flow, producing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine, and pale stools.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Crigler-Najjar syndrome impairs bilirubin conjugation and causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, usually presenting early in life; it does not cause acholic stools.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Gilbert syndrome causes mild, intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, often during fasting, illness, or stress, and does not cause dark urine with pale stools.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Viral hepatitis typically causes marked aminotransferase elevation and a mixed bilirubin pattern; it does not fit the near-normal AST/ALT or classic obstructive stool/urine findings.

A.text: Hemolysis is listed among causes of unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia, unlike this patient's predominant direct bilirubin.

B.text: Gallstones are a cause of biliary obstruction; page 400 classifies biliary tract obstruction as a cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

C.text: Crigler-Najjar syndrome is an inherited cause of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to absent or markedly reduced UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity.

D.text: Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, often with fasting, stress, or illness.

E.text: Hepatitis is listed as a cause of mixed hyperbilirubinemia, in contrast to the predominantly conjugated obstructive pattern here.

fa_summary: Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia suggests biliary obstruction or an excretion defect. Gallstones can obstruct the biliary tract; unconjugated bilirubin instead rises with hemolysis, Crigler-Najjar, or Gilbert syndrome. Hepatitis commonly produces mixed hyperbilirubinemia.

stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician for infertility evaluation. During the last 6 months she has had two positive pregnancy tests, but then menses began within days of the tests. She and her husband are healthy, with no known reproductive defects or chromosomal abnormalities. Which of the following laboratory findings in serum is most likely in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient's problem is that she is able to conceive but not able to maintain pregnancy. Spontaneous abortions very early in the pregnancy are usually due to chromosomal abnormalities but can be due to abnormal hormone secretion. The fertilized ovum remains in the oviduct for 2 to 3 days, then enters the uterus by day 3 or 4. Once in the uterus, the morula develops into a blastocyst, the zona pellucida is shed, and the blastocyst implants into the uterine wall on day 7. The movement from the oviduct to the uterus is largely regulated by progesterone and estrogen, so a decrease in progesterone could prevent implantation. However, this woman did obtain a positive pregnancy test, implying hCG production. Around 6 to 8 days postfertilization, hCG production begins and can be detected by a pregnancy test. Normally, hCG acts like LH to increase luteal progesterone production, which prevents menses. If hCG is ineffective in maintaining the corpus luteum, it will regress. The resulting loss of progesterone causes the endometrium to atrophy and the pregnancy will be terminated.

High plasma estrogen (choice A) and high plasma progesterone (choice D) are normal during pregnancy and would not lead to spontaneous abortion. However, estrogen levels rise more slowly during the first half of pregnancy than during the second half, so severely elevated estrogen would not be seen until later in the pregnancy. High plasma hCG (choice B) would be expected during pregnancy. The plasma levels of hCG double every 2 to 3 days in early pregnancy until about 10 to 15 weeks' gestation, when placental progesterone negatively feeds back to greatly reduce hCG production. At this point, the placenta produces the majority of hormones responsible for maintenance of pregnancy. High plasma human placental lactogen (hPL; choice C) would not result in spontaneous abortion within a month of fertilization. hPL is produced by the same cells as hCG, and levels gradually rise from the third week of pregnancy until term. hPL promotes cell specialization in mammary glands similar to prolactin, but is less potent than prolactin in stimulating milk production. Its main action early in pregnancy is to maintain adequate fuel supply for the fetus; therefore, an elevation in hPL levels would not cause the patient to abort early in pregnancy.

choice_explanations.A: High estrogen is not the expected defect causing repeated very early pregnancy loss; estrogen normally rises during pregnancy.
choice_explanations.B: hCG is present because the pregnancy tests are positive; hCG normally supports the corpus luteum rather than causing its failure.
choice_explanations.C: hPL is produced by syncytiotrophoblast and rises with placental mass; it is not the hormone maintaining the corpus luteum at this stage.
choice_explanations.D: Progesterone should be adequate to maintain the endometrium; low rather than high progesterone explains the losses.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Inadequate progesterone support after corpus-luteum regression leads to endometrial atrophy and early pregnancy loss.

A.text: Placental estrogen rises during pregnancy, but the First Aid discussion does not identify elevated estrogen as a cause of this pattern of early loss.

B.text: Syncytiotrophoblast-derived hCG maintains the corpus luteum in the first trimester; the pregnancy test detects hCG.

C.text: hPL is a placental hormone that rises with placental mass; it is distinct from hCG-mediated corpus-luteum support.

D.text: Progesterone is mainly secreted by the corpus luteum during the first 10 weeks and maintains the endometrium.

E.text: hCG maintains the corpus luteum, increasing first-trimester progesterone; progesterone maintains the endometrium.

stem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 39 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. Another car struck the side of the car where she was a passenger. She was wearing her seat belt. She reports abdominal pain and has premature rupture of the amniotic membranes and contractions. Ultrasound reveals fetal tachycardia and placental abruption. Which of the following is she most likely to experience as a result of amniotic fluid entering the circulation?
explanation: The correct answer is D. Respiratory distress immediately follows amniotic fluid embolism. Emboli consisting of squamous cells, lanugo, and mucus deposit in the pulmonary microcirculation, producing numerous tiny pulmonary infarcts. Rupture of membranes allows amniotic fluid to enter the maternal circulation through a tear in the uterine or cervical veins. The dramatic respiratory distress may also reflect prostaglandins and other bioactive compounds present in high concentrations in the amniotic fluid embolus. Causes of amniotic fluid embolism include abdominal trauma, placental abruption or previa, amniocentesis, cesarean section, uterine rupture, and immediate cesarean delivery. Hemiplegia (choice A) would reflect ischemic injury to one cerebral hemisphere or one side of the brain stem resulting from arterial occlusion; a venous embolus would not produce such an insult. Preeclampsia (choice B) is a disorder of pregnancy characterized by hypertension and proteinuria (choice C) and occurs in the third trimester. Increased risk occurs with obesity, older maternal age, hypertension, and diabetes. Abnormal incomplete trophoblastic invasion of the spiral arteries can trigger release of vasoactive compounds, causing vasoconstriction, endothelial damage, and platelet dysfunction. Splinter hemorrhages (choice E) are small hemorrhages seen on toes and fingers due to a shower of microemboli arising in the arterial circulation. Amniotic fluid emboli arise in the veins and deposit in the lungs.

choice_explanations.A: Hemiplegia is a focal neurologic deficit and is not the characteristic immediate presentation of amniotic fluid embolism.
choice_explanations.B: Preeclampsia is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, not the acute pulmonary manifestation of amniotic fluid entering maternal circulation.
choice_explanations.C: Proteinuria can accompany preeclampsia but is not the immediate consequence tested here.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden respiratory distress from pulmonary microvascular obstruction and mediator effects; coagulopathy may also occur.
choice_explanations.E: Splinter hemorrhages are classically associated with infective endocarditis, not amniotic fluid embolism.

A.text: No direct First Aid 2026 reproductive-page discussion links hemiplegia to amniotic fluid embolism.

B.text: First Aid discusses preeclampsia separately, but not as a consequence of amniotic fluid embolism.

C.text: Proteinuria is discussed with preeclampsia, not as the acute manifestation of amniotic fluid embolism.

D.text: No direct First Aid 2026 reproductive-page entry for amniotic fluid embolism or its acute respiratory presentation was found; this mapping is supported by the source explanation.

E.text: No direct First Aid 2026 reproductive-page mapping connects splinter hemorrhages with this obstetric emergency.

stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of fever, chills, body aches, painful urination, and urinary urgency. His medical history includes well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes managed with oral hypoglycemic agents. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 134/88 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, hematocrit 40%, and leukocyte count 12,800/mm³. Physical examination shows mild abdominal tenderness. Digital rectal examination shows a diffusely enlarged, very tender prostate gland. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
explanation:
