stem: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician because of decreased libido and hot flashes. She states that her menstrual cycles have been sporadic and irregular for the past 6 months. Laboratory studies show elevated luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), with normal prolactin. Which of the following best explains these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Menopause usually occurs between the ages of 48 and 52, but the associated hormonal changes usually begin near age 45. Ovulation frequency begins to decline, and menses and fertility are reduced. Estrogen production is reduced as ovarian function fails, resulting in the characteristic hot flashes, as well as changes in secondary sex characteristics and bone density. The reduction in estrogens results in an increase in hypothalamic GnRH and pituitary gonadotropins. Estrogen normally feeds back to reduce the production of GnRH from the hypothalamus and LH and FSH from the pituitary. Therefore, GnRH, FSH, and LH levels would be increased in the absence of estrogen feedback regulation. Also, decreased libido occurs in women with ovarian failure due to a reduction in circulating testosterone.

While decreased GnRH (choice B) would result in secondary hypogonadism, LH and FSH would also be reduced. In this patient, LH and FSH are increased, and her complaints are caused by estrogen deficiency. This would suggest that the disorder is a loss of inhibitory feedback by estrogens. Androgens are produced in the theca cells in response to LH stimulation, then converted to estrogen in the granulosa cells. While increased LH levels could stimulate the production of androgens (choice C), the androgens would then be converted to estrogen. The estrogen would then feed back to decrease LH and FSH secretion. An increase in estrogen (choice D) would feed back to decrease LH and FSH. An increase in inhibin (choice E) would decrease FSH rather than increase it, as seen in this patient.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Declining ovarian estrogen removes negative feedback, increasing GnRH and pituitary LH/FSH; vasomotor symptoms are consistent with estrogen deficiency.
choice_explanations.B: Reduced GnRH would lower rather than raise LH and FSH.
choice_explanations.C: Androgens may rise relatively after menopause, but do not explain the increased gonadotropins and classic hot flashes as directly as reduced estrogen.
choice_explanations.D: Increased estrogen would provide negative feedback and lower LH/FSH.
choice_explanations.E: Increased inhibin would suppress FSH rather than accompany elevated FSH.

A.text: Menopause is associated with reduced estrogen from depletion of ovarian follicles and loss of negative feedback, with increased LH and FSH.

B.text: Reduced GnRH would not explain increased LH/FSH; menopause is associated with increased GnRH/gonadotropins after estrogen feedback falls.

C.text: First Aid notes relative androgen increase after menopause, but declining estrogen is the primary feedback change that explains elevated gonadotropins.

D.text: Estrogen normally feeds back to reduce gonadotropin secretion; menopause involves reduced estrogen, not increased estrogen.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly list increased inhibin as a menopause finding; increased inhibin would suppress FSH, opposite the measured pattern.

stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of epigastric discomfort. A proton pump inhibitor provided little relief. During the past month he has developed diarrhea and lost 10 lb. Upper endoscopy shows diffusely thickened gastric rugal folds. Gastric biopsy shows marked hyperplasia of superficial mucous cells with scant gastric glands. If untreated, loss of which of the following from his gastrointestinal tract is most likely to increase?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has Ménétrier disease, also known as protein-losing gastroenteropathy (note that this is distinct from Meniere disease, which affects the inner ear). This disease is a hyperplastic gastropathy characterized by enlarged rugal folds because of the increased proliferation of the mucus-producing cells of the stomach. Increased mucus production in Ménétrier disease leads to protein losses from excessive gastric secretions and may cause hypoalbuminemia and peripheral edema. It is associated with increased amounts of transforming growth factor alpha (TGF-alpha), although the exact mechanism is uncertain.

Absorption of carbohydrates (choice A), which occurs in the small intestine, is unimpaired in Ménétrier disease.

Ménétrier disease is associated with deficient production of gastric acid, so chloride loss (choice B) would be unlikely. This is in marked contrast to hypertrophic-hypersecretory gastropathy and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, in which there is hyperplasia of parietal cells rather than atrophy, as in Ménétrier disease.

Dietary fat loss (choice C) is generally due to enteric malabsorption, such as that which occurs in celiac disease or cystic fibrosis. Gastric mucus is poor in fats, and no appreciable fat loss accompanies Ménétrier disease.

Fluid losses (choice E) due to mucus overproduction in Ménétrier disease are reabsorbed in the gut. Ménétrier disease does not cause dehydration.

ReKaps: Ménétrier disease is a hyperplastic gastropathy characterized by enlarged rugal folds because of the increased proliferation of mucus-producing cells of the stomach. It presents as a protein-losing enteropathy.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Carbohydrate absorption occurs in the small intestine and is not impaired by this gastric mucosal disorder.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Ménétrier disease causes reduced acid production from loss/atrophy of parietal cells, so increased chloride loss is not expected.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Increased fat loss suggests small-intestinal or pancreatic malabsorption (eg, celiac disease or pancreatic insufficiency), not excess gastric mucus secretion.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Excess protein-rich gastric mucus is lost from the GI tract, producing protein-losing gastropathy and possible hypoalbuminemia/edema.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Excess mucus fluid is generally reabsorbed in the intestine; Ménétrier disease does not typically cause dehydration.

A.text: Only monosaccharides are absorbed by enterocytes in the small intestine; gastric mucosal disease does not directly impair this process.

B.text: Ménétrier disease causes parietal cell atrophy and decreased acid production; page 379 describes gastric acid secretion by parietal cells.

C.text: Malabsorption syndromes can cause steatorrhea; celiac disease primarily affects the small intestine and causes malabsorption, unlike this gastric protein-losing disorder.

D.text: Ménétrier disease is gastric mucosal hyperplasia with excess mucus production and resultant protein loss.

E.text: No direct First Aid 2026 statement was found that Ménétrier disease causes or prevents water loss; the source explanation states secreted fluid is reabsorbed and dehydration does not occur.

fa_summary: Ménétrier disease causes hyperplasia of gastric fundus/body mucosa with excess mucus, protein loss, edema, and parietal-cell atrophy with reduced acid production. It is a protein-losing gastropathy, not a small-intestinal carbohydrate/fat malabsorption syndrome.

stem: A 69-year-old man with Alzheimer disease and a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes is brought to the physician by his daughter for a follow-up examination. The patient is unable to give a clear account of how carefully he controls his blood glucose. His temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse is 74/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies are done to assess the level of glycosylated hemoglobin in his blood. Which of the following conditions may confound this measurement, resulting in falsely high values?
explanation:
Studies have shown that glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) is directly related to the level of glucose in the blood. Since HbA1c is a stable product, its concentration reflects mean glucose levels over the past 3–6 months, since the average red blood cell has a life span of 120 days. HbA1c levels are affected by red cell survival and turnover. Falsely high values are seen with low red cell turnover (long red cell life span), such as in patients with iron or vitamin B12/folate deficiency anemia. In these conditions, there is a disproportionate number of older red cells, resulting in a falsely elevated HbA1c value. Other causes that can alter HbA1c include: erythropoietin can lower HbA1c by causing increased red cell production and dilution of the amount of hemoglobin that can bind to glucose; anti-malarial drugs can falsely lower HbA1c due to increased red cell destruction; and HbA1c levels obtained from patients with hemoglobin disorders, such as sickle cell anemia and thalassemia, do not accurately represent blood glucose control. HbA1c forms as a result of nonenzymatic glycosylation, a fundamental biochemical abnormality that accounts for most of the histopathologic alterations in diabetes mellitus (e.g., hyaline arteriolosclerosis). In a diabetic patient, the recommended HbA1c level is less than 6–7% to minimize risk of microvascular complications. This reflects an estimated average glucose of less than 154 mg/dL. HbA1c levels above 8% would have an increased risk for microvascular complications, affecting kidney, retina, and arterioles. A normal person would have HbA1c level of 5% with an estimated average glucose (eAG) of 97 mg/dL.

Choice A: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia results from a proliferation of lymphocytes, most commonly with B-cell markers, and does not commonly affect red blood cells or hemoglobin levels.

Choice B: Iron supplementation or addition of B12/folate to the diet has the opposite effect of iron or B12/folate deficiency. Enhanced red blood cell turnover leads to a falsely decreased HbA1c level.

Choice C: G6PD deficiency can lead to periods of hemolysis, resulting in increased red blood cell turnover. The rapid turnover leads to a greater proportion of younger red cells and falsely low HbA1c values.

Choice D: Hemophilia A is a coagulopathy involving the coagulation cascade, not red blood cells or hemoglobin levels.

choice_explanations.A: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia results from a proliferation of lymphocytes, most commonly with B-cell markers, and does not commonly affect red blood cells or hemoglobin levels.
choice_explanations.B: Iron supplementation or addition of B12/folate to the diet has the opposite effect of iron or B12/folate deficiency. Enhanced red blood cell turnover leads to a falsely decreased HbA1c level.
choice_explanations.C: G6PD deficiency can lead to periods of hemolysis, resulting in increased red blood cell turnover. The rapid turnover leads to a greater proportion of younger red cells and falsely low HbA1c values.
choice_explanations.D: Hemophilia A is a coagulopathy involving the coagulation cascade, not red blood cells or hemoglobin levels.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Vitamin B12/folate deficiency reduces red-cell turnover and increases the proportion of older red cells, falsely elevating HbA1c.

fa_summary: Endocrine → Diabetes mellitus, diagnosis: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over the prior 3 months and is influenced by red-cell turnover.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of several stab wounds he sustained in a gang fight. Physical examination shows a 3-cm penetrating wound on the posterolateral aspect of the neck that has partially severed the C6 ventral ramus as it emerges through the scalene interval. The patient says he has pain in the region of the wound and there is significant bruising in this area. Which of the following additional findings will most likely be seen in this patient?

options.text: Anesthesia in skin covering the hypothenar eminence
Weakness in the ability to protract the scapula

explanation:
The affected muscle is the serratus anterior. The serratus anterior is innervated by the long thoracic nerve, which arises from the ventral rami of C5, C6, and C7. Weakness of the serratus anterior from a lesion of the long thoracic nerve results in protraction weakness and winging of the scapula.

Choice A: The skin of the hypothenar eminence is innervated mainly by the C8 ventral ramus.

Choice B: Weakness of the laryngeal muscles from lesions of the vagus nerve or its branches may result in hoarseness, but would not be evident in a lesion to C6. The vagus nerve passes through the neck within the carotid sheath, medial to the site of this injury.

Choice C: The thenar muscles are innervated mainly by the C8 ventral ramus.

Choice E: Weakness of thumb flexion would result from paresis of flexor pollicis longus in the forearm (innervated by C7 and C8 fibers in the anterior interosseous nerve) and flexor pollicis brevis in the thenar eminence (innervated by C8 and T1 fibers in the recurrent branch of the median nerve).
fa_subchapter: Anatomy and physiology — brachial plexus / shoulder

choice_explanations.A: The skin of the hypothenar eminence is innervated mainly by the C8 ventral ramus.
choice_explanations.B: Weakness of the laryngeal muscles from lesions of the vagus nerve or its branches may result in hoarseness, but would not be evident in a lesion to C6. The vagus nerve passes through the neck within the carotid sheath, medial to the site of this injury.
choice_explanations.C: The thenar muscles are innervated mainly by the C8 ventral ramus.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. The C6 ventral ramus contributes to the long thoracic nerve (C5–C7), which innervates serratus anterior; weakness impairs scapular protraction and causes winging.
choice_explanations.E: Weakness of thumb flexion would result from paresis of flexor pollicis longus in the forearm (innervated by C7 and C8 fibers in the anterior interosseous nerve) and flexor pollicis brevis in the thenar eminence (innervated by C8 and T1 fibers in the recurrent branch of the median nerve).

fa_summary: Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue → Anatomy and physiology: long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) innervates serratus anterior; injury causes winged scapula and impaired scapular stabilization/protraction (pp. 451–452).

stem: A 37-year-old woman is brought to the physician because of lack of coordination and unsteadiness. Physical examination shows impaired proprioception and locomotor ataxia. A complete blood count is within normal limits. MRI imaging shows degeneration of the dorsal columns and dorsal roots of the spinal cord. Which of the following is most likely present in this patient's history?
explanation:
The findings described are those of tabes dorsalis, a form of tertiary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Tabes dorsalis and other manifestations of tertiary syphilis are now uncommon in the United States because primary cases are treated expeditiously with antimicrobials. The hallmark lesion of tertiary syphilis is the gumma, a syphilitic granuloma that forms in the central nervous system and in the vasculature. Tertiary syphilis is preceded by secondary syphilis, in which there is a maculopapular, bronzing rash and condylomata lata (flat, wartlike growths in the perianal or perigenital area). Primary syphilis is characterized by a painless, ulcerated genital lesion. Neurosyphilis can take many forms, including acute syphilitic meningitis, meningovascular syphilis, tabes dorsalis, general paresis, Argyll-Robertson pupils, and/or optic atrophy. Tabes dorsalis is a slowly progressive degenerative neurologic disease that affects the dorsal columns with demyelination and the dorsal roots with inflammatory changes accompanied by fibrosis. There is loss of pain sensation and peripheral reflexes, accompanied by impairment of vibration and position senses, with progressive sensory ataxia.

Choice A: Ingestion of poorly cooked fish is the means of transmission of Diphyllobothrium latum, which competes with the host for vitamin B12. Infection may mimic pernicious anemia and cause degeneration of the dorsal columns and roots (subacute combined degeneration) that may closely mimic syphilis; the two conditions can be distinguished by the megaloblastic anemia in vitamin B12 deficiency.

Choice B: Leukorrheic vaginal discharge could be observed with Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection, but is not found in any stage of syphilis. N. gonorrhoeae usually does not cause neurologic deficits. Neisseria meningitidis can cause meningitis, with fever, headache, meningeal signs, and photophobia.

Choice D: Painful genital ulcers are caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; syphilitic chancres are painless and indurated.

Choice E: Travel to Africa may be relevant to granuloma inguinale (Klebsiella granulomatis) or lymphogranuloma venereum (Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes L1–L3), but is not a prerequisite for syphilis.

Choice F: Unknown immunization history would be important when evaluating poliovirus infection. Here, the pathology is in the dorsal columns, not the ventral horns, which would be diagnostic for poliovirus infection.

choice_explanations.A: Ingestion of poorly cooked fish is the means of transmission of Diphyllobothrium latum, which competes with the host for vitamin B12. Infection may mimic pernicious anemia and cause degeneration of the dorsal columns and roots (subacute combined degeneration) that may closely mimic syphilis; the two conditions can be distinguished by the megaloblastic anemia in vitamin B12 deficiency.
choice_explanations.B: Leukorrheic vaginal discharge could be observed with Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection, but is not found in any stage of syphilis. N. gonorrhoeae usually does not cause neurologic deficits. Neisseria meningitidis can cause meningitis, with fever, headache, meningeal signs, and photophobia.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. The maculopapular, bronzing rash is a feature of secondary syphilis, which can precede tertiary syphilis and tabes dorsalis.
choice_explanations.D: Painful genital ulcers are caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; syphilitic chancres are painless and indurated.
choice_explanations.E: Travel to Africa may be relevant to granuloma inguinale (Klebsiella granulomatis) or lymphogranuloma venereum (Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes L1–L3), but is not a prerequisite for syphilis.
choice_explanations.F: Unknown immunization history would be important when evaluating poliovirus infection. Here, the pathology is in the dorsal columns, not the ventral horns, which would be diagnostic for poliovirus infection.

fa_summary: Neurology and Special Senses → Neurology—pathology: tabes dorsalis is degeneration/demyelination of dorsal columns and roots due to T. pallidum (tertiary syphilis), causing impaired proprioception and progressive sensory ataxia (p. 544). First Aid also summarizes tertiary syphilis at p. 145.

stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination for her major depressive disorder. She states that despite the use of two different antidepressants, she has felt depressed for the past 2 months. She denies drug abuse or excessive drinking. After further evaluation, the physician prescribes a second-line medication. He warns her about possible side effects including dry mouth, constipation, increased heart rate, urinary retention, and orthostatic hypotension. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?

options.text: Inhibits the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine
Selectively inhibits the reuptake of serotonin

explanation:
Amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, and doxepin are tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) that work by blocking the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, thereby increasing the levels of these neurotransmitters in the synaptic space. Important common side effects of the TCAs are antimuscarinic effects such as dry mouth (xerostomia), tachycardia, urinary retention, increased intraocular pressure, and sedation. Orthostatic hypotension occurs as a result of alpha-adrenergic blockade. Important serious cardiac effects include QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, and AV block.

Choice A: Increasing central nervous system dopamine release is a mechanism of action of indirect-acting sympathomimetics such as amphetamine. Although associated with xerostomia and tachycardia, these drugs are used in the treatment of ADHD and narcolepsy, not major depressive disorder.

Choice B: Galantamine acts by reversibly binding to and inactivating acetylcholinesterase. It is indicated for treatment of Alzheimer disease; important side effects include severe bradycardia, fatigue, and tremor.

Choice C: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors such as tranylcypromine, phenelzine, and isocarboxazid are another class of antidepressants. Side effects include weakness, dizziness, anxiety, and orthostatic hypotension. They do not have antimuscarinic side effects.

Choice E: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates are sedative-hypnotics that act by potentiating GABA. Important benzodiazepine side effects include respiratory depression, amnesia, and hypotension.

Choice F: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine, paroxetine, and sertraline are generally considered first-line agents for depression. They can cause sexual dysfunction, insomnia, serotonin syndrome, and exacerbation of mania.

choice_explanations.A: Increasing central nervous system dopamine release is a mechanism of action of indirect-acting sympathomimetics such as amphetamine. Although associated with xerostomia and tachycardia, these drugs are used in the treatment of ADHD and narcolepsy, not major depressive disorder.
choice_explanations.B: Galantamine acts by reversibly binding to and inactivating acetylcholinesterase. It is indicated for treatment of Alzheimer disease; important side effects include severe bradycardia, fatigue, and tremor.
choice_explanations.C: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors such as tranylcypromine, phenelzine, and isocarboxazid are another class of antidepressants. Side effects include weakness, dizziness, anxiety, and orthostatic hypotension. They do not have antimuscarinic side effects.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. TCAs block reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine; antimuscarinic effects and alpha-adrenergic blockade account for the described adverse effects.
choice_explanations.E: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates are sedative-hypnotics that act by potentiating GABA. Important benzodiazepine side effects include respiratory depression, amnesia, and hypotension.
choice_explanations.F: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine, paroxetine, and sertraline are generally considered first-line agents for depression. They can cause sexual dysfunction, insomnia, serotonin syndrome, and exacerbation of mania.

fa_summary: Psychiatry → Psychiatry—pharmacology: tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, doxepin) inhibit 5-HT and NE reuptake; p. 593.

stem: A 29-year-old woman requests a paternity test to determine if her current boyfriend is the father of her child. Blood samples are taken from the patient, the son, and the patient's boyfriend. Which of the following procedures would be most appropriate for analyzing these samples?
explanation:
Microsatellite testing detects genetic differences between individuals due to different lengths of microsatellite repeats. Microsatellites are repeated units of typically 2–4 bp, and the length of the entire repeat is generally less than 150 bp. These simple tandem repeats (STRs) create a molecular fingerprint of an individual, as no two persons would have the same pattern of STRs. Using this technique, it is possible to identify the parents of a child due to the presence of STR bands in the child's sample that represent STR bands from each of the parents. In case 1, the tested male may be the father because he shares a band with the child. It is not certain, however, because other men in the population could have the same band. Matches are required at 9 to 10 different loci to indicate with high probability that a tested male is the father. In case 2, the tested male cannot be the father because neither of his bands is shared with the child.

Choice A: Chromosomal karyotyping detects chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomies or monosomies. It can be used to diagnose various genetic diseases, but it cannot be used to determine paternity.

Choice C: Northern blot analysis determines the expression pattern or expression levels of specific RNA molecules and is commonly used to compare mRNA levels among different tissue types. RNA levels or expression patterns cannot identify a particular individual or that individual's progeny.

Choice D: Promoter methylation analysis identifies epigenetic silencing of genes. Methylation of cytosines in promoters can prevent expression of the associated gene, a mechanism used by some cancers to inhibit tumor suppressors; this method cannot determine paternity.

Choice E: Western blot analysis detects specific proteins in a sample and can determine a protein's presence or absence, size, or expression level. Protein size or levels do not determine paternity.

choice_explanations.A: Chromosomal karyotyping detects chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomies or monosomies. It can be used to diagnose various genetic diseases, but it cannot be used to determine paternity.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Microsatellite analysis compares repeat-length patterns among the mother, child, and alleged father. The source notes that paternity testing is commonly performed using PCR probes to amplify microsatellite repeats; several probes are used, and matches across multiple loci provide high probability.
choice_explanations.C: Northern blot analysis determines the expression pattern or expression levels of specific RNA molecules and is commonly used to compare mRNA levels among different tissue types. RNA levels or expression patterns cannot identify a particular individual or that individual's progeny.
choice_explanations.D: Promoter methylation analysis identifies epigenetic silencing of genes. Methylation of cytosines in promoters can prevent expression of the associated gene, a mechanism used by some cancers to inhibit tumor suppressors; this method cannot determine paternity.
choice_explanations.E: Western blot analysis detects specific proteins in a sample and can determine a protein's presence or absence, size, or expression level. Protein size or levels do not determine paternity.

fa_summary: Biochemistry → Laboratory Techniques: First Aid describes Southern blot detection/size analysis of specific DNA sequences and repeat counts (including FMR1 CGG repeats), which is the nearest molecular sizing method; the text does not directly teach STR-based paternity testing (p. 51).

stem: During morning rounds, a medical resident is the first person to enter the room of a new patient. When the resident opens the door, she feels air rushing past the side of her face. She later describes the air moving from the hallway into the patient's room. Assuming the hospital is following appropriate treatment protocol for each of the listed disorders, this patient most likely has which of the following conditions?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The air pressure in a standard room is affected by whether air can enter and leave a room through gaps around windows and doors. Negative- and positive-pressure rooms are common in hospitals since they provide an appropriate environment for both patients and clinicians. A negative-pressure room (NPR) keeps its air inside the room with controlled venting only. Conversely, a positive-pressure room (PPR) keeps unfiltered air from outside the room out of the room altogether. NPRs are an isolation technique used in hospitals to prevent cross-contamination from room to room. An NPR has its own ventilation system that generates negative pressure to allow air to flow into the isolation room but not escape from the room. This ventilation system creates a “negative pressure” inside the room where air will flow from areas with higher pressure (outside the room) to areas with lower pressure (inside the room), thereby preventing contaminated air from escaping the room. NPRs are used to isolate patients with airborne contagious diseases such as tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox, SARS, and aspergillosis. Patients with heart failure (choice A) and herpes simplex encephalitis (choice B) can be placed in standard rooms. Patients with severe allergic asthma (choice C) and those with a recent bone marrow transplantation (choice E) are likely to be placed in positive-pressure rooms. A PPR creates a pressure within the patient's room that is greater than the environment outside the room, so when the door to the room opens, air will go out into the hallway. Hospitals most commonly use PPRs for patients with compromised immune systems to prevent infection with airborne microorganisms.

choice_explanations.A: Patients with heart failure can be placed in a standard room.
choice_explanations.B: Patients with herpes simplex encephalitis can be placed in a standard room.
choice_explanations.C: Patients with severe allergic asthma are likely to be placed in a positive-pressure room.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Air flowing from the hallway into the room indicates negative pressure, used to isolate patients with airborne contagious disease such as pulmonary tuberculosis.
choice_explanations.E: A patient after recent bone marrow transplantation is likely to be placed in a positive-pressure room.

fa_summary: Microbiology → Clinical bacteriology—Mycobacteria: First Aid describes M. tuberculosis and TB presentation on printed p. 138. The negative-pressure-room precaution itself is not directly covered there; this is the nearest disease-topic cross-reference.

stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a recent onset of a dry, nonproductive cough, difficulty breathing, and fever. He states that he was recently visiting family in southern China. Laboratory results show a positive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for serum coronavirus antibodies. Which of the following additional infection-control precautions should be taken in this patient compared to a patient with a noninfectious disease?

options.text: Handwashing before and after patient contact
Place the patient in a gown during transport
Place the patient in a negative-pressure room
Safe disposal or cleaning of examination instruments
Safe disposal or cleaning of linen
Use of eye protection as required

explanation: The correct answer is C. This patient likely has severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), which is classified as an airborne infection. A diagnosis of SARS is likely due to the positive ELISA test for coronavirus antibodies and recent travel to China. Severe respiratory illness caused by SARS is associated with fever and one or more clinical findings of respiratory illness (hypoxia, cough, dyspnea, breathing difficulties). Negative-pressure rooms (NPRs) are used to isolate patients with airborne contagious diseases, such as tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox, SARS, and aspergillosis. The air pressure in a standard room determines whether air can enter or leave through gaps around windows and doors. Negative- and positive-pressure rooms are common in hospitals since they provide an appropriate environment for both patients and clinicians. An NPR keeps its air inside the room with controlled venting only. An NPR ventilation system creates a negative pressure inside the room in which air will flow from areas with higher pressure (outside the room) to areas with lower pressure (inside the room), thereby preventing contaminated air from escaping the room. Conversely, a positive-pressure room (PPR) keeps unfiltered air in the hallway from entering the room altogether. The source also supplies this infection-control table: Standard precautions for all patients—handwashing before and after every patient contact; examination gloves, gowns, and eye protection as required; safe disposal or cleaning of instruments and linen; cough etiquette (clinicians, patients, and visitors cover the nose or mouth when coughing or sneezing, promptly dispose of used tissues, and practice hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions). Contact precautions—standard precautions plus minimizing environmental contamination during transport by placing the patient in a gown; washing hands with soap and water before and after leaving the room; preferring a private room; requiring gloves upon room entry and changing them after contact with contaminated secretions; requiring a clinician gown if clothing may contact the patient or environmental surfaces or if the patient has diarrhea; shoe covers when applicable; and dedicating noncritical items to one patient for disposal or appropriate disinfection. Droplet precautions—standard precautions plus wearing a mask within 3 feet of the patient, masking the patient during transport, and preferring a private room. Airborne precautions—standard precautions plus placing the patient in a negative-pressure room and wearing a mask.

choice_explanations.A: Handwashing before and after patient contact is a standard precaution used for all patients, not the added airborne precaution asked for.
choice_explanations.B: A gown for transport is an added contact precaution.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. SARS is treated as airborne here; place the patient in a negative-pressure room.
choice_explanations.D: Safe instrument disposal or cleaning is a standard precaution.
choice_explanations.E: Safe linen disposal or cleaning is a standard precaution.
choice_explanations.F: Examination gloves are a standard precaution.
choice_explanations.G: Eye protection is used as required under standard precautions.

fa_summary: Microbiology → Virology: SARS/coronavirus context is within the virology material (printed p. 163). First Aid does not directly give this negative-pressure isolation rule; it is a contextual pathogen cross-reference.

stem: Members of the endocrinology department at a community hospital are attempting to improve patient compliance with both blood glucose monitoring and dietary restrictions. They employ a methodology that uses a trial-and-error approach to reach their desired outcome of improved patient compliance. The group likely derived their concepts from which of the following?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The PDSA (plan, do, study, act) cycle is a common quality-improvement model that applies knowledge based on past actions to make an improvement by asking three questions. The interventions with the PDSA cycle are small-scale, rapid tests of new initiatives. Interventions with promising results are then selected for larger-scale implementation. These four steps are repeated over and over as part of a repeated cycle of continual improvement. PDSA can be described as: Plan—plan a change or a pilot test of a new intervention or innovation; Do—carry out the plan; Study—evaluate the results; Act—decide what actions should be taken to improve (i.e., implement the new intervention or start over with a new plan based on the prior results). This model takes the simple concept of “trial and error” and transforms it into the PDSA model that can be used to make improvements in health care. It asks: What are we trying to accomplish? How will we know whether a change is an improvement? What changes can we make that will result in an improvement? There are two basic types of flowcharts: high-level flowcharts (more conceptually focused, “big picture”) and detailed (low-level) flowcharts (more focused on specific, fine points) (choice A). Flowcharts allow health care teams to understand the steps involved in the delivery of patient-care service. A flowchart is a visual illustration of all the steps or parts of a process in patient care; they are more accurate and effective when all representative members of a health-care team actively participate in their design. Pareto charts (choice B) describe a large proportion of quality problems being caused by a small number of causes. They are based on the classic 80/20 rule from economics. In health care, the majority of patient-safety errors stem from only a few recurring contributing factors. Pareto charts help prioritize problems, highlighting that most problems are affected by a few factors and indicating which problems to solve and in what order. A Pareto chart includes the multiple factors that contribute to an effect arranged in descending order according to the magnitude of their effect, helping the team concentrate effort on the factors with the greatest impact. Run charts (or time plots) (choice D) are graphs of data collected over time that can help determine whether an intervention or enhancement in the patient-care process has resulted in true improvement over time. They can also help identify whether the intervention simply represents a random fluctuation that might be incorrectly interpreted as significant improvement. Run charts plot time along the X-axis and the quality measure on the Y-axis; the median (or 50th percentile) is measured using baseline historical data and compared to outcomes following the quality-improvement intervention. Shewhart (or control) charts (choice E) apply formal statistical calculations (statistical process control) to determine whether the observed rise and fall of a quality measure over time is within a predictable range of variation or indicates a significant system change. Control charts use upper and lower control limits that indicate the threshold at which process output is statistically unlikely, typically drawn at 3 standard errors from the center line. Six Sigma (choice F) is another quality-improvement model with origins in manufacturing. The term comes from the Greek letter sigma, used in statistics to denote standard deviation from the mean. By definition, 95% of a normally distributed population falls within 2 standard deviations of the mean, so 5% of observations are considered abnormal or unacceptable. Six Sigma is equivalent to 3.4 defects (or errors) per million, or 6 standard deviations from the population average. This system uses specific steps to reduce variation and improve performance.

choice_explanations.A: High-level and low-level flowcharts depict process steps; they are not the trial-and-error iterative model described.
choice_explanations.B: Pareto charts prioritize the few causes responsible for a large proportion of problems (80/20 concept).
choice_explanations.C: Correct. PDSA is the iterative plan-do-study-act cycle of small, rapid tests and repeated improvement.
choice_explanations.D: Run charts plot a measure over time to distinguish improvement from random fluctuation.
choice_explanations.E: Shewhart/control charts use statistical control limits to assess variation over time.
choice_explanations.F: Six Sigma uses steps to reduce process variation and defects.

fa_summary: Public Health Sciences: p. 255 introduces quality improvement among the subject areas, but First Aid does not directly explain PDSA; this is a topic-level cross-reference only.

stem: A 65-year-old man is scheduled for a surgical procedure. After the surgical procedure has started, it is determined that the surgeon is using instruments that were used in the previous surgery without being properly sterilized. The patient is later diagnosed with hepatitis C as a result of the error. Which of the following best characterizes this incident?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The term “never event” was originally introduced by the National Quality Forum (NQF) and refers to a particularly shocking, unacceptable medical error (such as serious injury associated with the use of contaminated devices) that should never occur. The current list was expanded to include adverse events that are unambiguous (clearly identifiable and measurable), serious (resulting in death or significant disability), and usually preventable. The most current list is grouped into six categories: surgical, product or device, patient protection, care management, environmental, radiologic, and criminal events. Examples include: Surgical events—surgery or another invasive procedure performed on the wrong body part or wrong patient; wrong surgical procedure performed on a patient; unintended retention of a foreign object. Product or device events—patient death or serious injury associated with contaminated drugs, biologics, or contaminated/dysfunctional devices provided by the health-care setting; patient death or serious injury due to air embolism. Patient-protection events—release of a patient/resident unable to make decisions to an unauthorized person, death due to disappearance, or patient suicide/attempted suicide while in care. Care-management events—death or serious injury associated with medication error, unsafe blood-product administration, or fall; maternal/neonatal death or serious injury associated with a low-risk pregnancy; wrong-donor artificial insemination; serious pressure ulcers; or death/serious disability from loss of an irreplaceable biological specimen. Environmental events—death/serious disability associated with electric shock, wrong gas (such as oxygen), serious burn, or injury from restraints. Radiologic events—death or serious injury associated with introducing a metallic object into the MRI area. Criminal events—care ordered or provided by someone impersonating a licensed health-care provider; patient abduction; sexual abuse/assault; or death/significant injury resulting from physical assault. Medical errors may be acts of commission (doing something wrong) or omission (failing to do the right thing) (choice B), leading to an undesirable outcome or potentially severe adverse event. Use of contaminated equipment is an error of commission, not omission. A surgical complication (choice D) is an event that can be reasonably expected as a result of a surgical procedure; this is not a reasonable event. A surgical hazard (choice E) is an event experienced by medical personnel as a result of the procedure, such as contact with the patient's blood.
fa_subchapter: Healthcare delivery — patient safety / medical errors

choice_explanations.A: The source identifies the incident as an unacceptable, preventable medical error, not an acceptable risk.
choice_explanations.B: This is an error of commission (using contaminated instruments), not omission (failing to do the right thing).
choice_explanations.C: Correct. A serious, preventable error from contaminated instruments is a never event.
choice_explanations.D: A surgical complication is an event reasonably expected as a result of the procedure; this is not one.
choice_explanations.E: A surgical hazard is a risk experienced by medical personnel, such as contact with the patient's blood.

fa_summary: Public Health Sciences → Healthcare Delivery: First Aid defines never events as serious, identifiable, usually preventable medical errors and lists contaminated devices among examples (p. 278).

stem:
A group of investigators is evaluating an outbreak of Salmonella poisoning at a local restaurant. They gather evidence of what patrons ate and which patrons became ill. The table shows the results of this investigation:

Based on these data, which of the following is the attack rate for those persons who ate raw clams?
explanation: The correct answer is D. An attack rate is the cumulative incidence of infection in a group of people observed over a period of time during an epidemic, usually in relation to food-borne illness. It is defined as the number of exposed people infected with the disease divided by the total number of exposed people. Out of the 40 people who ate raw clams, 28 became ill. The attack rate for raw clams is, therefore, 28/40. Because the question was focused only on raw clams, the presented data for egg-drop soup, the chicken special, and the total can all be ignored. The rule for handling these types of questions is: “Don't get distracted by irrelevant data.” Attack rate is a type of incidence rate in which the denominator is further reduced for some known exposure. In epidemiology, attack rate is usually used for food-borne illnesses.
fa_subchapter: Epidemiology and biostatistics — measures of disease frequency

choice_explanations.A: Uses the number of healthy people exposed over the ill people; attack rate numerator and denominator are reversed.
choice_explanations.B: Reverses the number ill and total exposed.
choice_explanations.C: Uses all patrons as the denominator instead of only those who ate raw clams.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. 28 of the 40 people who ate raw clams became ill, so the attack rate is 28/40.
choice_explanations.E: Uses all ill patrons rather than all exposed persons who ate raw clams as denominator.

fa_summary: Public Health Sciences → Epidemiology and Biostatistics: attack rate is the proportion of exposed people who become ill (p. 259).

stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for a routine well-child examination. Physical examination shows a palpable, large nontender abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. CT scan of the abdomen shows a 6-cm mass that is present within the superior pole of the left kidney and does not cross the renal capsule. Which of the following findings is most likely present on histologic examination of the mass?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has a tumor of the kidney and most likely has Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), the most common malignant renal tumor in children. The tumor is commonly present in children less than age 5 and has a 90% survival rate, thanks to modern management. Note: the differential diagnosis for an abdominal mass in a child <5 years of age also includes neuroblastoma, which arises from the adrenal gland. Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumor of infancy and childhood.

Microscopically, there is a triphasic pattern: embryonic undifferentiated cells (blastema), immature glomerular and tubular structures (epithelium), and a spindle-cell stroma (mesenchyme). They may also contain smooth muscle, striated muscle, bone, cartilage, fat, and fibrous tissue. On gross examination, the tumor appears as a very large, well-demarcated, tan mass, usually occurring unilaterally, but may be bilateral if familial. It can be caused by deletion of a tumor suppressor gene (WT1) on chromosome 11p13 or (WT2) on chromosome 11p15.

Wilms tumor generally presents as a large, unilateral mass. Other symptoms include abdominal pain, hypertension (because of renin release), and hematuria. The majority of cases are sporadic, but a small percent occur as part of multiple malformation syndromes, such as WAGR (Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genital abnormalities, mental and motor Retardation), Denys-Drash syndrome, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes.

Abundant clear cells (choice A) are a feature of renal cell carcinoma (clear cell type). Renal cell carcinoma is usually seen as a sporadic (non-inherited) tumor in older adults who have a history of tobacco smoking, chronic renal failure on hemodialysis, chronic analgesic use, and asbestos exposure. Gross examination shows a yellow tumor, and if present near the renal hilum, can invade the renal vein and spread hematogenously to the right heart. It presents with the classic triad of hematuria, palpable mass, and flank pain. Many patients have accompanying paraneoplastic syndromes. It also develops in nearly 40% of patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease.

Eosinophilic cells packed with mitochondria (choice C) suggest oncocytoma, which are often benign. On light microscopy, epithelial cells have an eosinophilic and granular cytoplasm. Electron microscopy confirms the presence of increased mitochondria. Oncocytomas can also occur in the salivary and thyroid glands.

Hamartomatous blood vessels (choice D) suggest angiomyolipoma, a benign tumor of the kidney which can occur sporadically or is associated with tuberous sclerosis.

Primitive cells with neuropil (choice E) suggest neuroblastoma, a malignant neuroendocrine tumor of the adrenal medulla. It is common among children age less than 5 years and can present with high blood pressure, opsoclonus myoclonus, and distant metastases. Histologically, tumor cells are small, with blue cytoplasm, surrounding neuropil, and forming rosettes (Homer-Wright rosettes). It is associated with N-myc oncogene amplification.

Gross examination shows a yellow tumor, and if present near the renal hilum, can invade the renal vein and spread hematogenously to the right heart. It presents with the classic triad of hematuria, palpable mass, and flank pain. Many patients have accompanying paraneoplastic syndromes. It also develops in nearly 40% of patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease.

choice_explanations.C: Eosinophilic cells packed with mitochondria (choice C) suggest oncocytoma, which are often benign. On light microscopy, epithelial cells have an eosinophilic and granular cytoplasm. Electron microscopy confirms the presence of increased mitochondria. Oncocytomas can also occur in the salivary and thyroid glands.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of an abdominal mass on the left side. The child is otherwise healthy. The mass was noted by the child's mother while bathing him. Physical examination shows a left upper quadrant abdominal mass. Otherwise, the child is able to run around the examination room without difficulty. CT-guided biopsy of the mass is undertaken. Microscopic examination of the specimen shows dense, immature islands of epithelial cells, ribbons of spindled fibroblastic stromal cells, and poorly formed tubular structures. Which of the following is the most likely underlying disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Wilms tumor, a neoplasm with triphasic pattern comprised of the embryonic renal blastema, islands of stromal or epithelial cells, and recognizable glomerular and/or tubular structures (may represent a minority or sizable component of the tumor). Children with Wilms tumors are typically healthy. The palpable mass is usually found by the child's parent, typically while bathing.

Wilms tumor can present as an abdominal mass with hypertension, nausea, hematuria, and intestinal obstruction. It may also be associated with other congenital anomalies: aniridia, genitourinary malformation, and mental-motor retardation (WAGR complex). The normal examination (with the exception of the abdominal mass) suggests that this child does not have WAGR syndrome. The gene mutation is in the WT-1 gene. Another tumor in the differential in a child would be neuroblastoma. These are actually generally extrarenal tumors, and cross the midline.

Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (choice A) is the most common soft tissue tumor in children. It is a malignancy of skeletal muscle origin, and the cells are recognized by their cytoplasmic content of eosinophilic muscle proteins (thin and thick filaments), which stain with desmin. Common sites include the head and neck (orbit and parameningeal regions), genitourinary tract, extremities, trunk, and retroperitoneum. Common sites for sarcoma botryoides, a variant of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, include genitourinary system and vagina. Rhabdomyosarcoma, in general, has embryonal, alveolar, and pleomorphic variants, but none demonstrates a triphasic histology.

Ewing sarcoma (choice B) appears as a monotonous mass of primitive, small, round cells with a thin rim of clear cytoplasm. Ewing sarcoma is a tumor of bone; presentation as an abdominal mass is distinctly unusual.

Hodgkin disease (choice C) is a lymphoid malignancy that presents with lymphadenopathy, typically in the cervical or mediastinal nodes. The cellular component contains varying amounts of inflammatory cells and Reed-Sternberg cells. There are different subtypes of Hodgkin disease, which affect young and older adults, but not children.

Neuroblastoma (choice D) frequently presents as an abdominal mass in children. It is a neuroendocrine tumor and does not have an epithelial component. The cell population of neuroblastoma ranges from primitive, small, blue, round cells to well differentiated neuritic cells resembling ganglion cells. A small percent of patients can have opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome.

Children with Wilms tumors are typically healthy and the palpable mass is usually found by the parent while bathing.

stem: A 45-year-old man returns to the physician for routine renal function tests. He has a history of glomerulonephritis. One year ago, his baseline creatinine clearance was 100 mL/min. Today, his creatinine clearance is 50 mL/min. Assuming that there has been no change in his diet, which of the following physiologic changes are most likely to have occurred in this patient in the year since his initial creatinine clearance studies?

options.text: A 2-fold decrease in blood urea nitrogen concentration
A 2-fold decrease in creatinine excretion rate
A 2-fold increase in creatinine excretion rate
A 2-fold increase in plasma creatinine concentration

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Creatinine is a metabolic waste product that muscle produces continually and must be excreted by the kidneys at an equivalent rate. Creatinine excretion is largely a passive process. Creatinine filters freely across the glomerular filtration barrier and passes through the tubule without being reabsorbed and is then excreted in urine. When plasma creatinine concentrations rise, excretion rates necessarily rise also.

The term "clearance" is a measure of the kidney's ability to excrete waste products and is defined as the volume of plasma that is completely cleared of any given substance per unit time. Note that the term does not reference concentration, only plasma volume. Creatinine clearance is calculated from a knowledge of plasma and urinary creatinine concentrations using the clearance formula. Creatinine clearance is calculated as Ccr = (Ucr x V)/Pcr, where Ccr = creatinine clearance (mL/min), Ucr = urinary concentration of creatinine (mol/L or mg/dL), V = urine flow rate (mL/min), and Pcr = plasma concentration of creatinine. Thus, creatinine clearance is calculated as the product of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and plasma creatinine concentration. When GFR decreases, the plasma creatinine concentration continues to increase until the rate of creatinine excretion matches the rate of creatinine production.

In the patient's case, the volume of blood cleared of creatinine per min dropped over the course of a year from 100 mL to 50 mL - a two-fold decrease. Since excretion rate must match the rate of creatinine production over the long term, urinary creatinine excretion stays constant.

For the purpose of demonstration, assume that the patient's serum creatinine level originally was 50 micromol/L. If his original creatinine clearance were 100 mL/min, then he was excreting 5 micromol/min (i.e., the amount of creatinine contained in 100 mL of blood).

Glomerulonephritis has caused the patient's glomerular filtration rate (GFR) to drop, meaning that less creatinine is excreted per minute. An acute two-fold decrease in GFR means that now only 2.5 micromoles/min are currently being excreted, which is less than the rate of creatinine production. Plasma creatinine levels inevitably rise as a result. When Pcr reaches 100 micromol/L (a two-fold increase over baseline), the normal urinary excretion rate of 5 micromol/min is restored.

Because creatinine is freely filtered at the glomerulus and plasma and urine concentrations are easy to measure, creatinine clearance is commonly used clinically to estimate GFR. Creatinine is actively secreted by the proximal tubule which introduces a small error (~10-40%), but changes in Ccr can be a useful indicator of kidney injury and disease.

The blood urea nitrogen concentration (choice A) increases when GFR is reduced.

At steady state, creatinine production and excretion rates are constant, so choices B and C are incorrect.

Creatinine is not reabsorbed during passage through the renal tubule, which excludes choice D.

choice_explanations.A: The blood urea nitrogen concentration (choice A) increases when GFR is reduced.
choice_explanations.B: At steady state, creatinine production and excretion rates are constant, so choices B and C are incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: At steady state, creatinine production and excretion rates are constant, so choices B and C are incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Creatinine is not reabsorbed during passage through the renal tubule, which excludes choice D.
choice_explanations.E: The correct answer is E. Because creatinine is freely filtered and not reabsorbed, when GFR falls the plasma creatinine concentration rises until the excretion rate again matches the constant rate of creatinine production; a two-fold fall in clearance is met by a two-fold rise in plasma creatinine.

fa_summary: Renal clearance Cx = (UxV)/Px; creatinine clearance is an approximate measure of GFR (slightly overestimates it because creatinine is moderately secreted).

stem: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of acute onset of cloudy urine and back pain. Laboratory studies show increases of both renal plasma flow (RPF) and glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of the increase of both RPF and GFR?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Dilation of the afferent arteriole decreases vessel resistance, thereby increasing renal plasma flow (RPF). Also, dilation of these vessels will increase glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure to increase GFR. Glomerular capillary pressure is the driving force behind glomerular filtration, so any factor that increases this pressure will most likely increase GFR.

Afferent and efferent arterioles can be thought of as tubes that fill (afferent) and empty (efferent) a bucket (glomerulus). The fuller the bucket, the greater the GFR. Dilating either tube will increase the flow through the bucket. Dilating the input fills the bucket (increases GFR), dilating the outflow empties the bucket (lower GFR). Constriction of the input lowers the bucket level (afferent constriction), constriction of the output (efferent) raises the level of the bucket.

Changes of either arteriole change RPF in the same direction; dilation increases flow, constriction decreases RPF. Dilation of any renal vessels increases RPF, but the effects on GFR differ.

Constriction of the afferent arteriole (choice A) will decrease RPF and glomerular capillary pressure by increasing vessel resistance and decreasing glomerular capillary pressure. Therefore, this answer is incorrect.

Constriction of the efferent arteriole (choice B) will decrease RPF but increase glomerular capillary pressure and GFR, so this answer is incorrect.

Dilation of the efferent arteriole (choice D) will increase RPF, but will decrease GFR by reducing glomerular capillary pressure.

Renal artery stenosis (choice E) will decrease renal blood flow and glomerular pressure, so both RPF and GFR would be decreased. Renal artery stenosis is a major cause of secondary hypertension.

Stenosis of the urethra (choice F) causes increased pressure in Bowman's space, which decreases net filtration pressure. GFR decreases, rather than increases. This is typical of urinary tract obstruction.

choice_explanations.A: Constriction of the afferent arteriole (choice A) will decrease RPF and glomerular capillary pressure by increasing vessel resistance and decreasing glomerular capillary pressure. Therefore, this answer is incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Constriction of the efferent arteriole (choice B) will decrease RPF but increase glomerular capillary pressure and GFR, so this answer is incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: The correct answer is C. Dilation of the afferent arteriole decreases vessel resistance, thereby increasing RPF, and increases glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure to increase GFR.
choice_explanations.D: Dilation of the efferent arteriole (choice D) will increase RPF, but will decrease GFR by reducing glomerular capillary pressure.
choice_explanations.E: Renal artery stenosis (choice E) will decrease renal blood flow and glomerular pressure, so both RPF and GFR would be decreased. Renal artery stenosis is a major cause of secondary hypertension.
choice_explanations.F: Stenosis of the urethra (choice F) causes increased pressure in Bowman's space, which decreases net filtration pressure. GFR decreases, rather than increases. This is typical of urinary tract obstruction.

fa_summary: Changes in glomerular dynamics: afferent arteriole constriction decreases RPF and GFR; efferent arteriole constriction decreases RPF and increases GFR. Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole.

stem:
A 36-year-old man comes to the physician because his urine has a dark-red color. He does not exercise regularly but states that yesterday he played racquetball for 4 hours. Physical examination of the heart, lungs, and abdomen are unremarkable. There is no costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness. Laboratory studies show:

Hemoglobin 14 g/dL
Hematocrit 42%

Urine:
Color reddish-brown
Dipstick positive for blood, negative for nitrates and leukocyte esterase
pH 5.5
Red blood cells/hpf 0/hpf
White blood cells/hpf 1/hpf

Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?

options.text: Ingestion of foods that contain red dye

explanation:
The correct answer is C. The appearance of dark-reddish urine is suggestive of a number of conditions, including hematuria; however, in the present case, no red blood cells are present on microscopic examination. Despite this, the dipstick test for blood is positive, which is suggestive of myoglobinuria. Myoglobin is a pigment that, if present in the urine, will produce a positive dipstick test for blood even in the absence of red blood cells. This occurs because the dipstick test detects peroxidase activity rather than specifically reacting to blood.

Myoglobinuria can be caused when a poorly conditioned individual takes part in intense physical exertion. This extreme physical activity leads to muscle cell breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) and the release of myoglobin into the blood, which is then filtered by the kidneys and excreted into the urine. Myoglobinuria may also be caused by rhabdomyolysis secondary to medications, crush injuries to muscle, malignant hyperthermia, or by severe or repeated seizures. Hydration and alkalinization of the urine is essential to prevent renal damage due to precipitation of myoglobin in the tubules, which causes obstruction and generation of reactive oxygen species.

If hemolyzed blood were in the urine (choice A) a few red blood cells should have been detected on urinalysis. A positive urine dipstick for blood can also indicate hemoglobinuria.

Ingestion of foods that contain red dye (choice B) can discolor the urine; however, this would not produce a positive dipstick test.

Nephrolithiasis (choice D) can cause a positive urine dipstick test for blood and generally results in the appearance of red blood cells in the urine.

Prostatitis (choice E), an inflammation of the prostate gland, is generally caused by an infection. Prostatitis produces symptoms of dysuria, urinary frequency, and cloudy urine; hematuria is rare.

choice_explanations.A: If hemolyzed blood were in the urine (choice A) a few red blood cells should have been detected on urinalysis. A positive urine dipstick for blood can also indicate hemoglobinuria.
choice_explanations.B: Ingestion of foods that contain red dye (choice B) can discolor the urine; however, this would not produce a positive dipstick test.
choice_explanations.C: The correct answer is C. Myoglobin is a pigment that produces a positive dipstick test for blood (peroxidase activity) even in the absence of red blood cells; myoglobinuria results from rhabdomyolysis after intense exertion.
choice_explanations.D: Nephrolithiasis (choice D) can cause a positive urine dipstick test for blood and generally results in the appearance of red blood cells in the urine.
choice_explanations.E: Prostatitis (choice E), an inflammation of the prostate gland, is generally caused by an infection. Prostatitis produces symptoms of dysuria, urinary frequency, and cloudy urine; hematuria is rare.

fa_summary: Acute tubular necrosis: nephrotoxic causes include myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis), which produces dipstick-positive blood without RBCs.

stem: A 43-year-old man with renal insufficiency comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. His diet shows normal intake of sodium, potassium, and protein. Laboratory studies show a relatively constant production of urea and creatinine. Estimated glomerular filtration using serum creatinine is 60 L/day. Plasma sodium is within the normal range and there is no sign of hypervolemia or hypovolemia. Further laboratory studies will most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Increased fractional excretion of filtered Na+

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) is a measure of tubular function. It is calculated as the excretion of sodium divided by the filtered load. Intake and excretion of sodium must be balanced to maintain normal sodium levels. If filtered load is decreased because of reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR), then the FENa must increase to maintain normal sodium balance.

GFR decreases in patients with renal insufficiency (chronic kidney disease, CKD). If Na+ and K+ intake remain unchanged, the fractional excretion of both of these ions must increase to maintain a constant excretion rate. If fractional excretion does not increase, plasma concentrations would increase. The observation that plasma Na+ is normal despite decreased filtered load implies that tubular function is able to compensate for reduced filtration; therefore, plasma K+ concentration would remain relatively constant rather than increase (choice D). Sodium intake and plasma sodium concentration are both normal, so urine excretion of sodium (choice E) is normal. Fractional excretion of sodium is increased because a higher percentage of a reduced filtered load is excreted. So long as aldosterone secretion and distal tubular flow are maintained, which are implied by the normal plasma sodium concentration in this patient, both plasma sodium and potassium concentrations usually remain near normal. If marked oliguria develops, both hypernatremia and hyperkalemia are more likely to occur.

The significance of the constant production of urea and creatinine lies in their dependence on glomerular filtration for regulation. Creatinine is almost completely excreted and urea is mostly excreted, with a small amount being reabsorbed. So, a decrease in glomerular filtration would initially result in a large decrease in creatinine and urea excretion rather than an increase (choices A and B). The equation for renal clearance of a substance is:

Clearance = (U x V)/P

U is urinary concentration, V is urine flow rate, and P is plasma concentration.

Because creatinine is freely filtered and only a small amount is secreted, creatinine clearance is used to measure GFR. So, P x glomerular filtration rate = U x V. A decrease in glomerular filtration rate increases plasma concentration so that urinary excretion rate (U x V) returns to normal. This is why rising serum creatinine concentration is a major clinical marker of decreased GFR.

choice_explanations.B: A decrease in glomerular filtration would initially result in a large decrease in creatinine and urea excretion rather than an increase (choices A and B).
choice_explanations.C: The correct answer is C. Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) is the excretion of sodium divided by the filtered load. With a decreased filtered load (reduced GFR), FENa must increase to maintain normal sodium balance.
choice_explanations.D: Plasma K+ concentration would remain relatively constant rather than increase (choice D), because tubular function compensates for reduced filtration when plasma Na+ is normal.
choice_explanations.E: Sodium intake and plasma sodium concentration are both normal, so urine excretion of sodium (choice E) is normal; it is the fractional excretion that is increased.

fa_summary: FENa = fractional excretion of sodium = (Na+ excreted/Na+ filtered) = (V x UNa)/(GFR x PNa) = (PCr x UNa)/(UCr x PNa).

A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a puffy face and eyes. His temperature is 37.3 C (99.1 F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 100/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows periorbital edema, but no erythema, no evidence of trauma, and no insect bite. Laboratory studies show:

Leukocyte count 8,500/mm3
Hemoglobin 13.5 mg/dL
Platelet count 400,000/mm3
Serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL
Serum albumin 2.0 g/dL
Cholesterol 210 mg/dL

Examination of a renal biopsy specimen shows normal-appearing glomeruli by light microscopy. Which of the following would most likely be found in the urine?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has minimal change disease, which presents with nephrotic syndrome, is commonly seen in children, and is characterized by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria. Although not mentioned in the vignette, the condition can follow an upper respiratory tract infection, an allergic reaction to bee sting, or NSAID use. It is usually self-limited. However, some children require steroid therapy, where the condition usually resolves by puberty. Minimal change disease in adults can be associated with Hodgkin disease. Adults can respond to steroid treatment, although at a slower rate.

Light microscopy is normal, but diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes is seen by electron microscopy. This is attributed to an altered cell-mediated immunologic response with abnormal secretion of T cell lymphokines. This alters the foot processes, thereby causing reduced negative charge of the glomerular basement membrane, which decreases the ability to repel negatively charged albumin and results in selective proteinuria. In addition, nephrotic syndrome also presents with edema (hypoalbuminemia causes decreased intravascular oncotic pressure, causing fluids to shift into the interstitial space), hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria. There is also increased risk for thrombosis due to loss of antithrombin III (normally responsible for lysing thrombin and factor Xa; heparin and low molecular weight heparin potentiates effect of antithrombin III).

Granular casts (choice A) are comprised of dead, necrotic epithelial cells, and are seen in acute tubular necrosis (ATN), not minimal change disease. Ischemic or toxic injury to renal tubule epithelial cells cause the cells to slough off, form a mold within the renal tubule lumen, and are then flushed out in the urine.

Lambda light chains (choice B) are associated with multiple myeloma (Bence-Jones proteins), not minimal change disease. They are filtered through the glomeruli, accumulate in renal tubules, and cause proteinuria, tubular damage, and renal failure. Light chain nephropathy can, of course, present with nephrotic syndrome.

Neutrophils (choice D) can be seen with any bacterial urinary tract infection. Neutrophil casts reflect accumulation of neutrophils within renal tubule lumen, such as that seen in pyelonephritis, whereas scattered neutrophils in urine would be seen in lower locations such as ureter, bladder, and urethra.

Red blood cells (choice E) in urine (hematuria) are associated with conditions such as trauma, nephritic syndrome, bacterial infection (cystitis), and malignancies of the kidney and bladder. Red blood cell casts reflect accumulation of red cells within renal tubule lumen (nephritic syndrome), whereas scattered red blood cells would be extravasated within lower locations such as the ureter, bladder, and urethra.

Ischemic or toxic injury to renal tubule epithelial cells cause the cells to slough off, form a mold within the renal tubule lumen, and are then flushed out in the urine.

stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of progressive swelling in her feet. She attends dance class and is unable to participate along with the other children because of her condition. Physical examination reveals bilateral lower extremity edema from the ankles to the calves. A 24-hour urine collection reveals 4 grams of protein, but no red cells or casts. Kidney biopsy is performed and electron microscopy is utilized. Which of the following is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?

options.text: Diffuse effacement of epithelial foot processes

explanation:
The correct answer is B. Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by severe proteinuria (>3.5 g/d), hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria. Minimal change disease (also called lipoid nephrosis and nil disease) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. The disease has peak incidence at ages 2 to 6. Light microscopy shows normal glomeruli with lipid accumulation in proximal tubule cells (lipoid nephrosis). Immunofluorescence is negative, with no immune deposits being visualized. Electron microscopy shows diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes but no immune complex deposits. The prognosis is excellent in children because treatment with corticosteroids produces a dramatic response. The majority have a complete recovery.

Other causes of nephrotic syndrome include focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and membranous nephropathy (also called membranous glomerulonephritis). Both are associated with visible glomerular pathology at the light microscopic level, unlike minimal change disease, which may appear essentially normal with light microscopy.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is a form of glomerular disease that affects both the glomerular mesangium and the basement membranes; it occurs in two types (type I and type II). Subendothelial deposits (choice D) are seen in type I MPGN. Dense deposits (choice A) within the glomerular basement membrane are seen in type II MPGN and described as intramembranous deposits.

Mesangial deposits (choice C) are a prominent feature of IgA nephropathy and are seen to a lesser degree in several other glomerulonephritides. IgA nephropathy can be associated with celiac sprue and Henoch-Schonlein purpura.

Subepithelial spikes (choice E) are a feature of membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN). Electron microscopy shows subepithelial deposits along the basement membranes with effacement of podocyte foot processes. The "spikes" reflect the thin area of basement membrane that is present between the immune complex deposits. Immunofluorescence shows a granular and linear pattern of IgG and C3.

choice_explanations.B: The correct answer is B. Electron microscopy in minimal change disease shows diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes but no immune complex deposits; light microscopy is normal.

choice_explanations.D: Subendothelial deposits (choice D) are seen in type I MPGN.

A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious at home. He regained consciousness in the ambulance and is able to state his name, date, and current year. He has no significant medical history. His temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 80/45 mmHg. Physical examination shows no abrasions or bruises, non-tender abdomen, and normal reflexes. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin is 9 g/dL, hematocrit is 27%, and platelet count is 350,000/mm3. An upper GI endoscopy shows a bleeding duodenal ulcer, which is surgically repaired. He receives 6 units of packed red blood cells. Two days later, laboratory studies show:

Hemoglobin 15 g/dL
Hematocrit 45%
Serum urea nitrogen 35 mg/dL
Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL

Urine microscopy shows presence of granular casts and few red blood cells. Fractional excretion of sodium is 5.5% (normal 1-3%) and osmolality is 300 mosmol/kg H2O. Two weeks later at a post-discharge follow-up appointment, the urine sediment is clear and renal function is normal. Which of the following histologic features of the kidney would most likely be present in this patient at this time?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The patient had acute tubular necrosis (ATN) from the hypotensive and hypovolemic episode. ATN can be caused by ischemic (hypotension, hemorrhage, sepsis) or nephrotoxic injury. The presence of elevated urea nitrogen, creatinine, granular casts, and elevated fractional excretion of sodium reflect the presence of ATN. ATN is reversible if treated and is fatal if untreated. When the patient's underlying condition is treated, recovery of the renal tissue can occur. The renal tubular epithelium can regenerate as long as the basement membrane is intact. In our patient, recovery and regeneration of tubular epithelium are reflected in the return of normal renal function and clear urine sediment.

Coagulative necrosis (choice A) is a form of necrosis where the cellular architecture is preserved ("ghost cells") for days to weeks. Occlusion of renal vessels leads to ischemia, resulting in coagulative necrosis. If extensive, patients would have hematuria and flank pain. Our patient does not have any cause for renal infarction that would lead to coagulative necrosis.

Fibrosis (choice B) and granulation tissue (choice C) are seen as part of wound healing from renal infarction associated with renal vessel occlusion (atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus, hypertension) or thrombosis. Our patient does not have any cause for renal infarction.

Hemosiderosis (choice D) is accumulation of granular iron pigment within organs from a systemic overload of iron levels. Histologically, there would be brown pigment present in hepatocytes that would stain positive with Prussian blue iron stain. Causes of hemosiderosis include hereditary hemosiderosis, hemolytic anemia, and repeated red cell transfusions. Our patient had 6 units of red cell transfusion, which would not contribute to hemosiderosis. In contrast, local hemosiderin accumulation can be seen with bruising of an affected region, where macrophages would engulf extravasated red cells.

Occlusion of renal vessels leads to ischemia, resulting in coagulative necrosis. If extensive, patients would have hematuria and flank pain. Our patient does not have any cause for renal infarction that would lead to coagulative necrosis.

The renal tubular epithelium can regenerate as long as the basement membrane is intact; recovery and regeneration of tubular epithelium are reflected in the return of normal renal function and clear urine sediment.
