choice_explanations.A: Antibodies to centromeres are found in limited scleroderma/CREST (found in <5% of SLE patients).
choice_explanations.B: Antibodies to the glomerular basement membrane are found in Goodpasture syndrome (linear deposition along the GBM with glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage).
choice_explanations.C: Antibodies to SS-A (Ro) ribonucleoprotein are found in Sjögren syndrome.
choice_explanations.D: The vasculitis and rash of SLE are associated with immune complex deposition in small-diameter blood vessels, followed by complement-mediated lysis (e.g., the malar "butterfly rash").
choice_explanations.E: Epstein-Barr virus has been implicated in the initiation of rheumatoid arthritis, not as a finding of SLE.

fa_summary: SLE 诊断依据 + 抗 Sm（Smith）抗体；其血管炎与面部皮疹由免疫复合物沉积于小血管后继发补体介导的溶解。

stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of dyspnea, tachycardia, and diaphoresis following a bee sting. A thorough medical history reveals that she has had similar severe responses to bee stings on two other occasions. Which of the following immunoglobulin classes was produced first during the initial response to this antigen?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The first immunoglobulin produced in response to any immunogen, upon initial exposure, is always IgM. This is because of the sequential transcription of the DNA coding for the immunoglobulin isotype genes. The first constant domain that is encoded downstream in the DNA from the idiotype coding is that for IgM and then IgD. These two isotypes are produced and expressed concomitantly. It is not possible for any other immunoglobulin to be made first. The symptoms that this patient is having are the result of a type I hypersensitivity reaction, but in these reactions the IgE antibody is preformed and already bound to mast cell receptors. IgE is not made during the hypersensitivity reaction itself and is only produced during the sensitization phase.

IgA (choice A), IgE (choice C), and IgG (choice D) can only be produced as a secondary response, i.e., one that follows the primary IgM response.

The DNA coding for the IgD (choice B) heavy chain follows that of IgM in the lymphocyte germ-line DNA. Mature, naive B lymphocytes express both IgM and IgD on their surfaces because of alternative RNA splicing, but the complete IgM molecule is always produced first.

choice_explanations.A: IgA is produced only as a secondary response, after the primary IgM response.
choice_explanations.B: IgD heavy chain is transcribed after IgM, and mature naive B cells co-express IgM and IgD, but the complete IgM molecule is always produced first.
choice_explanations.C: IgE is preformed and bound to mast cells in type I hypersensitivity; it is produced during sensitization, not during the symptomatic reaction.
choice_explanations.D: IgG is produced only as a secondary response, after the primary IgM response.
choice_explanations.E: IgM is always the first immunoglobulin produced on initial exposure to any immunogen.

fa_summary: 初次免疫应答最先产生的免疫球蛋白恒为 IgM（因基因顺序性转录，IgM 与 IgD 同时表达但 IgM 先成）。

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a sore throat, cough, and nasal congestion. His mother says that he has suffered from recurrent bacterial infections since he was 6 months old. Laboratory and genetic studies show that this patient has an inherited defect in one of the genes encoding a component of NADPH oxidase. A defect of which of the following processes is most likely responsible for the deficient leukocyte defense against microbes in this patient?

options.text: Transfer of lysosomal enzymes to phagosomes

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Phagocytosis is followed by rapid activation of oxygen-dependent enzymatic reactions referred to as the oxidative burst, which leads to generation of reactive oxygen radicals capable of killing bacteria. NADPH oxidase plays a fundamental role in the oxidative burst. NADPH oxidase is a multiprotein complex that oxidizes NADPH, producing superoxide anions (O2-) from molecular oxygen. Superoxide anions then convert to H2O2 by spontaneous dismutation. Hydrogen peroxide serves as the substrate for myeloperoxidase, which then acts to produce toxic halide radicals. Mutations in one of the genes encoding NADPH oxidase proteins are known to cause chronic granulomatous disease, a group of congenital disorders characterized by defective bacterial killing and chronic predisposition to infections with catalase-positive microbes. Patients with CGD are prone to persistent infections with catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, because these organisms destroy the hydrogen peroxide that they produce metabolically, so neither of the oxygen-dependent mechanisms can function in intracellular killing during these infections.

Other conditions due to defective leukocyte functions include genetic deficiencies in leukocyte adhesion molecules (leukocyte adhesion deficiencies 1 and 2; LAD1 and LAD2), which impair leukocyte adhesion and transmigration (choice A), leading to recurrent infections and defective wound healing. LAD1 is due to genetic alterations in the beta chain of the integrin. LAD2 is due to absence of sialyl-Lewis X, a carbohydrate that binds selectins expressed on activated endothelium.

Chemotaxis (choice B) is impaired in a number of acquired conditions, including diabetes mellitus, malignancy, thermal injury, and sepsis.

Myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency is a genetic condition characterized by absence of MPO and deficient production of HOCl (choice D). Myeloperoxidase converts H2O2 to HOCl in the presence of Cl-. HOCl is one of the most powerful bactericidal agents, killing bacteria by halogenation and oxidation of macromolecules. Patients with MPO deficiency tend not to be symptomatic unless they have a simultaneous inability to generate NADPH oxidase.

Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by a deficiency in the transfer of lysosomal enzymes into phagosomes (choice E). This defect also affects melanocytes, nerve cells, and platelets, resulting in a peculiar constellation of clinical features, i.e., susceptibility to infections, albinism, nerve deficits, and a bleeding diathesis.

choice_explanations.A: LAD1/LAD2 impair leukocyte adhesion and transmigration, causing recurrent infections and defective wound healing, but not the NADPH oxidase defect.
choice_explanations.B: Chemotaxis is impaired in acquired conditions such as diabetes, malignancy, thermal injury, and sepsis, not in this inherited NADPH oxidase defect.
choice_explanations.C: NADPH oxidase drives the oxidative burst, generating superoxide and H2O2 for intracellular killing; its deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease.
choice_explanations.D: Myeloperoxidase deficiency abolishes HOCl production but is usually asymptomatic unless NADPH oxidase is also impaired.
choice_explanations.E: Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is defective transfer of lysosomal enzymes into phagosomes (with albinism and bleeding diathesis).

fa_summary: NADPH oxidase deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease; the oxidative/respiratory burst generates reactive oxygen species that kill catalase-negative organisms.

stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of diffuse pelvic pain and a fever. She states that her husband was treated for a sexually transmitted infection one month ago, but she was not treated at that time. Her temperature is 38.2°C (101°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a tender mass around the left adnexa. Which of the following is most important in clearing the infection in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This woman has developed pelvic inflammatory disease, one of the sequelae of untreated sexually transmitted diseases (STDs). Ascending infections involving either gonococci or Chlamydia may enter the uterine tubes, producing salpingitis and eventually infecting the fimbriated ends and the ovaries. The palpable ovarian mass suggests tubo-ovarian abscess.

When you are not given diagnostic clues to distinguish between Neisseria and Chlamydia, the two likely causal agents, you should answer the question in reference to your knowledge of the epidemiology of the agents. In the United States, C. trachomatis causes the most common bacterial STD. Chlamydia are intracellular pathogens, and thus elicit a T-helper-1 (TH1) lymphocyte response. TH1 cells produce the cytokines that activate and clone all the effector cells of cell-mediated immunity. In the case of an obligate intracellular pathogen such as Chlamydia, the best effector cell is the cytotoxic T lymphocyte, which will be activated by the interleukin-2, interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor-beta produced by the TH cell. Unfortunately, this same immune response causes the damage to the fallopian tubes that can lead to infertility (a type IV hypersensitivity).

Antibodies (choice A) will not work because, as stated above, Chlamydia are intracellular pathogens and antibodies do not have a prominent role in clearing the infection.

Complement (choice B) plays a major role in inflammation and removal of immune complexes, but would not play a prominent role in clearing the infection of an intracellular pathogen such as Chlamydia.

Natural killer (NK) cells (choice C) are important in antitumor and antiviral immunology. Although Chlamydia are intracellular, cytotoxic lymphocyte activation via TH1 cells would be the predominant response.

TH2 lymphocytes (choice E) are involved in class-switching in B cells for the production of antibodies. Since Chlamydia are intracellular pathogens, however, antibody formation does not play a major role in immunity.

choice_explanations.A: Antibodies do not play a prominent role against intracellular pathogens such as Chlamydia.
choice_explanations.B: Complement aids inflammation and immune-complex removal but is not the key defense against an intracellular pathogen.
choice_explanations.C: NK cells are important in antitumor/antiviral immunity; for Chlamydia, cytotoxic T lymphocyte activation via TH1 cells predominates.
choice_explanations.D: Chlamydia are intracellular, eliciting a TH1 response that activates CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (cell-mediated immunity) to clear the infection.
choice_explanations.E: TH2 lymphocytes drive class-switching and antibody production, which does not play a major role against intracellular Chlamydia.

fa_summary: Intracellular pathogens (e.g., Chlamydia) elicit a TH1 response; TH1 cells secrete IFN-γ/IL-2 to activate macrophages and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (cell-mediated immunity).

stem: An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a severe headache and a high fever. The patient is incoherent. Physical examination shows nuchal rigidity. Examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) shows gram-negative diplococci. A review of the patient's records shows that he has had five previous episodes of infection with this pathogen, the earliest at age 6 years. Which of the following is most likely impaired in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. A wide variety of defects related to complement can produce immunodeficiency. The pattern of recurrent Neisseria (gram-negative diplococcus) infections described here is typical of deficiency of complement factors C6, C7, or C8. Recall that these are members of the membrane attack complex (MAC).

Deficiency of C1, C2, or C4 produces a combined immunodeficiency with a systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)-like syndrome. C1, C2, and C4 are proteins involved in the early classical complement pathway. Deficiency of C3 or C5 produces a tendency to pyogenic infections. C3 and C5 are involved in both complement pathways.

B-cell deficiencies (choice A) occur in a number of conditions and tend, in general, to be associated with an increased susceptibility to extracellular microorganisms.

Eosinophil deficiency (choice C) is not a usual cause of immunodeficiency, but it would impair the normal protective response against parasites.

Neutrophil abnormalities (choice D) are associated with increased susceptibility to extracellular microorganisms.

T-cell deficiencies (choice E) may present as severe combined immunodeficiencies or with infections with opportunistic organisms such as Candida, Pneumocystis, or Cytomegalovirus.

choice_explanations.A: B-cell deficiencies increase susceptibility to extracellular microorganisms, not the recurrent Neisseria pattern seen here.
choice_explanations.B: Recurrent Neisseria infections are typical of terminal complement (C6, C7, C8) deficiency, i.e., membrane attack complex components.
choice_explanations.C: Eosinophil deficiency is not a usual cause of immunodeficiency; it impairs defense against parasites.
choice_explanations.D: Neutrophil abnormalities increase susceptibility to extracellular microorganisms.
choice_explanations.E: T-cell deficiencies present as SCID or with opportunistic infections (Candida, Pneumocystis, CMV).

fa_summary: Terminal complement (C5-C9/MAC) deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria bacteremia; early complement (C1-C4) deficiency predisposes to SLE, and C3/C5 deficiency to pyogenic infection.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of purplish patches on his arms and thorax. The mother says that the boy also has a history of recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia and red, itchy rashes on the inside of his elbows and knees that leak fluid and crust over when scratched. Laboratory studies show thrombocytopenia and a selective decrease in IgM. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This child has Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, which is an X-linked, partial combined immunodeficiency disorder. It presents clinically as the triad of thrombocytopenic purpura, eczema, and recurrent opportunistic infections with organisms having polysaccharide capsules, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. The red, itchy rash in the question stem describes eczema. Patients characteristically have decreased serum IgM, normal IgG, elevated IgA/IgE, and T-cell deficits (which appear later in life). Most patients die before the second decade of life, either from infection or from non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Bone marrow transplantation has had some therapeutic success in these patients. A specific defect in the WAS protein, which plays a critical role in actin cytoskeleton rearrangement, has been implicated.

Ataxia telangiectasia (choice A) is a combined partial T- and B-cell deficiency that presents with ataxia, telangiectasia, and IgA and IgE deficiencies. The specific mutation is in a kinase involved in the cell cycle.

Common variable immunodeficiency (choice B) is a humoral deficiency that typically presents in the late teens and early twenties as a decrease in immunoglobulin levels.

Hyper-IgM syndrome (choice C) is an X-linked immunodeficiency that is a mutation in CD40L on activated TH cells that results in a deficiency in class-switching. Patients typically have elevated levels of IgM and low or deficient levels of the other antibody classes. Recurrent bacterial infections, particularly mucosal, are common.

Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (choice D) presents early in life with severe and recurrent infections with all pathogens: bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic. There are several different known causes.

choice_explanations.A: Ataxia telangiectasia presents with ataxia, telangiectasia, and IgA/IgE deficiency from a cell-cycle kinase mutation.
choice_explanations.B: Common variable immunodeficiency is a humoral deficiency presenting in late teens/early twenties with decreased immunoglobulin levels.
choice_explanations.C: Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40L defect) causes elevated IgM with low IgG/IgA/IgE and recurrent mucosal bacterial infections.
choice_explanations.D: Severe combined immunodeficiency presents early in life with severe infections by all pathogen classes.
choice_explanations.E: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked partial combined immunodeficiency with thrombocytopenia, eczema (the itchy rash), and recurrent polysaccharide-encapsulated infections, with decreased IgM.

fa_summary: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked combined (B- and T-cell) immunodeficiency with the triad of thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections with encapsulated organisms (decreased IgM).

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of alcoholism is brought to the emergency department after being found behind the neighborhood bar at 4 AM in freezing weather. He is lethargic and has shaking chills. His temperature is 39.2°C (102.5°F), pulse is 106/min, respirations are 12/min and labored, and blood pressure is 108/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor and cold extremities, and diffuse rales are heard on auscultation of the chest. His sputum is blood-tinged and contains numerous gram-positive, alpha-hemolytic cocci. Treatment with penicillin is begun and his condition improves over the next few days. Which of the following immune effector mechanisms is most important in completely clearing this infection?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The patient has typical pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. One of the most efficient mechanisms for eliminating extracellular pathogenic bacteria that are protected by polysaccharide capsules is by opsonization and phagocytosis by phagocytes. The IgG and IgM antibodies produced in response to the organism react with the capsular structure, stimulating the activation of the classical pathway of the complement system. This pathway produces large amounts of C3b that coat the organism, enhancing the speed and efficiency of phagocytosis. The reticuloendothelial system macrophages of the spleen function in clearing opsonized bacteria and cells from the circulation. In addition, IgG can function alone as a substance that can opsonize since phagocytic cells have receptors for the Fc portion of IgG (Fc receptor, CD16).

ADCC (antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity) (choice A) is a process whereby cells, such as macrophages and NK cells, find altered cells that have been coated with antibody, and destroy them. ADCC cells do not destroy antibody-coated bacteria, only altered self cells that are coated with antibody.

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (choice B) react only with cells that have antigen epitopes presented in association with class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules. An example would be a virus epitope from a virus-infected cell presented by class I molecules on the surface of the cell.

LAK cells (choice C) are natural killer (NK) cells that have been activated by high levels of IL-2 in vitro. They are considered to be superactivated NK cells. NK cells kill altered self cells such as tumor cells or virus-infected cells.

NK cells (choice D) are cells of the innate immune system that destroy virus-infected cells or tumor cells. This does not involve antibody and it does not involve extracellular pathogens.

choice_explanations.A: ADCC destroys antibody-coated altered self cells (via macrophages/NK cells), not antibody-coated bacteria.
choice_explanations.B: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognize antigen presented on class I MHC and kill altered self cells, not extracellular bacteria.
choice_explanations.C: LAK cells are IL-2-activated (superactivated) NK cells that kill tumor/virus-infected cells.
choice_explanations.D: NK cells destroy virus-infected or tumor cells without antibody and do not target extracellular pathogens.
choice_explanations.E: Opsonization by IgG/IgM plus complement (C3b) coats the encapsulated organism and greatly enhances phagocytosis, which is key to clearing S. pneumoniae.

fa_summary: C3b and IgG are the two primary opsonins; opsonization enhances phagocytosis of encapsulated extracellular bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae.

stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of difficulty swallowing, hard subcutaneous lesions, and hands that turn painful in cold weather. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 86/min, blood pressure is 122/69 mm Hg, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 99%. Physical examination shows markedly thickened, shiny skin on the fingers and hands. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be present in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The symptoms described in the question are classic for CREST syndrome. This condition is an example of localized scleroderma with slow progression to life-threatening complications. CREST syndrome is the combination of Calcinosis (calcified subcutaneous nodules)/anti-Centromere antibodies, Raynaud phenomenon (hypoperfusion of the digits causing color changes and pain), Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly (localized thickening and tightness of the skin), and Telangiectasia. Anticentromere antibodies are reported in a high percentage of patients who have CREST syndrome, but only in a small percentage of systemic scleroderma patients. Centromeres are the portion of the chromosome where spindle fibers attach sister chromatids during cell division.

Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies (choice A) are autoantibodies directed against acetylcholine receptors and are found in myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis is characterized by ptosis and muscle fatigability.

Antihistone antibody (choice C) is a marker for drug-induced lupus erythematosus. Drugs that can induce systemic lupus erythematosus are hydralazine, isoniazid, and procainamide. Common symptoms include fever, myalgias, rash, arthralgias, arthritis, and serositis. Removal of the drug generally leads to remission.

Anti-Ro or anti-SS-A (choice D) is a marker for Sjögren syndrome, which is characterized by dry eyes and dry mouth.

Rheumatoid factor (RF) (choice E) is generally an IgM autoantibody directed against the Fc portion of IgG. RF is found in 80% of patients who have rheumatoid arthritis and may also be found in low titers in patients who have chronic inflammatory diseases such as pulmonary, hepatic, or renal diseases.

choice_explanations.A: Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies occur in myasthenia gravis (ptosis, muscle fatigability).
choice_explanations.B: Anticentromere antibodies are found in CREST (limited scleroderma): calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia.
choice_explanations.C: Antihistone antibody is a marker for drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, isoniazid, procainamide).
choice_explanations.D: Anti-Ro/anti-SS-A is a marker for Sjögren syndrome (dry eyes and dry mouth).
choice_explanations.E: Rheumatoid factor is an IgM antibody against the Fc portion of IgG, found in rheumatoid arthritis and other chronic inflammatory diseases.

fa_summary: Anticentromere antibody is associated with limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome); anti-Scl-70 with diffuse scleroderma.

stem: A 28-year-old primigravid woman gives birth to a child at term. The father is homozygous RhD-positive and the mother is homozygous RhD-negative. The baby is born without any complications, but the mother is not given RhoGAM (anti-Rh IgG) following the delivery. Eighteen months later, she delivers another child, who is anemic, slightly jaundiced, and has an enlarged spleen and liver. Which of the following is the most likely underlying explanation for these findings in the second child?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The Rh factor is a red blood cell surface antigen; about 85% of people are Rh+. Rh incompatibility occurs when a woman with Rh(D)-negative (Rh-) blood type is exposed to Rh(D)-positive (Rh+) blood cells, leading to the development of Rh antibodies.

This is an example of type II hypersensitivity, in which antibody is produced against cells or receptors in the body. In this type of cytotoxic disease, the mother produced antibody against Rh+ cells to which she was exposed upon delivery of her first child. (This child must be Rh+ because the father is homozygous Rh+.) The Rh+ cells are foreign to the mother since she is Rh-, so she mounts an antibody response against the antigen. This will pose no problems during the first pregnancy because the mother's immune system will not usually encounter fetal blood cell antigens until placental separation at the time of birth. However, at that time, Rh+ fetal red blood cells will enter the maternal circulation and stimulate a T-dependent immune response, eventually generating memory B cells capable of producing IgG antibody. In a subsequent pregnancy with another Rh+ fetus, this maternal IgG can be transported across the placenta, react with fetal Rh+ red cells, and activate complement, producing a hemolytic disease in the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis), which can cause jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly. Hemolytic disease of the newborn can be prevented by treating the Rh- mother with RhoGAM, a preparation of human anti-RhD IgG antibody, at 28 weeks gestation and within 72 hours after birth. This antibody effectively eliminates the fetal Rh+ cells before they can generate RhD-specific memory cells in the mother.

Atopic disease (choice A) is a type I immediate hypersensitivity reaction that occurs in minutes following a second exposure to the offending allergen.

Type IV hypersensitivity is delayed-type hypersensitivity (choice C), developing in response to viral, fungal, and intracellular bacterial antigens. It involves CD4 T-helper lymphocytes, but not antibody.

Immediate hypersensitivity (choice D) is a type I reaction that occurs in minutes following a second exposure to the offending allergen.

Immune complex disease (choice E) is a type III hypersensitivity reaction. It involves antigen-antibody complexes, which deposit in small and medium vessels and cause disease via activation of complement. Systemic lupus erythematosus and serum sickness are examples of type III hypersensitivity.

choice_explanations.A: Atopic disease is a type I immediate hypersensitivity reaction occurring within minutes of re-exposure.
choice_explanations.B: This is a type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity: maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses the placenta and destroys fetal Rh+ red cells (hemolytic disease of the newborn).
choice_explanations.C: Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity is T-cell mediated and does not involve antibody.
choice_explanations.D: Immediate hypersensitivity is a type I reaction occurring within minutes of re-exposure.
choice_explanations.E: Immune complex disease is type III hypersensitivity (e.g., SLE, serum sickness).

fa_summary: Hemolytic disease of the newborn is a type II (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity: maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses the placenta and destroys fetal Rh+ erythrocytes.

stem: A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician for a pre-employment physical examination. She says that as a child she experienced two episodes of fever, headache, and sore joints following severe sore throats. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following sequelae of her childhood illness is most likely to develop in this patient as she grows older?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. After an initial attack of rheumatic fever, an affected individual is at increased risk for developing recurrent rheumatic disease after each pharyngeal infection by beta-hemolytic streptococci. Any one of the manifestations of rheumatic disease can recur, but will usually resolve. The damage to the heart valves caused by rheumatic fever can lead to fibrous scarring and deformity, producing valvular dysfunction (particularly mitral stenosis), which may lead to heart failure in late adulthood. This is an example of a type II hypersensitivity reaction in which tissue-specific autoantibodies cause damage to host tissues, also known as molecular mimicry. In this case, group A Streptococcus pyogenes' cell wall contains a particular protein called M protein. During Streptococcus infection, antibodies to the M protein form, which then cross-react with a cardiac antigen, producing valvular and endocardial damage and causing valvular damage, particularly in the mitral valve.

The arthritis (choice A) produced by rheumatic fever is transitory and resolves after the attack has run its course. There are no long-term complications of the arthritis.

Fibrinous pericarditis (choice B), like almost any fibrinous inflammatory response, is an acute process. Although the patient may develop some scarring of the pericardium, this is generally not sufficient to produce long-lasting consequences.

Myocardial involvement (choice C) by rheumatic fever is typically seen as Aschoff bodies, collections of fibrinoid necrosis, lymphocytes, plasma cells and histiocytes within the myocardium. When the event resolves, the Aschoff bodies will be replaced by discrete fibrous scars. No appreciable myocardial dysfunction ensues.

Sydenham chorea, the neurologic manifestation of acute rheumatic fever, causes no lasting neurologic effects (choice D).

choice_explanations.A: Rheumatic fever arthritis is transient and resolves without long-term complications.
choice_explanations.B: Fibrinous pericarditis is an acute process; any pericardial scarring is generally insufficient to cause long-lasting consequences.
choice_explanations.C: Myocardial involvement (Aschoff bodies) is replaced by discrete fibrous scars without appreciable myocardial dysfunction.
choice_explanations.D: Sydenham chorea causes no lasting neurologic effects.
choice_explanations.E: Rheumatic fever causes fibrous scarring and deformity of heart valves (particularly mitral stenosis), which may lead to heart failure in late adulthood.

fa_summary: Rheumatic fever (type II hypersensitivity from group A streptococcal molecular mimicry) causes permanent valvular damage, especially mitral stenosis.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the physician because of a pruritic, linear, vesicular rash on her leg. The rash developed 2 days after she returned from a hiking trip. She says that it began as a swollen, erythematous streak that developed into extremely itchy blisters and that she has experienced similar episodes in the past. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for the development of this rash in this patient?

options.text: Antigen-antibody complexes formed in the circulation and deposited in the tissue
Cytotoxic antibodies against cell surface antigens
Release of histamine from mast cells
Release of interferon-gamma from activated TH1 cells

explanation:
The correct answer is E. This woman most likely has been exposed to poison ivy, which caused a contact, type IV cell-mediated sensitivity response to urushiol, an oil found in poison ivy. Contact with this oil leads to a reaction that appears as a linear, streaklike rash in sensitized individuals. Redness, swelling, and pruritic blisters occur at the sites of contact. Sensitivity usually develops after the first contact with poison ivy, and the reaction described typically occurs after subsequent exposures. Antigenic activation of TH1 lymphocytes causes the production of interferon-gamma, which stimulates macrophages and cytotoxic T lymphocytes to destroy the oil-coated cells. This reaction does not require the formation of antibodies.

Antigen-antibody complexes formed in the circulation and deposited in the tissue (choice A) underlie type III hypersensitivity reactions. Diseases mediated by this type of hypersensitivity include systemic lupus erythematosus and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Cytotoxic antibodies against cell surface antigens (choice B) produce type II hypersensitivity reactions. Diseases mediated by this type of hypersensitivity include autoimmune hemolytic anemia, pemphigoid, pemphigus, and Goodpasture disease.

IgE antibody-mediated basophil degranulation (choice C) and the release of histamine from mast cells (choice D) are the mechanisms responsible for type I immediate hypersensitivity reactions. IgE antibodies are formed in response to exposure to a specific antigen. Re-exposure to that antigen results in the cross-linking of the IgE molecules on the surface of mast cells and basophils, and subsequent degranulation to release mediators that cause the classic manifestations of type I hypersensitivity reactions. Examples are hives, hay fever, and anaphylactic reactions.

choice_explanations.A: Circulating antigen-antibody complexes deposited in tissue underlie type III hypersensitivity (e.g., SLE, poststreptococcal GN).
choice_explanations.B: Cytotoxic antibodies against cell-surface antigens produce type II hypersensitivity (e.g., autoimmune hemolytic anemia).
choice_explanations.C: IgE-mediated basophil degranulation is the mechanism of type I immediate hypersensitivity.
choice_explanations.D: Histamine release from mast cells is the mechanism of type I immediate hypersensitivity.
choice_explanations.E: Poison ivy contact dermatitis is a type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity: TH1 cells release interferon-gamma, activating macrophages and CD8+ CTLs to destroy the oil-coated cells.

fa_summary: Poison ivy contact dermatitis is a type IV (delayed-type, cell-mediated) hypersensitivity mediated by TH1 cells and macrophages, not antibodies.

stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of recurrent infections. He has a history of infections with Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa that have occurred over the past 6 months. Laboratory studies show serum IgG levels of 900 mg/dL and decreased C3 levels. To which of the following does this patient have an increased susceptibility?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Individuals with C3 deficiency have an increased susceptibility to immune complex diseases (type III hypersensitivity). The most important functions of C3 are removing immune complexes from the bloodstream and enhancing opsonization. Type III hypersensitivity reactions result from immune complexes of self or foreign antigens bound to an antibody; these will activate complement, leading to tissue damage. Examples of type III hypersensitivity reactions include systemic lupus erythematosus, and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Human immunodeficiency virus-1 (choice A), which is the cause of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), is an intracellular pathogen that depends on the activation of TH1 cells and their cytokines for a protective immune response. A patient with C3 deficiency would not be expected to be any more susceptible to an intracellular pathogen such as this one than the population at large would be.

Measles (choice B) is caused by rubeola virus, which is an intracellular pathogen and would not be affected by deficiencies in complement.

Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (choice C) is an intracellular bacterium that infects phagocytic cells. It is controlled by a cell-mediated response, not a complement-mediated response.

Type IV hypersensitivity (choice E) is a disease that depends on the action of TH1 cells, macrophages, and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. It does not depend on the presence of antibody and complement.

choice_explanations.A: HIV-1 is an intracellular pathogen controlled by TH1 cytokines; C3 deficiency does not increase susceptibility.
choice_explanations.B: Measles (rubeola) is an intracellular pathogen unaffected by complement deficiency.
choice_explanations.C: Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare is controlled by cell-mediated immunity, not complement.
choice_explanations.D: C3 deficiency impairs clearance of immune complexes from the bloodstream, predisposing to type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity such as SLE and poststreptococcal GN.
choice_explanations.E: Type IV hypersensitivity depends on TH1 cells, macrophages, and cytotoxic T lymphocytes, not on antibody and complement.

fa_summary: C3 deficiency impairs opsonization and immune-complex clearance, causing increased susceptibility to type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity.

stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of pain and swelling in his knees and ankles along with a recent onset of fever. He had an upper respiratory infection two weeks ago, for which he received acetaminophen. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 115/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows erythematous skin macules with a clear center, arthritis, and small subcutaneous nodules on the dorsal aspect of the arms. A systolic murmur in the mid-precordial area is heard on auscultation of the chest. Which of the following hypersensitivity reactions best explains this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has rheumatic fever. Rheumatic fever is a condition characterized by pancarditis, arthritis, subcutaneous nodules, chorea, and erythema marginatum. Infection with group A Streptococcus (GAS) often precedes the onset of the disease by 2-3 weeks and is typically elicited in the patient's history as pharyngitis. GAS incites the production of antistreptococcal antibodies, which cross-react with antigens of heart, dermis, joints, etc. The antibodies bind and trigger an acute inflammatory response that eventually resolves. However, patients often suffer permanent sequelae, such as valvular heart disease.

This type of hypersensitivity response, in which autoantibodies bind antigens on cells or tissues, is classified as type II. Other examples of type II hypersensitivity-mediated diseases include Graves disease, in which the autoantibodies stimulate thyroid hormone production by binding thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptors, and myasthenia gravis, in which the autoantibodies interfere with cholinergic neuromuscular transmission by binding nicotinic receptors.

Type I hypersensitivity (choice A) is mediated by IgE. Antigens bind IgE on the surface of mast cells and trigger the release of inflammatory mediators such as histamine and heparin. Activation of the arachidonic acid cascade causes production of prostaglandins and leukotrienes. Asthma and urticaria are classic examples.

Contrast direct antibody interaction with immune complex formation and deposition. In type III hypersensitivity (choice C), immune complexes (antigen-antibody protein complexes) form in the blood and deposit in tissues, especially within vascular beds. The glomeruli of children are especially sensitive to immune complex deposition after GAS infection, so-called acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Serum sickness and systemic lupus erythematosus are other examples of type III hypersensitivity-mediated diseases.

Diseases caused by type IV hypersensitivity (choice D) (aka. delayed-type or cell-mediated hypersensitivity) are due to inappropriate helper T cell activation of phagocytes and direct killing by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells. One example of this reaction is pancreatic beta-cell death in type 1 diabetes.

choice_explanations.A: Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated (mast cells/basophils), e.g., asthma and urticaria.
choice_explanations.B: Rheumatic fever is a type II hypersensitivity reaction: antistreptococcal antibodies cross-react with cardiac tissue (molecular mimicry), as in Graves disease and myasthenia gravis.
choice_explanations.C: Type III hypersensitivity involves immune complex deposition in tissues/vascular beds (e.g., poststreptococcal GN, SLE, serum sickness).
choice_explanations.D: Type IV hypersensitivity is T-cell (delayed-type) mediated, e.g., pancreatic beta-cell death in type 1 diabetes.

fa_summary: Rheumatic fever is a type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity via molecular mimicry between group A streptococcal antigens and cardiac tissue.

stem: A 4-year-old boy with a history of multiple bacterial and viral respiratory infections is brought to the physician because of epistaxis. The patient's mother states that her brother had similar problems with recurrent nosebleeds. His vital signs are normal. Multiple petechial lesions are identified on the mucous membranes and legs. Which of the following genes is most likely to be deficient or mutated in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is F. This patient has Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, which is an X-linked condition characterized by thrombocytopenia, immunodeficiency ("TIE"), and eczema. This syndrome is categorized as a combined partial B- and T-cell deficiency. Affected children may present with bleeding and often succumb to complications of bleeding, infection, or lymphoreticular malignancy. The platelets are small, have a shortened half-life, and appear to be deficient in surface sialophorin (CD43). Serum IgM is usually decreased, whereas IgE and/or IgA is frequently increased. The inability to mount an antibody response to polysaccharide antigens supports recurrent infections from polysaccharide containing bacteria. Mutations in the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) gene on the short arm of the X chromosome is responsible for this disease. WAS protein is expressed in hematopoietic cells and functions in reorganizing actin cytoskeleton in order for cells to communicate with other cells.

Adenosine deaminase (choice A) is the enzyme deficient in a form of severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID). Such deficiency causes accumulations of toxic metabolites in lymphocytes. In SCID, patients have no immunity to bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites. Eczema and thrombocytopenia are not associated with adenosine deaminase deficiency.

Bruton tyrosine kinase (choice B) is the enzyme deficient in X-linked agammaglobulinemia. In this disorder, patients are susceptible to frequent and severe infections with extracellular microbes and have no circulating B lymphocytes. These patients have a severe deficiency of antibodies, including IgG, IgM, and IgA in particular. It would not be associated with eczema and thrombocytopenia.

CD18 (choice C) is a cell adhesion marker that is deficient in leukocyte adhesion deficiency. Patients usually present early in life with omphalitis, and also have difficulty with extracellular infections. It causes patients to be unable to produce pus or abscesses and would not typically be associated with eczema and thrombocytopenia.

Myeloperoxidase (choice D) is an enzyme found in lysosomal granules that acts on H2O2 to produce HOCl. Deficiencies in this enzyme are usually asymptomatic because if NADPH oxidase is functional, it is usually sufficient for intracellular killing.

NADPH oxidase (choice E) is the enzyme that is deficient in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). In CGD, neutrophils cannot generate toxic oxygen radicals and have difficulty clearing infections with catalase-positive bacteria.

choice_explanations.A: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes SCID (no immunity to all pathogens) without eczema or thrombocytopenia.
choice_explanations.B: Bruton tyrosine kinase deficiency causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia (no B cells, antibody deficiency), not eczema/thrombocytopenia.
choice_explanations.C: CD18 deficiency causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency (omphalitis, no pus/abscesses), not eczema/thrombocytopenia.
choice_explanations.D: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is usually asymptomatic if NADPH oxidase is functional.
choice_explanations.E: NADPH oxidase deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease (catalase-positive organisms), not eczema/thrombocytopenia.
choice_explanations.F: Mutations in the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) gene cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (thrombocytopenia, immunodeficiency, eczema).

fa_summary: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is caused by mutations in the WASP gene (X-linked); clinically it is thrombocytopenia + immunodeficiency + eczema with small platelets.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a deep puncture wound to her right hand. A shard of glass is removed from the wound, and the wound is cleaned and dressed. The patient is taking medication that decreases chemotaxis of white blood cells via a novel mechanism. A side effect of the drug is poor wound healing and increased infection risk. The drug most likely blocks which of the following molecules?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. In active inflammation, the complement system is activated and C5a is produced. C5a is a strong chemoattractant to neutrophils and other phagocytic cells. Other chemotactic factors for neutrophils include IL-8, fibrinopeptides, leukotriene B4, and formyl methionyl peptides from bacteria.

Blocking C5a would significantly reduce neutrophil chemotaxis into the wound of the patient in the question stem. As with other drugs that decrease the immune response, poor wound healing and increased risk for infection would result. As an example, eculizumab is one such anti-C5a agent. One major side effect of this drug is, in fact, increased infection risk.

C3b (choice A) is an opsonin. When an organism is coated with C3b, it is more easily phagocytized. C3b is formed via the classical and alternative complement pathways, but it is not chemotactic for neutrophils.

IgM (choice C) is the first immunoglobulin produced in the primary immune response. It is not chemotactic for neutrophils.

IL-2 (choice D) is a powerful interleukin that stimulates proliferation of TH cells, natural killer cells, and CD8+ cytotoxic lymphocytes, but it is not chemotactic for neutrophils.

Lysozyme (choice E) is a material present in tears, mucus, vaginal secretions, and other body fluids. It is active against the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls, splitting the backbone structure of the peptidoglycan (N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramic acid polymers). It is not chemotactic for neutrophils.

choice_explanations.A: C3b is an opsonin (enhances phagocytosis) but is not chemotactic for neutrophils.
choice_explanations.B: C5a is a strong chemoattractant for neutrophils and other phagocytic cells; blocking it impairs chemotaxis, wound healing, and host defense.
choice_explanations.C: IgM is the first immunoglobulin of the primary response; it is not chemotactic for neutrophils.
choice_explanations.D: IL-2 stimulates proliferation of T cells and NK cells but is not chemotactic for neutrophils.
choice_explanations.E: Lysozyme cleaves bacterial peptidoglycan in body fluids but is not chemotactic for neutrophils.

fa_summary: C5a is a complement anaphylatoxin and a strong neutrophil chemoattractant; other neutrophil chemotactic factors include IL-8, LTB4, and bacterial formyl peptides.

stem: A 37-year-old man who is a herpetologist is brought to the emergency department because he was bitten by a rattlesnake. He had two prior rattlesnake bites for which he received appropriate treatment. Treatment is begun with an antivenin that is raised in horses. Two weeks later, the patient returns to the emergency department because of generalized edema, malaise, skin rash, and arthralgias. His serum urea nitrogen concentration is 20 mg/dL and serum creatinine concentration is 3.2 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of this patient's illness?

options.text: Direct antibody binding to the glomerular basement membrane
Immune complex deposition in the kidney

explanation:
The correct answer is D. This is a form of type III hypersensitivity; in essence this is a serum sickness reaction. Snake antivenin consists of antibodies against the specific venom. Furthermore, this patient has received prior passive treatments with immunoglobulin. When administered, this can cause the production of antigen-antibody immune complexes that should be cleared, usually efficiently by cells of the monocyte-phagocyte system.

In this type III hypersensitivity reaction, these complexes lodge into tissues, in particular the kidney and lung, because they cannot be cleared from the circulation in the small-diameter vasculature of these organs. In these locations, complement is activated by the presence of the immune complexes and the tissue is damaged by complement-mediated lysis and activation of neutrophils. Acute renal failure can develop as evidenced by the significantly increased creatinine in this patient. Laboratory analysis may also reveal decreased levels of complement C3 and C4. This type of reaction can also occur upon administration of many different drugs e.g. sulfonamides, allopurinol, penicillins, and cephalosporins.

Delayed-type hypersensitivity (choice A) is also known as type IV hypersensitivity. It is the only form of hypersensitivity that depends entirely on the action of TH1 cells and their mediators. It does not involve antibody in any way, and therefore can be ruled out in this case.

Direct antibody binding to the glomerular basement membrane (choice B), or type II hypersensitivity, occurs when autoantibodies are produced that bind to self cells or tissues. Type II hypersensitivity can cause cytotoxic reactions, where cells are damaged or destroyed, or non-cytotoxic reactions, where cell function is inhibited but the cells remain viable. Activation of complement in these areas causes damage that is tissue-specific, not system-wide as seen in type III hypersensitivities. The antibody injected in this case was specific for the rattlesnake venom, not a self-tissue constituent.

IgE-mediated anaphylaxis (choice C), or type I hypersensitivity, depends on the degranulation of mast cells and basophils following the crosslinking of preformed IgE antibody molecules on their cell surfaces. The symptoms of IgE-mediated hypersensitivity are due to the release of vasoactive amines and activation of the arachidonic acid cascade and will be manifested in minutes, not the weeks described here. Kidney failure is not a common outcome.

Rattlesnake venom nephrotoxicity (choice E) is not likely since the patient was promptly treated with antivenin to neutralize the action of the venom.

choice_explanations.A: Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity is T-cell mediated and does not involve antibody.
choice_explanations.B: Type II hypersensitivity (direct antibody to GBM) is tissue-specific; here the injected antibody targets venom, not self tissue.
choice_explanations.C: Type I (IgE-mediated) anaphylaxis occurs within minutes, not weeks, and does not typically cause kidney failure.
choice_explanations.D: Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity: antigen-antibody immune complexes deposit in small vessels (kidney, lung), activate complement, and cause tissue damage (↑ creatinine, ↓ C3/C4).
choice_explanations.E: Venom nephrotoxicity is unlikely because the patient was promptly treated with antivenin.

fa_summary: Serum sickness is the prototypic type III hypersensitivity: antibody-antigen immune complexes deposit in small vessels 1-2 weeks after antigen exposure, causing fever, urticaria, arthralgia, and proteinuria (↓ C3/C4).

stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a feeling that she has "sand in her eyes" and difficulty swallowing foods such as crackers and toast. Physical examination reveals irritated dry conjunctiva, an oral cavity that is erythematous with presence of few dental caries, and slightly enlarged parotid glands, bilaterally. She states that she brushes and flosses regularly and sees a dentist on a regular basis. Histologic examination of the salivary gland biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltration, small germinal follicles, and destruction of glandular tissue. Which of the following tests will most likely yield positive results in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient has Sjögren syndrome, which is an autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of exocrine glands resulting in dry mouth (xerostomia) and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). Patients have an increased risk of malignant B cell lymphoma arising in the affected organ. Autoantibodies produced include anti-Ro (SS-A), anti-La (SS-B), and antinuclear antibodies (ANA).

Anticentromere antibodies (choice A) are a very specific marker for CREST syndrome, the limited form of scleroderma. Esophageal dysmotility and difficulty swallowing are seen with CREST syndrome; other signs such as skin tightening, telangiectasia, and Raynaud phenomenon, are not mentioned.

Anti-Smith antibody and anti-double stranded DNA antibody (choice B) are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Salivary gland involvement is not seen with SLE.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies (choice C) are seen in anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (kidney limited) and Goodpasture syndrome. Goodpasture syndrome affects the lung and kidney only, which is not seen in our patient.

Anti-Scl-70 antibodies (choice D) are seen in patients with systemic/diffuse scleroderma. Esophageal dysmotility and difficulty swallowing are seen with systemic scleroderma, but other signs such as sclerodactyly, dyspnea (lung involvement), and skin tightening are not mentioned.

choice_explanations.A: Anticentromere antibody marks CREST (limited scleroderma).
choice_explanations.B: Anti-Smith and anti-dsDNA antibodies are associated with SLE, which does not cause salivary gland destruction.
choice_explanations.C: Anti-GBM antibodies occur in Goodpasture syndrome / anti-GBM disease, affecting lung and kidney only.
choice_explanations.D: Anti-Scl-70 marks systemic/diffuse scleroderma.
choice_explanations.E: Sjögren syndrome produces anti-Ro (SS-A) and anti-La (SS-B) antibodies with lymphocytic destruction of exocrine glands (xerostomia, keratoconjunctivitis sicca).

fa_summary: Sjögren syndrome is associated with anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies and causes lymphocytic destruction of exocrine glands (dry eyes and dry mouth).

stem: A 37-year-old woman with chronic active hepatitis B develops a low-grade fever. Her temperature is 37.4°C (99.4°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/88 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals a generalized petechial rash. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein, 1+ blood, 2+ bilirubin; fat globules and casts are present on microscopy. Examination of tissue obtained on needle biopsy of the kidney shows the presence of irregular deposits of antigen-antibody complexes with underlying areas of neutrophilic infiltration and tubular damage. Which of the following is most important in the removal of these immune complexes from the bloodstream?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The classical complement pathway is activated when C1-complex binds to the constant heavy domain of two IgG molecules or one IgM molecule that has reacted with the pathogen surface epitope. Downstream, C3, the most abundant protein of all the complement proteins, is cleaved into C3a and C3b. C3b attaches to bacterial surfaces for opsonization by phagocytes. C3a binds to mast cells and basophils activating them and producing histamine release. C3b is also critically involved in the removal of immune complexes from the serum. Immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis is common in many infectious diseases, where the chronic persistence of antigen and antibody mediate damage in the small vasculature by immune complex-mediated (type III) hypersensitivity. Most likely, this patient has membranous glomerulonephritis, which can present as a nephrotic picture: edema, proteinuria, lipiduria, and hypotension (as above). Subepithelial dense deposits would be present on electron microscopy.

The alternative complement pathway (choice A) is part of the innate immune system. It is continuously activated at a low level and is triggered by the spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 or by antigens directly, that are not bound by antibodies (unlike the classic complement pathway).

Antibody mediated response (choice B) is part of the adaptive immune system and functions to destroy extracellular bacteria.

Natural killer cells (choice D) are part of the innate immune system. Natural killer cells are not involved directly in killing pathogens, but they kill host cells that are compromised. These host cells are recognized by exhibiting a "missing self" signal of low levels of a cell-surface marker MHC class I.

T-mediated response (choice E) is part of the adaptive immune system. T-mediated response occurs in response to cells that are infected with viruses or other intracellular pathogens.

choice_explanations.A: The alternative pathway is innate, continuously activated at low level, and triggered by spontaneous C3 hydrolysis or antibody-independent antigens.
choice_explanations.B: The antibody-mediated response destroys extracellular bacteria but is not the main complement pathway removing immune complexes here.
choice_explanations.C: The classical complement pathway is activated by antigen-antibody complexes; C3b generated here clears immune complexes and opsonizes pathogens.
choice_explanations.D: NK cells of the innate immune system kill compromised host cells via the missing-self signal; they do not remove immune complexes.
choice_explanations.E: T-cell-mediated responses target virus-infected or intracellular pathogen-infected cells, not immune complex clearance.

fa_summary: The classical complement pathway is activated by antigen-antibody (IgG/IgM) complexes; C3b mediates opsonization and clearance of immune complexes from the serum.

stem: A 73-year-old woman with a history of diabetes comes to the physician because of left ear pain and drainage of pus from the ear canal. Physical examination shows swelling and tenderness over the left mastoid bone. The most likely causal organism is also responsible for causing which of the following?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes malignant otitis externa, which is a severe necrotizing infection of the external ear canal. Infection tends to spread to the mastoid bone, temporal bone, sigmoid sinus, base of the skull, meninges, and brain. Patients at increased risk include the elderly, people with diabetes, and the immunocompromised. Pseudomonas is also associated with many other clinical syndromes, including infection following traumatic wounds to the feet in persons wearing sneakers or rubber-soled shoes (since the organism can be cultured from the shoes), burn infections, and pneumonia in cystic fibrosis patients. Ecthyma gangrenosum is the name of the characteristic lesion that occurs during Pseudomonas septicemias. It has a black, necrotic center and a raised hemorrhagic ring outside. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative organism that causes several infectious processes such as urinary tract infections (catheterized patients), recurrent pneumonias (cystic fibrosis patients), and rarer infections such as ecthyma gangrenosum. Ecthyma gangrenosum is a black, necrotic skin lesion that is seen in septicemic patients.

The treatment of malignant otitis externa generally involves the use of oral or intravenous fluoroquinolones, such as ciprofloxacin. Topical otitis externa treatments are used for less severe cases and include ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin otic preparations. It should also be noted that both gentamicin and tobramycin "eye" drops can also be used. Although not tested on Step 1, a good clinical pearl to remember is that eye drops can be put in the ear BUT ear drops CANNOT be put in the eye.

Erythema migrans (choice B) is the target-shaped rash that occurs in the early stages of Lyme disease. Lyme disease is caused by an infection with the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi and the body's subsequent immune response to this organism. Borrelia burgdorferi is transmitted to humans via tick bites, from infected ticks of the genus Ixodes.

Food poisoning (choice C) is not commonly caused by Pseudomonas. The most common pathogens are Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens, Campylobacter, and Staphylococcus aureus, as well as Norovirus.

Non-mycotic mycetoma (choice D) is caused by Actinomyces and Nocardia. This type of infection causes granulomatous inflammatory response in the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue, which can also extend to the underlying bone.

Pharyngitis (choice E) is not commonly caused by Pseudomonas. The most common and important bacterial cause of pharyngitis is Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).

choice_explanations.A: Ecthyma gangrenosum is the characteristic black, necrotic skin lesion with a raised hemorrhagic ring seen in Pseudomonas septicemias.
choice_explanations.B: Erythema migrans is the target-shaped rash of early Lyme disease caused by Borrelia burgdorferi.
choice_explanations.C: Food poisoning is not commonly caused by Pseudomonas; typical pathogens include E coli, Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens, Campylobacter, Staphylococcus aureus, and Norovirus.
choice_explanations.D: Non-mycotic mycetoma is caused by Actinomyces and Nocardia.
choice_explanations.E: Pharyngitis is not commonly caused by Pseudomonas; the most important bacterial cause is Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).

fa_summary: 糖尿病老年患者恶性外耳道炎（铜绿假单胞菌）可累及乳突；该菌亦可致脓毒症中的坏疽性臁疮（ecthyma gangrenosum）。

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a mass in her left breast. A diagnosis of breast cancer is made and a mastectomy is planned. During the procedure, involvement of the muscle deep to the fatty tissue is seen and a radical mastectomy with removal of the breast, underlying chest muscles, and lymph nodes is performed. Removal of this muscle will most likely compromise which of the following functions?

options.text: Abduction of the humerus at the shoulder
Adduction of the humerus at the shoulder
External rotation of the humerus at the shoulder

explanation: The correct answer is B. The muscle deep to the breast is the pectoralis major. Breast cancer can invade this muscle, but usually does not because the relatively thick deep fascial layer serves as a barrier. Formerly, the pectoralis major was removed during radical mastectomy, leaving the patient with a major loss of function of the adjacent arm. The modified radical mastectomy, now more frequently used, spares the pectoralis major. The major actions of the muscle, which attaches to the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus, is to adduct and internally rotate the humerus at the shoulder. The deltoid muscle and the supraspinatus muscle act to abduct the humerus at the shoulder (choice A). External rotation of the humerus at the shoulder (choice C) is performed by the infraspinatus, teres minor, and posterior fibers of the deltoid muscles. The trapezius and the rhomboids are the retractors of the scapula (choice D). The pectoralis major can protract the scapula indirectly, by way of the humerus. Supinators (choice E) include the biceps brachii and supinator muscles.

choice_explanations.A: The deltoid and supraspinatus muscles abduct the humerus at the shoulder.
choice_explanations.B: The pectoralis major adducts and internally rotates the humerus at the shoulder; it is the muscle deep to the breast removed during radical mastectomy.
choice_explanations.C: External rotation is performed by the infraspinatus, teres minor, and posterior fibers of the deltoid.
choice_explanations.D: The trapezius and rhomboids retract the scapula; the pectoralis major can protract the scapula indirectly.
choice_explanations.E: Supinators include the biceps brachii and supinator muscles.

fa_summary: Pectoralis major lies deep to the breast; radical mastectomy removes it, impairing humeral adduction and internal rotation.

stem: A 59-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious by his wife. On examination, he is unable to move his extremities and has decerebrate posturing. The patient is unable to speak or move his face. He is able to answer yes/no questions by using eye blinks or vertical eye movements, but has no horizontal eye movements. He is unable to move his limbs in response to commands and has upgoing plantar responses bilaterally. Pathology of which of the following vessels is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
explanation: The correct answer is B. One large clinical clue is that patient has bilateral symptoms—all four limbs are affected and he has bilateral Babinski signs. In addition, the patient has awareness and is able to move his eyes vertically and blink. The only vessel listed that can cause bilateral signs and symptoms is the basilar artery, which supplies both sides of the ventral and medial pons. Note on the figure below that the basilar artery is formed by the joining of the 2 vertebral arteries; it ascends along the ventral midline of the pons, and then divides into the 2 posterior cerebral arteries. This patient has locked-in syndrome, which is characterized by: preserved alertness and cognitive abilities (reticular formation and cortex is spared); preserved vertical eye movements and blinking (these are controlled in the midbrain); and paralysis of limbs and oral structures. The patient cannot move their limbs or speak (lesioned corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers). Bilateral ventral pontine lesions will involve the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, which both course through the ventral pons. Damage to the corticospinal tracts will lead to quadriplegia and bilateral upgoing plantar responses (Babinski signs). Corticobulbar neurons normally synapse on lower motor neurons involved in motor functions of the mouth, tongue, pharynx, and jaws. Bilateral lesions of these fibers lead to a loss of voluntary mouth and tongue movements, and a loss of speech and the ability to swallow. The abducens nuclei (CN VI) are also affected, impairing horizontal eye movement. The reticular formation, which is involved in consciousness and the control of respiratory, cardiac, and vasomotor functions is spared. It is extremely important to recognize the vertical eye movements (controlled in the midbrain) in a patient who appears unresponsive because they can be misdiagnosed as a patient in a coma. Locked-in syndrome can also be caused by central pontine myelinolysis (damage to pons caused by overly rapid correction of hyponatremia), pontine abscess, and pontine tumors. The rest of the options can be eliminated because they produce combinations of ipsilateral and contralateral (but not bilateral) signs: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) (choice A) is a branch of the basilar artery. Occlusion of this vessel can lead to a lateral pontine syndrome, characterized by many ipsilateral or contralateral signs and symptoms. Symptoms include ipsilateral ataxia, vertigo/nausea/vomiting/nystagmus, facial nucleus and nerve signs (ipsilateral facial paralysis, loss of taste anterior 2/3 of tongue; loss of lacrimation, salivation, and corneal reflex; hyperacusis), ipsilateral pain/temperature loss (face), contralateral pain/temperature loss (body), ipsilateral hearing loss, and ipsilateral Horner's syndrome. The middle cerebral artery (choice C) is a large terminal branch of the internal carotid artery. Occlusion results in spastic paresis and anesthesia of the contralateral lower face and upper limb. Aphasia or hemineglect can also result depending on which hemisphere is affected. A contralateral superior quadrantanopia visual field defect can also occur. The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) (choice D) is a branch of the vertebral artery. Occlusion of this vessel can lead to a lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome), characterized by many ipsilateral or contralateral signs and symptoms. Symptoms include ipsilateral limb ataxia, vertigo/nausea/vomiting/nystagmus, nucleus ambiguus symptoms (CN IX, X: dysarthria, dysphagia, loss of gag reflex), ipsilateral pain/temperature loss (face), contralateral pain/temperature loss (body), and ipsilateral Horner syndrome. The vertebral artery (choice E) is a branch of the subclavian artery that ascends to the brain through the foramen magnum. Branches of the vertebral artery include the anterior spinal artery and PICA. Occlusion of this artery can lead to different syndromes depending on the location affected. Potential syndromes include the medial medullary syndrome and lateral medullary syndrome. Regardless of where the pathology is, bilateral symptoms would not be expected.

choice_explanations.A: AICA occlusion causes a lateral pontine syndrome with ipsilateral/contralateral (not bilateral) signs.
choice_explanations.B: The basilar artery supplies both sides of the ventral and medial pons; its occlusion causes bilateral signs and locked-in syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: MCA occlusion causes contralateral hemiparesis/anesthesia of the lower face and upper limb, not bilateral signs.
choice_explanations.D: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, not bilateral signs.
choice_explanations.E: Vertebral artery occlusion causes medial or lateral medullary syndromes but not bilateral symptoms.

fa_summary: Basilar artery occlusion damages both sides of the ventral pons, causing locked-in syndrome with preserved alertness and vertical eye movements.

stem: A 21-year-old man is bitten by a stray cat. The wound becomes erythematous and swollen despite appropriate wound care. Five days later, the patient notices a pustule at the wound site that was not previously present and develops a low grade fever. His symptoms persist, and two weeks later, he complains of pain in the back of his leg. Physical examination reveals a swollen tender lymph node in the popliteal fossa. An infected cat bite in which of the following sites would most likely induce lymphadenopathy in this region?

options.text: Lateral side of the dorsum of the foot
Medial side of the leg below the knee
Medial side of the sole of the foot

explanation: The correct answer is A. This patient has cat scratch disease, which occurs as a result of a Bartonella henselae infection, and is diagnosed with a Warthin-Starry stain. It can occur as a result of either a cat bite or a cat scratch. It typically presents with a primary cutaneous lesion within 3-10 days of primary injury before spreading to adjacent lymph nodes. The affected lymph nodes are usually tender and enlarged. There is also typically evidence of fever and sometimes, there may be visceral organ involvement. Bartonella can also rarely produce hepatitis and affect the spleen, eye, or CNS. Lymphatic drainage from skin of the lower limb generally follows the course of the superficial veins (see figure). Most of the venous drainage of the skin of the lower limb is to the great saphenous vein; the accompanying lymphatics drain into the superficial group of the inguinal lymph nodes. However, the skin drained by the small saphenous vein, including that of the lateral aspect of the dorsum of the foot, is an exception to this rule. Lymphatic fluid from this area drains into lymphatics accompanying the small saphenous vein, then drains into lymph nodes behind the knee in the popliteal fossa. The lateral side of the thigh (choice B), the medial side of the leg below the knee (choice C), the medial side of the sole of the foot (choice D), and the medial side of the thigh (choice E) are all regions for which venous drainage is to the great saphenous vein and, therefore, the lymphatics from these regions all drain to the superficial inguinal nodes. The following table summarizes the venous drainage of the lower extremities: the long saphenous vein drains and runs on the medial side of the leg and drains into the inguinal lymph nodes; the short saphenous vein drains the lateral side of the dorsum of the foot and runs on the posterior side of the leg, draining into the lymph nodes in the popliteal fossa.

choice_explanations.A: The lateral aspect of the dorsum of the foot drains via lymphatics that accompany the small saphenous vein into the popliteal lymph nodes.
choice_explanations.B: The lateral side of the thigh drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
choice_explanations.C: The medial side of the leg below the knee drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
choice_explanations.D: The medial side of the sole of the foot drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
choice_explanations.E: The medial side of the thigh drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

fa_summary: Lymphatics of the lateral dorsum of the foot accompany the small saphenous vein and drain to the popliteal lymph nodes.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of hypertension is admitted to the intensive care unit after sustaining a stroke. He describes recent onset dizziness and difficulty standing upright without falling over. Physical examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the face and the left side of the body. The right eye exhibits partial ptosis and pupillary miosis. He is discharged 6 days later and is transferred to a rehabilitation center. A more comprehensive physical examination also reveals difficulty in elevating the tongue to the roof of the mouth. Dysfunction of which of the following muscles is most likely responsible for this finding in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is C. This patient is displaying lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome), usually resulting from occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Among the cranial nerves affected by this syndrome is the vagus nerve. Elevation of the tongue is carried out by the styloglossus (innervated by the hypoglossal nerve, CN XII) and the palatoglossus (innervated by the vagus nerve, CN X). Other structures affected in this syndrome include: Vestibular nuclei: vertigo, nausea/vomiting, nystagmus (away from the lesion); Spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus: ipsilateral pain/temperature loss (face); Spinothalamic tract: contralateral pain/temperature loss (body); Descending hypothalamics: ipsilateral Horner syndrome; Inferior cerebellar peduncle: ipsilateral limb ataxia; Nucleus ambiguus: dysarthria, dysphagia, loss of gag reflex. The medial and lateral medullary lesions are shown below (Lesion A: Medial medullary syndrome; Lesion B: Lateral medullary syndrome). Note that tongue movement would also be affected by a medial medullary lesion due to damage to the hypoglossal nerve or nucleus. The buccinator (choice A) functions to maintain the contours of the cheek and to keep food between the teeth while chewing. The buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve, CN VII. The geniohyoid (choice B) elevates and moves the hyoid anteriorly to help in elevation of the pharynx. The geniohyoid is innervated by cervical spinal nerves. The palatopharyngeus (choice D) assists in elevation of the pharyngeal wall during swallowing. It does not cause movement of the tongue. The palatopharyngeus is innervated by the vagus nerve, CN X. The tensor palati (choice E) tenses the soft palate during swallowing and speech. It does not move the tongue. The tensor palati is innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, CN V.

choice_explanations.A: The buccinator maintains the contours of the cheek and keeps food between the teeth while chewing; innervated by CN VII.
choice_explanations.B: The geniohyoid elevates and moves the hyoid anteriorly to help elevate the pharynx; innervated by cervical spinal nerves.
choice_explanations.C: The palatoglossus (CN X) and styloglossus (CN XII) elevate the tongue; the palatoglossus is affected in Wallenberg syndrome.
choice_explanations.D: The palatopharyngeus assists in elevation of the pharyngeal wall during swallowing and does not move the tongue; innervated by CN X.
choice_explanations.E: The tensor palati tenses the soft palate during swallowing and speech and does not move the tongue; innervated by CN V3.

fa_summary: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome from PICA occlusion affects CN X; palatoglossus (CN X) helps elevate the tongue.

stem: A 24-year-old man who is a truck driver is brought to the emergency department because of a fracture of the right humerus. Physical examination shows an inability to extend the right hand at the wrist. The patient can flex all of the fingers but he cannot make a tight fist with the right hand. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured as a result of this fracture?
explanation: The correct answer is E. The radial nerve lies in the musculospiral groove of the humerus and is subject to injury in association with a fracture of the midshaft of the humerus. The radial nerve innervates the extensor muscles of the forearm, including the muscles that extend the wrist; paralysis of these muscles results in a wrist drop. Although the muscles responsible for flexing the digits are not innervated by the radial nerve, the making of a tight fist requires that the wrist be stabilized with the wrist extensors. The radial nerve is accompanied in the musculospiral groove by the profunda brachii artery and vein. The axillary nerve (choice A) leaves the axilla through its posterior wall through the quadrangular space. It is not located in the region of the midshaft of the humerus. This nerve may be injured by fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus, which forms the lateral border of the quadrangular space. The axillary nerve innervates the deltoid and the teres minor muscles, neither of which has any function in the hand. Lesion of the axillary nerve results in inability to abduct the arm at the shoulder and weakness of lateral rotation at the shoulder. The medial brachial cutaneous nerve (choice B) innervates the skin of the medial side of the arm. It lies in the superficial fascia of the arm and is not near the humerus, therefore not in danger of being injured with a fracture of the humerus. The median nerve (choice C) passes through the arm but is not in close contact with the humerus in the midshaft region. The nerve is separated from the bone by the brachialis muscle. The median nerve innervates many muscles of the anterior compartment of the forearm responsible for flexion of the wrist and digits. Lesion of the nerve results in loss of sensation of the palmar surface of the first three fingers and half of the fourth. Chronic injury of the median nerve results in clawing of the second and third fingers due to paralysis of the first and second lumbrical muscles. The musculocutaneous nerve (choice D) is not in contact with the humerus. It innervates the muscles in the anterior compartment of the arm. These muscles cause flexion at the elbow and supination.

choice_explanations.A: The axillary nerve is injured at the surgical neck of the humerus; it supplies deltoid and teres minor and has no hand function.
choice_explanations.B: The medial brachial cutaneous nerve supplies skin of the medial arm and lies in superficial fascia, far from the humerus.
choice_explanations.C: The median nerve is separated from the midshaft humerus by the brachialis; it supplies anterior forearm flexors.
choice_explanations.D: The musculocutaneous nerve is not in contact with the humerus; it supplies anterior arm muscles (elbow flexion, supination).
choice_explanations.E: The radial nerve lies in the musculospiral groove of the humerus; midshaft fracture injures it, causing wrist drop and impaired tight fist.

fa_summary: Radial nerve injury with midshaft humerus fracture causes wrist drop; wrist extensor stabilization is needed for a tight fist.

stem: A 35-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of pain and tingling in her hands. She also says that at times her hands feel numb, however she cannot pinpoint exactly where the numbness is centered. She reports no issues with her pregnancy. Physical examination shows wasting of the thenar eminence. Physical examination will most likely also reveal loss of sensation in which of the following sites?

options.text: Dorsal aspect of the hand (not fingers) on the medial side
