Dorsal aspect of the hand (not fingers) on the lateral side
Dorsal aspect of the proximal part of the forefinger
Dorsal aspect of the proximal part of the thumb
Nail bed of the third digit

explanation: The correct answer is E. This patient's presentation is fairly classic for carpal tunnel syndrome, in which the median nerve is compressed as it passes underneath the flexor retinaculum of the wrist. Many conditions predispose patients to this pathology, including hypothyroidism, pregnancy, amyloidosis, acromegaly, obesity, diabetes, and work with vibrating tools. For our patient, high levels of progesterone from pregnancy promote water retention, which leads to synovial swelling and makes the median nerve prone to compression. The primary clue to involvement of the median nerve is the physical exam finding of wasting of the thenar eminence. Although the ulnar nerve innervates a significant portion of the intrinsic muscles of the hand, the muscles of the thenar eminence are solely innervated by the recurrent branch of the median nerve. These muscles include the abductor pollicis brevis, the flexor pollicis brevis, and the opponens pollicis, which control abduction, flexion, and opposition of the thumb, respectively. The median nerve also provides innervation to the lateral two lumbrical muscles for digits 2 and 3. These muscles enable flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joint and extension at the interphalangeal joints. Thus, some patients with median nerve damage will display "clawing" of these two digits. However, the answer choices presented ask about the sensory distribution of the median nerve. The median nerve supplies sensory innervation from the thumb to the lateral half of the fourth (ring) finger, with extension to the distal dorsal aspect of each of these fingers, including the nail beds (choice E). The median nerve also provides innervation to the skin overlying the thenar eminence; however, this is mediated by the palmar branch, which does not actually pass through the carpal tunnel, but rather travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum. Thus this nerve and its associated sensory distribution would not be affected in carpal tunnel syndrome. The dorsal aspect of the hand on the medial (ulnar) side (choice A) of the hand is supplied by the ulnar nerve. The dorsal aspect of the hand, with the exception of the distal fingers, on the lateral (radial) side (choice B) of the hand is supplied by the radial nerve. The dorsum of the proximal part of the forefinger (choice C) and the dorsum of the proximal part of the thumb (choice D) are supplied by the radial nerve.

choice_explanations.A: The dorsal hand on the medial (ulnar) side is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
choice_explanations.B: The dorsal hand (except distal fingers) on the lateral (radial) side is supplied by the radial nerve.
choice_explanations.C: The dorsum of the proximal forefinger is supplied by the radial nerve.
choice_explanations.D: The dorsum of the proximal thumb is supplied by the radial nerve.
choice_explanations.E: The median nerve supplies the distal dorsal aspect of the lateral 3.5 digits, including the nail beds.

fa_summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome compresses the median nerve; thenar wasting and sensory loss over the lateral 3.5 digits/nail beds.

stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a severe sore throat. She describes significant pain with swallowing and general feelings of malaise. Her parents report that the patient has had a high fever for the past several days. Physical examination shows an erythematous patch on the upper posterior pharynx and tenderness of the cervical lymph nodes. Her temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F). The nerve responsible for this patient's throat pain is also involved in which of the following functions?

options.text: Sensory input from carotid sinus baroreceptors
Taste in the anterior 2/3 of the tongue

explanation: The correct answer is D. Recall that afferent nerve traffic (sensory) travels toward the central nervous system (CNS) and efferent nerve traffic (motor) travels away from the CNS. The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX): carries general somatic sensation from the posterior part of the upper pharynx, eustachian tube, middle ear, and posterior one-third of the tongue; conveys afferent fibers from the carotid sinus baroreceptors and carotid body chemoreceptors; carries taste sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue; sends efferent fibers to the stylopharyngeus muscle; carries parasympathetic fibers that synapse in the otic ganglion in the pathway for innervation of the parotid gland. Difficulty in swallowing (dysphagia) can result from a variety of causes including pain carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve, abnormal motor innervation to the muscles of the pharynx or esophagus (vagus nerve), muscle weakness (e.g., myasthenia gravis), disorders of esophageal motility and of the lower esophageal sphincter (achalasia), and compression of the pharynx or esophagus from nearby structures (e.g., left atrial enlargement, tumors in the neck or thorax). Head rotation to the opposite side (choice A) is accomplished by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), which innervates the sternocleidomastoid muscle. CN XI also elevates and upwardly rotates the scapula (trapezius). Movement of the intrinsic tongue muscles (choice B) is predominately controlled by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). CN XII innervates the intrinsic and extrinsic skeletal muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus muscle (which is innervated by CN X). Sensation of the lower jaw (choice C) is carried by the mandibular (V3) branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V). CN V receives somatic sensation from the face, lips, gums, teeth, palate, and anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and provides motor innervation to muscles of mastication (chewing). Taste in the anterior 2/3 of the tongue (choice E) is carried by the facial nerve (CN VII). CN VII also supplies motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression and to the stapedius muscle, and sends parasympathetic fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion (lacrimal gland) and submandibular ganglion (submandibular and sublingual glands).

choice_explanations.A: Head rotation to the opposite side is via the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) to the sternocleidomastoid.
choice_explanations.B: Intrinsic tongue muscles are controlled by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
choice_explanations.C: Sensation of the lower jaw is carried by the mandibular (V3) branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).
choice_explanations.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) conveys afferent fibers from the carotid sinus baroreceptors and carotid body chemoreceptors.
choice_explanations.E: Taste in the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is carried by the facial nerve (CN VII).

fa_summary: CN IX carries general sensation from the upper posterior pharynx/posterior 1/3 tongue and afferents from carotid sinus/body.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has worked out twice a week for several months at a local exercise club. Recently she developed a severe weakness in abduction of her thighs against resistance using an exercise machine. It is determined that this weakness began soon after she received an intramuscular injection of a vaccine. Damage to which of the following nerves is most likely responsible for this loss of function?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The patient has a deficit in hip abduction. The major hip abductors are the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus. Both muscles are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve, from roots L4 through S1. An intragluteal injection can injure this nerve. The deep fibular nerve (choice A) innervates the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg, which include the tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, and extensor hallucis longus. These muscles all contribute to dorsiflexion at the ankle. Injury to the deep fibular nerve causes "foot drop." The femoral nerve (choice B) innervates the muscles of the anterior compartment of the thigh, which include the quadriceps femoris, sartorius, and pectineus. The major functions of these muscles are hip flexion and knee extension. The obturator nerve (choice C) innervates the muscles of the medial compartment of the thigh, which include the gracilis, the adductor longus, adductor brevis, and the anterior part of the adductor magnus. These muscles are responsible for hip adduction. The tibial nerve (choice E) innervates all of the muscles of the posterior compartment of the thigh (responsible for hip extension and knee flexion), posterior muscles of the leg (responsible for plantar flexion and digit flexion), and the muscles of the plantar compartment of the foot (responsible for digit flexion, abduction, and adduction).

choice_explanations.A: The deep fibular nerve supplies the anterior leg compartment (dorsiflexors); injury causes foot drop.
choice_explanations.B: The femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh compartment (quadriceps, sartorius, pectineus) for hip flexion and knee extension.
choice_explanations.C: The obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh compartment (adductors) for hip adduction.
choice_explanations.D: The superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1) supplies gluteus medius and minimus, the major hip abductors; intragluteal injection can injure it.
choice_explanations.E: The tibial nerve supplies posterior thigh/leg and plantar foot muscles.

fa_summary: Superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1) innervates gluteus medius/minimus, the major hip abductors; intragluteal injection can injure it.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a skiing accident. She tells the physician that she was going too fast and grabbed a tree with her right arm to avoid colliding with another skier. Following the injury, the patient complained of weakness and numbness in her right upper extremity. Physical examination shows pain and numbness in the medial two fingers, the medial aspect of the palm, and in the medial aspect of the arm and forearm on the right. Examination also reveals clawing of digits in the right hand. This patient most likely injured which of the following?

options.text: The lower trunk of the brachial plexus
The upper trunk of the brachial plexus

explanation: The correct answer is B. Grabbing at something to stop oneself (as in this example, or when a skidding motorcyclist tries to catch a lamppost) is one of the more common mechanisms by which the lower trunk of the brachial plexus is damaged. Delivering the arms in an extended position above the head during a breech delivery is another means by which the lower trunk of the brachial plexus can be damaged. In both cases, there is excessive traction on the arm while it is in an abducted position. Thoracic outlet syndrome and superior sulcus tumors (e.g., Pancoast tumor of the apical lung) may also produce compromised function of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. The resulting condition from lower trunk injury is known as Klumpke paralysis. Keep in mind that the lower trunk of the brachial plexus receives input from C8-T1 of the spinal cord and contributes to the medial cord. The medial cord, in turn, provides innervation to the ulnar nerve, medial cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm, and a portion of the median nerve. Thus, the result of lower trunk injury is loss of motor function of the intrinsic hand muscles, and numbness along the inner aspect of the hand (ulnar side), forearm, and upper arm. In particular, loss of all lumbrical function (critical for flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joint and extension at both interphalangeal joints) produces the characteristic "total claw hand." If T1 injury is involved, Horner syndrome (ipsilateral miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis) may be present due to loss of sympathetic input to the superior cervical ganglia. The axillary nerve (choice A) can be damaged if there is a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or a dislocation of the head of the humerus. The axillary nerve innervates the deltoid muscle and teres minor, thus damage produces weakness of abduction and lateral rotation of the arm at the shoulder. There will also be some sensory loss in the upper lateral portion of the arm. Damage to the median nerve (choice C) can happen in carpal tunnel syndrome, supracondylar fractures, and suicide attempts via wrist slashing. Depending on the location, injury can result in loss of innervation to many flexor compartment muscles of the forearm, weakness of the thenar muscles ("flattening of the thenar eminence" and "ape hand"), and weakness of the lateral lumbricals (producing clawing of the 2nd and 3rd digits). It is true that many of the median nerve's intrinsic hand muscle functions are compromised with lower trunk injury due to lost contributions from the medial cord. However, there would not be a "total claw hand" or medial sensory loss with median nerve damage alone. The radial nerve (choice D) can be damaged with mid-humeral fractures or when a person falls asleep with the arm over the back of a chair (e.g., Saturday night palsy). Injury results in inability to extend the digits and wrist ("wrist drop"), due to the radial nerve's contribution to major extensor muscles of the arm and forearm. There would also be sensory loss on the dorsolateral portion of the hand. The ulnar nerve (choice E) is frequently injured by trauma to the elbow due to the nerve's passage through the cubital tunnel at this location. Although the ulnar nerve controls many intrinsic muscles of the hand, damage would produce clawing of the medial two digits, rather than all digits. Additionally, the ulnar nerve provides sensory innervation to the medial hand, but not the forearm and arm, which rely on cutaneous branches from the medial cord. The upper trunk of the brachial plexus (choice F) can be damaged when the person falls on the point of the shoulder or has a hyperextension injury of the neck (frequently after motor vehicle accidents or following a difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia). Patients may have altered sensation over the C5 and C6 dermatomes and a "waiter's tip" sign in the upper limb due to loss of function of the axillary, suprascapular, and musculocutaneous nerves.

choice_explanations.A: The axillary nerve is injured at the surgical neck of the humerus/dislocation; supplies deltoid and teres minor.
choice_explanations.B: Lower trunk (C8-T1) injury (Klumpke) causes total claw hand and numbness of the medial hand, forearm, and arm; may include Horner syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: Median nerve injury can cause thenar wasting and clawing of digits 2-3 but not total claw hand or medial sensory loss.
choice_explanations.D: Radial nerve injury (mid-humeral fracture or Saturday night palsy) causes wrist drop and dorsolateral hand sensory loss.
choice_explanations.E: Ulnar nerve injury causes clawing of the medial two digits and medial hand sensory loss, sparing forearm/arm.
choice_explanations.F: Upper trunk injury (shoulder trauma/neck hyperextension) gives C5-C6 sensory changes and a "waiter's tip" sign.

fa_summary: Lower trunk (C8-T1) brachial plexus injury = Klumpke paralysis: total claw hand plus medial arm/forearm/hand numbness.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after sustaining multiple knife wounds, including one into the axilla. Neurologic examination suggests an injury to the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. Further evaluation reveals no major vascular injury. Which of the following muscles is most likely to be paralyzed?
explanation: The correct answer is B. The posterior cord gives rise to the axillary and radial nerves. Of the muscles listed, only the deltoid is supplied by one of these two nerves, specifically the axillary nerve. The other muscle that is supplied by the axillary nerve is the teres minor muscle. The radial nerve innervates the posterior compartment muscles of the arm and forearm. The deltoid is a major abductor at the shoulder, as well as a flexor, extensor, medial rotator and lateral rotator at the shoulder. The teres minor is an external rotator and adductor at the shoulder. The brachialis (choice A) is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve, which arises from the lateral cord. The flexor digitorum superficialis (choice C) is innervated by the median nerve, which arises from branches of the lateral cord and the medial cord. The pronator teres (choice D) is innervated by the median nerve, which arises from branches of the lateral cord and the medial cord. The rhomboideus major and minor (choice E) are innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve, which arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus in the neck. This is proximal to the formation of any of the cords.

choice_explanations.A: The brachialis is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve from the lateral cord.
choice_explanations.B: The posterior cord gives off the axillary and radial nerves; of the listed muscles only the deltoid (axillary nerve) is supplied by them.
choice_explanations.C: The flexor digitorum superficialis is innervated by the median nerve (lateral and medial cords).
choice_explanations.D: The pronator teres is innervated by the median nerve (lateral and medial cords).
choice_explanations.E: The rhomboideus major and minor are innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve from the upper trunk.

fa_summary: The posterior cord divides into the axillary and radial nerves; the deltoid is supplied by the axillary nerve.

stem: A 54-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit because of sepsis secondary to a urinary tract infection. The decision is made to place a central line catheter in the lumen of the right internal jugular vein to better track hemodynamic information. A resident performs the procedure guided by ultrasound, but during the course of the procedure, inadvertently pierces through the vein and damages structures located posterior to the carotid sheath. Which of the following is most likely to occur?

options.text: Inability to abduct the right eye
Inability to close the right eye
Paralysis of the platysma muscle on the right side

explanation: The correct answer is A. The right sympathetic trunk lies posterior to the right carotid sheath, and may be injured in this procedure. Preganglionic sympathetic nerve fibers arising from the T1 spinal cord segment and ascending through the cervical sympathetic chain will be damaged. These nerve fibers synapse in the superior cervical ganglion on postganglionic sympathetic neurons that innervate structures in the head. The dilator pupillae muscle (smooth muscle of the iris that dilates the pupil) is sympathetically innervated; paralysis of this muscle due to interruption of its innervation results in constriction of the pupil (miosis). Dilation of the pupil (choice B) would result from paralysis of the sphincter pupillae muscle (smooth muscle of the iris that constricts the pupil). This muscle is innervated by the parasympathetic nervous system (CN III) and would not be affected by this injury. The preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arise from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain and exit the brain stem in the oculomotor nerve. They synapse in the ciliary ganglion and the postganglionic fibers enter the globe with the short ciliary nerves. An inability to abduct the eye (choice C) would result from paralysis of the lateral rectus muscle, an extraocular muscle that is innervated by the abducens nerve. It would not be affected by this injury. An inability to close the eye (choice D) would result from paralysis of the orbicularis oculi muscle, a skeletal muscle of the face. This muscle is innervated by the facial nerve and would not be affected by this injury. The platysma muscle (choice E) is a skeletal muscle in the superficial fascia of the neck. It is innervated by the facial nerve and would not be affected by this injury.

choice_explanations.A: Sympathetic trunk injury causes loss of the dilator pupillae (mydriasis muscle), giving unopposed miosis of the right pupil.
choice_explanations.B: Pupillary dilation results from paralysis of the sphincter pupillae (CN III parasympathetic), not affected here.
choice_explanations.C: Inability to abduct the eye is from lateral rectus/abducens (CN VI) injury, not affected here.
choice_explanations.D: Inability to close the eye is from orbicularis oculi/facial nerve (CN VII) injury, not affected here.
choice_explanations.E: The platysma is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII) and is not affected here.

fa_summary: The right sympathetic trunk lies posterior to the carotid sheath; injury causes ipsilateral miosis (Horner syndrome).

stem: A 58-year-old man is brought to his general physician by family members because of recent cognitive changes. His family is concerned that he is no longer able to recognize common objects in his surroundings. Neurologic examination shows that when he is presented with a picture of a dog, he is able to copy the picture but is unable to recognize the animal as a dog. This finding is most likely caused by a lesion to which of the following areas?
explanation: The correct answer is F. This patient has agnosia, which is the inability to recognize, despite adequate sensation. This patient has a type of agnosia known as visual agnosia, which is the inability to recognize familiar objects despite the ability to see. The fact that this man can copy a picture of the dog indicates that he has adequate visual acuity, visual fields, and perception. If this patient had only visual agnosia and were to hear a dog bark (auditory) or to pet a dog (tactile), then he would be able to recognize and identify the dog as a dog. Prosopagnosia is a special type of visual agnosia in which a person is unable to recognize faces. There are also other types of agnosias, including auditory and tactile agnosias. Visual information is first processed in the primary visual cortex (area 17) and then in visual association cortices (areas 18 and 19). There are two main streams of higher-order visual processing that stem from these areas. The ventral pathway, or the "what" pathway projects to temporo-occipital association cortex (cortex that bridges the occipital and temporal lobes and also called occipitotemporal cortex). This pathway is the stream that processes colors, faces, letters and other visual stimuli. Our patient has a lesion in this area. The dorsal pathway, or the "where" pathway projects to parieto-occipital association cortex (choice C) (cortex that bridges the occipital and parietal lobes). This pathway analyzes spatial relationships between objects, between the body and visual stimuli, and motion. The angular gyrus (choice A) is located in the dominant inferior parietal lobe. A lesion of this area produces Gerstmann syndrome, which consists of: 1) agraphia (inability to write); 2) acalculia (loss of ability to calculate mathematical problems); 3) right-left disorientation (difficulty identifying right vs. left body parts); 4) finger agnosia (inability to name or identify individual fingers). The frontal eye fields (choice B) are in the frontal cortex and are the cortical centers for contralateral horizontal gaze. A lesion in this area results in an inability to make voluntary eye movements to the contralateral side. Because of the activity of the intact frontal eye field would be unopposed after this lesion, the result would be a conjugate slow deviation of the eyes toward the lesion ("looks toward the lesion"). The central sulcus (of Rolando) separates the frontal cortex from the parietal cortex. The precentral gyrus (choice D) is immediately rostral to this sulcus and is the primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe. A lesion in this area would cause contralateral upper motor neuron symptoms. (In contrast, the postcentral gyrus is just caudal to this sulcus and is the primary somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe.) The prefrontal cortex (choice E) is located in front of (rostral to) the premotor cortex and is where much of one's personality is located. This area is involved in organizing and planning the intellectual and emotional aspects of behavior. A lesion of this area produces frontal lobe syndrome, in which patients can have a variety of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral problems.

choice_explanations.A: The angular gyrus (dominant inferior parietal lobe) lesion produces Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, right-left disorientation, finger agnosia).
choice_explanations.B: Frontal eye field lesions impair voluntary contralateral horizontal gaze, with eyes deviating toward the lesion.
choice_explanations.C: The dorsal "where" pathway projects to parieto-occipital association cortex, analyzing spatial relationships and motion.
choice_explanations.D: The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex; lesions cause contralateral upper motor neuron signs.
choice_explanations.E: The prefrontal cortex organizes/plans behavior; lesions produce frontal lobe syndrome.
choice_explanations.F: The ventral "what" pathway projects to temporo-occipital association cortex; lesions cause visual agnosia.

fa_summary: Visual agnosia (inability to recognize objects despite seeing) results from a lesion of the temporo-occipital association cortex.

stem: A 53-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her family because of increased irritability, agitation, and sexually inappropriate behavior. She has a history of major depressive disorder and recently started taking sertraline. She says that she has recently had increased energy, and says, "I've been able to stay up all night to clean the house and have not felt this good in a long time." She denies any current hallucinations, but states that she has heard voices in the past, telling her to kill herself. She denies current suicidal ideation and states that life is "just great," except that she is worried about her grandchildren while she is in the hospital. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is B. Bipolar disorder is associated with symptoms of major depression PLUS symptoms of mania. Mania is described as a period of abnormal and persistent elevated, expansive, or irritable mood. The patient has a history of depression and is receiving the SSRI, sertraline. She now presents with symptoms of mania, including increased goal-directed activity, possible hypersexuality, irritability, and decreased need for sleep as well as elated or euphoric mood and racing thoughts. While the primary diagnosis has been major depressive disorder, the current presentation is consistent with bipolar disorder (manic-depressive). SSRIs have been shown to precipitate or worsen manic episodes in bipolar disorder; this is a reason why clinicians screen for bipolar disorder before prescribing an SSRI. The characteristics of mania can be summarized in the DIG FAST mnemonic: Distractibility (inability to concentrate); Irresponsibility/Indiscretion/Interest (reckless pleasure-seeking without regard for consequences); Grandiosity; Flight of Ideas (racing thoughts); Activity Increase (increased energy); Sleep (decreased need); Talkativeness (pressured speech). A healthy individual should be able to adjust to new conditions, such as a new neighbor, but this patient is clearly exhibiting symptoms of an affective disorder rather than an adjustment disorder (choice A). A diagnosis of adjustment disorder may only be given when another Axis I diagnosis does not apply. Brief psychotic disorder (choice C) is characterized by at least one of the following symptoms: delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech. Patients may also have grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior. The duration of the episodes is at least 1 day but must be less than 1 month. The patient in this question does not meet these criteria; hence this is an incorrect answer. Generalized anxiety disorder (choice D) is characterized by the presence of anxiety more often than not over a six month period. However, there is more than simple anxiety present here. Increased irritability, sexually inappropriate behavior, and the ability to stay up all night are all symptoms more consistent with mania than anxiety. Schizophrenia (choice E) is associated with 2 or more of the following, each present for a significant portion of the time during a 1-month period and at least one of the following symptoms must be delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech. The other symptoms in criterion A include grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior and negative symptoms (diminished emotional expression or avolition). Although the patient indicates that she heard voices in the past, the brief auditory hallucinations are likely related to the manic phase of bipolar disorder. In fact, auditory hallucinations are seen in a variety of psychiatric disorders. It has been estimated that around 75% of patients with schizophrenia experience auditory hallucinations. These hallucinations are also relatively common in bipolar disorder (20% to 50%), major depressive disorder with psychotic features (10%), and in posttraumatic stress disorder (40%). Furthermore, the timeframe of her symptom appearance can rule out schizophrenia.

choice_explanations.A: Adjustment disorder may only be given when another Axis I diagnosis does not apply.
choice_explanations.B: Bipolar disorder is major depression PLUS mania; SSRIs can precipitate mania in bipolar disorder.
choice_explanations.C: Brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month.
choice_explanations.D: Generalized anxiety disorder is anxiety more often than not over a 6-month period; mania better explains the irritability, hypersexuality, and staying up all night.
choice_explanations.E: Schizophrenia requires 2+ symptoms for a significant portion of a 1-month period; the timeframe and picture here rule it out.

fa_summary: Bipolar disorder combines depressive and manic symptoms; SSRIs can precipitate mania, so screen for bipolar disorder before starting an SSRI.

stem: A 22-year-old woman who is a college student comes to the physician for a routine examination. She says that she sometimes experiences very vivid and detailed visual images in the room about her as she wakes up in the morning. She has learned to recognize that what she is seeing is not real because some details will be inappropriate, such as summer clothes on the chair when she knows it is December. She reports no difficulties going to sleep, although she says she feels tired during the day. More detailed examination of this patient is likely to reveal which of the following additional symptoms?

options.text: Inability to move after waking up
Sensations moving up and down her legs while going to sleep

explanation: The correct answer is A. This patient, who likely has narcolepsy, is reporting hypnopompic hallucinations, which occur upon awakening. Hypnagogic hallucinations, which take place when going to sleep, also occur. These hallucinations are vivid, can be frightening, and can involve visual, tactile, or auditory sensations. These hallucinations are most often brief and simple, such as hearing a bell ring or a name called. However, they can be complex and of long duration, such as the one in the question stem. It is hypothesized that this results from the intrusion of the REM phase of sleep into the waking state, whereas REM sleep is the active inhibition of skeletal muscle leading to paralysis. Medications that disrupt sleep architecture, such as serotonergic and anticholinergic antidepressants, can also produce hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations. Patients with narcolepsy frequently enter REM sleep within a few minutes of falling asleep. Hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations along with sleep paralysis (episodes of paralysis on awakening), cataplexy (loss of muscle tension while awake; often triggered by strong emotions such as fear, anger, stress, excitement, or humor), and excessive daytime sedation with sleep attacks (paroxysms of falling asleep without warning) are the classic symptoms of narcolepsy. Onset is typically in the teens and early twenties. A deficiency of the hypothalamic neuropeptides, orexin-A and orexin-B (also known as hypocretin-1 and -2) are hypothesized to underlie this disorder when cataplexy is present. Modafinil, methylphenidate, and amphetamines are used to treat excessive daytime sleepiness. Loud snoring while sleeping (choice B) is one of the primary presenting symptoms for obstructive sleep apnea, in which there is obstruction of the airway while sleeping, making breathing difficult. Obstructive (upper airway) sleep apnea is associated with middle-age, being overweight, and making a "rasping" sound while snoring. Patients with apnea may be tired during the day, but lack any of the other narcolepsy symptoms. Treat obstructive apnea by changing patients sleeping position, weight loss, and/or continuous positive airway pressure. Sensations moving up and down her legs while going to sleep (choice C) is suggestive of restless legs syndrome often making it difficult for the patient to sleep. Treat with ropinirole, gabapentin, or benzodiazepines. Sleep walking (choice D), also known as somnambulism, occurs in Stage 3 (formerly Stage 4) sleep. If awakened, the person will be confused and disoriented, just as anyone awakening from Stage 3 sleep. Note the person is NOT dreaming during sleep walking. Teeth grinding while sleeping (choice E), also known as bruxism, occurs in Stage 2 sleep. Symptoms can be reduced by use of oral devices or amelioration of waking time anxiety.

choice_explanations.A: Narcolepsy features sleep paralysis (inability to move after waking up) along with hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, cataplexy, and sleep attacks.
choice_explanations.B: Loud snoring is one of the primary presenting symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea.
choice_explanations.C: Sensations moving up and down the legs while going to sleep suggest restless legs syndrome.
choice_explanations.D: Sleep walking (somnambulism) occurs in Stage 3 (formerly Stage 4) sleep.
choice_explanations.E: Teeth grinding (bruxism) occurs in Stage 2 sleep.

fa_summary: Narcolepsy: hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, sleep paralysis, cataplexy, and sleep attacks, with REM sleep intrusion into wakefulness.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is robbed by a man wearing a ski mask while walking home from work. Six weeks later, she comes to the physician because of recurrent, intrusive thoughts about the experience. She states that she feels "numb", is easily startled whenever she sees a stranger on the street, and avoids the neighborhood where the attack occurred. Three months after the incident, the symptoms have subsided. In the coming year, this patient will most likely experience which of the following?

options.text: Repetitive behaviors that are beyond her control

explanation: The correct answer is B. This woman has post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which is now classified as a trauma- and stressor-related disorder in DSM-5. It was formerly classified as an anxiety disorder in DSM-IV. In DSM-5, a patient may also be diagnosed with PTSD if they also experience symptoms after "learning that traumatic events occurred to a close friend or family member." The traumatic event is commonly reexperienced by the individual in the form of recurrent, intrusive recollections, flashbacks, and nightmares. The condition is triggered by exposure to a traumatic event outside the realm of normal human experience, often involving the threat of death or serious bodily harm to oneself or others. Because of the event, the person may feel helpless and/or intensely fearful. Typically, patients with PTSD avoid thoughts, emotions, and discussion of the traumatic event. Once symptoms abate, however, they usually do not return. Note that if symptoms last less than 1 month, we use the diagnosis of acute stress disorder. Once PTSD has abated, there is no reason to expect continued deterioration in functioning (choice A). This type of deterioration is more common in psychotic states or dementia. Persistent flashbacks (choice C) are associated with PTSD, but would not be expected once symptoms abate. Once the patient has regained functioning, we do not expect continued symptoms. Depressive mood (choice D) is associated with PTSD in 30 - 50% of cases; however, since this patient has had abatement of her PTSD, it is not likely to occur in the future. Repetitive behaviors that are beyond her control (choice E; e.g., compulsions), usually focused on being safe, are associated with PTSD, but would not be expected after symptoms have abated.

choice_explanations.A: Continued deterioration in functioning is more common in psychotic states or dementia.
choice_explanations.B: After PTSD abates, symptoms usually do not return; the expected outcome is no recurrence of symptoms.
choice_explanations.C: Persistent flashbacks are part of active PTSD and would not be expected after symptoms abate.
choice_explanations.D: Depressive mood occurs in 30-50% of PTSD cases but is unlikely after the PTSD has abated.
choice_explanations.E: Trauma-related repetitive safety behaviors would not be expected after symptoms abate.

fa_summary: PTSD (trauma- and stressor-related disorder) typically resolves: once symptoms abate they usually do not return.

stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine examination. She denies engaging in risky sexual behaviors, but does admit to being involved in a number of brief, superficial relationships. She fidgets and appears anxious during the interview. As she leaves, she puts on a fur coat over a bright green shirt and miniskirt. On her way out, she hugs the physician. Which of the following is most likely associated with this patient's condition?

options.text: Has a grandiose sense of self-importance
Has a restricted range of emotion

explanation: The correct answer is E. This individual has histrionic personality disorder, characterized by her acting in a theatrical manner. These patients dress in a colorful, dramatic, and extroverted manner, have an inability to maintain long-lasting relationships, are "attention-seeking" (constantly wanting the spotlight), and are sexually provocative. This is a cluster B (dramatic and emotional) personality disorder. According to DSM-5, the diagnostic criteria for histrionic personality disorder are as follows: A pervasive pattern of excessive emotionality and attention seeking, beginning by early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts, as indicated by five or more of the following: uncomfortable in situations in which he or she is not the center of attention; interaction with others is often characterized by inappropriate sexually seductive or provocative behavior; displays rapidly shifting and shallow expression of emotions; consistently uses physical appearance to draw attention to self; has a style of speech that is excessively impressionistic and lacking in detail; shows self-dramatization, theatricality and exaggerated expression of emotion; is suggestible; considers relationships to be more intimate than they actually are. Patients with antisocial personality disorder often find it difficult to maintain a stable job (choice A), and exhibit a persistent pattern of disregard for the rights and wishes of others that begins in childhood or early adolescence. As such, patients with this disorder can be prone to crime and violence. Patients with a grandiose sense of self-importance (choice B) are usually diagnosed with narcissistic personality disorder. Other characteristics include preoccupation with fantasies of unlimited success, requires of excessive admiration, strong sense of entitlement, arrogance, and lack of empathy. Instead of being limited in expression of feelings (choice C), such as a patient with schizoid personality disorder, this patient expresses feelings openly, often in a very superficial manner. Patients who seek constant reassurance from their partners (choice D) fear rejection, and are sometimes diagnosed with dependent personality disorder.

choice_explanations.A: Difficulty maintaining a stable job is seen in antisocial personality disorder.
choice_explanations.B: A grandiose sense of self-importance is characteristic of narcissistic personality disorder.
choice_explanations.C: A restricted range of emotion is seen in schizoid personality disorder; this patient expresses feelings openly and superficially.
choice_explanations.D: Seeking constant reassurance from partners reflects dependent personality disorder (fear of rejection).
choice_explanations.E: Sexually provocative behavior is characteristic of histrionic personality disorder, as in this patient.

fa_summary: Histrionic personality disorder (cluster B): attention-seeking, theatrical dress, shallow emotion, and sexually provocative behavior.

stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine examination. The physician has known this patient for more than 10 years. During this period, the patient has been emotionally cold and distant. He has not developed friendships with either men or women and has always appeared preoccupied with his own concerns. He does not appear to specifically trigger confrontations and does not show bizarre ideation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is D. This patient has schizoid personality disorder. These individuals tend to have cold, introverted personalities that limit the degree to which they form strong bonds with other people. They tend to fear closeness and to be given to daydreaming rather than action. They have a lifelong pattern of social withdrawal and are seen by others as eccentric, isolated, and withdrawn. According to DSM-5, the diagnostic criteria for schizoid personality disorder are as follows: Schizoid personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of expression of emotions in interpersonal settings, beginning by early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts, as indicated by four or more of the following: neither desires nor enjoys close relationships, including being part of a family; almost always chooses solitary activities; has little if any interest in having sexual experiences with another person; takes pleasure in few, if any, activities; lacks close friends or confidants other than first-degree relatives; appears indifferent to the praise or criticism of others; shows emotional coldness, detachment, or flattened affect. Does not occur exclusively during the course of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or depressive disorder with psychotic features or another psychotic disorder. Patients with histrionic personality (choice A) tend to have exaggerated, childlike emotions, sometimes with a sexual overlay and have an inability to maintain long-lasting relationships. They are continually seeking attention and will do what is necessary to obtain their desired attention. These patients often dress in a colorful, dramatic, and extroverted manner. Patients with narcissistic personality (choice B) tend to be grandiose and preoccupied with self, wealth, and power. They demand constant attention and have a fragile self-esteem. Patients with paranoid personality (choice C) tend to be very suspicious of other individuals' motivations. They are preoccupied with issues of trust and read hidden meaning into comments or events. Schizotypal personality (choice E) is similar to schizoid personality, but is also associated with oddities of thinking (much less severe than in schizophrenia), such as magical thinking, clairvoyance, or paranoid ideation.

choice_explanations.A: Histrionic personality features exaggerated, childlike emotions with a sexual overlay and attention-seeking.
choice_explanations.B: Narcissistic personality features grandiosity and preoccupation with self, wealth, and power.
choice_explanations.C: Paranoid personality features pervasive suspiciousness and preoccupation with trust.
choice_explanations.D: Schizoid personality features detachment from social relationships with a restricted range of emotional expression.
choice_explanations.E: Schizotypal personality is similar to schizoid but adds oddities of thinking (magical thinking, clairvoyance, paranoid ideation).

fa_summary: Schizoid personality disorder: pervasive social detachment with restricted emotional expression, without bizarre ideation.

stem: A 25-year-old man comes to the emergency department for severe abdominal pain. His medical record shows multiple visits to the emergency department to request narcotics. Physical examination shows no abnormalities with symptoms disproportionate to physical findings. When the physician refuses to provide narcotics, the patient leaves. One week later, the patient is arrested and sentenced to court-mandated drug rehabilitation. While in the drug rehabilitation program, the patient repeatedly engages in small thefts. He fails to show guilt or remorse about his activities, and is perceived to be manipulative by the staff and other program participants. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is A. This is antisocial personality disorder, formerly called sociopathic personality disorder. This personality disorder is characterized by a callous disregard for the feelings of others as well as the rules and norms of society, with a tendency to exploit others for personal gain. Many of these individuals are very good at glib rationalizations of their behavior, and there is often associated alcoholism, drug addiction, infidelity, promiscuity, job failure, and/or imprisonment. Punishment rarely modifies behavior or improves judgment. Patients with avoidant personality (choice B) show intense sensitivity to criticism, disapproval, or rejection, leading to avoidance behaviors including isolation. Patients with avoidant personality disorder desire relationships and dislike their isolation. They are hypersensitive and fear rejection. Patients with borderline personality (choice C) alternate between "poor waif" behavior and intense anger. Patients generally have problems in affect regulation, interpersonal functioning, impulse control as well as cognitive-perceptual issues. Splitting is a defense mechanism common to many patients with borderline disorder in which people see things or people as all good or all bad, depending on whether they help to gratify their wishes or frustrate them. Conduct disorder (choice D) is a serious behavioral and emotional disorder that occurs in children and teens. It includes aggressive, destructive, deceitful behaviors, and the violation of rules of society. This individual is an adult, and therefore the diagnosis of conduct disorder does not apply. Patients with histrionic personality (choice E) show very dramatic, childlike presentations, often coupled with sexual overtones. There is an excessive need for approval, and often, inappropriately seductive behavior to get attention. Narcissistic personality disorder (choice F) is characterized by grandiose self-images, fantasies of glory, exploitative behavior, a sense of entitlement, and a lack of empathy and concern for others. Patients with this disorder demand constant attention and have fragile self-esteem. There is genuine surprise and associated anger when they do not obtain their goals. It is more commonly diagnosed in men.

choice_explanations.A: Antisocial personality disorder: callous disregard for others' rights and societal rules, deceit, theft, lack of remorse, manipulation.
choice_explanations.B: Avoidant personality disorder: hypersensitivity to criticism/rejection with social avoidance despite wanting relationships.
choice_explanations.C: Borderline personality disorder: unstable affect/relationships, impulsivity, splitting, fear of abandonment.
choice_explanations.D: Conduct disorder occurs in children/teens; this patient is an adult, so the diagnosis does not apply.
choice_explanations.E: Histrionic personality disorder: dramatic, childlike, attention-seeking with sexual overtones.
choice_explanations.F: Narcissistic personality disorder: grandiosity, entitlement, exploitativeness, and lack of empathy.

fa_summary: Antisocial personality disorder: disregard for others' rights and societal rules with deceit, theft, and lack of remorse.

stem: A 10-year-old boy exhibits a fear of water during his first day of swimming lessons. The teacher helps him sit on the edge of the pool and splash the water with his feet. After he becomes more comfortable, she then goes one step further and shows him how to wet his knees. It takes her an hour to have him float on the water while she is holding his hand. At the end of the lesson, the teacher compliments the boy on his excellent progress at his first lesson. Which of the following best describes the technique used to help this boy lose the fear of water?
explanation: The correct answer is B. Desensitization is an effective therapy for phobia. The therapist models and guides the patient through progressive steps, starting with the least fearful step, until the fear and anxiety associated with phobic object are extinguished. In classical conditioning (choice A), which was first described by Pavlov in animal models, a neutral stimulus is paired with a stimulus that produces a response. The goal is to have the neutral stimulus alone produce the response. If food plus the ringing of a bell produce salivation in a dog, for example, repeated conditioning will cause the dog to salivate upon hearing the bell alone. The goal in extinction (choice C) is to change a response by denying a reward that has maintained that response. If a child gets his parents' attention by misbehaving, for example, ignoring him can produce extinction of the misbehavior. In flooding (choice D), the therapist encourages the patient to confront the feared object or situation without a gradual or graded exposure. In operant conditioning (choice E), the goal is to increase the likelihood of a response by reinforcement. A desired behavior is rewarded so it will be repeated and strengthened. In the present case, complimenting the boy is a type of reward. However, it was the desensitization process that helped him conquer his fear of water.

choice_explanations.A: Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus (eg, Pavlov's dogs).
choice_explanations.B: Desensitization guides the patient through progressive, least-to-most fearful steps until the phobic anxiety is extinguished.
choice_explanations.C: Extinction changes a response by denying a reward that maintained it.
choice_explanations.D: Flooding has the patient confront the feared object without gradual/graded exposure.
choice_explanations.E: Operant conditioning increases a response via reinforcement; the compliment here is a reward, but desensitization produced the change.

fa_summary: Systematic desensitization is used for phobias: graded exposure from least to most fearful, replacing anxiety with relaxation.

stem: A 50-year-old man who is a teacher is admitted to the hospital because he threatened to kill his wife and another teacher at his school. His wife says that her husband began accusing her of having an affair with the other teacher 8 months ago. He has also recently begun accusing her of having affairs with their neighbors and the local priest. She says that her husband has no history of medical or psychiatric problems prior to these episodes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is B. Delusional disorder is characterized by one or more fixed and unshakable delusions. The patient's delusion is non-bizarre (i.e., it is plausible or at least possible) and has to be present for at least a month. It should be noted that in DSM-5, the patient's delusions can be bizarre or non-bizarre. Apart from the impact of the delusion(s), functioning is not markedly impaired in other areas of life. Delirium (choice A) is an acute, reversible mental disorder characterized by confusion and some impairment of consciousness, generally associated with emotional lability, hallucinations, inappropriate and, sometimes, agitated behavior. The changes in mentation are waxing and waning. Patients usually have times during which they act normal and have perfect mentation, but then they can rapidly switch over to being confused and disoriented. Delirium can be caused by infections, metabolic abnormalities, electrolyte abnormalities, medication usage, or just simply being in the intensive care unit for long periods of time. Dementia (choice C) is a mental disorder characterized by progressive, nonreversible, general impairment of intellectual functioning typically seen as failing memory, difficulty calculating, distractibility, alterations in mood and affect, impaired judgment and abstraction, reduced facility in language, and disturbance of orientation. Dementia does not usually wax and wane like delirium, but rather follows a slowly progressive course of cognitive deterioration. Dementia usually affects older people as well. Paranoid personality disorder (choice D) is characterized by pervasive distrust and suspicion of others. It begins in early adulthood, and at least four of the following must be present: increased suspiciousness without sufficient basis, preoccupation with unjustified doubts, reluctance to confide in others, finding hidden meaning in benign remarks, being persistently unforgiving about insults, and perception of attacks on oneself even if it is not apparent to others. This patient does not have paranoid personality disorder because he does not have a long-standing history of mistrust. He was apparently normal before 8 months ago. Furthermore, he is exhibiting mistrust in only one area of his life. Schizophrenia (choice E) is defined by the presence of active symptoms of delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized speech or behavior in the past month. The continuous signs must be present for longer than 6 months and cause significant impairment in social or occupational functioning.

choice_explanations.A: Delirium is an acute, reversible, waxing-and-waning confusional state, not a fixed delusion.
choice_explanations.B: Delusional disorder: one or more fixed, unshakable (often non-bizarre) delusions for at least a month with otherwise preserved functioning.
choice_explanations.C: Dementia is a progressive, nonreversible global cognitive decline, usually in older patients.
choice_explanations.D: Paranoid personality disorder requires a long-standing pervasive pattern of mistrust, not an 8-month focus on one theme.
choice_explanations.E: Schizophrenia requires continuous signs for longer than 6 months with disorganized speech/behavior or negative symptoms.

fa_summary: Delusional disorder: fixed, unshakable (often non-bizarre) delusions for at least 1 month with otherwise preserved functioning.

stem: A 39-year-old man with atypical depression comes to the physician because of insomnia. He states that he has a difficulty falling asleep and that when he finally does fall asleep, he experiences a multitude of intense, colorful dreams. He also states that he has not taken his phenelzine for the past two weeks. Which of the following best explains this finding?
explanation: The correct answer is C. Phenelzine is a monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitor used in the treatment of atypical depression. Barbiturates, alcohol, benzodiazepines, phenothiazines, and MAO inhibitors decrease the amount of REM sleep while the patient is taking them. Withdrawal of phenelzine (or any of the other medications listed) allows the body to compensate for "missed" REM sleep, and REM rebound develops. This phenomenon is characterized by an increase in the number and intensity of dreams for several days after discontinuation of the drug in question. Hypnopompic hallucinations (choice A) occur as the patient is awakening, not while in a deep sleep. They are commonly seen in narcolepsy. Night terrors (pavor nocturnus; choice B) generally occur in children, and are not associated with dreams at all, as they occur in delta (also called stage 4) sleep rather than in REM sleep. Note: night terrors (in contrast to nightmares) are often not remembered upon awakening. Sensitization (choice D) is a process in which prior exposure to an agent leads to an increased effect upon readministration of that agent. This effect is generally associated with psychostimulant drugs. Tolerance (choice E) refers to a progressive decrement in the effectiveness of a particular dose of a drug.

choice_explanations.A: Hypnopompic hallucinations occur on awakening (seen in narcolepsy), not while asleep.
choice_explanations.B: Night terrors occur in delta (stage N3/4) non-REM sleep in children and are not associated with dreams.
choice_explanations.C: MAO inhibitors suppress REM sleep; stopping phenelzine causes REM rebound with more intense dreaming.
choice_explanations.D: Sensitization is an increased effect on readministration, typically with psychostimulants.
choice_explanations.E: Tolerance is a progressive decrease in a drug's effectiveness at a given dose.

fa_summary: Drugs that suppress REM sleep (barbiturates, alcohol, benzodiazepines, MAO inhibitors) cause REM rebound on withdrawal, with vivid dreams.

stem: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician 1 year after his wife died in a motor vehicle accident. Over the course of the year, he has had increased feelings of worthlessness and no longer is proud of his accomplishments. He continues to feel that his wife's passing was his fault and blames himself for the event. Over this time, he has had continued difficulty sleeping, which he attributes to his decreased energy at work and why he no longer plays golf with his friends. He has maintained his job, but feels his work is not up to the same standard it was before the accident. As his work has been suffering, he has also been spending a lot less time with friends who have noticed he turns down their offers to socialize much more frequently. He has also lost 6.8 kg (15 lb) since his last office visit. He says that his symptoms have been worsening but he assures the physician that he does not want to hurt himself. Which of the following is most likely associated with this patient's condition?
explanation: The correct answer is B. This patient most likely has major depressive disorder. Major depression manifests with at least five of the following nine symptoms and one of these symptoms must be depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure (new requirement in DSM-5): Depressed mood; Loss of interests/pleasure; Change in sleep (insomnia or hypersomnia); Change in appetite or weight; Change in psychomotor activity; Loss of energy; Trouble concentrating; Thoughts of worthlessness or guilt; Thoughts about death or suicide. The symptoms must be present most of the day nearly every day for a minimum of 2 consecutive weeks. These symptoms cause severe distress and functional impairment. They are severe enough to meet the criteria for a major depressive episode, and are not better accounted for by normal grief and bereavement. An easy way to remember the symptoms of major depressive disorder is with the mnemonic SIG-E-CAPS: Sleep changes: increase during day or decreased sleep at night; Interest (loss): of interest in activities that used to interest them; Guilt (worthless): depressed persons may devalue themselves; Energy (lack): common presenting symptom (fatigue); Cognition/Concentration: reduced cognition &/or difficulty concentrating; Appetite (weight loss): usually declined, occasionally increased; Psychomotor: agitation (anxiety) or lethargic; Suicide/preoccupation with death. Patients with major depressive disorder have increased REM sleep, although they often complain of insomnia. They usually exhibit decreased REM latency and decreased stage N3 (deep) sleep. Episodes of increased energy (choice A) in a patient who also appears to have depressive symptoms implies the presence of manic episodes, which occur in patients with bipolar disorder. While suicidal ideation is rare (choice C) in patients with normal grief, up to 60% of patients with depression have some degree of suicidal ideation. Up to 15% of patients die by suicide. Tactile hallucinations (choice D) are most commonly associated with alcohol withdrawal where patients may experience the feeling of bugs crawling on their skin. It should be noted that in pathological grief, patients may experience brief auditory and visual hallucinations pertaining to the loss of a loved one. For example, they may hear their loved one calling their name or see them in a crowded area. Seasonal affective disorder is a mood disorder that is associated with seasonal changes and is worse during winter months (choice E). It can be treated with bright-light therapy.

choice_explanations.A: Episodes of increased energy suggest mania/bipolar disorder.
choice_explanations.B: Major depressive disorder is associated with increased REM sleep (and decreased REM latency and decreased deep sleep).
choice_explanations.C: Suicidal ideation is not rare in depression (up to 60%); it is rare in normal grief.
choice_explanations.D: Tactile hallucinations are more typical of alcohol withdrawal; pathological grief may have brief auditory/visual hallucinations.
choice_explanations.E: Worsening in winter months is characteristic of seasonal affective disorder.

fa_summary: Major depressive disorder is associated with increased REM sleep, decreased REM latency, and decreased deep (N3) sleep.

stem: A 22-year-old woman who is a college student is brought to the emergency department by police because she was found talking to herself while walking back and forth across a busy street. She appears to be oriented to person, place, and time. Her sister comes to the hospital and says that the patient dropped out of school 3 months ago and has been living on the streets. A review of her records shows a hospital admission 2 months ago for a similar condition. Psychiatric examination shows difficulty concentrating and talking to unheard voices. Urine toxicology is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is E. This patient is suffering from schizophreniform disorder. There has been a marked decline in the level of functioning, and she was endangering herself in the middle of the street. Schizophreniform disorder is characterized by schizophrenia-like symptoms, but the duration of symptoms is less than 6 months (but more than 1 month). Fully developed psychotic symptoms are typical. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for schizophreniform disorder are as follows: Two or more of the following, each present for a significant portion of the time during a 1-month period. At least one of these must be 1, 2, or 3: Delusions; Hallucinations; Disorganized speech; Grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior; Negative symptoms (i.e., diminished emotional expression or avolition). The episode lasts at least 1 month but less than 6 months. Schizoaffective disorder and depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features have been ruled out. Disturbance is not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Brief psychotic disorder (choice A) is characterized by the presence of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and one of the symptoms must be 1, 2, or 3. The duration of an episode of the disturbance is at least 1 day but less than 1 month. The patient in this question has a duration between 1 and 6 months. In schizoaffective disorder (choice B), alterations in mood are present during a substantial portion of the illness. This condition requires the presence of symptoms of schizophrenia and a major affective disorder, such as mania or depression. This patient does not demonstrate the latter, as there is no apparent mood disorder. Although schizoid personality disorder (choice C) produces detachment from social relationships and is characterized by restriction of emotional expression, it is not accompanied by a marked decline in occupational functioning or hallucinations. If the symptoms do not remit after 5 months or more, then the diagnosis of schizophrenia (choice D) should be made. Schizotypal personality disorder (choice F) is characterized by eccentricities of behavior, odd beliefs or magical thinking, and difficulties with social and interpersonal relationships. Unlike schizophrenia, schizotypal personality disorder is not characterized by a formal thought disorder.

choice_explanations.A: Brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month.
choice_explanations.B: Schizoaffective disorder requires mood episodes during a substantial portion of the illness; no mood disorder is evident here.
choice_explanations.C: Schizoid personality disorder lacks the marked functional decline and hallucinations seen here.
choice_explanations.D: Schizophrenia is diagnosed if symptoms persist 6 months or more; this patient's duration is 1-6 months.
choice_explanations.E: Schizophreniform disorder: schizophrenia-like symptoms lasting more than 1 month but less than 6 months.
choice_explanations.F: Schizotypal personality disorder features eccentric behavior/odd beliefs without a formal thought disorder.

fa_summary: Schizophreniform disorder: schizophrenia-like symptoms lasting between 1 and 6 months.

stem: A 36-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine examination, but arrives 2 hours late and the physician has already left. The patient states in a very loud and pressured speech that his time is precious, he cannot return on another day, and demands to be seen by another physician. The receptionist has seen this patient act this way on many occasions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is F. This patient most likely has narcissistic personality disorder, which is characterized by grandiose self-images, fantasies of glory, exploitative behavior, a sense of entitlement, and a lack of empathy and concern for others. Patients with this disorder demand constant attention and have fragile self-esteem. There is genuine surprise and associated anger when they do not obtain their goals. It is more commonly diagnosed in men. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for narcissistic personality disorder are as follows: A pervasive pattern of grandiosity, need for admiration and lack of empathy, beginning in early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts, as indicated by 5 or more of the following: Has a grandiose sense of self-importance; Is preoccupied with fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, beauty, or ideal love; Believes that he or she is special and unique and can only be understood by, or should associate with, other special or high-status people; Requires excessive admiration; Has a sense of entitlement; Is interpersonally exploitative; Is often envious of others or believes that others are envious of him or her; Shows arrogant, haughty behaviors or attitudes. Antisocial personality disorder (choice A) is associated with a complete disregard for the rules and norms of society. These individuals are often men who lie, steal, and endanger the lives of others. They are aggressive, commit crimes, and often end up in prison. Bipolar disorder (choice B) and narcissistic personality disorder have some similar characteristics. They are both associated with grandiosity, potentially pressured speech, and agitation. However, the patient in this question does NOT have a history of depression and also lacks other key symptoms of mania which are both needed to make a diagnosis of bipolar disorder. Patients in a manic episode often have an elated or euphoric mood and racing thoughts. Other symptoms of mania include increased energy, hypersexuality (increased sexual activity), grandiosity, and increased talkativeness. In some patients, irritability, rather than euphoria, is characteristic. The onset of insomnia in patients vulnerable to bipolar disorder is the single best indication that a manic episode is about to begin. The most common characteristics of mania can be summarized with the DIG FAST mnemonic: Distractibility, Increased energy/Indiscretion/Irresponsibility, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep decreased and Talkativeness (pressured speech). Individuals with borderline personality disorder (choice C) have unstable relationships, have "black and white thinking," and lack self-esteem and impulse control. They often fear abandonment and engage in self-destructive behavior. They are commonly observed to be using "splitting" as a defense mechanism, where they fail to see individuals as a cohesive whole and instead judge a person as to be wholly good or wholly evil. This disorder is more commonly diagnosed in women. Generalized anxiety disorder (choice D) is characterized by the presence of anxiety more often than not over a six month period. However, there is more than simple anxiety present here. Although the patient is anxious, he does not have worry about his current situation. Histrionic personality disorder (choice E) is characterized by attention seeking behavior and labile emotions. These individuals often wear dramatic clothing, have theatrical and exaggerated behavior, and are inappropriately seductive.

choice_explanations.A: Antisocial personality disorder features disregard for societal rules with lying, stealing, and aggression.
choice_explanations.B: Bipolar disorder requires a manic episode (with mood change) or history of depression; neither is present here.
choice_explanations.C: Borderline personality disorder features unstable relationships, black-and-white thinking, and fear of abandonment.
choice_explanations.D: Generalized anxiety disorder is persistent anxiety over 6 months without the grandiosity seen here.
choice_explanations.E: Histrionic personality disorder features attention-seeking and labile emotions with dramatic, seductive behavior.
choice_explanations.F: Narcissistic personality disorder: grandiosity, sense of entitlement, need for admiration, and lack of empathy.

fa_summary: Narcissistic personality disorder: grandiosity, entitlement, exploitativeness, need for admiration, and lack of empathy.

stem: A 17-year-old girl whose father is a church minister is troubled by sexual dreams. She does not discuss the dreams with anyone, but begins to tell her friends that she is considering becoming a nun. This is most likely an example of which of the following?
explanation: The correct answer is E. This can be considered an example of reaction formation, in which there is an unconscious adoption of behavior opposite to that which would reflect true feelings and intentions. There can be a global reversal, for example, in which love is expressed as hate. Another example of reaction formation is a married woman who is disturbed by feeling attracted to another man and treats him rudely. Excessive overreaction can also be a sign of reaction formation, as if the person is trying to convince himself or anyone else that the original feeling or impulse did not exist. From Shakespeare: "The lady doth protest too much, methinks." Displacement (choice A) is a transfer of emotion from one setting to another that is generally more manageable. In other words, the source stays the same but the emotions are redirected elsewhere. An example is a mother taking her anger out on her son, who in turn yells at his little sister. Identification (choice B) is the unconscious adoption of someone else's traits or activities. For example, a medical student begins to dress and act like an attending physician in an effort to bolster their self-esteem. Projection (choice C) occurs when someone attributes their own wishes, desires, thoughts, or emotions to someone else. Internal states are perceived as a part of someone else or of the world in general. A classic example is a man who has committed adultery becoming convinced that his wife is having an affair even though there is no evidence of it. Rationalization (choice D) is the unconscious offering of a false but acceptable explanation for unacceptable behavior. An example is a student stealing from a wealthy friend and thinking that he is rich enough that he can afford to lose it.

choice_explanations.A: Displacement is a transfer of emotion (the source stays the same but the target changes), e.g., a mother taking her anger out on her son; it does not describe adopting the opposite behavior.
choice_explanations.B: Identification is the unconscious adoption of someone else's traits or activities (e.g., a student dressing like an attending); it is not a reversal of feeling.
choice_explanations.C: Projection occurs when someone attributes their own unacceptable wishes, thoughts, or emotions to another person; it is not a reversal of feeling.
choice_explanations.D: Rationalization is the unconscious offering of a false but acceptable explanation for unacceptable behavior; it is not a reversal of feeling.
choice_explanations.E: Reaction formation is the unconscious adoption of behavior opposite to the true feeling or impulse (here, religious devotion opposite to sexual feelings).

fa_summary: Reaction formation is an immature ego defense mechanism in which unacceptable feelings or impulses are transformed into their opposites (e.g., a girl troubled by sexual dreams who adopts religious devotion).

stem: A 27-year-old man is arrested by police officials because of domestic violence. The wife states that he also regularly hits their 7-year-old son with a leather belt and often strikes the boy with his hand. When the man is asked why he does this, he says, "This is how my father treated me. It's how men should act." Which of the following types of learning best accounts for his behavior?
explanation: The correct answer is E. In social learning, also known as modeling or observational learning, behavior is acquired by watching other persons and assimilating their actions into the behavioral repertoire. Note that we are more likely to adopt the behaviors of those we believe to be high status (a father), and people we see getting reinforced (e.g., getting what they want as a result of their behavior). Because behaviors such as spousal abuse, child abuse, and elder abuse are all based on observing and incorporating behaviors from significant others, the person displaying the behaviors does not realize the behaviors are inappropriate and is typically very resistant to change. The fact that the learning is nonverbal and not dependent upon reinforcement contributes to the resistance to change. For classical conditioning (choice A), a new stimulus evokes an old response (salivating to the bell). The Pavlovian experiment paired the ringing of the bell (conditioned stimulus) with the bringing of food (unconditioned stimulus) so that, eventually, the sound of the bell elicited the salivatory response (conditioned response), which previously only occurred with the sight of food (unconditioned response). The aggressive behavior in this question is an acquired response, and so is not classical conditioning. The behavior in focus here is nonverbal and reflects a behavioral reaction, not a cognitive process or rehearsal (choice B). Imprinting (choice C) is a critical attachment instinct in animals such as geese, ducks, and quail and does not apply to people. For example, some animals will follow the first object they see following birth. With operant conditioning (choice D), a new response is emitted, perhaps randomly at first, which results in a consequence. This consequence acts as reinforcement and changes the probability of the response's future occurrence. In this question, this was a behavior the man observed (as a child), not one that he was able to practice when young, as in operant conditioning. The key is that he watched another, not himself, be reinforced.

choice_explanations.A: Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned one; the aggressive behavior here is an acquired response, not a conditioned reflex.
choice_explanations.B: Cognitive learning involves a cognitive process or rehearsal; this behavior is a nonverbal behavioral reaction.
choice_explanations.C: Imprinting is a critical-period attachment instinct in some animals (e.g., geese) and does not apply to humans.
choice_explanations.D: Operant conditioning requires the person to emit a response and be reinforced; here the man only observed his father's behavior.
choice_explanations.E: Social learning (modeling/observational learning) is acquisition of behavior by watching significant others; it matches observing the father's aggression.

fa_summary: Social (observational/modeling) learning is acquisition of behavior by watching others; it is nonverbal, does not require reinforcement, and is resistant to change.

stem: A 55-year-old man begins group therapy. After the first session, he befriends one of the other clients, and begins telling her how intelligent and talented the facilitator is. At the next session, he and the facilitator disagree. After the session, he tells his fellow group member that the facilitator is incompetent and that they should sue for malpractice. This is an example of which of the following?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Splitting is a primitive defense mechanism in which objects or people are thought of as either "all bad" or "all good." The world is pictured in extreme terms rather than a more realistic blend of good and bad qualities. This defense mechanism is normal in young children, but also occurs in adults with borderline personality disorder (the man in group therapy) or psychosis. For example, a patient with borderline personality disorder may say "This doctor is a miracle worker, but that doctor is totally incompetent." This patient is showing "splitting," which is a defense mechanism. Displacement (choice A) is an unconscious defense mechanism in which one's feelings or desires are unconsciously transferred from their original object to a more acceptable substitute. For example, an attending physician scolds a resident who later expresses his anger by yelling at a medical student. Fixation (choice B) refers to an arrest of development at a particular developmental stage. It is generally a partial or incomplete arrest of development, but can contribute to the development of emotional problems if protracted. For example, an adult male who continually plays video games as their primary form of entertainment. Reaction formation (choice C) refers to an unconscious defense mechanism in which the person takes on an attitude or belief that is the opposite of his or her true beliefs and desires. Reaction formation can also be described as an unacceptable impulse that is transformed into its opposite. For example, having a bias against a particular race or culture and then embracing that race or culture to the extreme. Reaction formation (along with undoing) is commonly seen in patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder. Regression (choice D) is a return to an earlier (often infantile) stage of development that occurs in many mental illnesses and in normal individuals experiencing tragic or extremely stressful events. For example, a child who starts to wet the bed after the birth of a sibling.

choice_explanations.A: Displacement redirects emotion from its original object to a safer substitute; here the patient's view of the facilitator flips entirely rather than being redirected.
