choice_explanations.B: Fixation is an arrest of development at a particular stage; it does not describe the all-good/all-bad flip.
choice_explanations.C: Reaction formation transforms an unacceptable impulse into its opposite; it differs from the all-good to all-bad shift seen here.
choice_explanations.D: Regression is a return to an earlier developmental stage (e.g., bed-wetting after a new sibling); it is not the same as splitting.
choice_explanations.E: Splitting is the primitive tendency to view people as entirely good or entirely bad, as the patient does with the facilitator.

fa_summary: Splitting is a primitive defense mechanism in which people or objects are viewed as all good or all bad; it is characteristic of borderline personality disorder and psychosis.

stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On history, the mother explains that her daughter can identify body parts by pointing to them, play with other children her age in parallel, ride a tricycle, can build a tower of 7-9 blocks, and speak in full sentences that both her parents and strangers can understand. Which of the following is an accurate assessment of this patient's development?

options.text: Delayed gross motor, delayed fine motor, and normal language development
Delayed gross motor, normal fine motor, and normal language development
Normal gross motor, delayed fine motor, and normal language development
Normal gross motor, normal fine motor, and delayed language development
Normal gross motor, normal fine motor, and normal language development

explanation: The correct answer is E. This patient has normal developmental milestones. A 3-year-old child should be able to ride a tricycle, balance on each foot for 1 second, build a tower of 7-9 blocks, copy and draw a vertical line, and speak with almost understandable sentences by both parents and strangers. It should be noted that the mother also mentions that her daughter can identify body parts by pointing to them and plays with other children her age in parallel. These two milestones are generally achieved during the second year of life. However, the overall development of the child can be assessed based on their most advanced milestones. This patient is not delayed in any area, making choices A, B, C, and D incorrect. Common developmental milestones are: Newborn - regards faces, suckle, Moro, and grasp reflexes; 6 months - babbles, sits upright alone, passes a cube; 12 months - says 1-2 words, begins to walk, waves bye-bye; 24 months - 200-250 word vocabulary, combines words, can build a tower of 4-6 cubes, kicks a ball; 3 years - 900-1000 word vocabulary, combines words to form almost understandable sentences, rides a tricycle, builds a tower of 7-9 cubes.

choice_explanations.A: Gross and fine motor milestones (tricycling, 7-9 block tower) are age-appropriate, so both are not delayed.
choice_explanations.B: Gross motor milestones are age-appropriate, so gross motor is not delayed.
choice_explanations.C: Fine motor milestones are age-appropriate, so fine motor is not delayed.
choice_explanations.D: Language is age-appropriate (full sentences understood by strangers), so language is not delayed.
choice_explanations.E: All domains (gross motor, fine motor, language) are appropriate for a 3-year-old; development is normal.

fa_summary: A 3-year-old should ride a tricycle, balance on each foot briefly, build a tower of 7-9 blocks, and speak in almost fully understandable sentences; the child in this vignette is developmentally normal.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the physician by his wife because of recent changes in behavior, including irritability and restlessness. He tells the physician that he has had a decreased need for sleep and increased energy. In the past week, he has not been going to work, but has been visiting local banks, seeking a loan to solve the nation's energy problems with a "wonderful new idea." The presence of which of the following would help to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Belief that he is being followed
Reliving of previous events in dreams

explanation: The correct answer is C. The presentation suggests a manic or hypomanic episode of bipolar disorder. Patients in a manic episode often have an elated or euphoric mood and racing thoughts. Other symptoms of mania include increased energy, hypersexuality (increased sexual activity), grandiosity, and increased talkativeness. In some patients, irritability, rather than euphoria, is characteristic. The onset of insomnia in patients vulnerable to bipolar disorder is the single best indication that a manic episode is about to begin. The most common characteristics of mania can be summarized with the DIG FAST mnemonic: Distractibility (inability to concentrate); Indiscretion/Irresponsibility (pleasure seeking without regard to consequences); Grandiosity (inflated self-esteem); Flight of ideas (racing thoughts); Activity increase (increase in goal-directed activity)/Agitation/Appetite increase; Sleep (decreased need for sleep); Talkativeness (pressured speech). The DSM-5 criteria for diagnosis of mania are as follows: a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy, lasting at least 1 week and present most of the day, nearly every day. During the period of the mood disturbance and increase in activity, three (or more) of the following symptoms (four if the mood is only irritable) are present to a significant degree and represent a noticeable change from usual behavior: inflated self-esteem or grandiosity; decreased need for sleep; talkative or pressured speech; flight of ideas; distractibility; increase in goal-directed activity (at home, at work, or sexually) or psychomotor agitation; excessive involvement in activities with a high potential for painful consequences (e.g., unrestrained buying sprees, sexual indiscretions, foolish business investments). The belief that one is being followed (choice A) suggests paranoid ideation. This paranoid delusion may accompany certain types of schizophrenia or the non-schizophrenic delusional disorder, paranoid subtype. However, it is not commonly found in patients with bipolar disorder.

choice_explanations.A: A belief of being followed suggests paranoid ideation (schizophrenia/delusional disorder), not mania.
choice_explanations.B: Hearing voices suggests a psychotic disorder rather than mania.
choice_explanations.C: Increased sexual activity (hypersexuality) is a DIG FAST feature of mania and would help confirm the diagnosis.
choice_explanations.D: Recurrent thoughts and actions suggest obsessive-compulsive disorder, not mania.
choice_explanations.E: Reliving previous events in dreams suggests PTSD, not mania.

fa_summary: A manic episode (bipolar disorder) is a distinct period of elevated/expansive/irritable mood with increased energy lasting >=1 week, with DIG FAST features (Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep decreased, Talkativeness).

stem: A 75-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and exhaustion. A review of her records shows that her spouse died 4 months ago in a motor vehicle collision and that she was a passenger in that vehicle. She states that she has bouts of crying for no reason, and that she sometimes thinks she hears her husband calling. For the most part, when she is outside or around friends she does not experience any of those symptoms. It is only when she is alone at home or looking at past pictures that she experiences sadness. She is still able to drive around and perform her activities of daily living and says that she does not have nightmares about the accident or flashbacks in which she re-experiences the event. Her vital signs are within normal limits, however, her weight has decreased by about 10 pounds since the death of her husband. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: "Do you think about your husband often?"
"I'm going to admit you to the hospital for overnight observation so we can run a few tests"
"I'm going to give you something to help you feel better and make it easier for you to sleep."
"I'm going to schedule you for an evaluation with a colleague of mine who can help us understand why you are feeling this way."
"It sounds like the loss of your husband was difficult for you, but it is time for you to think about your own life now."

explanation: The correct answer is A. This case presents a woman who is having a normal grief and mourning reaction to the loss of her husband. This is also known as bereavement. The grief response is likely exacerbated by the fact that she survived the accident and he did not, which is called "survivor's guilt." The key to this question is that the physician must recognize that although some of the symptoms of depression are present, this woman is experiencing normal grief. Depression lingers for years; grief resolves itself. Grief usually comes and goes and is normally triggered by memories that are associated with the deceased such as a birthday or special location or object. She does not need diagnosis or drugs, but does need someone to talk to and listen to her. When patients are grieving, the physician should take the time to talk with them. Let them know that grief is normal (many people begin to feel that it is not), and that moving through grief takes time. Normal grief can last up to 1 year. Asking about her husband encourages her to talk about her reactions and her memories of the relationship. Both are a part of the healing process and the most appropriate next response by the physician. If the patient would have met the criteria for a major depressive disorder, then the recommended treatment would be psychotherapy with or without medications, such as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). This woman is having a normal grief response and does not need to be hospitalized (choice B). She is not unable to care for herself, nor is there any mention of suicidal ideation, which would necessitate admission to the hospital. As a general rule, grief should not be medicated (choice C). To work through the grief, the patient needs to come to grips with reality, an unpleasant reality. The physician's job is not to reduce the patient's emotional reactions with pharmacology, but to allow her to come to psychological acceptance of that reality by helping her think about and talk about that reality. There is no need to refer someone to a colleague (choice D). The physician should recognize what is going on and is perfectly able to provide support and comfort on his/her own. Note that referring a patient to an outside source is virtually never the correct answer on the USMLE. Telling the patient to get on with her life (choice E) is premature and suggests that something is wrong with her for having the reactions that she is having.

choice_explanations.A: Asking whether she thinks about her husband often invites the patient to verbalize her feelings and memories, the appropriate response for normal grief.
choice_explanations.B: Hospitalization is unnecessary; she is functioning, not suicidal, and can care for herself.
choice_explanations.C: Grief should not be medicated; the physician's role is to help her accept the reality rather than suppress her emotions.
choice_explanations.D: Referring the patient to a colleague is almost never the correct answer; the physician can provide support directly.
choice_explanations.E: Telling her to move on is premature and implies her normal grief reactions are abnormal.

fa_summary: Normal grief/bereavement is an expected, time-limited reaction to loss; it does not require medication or hospitalization, and the physician should encourage the patient to talk about the deceased.

stem: A 78-year-old woman comes to the physician because of not feeling fully rested after a night's sleep. Physical examination and routine laboratory studies show no abnormalities. She reports no headaches upon wakening or dysesthetic sensations. Her husband says she does not snore often. Which of the following best explains her symptoms?
explanation: The correct answer is A. Sleep consists of two distinct states: NREM and REM. NREM or Non-rapid Eye Movement sleep is divided into stages on the basis of EEG criteria. NREM alternates with REM sleep throughout the sleep period and is characterized by a slowing of the EEG rhythms, higher muscle tone, absence of eye movements, and absence of "thought-like" mental activity. REM or Rapid Eye Movement sleep is characterized by an aroused EEG pattern, sexual arousal, saccadic eye movements, and elaborate visual imagery (dreaming). In the elderly: total sleep time declines; REM percentage remains constant (20%) up to around 80 years of age, then declines further; Stage 4, then stage 3 NREM sleep decrease significantly; there is more awakening and arousal at night, leading to feelings of being unrested after a night's sleep. Sleep patterns differ from person to person, however some generalizations can be made regarding age and sleep. Elderly individuals have more awakening and arousal at night, tend to awaken earlier, and have less total sleep. REM percentage remains constant (20%) up to around 80 years of age, then declines further. Stage 4, and then stage 3 NREM (slow wave) sleep almost vanishes. Multiple factors can contribute to sleep disturbances in the elderly, including primary sleep disorders, sleep disorders secondary to other physical and psychiatric conditions, as well as medication-induced sleep problems. However, many elderly complain of sleep problems when they are simply experiencing normal age-related sleep patterns. K-complexes (choice B) are a sign of stage 2 sleep, the most common stage of sleep. Although more sleep time for the elderly person is spent in Stage 2 sleep, the decline in total sleep time also means that Stage 2 sleep and K-complexes would also decrease. During the adult years, about 20% of sleep time is REM sleep. For the elderly, this proportion may decline even further. Because total sleep time declines, REM sleep time would also decline (choice C). Sleep apnea (choice D) does increase with normal aging, although it is much more common in men. However, the lack of snoring and no headaches in the morning, along with normal laboratory values, tend to rule out sleep apnea in the present case. Restless legs syndrome (RLS) (choice E) is a neurologic movement disorder of the limbs. RLS is often associated with a sleep complaint as well as unpleasant sensations, such as an almost irresistible urge to move the legs. RLS patients generally report dysesthetic sensations commonly described as "pins and needles" or an "internal itch" sensation. Although patients with this condition would likely not feel fully rested (as described in the question stem), the absence of other key RLS symptoms makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

choice_explanations.A: A decrease in slow-wave (Stage 3/4 NREM) sleep is a normal age-related change and best explains not feeling rested.
choice_explanations.B: K-complexes are a Stage 2 feature; total Stage 2 sleep time also declines with age, so they do not increase.
choice_explanations.C: REM sleep time decreases rather than increases with age, since total sleep time declines.
choice_explanations.D: The absence of snoring and morning headaches makes sleep apnea unlikely.
choice_explanations.E: The absence of dysesthetic sensations or an urge to move the legs makes restless legs syndrome unlikely.

fa_summary: With aging, total sleep time declines and Stage 3/4 (slow-wave) NREM sleep almost vanishes, with more night-time awakening causing a feeling of being unrested.

stem: A 76-year-old woman comes to the physician every week because of various minor health problems. Despite the physician's repeated assurances that the woman is basically healthy and capable of making minor medical decisions herself, she remains unconvinced and repeatedly returns to the physician. She explains to the physician that she feels uncomfortable with making decisions for herself and wants the physician to make medical decisions for her. At the end of each interview, she always thanks the physician for his help. Which of the following is a common feature of this patient's likely personality disorder?
explanation: The correct answer is D. This patient is exhibiting signs of dependent personality disorder, a Cluster C disorder, which is evidenced by a marked tendency to surrender control of major areas of the person's life to other individuals. Patients with this disorder often lack self-confidence, feel an excessive need to be taken care of, and are submissive and clinging. Other characteristics include needing others to assume responsibility, having difficulty initiating projects, feeling uncomfortable when alone, and often having an unrealistic preoccupation with fears of being left to take care of oneself. As a result, many physicians become the target of this dependent relationship. Patients with this disorder are often in abusive relationships. Other Cluster C disorders include avoidant personality disorder and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder; all three personality disorders share a high level of anxiety. Masked dependency can also occur as part of other personality disorders, including histrionic and borderline personality disorders. Distrust and suspiciousness (choice A) are hallmarks of paranoid personality disorder. Other characteristics include reading hidden meaning in comments or events and carrying grudges. Excessive emotionality (choice B), somatization, attention-seeking, and sexual provocation are signs of histrionic personality disorder. Grandiose sense of self-importance (choice C), preoccupation with fantasies of unlimited success, requiring excessive admiration, believing that they are special, a sense of entitlement, arrogance, being interpersonally exploitative, and lacking empathy are all characteristics of narcissistic personality disorder. Patients with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder are often preoccupied with order (choice E), to the extent that this preoccupation interferes with day-to-day function. Patients with avoidant personality disorder are socially inhibited and usually are sensitive to rejection (choice F).

choice_explanations.A: Distrust and suspiciousness are hallmarks of paranoid personality disorder, not dependent personality disorder.
choice_explanations.B: Excessive emotionality and attention-seeking are features of histrionic personality disorder.
choice_explanations.C: A grandiose sense of self-importance is characteristic of narcissistic personality disorder.
choice_explanations.D: Low self-confidence (with excessive need to be cared for and difficulty deciding things alone) is a core feature of dependent personality disorder.
choice_explanations.E: Preoccupation with order is characteristic of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder.
choice_explanations.F: Sensitivity to rejection is characteristic of avoidant personality disorder.

fa_summary: Dependent personality disorder (Cluster C) is characterized by a pervasive need to be taken care of, submissiveness, clinging, and low self-confidence, with difficulty making decisions without others' assurance.

stem: A 45-year-old man comes to his physician for a routine examination. He drinks 5-6 alcoholic drinks per day. Laboratory studies show a plasma glucose of 40 mg/dL. Which of the following metabolic alterations is most likely a consequence of this patient's alcohol consumption?

options.text: Increased conversion of glycerol-3-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate
Increased conversion of malate into oxaloacetate
Increased conversion of pyruvate to lactate

explanation:
The correct answer is D. The principal route of metabolism of ethanol is via alcohol dehydrogenase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, both of which reduce NAD+ to NADH, markedly increasing the ratio of NADH to NAD+. The high NADH/NAD+ ratio favors the formation of the product on the right in the following reactions: Pyruvate + NADH ⇌ Lactate + NAD+ and Dihydroxyacetone-P + NADH ⇌ Glycerol-3-P + NAD+. These reactions should go to the left to promote entry of substrates into gluconeogenesis. Thus, gluconeogenesis slows. The higher-than-normal ratio of [NADH]/[NAD+] would increase conversion of pyruvate to lactate.

The higher-than-normal [NADH]/[NAD+] favors the formation of glycerol-3-phosphate from dihydroxyacetone phosphate, so increased conversion of glycerol-3-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (choice A) is incorrect.

The higher-than-normal [NADH]/[NAD+] would decrease the conversion of malate to oxaloacetate rather than stimulating it (choice B).

The relative excess of NADH decreases rather than increases fatty acid oxidation, which would decrease rather than increase conversion to ketone bodies (choice C). Choice C is also incorrect because the patient is presumed to be a long term alcoholic and likely has alcoholic cirrhosis of the liver; therefore, any pathway normally conducted by the liver, such as gluconeogenesis, will be impaired, and there would be decreased production of ketone bodies.

The higher-than-normal [NADH]/[NAD+] would increase conversion of pyruvate to lactate (choice D is correct).

The relative excess of NADH decreases, rather than increases, fatty acid oxidation (choice E).

The borderline fasting hypoglycemia is likely due to impaired gluconeogenesis, which is a consequence of decreased pyruvate, decreased dihydroxyacetone phosphate, and decreased oxaloacetate from the higher-than-normal ratio of [NADH]/[NAD+]. In each instance, those gluconeogenic precursors are being shunted away from gluconeogenesis rather than shunted into the pathway of glucose synthesis. NADH + DHAP ⇌ Glycerol-3P + NAD+; NADH + Pyruvate ⇌ Lactate + NAD+; NADH + Oxaloacetate ⇌ Malate + NAD+. When [NADH] increases and [NAD] decreases, the equilibrium of the reactions above is shifted to the right. In order to promote gluconeogenesis, the equilibrium of these reactions must favor the formation of oxaloacetate, dihydroxyacetone phosphate, and pyruvate so these substrates can be converted to glucose.

choice_explanations.A: The higher-than-normal [NADH]/[NAD+] favors the formation of glycerol-3-phosphate from dihydroxyacetone phosphate, so increased conversion of glycerol-3-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (choice A) is incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: The higher-than-normal [NADH]/[NAD+] would decrease the conversion of malate to oxaloacetate rather than stimulating it (choice B).
choice_explanations.C: The relative excess of NADH decreases rather than increases fatty acid oxidation, which would decrease rather than increase conversion to ketone bodies (choice C). Choice C is also incorrect because the patient is presumed to be a long term alcoholic and likely has alcoholic cirrhosis of the liver; therefore, any pathway normally conducted by the liver, such as gluconeogenesis, will be impaired, and there would be decreased production of ketone bodies.
choice_explanations.D: The higher-than-normal [NADH]/[NAD+] would increase conversion of pyruvate to lactate (choice D is correct).
choice_explanations.E: The relative excess of NADH decreases, rather than increases, fatty acid oxidation (choice E).

fa_summary: Ethanol metabolism raises the NADH/NAD+ ratio, shunting pyruvate to lactate and impairing gluconeogenesis.

stem: A 3-month-old boy has delayed motor development. Nine months later, he develops spasticity and writhing movements. Two years later, he exhibits compulsive biting of fingers and lips and constantly bangs his head. By age 14, he develops arthritis and by age 20, he develops renal failure. Which of the following is most likely to be increased in serum in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has a classic case of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder due to near-complete deficiency of the purine salvage enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HPRT, or sometimes referred to as HGPRT). This enzyme recycles purine bases back into nucleotide synthesis and thereby prevents their degradation to uric acid. The deficiency of HPRT is associated with excessive de novo purine synthesis, hyperuricemia (elevated levels of uric acid in the blood), and the clinical signs and symptoms described in the question stem. The biochemical basis of the often striking self-mutilation, which may require restraints and even tooth extraction, has never been established. Treatment with allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase and its production of uric acid, and reduces the gouty arthritis, urate crystal formation, urate nephropathy and subcutaneous deposits of urate crystals (tophi) associated with hyperuricemia. It does not, however, modify the neurologic/psychiatric presentation.

Galactosemia is an autosomal recessive trait that results from a defective gene encoding galactokinase; galactose 1-P is reduced to galactitol (choice A) in the lens. Galactitol in the lens causes swelling and cataracts.

Glucocerebroside (choice B) is the sphingoglycolipid substrate accumulating in inclusion bodies of individuals with glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher disease). The disease is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, erosion and fractures of bones, thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia, and characteristic macrophages (crumpled-paper inclusions).

Orotic aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the pyrimidine synthesis pathway. Orotic acid (choice D) accumulates and spills into the urine, resulting in orotic acid crystals. Infants with some forms of this disorder can present with severe megaloblastic anemia that does not respond to supplementation with vitamin B12 or folic acid.

Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency results in phenylketonuria (PKU), in which the accumulation of phenylalanine (choice E) results in slow development, severe intellectual disability, autistic symptoms, and loss of motor control. There is mandatory newborn screening for PKU in all states in the US, because early diagnosis and treatment (dietary restriction) prevent pathology.

choice_explanations.A: Galactosemia is an autosomal recessive trait that results from a defective gene encoding galactokinase; galactose 1-P is reduced to galactitol (choice A) in the lens. Galactitol in the lens causes swelling and cataracts.
choice_explanations.B: Glucocerebroside (choice B) is the sphingoglycolipid substrate accumulating in inclusion bodies of individuals with glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher disease). The disease is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, erosion and fractures of bones, thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia, and characteristic macrophages (crumpled-paper inclusions).
choice_explanations.D: Orotic aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the pyrimidine synthesis pathway. Orotic acid (choice D) accumulates and spills into the urine, resulting in orotic acid crystals. Infants with some forms of this disorder can present with severe megaloblastic anemia that does not respond to supplementation with vitamin B12 or folic acid.
choice_explanations.E: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency results in phenylketonuria (PKU), in which the accumulation of phenylalanine (choice E) results in slow development, severe intellectual disability, autistic symptoms, and loss of motor control. There is mandatory newborn screening for PKU in all states in the US, because early diagnosis and treatment (dietary restriction) prevent pathology.

fa_summary: HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan syndrome) causes hyperuricemia with increased serum monosodium urate.

stem: An infant is lethargic and intermittently responsive, tachypneic with hyperventilation, and has hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show: Na 145 mEq/L, Cl 108 mEq/L, HCO3 14 mEq/L, serum urea nitrogen 4 mg/dL, creatinine 0.2 mg/dL, glucose 95 mg/dL, and ammonia 165 μmol/L (10-60 μmol/L). Urine studies show a decreased citrulline level. Which of the following is most likely deficient in this child?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The patient is presenting with ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC) deficiency, which is an X-linked deficiency in an enzyme involved in the urea cycle. The urea cycle is the metabolic pathway that transforms nitrogen to urea for excretion from the body. Neonates typically present at 24 to 48 hours of age with lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, hyperventilation, seizures, and cerebral edema. Typical laboratory values are hyperammonemia with a decrease in urea in the serum (BUN) due to inability to convert nitrogen to urea, as demonstrated in this patient. The treatment for ornithine transcarbamoylase deficiency is a low protein diet and administering supplements to help bypass the enzyme defect.

A deficiency in branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase (choice A) is the cause of maple-syrup urine disease, which is a deficiency in amino acid metabolism. Patients with maple syrup urine disease present with a distinct sweet odor, cognitive impairment, and hypotonia that progresses to seizures and death if not diagnosed in a timely manner.

A deficiency in homogentisate oxidase (choice B) is the cause of alkaptonuria, which is another deficiency in amino acid metabolism. These patients present with dark urine, arthritis, and ochronosis (ie, yellowish-darkish discoloration of the connective tissues).

A deficiency in phenylalanine hydroxylase (choice D) is the cause of phenylketonuria, which is another deficiency in amino acid metabolism. Patients present with a musty odor, albinism and if not treated in time, cognitive impairment. Prompt diagnosis is imperative in order to avoid foods with phenylketones and prevent cognitive effects on the brain.

The cofactor for this enzyme is tetrahydrobiopterin (choice E). Patients deficient in this cofactor have a similar clinical presentation as those with the enzyme deficiency.

Patients with maple syrup urine disease present with a distinct sweet odor, cognitive impairment, and hypotonia that progresses to seizures and death if not diagnosed in a timely manner.

Patients present with a musty odor, albinism and if not treated in time, cognitive impairment. stem: A 4-year-old girl with a history of mental retardation is brought to the physician because of poor vision. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 98/65 mm Hg. Physical examination shows long limbs, tall stature, and kyphosis. Funduscopic examination shows bilateral lens dislocations. Laboratory studies are most likely to show a selective elevation of which of the following amino acids in serum?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The child has cystathionine synthase deficiency, also known as homocystinuria. This enzyme occurs in the pathways involving the metabolism of sulfur-containing amino acids, and normally catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine. When the enzyme is blocked, homocysteine (which is normally a degradation product of methionine) is remethylated by a salvage pathway, resulting in the resynthesis of methionine. Plasma methionine and homocysteine levels are elevated as a result. The clinical features illustrated in the question stem are typical and likely to be mistaken for Marfan syndrome. Note however that the history of mental retardation is not consistent with Marfan syndrome. Children with cystathionine synthase deficiencies also have limited joint mobility in contrast to the hyperextensible joints in Marfan syndrome. These patients are also vulnerable to (potentially fatal) thrombotic episodes, particularly in postoperative and postpartum periods. Note that the question asked for the most likely laboratory result in this patient, and mutations in the CBS (cystathionine beta-synthase) gene is the most common form of homocystinuria.

Cystathionine (choice A) and cysteine (choice B) occur in the pathway after the enzyme blockage, and so are reduced.

Cystathionine (choice A) and cysteine (choice B) occur in the pathway after the enzyme blockage, and so are reduced.

Associate abnormalities of phenylalanine (choice D) with phenylketonuria.

Associate abnormalities of tyrosine metabolism (choice E) with tyrosinemia, albinism, and alkaptonuria.

choice_explanations.B: Cystathionine (choice A) and cysteine (choice B) occur in the pathway after the enzyme blockage, and so are reduced.

fa_summary: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency elevates methionine and homocysteine and causes Marfan-like features with lens dislocation.

stem: An infant, born at 37 weeks' gestation, is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit because of a spontaneous pneumothorax. Two days later, the pneumothorax resolves and the newborn is transferred to the nursery where he is fed a standard cow's-milk formula. Within 24 hours, the baby vomits all feeds, is tachypneic, and has progressive lethargy. Laboratory studies show: arterial pH 7.41, plasma NH4+ 300 μM, plasma amino acids with elevated glutamine and absent citrulline, and urine orotic acid is high. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, the most common of the urea cycle disorders, is a rare metabolic disorder that occurs in 1 out of every 80,000 births. OTC deficiency is an X-linked genetic disorder affecting predominantly males, although there is significant, though milder, symptomatology in heterozygous females. Like other urea cycle disorders, OTC deficiency affects the body's ability to eliminate ammonia, a toxic byproduct of the body's use of protein. As a result, ammonia accumulates in the blood, causing hyperammonemia. Ammonia travels to the various organs of the body, including the brain, where it can cause coma, brain damage, and death. This phenomenon is called hepatic encephalopathy. An infant with ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency may be lethargic or unwilling to eat, and may have poorly controlled breathing rate or body temperature. Some babies with this disorder may experience seizures or unusual body movements. Typical plasma findings with OTC deficiency are elevated levels of glutamine. Because carbamoyl phosphate is not used for synthesis of citrulline, plasma citrulline levels are low or absent in persons with OTC deficiency. The excess carbamoyl phosphate leaves the mitochondria, and enters the cytosol where it stimulates pyrimidine synthesis, leading to accumulation of orotate.

The major symptoms of arginase deficiency (choice A) are all progressive and include psychomotor retardation, spastic tetraplegia (where the lower limbs are more affected than the upper), hyperactivity, growth failure and seizures.

Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (choice B) is characterized by the accumulation of ammonia and glutamine.

Deficiencies in carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (choice C) result in the most severe levels of hyperammonemia associated with any defect in the urea cycle.

choice_explanations.A: The major symptoms of arginase deficiency (choice A) are all progressive and include psychomotor retardation, spastic tetraplegia (where the lower limbs are more affected than the upper), hyperactivity, growth failure and seizures.
choice_explanations.B: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (choice B) is characterized by the accumulation of ammonia and glutamine.
choice_explanations.C: Deficiencies in carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (choice C) result in the most severe levels of hyperammonemia associated with any defect in the urea cycle.

fa_summary: OTC deficiency (X-linked) causes hyperammonemia with orotic aciduria and low/absent citrulline.

stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician because of recent fatigue and a pallor that she noticed in the sclera of both eyes. She says that her sister and older brother have been diagnosed with hemolytic anemia but that two younger brothers are asymptomatic. The patient's mother and father are second cousins. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely to cause this patient's disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. In general, you should associate primary hemolytic anemia with defects in glycolysis or the hexose monophosphate shunt (pentose phosphate pathway) because those are pathways of energy generation and antioxidant defense in the red cell. A salient feature of the patient's presentation is that the disorder appears to be hereditary and that it is not X-linked, because there is not a male-bias in the inheritance. Only one enzyme of those listed in the answer choices specifically involves these pathways, causes hemolytic anemia when deficient and is inherited in an autosomal fashion: pyruvate kinase (PK). PK is a glycolytic enzyme; PK deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder, affecting males and females approximately equally. Consanguinity increases the incidence of any autosomal recessive condition. Deficiency of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH), which may be related to hemolytic anemia, is X-linked. A hemolytic anemia from inherited deficiency of G6PDH in a woman is expected to be very rare. If this enzyme is deficient, red cells are defective in their ability to produce sufficient ATP to maintain the Na+/K+ pump on the plasma membrane, secondarily causing swelling and lysis. Severe forms of PK deficiency are usually symptomatic in newborns and may be life-threatening. Milder cases of PK deficiency are often missed earlier in life and may or may not produce symptoms later in life. Increased concentrations of glycolytic intermediates in red blood cells occur. 2 to 3 times the normal levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG or 2,3-DPG) in red cells are present, leading to a lower affinity of Hb for O2.

Debranching enzyme (alpha-1,4, alpha-1,4 transferase) (choice A) deficiency is characterized by mild fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperuricemia.

Defects in glucose-6-phosphatase (choice B) produce profound fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperuricemia.

Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice C) deficiency decreases NADPH production in the red cell and decreases the red cell's ability to handle oxidative stress; it can also lead to a hemolytic anemia but is less likely in this case because the G6PDH gene is X-linked.

Deficiency of muscle phosphorylase (myophosphorylase) (choice D) produces weakness and cramping during the initial phase.

choice_explanations.A: Debranching enzyme (alpha-1,4, alpha-1,4 transferase) (choice A) deficiency is characterized by mild fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperuricemia.
choice_explanations.B: Defects in glucose-6-phosphatase (choice B) produce profound fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperuricemia.
choice_explanations.C: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice C) deficiency decreases NADPH production in the red cell and decreases the red cell's ability to handle oxidative stress; it can also lead to a hemolytic anemia but is less likely in this case because the G6PDH gene is X-linked.
choice_explanations.D: Deficiency of muscle phosphorylase (myophosphorylase) (choice D) produces weakness and cramping during the initial phase.

fa_summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency, an autosomal recessive glycolytic defect, causes intrinsic hemolytic anemia.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of digestive problems. His mother says that he often experiences severe abdominal cramps after eating a high-fat meal. Diagnosis of a genetic defect resulting in a deficiency of lipoprotein lipase is made. Which of the following substances is most likely increased in this patient's plasma following a fatty meal?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. After a person eats a high-fat meal, triglycerides are processed by the intestinal mucosal cells. They are assembled in chylomicrons and eventually sent into the circulation for delivery to adipocytes and other cells. Chylomicrons are too large to enter cells, but are degraded while in the circulation by lipoprotein lipase, an enzyme associated with the luminal surface of endothelial cell membranes. Lipoprotein lipase catalyzes the breakdown of triacylglycerides in chylomicrons to free fatty acids and glycerol. A defect in this enzyme would result in the accumulation of chylomicrons in the plasma, causing the plasma to appear milky (lactescence), even in a fasting blood sample. Deficiency of this enzyme would lead to elevated levels of chylomicrons (mainly chylomicronemia) and VLDL.

Albumin-bound free fatty acids (choice A) is incorrect because fatty acids leave the intestine esterified as triglycerides in chylomicrons. Free fatty acids increase in plasma when they are released from adipose tissue.

HDL (choice C) is not a carrier of dietary fat from the intestine.

LDL (choice D) would not be elevated in this patient after a high-fat meal.

Thus, a defect in lipoprotein lipase would cause a decrease, not an elevation, of unesterified fatty acids (choice E).

choice_explanations.A: Albumin-bound free fatty acids (choice A) is incorrect because fatty acids leave the intestine esterified as triglycerides in chylomicrons. Free fatty acids increase in plasma when they are released from adipose tissue.
choice_explanations.C: HDL (choice C) is not a carrier of dietary fat from the intestine.
choice_explanations.D: LDL (choice D) would not be elevated in this patient after a high-fat meal.
choice_explanations.E: Thus, a defect in lipoprotein lipase would cause a decrease, not an elevation, of unesterified fatty acids (choice E).

fa_summary: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes chylomicronemia and eruptive xanthomas.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled insulin-requiring diabetes mellitus is admitted to the hospital because of severe hyperglycemia. The patient has experienced increased thirst and frequent urination and has had episodes of nausea and vomiting. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 138/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry skin and dry mucous membranes and his breath smells like nail polish remover. An arterial blood gas shows: arterial CO2 29 mm Hg and arterial HCO3 15 mEq/L. Which of the following measurements is most likely to be decreased in this patient compared to the normal range?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient's blood gases reveal a metabolic acidosis (low pH, low HCO3). The decrease in arterial CO2, resulting from increased respiratory rate, is an appropriate compensatory response to the acidosis. The smell of acetone (the primary solvent in nail-polish remover) on the breath of a diabetic suggests ketoacidosis. This occurs when uncontrolled diabetes mellitus leads to overproduction of ketoacids and high levels of plasma acetone. Together, these are referred to as diabetic ketoacidosis. Because acetone is highly volatile, it is excreted mainly by the lungs and can be detected in the breath. Ketoacids, which include acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate, are normally produced in roughly equal amounts. However, in pathologic conditions such as poorly controlled diabetes and alcoholism, in which the concentration of NADH is high, the ratio shifts and 3-hydroxybutyrate predominates. Therefore, the ratio of acetoacetate to 3-hydroxybutyrate actually decreases, while the net amount of ketoacids increases.

Plasma levels of acetone (choice A) are actually increased during ketoacidosis, which leads to the smell of nail polish remover on the patient's breath.

Plasma catecholamines (choice B) as well as glucagon (choice C) are increased during ketoacidosis due to a shift in metabolism to that resembling the starvation state as a result of insufficient insulin.

Plasma catecholamines (choice B) as well as glucagon (choice C) are increased during ketoacidosis due to a shift in metabolism to that resembling the starvation state as a result of insufficient insulin.

Plasma 3-hydroxybutyrate (choice D) will increase (as a result of an increase in NADH), which contributes to the decrease in the acetoacetate/3-hydroxybutyrate ratio.

choice_explanations.B: Plasma catecholamines (choice B) as well as glucagon (choice C) are increased during ketoacidosis due to a shift in metabolism to that resembling the starvation state as a result of insufficient insulin.
choice_explanations.C: Plasma catecholamines (choice B) as well as glucagon (choice C) are increased during ketoacidosis due to a shift in metabolism to that resembling the starvation state as a result of insufficient insulin.

fa_summary: In diabetic ketoacidosis the high NADH/NAD+ ratio increases 3-hydroxybutyrate more than acetoacetate, lowering their ratio.

stem: A 7-day-old newborn is brought to a physician because of multiple bruises and bleeding at the umbilical stump. The infant has been breast fed and the mother reports taking a cephalosporin for a respiratory tract infection she acquired after delivery. Laboratory studies show a prothrombin time that is four-times the reference value. Which of the following biochemical processes is most likely abnormal in this newborn?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Deficiency of vitamin K produces a clotting disorder characterized by an elevated prothrombin time and easy bleeding, particularly in neonates (hemorrhagic disease of the newborn). The biochemical basis for this hemorrhagic tendency is that glutamate residues on factors II (thrombin), VII, IX, and X must be converted to gamma-carboxyglutamate residues (in a vitamin K-requiring reaction) for optimal activity. In breast-feeding mothers, certain antibiotics, eg, cephalosporins, can interfere with the production of vitamin K in breast milk.

The conversion of homocysteine to methionine (choice A) requires vitamin B12.

Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA (choice B) requires vitamin B12.

Cystathionine is further degraded (choice C) by other enzymes to products that can be oxidized in the TCA cycle.

Hydroxylation of proline (choice E) requires vitamin C. Vitamin C deficiency can cause easy bruising, but will not prolong the prothrombin time.

choice_explanations.A: The conversion of homocysteine to methionine (choice A) requires vitamin B12.
choice_explanations.B: Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA (choice B) requires vitamin B12.
choice_explanations.C: Cystathionine is further degraded (choice C) by other enzymes to products that can be oxidized in the TCA cycle.
choice_explanations.E: Hydroxylation of proline (choice E) requires vitamin C. Vitamin C deficiency can cause easy bruising, but will not prolong the prothrombin time.

fa_summary: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X.

stem: A 8-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of increased crying, sweating, and shaking chills. The mother states that until recently the child had been exclusively breast-fed but she was now trying to see whether the child might enjoy other foods. The symptoms started soon after feeding the child applesauce and puréed pears, which at first she ate eagerly. Onset of symptoms began approximately 1 hour later. Based on the history and laboratory results, a tentative diagnosis is made. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Fructose-1-phosphate aldolase (aldolase B) deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder of fructose metabolism resulting in accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate because of the inability to cleave it to glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. The accumulated fructose-1-phosphate inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, causing severe hypoglycemia after ingestion of fructose. These processes are inhibited because free inorganic phosphate (Pi) levels are reduced. Pi is required for glycogen phosphorylase of glycogenolysis. Pi is also required for ATP production, and ATP is needed for gluconeogenesis. As ATP levels fall, AMP levels rise. AMP is degraded to uric acid and hyperuricemia may be seen. Because urate and lactate compete for the same transporters in the kidneys, lactic acidosis may be seen. Prolonged fructose ingestion in infants leads ultimately to hepatic failure and death. This condition is known as hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI). Treatment is removal of fructose (and sucrose, a disaccharide of glucose and fructose) from the diet. Free fructose is found in fruits, honey, and high-fructose corn syrup.

Aldose reductase (choice A) reduces glucose to sorbitol and galactose to galactitol. In patients with recurring hyperglycemia (as in diabetes) or galactosemia (as in galactokinase deficiency or UDP-galactosyltransferase deficiency), increased flux through this pathway can cause osmotic damage in the lens.

Essential fructosuria involves a defect in fructokinase (choice B) and is a benign, asymptomatic condition.

Hexokinase (choice D) catalyzes the first step in glycolysis.

Lactase (choice E) breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose.

choice_explanations.A: Aldose reductase (choice A) reduces glucose to sorbitol and galactose to galactitol. In patients with recurring hyperglycemia (as in diabetes) or galactosemia (as in galactokinase deficiency or UDP-galactosyltransferase deficiency), increased flux through this pathway can cause osmotic damage in the lens.
choice_explanations.B: Essential fructosuria involves a defect in fructokinase (choice B) and is a benign, asymptomatic condition.
choice_explanations.D: Hexokinase (choice D) catalyzes the first step in glycolysis.
choice_explanations.E: Lactase (choice E) breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose.

fa_summary: Aldolase B deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance) impairs glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis, causing hypoglycemia after fructose ingestion.

stem: A 47-year-old man with a history of alcoholism is brought to the emergency department because he was found wandering in the streets. He appears disoriented and walks unsteadily. Physical examination shows an inability to adduct the right eye or to abduct the left eye. When asked about recent events that may have resulted in his condition, he responds with several elaborate but obviously fictitious stories. Altered activity of which of the following enzymes is most likely contributing to his symptoms?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion, and a memory deficit, which he tries to cover by inventing bizarre explanations (confabulation). This constellation of neurologic symptoms is characteristic of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is caused by thiamine deficiency. In the United States, severe thiamine deficiency is seen most commonly in chronic alcoholics. Thiamine deficiency can also damage peripheral nerves ("dry" beriberi) and the heart ("wet" beriberi). Dietary deficiency is more common in countries in which "polished rice" (rice with hulls removed) is a dietary staple. Pyruvate dehydrogenase is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. Cofactors and coenzymes used by pyruvate dehydrogenase include thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, from the vitamin thiamine), lipoic acid, coenzyme A (from the vitamin pantothenate), FAD[H2] (from the vitamin riboflavin), and NAD[H] (from the vitamin niacin). TPP is also a coenzyme for alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase, and transketolase. Treatment is with thiamine. Thiamine must be administered prior to glucose. Administration of glucose to malnourished patients can exhaust their thiamine supplies (because the complete oxidation of glucose is a thiamine-intensive process) and precipitate or worsen Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. If treated quickly and effectively, Wernicke encephalopathy can be reversible.

Deficiency of fructose 1-phosphate aldolase (also known as aldolase B; choice A) causes hereditary fructose intolerance, a disorder resulting in accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate in the liver and renal proximal tubules. Symptoms include lethargy, vomiting, hyperbilirubinemia, hypoglycemia, hyperuricemia, and renal proximal tubule defects (Fanconi syndrome).

Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice B) deficiency, an X-linked disorder, is the most common genetic deficiency that causes a hemolytic anemia.

Pyruvate carboxylase (choice C) is a mitochondrial enzyme activated by acetyl-CoA.

Pyruvate kinase (choice E) deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder, is the second most common genetic deficiency that causes a hemolytic anemia.

choice_explanations.A: Deficiency of fructose 1-phosphate aldolase (also known as aldolase B; choice A) causes hereditary fructose intolerance, a disorder resulting in accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate in the liver and renal proximal tubules. Symptoms include lethargy, vomiting, hyperbilirubinemia, hypoglycemia, hyperuricemia, and renal proximal tubule defects (Fanconi syndrome).
choice_explanations.B: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice B) deficiency, an X-linked disorder, is the most common genetic deficiency that causes a hemolytic anemia.
choice_explanations.C: Pyruvate carboxylase (choice C) is a mitochondrial enzyme activated by acetyl-CoA.
choice_explanations.E: Pyruvate kinase (choice E) deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder, is the second most common genetic deficiency that causes a hemolytic anemia.

fa_summary: Thiamine (TPP) is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase; deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

stem: A 8-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of persistent weakness. Laboratory studies show hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia, and myoglobinuria. A diagnosis of defective carnitine biosynthesis is made. This molecule is necessary for which of the following biochemical functions?

options.text: Carrier of free fatty acids in the blood
Importing nascent proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum
Transfer of digestive enzymes from the Golgi apparatus to lysosomes
Transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Carnitine is a methylated derivative of lysine that is used by the enzyme carnitine palmitoyltransferase (CPT/CAT). This enzyme catalyzes the movement of a long-chain fatty acyl group from CoA to carnitine, and then the fatty acid attached to carnitine is carried across the inner mitochondrial membrane and into the mitochondrial matrix. Within the mitochondrion, fatty acyl-CoA is regenerated and undergoes beta-oxidation. Carnitine is obtained to some degree from the diet and to a greater degree by endogenous synthesis. Carnitine deficiency can result either from increased demand (e.g., ketosis) coupled with inadequate diet or from defects in the carnitine metabolic pathways. In addition to features noted in the question stem, carnitine deficiency may cause fatty liver, lipid storage myopathy, and confusion.

Serum albumin carries free fatty acids in the blood (choice A) for distribution to tissues that can oxidize them, such as liver and muscle.

An N-terminal hydrophobic signal sequence is required to import nascent proteins into the lumen of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (choice B).

Targeting misfolded proteins to proteasome (choice C) requires ubiquitin.

Transfer of digestive enzymes from the Golgi apparatus to lysosomes (choice D) requires phosphorylation of mannose in the glycosylated enzyme to form mannose-6-P.

choice_explanations.A: Serum albumin carries free fatty acids in the blood (choice A) for distribution to tissues that can oxidize them, such as liver and muscle.
choice_explanations.B: An N-terminal hydrophobic signal sequence is required to import nascent proteins into the lumen of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (choice B).
choice_explanations.C: Targeting misfolded proteins to proteasome (choice C) requires ubiquitin.
choice_explanations.D: Transfer of digestive enzymes from the Golgi apparatus to lysosomes (choice D) requires phosphorylation of mannose in the glycosylated enzyme to form mannose-6-P.

fa_summary: Carnitine shuttles long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation.

stem: A 5-day-old newborn develops poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy that progresses to convulsions, coma, and apnea. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 135/min, respirations are 55/min, and blood pressure is 84/58 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a minimally responsive neonate with hypotonic limbs. Urinalysis shows ketones but no acetoacetate or 3-hydroxybutyrate. Specialized laboratory studies show a deficiency of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase activity. Which of the following amino acids should be eliminated from this baby's diet?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The disease is maple-syrup urine disease, which is also known as branched-chain ketoaciduria. This is a rare autosomal recessive disease, with an incidence of 1 in 200,000 in most of the United States, although a Mennonite community in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, has been found with an incidence of 1 in 176. The defective enzyme, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, normally is involved in the catabolism of branched-chain amino acids that have been previously transaminated to form their ketoacid derivatives. The branched chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, and valine) and their by-products build up in the organs and brain. Because they are toxic to these organs, the build up leads to poor feeding, hypotonia, vomiting, and lethargy initially that progresses to seizures and death if not promptly recognized. Onset of the progressive neurologic decline is several days after birth. Because neonates do not normally produce acetoacetate, ketones detected on urinalysis should prompt consideration of an organic aciduria. Leucine, isoleucine, and valine should be minimized in the diet.

Associate abnormal histidine metabolism (choice A) with histidinemia. This is a rare metabolic, autosomal recessive deficiency of the enzyme histidine decarboxylase, which leads to accumulation of histidine. Most individuals with this condition are asymptomatic.

For the USMLE, associate methioninemia (choice C) with homocystinuria. Classic homocystinuria is caused by deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase (the CBS enzyme). Homocystinuria is associated with an increased risk of atherosclerosis, stroke, deep vein thrombosis, Marfan-like habitus, mental retardation, and restricted joint mobility.

Associate abnormal phenylalanine metabolism (choice D) with phenylketonuria (PKU).

Associate abnormal tyrosine metabolism (choice E) with albinism, in which there is a congenital deficiency of tyrosinase.

choice_explanations.A: Associate abnormal histidine metabolism (choice A) with histidinemia. This is a rare metabolic, autosomal recessive deficiency of the enzyme histidine decarboxylase, which leads to accumulation of histidine. Most individuals with this condition are asymptomatic.
choice_explanations.C: For the USMLE, associate methioninemia (choice C) with homocystinuria. Classic homocystinuria is caused by deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase (the CBS enzyme). Homocystinuria is associated with an increased risk of atherosclerosis, stroke, deep vein thrombosis, Marfan-like habitus, mental retardation, and restricted joint mobility.
choice_explanations.D: Associate abnormal phenylalanine metabolism (choice D) with phenylketonuria (PKU).
choice_explanations.E: Associate abnormal tyrosine metabolism (choice E) with albinism, in which there is a congenital deficiency of tyrosinase.

fa_summary: Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency (maple syrup urine disease) requires dietary restriction of isoleucine, leucine and valine.

stem: A 38-year-old man collapses while running a marathon and is brought to the emergency department. His wife states that he is not in shape but still decided to run. Arterial blood gas on room air shows PO2 of 100 mm Hg, PCO2 of 42 mm Hg, and pH of 7.30. Further evaluation reveals a metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap. Increased activity of which of the following biochemical pathways is the basis for the clinical findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Under normal conditions, when oxygen is readily available, the pyruvate generated in glycolysis enters the mitochondria and is decarboxylated to acetyl CoA by the action of pyruvate dehydrogenase. In severe exercise, particularly by individuals in poor physical condition, the oxygen demands of the skeletal muscle may exceed the ability of the heart and lungs to provide oxygen. Consequently, oxidation of NADH by the electron transport chain is decreased, as is ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation. In this setting, the muscles switch to anaerobic glycolysis and the pyruvate that is produced is reduced to lactate by the action of lactate dehydrogenase as NADH is oxidized. The NAD+ generated allows glycolysis to continue and ATP is generated by substrate-level phosphorylation. Much of the lactic acid thereby produced is released into the bloodstream, where it causes metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap. In addition to the setting of severe exercise, lactic acidosis can also be seen in tissue hypoxia (seizures, cardiac failure, hypotension, carbon monoxide poisoning, severe anemia), with drug toxicity and toxins (phenformin, catecholamines, salicylate, isoniazid, cyanide), in congenital defects in processes that utilize pyruvate such as gluconeogenesis, and in many severe illnesses.

Beta-oxidation of fatty acids (choice B) can produce acetyl-CoA, which, in the liver mitochondria, may be converted to ketone bodies such as acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate if the acetyl-CoA is not used in the citric acid cycle. When the production of these ketone bodies exceeds their use, ketoacidosis (a type of high anion gap metabolic acidosis) can result. This would not explain this patient's findings.

The citric acid cycle (choice C) oxidizes acetyl CoA from the oxidation of glucose, fatty acids, and some amino acids and produces CO2, NADH, and FADH2. Increasing the activity of the cycle would not cause a metabolic acidosis.

In mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (choice D), the NADH and FADH2 from the citric acid cycle (and other sources) are used to generate ATP.

The pentose phosphate shunt (choice E) is an important producer of NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate.

choice_explanations.B: Beta-oxidation of fatty acids (choice B) can produce acetyl-CoA, which, in the liver mitochondria, may be converted to ketone bodies such as acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate if the acetyl-CoA is not used in the citric acid cycle. When the production of these ketone bodies exceeds their use, ketoacidosis (a type of high anion gap metabolic acidosis) can result. This would not explain this patient's findings.
choice_explanations.C: The citric acid cycle (choice C) oxidizes acetyl CoA from the oxidation of glucose, fatty acids, and some amino acids and produces CO2, NADH, and FADH2. Increasing the activity of the cycle would not cause a metabolic acidosis.
choice_explanations.D: In mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (choice D), the NADH and FADH2 from the citric acid cycle (and other sources) are used to generate ATP.
choice_explanations.E: The pentose phosphate shunt (choice E) is an important producer of NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate.

fa_summary: During intense exercise muscle shifts to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactate and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

stem: A 53-year-old man with a history of alcoholism is brought to the emergency department by the police after having been found lying on the street. He has multiple lesions on his body, but denies being involved in a fight. Physical examination shows multiple ecchymoses on the extremities and thorax, and hemorrhages around hair follicles. His BMI is 16 kg/m2. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is most likely responsible for these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This alcoholic, malnourished patient suffers from scurvy due to a deficiency of dietary vitamin C. Absence of vitamin C leads to impaired hydroxylation of proline residues in nascent procollagen chains. The hydroxyl groups of hydroxyproline are involved in hydrogen bonding that stabilizes the triple helical procollagen. Its absence results in decreased tensile strength of the collagen, leading to weakness of blood vessel walls. Alcoholism is associated with deficiencies of several nutrients and vitamins. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is necessary for the hydroxylation of proline residues in procollagen chains. Deficiency of vitamin C results in scurvy, which is characterized by perifollicular hemorrhages, fragmentation of hairs, purpura, ecchymoses, splinter hemorrhages, gum changes, and hemorrhages into muscle.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency (choice A) can cause Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff psychosis, peripheral neuropathy ("dry" beriberi), and congestive heart failure resulting from a cardiomyopathy ("wet" beriberi).

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency (choice B) can cause microcytic sideroblastic anemia.

Cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency (choice C) can cause megaloblastic anemia and potentially a peripheral and progressive neuropathy.

Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) deficiency (choice E), or the inability to activate D2 in an alcoholic liver, can result in osteoporosis and bone disease.

choice_explanations.A: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency (choice A) can cause Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff psychosis, peripheral neuropathy ("dry" beriberi), and congestive heart failure resulting from a cardiomyopathy ("wet" beriberi).
choice_explanations.B: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency (choice B) can cause microcytic sideroblastic anemia.
choice_explanations.C: Cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency (choice C) can cause megaloblastic anemia and potentially a peripheral and progressive neuropathy.
choice_explanations.E: Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) deficiency (choice E), or the inability to activate D2 in an alcoholic liver, can result in osteoporosis and bone disease.

fa_summary: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) impairs proline hydroxylation in collagen, causing perifollicular hemorrhage and easy bruising.

stem: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of the onset of seizures. The parents say that the seizures occur several hours after each feeding. The mother also reports that she did not have any prenatal care. Physical examination of the infant shows growth retardation and a demonstrably palpable liver. Laboratory studies show elevated lactate and lipidemia in addition to a glucose level of 4 mg/dL. A defect involving which of the following enzymes is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The demonstrably palpable liver indicates the infant has pronounced hepatomegaly. Hepatomegaly and hypoglycemic seizures strongly suggests a glycogen storage disease (GSD). Three of the enzymes listed are related to glycogen storage diseases: Glucose-6-phosphatase (choice C; deficiency produces von Gierke disease, from which this patient is suffering); Acid maltase (choice A; also called lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase; deficiency results in Pompe disease); and Muscle phosphorylase (choice E; deficiency produces McArdle disease). Von Gierke disease is a glycogen storage disease caused by a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase (GSD type Ia) or the glucose-6-phosphate translocase (GSD type Ib). It typically presents between 3 months of age with hypoglycemia, hyperlipidemia, and lactic acidosis. Failure to thrive is also common in early life; convulsions may occur during episodes of profound hypoglycemia. The glycogen accumulation in von Gierke disease occurs primarily in the liver and kidneys, accounting for the enlargement of these organs. Gout may develop later because of the derangement of glucose metabolism. Due to allelic heterogeneity, the onset of symptoms may be delayed and, in some cases, symptoms may be milder.

Pompe disease (choice A) is a muscle glycogenosis disorder associated with skeletal and cardiac muscle involvement.

Beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency (choice B) causes Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disease, which is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly and glucocerebroside accumulation in phagocytic cells.

Hexosaminidase A (choice D) deficiency is associated with Tay-Sachs disease, a lysosomal storage disease.

McArdle disease (choice E) is also a muscle glycogenosis.

choice_explanations.A: Pompe disease (choice A) is a muscle glycogenosis disorder associated with skeletal and cardiac muscle involvement.
choice_explanations.B: Beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency (choice B) causes Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disease, which is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly and glucocerebroside accumulation in phagocytic cells.
choice_explanations.D: Hexosaminidase A (choice D) deficiency is associated with Tay-Sachs disease, a lysosomal storage disease.
choice_explanations.E: McArdle disease (choice E) is also a muscle glycogenosis.

fa_summary: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) causes fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia.

stem: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after having a brief generalized seizure, which left him semicomatose. Laboratory studies show elevated C8-C10 acylcarnitines. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is C. This infant most likely has medium-chain acyl CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency. MCAD is important in the beta-oxidation of fatty acids after the initial cycles of this process are carried out by long-chain acyl CoA dehydrogenase (LCAD) to yield acetyl CoA plus fragments 8 to 10 carbons in length. Without the MCAD enzyme, these medium chain length fatty acids accumulate, eventually spilling out of the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle. The resultant C8-C10 acylcarnitines are sufficiently amphipathic that they can exit the cells and spill into the bloodstream. Levels of C8-C10 acylcarnitines in the blood are measured by mass spectrometry to diagnose MCAD deficiency. The decreased ability to complete fatty acid beta-oxidation (which requires the MCAD enzyme) in the liver during fasting conditions results in low ATP levels because of decreased production of acetyl CoA, the product of beta-oxidation. Decreased beta-oxidation in fasting increases reliance on proteolysis to supply glucose and ATP. Amino acid degradation produces toxic ammonia that is converted to nontoxic urea in the urea cycle, an ATP-requiring process. With low ATP levels, the activity of the urea cycle decreases, and ammonia builds up in the bloodstream. In the early neonatal period, the newborn is often asymptomatic because frequent feedings protect the newborn from the need to cope with the metabolic stresses of fasting. The family is typically initially unaware of the problem, especially as this is an autosomal recessive condition, so close relatives may be unaffected. As the infant gets older and feeding frequency decreases, symptoms that may develop (particularly at night) are often related to hypoglycemia, such as irritability before meals, lethargy, jitteriness, sweating, and, possibly, seizures. By about 3 months of age, the infant may become seriously ill after a viral illness that decreases nutrient intake, with hypoglycemia and hypoketonemia. MCAD deficiency results in fasting hypoglycemia and hypoketonemia; failure of the urea cycle to operate leads to ammonia accumulation in blood.
fa_summary: MCAD deficiency impairs beta-oxidation, causing hypoglycemia, hypoketonemia and hyperammonemia.

stem: A 37-year-old woman with a history of acute intermittent porphyria comes to the physician because of acute gastroenteritis. She has severe abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypertension, and proximal muscle weakness. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely to be seen during an episode of this illness?

options.text: Increased porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD) activity in erythrocytes
Increased urinary delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG)

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is one of the most common of the porphyrias. It is an autosomal dominant condition that results from partial deficiency of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD), also known as hydroxymethylbilane synthase, which catalyzes the reaction. In AIP, patients excrete delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG) in the urine during the acute attacks. Attacks are characterized by abdominal pain, tachycardia, and neurologic effects. Patients are not photosensitive.

Increased erythrocyte Zn-protoporphyrin (choice A) results when the last step in heme synthesis does not take place.

Increased serum porphyrins (choice C) is incorrect because there would be an inability to synthesize sufficient amounts of porphyrins due to a partial defect in PBGD.

A decrease in urinary coproporphyrins (choice D) is found in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency and congenital erythropoietic porphyria (decreased activity of uroporphyrinogen III synthase).

In AIP, patients excrete delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG) in the urine during the acute attacks (choice E is correct).
fa_subchapter: Heme synthesis, porphyrias, and lead poisoning

choice_explanations.A: Increased erythrocyte Zn-protoporphyrin (choice A) results when the last step in heme synthesis does not take place.
choice_explanations.C: Increased serum porphyrins (choice C) is incorrect because there would be an inability to synthesize sufficient amounts of porphyrins due to a partial defect in PBGD.
choice_explanations.D: A decrease in urinary coproporphyrins (choice D) is found in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency and congenital erythropoietic porphyria (decreased activity of uroporphyrinogen III synthase).
choice_explanations.E: In AIP, patients excrete delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG) in the urine during the acute attacks (choice E is correct).

fa_summary: Acute intermittent porphyria (PBGD deficiency) increases urinary ALA and PBG during attacks.

stem: A physician from the United States decides to take a sabbatical from his responsibilities at a teaching hospital to work in a clinic in a remote part of Africa. During his first week at the clinic, he is told that he will be seeing a patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Which of the following will be the most likely clinical presentation of this patient?

options.text: A child with short stature, radial abnormalities, absent thumbs, and café-au-lait spots develops severe anemia
A child who develops myoglobinuria following vigorous exercise
A neonate with an enlarged spleen and severe anemia
An adult who develops anemia following use of antimalarial drugs
An adult who develops severe shortness of breath during an airplane ride

explanation:
The correct answer is D. There are several variants of G6PD deficiency (X-linked recessive) in Africa. The most common clinically significant variant is the so-called A-type, which produces an unstable G6PD enzyme. This variant is found in up to 11% of African-American males. In red cells, NADPH from the HMP shunt is essential for detoxifying reactive oxygen species that otherwise would damage proteins and lipids in the RBC. Glutathione reductase and glutathione peroxidase are involved in the normal detoxification process. The A-variant renders the individual's red cells susceptible to oxidative stresses, such as those that occur with administration of the antimalarial drug primaquine. Sulfonamides and dapsone are other agents that can trigger hemolytic episodes. Infections (bacterial or viral) are another important trigger for hemolysis in these individuals. Rarely, G6PD deficiency presents as neonatal jaundice or with chronic hemolysis. In Mediterranean populations, G6PD deficiency-associated hemolysis may occur in individuals who eat a meal of fava beans (Vicia fava) and several hours later develop hemoglobinuria and peripheral vascular collapse secondary to intravascular hemolysis as a result of the oxidant injury initiated by the fava beans.

Fanconi anemia (choice A) is caused by a mutation in one of several genes encoding a multiprotein nuclear complex that functions in the BRCA pathway, which repairs damage to DNA caused by cross-linking agents. All bone marrow elements are affected. In addition to the often-fatal leukemia, pigmentary changes in the skin and malformations of the heart, kidney, and limbs (aplasia of the radius, thumb deformity) are associated features.

Myoglobinuria following strenuous exercise, especially in the initial phase (choice B) is characteristic of myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease), a defect in muscle glycogenolysis.

A neonate with an enlarged spleen and chronic hemolysis (choice C) is consistent with pyruvate kinase deficiency, the neonatal form of which is often fatal. Transfusions coupled with splenectomy often lessen the symptoms.

choice_explanations.A: Fanconi anemia (choice A) is caused by a mutation in one of several genes encoding a multiprotein nuclear complex that functions in the BRCA pathway, which repairs damage to DNA caused by cross-linking agents. All bone marrow elements are affected. In addition to the often-fatal leukemia, pigmentary changes in the skin and malformations of the heart, kidney, and limbs (aplasia of the radius, thumb deformity) are associated features.
choice_explanations.B: Myoglobinuria following strenuous exercise, especially in the initial phase (choice B) is characteristic of myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease), a defect in muscle glycogenolysis.
choice_explanations.C: A neonate with an enlarged spleen and chronic hemolysis (choice C) is consistent with pyruvate kinase deficiency, the neonatal form of which is often fatal. Transfusions coupled with splenectomy often lessen the symptoms.

fa_summary: G6PD deficiency causes episodic hemolysis triggered by antimalarials, sulfonamides, dapsone, fava beans and infection.

stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of increasing irritability, poor attention span, and lethargy. She also has anorexia, vague abdominal pain, and constipation. Physical examination shows a pale girl who is somewhat somnolent, with reduced reflexes in all extremities. Treatment is begun with intravenous dimercaprol (BAL) and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA). The toxicity responsible for this patient's condition most likely results from inhibition of which of the following enzymes?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This child is presenting with the typical signs and symptoms of lead poisoning, which affects the activity of the enzymes aminolevulinate (ALA) dehydratase in the heme biosynthetic pathway. Lead poisoning is a chronic disorder often seen in children who are exposed to environmental sources of lead, such as paint chips, putty, or plaster from old buildings, which the child may ingest.
