Lead poisoning can lead to a variety of constitutional symptoms, including lethargy, headache, memory loss, nausea, abdominal pain, and diarrhea or constipation. With high blood lead levels, lead lines may appear in the gums (usually seen in adults more than in children) and in bones on x-ray (lead lines that are opaque metaphysial bands in growing bone). Inhibition of ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase can result in microcytic, hypochromic anemia due to impaired heme synthesis. Ferrochelatase inhibition also results in the accumulation of free erythrocyte protoporphyrin. Treatment involves chelation of lead (EDTA, dimercaprol, succimer).

Ceruloplasmin (a ferroxidase) (choice B) catalyzes the oxidation of ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+) iron.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice C) deficiency, an X-linked disease that affects the pentose phosphate pathway, results in episodic hemolysis triggered by infections, certain drugs, including primaquine and sulfamethoxazole, and ingestion of fava beans.

Porphobilinogen deaminase (choice D) deficiency can lead to acute intermittent porphyria, with increased urine excretion of ALA and porphobilinogen resulting in a port-wine urine in some patients.

Pyruvate kinase (choice E) deficiency, an AR disease that affects glycolysis primarily in RBCs, would produce a chronic hemolytic anemia whose severity can be mild to life-threatening.
fa_subchapter: Heme synthesis, porphyrias, and lead poisoning

choice_explanations.B: Ceruloplasmin (a ferroxidase) (choice B) catalyzes the oxidation of ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+) iron.
choice_explanations.C: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice C) deficiency, an X-linked disease that affects the pentose phosphate pathway, results in episodic hemolysis triggered by infections, certain drugs, including primaquine and sulfamethoxazole, and ingestion of fava beans.
choice_explanations.D: Porphobilinogen deaminase (choice D) deficiency can lead to acute intermittent porphyria, with increased urine excretion of ALA and porphobilinogen resulting in a port-wine urine in some patients.
choice_explanations.E: Pyruvate kinase (choice E) deficiency, an AR disease that affects glycolysis primarily in RBCs, would produce a chronic hemolytic anemia whose severity can be mild to life-threatening.

fa_summary: Lead poisoning inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, causing microcytic hypochromic anemia.

stem: A 35-year-old man who is a marathon runner experiences cutaneous vasodilation to help cool his body while running on a hot summer day. Increased blood flow leads to the release of a chemical mediator from endothelial cells causing vasodilation in arterioles. Which of the following enzymes is directly activated by this chemical mediator?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Nitric oxide (NO) is a short-acting (about 100 msec) physiologic messenger that is released from endothelial cells. NO diffuses to a nearby smooth muscle cell, enters the cell, and activates soluble (cytosolic) guanylate cyclase. Guanylate cyclase makes the second messenger cGMP, which triggers smooth muscle relaxation by facilitating the dephosphorylation of myosin light chains. This prevents the interaction of myosin with actin. This is also the mechanism by which NO causes vasodilation in the corpus cavernosum of the penis, leading to penile erection.

Adenylate cyclase (choice A) is a plasma membrane-bound enzyme that is activated by ligand binding to a Gs protein-coupled receptor.

Heme oxygenase (choice C) is the enzyme that initiates the conversion of heme to bilirubin.

NO synthase (choice D) synthesizes NO from arginine.

Phospholipase C (choice E) cleaves phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate (PIP2) into diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol trisphosphate (IP3).

choice_explanations.A: Adenylate cyclase (choice A) is a plasma membrane-bound enzyme that is activated by ligand binding to a Gs protein-coupled receptor.
choice_explanations.C: Heme oxygenase (choice C) is the enzyme that initiates the conversion of heme to bilirubin.
choice_explanations.D: NO synthase (choice D) synthesizes NO from arginine.
choice_explanations.E: Phospholipase C (choice E) cleaves phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate (PIP2) into diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol trisphosphate (IP3).

fa_summary: Endothelial nitric oxide activates soluble guanylate cyclase, raising cGMP and relaxing vascular smooth muscle.

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of repeated shoulder dislocations. His mother states that the shoulder typically "pops back by itself." The patient appears short for his age. Physical examination shows a small jaw for head size, several bruises on the shins and elbows, and hyperextensible joints. Otherwise, he appears to be healthy. Which of the following is most likely deficient in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This boy presents with the symptoms consistent with the collagen disorder Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), including hyperextensible joints, frequent joint dislocations, and easy bruising. There are several different forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, many of which are due to mutations in the genes encoding collagen. However, one form, known as EDS type VI, is caused by a mutation in the gene that encodes the enzyme lysyl hydroxylase (Step 3 in collagen synthesis). Lysyl hydroxylase is responsible for the hydroxylation of lysine residues during the processing of collagen. Absence of hydroxylated lysines leads to defective collagen fiber synthesis, resulting in the clinical symptoms of hyperextensible joints, easy bruising, and frequent joint dislocations.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin (choice A) is a protein that inhibits the activity of the enzyme elastase. This patient does not have respiratory issues, so it is not likely that he is deficient in alpha-1-antitrypsin.

Ascorbic acid deficiency (choice B) is responsible for the disease scurvy.

In individuals with Menkes disease, a mutation has occurred in the ATP7A gene, which results in an ATP-dependent copper transporter deficiency (choice C).

Fibrillin (choice D) is a protein that polymerizes to form microfibrils. The microfibrils combine with elastin to form elastic fibers.

choice_explanations.A: Alpha-1 antitrypsin (choice A) is a protein that inhibits the activity of the enzyme elastase. This patient does not have respiratory issues, so it is not likely that he is deficient in alpha-1-antitrypsin.
choice_explanations.B: Ascorbic acid deficiency (choice B) is responsible for the disease scurvy.
choice_explanations.C: In individuals with Menkes disease, a mutation has occurred in the ATP7A gene, which results in an ATP-dependent copper transporter deficiency (choice C).
choice_explanations.D: Fibrillin (choice D) is a protein that polymerizes to form microfibrils. The microfibrils combine with elastin to form elastic fibers.

fa_summary: Ehlers-Danlos type VI is caused by lysyl hydroxylase deficiency, a collagen cross-linking defect.

stem: An investigator is measuring the activity of various enzymes involved in reactions of intermediary metabolism. The activity of one of the enzymes is greatly decreased compared to reference values. The buffer used for the enzyme assay contains sodium citrate. The activity of which of the following enzymes will most likely be directly affected by the use of citrate?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Citrate is produced by citrate synthase from acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate. This is a reaction of the mitochondrial citric acid cycle, but citrate can move freely from the mitochondria into the cytosol using the citrate shuttle. When the citric acid cycle slows down, citrate accumulates and enters into the cytosol. In the cytosol, it acts as a negative allosteric regulator of phosphofructokinase I (PFK-1), the enzyme that catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis. This prevents excess substrate from entering the cycle. Citrate is a positive allosteric effector of cytosolic acetyl CoA carboxylase, the rate-limiting and regulated enzyme of fatty acid synthesis.

Fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase (choice A) is an activity of the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2. It breaks down fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

Isocitrate dehydrogenase (choice B) converts isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate in the citric acid cycle. This reaction produces NADH and CO2.

Pyruvate carboxylase (choice D) is a mitochondrial enzyme that converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in a biotin and ATP-dependent reaction.

6-Phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (choice E) converts 6-phosphogluconate to ribulose 5-phosphate in the pentose phosphate shunt (pathway), and in the process reduces NADP+ to NADPH for biosynthesis (liver), for generating superoxide to kill bacteria (neutrophil) and for protecting erythrocyte membranes from oxidative damage and hemolysis.

choice_explanations.A: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase (choice A) is an activity of the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2. It breaks down fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.
choice_explanations.B: Isocitrate dehydrogenase (choice B) converts isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate in the citric acid cycle. This reaction produces NADH and CO2.
choice_explanations.D: Pyruvate carboxylase (choice D) is a mitochondrial enzyme that converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in a biotin and ATP-dependent reaction.
choice_explanations.E: 6-Phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (choice E) converts 6-phosphogluconate to ribulose 5-phosphate in the pentose phosphate shunt (pathway), and in the process reduces NADP+ to NADPH for biosynthesis (liver), for generating superoxide to kill bacteria (neutrophil) and for protecting erythrocyte membranes from oxidative damage and hemolysis.

fa_summary: Citrate is a negative allosteric regulator of phosphofructokinase-1 and a positive effector of acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

stem: A 27-year-old man completes a 10K race and drinks a 16-oz bottle of a sugar-containing drink. This drink transiently raises his blood glucose and triggers a release of insulin. The released insulin subsequently increases glucose absorption by skeletal muscle. Which of the following glucose transporters (GLUT) is most likely principally involved in this latter process?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. GLUT is an abbreviation for glucose transporter, and describes a family of sugar transporters with varying distribution and activity. GLUT 4 is found in fat, skeletal muscle, and heart muscle, and mediates insulin-stimulated glucose uptake. Insulin acts to translocate GLUT 4 to the plasma membrane. When this happens, more glucose is transported into tissues that express GLUT 4. GLUT 4 in skeletal and cardiac muscle is also stimulated by exercise through an insulin-independent pathway.

GLUT 1 (choice A) is found in red blood cells, brain microvessels, kidney, colon, and other cells. It is thought to be part of the blood-brain barrier and may limit glucose transport into the brain. GLUT 1 is not responsive to insulin levels.

GLUT 2 (choice B) is found in liver, pancreatic beta cells and the basolateral surface of the small intestine.

GLUT 3 (choice C) is found on neurons, placenta, and testes. This form of glucose transporter has a very high affinity for glucose.

GLUT 5 (choice E) is found in small intestine, testes and sperm; low levels are also found in kidney, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue.

choice_explanations.A: GLUT 1 (choice A) is found in red blood cells, brain microvessels, kidney, colon, and other cells. It is thought to be part of the blood-brain barrier and may limit glucose transport into the brain. GLUT 1 is not responsive to insulin levels.
choice_explanations.B: GLUT 2 (choice B) is found in liver, pancreatic beta cells and the basolateral surface of the small intestine.
choice_explanations.C: GLUT 3 (choice C) is found on neurons, placenta, and testes. This form of glucose transporter has a very high affinity for glucose.
choice_explanations.E: GLUT 5 (choice E) is found in small intestine, testes and sperm; low levels are also found in kidney, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue.

fa_summary: Insulin translocates GLUT4 to the plasma membrane of fat and skeletal/cardiac muscle, increasing glucose uptake.

stem: An otherwise healthy 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a swollen and extremely tender great toe. A review of his records shows that he has had 4 episodes of severe flank pain radiating to the groin over the past 5 months. Polarized light microscopy examination of synovial fluid from the great toe shows negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals. Which of the following conditions is most likely in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has gout, characterized by painful joints due to the precipitation of sodium urate crystals caused by either underexcretion (majority) or excessive production of uric acid (minority). Acute gouty arthritis is seen most commonly in males. The crystals, identified as negatively birefringent and needle-shaped, initiate neutrophil-mediated acute inflammation, often first affecting the big toe (although other joints such as the ankle, heel, and wrist can also be affected). Kidney disease is also seen due to accumulation of uric acid in the tubules, leading to repeated episodes of renal colic (severe flank pain radiating to the groin). Acute attacks are treated with colchicine or indomethacin to reduce the inflammation. Overproduction of uric acid and chronic gout are treated with allopurinol, which inhibits xanthine oxidase and can indirectly reduce purine synthesis through inhibition of PRPP-amidotransferase. Xanthine oxidase catalyzes the sequential oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine to uric acid.

A defect in urea synthesis (choice A) would result in the accumulation of ammonia.

A defect in pyrimidine synthesis (choice C) (UMP synthase deficiency) could cause deposition of orotic acid crystals, causing an orotic uropathy.

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (choice D) would show many of the same symptoms as gout.

Ethylene glycol poisoning (choice E) would produce a metabolic acidosis from an increase in glycolate, and deposition of calcium oxalate crystals.

choice_explanations.A: A defect in urea synthesis (choice A) would result in the accumulation of ammonia.
choice_explanations.C: A defect in pyrimidine synthesis (choice C) (UMP synthase deficiency) could cause deposition of orotic acid crystals, causing an orotic uropathy.
choice_explanations.D: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (choice D) would show many of the same symptoms as gout.
choice_explanations.E: Ethylene glycol poisoning (choice E) would produce a metabolic acidosis from an increase in glycolate, and deposition of calcium oxalate crystals.

fa_summary: Gout is caused by a defect in purine metabolism leading to monosodium urate crystal deposition.

stem: In a 28-year-old man, the left ventricle of the heart shows classic contraction band necrosis of the myocardium. Cocaine and its metabolites are detected in body fluids. Assuming that the cocaine intoxication contributed to the patient's death, which of the following enzymes was most likely increased in its activity in the patient's myocardial cells prior to his death?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine, resulting in tachycardia as well as excessive vasoconstriction of coronary vessels, leading to ischemia and infarction of heart tissue known as contraction band necrosis. Under these pathologic conditions, myocardial cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and therefore, glycolysis becomes the major source of ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase. Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, and its activity would therefore be increased.

Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice A) is an enzyme of glycolysis that produces 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, a substrate for the ATP-producing enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase. Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase is not a regulated enzyme of glycolysis and is not expected to increase in activity under hypoxic conditions or under a shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism.

Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (choice B) is a regulatory enzyme in gluconeogenesis, which is induced by cortisol, epinephrine, and glucagon. It functions in the hepatic synthesis of glucose when energy levels from beta-oxidation of fatty acids are adequate.

Pyruvate dehydrogenase (choice D) produces acetyl-CoA from pyruvate and coenzyme A, bridging glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. It requires 5 cofactors, including NAD and FAD, which would no longer be produced by the electron transport under hypoxic conditions, decreasing its activity.

Succinate dehydrogenase (choice E) is a key enzyme of the TCA cycle, producing a reduced equivalent of FAD to feed into the electron transport chain. It is also known as Complex II. The TCA cycle only functions if oxygen is in appropriate supply. The absence of oxygen leads to an accumulation of NADH and a subsequent decrease in the enzyme activities of the cycle.

choice_explanations.A: Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (choice A) is an enzyme of glycolysis that produces 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, a substrate for the ATP-producing enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase. Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase is not a regulated enzyme of glycolysis and is not expected to increase in activity under hypoxic conditions or under a shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism.
choice_explanations.B: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (choice B) is a regulatory enzyme in gluconeogenesis, which is induced by cortisol, epinephrine, and glucagon. It functions in the hepatic synthesis of glucose when energy levels from beta-oxidation of fatty acids are adequate.
choice_explanations.D: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (choice D) produces acetyl-CoA from pyruvate and coenzyme A, bridging glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. It requires 5 cofactors, including NAD and FAD, which would no longer be produced by the electron transport under hypoxic conditions, decreasing its activity.
choice_explanations.E: Succinate dehydrogenase (choice E) is a key enzyme of the TCA cycle, producing a reduced equivalent of FAD to feed into the electron transport chain. It is also known as Complex II. The TCA cycle only functions if oxygen is in appropriate supply. The absence of oxygen leads to an accumulation of NADH and a subsequent decrease in the enzyme activities of the cycle.

fa_summary: Anaerobic metabolism from cocaine-induced cardiac ischemia increases phosphofructokinase-1 activity.

stem: A standard urine test used to detect cocaine has a sensitivity of 97%, a specificity of 4%, a positive predictive value of 90%, and a negative predictive value of 95%. Recent data suggest that the use of cocaine in all age groups has declined since the screening test properties were determined. A decline in cocaine usage will most likely have which of the following impacts on the results of this screening test?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This question provides a lot of numbers to ask a simple question: What happens to screening test values when prevalence declines? The numbers given are a distraction, and are not needed to answer this question.

As prevalence declines, sensitivity and specificity are unchanged. On the other hand, a decline in prevalence will increase negative predictive value (NPV) and decrease positive predictive value (PPV). With NPV, the inverse relationship exists with prevalence because as the number of patients with the disease changes so will the number of TN's and FN's. This is true because predictive value is a function of the properties of the screening test in conjunction with the disease prevalence in the population.

Positive predictive value (PPV) and NPV are affected by prevalence, while sensitivity and specificity are not. An increase in the prevalence increases the PPV and decreases the NPV, and vice versa.

NPV is the probability that a person with a negative test is a true negative (TN). The probability that a person with a negative test is a true negative (person does not have the disease) is referred to as the "predictive value of a negative test". The NPV measures only the distribution of persons who receive a negative test result. It can be calculated as follows: NPV = TN/(TN + FN). (FN, false negative)

This table summarizes the relationship between screening test results. NOTE: The NPV uses the data from the bottom row of the following 2 X 2 table.

[2X2 table: disease present/absent vs test positive/negative; row/column totals TP+FN, TN+FP, and grand total TP+TN+FP+FN]
TP = True Positive, FP = False Positive, FN = False Negative, TN = True Negative

choice_explanations.A: Sensitivity is a property of the test and is unchanged when prevalence declines.
choice_explanations.B: Specificity is a property of the test and is unchanged when prevalence declines.
choice_explanations.C: A decline in prevalence increases the negative predictive value (the probability that a person with a negative test is a true negative) (the correct answer).
choice_explanations.D: A decline in prevalence decreases, not increases, the positive predictive value.
choice_explanations.E: Sensitivity is unchanged when prevalence declines.
choice_explanations.F: Specificity is unchanged when prevalence declines.

fa_summary: When disease prevalence declines, sensitivity and specificity are unchanged, but NPV increases and PPV decreases.

stem: The American Diabetes Association (ADA) lowered the cutoff value for fasting blood glucose used in diagnosing diabetes mellitus from two or more fasting glucose levels of >/= 140 mg/dL to >/= 126 mg/dL. This reference interval change is most likely to produce which of the following alterations?

options.text: Increase the test's false negative rate
Increase the test's negative predictive value
Increase the test's positive predictive value

explanation:
The correct answer is C. This question evaluates the use of a screening test, which is used to identify people that are healthy vs. diseased. Changing the reference interval of a test alters its sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV, PV+), and negative predictive value (NPV, PV-).

The negative predictive value of a test (NPV or PV-) refers to the probability that a negative test result is a true negative (TN) rather than a false negative (FN). It is expressed by the following formula:
NPV = TN/(TN + FN)
Note: Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN)
- TN = true negative, healthy person with a normal test result
- FN = false negative, diseased person with a normal test result
- TP = true positive, an abnormal test result in an individual with disease
- FP = false positive, an abnormal test result in a healthy person
- Negative predictive value = TN/(TN + FN)

Let's say that we are changing our cutoff from Line C (140 mg/dL) to Line B (126 mg/dL) in the graph below. From Line B, looking to the right, we do a much better job at labeling all of the diseased people. Therefore, we have really good sensitivity, TP/(TP+FN). Sensitivity is the probability of correctly identifying a case of disease. If you look to the left of line B, there are only healthy people. This means that the negative predictive value (NPV; the probability of no disease in a patient who receives a negative test result) is excellent.

At line C, we are doing a pretty good job at identifying healthy people, but there are some diseased people on the left of line C. Therefore my NPV at line C is not as good as with line B.

Note that NPV is directly related to sensitivity. Many people make the connection of sensitivity to positive predictive value (PPV) because they share a common numerator (TP). Similarly, people often relate specificity to NPV because their common numerator is TN, but this is not the correct way to look at it. The key in these ratios are the denominators. Since sensitivity and NPV both have FN in their denominator, when the FN falls to 0, we have perfect sensitivity and perfect NPV. In the same way, when FP falls to 0, we have perfect specificity and perfect PPV.

Lowering of the clinical cutoff for disease lowers the diagnostic threshold and increases the test's sensitivity, which will decrease the false negatives.

The test's sensitivity is increased rather than decreased (choice A) by decreasing our cutoff. Because the diagnostic blood glucose level was lowered, the test is more likely to diagnose patients with diabetes. However, if the diagnostic glucose level was increased above 140 mg/dL, then the test's sensitivity would be decreased.

Since the test's sensitivity is increased, the FN rate at the new reference level is decreased (choice B).

The positive predictive value of a test reflects the probability that an abnormal test result represents a TP rather than a FP. The test's positive predictive value (choice D) decreases, since the test's specificity, which ultimately determines its FP rate, decreases as the test's sensitivity increases. Stated another way, a greater number of normal individuals will have FP fasting glucose levels when the test's upper limit is decreased to 126 mg/dL.

A test's sensitivity is inversely related to its specificity (the probability of correctly identifying disease-free people). Changing the reference interval of a test to increase its sensitivity automatically lowers its specificity (choice E), since the number of FPs will increase. Similarly, when altering a reference interval to increase a test's specificity, its sensitivity is reduced because of an increase in the number of FNs.

In summary, lowering a test's upper limit of normal increases the test's sensitivity, which decreases the FN rate, and increases the NPV. Increasing the test's sensitivity also decreases the test's specificity. Decreasing a test's specificity increases the FP rate and decreases the PPV.

choice_explanations.A: Sensitivity is increased, not decreased, by lowering the cutoff; a higher cutoff above 140 mg/dL would decrease sensitivity.
choice_explanations.B: Since sensitivity increases, the false negative rate is decreased, not increased.
choice_explanations.C: Lowering the cutoff increases sensitivity, which decreases false negatives and increases the negative predictive value (the correct answer).
choice_explanations.D: The positive predictive value decreases, because specificity (which determines the FP rate) decreases as sensitivity increases.
choice_explanations.E: Specificity decreases (not increases) when sensitivity is increased by lowering the cutoff.

fa_summary: Lowering a test's cutoff increases sensitivity, decreases false negatives, and increases the negative predictive value.

stem: In a city with a population of 1 million, 10,000 individuals have AIDS. There are 1,000 new cases of AIDS and 200 deaths each year from the disease. There are 2,500 deaths per year from all causes. Assuming no net emigration from or immigration to the city, the incidence of AIDS in this city is given by which of the following expressions?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The incidence of a disease is given by the number of new cases in a given period divided by the total susceptible population.
Incidence Rate = # new cases / # of people at risk

In this case, this is equal to 1,000 (# of new cases) / 990,000 (# of people at risk). There are 990,000 people at risk out of 1 million total people. Remember that the 10,000 people that have the disease are no longer at risk for contracting it; therefore, this number is subtracted from 1 million to get 990,000.
Incidence Rate: rate of new cases occurring in a population over a given time period.
Incidence = number of new events in a period / number of people at risk.

Although on average, the number of AIDS patients increases only by 800 (1,000 new cases minus 200 deaths), the term "incidence" does not take the number of deaths into consideration. Therefore, the incidence is not 800/990,000 (choice A).

The rate of increase of a disease is given by the number of new cases per year minus the number of deaths (or cures) per year, divided by the total population. Since there is (as yet) no cure for AIDS, the number of cures is zero. In this case, the rate of increase is (1,000 - 200)/1,000,000 = 800/1,000,000 (choice B).

The incidence of a disease is the number of new cases divided by the total susceptible population. Since the 10,000 AIDS patients are already affected, the total susceptible population is 990,000, not 1,000,000. Hence, the incidence cannot be 1,000/1,000,000 (choice D).

The crude mortality rate is given by the number of deaths from all causes divided by the population; in this case, 2,500/1,000,000 (choice E).

Prevalence Rate: all persons who experience a disease or event in a population. Prevalence = all cases of disease at a given period / total population. Prevalence = Incidence x Duration.

choice_explanations.A: 800/990,000 ignores that incidence counts new cases (1,000), not the net increase after deaths.
choice_explanations.B: 800/1,000,000 is the rate of increase of the disease (new cases minus deaths over total population), not the incidence.
choice_explanations.C: 1,000/990,000 = new cases divided by the susceptible population (the correct answer).
choice_explanations.D: 1,000/1,000,000 wrongly uses the total population; the 10,000 already-affected are no longer at risk (susceptible = 990,000).
choice_explanations.E: 2,500/1,000,000 is the crude mortality rate (all-cause deaths over total population).

fa_summary: Incidence = new cases in a period / population at risk (subtract those already diseased from the denominator).

stem: A study is conducted to determine the efficacy of a new drug in preventing hospitalization of patients from HIV-related pneumonia. Medical records from participating physicians are used to select one group of patients who received the drug in the year preceding the observation period (Group A), and a second group of patients who had not received the drug in the preceding year (Group B). Both groups are followed for a 3-year period to determine the number of hospitalizations and the number of deaths from all causes. The number of hospitalizations for Group A was lower (p = 0.001) than for the control group. However, the mortality rate from all causes was found to be higher (p = 0.01) in Group A. Based on these results, the researchers conclude that the drug should not be used. This conclusion is most likely invalid because of which of the following scenarios?

options.text: Expectations of the researchers affected the outcome of the study
Knowledge about whether patients had taken the drug or not biased the measurement of the outcome variables
Patients who received the new drug may be less healthy than those who did not
Subjects fail to accurately recall events in the past
The existence of a Hawthorne effect

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Because all patients enrolled in the study came from the records of the same physicians, whether or not the patients received the new drug depended on the assessment and treatment decisions made by each physician. It is very likely that those patients to whom the physicians administered the new drug were different than those for whom they prescribed some alternative. In other words, this is a type of selection bias where the sample selected (those who received the new drug) is not representative of the general HIV/AIDS population. In this question, one likely difference is that patients who received the new drug were "sicker" and that this alone caused the physicians to use the new drug. The higher mortality rate in the group who received the drug supports this possibility. Failing to control for disease severity in patients in different treatment arms of a study is a major confounding element in this type of research.

Selection or sampling bias is the most common type of bias associated with cohort study designs in which the sample is not representative of the population. Failure to control for disease severity in patients in different arms of the treatment during sample selection can distort the results of the study.

Experimenter expectancy or Pygmalion effect is where the experimenter's expectations or beliefs affect the results of the study (choice A). For example, the researcher's expectations are inadvertently communicated to subjects, who then produce the desired effects. This type of bias can be averted by using a double-blind design, where neither the subject nor the investigators know which group receives the intervention or is in the control group.

For choice B to be true, it would have to be argued that patients' knowing which arm of the study they were in made them more likely to go to the hospital or to die. The outcome variables used here are clean, easily measured, and unlikely to be changed due to knowledge of which study group the patients were in.

Choice D is incorrect. Recall bias is where subjects fail to accurately recall events in the past. Since this study is based on a review of medical records, a patient's memory of past events is not relevant.

The most common type of measurement bias is the Hawthorne effect. The Hawthorne effect (choice E) states that people act differently when they know they are being watched or measured. As noted in the discussion of choice B, this is unlikely in this case. Also, the existence of a control group, as in this case, offers a simple solution to the Hawthorne effect. Participants in both the treatment and the control group know they are being watched, so this factor will not contaminate any comparison between the two groups.

Lead-time bias (choice F) gives a false estimate of survival rates. For example, patients seem to live longer with the disease after it is uncovered by a screening test. However, there is no actual increase in survival. When the disease is discovered sooner, patients who are diagnosed earlier only "seem" to live longer.

choice_explanations.A: Experimenter expectancy (Pygmalion effect) is where the experimenter's expectations or beliefs affect the results; it can be averted with a double-blind design.
choice_explanations.B: Patients' knowledge of their study arm is unlikely to change these clean, easily measured outcome variables (hospitalization and death).
choice_explanations.C: Selection (sampling) bias: patients who received the new drug may have been sicker, so the groups are not comparable (the correct answer).
choice_explanations.D: Recall bias (subjects failing to accurately recall past events) is not relevant, since the study is based on a review of medical records.
choice_explanations.E: The Hawthorne effect (people act differently when watched) is unlikely here, and a control group offers a simple solution to it.
choice_explanations.F: Lead-time bias produces a false estimate of survival after screening; it is not relevant to this study design.

fa_summary: Selection (sampling) bias occurs when the study sample is not representative of the population, e.g., failing to control for disease severity.

stem: A neuronal cell line shows normal morphology and axonal extension, but has abnormalities in fast anterograde axonal transport caused by a defect in the movement of secretory vesicles from the Golgi to the plasma membrane. The defect is caused by mutation in a single gene. Retrograde axonal transport and endocytosis are within normal limits. Which of the following cytoskeletal proteins is most likely deficient in this cell line?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The movement of vesicles within cells is predominantly due to motor proteins carrying those vesicles along microtubules. Microtubules are arranged throughout the cell with their (-) ends near the centrosome (MTOC) and their (+) ends radiating outward. Therefore, movement from the Golgi apparatus to the plasma membrane and from the cell body to the end of the axon are both movements toward the (+) ends of microtubules. The great majority of kinesins are (+)-directed microtubule motor proteins. Remember, kinesins are involved in anterograde transport and dyneins are involved in retrograde transport.

Deficient actin (choice A) would prevent normal microfilament formation or function. Although this function is not involved in axonal transport or secretion, it would probably interfere with axonal extension, which relies on rapid microfilament polymerization.

Dyneins (choice B) are (-)-directed microtubule motor proteins. They function in retrograde transport.

Myosins (choice D) are all (+)-directed microfilament proteins.

Deficient tubulin (choice E) would interfere with the microtubule structure, which would interfere with normal neuron morphology and with both retrograde and anterograde vesicle movements.

Also note that intermediate filaments serve primarily a structural role within cells. They have different proteins attached to them, depending on the cell tissue type.

Comparison of cytoskeletal proteins: Actin—monomeric units that comprise microfilaments; Myosin—microfilament proteins that are directed toward the (+) end of the filament; Tubulin—monomeric units that comprise microtubules; kinesin—motor protein that moves cargo toward the (+) end of the microtubule (anterograde); Dynein—motor protein that moves cargo toward the (-) end of the microtubule (retrograde).

choice_explanations.A: Deficient actin would prevent normal microfilament formation or function; this is not involved in axonal transport or secretion but would interfere with axonal extension, which relies on rapid microfilament polymerization.
choice_explanations.B: Dyneins are (-)-directed microtubule motor proteins that function in retrograde transport.
choice_explanations.C: Kinesins are (+)-directed microtubule motor proteins that mediate anterograde transport from the Golgi to the plasma membrane and from the cell body to the axon terminal.
choice_explanations.D: Myosins are (+)-directed microfilament proteins.
choice_explanations.E: Deficient tubulin would interfere with microtubule structure and with both retrograde and anterograde vesicle movements.

fa_summary: Kinesin is the (+)-directed microtubule motor protein that mediates anterograde axonal transport; dynein mediates retrograde transport.

stem: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of pain in his calves and his knees. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 87/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows multiple yellow painful nodules on his calves and knees. His total serum cholesterol is 590 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol is 593 mg/dL, triglyceride level is 200 mg/dL, and HDL cholesterol is 57 mg/dL. Family history shows that his father died of a myocardial infarction at the age of 40. Which of the following cellular processes is most likely responsible for this boy's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The patient described in this case has all of the hallmarks of an individual with familial hypercholesterolemia, including xanthomas on his knees, described as “nodules”, and a very high serum cholesterol reading. Familial hypercholesterolemia is due to a mutation in the LDL receptor, which is a membrane protein found on the surface of cells that allows for the absorption of cholesterol. Normally, upon the binding of cholesterol molecules to the LDL receptor, a process called receptor-mediated endocytosis results in the internalization of the receptor-cholesterol complexes. Inside the cell, these complexes are sent to the lysosome, where the acidic environment causes the release of the cholesterol molecules from the receptors, making the free cholesterol available to the cell. In individuals with this disease, a mutation has occurred in the gene encoding the LDL receptor that results in the loss of functional receptors on the cell surface. The inability of the cells to absorb the cholesterol results in a dramatic accumulation of cholesterol in the blood, where it becomes deposited in certain areas of the body, most commonly on the knees, forming nodules called xanthomas. Cholesterol may also deposit in the arteries, leading to atherosclerosis and premature onset of cardiovascular disease, as seen in this patient's father. The typical laboratory pattern is an elevated total cholesterol, elevated LDL cholesterol, with normal HDL and triglyceride levels.

HMG-CoA reductase (choice A) is the enzyme responsible for the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonic acid, which is a key step in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway. Loss of HMG-CoA reductase activity would result in a lowering of cholesterol levels, the opposite of what we see in this patient. The family of cholesterol-lowering drugs known as statins work by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase and, effectively, lowering serum cholesterol levels in patients.

Lysosome-mediated proteolysis (choice B) is incorrect because the function of the lysosome is not affected by familial hypercholesterolemia. There are some diseases, however, that do occur as a result of the loss of lysosome function. These are known as lysosomal storage diseases and include Tay-Sachs and Gaucher disease, and are characterized by the accumulation of cellular components that would normally be degraded by the lysosome.

N-linked glycosylation (choice C) is a form of post-translational modification to proteins that is performed by enzymes present in the endoplasmic reticulum. Typically, these modifications are used to determine the ultimate destination of that protein. I-cell disease is caused by a deficiency in GlcNAc phosphotransferase, which phosphorylates mannose residues to mannose-6-phosphate on N-linked glycoproteins, such as some lysosomal enzymes. These modifications are necessary for enzymes to be sent to the lysosome, and individuals with this disease lack lysosomal function and have symptoms similar to those of other lysosomal storage diseases.

Loss of proteasome activity (choice D) would result in the accumulation of proteins that are marked for degradation. In familial hypercholesterolemia, the LDL receptor is not folded properly, and is marked for degradation in the proteasome. Therefore, a loss of proteasome activity would result in an accumulation of mis-folded LDL receptor protein, which is not seen in familial hypercholesterolemia.

Familial hypercholesterolemia is characterized by high serum cholesterol levels and the formation of cholesterol deposits in the skin and atherosclerosis. Absorption of serum cholesterol requires the binding of cholesterol molecules to LDL receptors on the surface of cells, followed by internalization through a process called receptor-mediated endocytosis.

choice_explanations.A: HMG-CoA reductase converts HMG-CoA to mevalonic acid in cholesterol biosynthesis; loss of its activity would lower cholesterol, the opposite of this patient. Statins inhibit this enzyme.
choice_explanations.B: Lysosome function is not affected by familial hypercholesterolemia; lysosomal storage diseases (eg, Tay-Sachs, Gaucher) arise from loss of lysosome function.
choice_explanations.C: N-linked glycosylation occurs in the ER; a GlcNAc phosphotransferase deficiency (I-cell disease) impairs mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal enzymes.
choice_explanations.D: Loss of proteasome activity would cause accumulation of misfolded LDL receptor, which is not seen in familial hypercholesterolemia.
choice_explanations.E: Familial hypercholesterolemia is caused by a mutation in the LDL receptor, impairing receptor-mediated endocytosis and absorption of cholesterol, leading to xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis.

fa_summary: LDL delivers hepatic cholesterol to peripheral tissues and is taken up via receptor-mediated endocytosis; LDL-receptor mutations cause familial hypercholesterolemia.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of low grade fever, fatigue, and paroxysmal cough. His mother reports that he had a cold for about a week, but his coughing spells have become much more severe lately, sometimes causing him to vomit. His temperature is 37.7°C (99.8°F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pharyngeal erythema, post nasal drip, mildly enlarged tonsils, and soft palpable cervical lymph nodes. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Cultures from a nasopharyngeal swab reveal a gram negative, aerobic, encapsulated coccobacillus. The toxin from these bacteria is most likely causing which of the following effects on his cells?

options.text: Decreased activity of protein kinase A

explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has the classic clinical signs of a Bordetella pertussis infection, commonly referred to as whooping cough. Early symptoms of this illness are similar to those of the common cold, including mild cough, runny nose, and sneezing. However, approximately two weeks following initial infection, frequent, violent coughing spells develop, which may be followed by fainting or vomiting. Bordetella pertussis releases an AB5-type exotoxin known as pertussis toxin (PT). Inside the cell, this toxin is responsible for the ADP-ribosylation of the Gαi subunit of the heterotrimeric G protein complex. The ADP-ribosylation prevents the Gαi from inhibiting adenylyl cyclase, thus resulting in increased levels of cAMP in the cell.

PI3 kinase (choice A) is an enzyme that is responsible for the phosphorylation and conversion of the phosphatidylinositol PIP2 to PIP3. Through activation of the downstream components AKT and mTOR, this enzyme is a key modulator of cellular proliferation and survival. PI3 kinase is not a target of the pertussis toxin.

A decrease in the activity of adenylyl cyclase (choice B) would occur as a result of the activation of the Gαi subunit. Active Gαi normally functions to inhibit adenylyl cyclase activity, preventing the production of cAMP. Since the pertussis toxin inhibits Gαi activity, there would not be a decrease in cAMP but rather an increase in cAMP.

Decreased activity of protein kinase A (PKA) (choice C) would not be expected in this patient because PKA is activated by cAMP, resulting in an increase in cAMP levels inside the cell. A decrease in this enzyme's activity would be associated with inhibition of adenylyl cyclase. Since pertussis toxin prevents the inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, resulting in an increase in cAMP, higher activity of PKA would be expected.

An increase in IP3 levels (choice E) is associated with the activity of the Gαq subunit-associated heterotrimeric G protein complex. When active, the Gαq subunit activates phospholipase C. Phospholipase C then cleaves the phosphatidylinositol PIP2 to form IP3 and diacylglycerol (DAG), two second messengers that are responsible for release of calcium from intracellular stores and activating protein kinase C (PKC) as well as other intracellular kinases, respectively. This pathway is not affected by pertussis toxin.

Bordetella pertussis infection, commonly referred to as whooping cough, is characterized by early symptoms of the common cold, followed by frequent, violent coughing spells, which may be followed by fainting or vomiting. The responsible agent is an exotoxin called pertussis toxin, which ADP-ribosylates the Gαi subunit of the heterotrimeric G protein complex, resulting in an increase in cAMP levels inside the cell.

choice_explanations.A: PI3 kinase phosphorylates PIP2 to PIP3 and modulates proliferation/survival via AKT and mTOR; it is not a target of pertussis toxin.
choice_explanations.B: Decreased adenylyl cyclase activity would result from Gαi activation; pertussis toxin instead inhibits Gαi, increasing cAMP.
choice_explanations.C: PKA is activated by cAMP; since pertussis toxin raises cAMP, higher (not decreased) PKA activity is expected.
choice_explanations.D: Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gαi subunit, preventing it from inhibiting adenylyl cyclase and thus increasing cAMP levels.
choice_explanations.E: Increased IP3 results from Gαq-mediated phospholipase C activation, a pathway not affected by pertussis toxin.

fa_summary: Pertussis toxin (Bordetella pertussis) ADP-ribosylates the Gαi subunit, preventing inhibition of adenylate cyclase and increasing cAMP.

stem: A 5-year-old child is brought to the physician for a routine examination. Physical examination shows “gargoyle facies,” hepatomegaly, and multiple skeletal, cardiac, and central nervous system abnormalities. Laboratory studies show elevated levels of various proteases, glycosylases, and lipases. The biochemical basis of the disease is an inability of an enzyme to phosphorylate mannose residues present on other enzymes. In which of the following organelles does this step normally occur?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The disease is I-cell disease, a rare genetic disease that may receive disproportionate attention both because it is a mucolipidosis (a disorder with features that overlap the mucopolysaccharidoses and sphingolipidoses) characterized by the accumulation of “undigested” material in lysosomes, and because the biochemical basis illustrates an interesting mechanism for protein targeting. Specifically, the Golgi apparatus in cells of these patients has an abnormal phosphotransferase (UDP-N-acetylglucosamine: N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase) and is not able to phosphorylate (at carbon 6) mannose residues in an oligosaccharide on N-glycosylated enzymes destined to enter lysosomes. As a result of the absence of this mannose 6-phosphate marker, proteins that should function as lysosomal acid hydrolases are excreted from the body, and the molecules they should have degraded accumulate and form inclusions within the lysosomes. I-cell disease is, then, a defect in protein targeting. Presentation includes coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly, and failure to thrive. There currently is no cure.

Endoplasmic reticulum (choice A) receives the growing peptide chain of the enzymes but is not the site of addition of recognition markers.

Lysosomes (choice C) are the normal destination for the enzymes with the mannose 6-phosphate marker but do not receive them if the marker is not present.

Mitochondria (choice D) supply ATP, the ultimate source of the phosphate in the reaction.

Ribosomes (choice E) are the site of synthesis of the amino acid chains of proteins but not the site of addition of the destination marker.

Abnormal phosphotransferase (UDP-N-acetylglucosamine: N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase) in the Golgi apparatus is not able to phosphorylate (at carbon 6) mannose residues on N-glycosylated enzymes destined to enter lysosomes (the enzymes are secreted into the circulation and urine instead). Presentation includes coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly; there is currently no cure.

choice_explanations.A: The ER receives the growing peptide chain but is not the site of addition of the mannose-6-phosphate recognition marker.
choice_explanations.B: In I-cell disease the Golgi phosphotransferase (UDP-N-acetylglucosamine: N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase) fails to phosphorylate mannose residues on N-glycosylated enzymes destined for lysosomes.
choice_explanations.C: Lysosomes are the normal destination of mannose-6-phosphate-tagged enzymes but do not receive them if the marker is absent.
choice_explanations.D: Mitochondria supply ATP, the ultimate source of the phosphate in the reaction.
choice_explanations.E: Ribosomes synthesize the amino acid chains of proteins but do not add the destination marker.

fa_summary: Mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal enzymes occurs in the Golgi; its failure causes I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II).

stem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 32 weeks’ gestation comes to the physician because of fever, headache, and painful genital lesions. Physical examination shows two vesicular lesions on the labia and one similar cervical lesion. The physician explains that she should consider cesarean section prior to rupture of her membranes. Which of the following best describes the form of axonal transport that contributes to infection with this organism?

options.text: Transport moves proteins to the axon terminal
Transport moves vesicles to the axon terminal

explanation:
The correct answer is B. This woman has evidence of a primary herpes simplex infection with active lesions, just prior to labor and delivery. This is an indication for treatment with acyclovir and for elective cesarean section. This therapy affords the best chance of minimizing the intrapartum infection of the baby. The soma (cell body) of the neuron, with its many dendrites, resides in the central nervous system. Each neuron has a primary axon, beginning at the cell body and extending peripherally. The axon is covered with a myelin sheath. Axons use anterograde and retrograde axonal transport to move subcellular elements toward or away from the axon terminal. Retrograde transport uses microtubules, is mediated by dynein, and transports lysosomes and recycled membrane. Herpesvirus, poliovirus, rabies virus, and tetanus toxin are examples of exogenous substances that affect neuron cell bodies as a result of retrograde axonal transport.

Anterograde transport (choice A) uses microtubules, is mediated by kinesin (choice C), and moves vesicles (choice E) and proteins (choice D) to the axon terminal.

Herpesvirus, poliovirus, rabies virus, and tetanus toxin use retrograde transport to cause disease through retrograde transport along the microtubules of the axon.

choice_explanations.A: Anterograde transport uses microtubules and kinesin, moving vesicles and proteins to the axon terminal; herpesvirus travels via retrograde transport, not anterograde.
choice_explanations.B: Retrograde transport uses microtubules and is mediated by dynein; herpesvirus, poliovirus, rabies virus, and tetanus toxin reach the neuron cell body this way.
choice_explanations.C: Kinesin mediates anterograde transport.
choice_explanations.D: Transport of proteins to the axon terminal is anterograde.
choice_explanations.E: Transport of vesicles to the axon terminal is anterograde.

fa_summary: Retrograde axonal transport is mediated by dynein; herpesvirus, poliovirus, rabies virus, and tetanus toxin use it to reach the neuron cell body.

stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of large, fluid-filled blisters on his lower abdomen and upper thighs. He states that the lesions are itchy and denies recent travel or use of new soaps or detergent. His temperature is 37.6°C (99.6°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 132/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows several intact tense vesicular lesions that do not slip away or rupture when rubbed. The oral mucosa is normal and uninvolved. Microscopic examination of skin biopsies from these regions shows extensive separation of the epidermis from the underlying basal lamina. Blood tests show the presence of antibodies against dystonin. Which of the following cellular structures is most likely disrupted in his skin cells?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Hemidesmosomes are a type of membrane junction found on the basal surface of epithelial cells that connects the cells to the underlying basal lamina. They consist of the proteins dystonin and plectin, which form a plaque on the intracellular side of the plasma membrane. This plaque binds to the keratin filaments inside the cell and connects these cytoskeletal components to the extracellular matrix of the basal lamina via integrin molecules. In individuals with the autoimmune disease bullous pemphigoid, such as this patient, antibodies are made that bind to dystonin (bullous pemphigoid antigen) and disrupt the hemidesmosome structure. As a result, the epithelial sheet of skin separates from the basal lamina, allowing for accumulation of fluid in this space and resulting in the formation of tense subepidermal blisters. Nikolsky sign is negative.

Adherens junctions (choice A) are transmembrane structures found on the lateral surface of epithelial cells. The intracellular part of these structures connects to the actin filaments inside the cell. The extracellular domain contains cadherins, such as E-cadherin, which are responsible for homotypic, calcium-dependent, adhesive interactions with the cadherins of adherens junctions on adjacent cells. Adherens junctions are an important part of the link between adjacent epithelial cells.

Pemphigus foliaceus and pemphigus vulgaris, two other types of autoimmune disease, are associated with disruption of desmosomes (choice B). In these diseases, antibodies are made that recognize proteins that are components of the desmosome, desmoglein-1 and desmoglein-3, respectively. Because the desmosome is responsible for connecting the lateral surfaces of two adjacent cells together, a space between the cells develops when this structure is disrupted. This leads to accumulation of fluid between cells, resulting in the formation of flaccid intraepidermal blisters. Pemphigus vulgaris has oral mucous membrane involvement. The fact that dystonin-specific antibodies were found in the patient eliminates the possibility that desmosomes are disrupted in this patient.

Gap junctions (choice C) are channels formed through the alignment of connexon complexes in the plasma membrane of adjacent cells. The connexon complexes are composed of protein subunits called connexins. The function of gap junctions is to connect the cytoplasm of the two cells, allowing for communication via movement of soluble molecules from one cell to the other.

Tight junctions (choice E) are areas along the lateral surface of two adjacent epithelial cells that form a seal, preventing movement of molecules in between the cells. These structures are composed of a branching network of sealing strands made up of claudin and occludin proteins.

Antibodies against the hemidesmosome component dystonin (bullous pemphigoid antigen) disrupt the connection between the epithelium and the basal lamina, leading to formation of tense subepidermal blisters.

choice_explanations.A: Adherens junctions lie on the lateral surface and link actin filaments via cadherins (eg, E-cadherin) between adjacent cells; they are not the target in bullous pemphigoid.
choice_explanations.B: Desmosomes link keratin filaments of adjacent cells; autoantibodies to desmoglein-1/3 cause pemphigus foliaceus/vulgaris with flaccid blisters, not this dystonin-mediated picture.
choice_explanations.C: Gap junctions are connexon channels that connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells for communication.
choice_explanations.D: Hemidesmosomes connect keratin in basal cells to the basal lamina via dystonin/plectin and integrins; antibodies against dystonin (bullous pemphigoid) disrupt them, causing tense subepidermal blisters with a negative Nikolsky sign.
choice_explanations.E: Tight junctions form a seal via claudins and occludins, preventing paracellular movement.

fa_summary: Hemidesmosomes connect basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane; autoantibodies to dystonin cause bullous pemphigoid.

stem: A pediatrician is caring for two 12-year-old boys with muscular dystrophy (MD). Patient #1 has been wheelchair-bound since the age of 9 years, and Patient #2 is still ambulatory, with the help of canes. In both cases, the initial symptoms started with progressive weakness in the lower limbs, and both family histories show that the disease was transmitted in an X-linked recessive manner. Each boy had a maternal uncle who died early from complications of the disease. Patient #1's uncle died at the age of 19 years and Patient #2's uncle died at the age of 45 years. Which of the following is most likely affected in both of these patients?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The symptoms described indicate that Patient #1 suffers from Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), whereas Patient #2 has Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD). Both diseases are caused by mutations in the gene coding for dystrophin, a 427-kDa protein with a flexible, rod-like structure having globular structures at either end. In short, dystrophin is a cytoskeletal protein that plays a critical role in maintaining muscle fiber integrity; when it is absent or nonfunctional, the myofibril literally falls apart. DMD is caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene that significantly disrupt large segments; these mutations often are associated with frame-shift induced deletions or with other mutations that disrupt critical structural elements, usually in the actin-binding head of the molecule. BMD is generally caused by point mutations that permit residual function of the dystrophin molecule. As a result of these mutations, typically DMD is severe with less than 5% of normal dystrophin levels present, whereas BMD is a milder form and has 30-80% retained dystrophin function. Clinically, DMD and BMD can have proximal muscle weakness, presence of Gowers sign (climbing up the leg as they get up from sitting to standing position), hypertrophic calves, and elevated creatine phosphokinase levels (CPK, CK-MM). Patients can die from progression to dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure (diaphragm is affected).

Lysosome (choice B) storage diseases such as Tay-Sachs disease and Niemann-Pick disease can present with progressive neurodegeneration, hypotonia, and failure to thrive within the first year of life. These conditions are inherited via autosomal recessive trait and are not associated with skeletal muscle defects. Tay-Sachs disease is associated with the absence/defect of the alpha subunit of Hex A enzyme, resulting in accumulation of GM2 gangliosides within the lysosomes of neuronal and retinal cells. Niemann-Pick disease is a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme sphingomyelinase, resulting in accumulation of sphingomyelin in the monocyte-macrophage system (causes hepatosplenomegaly, recurrent respiratory infections). NOTE: Both conditions can have a “cherry-red” macula due to pallor of the retina from cellular lipid accumulation.

Mitochondrial (choice C) myopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke (MELAS) is a rare progressive neurodegenerative disorder that is either sporadic in origin or transmitted maternally via mitochondrial inheritance. Recall that the mitochondria has a key function in oxidative phosphorylation. Thus, multisystemic dysfunction in patients with MELAS due to oxidative phosphorylation dysfunction occurs. Patients can present in childhood age with seizures, stroke-like episodes, hearing loss, short stature, endocrine disorders, and exercise intolerance. Repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrates decrement over time.

Neuromuscular junction (choice D) can be affected in myasthenia gravis (MG) or Lambert-Eaton syndrome (LEMS). Both conditions can present with muscle weakness. MG is an autoimmune disorder that affects females, peak age in the 30s, and is associated with antibodies against the acetylcholine nicotinic postsynaptic receptors at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of the skeletal muscle. MG patients present with weakness of extra-ocular muscles, ptosis, and limb weakness that increases with exertion and are alleviated with rest. The ice pack test (placing ice over the eyelids) improves neuromuscular transmission and ptosis. Tensilon (edrophonium) test blocks the acetylcholinesterase enzyme and prolongs acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, thus improving symptoms. LEMS is associated with antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels, disrupting ACh release at the NMJ. The initial presentation may be similar to MG, but later has progressive proximal extremity weakness and autonomic dysfunction. Edrophonium test does not show muscle strength improvement in LEMS. Unlike MG, weakness improves temporarily upon exertion.

Protein kinase (choice E) mutation can be seen with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (myotonic dystrophy protein kinase; DMPK). It is an autosomal dominant pattern CTG trinucleotide repeat disorder affecting the DMPK gene. DM1 has a childhood form and adult onset form. Muscles of the face, eyes, forearm, hand and ankles are affected. Patients can also have cataracts, heart conduction defects, and endocrine dysfunction. Physical examination demonstrates a delayed grip release after a hand shake.

choice_explanations.A: Both Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy are caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene; dystrophin is a cytoskeletal protein that maintains muscle fiber integrity.
choice_explanations.B: Lysosomal storage diseases (Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick) cause neurodegeneration and are autosomal recessive, without skeletal muscle defects.
choice_explanations.C: MELAS is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder causing multisystem dysfunction, not this X-linked pattern.
choice_explanations.D: The neuromuscular junction is affected in myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton syndrome, which are autoimmune, not X-linked.
choice_explanations.E: DMPK (protein kinase) mutation causes myotonic dystrophy type 1, an autosomal dominant CTG repeat disorder.

fa_summary: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies are X-linked recessive disorders of the cytoskeletal protein dystrophin; Duchenne is severe, Becker milder.

stem: A 24-year-old woman and her 26-year-old husband come to the physician because of concerns about having children. The wife tells the physician that she has had regular menstrual cycles since the age of 13. The husband says that he has been generally healthy, but recalls getting numerous sinus infections, colds, and ear infections. He was tested for cystic fibrosis as a child, but showed no evidence of the disease. Semen analysis indicates that the infertility is due to a problem affecting sperm motility. Which of the following cardiac anomalies may also be present?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The man has Kartagener syndrome, which is characterized by an inherited defect in dynein protein. Cilia and flagella contain 9 peripheral pairs of microtubules and 2 central microtubules. The microtubules convey motility to cilia through the ATPase dynein. Dynein is a cellular motor that travels along microtubules, typically toward the “minus” end, which is anchored to the basal bodies in the axonemes of cilia or flagella. Ciliary or flagellar movement occurs when the dynein arms attached to an outer microtubule doublet move along the adjacent doublet's microtubules. The coordinated movement of the dynein arms attached to the nine outer microtubule doublets in an axoneme create normal ciliary or flagellar motion. Patients lacking axoneme structures due to defects in dynein or radial spoke proteins display symptoms associated with loss of ciliary and flagellar function. Sperm motility is reduced or absent, and respiratory and ear infections are common due to lack of respiratory epithelial cilia.

As originally described in 1904 by Manes Kartagener, this distinctive congenital syndrome had the unusual cluster of situs inversus, sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. The term situs inversus refers to a congenital condition in which the major visceral organs are reversed or mirrored from their normal positions. This anatomic variant is thought to occur in Kartagener syndrome because cells with normally functioning cilia help to determine the position of internal organs during development. The most obvious feature on physical examination of situs inversus is dextrocardia, in which the apex of the heart points to the right and auscultation of the heart is best over the right chest. None of the other options are associated with Kartagener syndrome.

Ostium primum septal defect (choice B), also known as endocardial cushion defect, causes a hole in the atrial septum near the tricuspid and mitral valves. These defects are the most common cardiac congenital defects in Down syndrome patients.

Patent foramen ovale (choice C) is a very common defect in which the foramen ovale between the atria fails to close after birth.

Tetralogy of Fallot (choice D) is a cyanotic congenital cardiac defect characterized by pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, ventricular septal defect, and right ventricular hypertrophy. It occurs with increased frequency with chromosome 22 deletions and DiGeorge syndrome. Tetralogy would most likely have been diagnosed in childhood.

Transposition of the great arteries (choice E) refers to the congenital cardiac condition in which the aorta arises from the morphologic right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the morphologic left ventricle. It is incompatible with life without the presence of a shunt such as a ventricular septal defect. This defect is more common in infants of diabetic mothers.

In Kartagener disease, the dynein motor that facilitates ciliary movement is nonfunctional through an inherited gene mutation. As a result, respiratory clearance of debris is inhibited. Additionally, the movement of sperm is inhibited due to dysfunction of the dynein motor, while the sperm count is unaffected. Situs inversus, which can cause dextrocardia, can be seen in Kartagener disease.

choice_explanations.A: Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia) features situs inversus, whose most obvious sign is dextrocardia, with the cardiac apex pointing to the right.
choice_explanations.B: Ostium primum septal defect (endocardial cushion defect) is the most common cardiac defect in Down syndrome, not Kartagener syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: Patent foramen ovale is a common defect in which the foramen ovale fails to close after birth.
choice_explanations.D: Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic defect associated with chromosome 22 deletions/DiGeorge syndrome.
choice_explanations.E: Transposition of the great arteries is more common in infants of diabetic mothers.

fa_summary: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) is an autosomal recessive dynein arm defect causing immotile cilia, situs inversus/dextrocardia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and infertility.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of poor vision and flashing lights in her left eye. She is unusually tall, with long limbs and slender fingers. Physical examination shows pectus excavatum and kyphoscoliosis. To view the cardiac examination, click on the "Play Media" button. The genetic disease most likely responsible for the findings seen in this patient is the result of a defect in which of the following types of protein?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has Marfan syndrome, which is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, and consists of a mutation in the fibrillin gene that increases the risk of an aneurysm at the base of the aorta. The classic features of Marfan syndrome are long, thin extremities, with skeletal changes such as pectus excavatum and kyphoscoliosis, ocular changes such as dislocation of the lens, myopia, and retinal detachment, and cardiovascular changes such as mitral valve prolapse (midsystolic click, as heard in this patient) and mitral regurgitation (holosystolic murmur). The life-threatening complications include aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, and aortic rupture. Fibrillins are large extracellular matrix proteins associated with both elastic and non-elastic microfibrils. Note: heart sounds can be heard best with headphones.

Autoantibodies to adhesion proteins (choice A) such as desmosomal or hemidesmosomal proteins may lead to pemphigus vulgaris or bullous pemphigoid, respectively.

Cytoskeletal proteins (choice B) include actin and tubulin, which form microfilaments and microtubules, respectively.

Membrane-bound proteins (choice D), such as ion channels and membrane receptors, are associated with disorders such as cystic fibrosis.

Nuclear proteins (choice E) may include histones and proteins involved in the transcription and DNA replication machinery, as well as those involved in RNA processing. These serve many specific functions. For instance, a defect in the transcription factor “sonic hedgehog” (SHH) can result in holoprosencephaly.

Marfan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations involving the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene. Major manifestations of the disease include: reduced upper to lower body-segment ratio; arm span exceeding height; arachnodactyly; scoliosis or kyphosis; dilation of the aorta (associated with aortic regurgitation); aortic dissection; ectopia lentis (lens subluxation).

choice_explanations.A: Autoantibodies to adhesion proteins (desmosomal or hemidesmosomal) cause pemphigus vulgaris or bullous pemphigoid.
choice_explanations.B: Cytoskeletal proteins include actin and tubulin, forming microfilaments and microtubules.
choice_explanations.C: Marfan syndrome results from a fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutation; fibrillin is a large extracellular matrix protein forming a sheath around elastin.
choice_explanations.D: Membrane-bound proteins include ion channels and receptors, associated with disorders such as cystic fibrosis.
choice_explanations.E: Nuclear proteins include histones and transcription/replication machinery; SHH defects cause holoprosencephaly.

fa_summary: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder due to defective fibrillin-1 (FBN1), an extracellular matrix protein that sheathes elastin.

stem: A 70-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and upper abdominal pain. He also reports recent loss of appetite and occasional vomiting. His family history is positive for gastric adenocarcinoma and infiltrating lobular carcinoma. The gene most likely mutated in this patient encodes a component of which of the following structures?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Adherens junctions are protein complexes found on the lateral surface of an epithelial cell that allow for cell-cell adhesion by linking the actin microfilaments of two adjacent cells. This adhesion is mediated by the homotypic interaction between E-cadherin proteins on the adjacent cells. Individuals who have inherited a mutation in the gene encoding E-cadherin, CDH1, are at high risk of developing gastric adenocarcinoma and infiltrating lobular carcinoma.

Desmosomes (choice B) are protein complexes found on the lateral surface of epithelial cells that link the keratin filaments of two adjacent cells. The intercellular linkage is mediated by the proteins desmoglein and desmoplakin. The blistering skin diseases pemphigus foliaceus and pemphigus vulgaris are autoimmune diseases that lead to the loss of desmosome function.

Gap junctions (choice C) are intercellular channels connecting the cytoplasm of two adjacent cells and allow for the passage of ions and small molecules. These channels are composed of protein subunits called connexins. While mutations in connexin genes are associated with some forms of congenital heart defects, there is no link between these mutations and gastric cancer.

Hemidesmosomes (choice D) are adhesion complexes found on the basal surface of epithelial cells and allow for the connection of the cell to the basal lamina. A form of blistering skin disease called bullous pemphigoid is caused by the body's production of antibodies that bind to a component of the hemidesmosome, dystonin, inhibiting its function.

Tight junctions (choice E) are areas along the lateral surface of two adjacent epithelial cells where the plasma membranes are joined together tightly to form a barrier that is impermeable to fluid, preventing molecules from passing in between the cells. The tight junctions are composed of proteins called occludin and claudins. Defects in tight junctions are not specifically associated with gastric adenocarcinoma.

Formation of some adherens junctions relies on a homotypic interaction between E-cadherin proteins on adjacent cells. Mutations in the gene encoding E-cadherin, CDH1, are found in gastric adenocarcinomas and infiltrating lobular carcinoma.

choice_explanations.A: Adherens junctions link actin microfilaments of adjacent cells via cadherins; inherited CDH1 (E-cadherin) mutations predispose to gastric adenocarcinoma and infiltrating lobular carcinoma.
choice_explanations.B: Desmosomes link keratin filaments of adjacent cells via desmoglein/desmoplakin; their loss causes pemphigus foliaceus/vulgaris.
choice_explanations.C: Gap junctions (connexins) connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells; connexin mutations cause some congenital heart defects, not gastric cancer.
choice_explanations.D: Hemidesmosomes connect the cell to the basal lamina via dystonin; antibodies cause bullous pemphigoid.
choice_explanations.E: Tight junctions (occludin/claudins) form a paracellular seal and are not specifically linked to gastric adenocarcinoma.

fa_summary: Adherens junctions use cadherins (E-cadherin/CDH1); loss of E-cadherin promotes metastasis and predisposes to gastric adenocarcinoma and infiltrating lobular carcinoma.

stem: A 2-day-old newborn is brought to the emergency department because of severe diarrhea. Electron microscopy performed on a duodenal biopsy shows abnormal enterocytes with sparse, short, irregularly arranged microvilli. Genetic analysis identifies a mutation in the gene that encodes myosin Vb. The function of which of the following cytoskeletal components is most likely affected in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The take home point in this question is that microvilli contain a core of actin microfilaments and act to increase the absorptive surface area of epithelial cells. Myosin, including non-muscle myosin in epithelial cells, is associated with actin microfilaments and thus contribute to the function of microvilli. Microvillus atrophy is the leading cause of secretory diarrhea in the first few weeks of life. Brush border microvilli are disorganized, short, and scanty. As a result, enterocytes cannot efficiently absorb ions and nutrients, causing a malabsorption syndrome. The diarrhea is primarily a result of active water and electrolyte secretion in the intestinal lumen. Mutations in MYO5B, the gene encoding myosin Vb, are commonly found in individuals with microvillus atrophy.

The centrosome (choice B) is the microtubule organizing center (MTOC) in animal cells. Its function is to nucleate, anchor, and organize the microtubules in interphase cells as well as the mitotic spindle apparatus during mitosis. As mentioned earlier, microvilli are composed of actin microfilaments, not microtubules (choice E). Also, myosin does not associate with microtubules.

Although keratin (choice C) is a type of intermediate filament that is abundant in epithelial cells, it does not contribute to microvilli.

Laminin (choice D) is a component of the basal lamina that underlies epithelial sheets. Being a component of the extracellular matrix, it does not have a function in maintaining microvilli structure or function.

Congenital microvillus atrophy reveals scanty, short, and disorganized microvilli; loss of microfilament (actin) function contributes to microvilli dysfunction.

choice_explanations.A: Microvilli contain a core of actin microfilaments; myosin Vb associates with actin microfilaments, so a MYO5B mutation impairs this function (congenital microvillus atrophy).
choice_explanations.B: The centrosome is the microtubule organizing center that nucleates and anchors microtubules; it does not maintain microvilli.
choice_explanations.C: Keratin is an intermediate filament abundant in epithelial cells but does not contribute to microvilli.
choice_explanations.D: Laminin is a basal lamina extracellular matrix component and is not involved in microvilli structure/function.
