choice_explanations.E: Microvilli are composed of actin microfilaments, not microtubules.

fa_summary: Microvilli have an actin (microfilament) core; MYO5B/myosin Vb mutations cause congenital microvillus atrophy with secretory diarrhea.

stem: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents, who are first cousins, for a well-child examination. The boy appears thin, small, and lethargic. Physical examination shows slightly misshapen long bones. Joint movements are restricted, the corneas are clouded, and the gums are hyperplastic. Laboratory studies of serum show elevated levels of acid hydrolases and glycosylases. Which of the following metabolic activities is most likely defective in this patient?

options.text: Degradation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate

explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient has I-cell disease, also known as mucolipidosis II, which is caused by a defective UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, the enzyme that phosphorylates mannose on enzymes destined for lysosomes. Proteins coded by nuclear DNA are synthesized on cytoplasmic ribosomes, which may be either “free” or associated with the endoplasmic reticulum to form the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER). Proteins synthesized in the RER are transferred into the Golgi apparatus, where they undergo further modifications that determine whether they remain part of the Golgi apparatus, become part of the plasma membrane, or are shipped to lysosomes or other locations. Proteins not marked for transport to a specific intracellular site follow the default pathway and are exported into the extracellular compartment. The signal for transport of the acid hydrolases (and other enzymes) to the lysosomes is phosphorylation of a terminal mannose moiety on an N-linked oligosaccharide to form mannose 6-phosphate. In I-cell disease, this terminal mannose moiety is not phosphorylated, and the acid hydrolases follow the default pathway and are secreted. Like many of the lysosomal storage diseases, the lack of lysosomal enzymes causes structural defects in the cells. One of the characteristics of I-cell disease is abnormal vacuolization and inclusion bodies in the cytoplasm. By the age of 6 months, there is a failure to thrive (and other developmental delays) as well as abnormal skeletal development, coarse facial features and restricted joint movement.

Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs disease) is one example of a condition in which ganglioside accumulation occurs (choice A).

Deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase results in lysosomal accumulation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate (choice B) in several conditions, such as mucopolysaccharidosis I, Hurler disease, and Hurler-Scheie syndrome.

There are several diseases in which glycogen degradation (choice C) is defective. These are collectively termed glycogen storage diseases because they result in abnormal cellular accumulation of glycogen. In Pompe disease, or type II glycogen storage disease, a lysosomal glucosidase is deficient, resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation.

Deficiency of sphingomyelinase (choice D), an enzyme involved in degradation of sphingomyelin, results in Niemann-Pick disease.

Phosphorylation of tyrosine moieties (choice F) is unrelated to lysosomes or lysosomal enzymes; however, decreased ability to phosphorylate tyrosine moieties might be associated with diabetes or dwarfism.

I-cell disease defect: phosphotransferase activity in the Golgi apparatus. Niemann-Pick disease defect: sphingomyelinase activity in the lysosome. Hurler disease defect: iduronidase activity in the lysosome.

choice_explanations.A: Ganglioside accumulation occurs in Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency).
choice_explanations.B: Deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase causes accumulation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate (mucopolysaccharidosis I/Hurler disease).
choice_explanations.C: Defective glycogen degradation causes glycogen storage diseases; in Pompe disease a lysosomal glucosidase deficiency causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation.
choice_explanations.D: Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease.
choice_explanations.E: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) is caused by defective UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, which phosphorylates mannose on enzymes destined for lysosomes.
choice_explanations.F: Tyrosine phosphorylation is unrelated to lysosomes or lysosomal enzymes.

fa_summary: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) results from defective mannose phosphorylation of lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi (phosphotransferase deficiency).

stem: A newborn is born with a deep fissure that extends from the left nostril through the upper lip. Physical examination shows no abnormalities of the mandible or palate. Which of the following developmental defects is most likely responsible for these findings?

options.text: Failure of the left lateral palatine process to fuse with the median palatine process
Failure of the left maxillary prominence to unite with the left medial nasal prominence
Failure of the primary palate to fuse with the secondary palate
Failure of the right and left medial nasal prominences to merge
Failure of the right palatine process to fuse with the left palatine process

explanation:
The correct answer is B. This neonate has a left (unilateral) cleft lip. In the formation of the upper lip, the right and left medial nasal prominences merge to form the philtrum of the upper lip. The left and right lateral maxillary prominences then merge with the merged medial nasal prominences. Failure of this merger to occur on one side results in a unilateral cleft lip.

Failure of a lateral palatine process to fuse with the median palatine process (choice A), which is synonymous with failure of the primary palate to fuse with the secondary palate (choice C), results in a primary cleft palate. Primary clefts of the palate are found anterior to the incisive foramen of the palate. Primary cleft palates may occur along with cleft lips but are the result of a separate developmental defect.

Failure of the right and left medial nasal prominences to merge (choice D) results in a median cleft lip. This is a rare anomaly. Normally, the right and left medial nasal prominences merge into a single prominence that forms the philtrum of the lip.

Failure of the right and left palatine processes to fuse (choice E) results in a secondary cleft palate. Secondary cleft palates are found posterior to the incisive foramen. Normally, the right and left palatine processes fuse together and fuse to the primary palate.

choice_explanations.A: Failure of a lateral palatine process to fuse with the median palatine process (synonymous with failure of the primary palate to fuse with the secondary palate) results in a primary cleft palate, located anterior to the incisive foramen.
choice_explanations.B: Failure of the left maxillary prominence to unite with the left medial nasal prominence on one side results in a unilateral cleft lip.
choice_explanations.C: Failure of the primary palate to fuse with the secondary palate results in a primary cleft palate (anterior to the incisive foramen).
choice_explanations.D: Failure of the right and left medial nasal prominences to merge results in a median cleft lip, a rare anomaly.
choice_explanations.E: Failure of the right and left palatine processes to fuse results in a secondary cleft palate (posterior to the incisive foramen).

fa_summary: Unilateral cleft lip results from failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the merged medial nasal prominences on one side.

stem: A healthy 10-year-old girl is seen by a physician for a routine health maintenance examination. The physician notes that the child has Tanner stage 1 breast development. Most of the oocytes in the ovary of this girl are in which meiotic stage?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. At birth, and until puberty (Tanner stage 1 is a prepubertal stage), all of the primary oocytes are arrested in the prophase stage of meiosis I, where DNA replication has yielded double-stranded chromosomes that condense and pair up at centromeres. Recombination by crossing over occurs during prophase of meiosis I. The oocytes reach this stage of development starting at about the fifth month of prenatal development. The bulk of oocytes in babies, girls, and premenopausal women are arrested at prophase of the first meiotic division (meiosis I).

Metaphase (choice B): The chromosomes align along the equator; the centromeres do not replicate.

Anaphase and telophase (choice E): One double-stranded chromosome of each homologous pair is distributed to each daughter cell. These daughter cells will be a secondary oocyte and a polar body. Cytokinesis: The cell divides into a secondary oocyte and a polar body. The polar body dies. The secondary oocyte is 2n and has 23 chromosomes. Each chromosome is double stranded. Each strand is referred to as a chromatid.

Meiosis II: Metaphase (choice C): The chromosomes align along the equator; the centromeres replicate. The secondary oocyte arrests at this stage prior to ovulation. It does not complete meiosis II unless it is fertilized. Anaphase (choice A) and telophase: Each chromosome splits into two single-stranded chromosomes, one to each daughter nucleus. This does not occur until after fertilization. Cytokinesis: The secondary oocyte divides into a definitive ovum that is haploid (1n) and a polar body. The polar body dies.

choice_explanations.A: Anaphase of meiosis II occurs only after fertilization, when each chromosome splits into two single-stranded chromosomes.
choice_explanations.B: Metaphase of meiosis I: chromosomes align along the equator and the centromeres do not replicate. Primary oocytes are not arrested here.
choice_explanations.C: Metaphase of meiosis II: chromosomes align along the equator and the centromeres replicate. Secondary oocytes arrest here prior to ovulation.
choice_explanations.D: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase of meiosis I from before birth until ovulation.
choice_explanations.E: Telophase of meiosis I: one double-stranded chromosome of each homologous pair is distributed to each daughter cell (a secondary oocyte and a polar body).

fa_summary: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase of meiosis I from fetal life until ovulation; meiosis I completes just prior to ovulation.

stem: A newborn is found at birth to have excess penile skin on the dorsal aspect of the penis. The urethral meatus is on the ventral aspect of the shaft of the penis. Physical examination shows no other genitourinary abnormalities. The newborn should undergo surgical correction of the hypospadias to prevent which of the following potential sequelae?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Hypospadias, which is congenital displacement of the urethral opening onto the ventral surface (underside) of the penis, is due to malformation of the urethral groove and canal. The displaced urethral meatus may range from the glans, the shaft of the penis, the scrotum, or perineum. Hypospadias may be accompanied by other genitourinary anomalies. An association with cryptorchidism is seen in intersexual abnormalities.

Isolated hypospadias are repaired for several reasons. First, the urethral meatus can be positioned onto the glans to allow for a normal urinary stream. Second, during sexual intercourse, ejaculate material can be propelled in an antegrade fashion to facilitate pregnancy; infertility can result without repair. Third, hypospadias is often associated with chordee (penile curvature), which can be addressed during hypospadias repair. Fourth, because hypospadias results in a shorter functional urethra, there is an increased risk of urinary tract infection. Repair of the hypospadias will address this.

Bladder exstrophy (choice A) is a completely unrelated congenital malformation in which the abdominal wall and anterior bladder wall form incompletely, and the bladder mucosa is exposed to the environment.

Hydrocele (choice B) is a serous accumulation in the tunica vaginalis, often producing a readily apparent scrotal mass. Hydrocele usually arises without any obvious cause.

Phimosis (choice D) is the condition in which the foreskin cannot be retracted over the head of the penis. It is usually either a congenital malformation or a consequence of scarring.

Urachal cysts (choice E) are produced by areas of persistent urachal epithelium, which may be present anywhere between the bladder and the umbilicus.

choice_explanations.A: Bladder exstrophy is an unrelated malformation in which the abdominal and anterior bladder walls form incompletely, exposing bladder mucosa.
choice_explanations.B: Hydrocele is a serous accumulation in the tunica vaginalis that usually arises without any obvious cause.
choice_explanations.C: Hypospadias can cause infertility because ejaculate may not be propelled in an antegrade fashion; repair also prevents chordee and urinary tract infection.
choice_explanations.D: Phimosis is the inability to retract the foreskin over the glans, usually congenital or a consequence of scarring.
choice_explanations.E: Urachal cysts are produced by persistent urachal epithelium between the bladder and the umbilicus.

fa_summary: Hypospadias (urethral opening on the ventral penile surface) is repaired to restore a normal urinary stream, prevent infertility, and address chordee and UTI risk.

stem: A newborn is born with Apgar scores of 8 and 9. Bottle feedings are begun and the newborn quickly vomits the formula. A nasogastric tube is placed and resistance is felt after several centimeters. A developmental defect of which of the following is most likely responsible for this finding?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This newborn has esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). The proximal atresia produces immediate vomiting with feedings. Between feedings, babies with esophageal atresia typically have copious, frothy secretions, and gagging. The distal fistula allows for air to enter the stomach from the trachea when the newborn cries. When a chest x-ray is taken, it shows the tube coiled high in the esophagus, and there is a significant amount of air in the stomach. However, if there were no fistula there would be a gasless abdomen, due to the proximal atresia. This is caused by a malformation of the tracheoesophageal septum. The tracheoesophageal septum is formed by the fusion of the right and left tracheoesophageal folds, and separates the respiratory diverticulum from the gut tube. This condition is often associated with polyhydramnios, due to the inability of the fetus to swallow amniotic fluid.

The respiratory diverticulum forms in the ventral wall of the foregut. The tracheoesophageal septum separates the foregut from the trachea. The distal end of the respiratory diverticulum (also called the laryngotracheal diverticulum, choice D) enlarges to form the lung bud, and the lung bud then divides into two bronchial buds (choice A), which branch into the main bronchi, lobar bronchi, and segmental bronchi.

The costodiaphragmatic recesses (choice B) are below the inferior borders of the lungs, where the costal and diaphragmatic pleura are in contact. The costomediastinal recess (choice C) is the space where the left costal and mediastinal parietal pleura meet, leaving a space caused by the cardiac notch of the left lung. It is occupied by the lingula of the left lung during inspiration.

choice_explanations.A: Bronchial buds arise from division of the lung bud and branch into the main, lobar, and segmental bronchi.
choice_explanations.B: The costodiaphragmatic recesses are below the inferior borders of the lungs, where the costal and diaphragmatic pleura are in contact.
choice_explanations.C: The costomediastinal recess is the space where the left costal and mediastinal parietal pleura meet, caused by the cardiac notch of the left lung.
choice_explanations.D: The laryngotracheal diverticulum is the distal end of the respiratory diverticulum that enlarges to form the lung bud.
choice_explanations.E: A malformation of the tracheoesophageal septum (failure of fusion of the right and left tracheoesophageal folds) produces esophageal atresia with TEF.

fa_summary: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula results from malformation of the tracheoesophageal septum; it presents with vomiting with feeds, frothy secretions, polyhydramnios, and failure to pass an NG tube.

stem: A 28-year-old woman delivers a boy at 42 weeks' gestation. She received minimal prenatal care during the pregnancy. A review of her records shows elevated levels of fetal α-fetoprotein but an ultrasound showed no neural tube defects. Physical examination of the newborn shows abdominal viscera, which are not covered by amnion, protruding through the abdominal wall adjacent to the midline. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings in the newborn?

options.text: Failure of the intestinal loop to retract from the umbilical cord
Failure of the yolk stalk (vitelline duct) to degenerate
Incomplete fusion of the lateral body folds

explanation:
The correct answer is D. During the fourth week of development, the lateral body folds move ventrally and fuse in the midline to form the anterior body wall and thereby internalize the dorsal part of the yolk sac to form the gut tube. Incomplete or imperfect fusion of these folds results in a defect or weakness in the abdominal wall that allows the abdominal viscera to herniate from the abdominal cavity, a condition known as gastroschisis. The viscera that protrude through the defect are not covered by the amnionic membrane covering the umbilical cord, and therefore are free in the amniotic cavity and are in contact with amniotic fluid during in utero life. Gastroschisis usually occurs on the right side of the midline.

During development, certain peritoneal organs fuse with the posterior abdominal wall to become secondarily retroperitoneal. Failure of this peritoneal fusion (choice A) will result in certain organs being mobile that are normally immobile (e.g., mobile cecum).

During development, the midgut normally herniates into the umbilical cord and then subsequently retracts into the abdominal cavity. The midgut usually remains in the umbilical cord from about the sixth week to the twelfth week of development. Failure of the intestinal loops to retract from the umbilical cord (choice B) results in omphalocele. In omphalocele, the abdominal viscera that are outside of the abdomen are inside of the umbilical cord and, therefore, covered by the amniotic membrane that covers the umbilical cord. Therefore, in omphalocele, in contrast to gastroschisis, the viscera are not free in the amniotic cavity and not in contact with amniotic fluid.

Failure of the yolk stalk (vitelline duct) to degenerate (choice C) results in an ileal (Meckel) diverticulum or a vitelline fistula or cyst. In the early embryo, the gut tube is connected to the yolk sac by a narrow connection known as the yolk stalk. Normally, this connection fuses and then degenerates.

Umbilical herniation (choice E) results from abdominal viscera protruding through a weakness in the abdominal wall in the umbilical region, after development. Such protrusions are covered by subcutaneous fascia and skin, distinguishing them from gastroschisis.

choice_explanations.A: Failure of peritoneal fusion results in organs that are normally secondarily retroperitoneal becoming abnormally mobile (e.g., mobile cecum).
choice_explanations.B: Failure of the intestinal loops to retract from the umbilical cord results in omphalocele, in which the viscera are covered by the amniotic membrane of the cord.
choice_explanations.C: Failure of the yolk stalk (vitelline duct) to degenerate results in an ileal (Meckel) diverticulum or a vitelline fistula/cyst.
choice_explanations.D: Gastroschisis results from incomplete fusion of the lateral body folds, leaving viscera uncovered by amnion and exposed to amniotic fluid.
choice_explanations.E: Umbilical herniation is a post-developmental protrusion through the umbilical region covered by subcutaneous fascia and skin.

fa_summary: Gastroschisis (viscera uncovered by amnion, paraumbilical) results from failure of the lateral body folds to fuse; it elevates AFP prenatally.

stem: A 23-year-old patient comes to the physician because of abdominal pain. The radiology report states that although there are no abdominal findings to explain the reported pain, it is noted that the patient has only one kidney. The physician explains to the patient that his right kidney is absent and explains that this is probably a result of a failure of an embryonic structure to form on the right side which normally induces the formation of the kidney. Which of the following structures is the physician referring to that normally induces the development of the adult kidney?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The ureteric bud (also called the metanephric duct) is a diverticulum of the mesonephric duct (choice B). It grows to the metanephric blastema of the urogenital ridge (choice E). It induces the development of the metanephros, which will give rise to the excretory units of the definitive kidney. The metanephros, in turn, induces the ureteric bud (metanephric duct) to divide into the calyces and the collecting tubules of the definitive kidney. The ureteric bud (metanephric duct) induces the development of the metanephros to give rise to the definitive kidney.

The allantois (choice A) is an endodermal diverticulum of the hind gut. It becomes incorporated into the urogenital sinus and contributes to the formation of the urinary bladder. The distal part of the allantois becomes the urachus. The adult remnant of this is the median umbilical ligament.

The mesonephric duct (choice B) is a mesodermal duct into which the mesonephric tubules drain. The mesonephric duct develops into the ductus deferens in the male; it degenerates in the female. In the early embryo, the mesonephric duct carries urine from the mesonephros to the cloaca.

The mesonephros (choice C) is the embryonic kidney, which functions in the embryo before the metanephros (or definitive kidney) develops. The mesonephros develops from the urogenital ridge.

The urogenital ridge (choice E) is a longitudinal elevation of the intermediate mesoderm. The embryonic and adult kidneys, as well as the gonads, develop from the urogenital ridge.

choice_explanations.A: The allantois is an endodermal diverticulum of the hindgut that contributes to the urinary bladder; its distal part becomes the urachus.
choice_explanations.B: The mesonephric duct is the duct from which the ureteric bud arises; it becomes the ductus deferens in males and degenerates in females.
choice_explanations.C: The mesonephros is the embryonic kidney that functions before the metanephros develops; it develops from the urogenital ridge.
choice_explanations.D: The ureteric bud (metanephric duct) induces the metanephros to form the excretory units of the definitive kidney.
choice_explanations.E: The urogenital ridge is a longitudinal elevation of intermediate mesoderm from which the kidneys and gonads develop.

fa_summary: The ureteric bud (metanephric duct) induces the metanephros to form the definitive kidney; absent kidney (renal agenesis) can follow failure of ureteric bud formation.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of the onset of fainting spells. A heart murmur is heard on auscultation of the heart. An echocardiogram shows a primum type atrial septal defect. Failure of which of the following processes is the most likely cause of these findings in this patient?

options.text: Ostium primum formation within the septum primum
Ostium secundum formation within the septum primum
Septum primum fusion with the endocardial cushions
Septum primum fusion with the septum secundum
Septum secundum fusion with the endocardial cushions

explanation:
The correct answer is C. The septum primum (first interatrial septum) develops by growing from the cranial end of the embryonic atrium toward the endocardial cushions. The gap that exists between the two atria during this period is the ostium primum. As the septum primum continues its growth, the ostium primum gets smaller. When the septum primum completes its growth and completely fuses with the endocardial cushions, the ostium primum is closed. Failure of the septum primum to fuse completely with the endocardial cushions leaves a persistent ostium primum, known as a primum type atrial septal defect. Endocardial cushions also contribute to the formation of the mitral and tricuspid valves and part of the interventricular septum. For this reason, ostium primum atrial septal defects (ASDs) are commonly associated with malformation of these structures. Remember also that ostium primum defects are commonly associated with Down syndrome.

The ostium primum does not form within the septum primum (choice A). The ostium primum is the communication between the two atria that exists during the formation of the septum primum; that is, the ostium primum is the space within the developing atrium not yet occupied by the septum primum.

The ostium secundum normally forms within the septum primum (choice B) before the ostium primum closes by fusion of the septum primum with the endocardial cushions. Failure of the ostium secundum to form would result in embryonic death because there would be no pathway for blood to pass from the right atrium to the left atrium when the ostium primum closes, thus depriving the embryo of oxygenated blood. If the ostium secundum is too large, then the septum secundum does not cover it over and a secundum type atrial septal defect would result.

During fetal life, the septum primum does not fuse with the septum secundum (choice D). The space between the two septa forms the foramen ovale, the pathway for blood to pass from the right atrium to the left atrium. After birth, reversal of the pressure gradient causes the septum primum to be pressed against the septum secundum, thus causing functional closure of the foramen ovale. Fusion does not normally occur at this time but usually occurs later in life in most people. In some people (~25% of the population), however, complete fusion never occurs (probe patency).

The septum secundum normally does not fuse with the endocardial cushions (choice E).

choice_explanations.A: The ostium primum does not form within the septum primum; it is the space between the two atria not yet occupied by the septum primum.
choice_explanations.B: The ostium secundum normally forms within the septum primum; failure to form it would be lethal, and if it is too large a secundum ASD results.
choice_explanations.C: Failure of the septum primum to fuse with the endocardial cushions leaves a persistent ostium primum (primum type ASD).
choice_explanations.D: The septum primum does not fuse with the septum secundum during fetal life; the space between them forms the foramen ovale.
choice_explanations.E: The septum secundum normally does not fuse with the endocardial cushions.

fa_summary: Ostium primum ASD results from failure of the septum primum to fuse with the endocardial cushions (AV canal/endocardial cushion defect).

stem: A researcher is studying the developmental origins of the arteries that supply blood to the brain. The investigation involves injecting contrast media into the hearts of fetal pigs and studying the arteries that develop in the pharyngeal arches. Which of the following pairs of pharyngeal arches gives rise to arteries that contribute to the blood vessels that supply the brain?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Each pharyngeal arch contains mesoderm. Some of this mesoderm gives rise to blood vessels that are within the pharyngeal arch. These blood vessels are called aortic arches. Arch 3 gives rise to an aortic arch that contributes to the common carotid artery and the internal carotid artery bilaterally, and arch 4 gives rise to an aortic arch that contributes to the arch of the aorta on the left and the right subclavian artery on the right.

The internal carotid arteries branch into the middle and anterior cerebral arteries that form the anterior circulation of the brain. The subclavian arteries give rise to the vertebral arteries that join to form the vertebrobasilar or posterior circulation of the brain. The anterior and posterior circulations are linked by the posterior communicating arteries to form the circle of Willis.

Pharyngeal arches 1 (choice A) and 2 (choices A and B) give rise to aortic arches that contribute to the maxillary artery and the stapedial artery, respectively.

Arch 5 (choice D) degenerates early in fetal development, and arch 6 (choice E) gives rise to an aortic arch that contributes to the pulmonary artery and the ductus arteriosus on the left and the pulmonary artery on the right.

choice_explanations.A: Arches 1 and 2 give rise to aortic arches contributing to the maxillary artery and the stapedial artery, respectively.
choice_explanations.B: Arch 2 gives rise to the aortic arch contributing to the stapedial artery.
choice_explanations.C: Arch 3 contributes to the common and internal carotid arteries; arch 4 contributes to the arch of the aorta (left) and right subclavian artery (right).
choice_explanations.D: Arch 5 degenerates early in fetal development.
choice_explanations.E: Arch 6 gives rise to an aortic arch contributing to the pulmonary artery and ductus arteriosus (left) and pulmonary artery (right).

fa_summary: Pharyngeal arches 3 and 4 give rise to the carotid arteries and the arch of the aorta/right subclavian artery, which supply the brain via the circle of Willis.

stem: A 16-year-old boy who recently immigrated to the United States is brought to the physician because of severe intellectual disability. He lives in a group home and a caretaker is present with him during the examination. Medical records reveal that he is barely able to brush his teeth. He cannot dress himself without assistance. He is able to walk without assistance. He speaks in 1-2 word sentences when asked a question, but the answers are not usually intelligible. Physical examination shows pallor, a protuberant abdomen, an edematous face, and an enlarged tongue. Which of the following substances is affected secondary to this patient's primary disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has cretinism. This condition is characterized by a profound lack of thyroid hormone in a developing child, leading to intellectual disability and the physical findings described in the question stem. Cretinism can be due to dietary deficiency of iodine (now rare in the United States because of the introduction of iodized salt), to developmental failure of thyroid formation, or to a defect in thyroxine synthesis. The thyroid gland concentrates iodine to iodinate tyrosine residues in thyroglobulin to ultimately produce T3 and T4, the thyroid hormones. Childhood deficiency produces short stature (deficient growth hormone secretion) with irreversible mental retardation (cretinism). Other symptoms include protruding tongue and coarse facial features.

Untreated cretinism results in a form of dwarfism. There is no evidence that thyroid hormones act directly on growth or bone formation. Rather, thyroid hormone appears to be permissive or act synergistically with growth hormone or growth factors acting directly on bone. There are also indications suggesting that thyroid hormone regulates GH secretion. In animal models, circulating thyroid hormone is required for continued GH synthesis and secretion. In humans, there is no such clear evidence, although there is clearly interplay between the two hypothalamic-pituitary axes involved in GH and thyroid hormone secretion. Anterior pituitary somatotropes (which secrete GH) and thyrotropes (which secrete thyroid stimulating hormone; TSH) are both under negative feedback control by somatostatin, which provides an opportunity for cross-talk and may explain why hyperthyroid patients have reduced GH.

None of the other substances listed are affected by the lack of thyroid hormone. Cortisol (choice A) is produced by the adrenal cortex and its release is controlled by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Although there is evidence of cross-talk between this and the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis (there is a reciprocal relationship between serum cortisol and TSH levels), cortisol actions are not thyroid hormone-dependent. Hypocortisolism results in Addison disease.

Iron (choice C), parathyroid hormone (choice D), and selenium (choice E) are also not affected by the lack of thyroid hormone.

choice_explanations.A: Cortisol is produced by the adrenal cortex under the control of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis; its actions are not thyroid hormone-dependent.
choice_explanations.B: In cretinism, the lack of thyroid hormone is associated with deficient growth hormone secretion, producing short stature and irreversible mental retardation.
choice_explanations.C: Iron status is not affected by the lack of thyroid hormone.
choice_explanations.D: Parathyroid hormone (calcium homeostasis) is not affected by the lack of thyroid hormone.
choice_explanations.E: Selenium (a cofactor for deiodinases) is not affected by the lack of thyroid hormone in the way described.

fa_summary: 克汀病（先天性甲状腺激素缺乏/碘缺乏）除智力障碍、舌大、面容粗陋外，伴生长激素分泌不足致矮小。

stem: A 3-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital after a right-sided abdominal mass extending across the midline is found on routine examination. The patient reports no symptoms. He undergoes surgical resection of the mass. Microscopic examination of the lesion shows sheets of small cells with hyperchromatic nuclei. The tumor cells encircle pink neurofibrillary structures. Which of the following oncogenes is most likely associated with this patient's tumor?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The tumor is a neuroblastoma, which is one of the most common non-cranial solid tumors in children. Neuroblastoma typically occurs before age 5 years, with many presenting before age 2. Patients typically present with a palpable abdominal mass crossing the midline detected on physical examination. Rarely, patients may present with opsoclonus-myoclonus and hypertension.

Neuroblastoma can arise from neural crest cells throughout the body, but the adrenal gland is the most common site. Neural crest cells populate both the adrenal medulla and the sympathetic chain, and their pluripotency results in varying degrees of differentiation of these tumors. A prominent histologic feature are Homer-Wright pseudorosettes, which are rings of tumor cells encircling nerve fibers that arise from the tumor cells. The hyperchromatic nuclei (small blue cells) is a nonspecific feature of many malignancies associated with the neural crest. Note: A rosette contains a central lumen (ependymoma, retinoblastoma, medulloblastoma), whereas a pseudorosette lacks a lumen and surrounds material or a blood vessel. However, the terms have been used interchangeably. The histopathology demonstrates small blue cells forming pseudorosettes. The typical presentation is an asymptomatic abdominal mass crossing the midline. Neuroblastoma is a relatively common malignancy in children younger than 5 years of age, and it arises from neural crest cells that populate the adrenal medulla and sympathetic chain.

Many cases of neuroblastoma are associated with amplification of the N-myc oncogene. These patients have a worse prognosis compared to patients without this mutation.

In children presenting with an asymptomatic abdominal mass, Wilms tumor, also known as nephroblastoma, associated with a mutation in the WT-1 tumor suppressor gene (chromosome 11) (choice E), should be the other major neoplasm on the differential. Wilms tumor arises from nephroblasts in the kidney, rather than from neural crest cells in the adrenal medulla. C-myc (choice A) is associated with Burkitt lymphoma; L-myc (choice B) with small cell lung cancer; and Ret (choice D) with MEN 2A/2B and medullary thyroid carcinoma.

choice_explanations.A: C-myc amplification is associated with Burkitt lymphoma.
choice_explanations.B: L-myc is associated with small cell lung cancer.
choice_explanations.C: Neuroblastoma is associated with amplification of the N-myc oncogene, which predicts a poorer prognosis.
choice_explanations.D: RET mutations are associated with MEN 2A/2B and medullary thyroid carcinoma.
choice_explanations.E: WT1 is a tumor suppressor gene mutated in Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), the other major pediatric abdominal mass on the differential.

fa_summary: 儿童中线跨越性腹部肿块 + 小蓝圆细胞环绕神经纤维（Homer-Wright 假菊形团）= 神经母细胞瘤，伴 N-myc 扩增、预后差。

stem: A 76-year-old woman passes away from lung cancer after a prolonged hospital stay complicated by pneumonia. She had smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for the past 45 years. An autopsy is performed and the cancerous lung is removed. Histologic examination shows the neoplasm consists of islands of mitotically active squamous cell carcinoma with central areas of coagulative necrosis. Which of the following is the underlying mechanism accounting for this type of tumor necrosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Tumor necrosis is usually due to ischemia caused by discrepancy between rapid neoplastic growth and vascular supply. In general, the more rapidly a tumor grows, the more malignant it is and the more likely that it will develop necrosis. When tumor growth outstrips vascular supply, the initial areas to undergo cell death are usually found in the center of the tumor. This is due to a greater density of vascular supply to the tumor periphery compared to the tumor core.

Surprisingly, neoplasms produce anti-angiogenesis factors (choice A) as well, which may slow the development of vascular supply to the tumor. This is probably part of the ability of tissues (including neoplasms) to regulate the degree of vascularity and, therefore, the rate of growth. However, there is no evidence suggesting that anti-angiogenesis factors are sufficient to produce tumor ischemia and necrosis.

Apoptosis (choice B) occurs in all neoplasms, especially lymphomas. Apoptosis is entirely different from necrosis, manifesting with pyknotic nuclei, shrunken cytoplasm, and lack of inflammatory reaction. Furthermore, in contrast to necrosis, apoptosis involves scattered single cells. It is a form of programmed cell death resulting from both intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Radiation therapy can result in apoptosis by inducing DNA damage and stimulating intracellular pro-apoptotic factors.

Tuberculosis and other granulomatous infections (choice C) can occur in immunocompromised patients, including those with malignancy. These infections usually cause caseous necrosis, termed due to the gross feature of "cheese-like" consistency of the affected tissue.

Host immune response (choice D) may cause single-cell apoptosis or necrosis by several mechanisms mediated by cytotoxic T lymphocytes, natural killer cells, and macrophages. Antitumor immunity is probably more important in immune surveillance (elimination of individual newly developing neoplastic clones) than in large tumor necrosis.

choice_explanations.A: Neoplasms produce anti-angiogenesis factors, which may slow the development of vascular supply to the tumor, but there is no evidence suggesting that anti-angiogenesis factors are sufficient to produce tumor ischemia and necrosis.
choice_explanations.B: Apoptosis occurs in all neoplasms, especially lymphomas. It is entirely different from necrosis, manifesting with pyknotic nuclei, shrunken cytoplasm, and lack of inflammatory reaction; in contrast to necrosis, apoptosis involves scattered single cells.
choice_explanations.C: Tuberculosis and other granulomatous infections can occur in immunocompromised patients with malignancy, and usually cause caseous necrosis ("cheese-like" consistency).
choice_explanations.D: Host immune response may cause single-cell apoptosis or necrosis via cytotoxic T lymphocytes, natural killer cells, and macrophages, but antitumor immunity is more important in immune surveillance than in large tumor necrosis.

fa_summary: Tumor necrosis is usually coagulative necrosis caused by ischemia from a discrepancy between rapid neoplastic growth and vascular supply.

stem: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain and swelling in his knees. He has a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes and a 5-year history of renal failure. He has been on hemodialysis for the past 4 years. He also has a history of carpal tunnel syndrome. Physical examination reveals bilateral knee effusions. The patient is able to ambulate albeit slowly. Joint aspiration produces synovial fluid that stains positively with Congo red and shows green birefringence with polarized light. Which of the following proteins is most likely associated with the observed staining?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Amyloid occurs in many different forms, and can be associated with a number of different precursor proteins. Amyloid deposits made of different proteins appear similar on light and electron microscopy, but actually represent a heterogeneous population of proteins that have a common tertiary structure forming a beta-pleated sheet.

Hemodialysis is a method for removing waste products such as potassium and urea, as well as free water, from the blood when the kidneys are failing. Beta-2 microglobulin (beta-2-M) is a large molecule and does not pass at all through the dialysis membranes, but instead begins to accumulate as an amyloid protein. After several years of being on hemodialysis (usually 5-7 years, but sometimes less), patients begin to develop complications from the accumulation of beta-2-M-derived amyloid, including carpal tunnel syndrome, bone cysts, and accumulation in joints and other tissues. Questions about the type of amyloid seen in different disease states (even though the type is usually not determined clinically) are favorites on USMLE examinations. The table below summarizes all five answer choices.

Amyloid type / associated disease / clinical manifestations:
- Amyloid-associated protein (choice A): secondary amyloidosis (autoimmune disease, chronic infection); deposition in kidney, spleen, liver; most commonly presents as renal insufficiency/nephrotic syndrome.
- Amyloid light chain (choice B): primary amyloidosis; systemic deposition, includes heart, kidney.
- Beta-2 microglobulin (choice C): long-term hemodialysis; most commonly musculoskeletal, with deposits in muscles, ligaments, synovium, bone, resulting in arthropathy, carpal tunnel, fractures.
- Calcitonin precursors (choice D): medullary thyroid carcinoma (related to calcitonin); deposition in the tumor; no known clinical consequence.
- Transthyretin (choice E): primary amyloidosis; mostly cardiac deposition.

choice_explanations.A: Amyloid-associated protein is seen in secondary amyloidosis (autoimmune disease, chronic infection), with deposition in kidney, spleen, and liver, most commonly presenting as renal insufficiency/nephrotic syndrome.
choice_explanations.B: Amyloid light chain is seen in primary amyloidosis, with systemic deposition including heart and kidney.
choice_explanations.C: Beta-2 microglobulin accumulates as an amyloid protein in long-term hemodialysis, most commonly causing musculoskeletal deposits (arthropathy, carpal tunnel, fractures).
choice_explanations.D: Calcitonin precursors deposit in medullary thyroid carcinoma, with no known clinical consequence.
choice_explanations.E: Transthyretin is seen in primary amyloidosis and produces mostly cardiac deposition.

fa_summary: Long-term hemodialysis accumulates beta-2 microglobulin as amyloid (Abeta2M), causing carpal tunnel syndrome and arthropathy.

stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of short stature and delayed puberty. She is 3 standard deviations below the mean for height. Physical examination shows thick folds of skin on the lateral neck, low-set ears, a fishlike mouth, and ptosis. Biopsy of her ovary shows fibrous stroma arranged in whorls. Chromosomal analysis shows a 45,X karyotype. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The 45,X karyotype results in Turner syndrome, which is characterized by ovarian dysgenesis and a variety of somatic abnormalities, including micrognathia, a fishlike mouth, a shield chest, low-set ears, ptosis, and a webbed neck. Other findings can include coarctation of the aorta, hypertension, and renal abnormalities.

Plasma levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) are markedly increased due to the lack of feedback inhibition by ovarian secretions. FSH levels are high during infancy and rise again after 9-10 years of age. Luteinizing hormone (LH) levels typically parallel FSH levels, and would be increased rather than decreased (choice B) at age 14. Combination estrogen and progesterone replacement therapy can induce the development of secondary sex characteristics and menses.

Short stature is invariably present. The cause is not known because plasma levels of growth hormone (choice A) are typically not decreased in Turner syndrome. Clinical studies have shown, however, that injections of human growth hormone can increase growth in patients with Turner syndrome; findings in Turner syndrome include increased follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), increased luteinizing hormone (LH), decreased estrogen, decreased inhibin, and normal growth hormone.

The ovaries usually are streak-like and exhibit only fibrous stroma. The ovarian dysgenesis leads to decreased secretion of estrogen (not increased, choice C). Inhibin (choice E) is also decreased. There is also persistent infantilism.

choice_explanations.A: Plasma growth hormone levels are typically not decreased in Turner syndrome; growth hormone injections can increase growth.
choice_explanations.B: LH levels typically parallel FSH levels and are increased rather than decreased at age 14.
choice_explanations.C: Ovarian dysgenesis leads to decreased (not increased) estrogen secretion.
choice_explanations.E: Inhibin is decreased in Turner syndrome due to ovarian dysgenesis.

fa_summary: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes ovarian dysgenesis with increased FSH/LH and decreased estrogen/inhibin.

stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious on a park bench. He smells of alcohol. His clothes are soiled and there is also the smell of feces on his pants and undergarments. In the emergency department, he is arousable and easily conversant. Physical examination reveals a man who looks older than his stated age. His pulse is 110/min and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. His lips are parched and his mouth is dry. The heart, lungs and abdomen are unremarkable. His extremities are dry and scaly. Laboratory studies show: Arterial CO2 28 mm Hg; arterial pH 7.32; serum Cl- 116 mEq/L; serum HCO3- 14 mEq/L; serum Na+ 140 mEq/L; serum K+ 3.3 mEq/L; serum creatinine 1.3 mEq/L; serum glucose 105 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from loss of bicarbonate in the feces. It is important to understand how to calculate the anion gap.

The anion gap is useful clinically to determine the basic cause of metabolic acidosis. The anion gap is defined as the difference between the plasma Na+ concentration and the sum of the plasma Cl- and HCO3- concentrations: Anion gap = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]) = 140 - (116 + 14) = 10.

The anion gap normally ranges from 8 to 16 (no units are used). Because the plasma must contain an equal number of positive and negative charges in accordance with the law of electroneutrality, the anion gap estimates the unmeasured anions in the plasma. Included among these unmeasured anions are organic acids such as lactate, acetoacetate, and others. Therefore, overproduction of endogenous acid or decreased ability to excrete acid increases the anion gap (and is referred to as normochloremic metabolic acidosis because plasma chloride is normal). Common causes of anion gap (normochloremic) metabolic acidosis (anion gap > normal) include diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, salicylate poisoning, and methanol ingestion.

Non-anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis (anion gap within normal range) is usually caused by a primary loss of HCO3-. Common causes of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis are diarrhea, as seen with this patient. Renal tubular acidosis is another common cause of metabolic acidosis. Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis can also be caused by ingestion of HCl.

The low bicarbonate ion indicates the patient is acidotic; this eliminates contraction alkalosis (choice A) and vomiting-induced alkalosis (choice F).

Ketoacidosis (choice B), lactic acidosis (choice C), and uremic acidosis (choice E) are all characterized by a high anion gap; this patient's anion gap is in the normal range.

choice_explanations.A: The low bicarbonate ion indicates the patient is acidotic; this eliminates contraction alkalosis.
choice_explanations.B: Ketoacidosis is characterized by a high anion gap; this patient's anion gap is in the normal range.
choice_explanations.C: Lactic acidosis is characterized by a high anion gap; this patient's anion gap is in the normal range.
choice_explanations.E: Uremic acidosis is characterized by a high anion gap; this patient's anion gap is in the normal range.
choice_explanations.F: The low bicarbonate ion indicates the patient is acidotic; this eliminates vomiting-induced alkalosis.

fa_summary: Diarrhea causes a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis from loss of bicarbonate in the feces.

stem: A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a several month history of body aches, joint pain, and flu-like symptoms. She has also had difficulty swallowing solids, recently progressing to liquids. Physical examination shows erythema of the nasal bridge and cheeks. Laboratory studies are performed and the following titers are obtained: Anti-ribonucleoprotein (anti-RNP) High titer; Rheumatoid factor (RF) High titer; Antinuclear antibody (ANA) High titer; Anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) Not detected; Anti-Smith antigen (anti-Sm) Not detected; Anti-Scl-70 Not detected. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient presents with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), a systemic autoimmune condition with clinical features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis. Patients may present with joint pain, myalgias, pleurisy, esophageal dysmotility, and Raynaud's phenomenon (vasospasm of distal extremities in response to cold temperatures). Because there is overlap of clinical features, it is suggested that the disease is not a distinct entity, but rather a subset of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis; over time, patients with MCTD may progress to SLE or systemic sclerosis.

One distinguishing feature of this disease is high antibody titers to ribonucleoprotein (RNP). The specific protein involved is U1-RNP, which is involved in splicing machinery. Elevated titers of RF and ANA are common features of MCTD. MCTD is readily treatable with steroid therapy.

Anti-centromere antibody is the distinctive marker for CREST syndrome (choice A), the limited form of scleroderma. CREST is an acronym for the hallmark features of this disease including calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia. Due to its association with scleroderma, there may be some overlap of autoantibody profiles.

Anti-Scl-70 is the distinctive marker for diffuse scleroderma (choice B) and represents antibodies against DNA topoisomerase I. There is early fibrotic involvement of viscera and more diffuse involvement of skin compared to CREST syndrome. Examples of resulting pathologies include diffuse interstitial fibrosis of the lung, restrictive pericarditis, and pulmonary hypertension.

High titers of anti-histone antibody without other autoantibodies is the distinctive marker for drug-induced lupus (choice C). This disorder is particularly associated with administration of hydralazine and procainamide. The clinical features will disappear when the medication is discontinued.

High titers of anti-dsDNA and/or anti-Smith antibodies are highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE; choice E). Other autoimmune conditions may present with low titers of these autoantibodies.

choice_explanations.A: Anti-centromere antibody is the distinctive marker for CREST syndrome, the limited form of scleroderma (calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia).
choice_explanations.B: Anti-Scl-70 (antibodies against DNA topoisomerase I) is the distinctive marker for diffuse scleroderma.
choice_explanations.C: High titers of anti-histone antibody without other autoantibodies mark drug-induced lupus, associated with hydralazine and procainamide and reversible when the medication is discontinued.
choice_explanations.E: High titers of anti-dsDNA and/or anti-Smith antibodies are highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus.

fa_summary: High anti-ribonucleoprotein (anti-U1 RNP) antibodies with RF and ANA are characteristic of mixed connective tissue disease.

stem: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with intractable chest pain. The patient reports a prior history of shortness of breath with exertion, relieved with rest. The patient develops a fatal arrhythmia in the emergency department. An autopsy is performed. Thrombosis of the left anterior descending artery with 100% occlusion is identified grossly and ischemic myocardial necrosis is confirmed histologically. How long after thrombosis of the coronary arteries will necrotic changes in the myocardium first be visible by light microscopy?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient's symptoms of severe, unrelenting chest pain is classic for a myocardial infarction (MI). The prior history of shortness of breath on exertion suggests the patient had angina and coronary artery disease. Following the AMI episode, the patient developed a fatal arrhythmia, typically ventricular fibrillation, which is a common cause of death. The timeline of an MI is highly tested on the boards. A summary table is provided below.

Timeline of myocardial infarction (microscopic appearance):
- 1-4 hours: no visible changes; wavy fibers, contraction bands.
- 4-12 hours: vague myocardial pallor and softening; coagulative necrosis.
- 1-3 days: yellow pallor; neutrophilic infiltrate.
- 3-7 days: yellow pallor; macrophage infiltrate.
- 7-28 days: central pallor with a red border; granulation tissue and blood vessel formation.

Following coronary artery occlusion and myocardial infarction (MI), microscopic changes showing infarction necrosis will first be seen at 4-12 hours.

Irreversible ischemic injury to the myocardium occurs following interruption of blood supply that lasts at least 20-30 minutes, which is why it is important to treat MI early ("time is muscle"). However, necrotic changes only become apparent on light microscopy 4 to 12 hours after ischemia. Note: some light microscopic changes (wavy fibers = stunned myocardial cells) can be seen as early as 1 hour (see table) after the episode.

Electron microscopic studies, on the other hand, reveal morphologic changes even at earlier stages, demonstrating sarcolemmal disruption and mitochondrial swelling following irreversible ischemia. Though this may seem like a minor point, during autopsies after sudden cardiac death, these pathologic features have important medico-legal and clinical implications. Note that the cellular changes of necrosis do not occur after death. Necrosis is a biologic phenomenon that, paradoxically, may only develop in a living organism.

In 3-5 days (choice D), coagulative necrosis will be advanced. Myocytes will have lost their nuclei and the cytoplasm will be disintegrating. Typically, there is abundant neutrophilic infiltration. Histiocytes (macrophages) start to arrive, which are necessary to remove necrotic debris prior to the development of granulation tissue. During this time, the inflammatory infiltrate may spread to the pericardium and produce symptoms of acute pericarditis. Keep in mind that this phenomenon is separate from the autoimmune pericarditis (Dressler's syndrome) that may occur several weeks following the MI.

Over 1 week (choice E) after ischemia marks the development of granulation tissue around the previously infarcted region of myocardium. This is a vulnerable time period because it is following the disintegrative inflammatory process described above but before strong tissue architecture can be established. Thus, during this time period, the heart is particularly prone to various "rupture" events including free wall rupture, septal rupture, and papillary muscle rupture.

choice_explanations.A: 10 seconds is far too early; irreversible injury requires at least 20-30 minutes of ischemia.
choice_explanations.B: 20-40 minutes is the threshold for irreversible ischemic injury, but necrotic changes are not yet visible by light microscopy.
choice_explanations.C: Necrotic changes in infarcted myocardium first become apparent on light microscopy at 4-12 hours after ischemia (the correct answer).
choice_explanations.D: At 3-5 days, coagulative necrosis is advanced with abundant neutrophilic infiltration and macrophages beginning to remove debris.
choice_explanations.E: Over 1 week marks granulation tissue formation, a vulnerable period for rupture events (free wall, septal, papillary muscle).

fa_summary: Necrotic (coagulative) changes in infarcted myocardium first become visible by light microscopy at 4-12 hours.

stem: A 34-year-old woman gives birth to a baby at 30 weeks' gestation after an uneventful pregnancy. A large, regular, red, flat lesion on the infant's face is observed in the delivery room. The facial lesion does not appear to cross the midline of the face and later persists into adulthood. This lesion is most likely associated with which of the following disorders?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is a rare congenital vascular disorder characterized by facial capillary malformation (port wine stain) and capillary-venous malformations that affect the brain and eye. The lesion described is a port-wine stain, a flat, vascular lesion that, unlike the more common strawberry nevus, does not usually regress with age. Facial port-wine stains can be a component of Sturge-Weber disease, and typically occurs in the ophthalmic and maxillary distribution of the trigeminal nerve (V1 and V2, respectively).

The characteristic findings of Sturge-Weber syndrome include:
- facial port-wine stain (V1 and V2 distribution), which does not regress and persists in adulthood
- leptomeningeal angiomatosis resulting in hemispheric atrophy
- non-specific neural findings (hemiparesis, seizures)
- glaucoma

Other features of the disease include similar vascular lesions of the meninges (leptomeningeal angiomatosis) occurring ipsilateral to the port-wine stain. CT of the brain demonstrates hemispheric atrophy due to venous infarction of vessels associated with leptomeningeal angiomas, with tram-track calcification along the cortical ribbon. Neurologic sequelae of these cerebral findings include seizures, mental retardation, and hemiparesis. Patients can also present with glaucoma and pheochromocytoma.

Sturge-Weber occurs sporadically and is not inherited.

Arnold-Chiari malformations (choice A) are a cluster of related brain and spinal cord malformations in which there is a downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils and vermis into the foramen magnum. Associated conditions include hydrocephaly, lumbar myelomeningocele, and syringomyelia. In myelomeningocele, a bony defect in the spine allows both the meninges and spinal cord to herniate into the sac. In syringomyelia, hydrocephalus of the central canal of the spine impinges on decussating C8T1 spinothalamic tract fibers, producing a bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature sensation. Skin defects are not associated with this disorder.

Dandy-Walker malformation (choice B) includes a large, distended fourth ventricle with a hypoplastic (or absent) cerebellum. These patients may also have associated spina bifida (bony defect in the spine without herniation). Though no skin findings are associated with spina bifida, there may be a tuft of hair overlying the site of the defect (spina bifida occulta).

Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) (choice C) is an inherited, autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome characterized by the presence of benign, subcutaneous neurofibromas arising from peripheral nerves. The involved NF1 gene is located on chromosome 17. Other findings can be encapsulated by the mnemonic CAFE-SPOT: Cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, eye Lisch nodules (hamartomas of the iris), scoliosis, pheochromocytoma, and optic tumors (usually optic glioma). The skin findings in NF1, namely cafe-au-lait spots, are usually brown and small, unlike the port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber.

Tuberous sclerosis (choice E) is also an inherited, autosomal dominant condition, characterized by renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, cortical tubers (malformed neural tissue), retinal hamartomas, lung cysts, seizures and mental retardation. The important cutaneous manifestations of this disease are ash-leaf spots (scattered hypopigmented macules) and adenoma sebaceum. Unlike port-wine stains, adenoma sebaceum, also known as a facial angiofibroma, appears like severe acne with raised red papules in a malar (butterfly) distribution across the nose and cheeks.

choice_explanations.A: Arnold-Chiari malformations involve downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils and vermis into the foramen magnum (hydrocephaly, myelomeningocele, syringomyelia); skin defects are not associated.
choice_explanations.B: Dandy-Walker malformation includes a large, distended fourth ventricle with a hypoplastic or absent cerebellum.
choice_explanations.C: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome (NF1 gene on chromosome 17) with cafe-au-lait spots (brown and small, unlike a port-wine stain), axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, and optic gliomas.
choice_explanations.E: Tuberous sclerosis is an autosomal dominant condition with renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, ash-leaf spots, and adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibroma in a malar distribution).

fa_summary: Sturge-Weber syndrome: facial port-wine stain (V1/V2) with leptomeningeal angiomatosis, seizures, and glaucoma.

stem: A study is conducted to determine transporter function in cardiac muscle cells isolated from papillary muscle. The study design includes patch-clamp studies, which analyze plasma membrane proteins, and cell-free studies, which analyze isolated organelles from different cell fractions. In these two studies, transporter function is correlated with the normal electrical sequence of events of the cardiac action potential. Under normal physiologic conditions, which of the following transporters is most likely to depolarize the sarcolemma by moving a net positive charge from extracellular fluid into resting cardiac muscle cells?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The sodium-calcium exchanger causes depolarization because three sodium ions enter the cell when one calcium ion is removed. Sodium (Na+) has a valence of +1, and calcium (Ca2+) has a valence of +2. This moves a net positive charge into the cell cytosol. During the cardiac action potential some calcium enters the cell through voltage-gated calcium channels; more is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. To restore resting conditions calcium must be resequestered and calcium that influxed must be pumped out of the cell. The Na+-Ca2+ exchanger is the predominant mechanism that removes calcium from cardiac cells during resting phase.

A plasma 3Na+-1Ca2+ exchanger, located in cardiac muscle, moves a net positive charge into the cell cytosol. The Na-Ca exchanger helps restore resting calcium level, by removing calcium that entered during the cardiac action potential. Sodium (Na+) has a valence of +1 and calcium (Ca2+) has a valence of +2, so +3 enters the cell.

Lysosomal V-type proton ATPases (choice A) move positively charged protons into the lysosome to acidify it.

Under physiologic conditions, positively charged protons move through the mitochondrial F-type ATP synthetases (choice B) from the intermembrane space of the mitochondria into the matrix of the mitochondria, forcing the transporter to make ATP.

The plasmalemma Na+-K+ ATPase (choice D) pumps three Na+ out of the cell in exchange for the two potassium (K+) being pumped into the cell; this moves a net positive charge out of the cell cytosol.

The sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA, choice E) pumps Ca2+, and thus a net positive charge, out of the cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. There is a plasma membrane calcium ATPase, a primary active transporter, that contributes to removal of calcium by pumping it into the extracellular fluid; this transporter makes the sarcolemma more negative because it removes cation from the cell.

choice_explanations.A: Lysosomal V-type proton ATPases move positively charged protons into the lysosome to acidify it.
choice_explanations.B: Mitochondrial F-type ATP synthetases move protons from the intermembrane space into the matrix, driving ATP synthesis.
choice_explanations.C: The plasma membrane Na+-Ca2+ exchanger (3 Na+ in, 1 Ca2+ out) moves a net positive charge into the cell and depolarizes the sarcolemma (the correct answer).
choice_explanations.D: The plasmalemma Na+-K+ ATPase pumps three Na+ out and two K+ in, moving a net positive charge out of the cell.
choice_explanations.E: SERCA pumps Ca2+ (a net positive charge) out of the cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, making the cell interior more negative.

fa_summary: The plasma membrane Na+-Ca2+ exchanger (3 Na+ in, 1 Ca2+ out) moves a net positive charge into the cell and depolarizes the sarcolemma.

stem: A 56-year-old woman who has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes each day for 30 years comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of limb weakness. She reports that her weakness seems to improve with activity. Physical examination reveals mild clubbing of fingertips and decreased breath sounds in the left upper lung lobe. She exhibits weakness in raising the upper arms and lifting lower legs. Edrophonium is administered intravenously and the patient's strength is assessed soon afterwards. A slight improvement in muscle strength is observed. This patient's muscle weakness is most likely due to dysfunction of which of the following?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a rare presynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission in which release of acetylcholine is impaired, resulting in proximal muscle weakness particularly of the limbs (patient has difficulty raising her arms and legs). Many cases of LEMS occur as part of a paraneoplastic syndrome, especially in small cell lung cancer. In this patient, the digital clubbing suggests hypoxemia, from chronic tobacco smoking as well as obstruction of the bronchial airway. Decreased breath sounds identified on physical examination also confirm bronchial airway obstruction, in this case, by a bronchogenic tumor.

During the course of the malignancy, autoantibodies are generated against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, inhibiting presynaptic release of acetylcholine. Patients present with weakness that is worse with inactivity and improves after exertion. By the same token, on electromyography (EMG), contraction strength increases with repeated nerve fiber stimulation. Patients may also have autonomic abnormalities (orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, dry mouth, blurry vision, constipation) though the pathophysiologic mechanism is unclear. There is no sensory loss in these patients.

Our patient also received an edrophonium (Tensilon) challenge test and demonstrated some mild reversal of symptoms. The application of edrophonium reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, thus increasing the amount of acetylcholine in synaptic clefts. In patients with myasthenia gravis, this causes immediate and profound clinical improvement; in LEMS, edrophonium may produce some improvement, but typically less than in myasthenia.

The most important disease in the differential diagnosis for LEMS is myasthenia gravis. In this disease, autoantibodies are directed against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (Nm) at the neuromuscular junction. These receptors are ligand-gated ion channels (choice B). Myasthenia gravis, like LEMS, also presents with muscle weakness without sensory findings. Important features of myasthenia gravis that distinguish it from LEMS include:
- No paraneoplastic association
- Prominent extraocular muscle involvement
- Weakness worsening with activity
- No autonomic findings
- Rapid and profound clinical improvement with edrophonium

Disorders of extracellular matrix molecules (choice A) such as proteoglycans can result in limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. This is an inherited condition characterized by proximal muscle weakness and wasting. It is not associated with malignancy and muscle strength would not improve with edrophonium.

Myotonic dystrophy results from congenital defects in a dystrophic myotonia protein kinase (DMPK) (choice C). Patients present with muscle wasting, cataracts, and heart block. The disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and associated with the CTG trinucleotide repeat.

Autoantibodies are usually directed at extracellular and membrane-bound proteins. Transcription factors (choice D) are intracellular and rarely the target in auto-inflammatory illnesses.

choice_explanations.A: Disorders of extracellular matrix molecules (eg, proteoglycans) can cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, an inherited condition not associated with malignancy and not improving with edrophonium.
choice_explanations.B: Postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in myasthenia gravis are ligand-gated ion channels; myasthenia gravis lacks a paraneoplastic association and worsens with activity.
choice_explanations.C: Myotonic dystrophy results from defects in dystrophic myotonia protein kinase (DMPK), with muscle wasting, cataracts, and heart block (CTG repeat, autosomal dominant).
choice_explanations.D: Transcription factors are intracellular and rarely the target in auto-inflammatory illnesses, since autoantibodies usually target extracellular and membrane-bound proteins.
choice_explanations.E: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (paraneoplastic, often small cell lung cancer); the correct answer.

fa_summary: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a paraneoplastic presynaptic disorder with autoantibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels (small cell lung cancer).

stem: A 57-year-old homosexual man comes to the physician because of a mass near his groin. Physical examination shows a painless and enlarged superficial inguinal lymph node. A biopsy of the lymph node is performed under ultrasound guidance and shows the presence of squamous cell carcinoma. Metastasis from which of the following sites has most likely occurred?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The lymph nodes of the groin are divided into superficial and deep groups. It is worth remembering that tumors from the penis, skin of the vagina, and anal canal below the dentate line drain to the superficial group of inguinal lymph nodes. Superficial inguinal lymph nodes also drain the lower extremity, gluteal region, and skin below the level of the umbilicus. Note that the tumor is a squamous cell carcinoma which indicates that the tumor arose from the mucosa located below the dentate (pectinate) line. Recall that the mucosa above the dentate (pectinate) line is simple columnar epithelium and would give rise to adenocarcinoma.

When the inguinal lymph nodes are involved, a search for the cause, focusing in the areas mentioned above should be done immediately. A melanoma from under the toe nail can be manifest as far away as the inguinal lymph nodes.

Anal squamous cell carcinoma is associated with HPV infection, especially HPV 16 and 18. These are the same high risk HPV types thought to predispose women to cervical cancer. Anal cancer risk is higher in men who have sex with men (MSM). Condylomas, or anal warts, are also caused by HPV infection, specifically HPV 6 and 11. These sometimes progress to verrucous carcinoma and/or squamous cell carcinoma.

Tumors from the colon (choices B, C and E) do not usually metastasize to easily palpable lymph nodes; they instead metastasize via the portal system to the liver.

Tumors from the rectum (choice D) do not usually metastasize to the inguinal lymph nodes. The flaw with this answer is that rectal tumors tend to travel to perirectal, internal iliac, external iliac, and sacral lymph nodes. In addition, the most common colorectal cancers are adenocarcinomas, not squamous cell carcinomas.

choice_explanations.A: Tumors of the anal canal below the dentate (pectinate) line drain to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes; the squamous cell carcinoma here metastasizes to the groin (the correct answer).
choice_explanations.B: Ascending colon tumors do not usually metastasize to palpable lymph nodes; they spread via the portal system to the liver.
choice_explanations.C: Descending colon tumors do not usually metastasize to palpable lymph nodes; they spread via the portal system to the liver.
choice_explanations.D: Rectal tumors drain to perirectal, internal iliac, external iliac, and sacral lymph nodes, and most colorectal cancers are adenocarcinomas, not squamous cell carcinomas.
choice_explanations.E: Transverse colon tumors do not usually metastasize to palpable lymph nodes; they spread via the portal system to the liver.

fa_summary: The anal canal below the dentate line drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes; squamous cell carcinoma there metastasizes to the groin.

stem: A 76-year-old man who died suddenly. He had recently complained of feelings of generalized fatigue and moderate shortness of breath. Previously performed physical examinations showed an elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) and a positive Kussmaul sign, but no further work-up was performed. Post-mortem microscopic examination of the tissues of the heart shows perivascular deposits of red extracellular material within the atria. When the tissue is stained with Congo red, the deposits show a bright green hue when viewed with polarized light. Which of the following additional findings was most likely present in this patient prior to his death?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The extracellular deposits with apple-green hue on polarization after staining with Congo red are suggestive of amyloid deposition. Amyloidosis is the accumulation of insoluble fibrillar material in tissues. Amyloidosis can be primary or secondary. Secondary amyloidosis is usually related to chronic inflammation (eg, rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis), while primary amyloidosis is often related to disorders of immune cells, such as multiple myeloma.

Cardiac amyloidosis is usually a primary amyloidosis, and it results from deposition of AL-type or ATTR-type amyloid. Cardiac amyloidosis causes restrictive cardiomyopathy, often known as "stiff heart syndrome". It may manifest with symptoms of palpitations, leg swelling, shortness of breath, and/or fatigue. However, the diagnosis is difficult to make, since findings from examination are not specific. Nevertheless, the disease may be complicated by atrial fibrillation or ventricular arrhythmias, which in some cases may be fatal.

Primary amyloidosis is characterized by the deposition of fibrillar immunoglobulin light chain (AL) systemically, or fibrillar TTR protein (ATTR) in the myocardium. Amyloid deposition in the myocardium typically presents as restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Apart from cardiac manifestations, amyloidosis is associated with a wide variety of systemic conditions resulting from extracellular deposition of amyloid fibrils. These include proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome (choice E), gastroparesis, peripheral neuropathy, various forms of organomegaly, and bleeding diathesis.

Pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles is more likely to be seen in amyloidosis than atrophy (choice A). This is a result of fluid or amyloid infiltration of the glenohumeral joint and surrounding structures.

Amyloidosis is more often associated with decreased functioning of coagulation factors rather than hypercoagulability (choice B). The bleeding tendency for these patients is thought to be due to a combination of vessel fragility (from amyloid infiltration in the vessel walls) and factor X deficiency.

Amyloidosis-induced cirrhosis (choice C) is extremely rare. More typically, amyloidosis will produce hepatomegaly due to infiltration, which may impair some of its synthetic function, but is unlikely to progress to cirrhosis.

Though amyloidosis does produce restrictive cardiomyopathy, it is unlikely to produce a pericardial knock (choice D), which is more related to constrictive pericarditis. The "knock" results from an expanding myocardium physically impinging on a fibrosed pericardium.

The table below lists a number of amyloid types and the amyloid precursor proteins associated with them.
- AA: secondary amyloidosis (autoimmune disease, chronic infection); deposition in kidney, spleen, liver, most commonly presenting as renal insufficiency/nephrotic syndrome.
- AB2M: long-term hemodialysis; most commonly musculoskeletal with deposits in muscles, ligaments, synovium, bone (resulting in arthropathy), carpal tunnel, fractures.
- ACal: medullary thyroid carcinoma (related to calcitonin); deposition in the tumor, no known clinical consequence.
- AL or ATTR: primary amyloidosis; AL is light chain deposition (systemic, includes heart and kidney); ATTR is mostly cardiac deposition.
- Amylin: type 2 diabetes; deposition in islet cells in pancreas, unclear clinical consequence.

choice_explanations.A: Pseudohypertrophy (not atrophy) of the shoulder muscles is more likely in amyloidosis, from fluid or amyloid infiltration of the glenohumeral joint and surrounding structures.
choice_explanations.B: Amyloidosis is more often associated with decreased functioning of coagulation factors (vessel fragility and factor X deficiency) rather than hypercoagulability.
choice_explanations.C: Amyloidosis-induced cirrhosis is extremely rare; amyloidosis more typically produces hepatomegaly with impaired synthetic function.
choice_explanations.D: A pericardial knock is more related to constrictive pericarditis, not amyloid restrictive cardiomyopathy.
choice_explanations.E: Proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome is a known systemic manifestation of amyloidosis (the correct answer).

fa_summary: Cardiac amyloidosis (AL/ATTR) causes restrictive cardiomyopathy and may present with proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome.

stem: A 58-year-old Japanese man, who recently came to the United States from Japan, comes to the physician because of an unintentional weight loss of 6.8 kg (15 lb) over the past 6 months.
