He has constant epigastric discomfort with no relation to meals. Rectal examination shows guaiac-positive stool. Upper endoscopy shows an irregular ulcerated mass in the antrum of the stomach with infiltration of the adjacent mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely predisposing risk factor for this disorder in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The Japanese, both in Japan and to a lesser extent in the United States, have an unusually high incidence of gastric adenocarcinoma. The Japanese diet, with its high concentration of polycyclic hydrocarbons present in smoked fish, has been strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of gastric adenocarcinoma. Nitrites are also potential carcinogens present in preserved foods, and have been shown to cause gastric cancer in laboratory animals.

The Japanese population is routinely screened for gastric adenocarcinoma (contrary to choice B), and as such is more frequently treated when the tumor is at an earlier stage. While screening can detect carcinoma at an earlier stage, it is not considered to alter the overall incidence of carcinoma, and so the lack of screening cannot be considered a "risk factor". In the United States, such screening is not routinely performed because the incidence of gastric carcinoma is much lower than in Japan.

Helicobacter pylori in the antral mucosa is highly associated with peptic ulcer disease, gastric lymphoma, and gastric adenocarcinoma. The bacterium is just as prevalent in the Japanese population as in the American population. There is a decreasing incidence of gastric adenocarcinoma in the United States, probably related to identification of H. pylori and its treatment.

Low fiber diet (choice C) is not associated with gastric adenocarcinoma. The role of fiber in cancer prevention is unclear, and the data on high-fiber diets reducing colon cancer risk is inconclusive. However, a healthy diet, including a diet high in fiber from fruits and vegetables, is probably protective against some forms of cancer. High fiber diet also protects against diverticulosis.

Ménétrier disease (or hypertrophic gastritis; choice D) is a very rare condition characterized by markedly thickened gastric rugal folds, accompanied by hyperplasia of mucous glands and protein-losing enteropathy. A few cases of gastric carcinoma arising in Ménétrier disease have been described, but this would not be the most likely scenario in an individual such as described in the question stem.

Schistosomiasis (choice E) may injure the liver, bladder, or intestines, depending upon the species, but it is not a risk factor for gastric carcinoma. Schistosoma hematobium infection is a risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

choice_explanations.A: The Japanese diet's food preservatives (nitrites) and polycyclic hydrocarbons in smoked fish have been strongly implicated in gastric adenocarcinoma (the correct answer).
choice_explanations.B: The Japanese population is routinely screened, so inadequate screening is not a risk factor; screening affects stage at diagnosis, not overall incidence.
choice_explanations.C: Low fiber diet is not associated with gastric adenocarcinoma; the role of fiber in cancer prevention is unclear.
choice_explanations.D: Ménétrier disease is a rare condition with thickened gastric rugal folds; only a few cases of gastric carcinoma have been described, not the most likely scenario.
choice_explanations.E: Schistosomiasis (eg, S. hematobium) is not a risk factor for gastric carcinoma; S. hematobium is a risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

fa_summary: Gastric adenocarcinoma is linked to dietary risk factors such as nitrites and polycyclic hydrocarbons in smoked/preserved foods (high incidence in Japan).

stem: A 29-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of premature contractions and vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound examination shows a nonviable fetus. Dilation and curettage is performed and the uterus is evacuated. Her doctor orders karyotype analysis of the aborted fetus. The result is most likely to reveal which of the following karyotypes?
explanation: The correct answer is C. Approximately half of all spontaneous abortions are of fetuses with major chromosomal defects, most commonly trisomy 16, triploidy (due to fertilization of an egg by two sperm), and 45,XO (Turner syndrome). Trisomy 16 and triploidy do not produce viable offspring, unlike 45,XO. Klinefelter syndrome (choice A) is a common genetic abnormality, involving aneuploidy of the X chromosome. Typically the embryo implants and carries to term. Individuals with Klinefelter syndrome are male, but their sexual development is impaired. Their phenotypic features include: small testes that are not able to produce sufficient amount of testosterone, resulting in delayed or incomplete puberty, gynecomastia, undescended testes, micropenis, and infertility. As adults, they tend to be taller than their peers. Trisomy 13 (choice B) is one of the more common live-birth trisomy syndromes (Patau syndrome). The major phenotypic features of trisomy 13 are the result of an early defect in development of the prechordal mesoderm, which is the origin of the midface, eye, and forebrain. These abnormalities include holoprosencephaly, absence of the olfactory nerve or bulb, sloping forehead, severe eye defects, deafness, and cleft lip and/or palate. Trisomy 18 (choice D), also known as Edwards syndrome, is the second most common autosomal trisomy observed in live births (1 in 5,500 live births). Trisomy 18 may involve any organ system. The major phenotypic features include: hypertonia, prominent occiput, small mouth, micrognathia, short sternum, horseshoe kidney, ectopic pancreatic tissue, small pelvis, and flexed fingers with overriding index fingers or third fingers. Congenital heart disease occurs in more than 50% of affected individuals. Trisomy 21 (choice E), also known as Down syndrome, is the most common chromosomal abnormality among live births (1 in 730 live births) and the most frequent form of mental retardation caused by a microscopically demonstrable chromosomal aberration. Trisomy 16 is the most common trisomy among miscarriages and is never encountered in live births.

choice_explanations.A: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is compatible with life and is not a cause of first-trimester spontaneous abortion.
choice_explanations.B: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) is a live-birth trisomy syndrome, not the most common abnormality in spontaneous abortion.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: trisomy 16 is the most common chromosomal abnormality in spontaneous abortion and is never seen in live births.
choice_explanations.D: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) is a live-birth trisomy syndrome, not the most common abnormality in spontaneous abortion.
choice_explanations.E: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is the most common chromosomal abnormality among live births, not in miscarriages.

fa_summary: Trisomy 16 is the most common chromosomal abnormality in spontaneous abortion and is never compatible with live birth.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of difficulty walking up stairs and muscle fatigue. His parents have noted a progressive decline in his motor abilities over the last 5-6 months. He has also had delays in speech development. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 88/48 mm Hg. On physical examination, the patient has enlargement of the muscles of his calves and a waddling gait. There is weakness in his proximal muscles and when arising from the floor, the patient uses his hands to push himself to an upright position. Laboratory studies show an elevated creatine kinase. The mode of inheritance of this boy's disease is most similar to which of the following inherited diseases?
explanation: The correct answer is B. The young boy is presenting with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive genetic disease caused by a defective gene that is responsible for the production of dystrophin. Dystrophin is a protein involved in stabilizing membrane proteins on muscle fibers. Loss of these proteins initiates the degeneration of muscle fibers, leading to weakness. Males usually present with proximal muscle weakness at age 2 to 3 years. Additional clinical features include dilated cardiomyopathy and scoliosis. Physical examination reveals pseudohypertrophy of the calf, a waddling gait, and hyporeflexia. Gowers sign, which is the use of a patient's hands/arms to push himself to an upright position, is usually present in patients. Laboratory values show an increase in creatine kinase due to muscle fiber degradation. Patients with DMD usually die in their late teens to twenties from respiratory insufficiency and/or dilated cardiomyopathy. The mode of inheritance of DMD is similar to that of hemophilia A. Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive genetic disease characterized by a deficiency in factor VIII. Patients with hemophilia experience spontaneous bleeding, particularly into joint spaces and muscles, and bleeding that is out of proportion to the degree of trauma. Diagnostic testing reveals an elevation in the partial thromboplastin time (PTT). Cystic fibrosis (choice A) is an autosomal recessive disease that is characterized by an abnormality in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein. The protein conducts chloride transportation in epithelial cells, especially those cells present in the lungs, pancreas, intestine, and reproductive tract. The consequence of abnormal chloride transport is viscous secretions in the lungs, pancreas, intestines, and reproductive tract. Patients present with recurrent, frequent respiratory infections including pulmonary and sinus disease; failure to thrive; bulky, foul smelling stools due to malabsorption secondary to pancreatic insufficiency; and infertility due to defective sperm transport. Huntington disease (choice C) is an autosomal dominant inherited neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia and abnormal choreiform movements. The disease is caused by a trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene. Fragile-X syndrome (choice D) is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by an expansion of a trinucleotide CGG repeat in the 5' untranslated region of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. The expansion causes a loss of function of the fragile X mental retardation protein. Males with this condition have characteristic physical features, particularly prominent in the adolescent, characterized by a long and narrow face with prominent forehead and chin, large ears, and testicular enlargement. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (choice E) is an autosomal dominant disease that is characterized by multiple physical findings including café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), and neurofibromas.

choice_explanations.A: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disease (CFTR mutation), unlike the X-linked recessive inheritance of DMD.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive, the same mode of inheritance as Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
choice_explanations.C: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant (CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene).
choice_explanations.D: Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked dominant disorder (CGG repeat expansion in FMR1).
choice_explanations.E: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant disease (café-au-lait macules, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas).

fa_summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive (dystrophin defect), the same inheritance pattern as hemophilia A.

stem: Hereditary hemochromatosis exhibits an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. The frequency of the disease in the general population is 1%. A man who is a known heterozygous carrier marries a woman from the general population. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in this population, which of the following is the probability that he and his partner will produce a child who has hemochromatosis?
explanation: The correct answer is B. One must first determine the probability that the man's mate will also be a heterozygous carrier. This is done by applying the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) rule (p² + 2pq + q² = 1), where: p² is the frequency of homozygous normal individuals; 2pq is the frequency of heterozygous individuals; q² is the frequency of homozygous affected individuals. If the frequency of affected homozygotes is 1% (q²), then the gene frequency (q) of the hemochromatosis mutation is the square root of 1%, or 0.10 (q² = 0.01, so q = √0.01, and then q = 0.1 and p = 0.9, since p + q = 1). Then, the estimated frequency of heterozygous carriers in the population, 2pq, is 2 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.18 (notice that we do not use the 2q approximation in this case because p is not approximately equal to 1). The probability that two heterozygous carriers will produce an affected offspring is 0.25 (25%), so the probability that the man mates with a carrier and the probability that they will in turn produce an affected offspring is obtained by multiplying the two probabilities together: 0.25 × 0.18 = 0.045. Additionally, there is a small chance (0.01) that the person he mates with will be a homozygote, and thus there is a chance (0.01/2) that the offspring of this mating will be affected, since the man has a 1 in 2 chance of transmitting the hemochromatosis gene. The correct answer, then, is 0.045 + 0.005 = 0.05. Exam tip: When faced with this type of problem on the exam, it is not necessary to perform all of the preceding calculations. Instead of considering all the possible matings, focus on the gametes in the population as a whole. We know that the man is heterozygous for the trait. We know that there is a 50% (0.5) chance that one of his sperm carrying an "h" will fertilize the egg. We know that if the population is in HWE, the frequency of eggs that carry h is equal to the allele frequency q, or 0.1. So the chance that he will have a child with hemochromatosis is (0.5) × (0.1) = (0.05).
fa_summary: For an autosomal recessive disease, the carrier frequency is 2pq; with q² = 0.01, q = 0.1, and the probability of an affected child is 0.5 × 0.1 = 0.05.

stem: A newborn girl is born premature at 36 weeks gestation age. The mother is 28 years old and lacked prenatal care. On physical examination, the newborn has hypotonia, microcephaly, wide set eyes with downward palpebral folds, small jaw, and a high-pitched cry. Chromosomal analysis reveals 46,XX with a large deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5. Which of the following is the most likely additional finding in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The presentation is classic for cri-du-chat syndrome, caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-). Approximately one-quarter of such patients have a ventricular septal defect. Other features of the syndrome include short stature, distorted laryngeal anatomy, profound mental retardation, microcephaly, micrognathia, wide nasal bridge, wide set eyes, and downward slanted eyes. The laryngeal malformation causes feeding and respiratory difficulties, as well as the cat-like cry, which typically disappears by age 1. Some patients survive to adulthood, but are usually institutionalized. Duodenal atresia (choice A) is seen with Down syndrome, trisomy 21. Infants with Down syndrome can also have congenital heart anomalies (VSD, ASD, AV canal defects), intellectual disability, upward slanted palpebral folds, and Hirschsprung disease. They would not have the distinct cry as seen with cri du chat. Mothers are usually older than 40 years of age (nondisjunction of chromosome 21), although Robertsonian translocations are seen in younger women who can have several children with Down syndrome. Obesity (choice B) is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome, a deletion of the functional paternal gene present on the short arm of chromosome 15. This genetic abnormality is associated with genomic imprinting (silencing) of the maternal chromosome and the lack of inheritance of the functional paternal gene. The inherited maternal Prader-Willi gene is silenced/unactivated and cannot be "turned on." Obesity would not be seen at birth, but would develop as the child grows due to an urge to constantly eat all the time. Children would also have mental retardation and fair hair and skin. NOTE: the opposite condition is Angelman syndrome in which the paternal Angelman gene is silenced with the lack of inheritance of the maternal gene. Renal cysts (choice C) are seen with childhood type autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD). Usually, both kidneys are enlarged with radially-arranged cysts that do not distort the renal capsule surface (adult type distorts). The condition is caused by a PKHD1 gene mutation associated with fibrocystin protein, which maintains the cilia of the renal tubules and hepatobiliary ducts, thus resulting in renal and hepatic cysts. Kidney enlargement and dysfunction may be present at birth with associated oligohydramnios, Potter's facies, and abnormally flexed extremities, but not with the findings seen in the question stem. Wilms tumor (choice E), also known as nephroblastoma, is associated with the WT1 gene mutation, located on the short arm of chromosome 11. It is the most common childhood tumor with peak age under 5 years of age. Wilms tumor is associated with WAGR syndrome: Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genito-urinary malformations, and mental Retardation, in which some of these are present at birth.

choice_explanations.A: Duodenal atresia is associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21), not cri-du-chat.
choice_explanations.B: Obesity is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome (chromosome 15 imprinting), not cri-du-chat.
choice_explanations.C: Renal cysts are seen with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD), not cri-du-chat.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: about one-quarter of cri-du-chat (5p deletion) patients have a ventricular septal defect.
choice_explanations.E: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is associated with WT1 mutation on chromosome 11, not cri-du-chat.

fa_summary: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-) and features a cat-like cry, microcephaly, and cardiac defects including VSD.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of excessive clumsiness. He often loses his balance, falls down, and has difficulty rising. He also has difficulty running, and climbing stairs. Physical examination shows enlarged calves and wasting of thigh muscles. A molecular genetic test shows defective dystrophin cytoskeletal protein. Which of the following individuals in the patient's family is most likely to also have this disease?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The disease is Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive muscular disease usually caused by a deletion involving the dystrophin gene. This defect produces accelerated muscle breakdown, leading initially to proximal muscle weakness, then later to generalized weakness that typically begins before age 5. A feature of X-linked recessive diseases is that carrier mothers pass the disease to half their sons; affected fathers can pass the abnormal allele to their daughters but not their sons. Since the mother is presumably normal (because the disease is X-linked), she must be a carrier to have an affected son, and there is a good chance that the grandmother is a carrier; therefore, the mother's brother (maternal uncle) may also have the disease. The father's (choice A) side of the family, including the father's brother (choice B), most likely does not carry the defective gene (since they themselves would most likely be affected; and furthermore, the father passes his Y chromosome to his son, not his X chromosome; therefore, he cannot pass the gene to a son). It would be extremely unlikely for a carrier female to marry an affected male (and the question does not mention any similar symptoms in the father). The patient's mother (choice C) and possibly his sister (choice E) are carriers of, but not affected by, the defective gene. In X-linked recessive diseases, carrier mothers pass the disease to half their sons. Affected fathers can have carrier daughters, but the daughters will not be affected.

choice_explanations.A: The father passes his Y chromosome to his son, so he cannot transmit an X-linked recessive disease to a son.
choice_explanations.B: The paternal side of the family most likely does not carry the defective gene.
choice_explanations.C: The mother is a carrier of, but not affected by, the defective gene.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: a maternal uncle (mother's brother) of an affected boy may also have the disease, because the mutation is X-linked recessive.
choice_explanations.E: A sister may be a carrier of, but is not affected by, the defective gene.

fa_summary: In X-linked recessive disease (e.g., Duchenne muscular dystrophy), carrier mothers transmit the disease to half their sons; a maternal uncle may be affected.

stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after sustaining a fracture of his right ulna in a fall. His parents are concerned because he has had several fractures of his bones over the past 9 years. Physical examination shows a bluish tinge to the sclerae. Which of the following best explains these findings?
explanation: The correct answer is E. The clinical presentation strongly suggests osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder affecting type 1 collagen. The most common mutations in OI are in the gene for type 1 collagen and result in abnormal collagen conformation or post-translational modification. This patient's presentation is a classic example of pleiotropy, which refers to the multiple, often seemingly unrelated, physical effects caused by a single genotype. Clinical manifestations of osteogenesis imperfecta include excess or atypical fractures, scoliosis, basilar skull deformities, blue sclerae, opalescent teeth, and laxity of ligaments and skin. Children with OI are often misdiagnosed with child abuse prior to discovery of the disorder. Allelic heterogeneity (choice A) refers to different alleles at the same gene locus resulting in a similar phenotype. This is observed in osteogenesis imperfecta, but this question asks about the findings of multiple unrelated phenotypes resulting from a gene lesion in an individual patient. A gain-of-function mutation (choice B) is inconsistent with the observed pathology. Locus heterogeneity (choice C) refers to mutations at different gene loci resulting in the same phenotype. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a good example of a disease in which locus heterogeneity is observed, because genes for type 1 procollagen are found on chromosome 7 and on chromosome 17. Mutations in either gene locus can result in imperfect formation of the type 1 collagen protein and OI. Though seen in OI, this principle does not explain the co-occurrence of fractures and blue sclerae, asked in this question. A single mutation at either the chromosome 7 or chromosome 17 locus is sufficient to cause the disease, so multiple mutations (choice D) do not explain the pattern. Pleiotropy refers to the multiple, often seemingly unrelated phenotypic effects exerted by a single mutation and thus describes the two features, blue sclera and multiple fractures, observed in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta.

choice_explanations.A: Allelic heterogeneity means different mutations in the same locus produce the same disease (e.g., β-thalassemia).
choice_explanations.B: A gain-of-function mutation is inconsistent with the pathology of osteogenesis imperfecta.
choice_explanations.C: Locus heterogeneity means mutations at different loci produce the same disease (OI involves COL1A1 on chromosome 17 and COL1A2 on chromosome 7); it does not explain the co-occurrence of fractures and blue sclerae.
choice_explanations.D: A single mutation at either collagen locus is sufficient to cause the disease, so multiple mutations do not explain the pattern.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: pleiotropy describes the multiple, seemingly unrelated effects (fractures and blue sclerae) of a single mutation.

fa_summary: Pleiotropy is the production of multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic effects (e.g., fractures and blue sclerae in osteogenesis imperfecta) by a single gene mutation.

stem: A 26-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because he has poor eye contact and keeps flapping his hands and chewing on them. He has delayed social, motor, and language skills. Physical examination shows a long narrow face, large ears, and flat feet. Which of the following best explains the findings seen in the boy?
explanation: The correct answer is A. The features described are typical of the familial form of intellectual disability known as fragile X syndrome. This disorder is the most common heritable cause of intellectual disability, impacting approximately 1:2000 males. Striking features of this disease are that the clinical features tend to worsen with each successive generation and that males are usually much more severely affected than females, although nearly 50% of females with the full mutation demonstrate characteristic physical features and developmental delay. The explanation apparently involves a region of DNA (FMR1 gene) on the X chromosome that normally contains 6 to 54 tandem repeats of the sequence CGG. Individual carriers of fragile X syndrome have a premutation that can contain up to 200 CGG repeats. Clinically affected individuals have full mutations with 200 to 4000 repeats of the CGG sequence. The expansion leads to methylation of the 5' region, an epigenetic change of gene expression, and gene silencing. Amplification of premutations to full mutations of the FMR1 gene is much more likely to occur during oogenesis than spermatogenesis. This is in contrast to another trinucleotide disorder, Huntington disease, in which paternal amplification is more prominent. Genomic imprinting (choice B) is a phenomenon in which the phenotypic expression of a gene differs if the gene is inherited from the mother rather than the father. An example of this effect is Angelman ("happy puppet") syndrome.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: fragile X syndrome is caused by expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene, leading to methylation and silencing of the gene.
choice_explanations.B: Genomic imprinting is a parent-of-origin effect (e.g., Angelman syndrome), not the mechanism of fragile X syndrome.

fa_summary: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, caused by CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 with methylation and silencing of the gene.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department at 22 weeks' gestation because of premature contractions and vaginal bleeding. She has a spontaneous abortion. A review of her records show that she has had three other pregnancies that ended with spontaneous abortion. Examination of the aborted fetus shows mature fetal tissue that contains Barr bodies. Which of the following is the most likely describes the fetus?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The Barr body, or X chromatin body, is an inactivated X chromosome seen as a small, perinuclear, dark-staining dot in somatic cells with two or more X chromosomes. Barr bodies are seen in any individual born with at least two X chromosomes, including normal females. 47,XXY, the classic karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome, is defined as male hypogonadism due to the presence of a Y chromosome and two or more X chromosomes. As in normal females, one of the X chromosomes becomes a Barr body in Klinefelter syndrome. Classic Turner syndrome females (choice A) and genotypically normal males (choice D) have only one X chromosome. Thus, no X chromosome is inactivated, and somatic cells do not show any Barr bodies. 47,XY,+18 is the karyotype of an Edwards syndrome male (choice B) fetus. Although this trisomic phenotype is associated with a characteristic syndrome of physical abnormalities, there is no programmed inactivation of the extra chromosome 18. Since the fetus is male, there is no Barr body formation from X-chromosome inactivation. XYY syndrome (choice E) is not associated with inactivation of any X chromosome because there is only one X. Barr bodies are not present. Like a trisomy involving any of the non-sex-linked chromosomes, the duplicated Y chromosome is not inactivated. If the embryo contains two or more X chromosomes, the extra ones will be inactivated until only one X chromosome remains active. In normal males and in aneuploidies with one X chromosome, Barr bodies are not formed.

choice_explanations.A: Classic Turner syndrome (45,XO) has only one X chromosome, so no Barr bodies form.
choice_explanations.B: 47,XY,+18 (Edwards syndrome male) has only one X chromosome; the extra chromosome 18 is not inactivated, so no Barr body forms.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) has two X chromosomes, so one is inactivated as a Barr body.
choice_explanations.D: A normal male (46,XY) has only one X chromosome and therefore no Barr body.
choice_explanations.E: XYY syndrome has only one X chromosome, so no Barr body is present.

fa_summary: Barr bodies form whenever two or more X chromosomes are present (normal females and Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY); they are absent in Turner syndrome and normal males.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with a history of intellectual disability is brought to the emergency department by her caregivers because of a 2-week history of fever, chills and productive cough. They also report that she has been showing signs of memory loss and depression recently. She is admitted to the hospital, and five days later she dies, despite appropriate treatment. Neuropathologic examination of her brain shows neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. Genetic analysis of this patient would most likely reveal which of the following?
explanation: The correct answer is C. Features of Down syndrome (trisomy 21, 47,+21) in children include intellectual disability (formerly mental retardation), epicanthal folds, dysplastic ears, hypotonia, a horizontal palmar crease (simian crease), redundant neck skin, and a short trunk. Congenital heart disease is present in about 1/3 of liveborn Down syndrome (DS) infants. Additional malformations are more common in DS, including duodenal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula. There is a 15-fold increase in leukemia. Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) develop a clinical dementia with clinical and pathologic characteristics that are virtually identical to Alzheimer disease (AD). Autopsy findings include intraneural neurofibrillary tangles, extracellular neuritic plaques, amyloid beta (Abeta) protein in senile plaques, and amyloid angiopathy. There are some differences because this neuropathology is superimposed on brain pathology unique to DS. One important clinical difference is the early age of onset of AD with DS patients. There is no treatment and prognosis is poor. AD causes a sharp decline in survival in DS patients older than 45 years. Many genes coding for proteins likely involved in AD development such as amyloid precursor protein (APP) and superoxide dismutase (SOD-1) are located in chromosome 21. The overexpression of these genes because of trisomy 21 is likely responsible for the early AD. Patients with the other listed conditions are not particularly prone to early AD: Common features of 45,XO (choice A), also known as Turner syndrome, include short stature, webbed neck, lymphedema in hands and feet, skeletal abnormalities, congenital heart defects, and infertility. Individuals show learning disabilities, though intelligence is usually normal. 47,+13 (choice B), also known as Patau syndrome or trisomy 13, is characterized by severe mental retardation, microcephaly, microphthalmia, polydactyly, cleft lip and palate, renal defects, and cardiac abnormalities. Affected infants typically die before the age of 1 year. Patients with 47,XXY, or Klinefelter syndrome (choice D), are male and have impaired sexual development. They typically have small testes that are not able to produce sufficient amounts of testosterone, resulting in delayed or incomplete puberty, gynecomastia, undescended testes, micropenis, and infertility. As adults, they tend to be taller than their peers. Fragile X syndrome (choice E) can occur in males and females, although females often have milder symptoms than males. It is associated with enlarged testes after puberty (macroorchidism, in males) as well as intellectual disability, large ears, prominent jaw and forehead. The condition is unusual in that it is related to expansion of a CGG repeat sequence located on the X chromosome. Fragile X syndrome is caused by mutation in the FMR1 gene.

choice_explanations.A: Turner syndrome (45,XO) features short stature, webbed neck, and infertility; it is not associated with early Alzheimer disease.
choice_explanations.B: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) causes severe malformations and death in infancy; it is not associated with early Alzheimer disease.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: trisomy 21 (47,+21) causes Down syndrome, which is associated with early-onset Alzheimer disease (APP and SOD-1 on chromosome 21).
choice_explanations.D: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes hypogonadism and tall stature; it is not associated with early Alzheimer disease.
choice_explanations.E: Fragile X syndrome (FMR1 CGG expansion) causes intellectual disability and macroorchidism, not early Alzheimer disease.

fa_summary: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is associated with early-onset Alzheimer disease because chromosome 21 carries the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene.

stem: An investigator is evaluating a large number of families with male and female children that have a disease caused by a small deletion on chromosome 15. In all patients affected by the disease, the deletion is inherited from the father. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this phenomenon?
explanation: The correct answer is A. Genomic imprinting refers to the differential expression of genes inherited from the father and the mother. Imprinting is a genomic "silencing" in which genes on the maternal chromosome are not expressed (maternal imprinting) or genes on the paternal chromosome are not expressed (paternal imprinting). If a defect occurs on the paternal chromosome in a gene that is maternally imprinted, then the offspring will express the defective gene and be at risk to show the disease. For example, Prader-Willi syndrome results from a deletion at a specific gene locus on the paternally derived chromosome 15 that is imprinted on the maternally derived chromosome. Interestingly, a deletion of a paternally imprinted gene in the same locus in the maternally derived chromosome 15 results in Angelman syndrome ("Happy Puppet syndrome"). This difference reflects the fact that the genes deleted in Prader-Willi syndrome are normally active only in the paternally transmitted chromosome while the genes whose deletion causes Angelman syndrome are normally active only in the maternally transmitted chromosome. In mitochondrial inheritance (choice B), only an affected mother can transmit the disease phenotype: the offspring of affected males are always unaffected. The other modes of inheritance would influence the relative proportions of affected individuals who belong to one gender or the other. Sex-dependent penetrance (choice C) occurs when there is differential penetrance depending on sex. X-linked recessive inheritance (choice D) will show a disproportionate number of males affected irrespective of the father's genotype. Y-linked inheritance (choice E) would be expected to only affect males, with no transmission from father to daughters.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: genomic imprinting means expression of a gene depends on the parent of origin; a paternally inherited deletion of a maternally imprinted gene causes disease.
choice_explanations.B: In mitochondrial inheritance only an affected mother transmits the disease phenotype.
choice_explanations.C: Sex-dependent penetrance depends on sex, not on the parent of origin of the deletion.
choice_explanations.D: X-linked recessive inheritance affects a disproportionate number of males regardless of the father's genotype.
choice_explanations.E: Y-linked inheritance affects only males and would not be transmitted from father to daughters.

fa_summary: Genomic imprinting causes parent-of-origin effects: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of the paternally derived (active) genes on chromosome 15.

stem: An 8-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician for follow-up of intellectual disability and hyperactivity. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse is 89/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 108/58 mm Hg. Physical examination shows the patient has a long, narrow face, prominent forehead and jaw, large testicles and large ears. His mother has mild intellectual disability but there is no other family history of intellectual disability. Detection of which of the following genetic abnormalities would most likely be diagnostic?

options.text: Absence of expression in paternal chromosome 15q11.2-13
Expansion of a trinucleotide CGG repeat in the 5' untranslated region
Genetic defect in the gene responsible for the production of dystrophin

explanation: The correct answer is B. The patient is presenting with Fragile X syndrome, which is the most frequently inherited form of intellectual disability. Fragile-X syndrome is an X-linked dominant genetic disorder caused by an expansion of trinucleotide CGG repeat in the 5' untranslated region of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. The expansion causes a loss of function of the fragile X mental retardation protein. Males with this condition have characteristic physical features, particularly prominent in adolescent, characterized by a long and narrow face with prominent forehead and chin, large ears, and testicular enlargement. They also characteristically have problems with hyperactivity and hyper-arousal. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is found in a majority of affected males. Females with the condition may present with normal intelligence or may present with the classic manifestations, but most are often less severely affected than males due to the variability in X-inactivation. An absence of expression in paternal chromosome 15q11.2-13 (choice A) is the cause of Prader-Willi syndrome. Patients with Prader-Willi syndrome present with hypotonia and feeding difficulties as a neonate that progress to hyperphagia and an insatiable appetite that may cause secondary co-morbidities due to morbid obesity. Patients with Prader-Willi syndrome typically have intellectual disability. Physical characteristics include small hands and feet, short stature, and almond shaped eyes. A genetic defect in the gene that is responsible for the production of dystrophin (choice C) is the cause of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Males usually present with proximal muscle weakness at age two to three years. Additional physical examination features include pseudohypertrophy of the calf, a waddling gait, and hyporeflexia. Trisomy 21 or three copies of chromosome 21 (choice D) is the cause of Down syndrome. Patients with Down syndrome typically have some component of intellectual disability. These patients typically have upslanting palpebral fissures, a flattened facial profile, hypotonia, short, broad hands, a single palmar crease, and a gap between the first and second toe. Patients with Down syndrome are at risk for congenital heart disease, hypothyroidism, and gastrointestinal issues. A karyotype demonstrating XXY (choice E) is characteristic of Klinefelter syndrome. Patients with Klinefelter syndrome have mild intellectual disability, tall stature, and hypogonadism and gynecomastia. Individuals will demonstrate characteristic decrease in serum testosterone and increase in follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH).

choice_explanations.A: Absence of expression of paternal chromosome 15q11.2-13 causes Prader-Willi syndrome (hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity), not fragile X.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1.
choice_explanations.C: A dystrophin gene defect causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy (proximal weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy).
choice_explanations.D: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome (upslanting palpebral fissures, single palmar crease, congenital heart disease).
choice_explanations.E: 47,XXY causes Klinefelter syndrome (tall stature, hypogonadism, gynecomastia).

fa_summary: Fragile X syndrome (CGG repeat expansion in FMR1) presents with intellectual disability, long narrow face, large ears, and macroorchidism.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of concerns for his apparent developmental delay and behavioral issues at school. Physical examination shows an elongated face with large, protruding ears, flat feet, and hypotonia. His mother states that his brother has a similar condition, although his three sisters appear to be unaffected. This child's condition is most likely caused by which of the following genetic defects?

options.text: CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion on a sex chromosome

explanation: The correct answer is A. This child possesses the traits associated with fragile X syndrome. This disorder is characterized by developmental delay and behavioral issues, as well as the physical features of an elongated face, large, protruding ears, flat feet, and hypotonia. Fragile X syndrome is caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion of the sequence CGG in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR-1 gene, located on the X chromosome. Genomic imprinting on chromosome 15 (choice B) is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome. This disorder is associated with intellectual delay, poor physical coordination, delayed puberty, and excessive weight gain. It is due to deletion of several genes on the paternal copy of chromosome 15. Another disorder, known as Angelman syndrome, is associated with deletion of genes on the maternal copy of chromosome 15. Microdeletion on chromosome 22 (choice C) causes DiGeorge syndrome, which is the most common microdeletion syndrome. A deletion of 22q11.2 results in cardiac abnormalities, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia/hypoparathyroidism. A translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (choice D) t(9;22)(q34;q11) results in the fusion of the genes encoding the proteins BCR and ABL kinase, resulting in the creation of an oncoprotein known as BCR-ABL. This translocation event is characteristic of Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Trisomy of chromosome 21 (choice E) results in Down syndrome. Individuals with this disorder are intellectually disabled, commonly have congenital heart defects, and are at increased risk for the development of leukemia. In addition, they have very distinct facial features including single palmar crease, slanted eyes, large, protruding tongue, and short stature.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR-1 gene on the X chromosome.
choice_explanations.B: Genomic imprinting on chromosome 15 is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome (paternal deletion) and Angelman syndrome (maternal deletion).
choice_explanations.C: Microdeletion of 22q11.2 causes DiGeorge syndrome (cardiac defects, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia).
choice_explanations.D: t(9;22) creates the BCR-ABL oncoprotein characteristic of chronic myeloid leukemia.
choice_explanations.E: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome (single palmar crease, slanted eyes, congenital heart defects, leukemia risk).

fa_summary: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR-1 gene on the X chromosome; physical features include an elongated face and large, protruding ears.

stem: A normal 30-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish woman comes to the physician with her husband for genetic counseling. She states that she has two siblings who died from Tay-Sachs disease. She states that there is no other family history of the disease that she is aware of and that her parents come from a small town and may be first cousins. Which of the following is the risk that this woman is a heterozygous carrier of the disease-causing mutation?

options.text: Not elevated above that of the general population

explanation: The correct answer is C. Tay-Sachs disease (TSD) is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by a deficiency in hexosaminidase A. Clinically, patients are identified early in life and exhibit developmental delay, progressive neurodegeneration, and have a cherry red macula on retinal examination. When approaching this question, we can start by identifying that because two of the woman's siblings had Tay-Sachs disease, her parents must both be carriers. This clearly elevates her risk above the general population and excludes choice E. Her risk of inheriting one copy of the disease gene at conception is 1/2 (choice B). However, the fact that she is phenotypically normal at age 30 means that she cannot have inherited copies of the disease gene from both parents. Therefore, the probability that she is a carrier of the gene for the condition is 2/3. Three possible scenarios are then possible: She inherited no copies of the mutation; she inherited a copy from her father; she inherited a copy from her mother. Each of these three possibilities is equally likely, and two of them lead to heterozygosity. Thus, the risk that she is a carrier is 2/3. This is illustrated in the Punnett square below. For an autosomal recessive condition, the parents are obligate carriers. Two of the three remaining possibilities are carriers of the trait; one must have TSD, so this possibility is eliminated.

choice_explanations.A: 1/4 is not the carrier risk for an unaffected sibling of an affected individual.
choice_explanations.B: 1/2 is the risk at conception of inheriting one disease allele, but she is known to be unaffected.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: an unaffected individual with an affected sibling has a 2/3 probability of being a carrier for an autosomal recessive disease.
choice_explanations.D: 3/4 is the risk of inheriting at least one disease allele, not the carrier risk among unaffected individuals.
choice_explanations.E: Because both parents are obligate carriers, her risk is clearly elevated above the general population.

fa_summary: An unaffected individual with an affected sibling has a 2/3 probability of being a carrier for an autosomal recessive disease such as Tay-Sachs.

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to a geneticist because of concerns about continued poor performance in school. His mother states that two years earlier, another physician had obtained a blood sample to test him for genetic anomalies, but the results were negative. His mother is requesting additional genetic testing. A skin biopsy is taken, and his skin cells are assessed for chromosomal abnormalities. It is found that his skin cells are positive for trisomy 21. Which of the following genetic mechanisms is most likely to account for the discrepancy between the two test results?
explanation: The correct answer is C. Down syndrome (DS) is primarily caused by three genetic variants: Trisomy of chromosome 21 due to meiotic nondisjunction, 95% of DS; chromosomal translocation that results in 3 copies of the critical region for Down syndrome: Robertsonian translocation; genetic material from chromosome 21 becomes attached to another chromosome (usually chromosome 14), resulting in 46 chromosomes with 1 chromosome having extra material from chromosome 21 attached, 3-4% of DS types; mosaicism: an event that takes place after fertilization, results in 2 cell lines: one with a free trisomy (47,+21) and one with a normal karyotype (46), 1-3% of DS. This patient has trisomy 21 mosaicism. Mosaicism is the term used when cells with more than one type of genetic constitution are present in the same organism. This occurs when nondisjunction of chromosome 21 occurs during mitosis (rather than meiosis) in one of the early cell divisions. Trisomy 21 mosaicism (47,+21/46), in which some cells will have 46 chromosomes and some will have 47 chromosomes, occurs in 1 to 3% of cases of Down syndrome. This form of DS can be more difficult to diagnose as it can occur in one cell line or across cell lines. The diagnosis of this form of Down syndrome is often later, and some individuals may be diagnosed as late as adulthood or possibly remain undiagnosed. The degree to which the individual expresses the characteristics of the syndrome depends on the number of cells involved and their distribution. Most individuals have developmental delay, but can range from the severity of trisomy 21 to not requiring special education. Balanced translocation (choice A) does not produce features of any syndrome because critical genetic material is not lost, although progeny may be affected when the translocated chromosome is added to a complement of otherwise normal chromosomes. Mitotic loss during embryogenesis (choice B) would result in monosomy mosaicism for the chromosome involved. Reciprocal or non-Robertsonian translocations (choice D) do not produce Down syndrome. These types of translocations may occur by chance at the somatic cell level throughout life. A classic example is Philadelphia chromosome, involving the long arms of chromosome 9 and 22. This translocation t(9;22) creates the bcr-abl fusion protein, which causes chronic myelogenous leukemia. Some cases of Down syndrome are caused by a Robertsonian translocation (choice E) in a parent between chromosome 21 and another chromosome, usually chromosome 14. A parent produces some gametes that have extra chromosome 21 material t(14;21). When this germ cell combines with a non-mutated germ cell from the other parent, the resulting offspring will have three copies of that fragment of chromosome 21 (two normal 21's and a third piece of 21 fused to chromosome 14). This produces the full-blown Down syndrome phenotype in that child, with a karyotype of 46,XY,t(14;21). This is different than the child in the question with mosaic DS; some of his cells (blood cells) have 46 chromosomes and some of his cells (skin cells) have 47 chromosomes.

choice_explanations.A: A balanced translocation does not produce features of a syndrome because critical genetic material is not lost.
choice_explanations.B: Mitotic loss during embryogenesis would result in monosomy mosaicism, not trisomy 21.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: mosaicism (a postfertilization mitotic nondisjunction) produces two cell lines (46 and 47,+21), so blood can be normal while skin cells show trisomy 21.
choice_explanations.D: Reciprocal (non-Robertsonian) translocations do not produce Down syndrome.
choice_explanations.E: A Robertsonian translocation causes translocation Down syndrome, but would not explain normal blood cells with trisomic skin cells.

fa_summary: Mosaicism is the presence of genetically distinct cell lines in one individual, arising from a postfertilization mitotic error; different tissues can show different karyotypes (e.g., trisomy 21 mosaicism).

stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. She has a history of developmental delay, particularly with language acquisition, and a seizure disorder. Her parents report she has a strange affect characterized by excessive laughter at inappropriate times and describe her as "happy." During the examination, she flaps her hands several times. Cytogenetic studies show an apparently normal genotype with 46 chromosomes. Which of the following best explains this patient's condition?

options.text: A point mutation in an autosome
Random inactivation of the X chromosome

explanation: The correct answer is D. The child described is exhibiting the features of Angelman (happy puppet) syndrome. This disorder is generally caused by a deletion of band q12 in the maternal copy of chromosome 15, i.e. [del (15)(q11q13)]. A similar deletion in the paternal chromosome 15 produces Prader-Willi syndrome. The disparate expression of the effects of deletions in the paternal vs. the maternal chromosomes is called genomic imprinting, and implies that the same genetic loci are expressed quite differently in maternal and paternal chromosomes. In genomic imprinting, the maternal or the paternal gene is "silenced" and only the gene inherited from the other parent is expressed. If the expressed gene is defective, then offspring can show a disease phenotype related to the gene defect. Angelman syndrome can also occur if the embryo receives two copies of the paternal chromosome 15 (uniparental disomy). Uniparental disomy occurs when a person receives two copies of a chromosome or part of a chromosome from one parent, but no copies from the other parent. Although Angelman syndrome is rarely caused by uniparental disomy, 30% of Prader-Willi syndrome cases are due to uniparental disomy. Point mutation in autosomes (choice A) has not been associated with Angelman syndrome. Confined placental mosaicism (choice B) is due to a mutation occurring within trophoblast or extraembryonic precursor cells of the inner cell mass and is an important cause of intrauterine growth retardation. Expansion of a trinucleotide repeat (choice C) is associated with fragile X syndrome and Huntington disease. Random inactivation of the X chromosome (choice E) occurs normally, as postulated in the Lyon hypothesis. Genomic imprinting means that the expression of a gene depends on the gender of the parent donating the gene. Angelman syndrome, associated with a microdeletion on chromosome 15, is an example of a defect in a maternally derived gene. Prader-Willi syndrome can be associated with microdeletion on chromosome 15 where the gene involved is expressed on the paternally-derived chromosome. Angelman syndrome, sometimes called the "happy puppet syndrome", is associated with severe developmental delay, especially in language acquisition, and an ataxia.

choice_explanations.A: A point mutation in an autosome has not been associated with Angelman syndrome.
choice_explanations.B: Confined placental mosaicism causes intrauterine growth retardation.
choice_explanations.C: Expansion of a trinucleotide repeat is associated with fragile X syndrome and Huntington disease.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: Angelman syndrome is generally caused by a microdeletion of the maternal copy of chromosome 15 (15q11-13).
choice_explanations.E: Random inactivation of the X chromosome occurs normally (Lyon hypothesis).

fa_summary: Angelman syndrome ("happy puppet") results from loss of the maternally derived active genes at chromosome 15q11-13 (imprinting), causing severe intellectual disability, inappropriate laughter, and seizures.

stem: A couple goes to a genetic counselor for family planning advice. Both male and female are of northern European ancestry and are concerned about offspring with cystic fibrosis, even though neither has a family history of the disease. The counselor learns that they recently heard of a family in their community whose son has cystic fibrosis. The counselor explains that the incidence of cystic fibrosis among populations of northern European ancestry is 1/2500. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, which of the following is the likelihood that this woman is a carrier for the cystic fibrosis gene mutation?
explanation: The correct answer is A. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the population incidence of carriers for a given autosomal recessive disease is 2pq, using the following equation: p² + 2pq + q² = 1. In this equation: p² equals the frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype; 2pq equals the frequency of the carrier genotype; q² equals the frequency of the affected genotype. Since there is no family history of cystic fibrosis, we can assume that the allele frequency of the individuals in this vignette is equal to that of the general population. Thus, if q² = 1/2500 then q = 1/50 and p = 49/50 (~1). Since the carrier frequency is equal to 2pq, the likelihood that the woman is a carrier for cystic fibrosis is 2(1/50)(~1) = 1/25. Assumptions of the Hardy-Weinberg equation are random mating, a population in equilibrium, and no selection for or against individual genotypes. For an autosomal recessive condition, the gene frequency and heterozygote frequencies can be calculated if the frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype is known. The carrier frequency is equal to 2pq or approximately 2q if the disease is rare and p ≈ 1.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: with q² = 1/2500, q = 1/50, and the carrier frequency is 2pq ≈ 2/50 = 1/25.
choice_explanations.B: 1/50 is the allele frequency (q), not the carrier frequency.
choice_explanations.C: 2/2500 is not the correct carrier frequency calculation.
choice_explanations.D: 1/2500 is the disease incidence (q²), not the carrier frequency.
choice_explanations.E: (1/2500)² is the square of the incidence and is not the carrier frequency.

fa_summary: For an autosomal recessive disease, the carrier frequency is 2pq; with an incidence of 1/2500 (q ≈ 1/50), the carrier frequency is approximately 1/25.

stem: A 2-year-old boy with Down syndrome participates in a study to determine the mechanism underlying the trisomy in their son. DNA is obtained from both parents and the child. A microsatellite marker adjacent to the centromere of chromosome 21 allows the researchers to track the inheritance of the chromosome. Four alleles at a locus are seen: A, B, C, and D. The father is found to have AC genotype; the mother BD genotype; and the affected child ABC. Nondisjunction most likely occurred in which of the following?

options.text: The child during the first mitotic division

explanation: The correct answer is B. The microsatellite marker detects a region near the centromere of chromosome 21. The region around the centromere exhibits a phenomenon called crossover suppression. Since genetic exchange cannot happen in this area, the probe is a reliable marker for the individual chromosomes. During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes that form the tetrad should separate, leading to haploid daughter cells containing a single chromosome composed of two sister chromatids (which are two identical copies of the same chromosome). During meiosis II, the sister chromatids should separate. One is able to determine that the nondisjunction event occurred in the father because the progeny received only a single allele from his mother (B) and two alleles from his father (A and C). The nondisjunction event occurred during paternal meiosis I because the progeny received two different alleles/chromosomes (A and C) from the father. This implies that alleles from each of the homologous chromosome 21's were inherited. If the nondisjunction event occurred during paternal meiosis II, the progeny would have received two copies of either the A or the C allele. Choice A (the child during the first mitotic division): If a nondisjunction event of chromosome 21 occurs early in development, a child that is likely to be a mosaic for trisomy 21 results. In addition, the child should only have two different alleles at this marker, not three (ABC). Approximately 1% of children with trisomy 21 exhibit mosaicism. Since some of their cells are normal, these individuals, as a population, tend to have a milder trisomy 21 phenotype. It is important to remember that each individual's phenotype will depend on which cells actually have each genotype; therefore, their phenotype can range from mild to severe. Choice C (the father during meiosis II): if the father had failure in meiosis II, either an AA gamete or a CC gamete would be produced, and the mother would pass a B gamete or a D gamete. Various combinations could produce BAA, DAA, BCC, or DCC. Choice D (the mother during meiosis I): If a BD woman had a failure in meiosis I, a BD gamete would be produced. When fertilized by the man's A or C sperm, a child that was ABD or BCD would result. Choice E (the mother during meiosis II): If a BD woman's sister chromatids failed to disjoin during meiosis II, BB or DD gametes would result. When fertilized by the A or C male's sperm, a child that was BBA, BBC, DDA, or DDC would result. If parental chromosomes can be distinguished by cytologic or molecular methods, it is possible to determine in which division and in which parent a nondisjunctional event occurred. Homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis I. Sister chromatids separate during meiosis II. Nondisjunction events during mitosis often result in mosaicism in the progeny.

choice_explanations.A: Early mitotic nondisjunction would produce mosaicism, and the child would show only two alleles at this marker, not three (ABC).
choice_explanations.B: Correct: receiving two different paternal alleles (A and C) indicates failure of homologous chromosomes to separate in paternal meiosis I.
choice_explanations.C: Paternal meiosis II failure would give two copies of one paternal allele (AA or CC), not A and C.
choice_explanations.D: Maternal meiosis I failure would produce a BD gamete, giving ABD or BCD.
choice_explanations.E: Maternal meiosis II failure would produce BB or DD gametes, giving BBA, BBC, DDA, or DDC.

fa_summary: Homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis I and sister chromatids during meiosis II; inheriting two different alleles of a centromeric marker indicates meiosis I nondisjunction.

stem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal examination. The patient says that her husband is affected with an inherited disease. Further evaluation reveals that the husband's father is affected with the disease as is his paternal aunt and her son. There are many generations of affected individuals in the husband's family. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.text: The child will not be affected
The inheritance risk cannot be determined until the sex of the child is known
There is a 25% chance of the child having the disease
There is a 50% chance of the child having the disease

explanation: The correct answer is E. The question points out the use of an algorithm for determining the mode of inheritance in a pedigree. Since there is female-to-male transmission (paternal aunt and her son), then the disease gene could be either X-linked or autosomal. Since there is male-to-male transmission (patient's father to the patient), the disease cannot be X-linked. Therefore, the disease gene must be autosomal. If multiple and successive generations are affected, the disease is most likely autosomal dominant and therefore has a 50% average recurrence risk for any progeny if one parent is affected. If multiple generations are not affected, the disease is more likely to be transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner, with a 25% recurrence risk if both parents are carriers. It is not possible to say that the child absolutely will be affected (choice A) or absolutely will not be affected (choice B). It is not necessary to know the sex of the child (choice C) since transmission of the disease is independent of the sex of the progeny. The chance of the child having the disease is not 25% (choice D) but 50%. In autosomal dominant inheritance, both female-to-male and male-to-female transmission are present, and multiple generations are affected, except in cases of incomplete penetrance. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of getting the disease. If both parents are heterozygous, the recurrence risk is 75%, assuming all genotypes are equally fit.

choice_explanations.A: It is not possible to say the child absolutely will be affected.
choice_explanations.B: It is not possible to say the child absolutely will not be affected.
choice_explanations.C: Transmission of an autosomal dominant disease is independent of the sex of the child.
choice_explanations.D: A 25% recurrence risk applies to autosomal recessive inheritance when both parents are carriers.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: with multiple affected generations and male-to-male transmission, the disease is autosomal dominant, giving a 50% recurrence risk with one affected parent.

fa_summary: With male-to-male transmission and multiple affected generations, the disease is autosomal dominant; each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of being affected.

stem: A 42-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician for a follow-up visit to receive the results of an amniocentesis. The physician explains that her child has a chromosomal abnormality that will likely result in intellectual disabilities and an increased risk for several other conditions including congenital heart defects and acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Her child most likely has which of the following chromosomal abnormalities?
explanation: The correct answer is C. In addition to the well-known intellectual disabilities associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21), affected individuals have an increased incidence of a variety of medical problems. Acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML) is seen in newborns and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is seen in older children. In addition, congenital malformations of the cardiac system are common (40-50% of cases), and include atrial and ventricular septal defects, tetralogy of Fallot, and patent ductus arteriosus. The development of the hypopharynx is often poor, predisposing to both aspiration pneumonia and obstruction by enlarged adenoids. Nearly all boys are infertile; girls are usually subfertile but can become pregnant. Epilepsy affects up to 10% of children with Down syndrome. On occasion, the malformed head and neck region can undergo atlantoaxial dislocation, causing a sudden or progressive quadriparesis. Other malformations that occur with lower frequency include duodenal atresia and imperforate anus. Acquired autoimmune hypothyroidism is frequent. Alzheimer-like changes develop in mid-adulthood. Visual problems related to strabismus, nystagmus, or myopia are common. Trisomy 13 (choice A) and trisomy 18 (choice B) arise from nondisjunction of an autosome, resulting in an individual in which all cells have three copies of 13 or 18, respectively, instead of the normal two copies. Both conditions are associated with severe intellectual disabilities and congenital heart defects. Both of these conditions are usually fatal within the first few weeks of life. Trisomy 13, also known as Patau syndrome, has "rocker-bottom" feet, cleft lip and palate, and polydactyly (extra fingers or toes), and cardiac and renal defects. Trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome, is characterized by "rocker-bottom feet", low birth weight, low set ears, micrognathia (small lower jaw), and clenched fists with overlapping fingers, and congenital heart defects. Although heart defects are common with both trisomy 13 and 18, neither is associated with an increased risk of ALL. Genotypes 45,XO (choice D) and 47,XXY (choice E) arise from nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes, resulting in either the absence of one X chromosome (45,XO) or the presence of an additional X chromosome (47,XXY). An individual with a 45,XO genotype has Turner syndrome, whereas an individual with 47,XXY has Klinefelter syndrome. Individuals with Turner syndrome are female, but the loss of the second X chromosome affects several aspects of development both before and after birth. Common features of Turner syndrome include short stature, webbed neck, lymphedema in the hands and feet, skeletal abnormalities, and congenital heart defects. In addition, they have nonfunctioning ovaries, due to ovarian tissue degeneration before birth, and are infertile. Individuals with Klinefelter syndrome are male, but their sexual development is impaired. They typically have small testes that are not able to produce sufficient amounts of testosterone, resulting in delayed or incomplete puberty, gynecomastia, undescended testes, micropenis, and infertility. As adults, they tend to be taller than their peers. Neither Turner syndrome nor Klinefelter syndrome are associated with an increased risk of ALL.

choice_explanations.A: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) is usually fatal within the first weeks of life and is not associated with an increased risk of ALL.
choice_explanations.B: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) is usually fatal within the first weeks of life and is not associated with an increased risk of ALL.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) causes intellectual disability, congenital heart defects, and increased risk of AML/ALL.
choice_explanations.D: 45,XO (Turner syndrome) causes short stature, webbed neck, and infertility, not an increased risk of ALL.
choice_explanations.E: 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) causes hypogonadism and tall stature, not an increased risk of ALL.

fa_summary: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is associated with intellectual disability, congenital heart disease (e.g., AVSD), and an increased risk of AML (in newborns) and ALL (in older children).

stem: A 38-year-old man with an autosomal recessive form of albinism marries a 34-year-old albino woman who also has an autosomal recessive form of the condition. Genetic analysis reveals that the man's condition is due to mutations in the TYR gene on chromosome 11, whereas the woman's albinism is due to OCA2 mutations on chromosome 15. Which of the following is the most likely probability that their first child will be affected with albinism?
explanation: The correct answer is A. The key is that the parents have albinism due to TWO independent genes, TYR and OCA2. This situation (when a similar phenotype is caused by mutations in two or more different genes or loci) is referred to as locus heterogeneity. Since each parent is homozygous for their respective disease, all of the offspring will be heterozygous carriers of both mutations, but none (0%) will be affected because homozygosity for the disease-causing mutation would be required to produce a recessive disease. In other words, each parent is homozygous for their respective disease and there is no possibility that an offspring will be homozygous with the disease (the other parent has two good copies of the other gene). None of the children will be affected by albinism. Locus heterogeneity means that a similar clinical phenotype can be caused by mutations in different genes. If two different autosomal recessive loci are causing the phenotype of a disease in the parents, the children will be heterozygous at both loci, and hence normal.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: because the two parents are homozygous for mutations in different genes (TYR and OCA2), all children are heterozygous at both loci and none is affected.
choice_explanations.B: 25% would apply if both parents were carriers of a mutation at the same locus.
choice_explanations.C: 50% does not apply because the mutations are at different loci.
choice_explanations.D: 75% does not apply because the mutations are at different loci.
choice_explanations.E: 100% would require that both parents carry the same defective locus in a dominant pattern.

fa_summary: Locus heterogeneity (e.g., albinism from TYR vs. OCA2 mutations) means a similar phenotype can result from mutations at different loci; children of two parents homozygous at different loci are unaffected carriers.

stem: A 23-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She has had no medical problems and has had an uncomplicated pregnancy to date. The physician recommends a screening test for cystic fibrosis because she comes from a population in which the incidence of the mutant allele for this disease is 1 in 10. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what is the likelihood that this patient is a carrier for the disease?
explanation: The correct answer is C. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disease caused by a mutation in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene located on chromosome 7. The gene encodes a chloride channel which, if defective, leads to secretion of thick mucus and high sodium/chloride levels in sweat and mucus. Fifteen percent of these patients present with meconium ileus at birth, and many also have recurrent pulmonary infections, infertility, pancreatitis, and malabsorption. CF is the most common lethal inherited disease in Caucasian people. The equations of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) can be used to find the estimated incidence of cystic fibrosis in this population. HWE can be expressed by the following: Let p + q = 1. The frequency of the dominant A allele = p. The frequency of the recessive a allele = q. The genotypic frequencies at that locus can be expressed as: p² + 2pq + q² = 1. p² = frequency of individuals with genotype AA; 2pq = frequency of individuals with genotype Aa; q² = frequency of individuals with genotype aa. If the frequency of the recessive allele is known in a population, it can be used to find the genotype frequencies in the current generation, which can then be used to solve for other variables. In the present problem, the frequency of the cystic fibrosis allele is equal to 1/10. This number is equal to q. The frequency of the normal allele, p, is equal to 9/10, since 1 - q = p. Thus, the frequency of those who are affected is expressed by q² and equals 0.01 (choice A). To determine the likelihood that our patient is a carrier we must first exclude the chance that she is affected since we know that she has no medical problems and it would be unusual for a patient to be asymptomatic at age 23 with cystic fibrosis. The Hardy-Weinberg equation would thus be: p² + 2pq + q² = 1, so (0.9)² + 2(0.9)(0.1) + (0.1)² = 1. We can calculate the likelihood that she is a carrier for the disease (2pq) as: 2(0.9)(0.1) = 0.18, which is the correct answer. 0.10 (choice B) is the frequency of the diseased allele (q). 0.81 (choice D) is the frequency of the homozygous normal genotype (p²). 0.99 (choice E) is the frequency of unaffected individuals (p² + 2pq). For an autosomal recessive condition, if the gene frequency of the recessive allele (q) is known, then p = 1 - q. The frequency of a given genotype in the population can then be calculated using the following equation: p² + 2pq + q² = 1. The carrier frequency is equal to 2pq or approximately 2q if the disease is rare and p ≈ 1.

choice_explanations.A: 0.01 is the frequency of affected individuals (q²).
choice_explanations.B: 0.10 is the frequency of the diseased allele (q).
choice_explanations.C: Correct: the carrier frequency (2pq) is 2(0.9)(0.1) = 0.18.
choice_explanations.D: 0.81 is the frequency of the homozygous normal genotype (p²).
choice_explanations.E: 0.99 is the frequency of unaffected individuals (p² + 2pq).

fa_summary: Given the recessive allele frequency q = 0.1 (p = 0.9), the carrier frequency 2pq = 0.18 for an autosomal recessive disease.

stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of failure to develop normal male secondary sexual characteristics. He is above normal height and average weight for his age. Physical examination shows small testes, a small penis, and gynecomastia. His parents report that he had to repeat the 8th and 9th grades, and he is still struggling in his classes. This patient's condition is most likely to be related to which of the following?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The boy probably has Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), which has the typical presentation described in the question. Klinefelter's syndrome is the most common congenital abnormality causing primary hypogonadism and occurs in approximately 1 in 1000 live births. The diagnosis is commonly made during adolescence or adulthood in males who have small testes with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and gynecomastia. The condition arises as a result of failure of separation (nondisjunction) of the sex chromosomes during meiotic division, and can be related to either paternal nondisjunction (slightly more common) or maternal nondisjunction. Two common symptoms leading to diagnosis include infertility and gynecomastia. Other symptoms include fatigue, erectile dysfunction, language impairment, academic difficulty, subnormal libido, osteoporosis, and behavioral problems. Examples of nondisjunction of autosomes (choice B) include trisomies such as most cases of Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18), and Patau syndrome (trisomy 13). There are two types of translocations: non-Robertsonian (choice D) and Robertsonian (choice E). Non-Robertsonian (reciprocal) translocations result when two non-homologous chromosomes exchange genetic material. Robertsonian translocations are a special type of translocation that involve exchange of genetic material from the long arms of one acrocentric chromosome to the long arms of another acrocentric chromosome, with fusion of the centromeres. Four percent of cases of Down syndrome are caused by this mechanism. Klinefelter syndrome is the most common congenital abnormality causing primary hypogonadism. The most common genotype is 47,XXY, resulting from nondisjunction of sex chromosomes during meiotic division of germ cells.

choice_explanations.A: A deletion does not cause Klinefelter syndrome.
choice_explanations.B: Nondisjunction of an autosome causes trisomies such as Down, Edwards, and Patau syndromes.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) results from nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes during meiotic division.
choice_explanations.D: Non-Robertsonian (reciprocal) translocations involve exchange between non-homologous chromosomes.
choice_explanations.E: Robertsonian translocations involve acrocentric chromosomes and cause ~4% of Down syndrome cases.

fa_summary: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common cause of primary hypogonadism and results from nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes during meiosis.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a six-month history of burning, tingling pain of his hands and feet. Physical examination shows angiokeratomas and corneal opacities. The pedigree shows that his two older sisters have children who have developed the same condition as the patient. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is A. Fabry disease is a lysosomal storage disease resulting from the absence of alpha-galactosidase A. Notably, Fabry disease follows an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance. The clinical presentation includes: burning sensations in the hands which get worse with exercise and hot weather; small, raised reddish-purple blemishes on the skin (angiokeratomas); eye manifestations, especially cloudiness of the cornea; impaired arterial circulation and increased risk of heart attack or stroke; enlargement of the heart and kidneys; renal failure is often the cause of death. Onset is usually during late childhood or adolescence. For this question, even if you cannot remember the features of the individual lipid storage diseases, it is worth remembering that Fabry disease is the only X-linked lipid-storage disease; the rest are autosomal recessive.
