As a general rule, associate all of the lipid storage diseases with severe neurologic deterioration. The exception is Gaucher disease (choice B), which tends to affect the liver and spares the brain (Gaucher disease; which tends to affect the liver and spares the brain). Characteristics of X-linked recessive inheritance include: More frequent in males because males require only one copy of the mutation to express the disease, whereas females require 2 copies. Skipped generations are common because an affected male can transmit the disease-causing mutation to a heterozygous daughter who is unaffected, but who can transmit the disease causing allele to her sons. Male-to-male transmission is not seen; this helps distinguish it from autosomal inheritance. Gaucher disease (choice B) is an autosomal recessive lipid storage disease caused by a deficiency in the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. Findings generally include hepatosplenomegaly, bone abnormalities, and Gaucher cells. The disease is more prevalent in individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish descent. Associate Krabbe disease (choice C) with the presence of "globoid" cells in degenerating white matter in the brain as well as peripheral neuropathy. The enzyme affected in this disease is galactocerebrosidase. Krabbe disease follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Metachromatic leukodystrophy (choice D) is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme arylsulfatase A, and follows autosomal recessive inheritance. Patients present with ataxia and dementia. Niemann-Pick disease (choice E) and Tay-Sachs disease (choice F) are autosomal recessive lysosomal storage diseases. Niemann-Pick disease is caused by deficiency in sphingomyelinase and Tay-Sachs is caused by a deficiency in hexosaminidase A. They each have findings of a cherry red spot on the macula on exam but are differentiable by the presence or absence of hepatosplenomegaly (HSM in Niemann-Pick, no HSM in Tay-Sachs). Both diseases occur with greater frequency in Ashkenazi Jews.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A deficiency) is the only X-linked lipid-storage disease and causes burning pain of the hands/feet, angiokeratomas, and corneal clouding.
choice_explanations.B: Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase deficiency) is autosomal recessive and affects the liver, sparing the brain.
choice_explanations.C: Krabbe disease (galactocerebrosidase deficiency) is autosomal recessive and features globoid cells in white matter and peripheral neuropathy.
choice_explanations.D: Metachromatic leukodystrophy (arylsulfatase A deficiency) is autosomal recessive and presents with ataxia and dementia.
choice_explanations.E: Niemann-Pick disease (sphingomyelinase deficiency) is autosomal recessive with a cherry red spot and hepatosplenomegaly.
choice_explanations.F: Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency) is autosomal recessive with a cherry red spot but no hepatosplenomegaly.

fa_summary: Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A deficiency) is the only X-linked lipid-storage disease; it causes burning pain of the hands/feet, angiokeratomas, and corneal cloudiness.

stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up examination because of easy bruising and petechiae. She has been otherwise healthy. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 76/min, blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg, and respirations are 12/min. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 10,200/mm3; Erythrocyte count 4.5 million/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This clinical scenario is most consistent with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), which is an immune-mediated destruction of platelets by the spleen. Antibodies to platelet receptors (GP Ib or GP IIb/IIIa) are formed. There are 2 types of ITP: acute and chronic. The acute form is seen in children and young adults, is preceded by a viral infection, and is self-limited. The chronic type is seen in female adults and may require intravenous immune globulin (IVIG; prevents the spleen from recognizing platelets and platelet destruction), corticosteroid, or splenectomy as therapy. The peripheral smear and bone marrow show the features described. Immature giant platelets and increased megakaryocytes are compensatory mechanism in the bone marrow in response to the increased platelet destruction. Decreased platelets and normal red blood cells on peripheral smear help establish this diagnosis.

In both Glanzmann thrombasthenia (choice A) and von Willebrand disease (choice F), the platelet count will be normal. Platelet aggregation will be impaired with Glanzmann thrombasthenia, while platelet adhesion will be impaired with von Willebrand disease.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (choice B; HUS) is usually associated with exposure to enterohemorrhagic, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 infection. Shigella, Campylobacter, and viruses (HIV, Coxsackie virus, Echovirus) may also cause this condition. Patients (most commonly children) may have eaten contaminated foods (e.g., hamburgers). Patients present with fever, bloody diarrhea, and subsequent (2-7 days afterwards) thrombocytopenia, bruising, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and acute renal failure (oliguria, elevated renal function tests). Patients may also have irritability, lethargy and seizures. Histologic changes in the renal glomeruli show presence of microthrombi. Peripheral blood smear reveals decreased platelets and schistocytes.

Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura is distinguished from microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (choice D) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (choice E; TTP) by the absence of fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on peripheral blood smear. TTP is due to ADAMTS13 enzyme deficiency, microthrombi formation, and has a characteristic pentad: fever, thrombocytopenia, neurologic dysfunction (altered mental status), renal dysfunction, and schistocytes (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia).

choice_explanations.A: In Glanzmann thrombasthenia the platelet count is normal; platelet aggregation is impaired (defective GP IIb/IIIa).
choice_explanations.B: Hemolytic uremic syndrome typically follows Shiga toxin-producing E coli O157:H7 and causes thrombocytopenia, bruising, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and acute renal failure with schistocytes.
choice_explanations.C: ITP is immune-mediated platelet destruction (antibodies to GP Ib or GP IIb/IIIa); peripheral smear shows decreased platelets and normal red blood cells without schistocytes.
choice_explanations.D: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia has normal platelets with fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on smear.
choice_explanations.E: TTP (ADAMTS13 deficiency) causes a pentad of fever, thrombocytopenia, neurologic dysfunction, renal dysfunction, and schistocytes.
choice_explanations.F: In von Willebrand disease the platelet count is normal; platelet adhesion is impaired.

fa_summary: ITP: immune-mediated platelet destruction; isolated thrombocytopenia with petechiae/bruising; anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies.

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of persistent bleeding after a tooth extraction. His mother reports that in the past, whenever he had a bloody nose, it would last longer than expected. She says that they have never seen any blood in his urine or stool. Laboratory studies show: Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) 42 sec, Prothrombin time (PT) 13 sec, Bleeding time 11 min. Which of the following is most likely to be abnormal in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is an autosomal-dominant bleeding disorder caused by either a deficiency or qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor (vWF), a multimeric protein that is required for platelet adhesion by binding to platelet GpIb. vWF is normally produced by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. An abnormal vWF causes a defect in the initial adhesion of normal platelets to a damaged vessel wall. vWF also carries factor VIII in the blood, so factor VIII levels are also consequently low, and the partial thromboplastin time is also prolonged. Defects in platelet adhesion are also seen in Bernard-Soulier disease (which is caused by a deficiency of GpIb platelet receptor).

Clinical features include spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes, prolonged bleeding from wounds, and menorrhagia in young females; bleeding into joints is uncommon. Laboratory studies show a normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time (indicating platelet pathology), normal PT, and often a prolonged PTT (indicating an intrinsic pathway defect). Abnormal platelet aggregation response to ristocetin is an important diagnostic test. Ristocetin will only cause platelet agglutination in the presence of vWF, so if it is added to blood without vWF, aggregation will not occur. Treatment is with desmopressin (DDAVP) in type 1 vWD (deficiency of vWF), which releases vWF from Weibel-Palade bodies of endothelial cells.

This patient has an increased bleeding time, prolonged PTT, and spontaneous, prolonged bleeding, all of which leads to the diagnosis of vWD.

Abnormal platelet morphology (choice B) is not seen in vWD, but may be observed with infiltration of the bone marrow by tumor or fibrosis, after splenectomy, and even platelet granule disorder (grey platelet syndrome). Platelet dysfunction would cause prolonged bleeding time. This, however, would not cause the prolonged thromboplastin time as seen in this patient.

Defects in primary platelet aggregation (choice C) are seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, which is caused by a deficiency or defect in the glycoprotein GpIIb-IIIa complex. A prolonged bleeding time would be seen. However, this would not cause the prolonged thromboplastin time as seen in this patient.

Defects in release of platelet vesicles (choice D) or secondary aggregation (choice E) are seen in storage pool disease and aspirin use. These conditions would have a prolonged bleeding time. Neither of these choices would cause the prolonged thromboplastin time as seen in this patient.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: von Willebrand disease causes a deficiency or qualitative defect of vWF, which is required for initial platelet adhesion (binding platelet GpIb); bleeding time and PTT are prolonged.
choice_explanations.B: Abnormal platelet morphology is not seen in vWD; it may be seen with marrow infiltration by tumor or fibrosis, after splenectomy, or in grey platelet syndrome, and it would not prolong the PTT.
choice_explanations.C: Defective primary platelet aggregation is seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa defect); bleeding time is prolonged but the PTT is not.
choice_explanations.D: Defective release of platelet vesicles is seen in storage pool disease and with aspirin use; bleeding time is prolonged but the PTT is not.
choice_explanations.E: Defective secondary aggregation is seen in storage pool disease and with aspirin use; bleeding time is prolonged but the PTT is not.

fa_summary: Von Willebrand disease: deficiency/defect of vWF impairs platelet adhesion (GpIb binding) and lowers factor VIII, prolonging bleeding time and PTT.

stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of tenderness in her neck. She has had low-grade fever intermittently for a few weeks. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows two 1.5 cm anterior cervical nodes that are tender to palpation and freely moveable. A biopsy of one of the lymph nodes shows preserved lymph node architecture with multiple, large round germinal centers with distinct dark and light zones. Many macrophages containing debris and frequent mitoses are present. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Evaluation of palpable lymph nodes is an important role of a physician. In any patient, consideration must be given to all possible benign and malignant causes of lymphadenopathy. In this patient, given the age range, a reactive lymphadenitis, Burkitt lymphoma, or Hodgkin lymphoma should be ruled out. Tender, mobile lymphadenopathy usually implies infection/inflammation, whereas a nontender, fixed lymphadenopathy implies lymphoma/metastatic carcinoma.

Localized cervical lymphadenitis may be caused by drainage from infections of the teeth or tonsils. Given this patient's age, it is appropriate to biopsy. Within the lymph node, the germinal center is the major site of antigen-dependent B-lymphocyte selection and maturation. The biopsy describes findings of benign follicular hyperplasia: preserved lymph node architecture, multiple large germinal centers with recognizable light and dark zones, and frequent mitoses. Macrophages containing debris from ingested lymphocytes, known as "tingible body macrophages," are characteristic of a reactive follicular center in benign reactive lymphadenitis.

Note: Increased mitoses and proliferation of cells may also be seen with malignant lymphoma, but the lymph node architecture would not be preserved. You cannot recognize cortex, paracortex, and medullary regions. Malignant lymphoma cells would not preserve the normal architecture and would have a non-organized growth pattern. Tingible body macrophages are also seen with Burkitt lymphoma, where these are normal reactive cells.

Hodgkin disease (choice B) is a type of lymphoma that spreads contiguously from node to node. There are five types of the disease. Some types have bimodal age presentation, while others may present in older age. Histologically, the characteristic cell finding is the Reed-Sternberg cell. Hodgkin disease usually presents with painless cervical adenopathy, fever, chills, night sweats, and weight loss. Microscopically, the lymph node architecture is lost or distorted due to the increased cellular proliferation.

Malignant histiocytosis (choice C) is a common subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The characteristic cell appears large with a vesicular nucleus and prominent nucleolus. The disorder can present with nodal enlargement (usually nontender) or with extranodal involvement.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (choice D) is the name for a varied group of lymphomas that are not associated with Reed-Sternberg cells. They usually present with nontender lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. They do not spread in contiguity, and 30% present extranodally. The histologic presentation varies, but all contain proliferation of atypical lymphocytes. Follicular B-cell lymphoma would be seen in older age patients (> 40 years), and have increased mitoses and numerous germinal follicles that distort the lymph node architecture (would not recognize cortex from medullary regions).

Sezary syndrome (choice E) is the leukemic form of a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Mycosis fungoides). Neoplastic T cells are found in the upper dermis and also within the peripheral blood. Patients are older and present with lymphadenopathy, pruritic erythroderma, and exfoliation.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: preserved lymph node architecture, large germinal centers with light/dark zones, frequent mitoses, and tingible body macrophages indicate benign reactive follicular hyperplasia (reactive lymphadenitis).
choice_explanations.B: Hodgkin disease spreads contiguously node to node; its characteristic cell is the Reed-Sternberg cell, and normal lymph node architecture is lost or distorted.
choice_explanations.C: Malignant histiocytosis is a subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma with large cells showing a vesicular nucleus and prominent nucleolus; it presents with (usually nontender) nodal enlargement or extranodal involvement.
choice_explanations.D: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma lacks Reed-Sternberg cells, usually presents with nontender lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, and does not preserve normal nodal architecture.
choice_explanations.E: Sezary syndrome is the leukemic form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides), seen in older patients with lymphadenopathy, pruritic erythroderma, and exfoliation.

fa_summary: Benign reactive follicular hyperplasia preserves lymph node architecture with germinal centers and tingible body macrophages, unlike malignant lymphoma.

stem: A primigravid 32-year-old woman at 37 weeks' gestation develops severe lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding and is brought to the emergency department. After examination, she is rushed to the operating room for emergency cesarean section. Following cesarean section, the patient develops shortness of breath, cyanosis, and copious bleeding from her surgical wounds. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 76,000/mm3, prothrombin time (PT) of 30 sec, partial thromboplastin time (PTT) of 56 sec, decreased fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimers. Which of the following factors best accounts for her bleeding disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The patient most likely experienced placental abruption. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), or consumptive coagulopathy, develops when blood is exposed to large amounts of tissue factor over a brief period of time, with massive generation of thrombin, resulting in the acute triggering of coagulation. DIC is seen in more than 50% of cases of amniotic fluid embolism and abruptio placentae.

The human decidua is immensely abundant in tissue factor, which is the primary initiator of the clotting cascade through thrombin generation. Clinically, there is profound systemic bleeding. Thromboembolism and dysfunction of the kidney, liver, lungs, and central nervous system often develop because of widespread intravascular fibrin deposition. Diagnosis of DIC is confirmed by laboratory studies that reveal decreased platelets, prolonged PT and PTT, decreased fibrinogen and elevated fibrin degradation products (FDPs) and D-dimers.

Antiplatelet antibodies (choice A) against epitopes on glycoprotein IIb/IIIa are seen in idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), an acquired disorder related to increased platelet destruction. Clinically, patients most often present with petechiae and easy bruising and thrombocytopenia of insidious onset.

Bacterial toxins (choice B) can be an important initiator of DIC. Gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria may cause endothelial damage and ultimately enhance expression of tissue factor. However, there is no indication that bacterial infection was the primary initiating event in this patient.

Lidocaine (choice C) is not known to be related to development of DIC. It is used in regional anesthesia for cesarean delivery and does not enter the peripheral circulation.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura-hemolytic uremic syndrome (TTP-HUS) describes acute syndromes with abnormalities in multiple systems. Excessive release of the multimeric form of von Willebrand factor (vWF, choice E) from systemic endothelial cells results in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). In TTP, there is aggregation of platelets that reversibly obstructs the arterioles and capillaries of organs, resulting in ischemia and sometimes infarction. The characteristic pentad of signs and symptoms of TTP consists of: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenic purpura, neurologic abnormalities, fever, and renal disease. Laboratory studies typically show mild anemia and low platelet counts (20,000-50,000/uL). The peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes due to the microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. D-dimers are usually normal or only slightly elevated.

choice_explanations.A: Antiplatelet antibodies against GpIIb/IIIa are seen in ITP; patients present with petechiae, easy bruising, and thrombocytopenia, not the prolonged PT/PTT, hypofibrinogenemia, and elevated D-dimers of DIC.
choice_explanations.B: Bacterial toxins can initiate DIC (endothelial damage with enhanced tissue factor expression), but there is no evidence of bacterial infection as the primary trigger in this patient.
choice_explanations.C: Lidocaine is used in regional anesthesia for cesarean delivery and is not known to cause DIC; it does not enter the peripheral circulation.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: exposure of blood to abundant tissue factor (e.g., from the decidua in placental abruption) initiates DIC, with massive thrombin generation and consumption of platelets and factors.
choice_explanations.E: Excess multimeric von Willebrand factor release causes TTP (a primary platelet-activation disorder with normal PT/PTT and normal-to-mildly elevated D-dimers), not tissue-factor-driven DIC.

fa_summary: DIC is driven by tissue factor exposure (e.g., placental abruption/decidua), causing consumption of platelets and clotting factors with prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimers.

stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of nosebleeds. She also says that she has easy bruising and excessively heavy bleeding during her periods. She does not take any medications. Physical examination shows scattered petechiae. The spleen is normal-sized. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 45,000/mm3 and a bleeding time of 17 minutes. A bone marrow aspirate shows an increased number of megakaryocytes. Antinuclear antibodies are negative. Autoantibodies against which of the following antigens are most likely present in this patient's serum?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The history of nosebleeds and menorrhagia, the petechiae, the thrombocytopenia, and the increased bleeding time all suggest a platelet disorder. Platelet disorders include thrombocytopenia (decreased numbers) and platelet function disorders (abnormal function despite adequate numbers). Thrombocytopenia can occur due to impaired production or accelerated destruction of platelets. The decreased platelet count suggests a thrombocytopenic disorder rather than a platelet function disorder.

The absence of antinuclear antibody argues against systemic lupus erythematosus (a significant cause of thrombocytopenia). The negative drug history rules out drug-associated thrombocytopenia. After other causes have been ruled out, a tentative diagnosis of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) can be made. ITP, also called immune thrombocytopenic purpura, is an acquired thrombocytopenia caused by formation of autoantibodies directed against the platelet membrane proteins glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (which function as a fibrinogen receptor in platelet aggregation). This is then followed by splenic destruction of opsonized platelets.

The disease typically occurs in children or women (20 to 40 years of age). Depending on the particular case, immunosuppressive therapy and/or splenectomy can be used to control the thrombocytopenia.

Antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor (choice A) are seen in myasthenia gravis. Patients develop weakness, especially as the day goes on.

Antibodies to erythrocyte membrane proteins (choice B) are seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Patients present with weakness, tachycardia, decreased hematocrit and may, in some cases, exhibit jaundice or dark-colored urine.

Antibodies to intrinsic factor (choice D) are seen in pernicious anemia. In this disorder, impaired absorption of vitamin B12 leads to megaloblastic anemia.

Antibodies to type IV collagen (choice E) are seen in Goodpasture syndrome, which features anti-glomerular membrane disease leading to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage signaled by hemoptysis.

choice_explanations.A: Antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor cause myasthenia gravis (weakness worsening through the day), not isolated thrombocytopenia.
choice_explanations.B: Antibodies to erythrocyte membrane proteins cause autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: ITP is caused by autoantibodies against platelet membrane glycoproteins (GpIIb/IIIa, a fibrinogen receptor), leading to splenic destruction of opsonized platelets and isolated thrombocytopenia.
choice_explanations.D: Antibodies to intrinsic factor cause pernicious anemia (megaloblastic anemia).
choice_explanations.E: Antibodies to type IV collagen cause Goodpasture syndrome (anti-glomerular basement membrane disease with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage).

fa_summary: ITP is caused by autoantibodies against platelet GpIIb/IIIa, causing isolated thrombocytopenia via splenic platelet destruction.

stem: A 26-year-old primigravid woman at 37 weeks' gestation presents to the emergency department because of vaginal bleeding. Vaginal ultrasound confirms the diagnosis of placental abruption. She undergoes a C-section and receives multiple transfusions. On the third day of admission, she develops increasing confusion. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 84/min, blood pressure is 100/66 mm Hg, and respirations are 18/min. Oxygen saturation on room air is 80%. Petechiae are present on the face and oral mucosa, while purpura and ecchymosis are present on the arms, trunk, and legs. Rales are noted in the lungs bilaterally. Foley catheter reveals decreased urine output, which is red-tinged. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the workup of this patient?

options.text: Bleeding time, partial thromboplastin time, and von Willebrand factor levels
Partial thromboplastin time and factor VIII levels
Partial thromboplastin time and factor XI levels
Platelet count and platelet aggregation studies with ADP and epinephrine
Platelet count, prothrombin time, and fibrin degradation products

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is characterized by consumption of platelets, fibrinogen and clotting factors, bleeding, and organ dysfunction. The best tests to order are platelet count (which will be markedly decreased), prothrombin time/partial thromboplastin time (PT/PTT; which will be prolonged), serum fibrinogen level (which will be low), and fibrin degradation products (which will be high).

Causes of DIC include sepsis, trauma, obstetrical complications (placental abruption; as in our patient), acute pancreatitis, malignancy (adenocarcinoma, acute promyelocytic leukemia), nephrotic syndrome, and incompatible transfusion reactions ("STOP Making New Thrombi").

The common underlying mechanism for DIC is endothelial cell damage, which triggers release of tissue factor and stimulation of the coagulation cascade, resulting in consumption of platelets, clotting factors, and fibrinogen to form microthrombi. Concurrent stimulation of the fibrinolytic system occurs to break down clots, resulting in elevated levels of fibrin degradation products, fibrin split products, and D-dimers. This sequence becomes a vicious cycle, which does not stop, and the body cannot adequately produce and replenish clotting factors, platelets, and fibrinogen.

Clinically, patients will clot first, then bleed out (venipuncture sites, mouth, skin, bladder). Organ dysfunction occurs in the brain (altered mental state), lungs (dyspnea), liver (elevated liver enzymes, jaundice), and kidneys (oliguria, elevated creatinine/urea nitrogen). Schistocytes are present in the peripheral blood smear, which reflects red blood cell damage as they pass through microthrombi in the circulation (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia).

Treatment is removal of the underlying cause. In this case, IV fluid administration, blood transfusion, fetal monitoring, removal of the placental abruption, delivery via cesarean section, and postpartum care are considered. Administration of platelets and fresh frozen plasma may be needed, which is a sensitive balance since both will try to prevent bleeding, but will create more clots. Note: in our patient, it is assumed that she received compatible blood transfusion.

Bleeding time, partial thromboplastin time and von Willebrand factor levels (choice A) reflects von Willebrand disease, a common autosomal dominant inherited bleeding disorder. Bleeding time and PTT will be prolonged. PTT is prolonged because von Willebrand factor promotes the half-life of clotting factor VIII. Patients present with bleeding with trauma or surgical procedures. It is not associated with placental abruption, microthrombi formation, or organ dysfunction.

Partial thromboplastin time and factor VIII levels (choice B) reflects hemophilia A, an X-linked inherited bleeding disorder that presents with hemarthrosis, purpura, and ecchymosis. Clotting factor VIII is present in the intrinsic coagulation cascade pathway. A deficiency is reflected by prolonged PTT. It is not associated with placental abruption, microthrombi formation, or organ dysfunction.

Partial thromboplastin time and factor XI levels (choice C) reflects factor XI (Hageman factor) deficiency. Clotting factor XI is present in the intrinsic coagulation cascade pathway. A deficiency is reflected by prolonged PTT. Patients are usually asymptomatic, but some may present with paradoxical thromboembolism. Spontaneous miscarriages may occur in pregnancy.

Platelet count and platelet aggregation studies with ADP and epinephrine (choice D) reflects platelet aggregation disorders such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a dysfunction or deficiency of platelet receptor glycoprotein IIb/IIIa. Patients would have a normal platelet count and an abnormal platelet aggregation study with ADP and epinephrine (platelet agonists for platelet aggregation). The glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor binds to fibrinogen for platelet aggregation.

choice_explanations.A: Bleeding time, PTT, and von Willebrand factor levels reflect von Willebrand disease; it is not associated with placental abruption, microthrombi, or organ dysfunction.
choice_explanations.B: PTT and factor VIII levels reflect hemophilia A; it is not associated with placental abruption, microthrombi, or organ dysfunction.
choice_explanations.C: PTT and factor XI levels reflect factor XI (Hageman factor) deficiency; it is not associated with placental abruption, microthrombi, or organ dysfunction.
choice_explanations.D: Platelet count and aggregation studies with ADP and epinephrine reflect platelet aggregation disorders such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia, not DIC.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: DIC is evaluated with platelet count, PT/PTT, fibrinogen, and fibrin degradation products.

fa_summary: DIC workup: decreased platelet count, prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, and elevated fibrin degradation products/D-dimers.

stem: A 7-year-old boy has fatigue and poor cognition at school. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals weight and height in the 50th percentile, scleral icterus, oral mucosal pallor, and a systolic murmur. The physician suspects an inherited blood cell disorder. He is considering sickle cell anemia and thalassemia major in the differential diagnosis. Which of the following features is common to both disorders?

options.text: Bone marrow expansion in the calvarium

explanation:
The correct answer is B. Under normal conditions, hematopoiesis occurs in the marrow of long bones. Both sickle cell anemia and thalassemia have chronic anemia, which requires compensatory increased hematopoiesis to meet the demands for oxygen transport. The flat bones of the skull (calvarium, maxilla) will have prominent marrow hematopoiesis, which will eventually cause expansion of the marrow space. This can be identified on radiographs as a "crew-cut" or "hair on end" appearance.

If the marrow of the skull and flat bones cannot adequately maintain erythropoiesis, extramedullary hematopoiesis will occur in the spleen and the liver. In addition, other common findings include: 1) fatigue, shortness of breath, and growth and developmental delay due to poor oxygen transport to tissues, 2) jaundice and icterus from red cell destruction, and 3) a systolic functional murmur due to low blood volume/anemia.

In this vignette, the child's clinical symptoms provided cannot distinguish sickle cell anemia from thalassemia. (Recall that normal adult hemoglobin A1 is composed of 2 alpha and 2 beta chains.) The pathogenic mechanisms responsible for anemia differ in these two conditions:

Sickle cell anemia is caused by a point mutation leading to substitution of valine for glutamate at the 6th position of the beta-globin chain. This hemoglobin variant is called hemoglobin S. Patients with sickle cell anemia are homozygous for hemoglobin S (SS), whereas patients with sickle cell trait are heterozygous (AS). Sickle cell anemia results in shortening of erythrocyte life due to extravascular hemolysis (removal of irreversibly sickled cells). Sickle cell anemia patients have episodes of sickling crises, autosplenectomy, increased risk for certain bacterial infections, osteomyelitis, and acute chest syndrome.

Thalassemia major (homozygous beta-thalassemia) has severely deficient or absent synthesis of beta-globin chains. Beta-thalassemia causes formation of excess free alpha-globin chains, which precipitate within the normoblasts, resulting in premature apoptosis of red cell precursors (ineffective erythropoiesis).

The remaining options are characteristics of sickle cell anemia, but not thalassemia major.

Autosplenectomy (choice A) is characteristic of sickle cell anemia. It results from repeated splenic infarcts due to recurrent occlusion of splenic sinusoids by sickled red cells.

Osteomyelitis (choice C), particularly with Salmonella, occurs frequently in patients with sickle cell anemia because of the autosplenectomy, but does not have significantly increased frequency in patients with thalassemia compared to normal individuals.

Sickle cell patients have a marked predisposition to infections by Haemophilus influenzae (choice D) and Streptococcus pneumoniae, both of which are encapsulated bacteria, due to autosplenectomy.

Erythrocyte sickling (choice E) is pathognomonic of sickle cell anemia. This occurs when HbS molecules undergo polymerization and aggregation in conditions of lower O2 tension or acidic pH. HbS aggregates cause distortion of erythrocytes, which acquire a sickle shape, and contributes to small vessel occlusion.

choice_explanations.A: Autosplenectomy is characteristic of sickle cell anemia (repeated splenic infarcts from sickled cells) but not thalassemia major.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: chronic anemia drives compensatory marrow hyperplasia in the flat bones (calvarium, maxilla), causing marrow expansion ("crew-cut" skull) in both sickle cell anemia and thalassemia major.
choice_explanations.C: Osteomyelitis (especially Salmonella) occurs frequently in sickle cell anemia (due to autosplenectomy) but not significantly more in thalassemia.
choice_explanations.D: Predisposition to Haemophilus influenzae (and Streptococcus pneumoniae) infection results from autosplenectomy in sickle cell anemia, not from thalassemia.
choice_explanations.E: Erythrocyte sickling is pathognomonic of sickle cell anemia, not thalassemia.

fa_summary: Both sickle cell anemia and thalassemia major cause marrow expansion of the skull ("crew-cut"/hair-on-end) from compensatory erythropoiesis.

stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of right knee pain that started ten days ago when he fell off his motorcycle. Initially, he was able to ambulate; however, he has had progressive swelling, redness, and limitation of movement of his knee. The process causing destruction of cartilage in this individual's knee is worsened because of which of the following?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient is showing symptoms of a bacterial infection of the knee joint (septic arthritis), which was triggered by this accident. Hyaline cartilage, found in the knee joint, contains very few, sparsely distributed, small blood vessels. The tissue consequently is very vulnerable to infection because the immune system (white cells and serum with clotting factors and antibodies) cannot access the cartilage in an efficient fashion.

Chondroitin sulfate (choice A) is an important constituent of cartilage that can be attacked by bacteria, but this is not the cause of uncontrollable infections in the cartilage, because if the infection is controlled, chondrocytes will continue to synthesize chondroitin.

Collagen (choice B) is present in cartilage, but does not predispose the cartilage for uncontrollable infection.

Cartilage is not innervated (choice C), but this does not contribute to the development of uncontrollable infection.

The tendency of cartilage to undergo calcification (choice E), even when not acting as the site of ossification, does not predispose for uncontrollable infection.

choice_explanations.A: Chondroitin sulfate is an important constituent of cartilage and can be attacked by bacteria, but this is not what makes the infection uncontrollable, because if the infection is controlled chondrocytes will continue to synthesize chondroitin.
choice_explanations.B: Collagen is present in cartilage but does not predispose the cartilage to uncontrollable infection.
choice_explanations.C: Cartilage is not innervated, but this does not contribute to the development of uncontrollable infection.
choice_explanations.D: Hyaline cartilage contains very few, sparsely distributed, small blood vessels; it is relatively avascular, so the immune system cannot access the cartilage efficiently, allowing infection to become uncontrollable.
choice_explanations.E: The tendency of cartilage to undergo calcification does not predispose for uncontrollable infection.

fa_summary: Septic arthritis: hyaline cartilage is relatively avascular, so immune cells/serum cannot reach it efficiently, allowing uncontrolled infection.

stem: An investigator is isolating mucin-secreting cells from various tissues to compare surface receptor types on these cells. Which of the following tissues would most likely yield the highest percentage of mucin-secreting cells?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. In their acini, salivary glands can contain predominantly serous cells, predominantly mucous cells, or both. The sublingual gland is almost purely mucous, while acini in the submandibular gland (choice E) contain a mixture of serous and mucous cells. Acini in the parotid gland (choice C) are mostly pure serous cells.

The esophageal mucosa (choice A) and the oral mucosa (choice B) are squamous epithelia that do not form acini. The types of acinar cells in major salivary glands vary with the specific gland: the sublingual gland is almost purely mucous; the submandibular gland is mixed mucous and serous; the parotid gland is majority serous.

choice_explanations.A: Esophageal mucosa is a squamous epithelium that does not form acini.
choice_explanations.B: Oral mucosa is a squamous epithelium that does not form acini.
choice_explanations.C: Acini in the parotid gland are mostly pure serous cells.
choice_explanations.D: The sublingual gland is almost purely mucous, so it yields the highest percentage of mucin-secreting cells.
choice_explanations.E: Acini in the submandibular gland contain a mixture of serous and mucous cells.

fa_summary: Major salivary glands differ in acinar cell type: sublingual is almost purely mucous, submandibular is mixed, parotid is mostly serous.

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being hit by a motorist while crossing the street and sustaining an abrasion injury on his left elbow. There is a total loss of epidermis over a large area of his left arm. One month later, the abrasion has healed, with regrowth of the epidermis. Which of the following best explains the restoration of the epidermis over the abraded area?

options.text: Growth of epidermis from stem cells in hair follicles and sweat glands in the dermis
Migration of endothelial cells from newly grown capillaries
Transformation of dermal fibroblasts into epidermal cells
Transformation of macrophages into epidermal cells
Transformation of melanocytes into epidermal cells

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The dermis contains skin appendages (e.g., hair follicles) that contain epithelial stem cells. In the process of healing a large area where the epidermis has been lost but the dermis is intact, re-epithelialization occurs by ingrowth of epidermal cells from the underlying skin appendages, as well as from the intact epidermis along the wound edges.

Recall that in addition to forming the epithelium of the epidermis, the embryonic ectoderm also forms the skin appendages such as hair follicles and sweat glands. The epithelial cells from these appendages can serve as the source of new epithelial cells for the epidermis. Even though the dermis itself is derived from mesoderm, the ectodermal skin appendages migrate into the dermis during their development.

None of the other cell types (choices B, C, D, and E) are known to directly contribute to the regeneration of epidermis over abraded skin.

choice_explanations.A: Epithelial stem cells within skin appendages (hair follicles and sweat glands) migrate to resurface the abraded area, together with the intact epidermis at the wound edges.
choice_explanations.B: Endothelial cells give rise to capillaries and do not become epidermis.
choice_explanations.C: Dermal fibroblasts (mesoderm-derived) do not transform into epidermal cells.
choice_explanations.D: Macrophages do not transform into epidermal cells.
choice_explanations.E: Melanocytes do not transform into the keratinocytes that reconstitute the epidermis.

fa_summary: After epidermal loss with an intact dermis, the epidermis is restored by epithelial stem cells in skin appendages (hair follicles, sweat glands) and from the wound edges.

stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of heartburn and a sour taste in his throat that occurs after meals. These symptoms have not been alleviated by over-the-counter medications. Endoscopy is performed, and a biopsy of the distal esophagus shows no abnormalities. Histologic examination of the biopsy is most likely to show which of the following cell types in the mucosal lining?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The esophagus is covered by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium for its entire length.

Heartburn is usually a sign of gastric regurgitation of the acidic contents in the lower esophagus (acid reflux disease). Acid reflux disease is a serious problem that may be associated with a precancerous condition (Barrett esophagus, in which the squamous mucosa becomes replaced by a columnar mucosa with alternating tall columnar cells and goblet cells in surface epithelium and glandular epithelium, which is a type of metaplasia). On endoscopy, normal esophagus mucosa would have a white-tan color, whereas in Barrett esophagus, metaplastic glandular mucosa would have a pink-tan or salmon color. With this patient, the endoscopy shows a normal appearance.

Ciliated columnar epithelium (choice A) is typically found in the uterine tubes and the ependyma of the central canal.

Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (choice B) is found in the epidermis of the skin.

Nonciliated columnar epithelium (choice C) is found in the absorptive portion of the digestive system (small intestine).

Nonkeratinized simple squamous epithelium (choice D) is found in the alveoli of the lung, the blood vessels, Bowman's capsule of the kidney, among other places. It is well suited for easy passage of material across the cell.

Pseudostratified columnar epithelium (choice F) is often called respiratory epithelium, and lines the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, trachea and bronchi.

choice_explanations.A: Ciliated columnar epithelium is typically found in the uterine tubes and the ependyma of the central canal.
choice_explanations.B: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium is found in the epidermis of the skin.
choice_explanations.C: Nonciliated columnar epithelium is found in the absorptive portion of the digestive system (small intestine).
choice_explanations.D: Nonkeratinized simple squamous epithelium is found in the alveoli, blood vessels, and Bowman's capsule, among other places.
choice_explanations.E: The esophagus is lined throughout by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
choice_explanations.F: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium (respiratory epithelium) lines the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, trachea and bronchi.

fa_summary: The entire esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium; Barrett esophagus (from chronic GERD) replaces it with intestinal-type columnar mucosa.

stem: An investigator is examining the distribution of an ion channel protein in the kidney. Slices of kidney tissue are incubated in a dilute solution of a specific antibody directed against the protein. The immunoperoxidase method is then used to localize the ion channel proteins. In one area, the investigator notes epithelial cells with a brush border that are positive for the ion channel protein. Which of the following areas is most likely to show these microscopic characteristics?

options.text: Deep portion of loop of Henle

explanation:
The correct answer is E. The immunoperoxidase method uses horseradish peroxidase to produce a visible pigment when a specific antibody binds to antigenic sites in the tissue. The positive immunoperoxidase results obtained here suggest that the channel protein is expressed in proximal convoluted tubular epithelium, because this is the only site in the kidney at which the epithelial cells have a "brush border." The brush border is made of microvilli which enhance the proximal tubules' ability to reabsorb plasma constituents filtered at the glomeruli.

The collecting ducts (choice A) are formed by regular simple cuboidal epithelial cells, and they do not have a brush border.

The thin segment of the loop of Henle (choice B) is simple squamous epithelium without a brush border.

The distal convoluted tubule (choice C) is composed of cuboidal cells without a brush border. It functions to reabsorb sodium and chloride from the tubular filtrate.

The glomerulus (choice D) is composed of capillary loops in between an afferent and an efferent arteriole. The cells are simple squamous epithelial and fenestrated.

choice_explanations.A: Collecting ducts are formed by regular simple cuboidal epithelial cells and do not have a brush border.
choice_explanations.B: The thin segment of the loop of Henle is simple squamous epithelium without a brush border.
choice_explanations.C: The distal convoluted tubule is composed of cuboidal cells without a brush border; it reabsorbs sodium and chloride.
choice_explanations.D: The glomerulus is composed of simple squamous, fenestrated capillary loops between an afferent and an efferent arteriole.
choice_explanations.E: The proximal convoluted tubule is the only site in the kidney whose epithelial cells have a microvillus "brush border," enhancing reabsorption.

fa_summary: The proximal convoluted tubule is the only nephron segment with a microvillus brush border (enhances reabsorption); immunohistochemistry can localize specific proteins.

stem: A 41-year-old Japanese man comes to the physician because of difficulty swallowing solid food for the past 4 months. Endoscopy reveals a polypoid mass inferior to the cricopharyngeus muscle. Examination of tissue obtained on biopsy shows malignant-appearing squamous epithelium and normal striated muscle in the same section. No smooth muscle is observed. Which of the following is the most likely site of the mass?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The muscle of the esophageal wall gradually transitions from skeletal muscle at the top to smooth muscle at the bottom with a gradient of mixtures in between. The muscularis of the upper 10% of the esophagus is composed entirely of striated muscle. Some authors identify the cricopharyngeus muscle as an upper esophageal sphincter (choice D), despite the fact that unlike a true sphincter, this muscle does not completely encircle the esophagus. We are told that the mass is located below the cricopharyngeus muscle, so the upper 10% of the esophagus is the best answer.

The lower one-third (choice B) of the esophagus, including the lower esophageal sphincter (choice A), contains only smooth muscle.

The middle one-third of the esophagus (choice C) contains both striated and smooth muscle.

choice_explanations.A: The lower esophageal sphincter contains only smooth muscle.
choice_explanations.B: The lower one-third of the esophagus contains only smooth muscle.
choice_explanations.C: The middle one-third of the esophagus contains both striated and smooth muscle.
choice_explanations.D: The cricopharyngeus is sometimes called the upper esophageal sphincter, but the question states the mass is inferior to it; the section shown is striated muscle only.
choice_explanations.E: The upper 10% (upper third) of the esophagus is composed entirely of striated muscle, matching the biopsy.

fa_summary: Esophageal muscularis: upper third is striated muscle, middle third is mixed, lower third (and LES) is smooth muscle.

stem: A sexually active 18-year-old woman has had a fever of 38.9°C (102°F) for the past 24 hours as well as a 5-day history of lower abdominal pain and anorexia. Physical examination shows a generalized tenderness of the abdomen, erythema of the cervix, and motion tenderness. There are no lesions on the external genitalia. Microscopic examination of the cervical discharge shows sloughed epithelial cells and scant neutrophils. Which of the following additional findings will most likely be found on examination of the discharge?

options.text: A naked, icosahedral, double-stranded, circular DNA virus
Intranuclear inclusion bodies surrounded by halos

explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient's presentation is typical for pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D-K) is the most common bacterial cause of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in the United States and is the most likely agent on the list to produce the symptoms described. It is an ATP scavenger that must therefore live intracellularly in the human host and can be visualized inside epithelial cells with iodine, Giemsa, or fluorescent-antibody stains. The remainder of the answer choices refer to other agents that could be found in the female genital tract, either by sexual transmission or by contamination with fecal flora, but they are not the best choices.

A naked, icosahedral, double-stranded, circular DNA virus (choice A) refers to human papillomavirus (HPV), which is the most common cause of anogenital warts, cervical dysplasia and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in the United States, but is not a cause of pelvic inflammatory disease.

Intranuclear inclusion bodies surrounded by halos ("owl's eyes") (choice B) refers to cytomegalovirus, a common infection in the United States but not a common agent of PID. Most cases in average adults are manifested by mononucleosis-like symptoms.

Lactose-fermenting, gram-negative bacilli (choice D) would be consistent with Escherichia coli. Although this organism is the most common cause of urinary tract infections in women in the United States, it would not be expected to cause PID.

Pear-shaped, flagellated protozoa (choice E) refers to the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis, the only protozoan to cause an STI in the world. Infection is characterized by a malodorous, often green to yellowish discharge, and there is presence of a "strawberry" cervix (a red, friable cervix).

Pleomorphic, gram-negative rods (choice F) are consistent with Haemophilus ducreyi, which causes chancroid and presents as a painful, soft genital lesion. It rarely causes PID.

choice_explanations.A: A naked, icosahedral, double-stranded, circular DNA virus refers to human papillomavirus (HPV), the most common cause of anogenital warts and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, but not a cause of PID.
choice_explanations.B: Intranuclear inclusion bodies surrounded by halos ("owl's eyes") refer to cytomegalovirus, a common infection but not a common agent of PID; most cases in adults are mononucleosis-like.
choice_explanations.C: Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D-K), the most common bacterial STI and a common cause of PID, lives intracellularly and is visualized inside epithelial cells with iodine, Giemsa, or fluorescent-antibody stains.
choice_explanations.D: Lactose-fermenting, gram-negative bacilli are consistent with Escherichia coli, the most common cause of urinary tract infections in women, but it would not be expected to cause PID.
choice_explanations.E: Pear-shaped, flagellated protozoa refers to Trichomonas vaginalis, which causes a malodorous green-yellow discharge and a "strawberry" cervix, not PID.
choice_explanations.F: Pleomorphic, gram-negative rods are consistent with Haemophilus ducreyi, which causes chancroid (a painful, soft genital lesion) and rarely causes PID.

fa_summary: Pelvic inflammatory disease: Chlamydia trachomatis (D-K) is the most common bacterial STI and a common cause; it lives intracellularly and is seen with iodine/Giemsa stains.

stem: A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being involved in a near-fatal fire. Over the next several days, he develops pneumonia and progressive shortness of breath and is intubated. Gram stain of the sputum shows a gram-negative, encapsulated, oxidase-positive aerobic rod. Antibiotic susceptibility tests reveal a resistance to aminoglycosides. Which of the following mechanisms allows the most likely causal organism to be resistant to this antibiotic?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a very common opportunist in burn patients, in whom it classically causes secondary wound infections and septicemia. It may also cause cystitis in patients with urinary catheters, and pneumonia in patients with cystic fibrosis. The organism is found in water and usually gains access to the body as a contaminant in the water used in respirators or in the water baths used to cleanse wounds. Pseudomonas is resistant to many antibiotics, and mutates to even more resistant strains during therapy. Aminoglycoside resistance can be mediated through the bacteria's ability to enzymatically inactivate the drug by acetylation. Other possible mechanisms of Pseudomonas resistance include the bacteria's ability to increase the number of efflux systems that pump out antibiotics, including beta-lactams and aminoglycosides, and decreased permeability of the outer membrane.

Mutation of a penicillin-binding protein (choice B) is a chromosomally mediated mechanism of resistance exhibited by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Mutation of a topoisomerase (choice C) is a chromosomally mediated mechanism of resistance to ciprofloxacin that is exhibited by Pseudomonas and Escherichia coli. It is not, however, considered the major mechanism of drug resistance to a wide variety of drugs.

Plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase production (choice D) is expressed in Pseudomonas and contributes to resistance to penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems. It does not confer resistance to as many drugs as the alteration of the porin proteins, but is still a significant cause of resistance. Plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase production is also seen with Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Klebsiella spp., and Enterobacter spp.

Shift in D-ala to D-lactate (choice E) is the mechanism of high-level vancomycin resistance, which is common in some gram-positive bacteria, such as enterococci. A low level of vancomycin resistance in enterococci is explained by the fact that the D-alanyl-D-serine terminus of peptidoglycan precursors has moderately reduced affinity for this drug.

choice_explanations.A: Pseudomonas resists aminoglycosides mainly by enzymatically inactivating the drug (e.g., acetylation, adenosylation, or phosphorylation); it also uses efflux pumps and decreased outer-membrane permeability.
choice_explanations.B: Mutation of a penicillin-binding protein is a chromosomally mediated resistance mechanism of S pneumoniae, H influenzae, S aureus, and N gonorrhoeae.
choice_explanations.C: Mutation of a topoisomerase mediates ciprofloxacin resistance in Pseudomonas and E coli, but it is not the major mechanism of broad drug resistance.
choice_explanations.D: Plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase production contributes to resistance to penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems, but does not confer resistance to as many drugs as porin alteration.
choice_explanations.E: Shift in D-ala to D-lactate is the mechanism of high-level vancomycin resistance seen in gram-positive bacteria such as enterococci.

fa_summary: Burn patient with a gram-negative, encapsulated, oxidase-positive rod = Pseudomonas aeruginosa; aminoglycoside resistance is via enzymatic inactivation (acetylation).

stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of an ulcerative genital lesion. The lesion first appeared 1 month ago as a papule with a red base, and then became ulcerated and painful. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.9°F). Physical examination shows an ulcerative lesion on the prepuce, with unilateral inguinal adenopathy. Microscopic examination of scrapings from the lesion will most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Epithelial cells with intranuclear inclusion bodies
Pleomorphic gram-negative rods in parallel short chains

explanation:
The correct answer is F. This is a typical case description of chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, a pleomorphic, gram-negative rod that displays a characteristic pattern ("school of fish") on Gram-stained slides. It grows on chocolate agar or on whole blood agar with a satellite phenomenon (around Staphylococcus aureus).

Chancroid initially causes an erythematous papule that rapidly turns into a pustule, and then a "painful" ulcer. One way to differentiate chancroid from syphilis is to remember the phrase "You do cry with ducreyi." Unlike the chancroid ulcer, the syphilitic ulcer is not painful. Patients with Haemophilus ducreyi generally have more than one ulcer and the most common sites are as follows: men (prepuce, corona, or glans penis) and women (labia, vaginal introitus, and perianal areas). A characteristic chancroid ulcer is 1 to 2 cm in diameter with a demarcated border and is covered a gray or yellow purulent exudate. The ulcer bleeds when friction is applied. Treat with azithromycin or ceftriaxone.

Encapsulated bacteria inside mononuclear cells (choice A) describes Klebsiella granulomatis, the agent of granuloma inguinale also known as donovanosis. This disease is rare in the United States, and would be expected most commonly in the tropics of Africa. It is generally a painless genital or perianal lesion that begins as a beefy-red bump and then breaks into granulation tissue that bleeds easily.

Epithelial cells with intranuclear inclusion bodies (choice B) are found with herpes simplex infections, but these lesions would be vesicular coalescing, painful and recurring.

Iodine-staining intracellular inclusion bodies (choice C) would be found during infections with Chlamydia trachomatis, the causative agent of lymphogranuloma venereum, but this lesion is generally nonpainful. It is associated with lymphadenopathy and genital elephantiasis.

Koilocytotic squamous epithelial cells (choice D) are found in infections with human papillomavirus (HPV), which is associated with genital warts, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, and penile cancer.

Neutrophils containing gram-negative diplococci (choice E) would be found if this were gonorrhea. However, in gonorrhea, the patient would have a leukorrheic urethral discharge, and not the ulcerative genital lesion described here.

choice_explanations.A: Encapsulated bacteria inside mononuclear cells describe Klebsiella granulomatis (granuloma inguinale/donovanosis), a painless beefy-red genital lesion seen in the tropics.
choice_explanations.B: Epithelial cells with intranuclear inclusion bodies are found with herpes simplex, whose lesions are vesicular, coalescing, painful, and recurring.
choice_explanations.C: Iodine-staining intracellular inclusion bodies occur with Chlamydia trachomatis (lymphogranuloma venereum), which is generally nonpainful and associated with lymphadenopathy.
choice_explanations.D: Koilocytotic squamous epithelial cells occur with human papillomavirus (HPV), associated with genital warts and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.
choice_explanations.E: Neutrophils containing gram-negative diplococci would indicate gonorrhea, which presents with a leukorrheic urethral discharge rather than the ulcerative lesion described.
choice_explanations.F: Haemophilus ducreyi, a pleomorphic gram-negative rod arranged in "schools of fish"/parallel short chains, causes chancroid: a painful genital ulcer with unilateral inguinal adenopathy.

fa_summary: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi): painful genital ulcer with unilateral inguinal adenopathy; a pleomorphic gram-negative rod in "schools of fish"/parallel short chains.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of a painful, enlarged lymph node in her right axilla for the past week. She reports that for about two weeks, she has been having intermittent chills and subjective fevers. Vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination shows a single enlarged, tender to palpation lymph node in the right axilla. There are no other enlarged lymph nodes palpated on examination. Hemoglobin and hematocrit are within the reference ranges. Histologic examination of tissue obtained on biopsy of the lymph node shows granulomas filled with necrotic debris. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Bartonella henselae is a gram-negative rod. Cats and dogs are the reservoir, transmitting the organism through bites or scratches. B. henselae causes cat-scratch fever, which presents as regional lymphadenopathy with or without low-grade fever and headaches. When available, pathology demonstrates a necrotizing/suppurative granulomatous response with foci of microabscesses. In the immunocompromised patient, it can cause bacillary angiomatosis, which is the vascular proliferative form of infection and can affect any organ system, although it most commonly affects the skin and subcutaneous tissue. Treatment is with azithromycin or doxycycline.

Borrelia burgdorferi (choice B) is a spirochetal organism that is transmitted by a tick bite (Ixodes sp.), producing Lyme disease. Lyme disease progresses from a skin rash to fevers, headache, and pain for about a month. It may produce lymphadenopathy but is not associated with granuloma formation.

Chlamydophila psittaci (choice C) infection occurs after contact with infected bird droppings and produces an atypical pneumonia. The central nervous system may also be involved, but lymph nodes are spared. Chlamydia trachomatis is the chlamydial species that typically produces suppurative nodal granulomas (lymphogranuloma venereum).

Coxiella burnetii (choice D) infection is transmitted by inhaling dust or drinking milk from infected mammals, especially sheep and cows. The disease in humans, Q fever, is marked by mild nonspecific symptoms or pneumonia, and may progress to myocarditis or hepatitis.

Rickettsia prowazekii (choice E) produces epidemic (louse-borne) typhus, which is transmitted by body lice and produces a rash similar to Rocky Mountain spotted fever, except that it moves from the trunk to the extremities. Although the organism may reside in the lymph nodes in dormancy, it does not elicit granuloma formation.

choice_explanations.A: Bartonella henselae is a gram-negative rod transmitted by cat/dog bites or scratches; it causes cat-scratch fever with regional lymphadenopathy and necrotizing/suppurative granulomas.
choice_explanations.B: Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by Ixodes ticks, produces Lyme disease; it may cause lymphadenopathy but not granuloma formation.
choice_explanations.C: Chlamydophila psittaci follows contact with infected bird droppings and causes atypical pneumonia, sparing lymph nodes.
choice_explanations.D: Coxiella burnetii is transmitted by inhaling dust or drinking milk from infected mammals and causes Q fever with mild symptoms or pneumonia.
choice_explanations.E: Rickettsia prowazekii produces epidemic (louse-borne) typhus; it does not elicit granuloma formation.

fa_summary: Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease): gram-negative rod, regional lymphadenopathy with necrotizing/suppurative granulomas.

stem: Several employees at a large company come to employee health services because of a 2-day history of multiple episodes of watery diarrhea. Some have had blood-tinged stools and some have had profound abdominal cramping and fever. All the affected individuals attended a dinner party several days ago. An overnight stool culture at 42°C (107.6°F) grows microaerophilic, oxidase-positive, gram-negative, curved rods with polar flagella. Which of the following is the most likely source of this infection?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This case history and culture characteristics describe a typical gastroenteritis due to Campylobacter jejuni, the most common bacterial gastroenteritis in the United States. Contaminated poultry or poultry products are responsible for more than 50% of all infections. This bacteria is a microaerophilic, oxidase-positive, gram-negative, curved rod with polar flagella.

Carriers (choice A) are not known to occur with Campylobacter, and are best known with Salmonella typhi. Typhoid fever is an enteric fever that presents with fever, lymphadenopathy and constipation.

Custard and potato-salad dishes (choice B) would be the most likely source if the agent was Staphylococcus aureus, but this would have had an onset of 2 hours, and a gram-positive coccus would have been seen on culture.

Poorly canned green vegetables (choice C) are the usual source of Clostridium botulinum, which would cause a flaccid paralysis. Clostridium is a genus of gram-positive rods.

Poorly washed salad greens (choice D) could be sources of infection with multiple agents such as Escherichia coli, Entamoeba histolytica, Salmonella, or Shigella. The E. coli strains that cause non-bloody diarrhea are usually associated with travel out of the home country (traveler's diarrhea). E. coli is a gram-negative rod that is oxidase-negative. Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite that does not occur commonly in the United States but instead requires travel to a tropical country. Salmonella and Shigella are both gram-negative rods that are oxidase-negative, and would be more likely to cause frankly bloody stools.

Rare red meat dishes (choice F) would be good sources for Escherichia coli or Trichinella spiralis. E. coli is a gram-negative, oxidase-negative rod and Trichinella is a nematode. The serotype of E. coli associated with rare meat dishes in the United States causes bloody diarrhea without leukocytes. Trichinosis causes myalgia, fever, eosinophilia, splinter hemorrhages and periorbital edema.

choice_explanations.A: Carriers are not known with Campylobacter; the carrier state is best known with Salmonella typhi (typhoid fever).
choice_explanations.B: Custard and potato-salad dishes fit Staphylococcus aureus, which has a 2-hour onset and would show a gram-positive coccus on culture.
choice_explanations.C: Poorly canned green vegetables are the usual source of Clostridium botulinum, a gram-positive rod causing flaccid paralysis.
choice_explanations.D: Poorly washed salad greens can carry E coli, Entamoeba histolytica, Salmonella, or Shigella, none of which matches the oxidase-positive curved rod.
choice_explanations.E: Campylobacter jejuni, a microaerophilic oxidase-positive gram-negative curved rod, is the most common bacterial gastroenteritis; contaminated poultry causes >50% of infections.
choice_explanations.F: Rare red meat dishes fit Escherichia coli or Trichinella spiralis, not the organism described.

fa_summary: Campylobacter jejuni = most common bacterial gastroenteritis; contaminated poultry/poultry products cause >50% of cases; microaerophilic, oxidase-positive, curved rod.

stem: A 28-year-old man drinks a glass of fresh fruit juice from a street vendor while traveling in Colombia. Three days later, he develops watery diarrhea and comes to the physician. His vital signs are stable. Physical examination is only notable for dry mucous membranes. He has no abdominal tenderness, distension, guarding, or rebound. Fecal occult blood test is negative. The most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is infection with which of the following pathogenic strains of Escherichia coli?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC), an important cause of traveler's diarrhea, produces toxins that activate intestinal adenylate or guanylate cyclase. Consequently, the intestinal mucosa overproduces cAMP, resulting in a mild and self-limited secretory diarrhea.

Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC; choice A) does not express a toxin but is seen to cluster over the colonic mucosa in some individuals. Although EAEC is occasionally found in patients with chronic diarrhea, no clear mechanism for mucosal pathophysiology has been determined for it.

Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC; choice B), classically associated with strain O157:H7 and present in undercooked hamburgers, expresses a Shiga-like toxin that causes bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). HUS is characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure; the Shiga-like toxin damages the 60S ribosomal subunit and protein synthesis.

choice_explanations.A: Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) does not express a toxin; it clusters over the colonic mucosa and lacks a clear mechanism of mucosal pathophysiology.
choice_explanations.B: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), classically O157:H7 from undercooked hamburgers, expresses a Shiga-like toxin causing bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
choice_explanations.E: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is an important cause of traveler's diarrhea; its toxins activate adenylate/guanylate cyclase, overproducing cAMP and causing mild, self-limited secretory diarrhea.

fa_summary: ETEC is the classic cause of traveler's diarrhea; heat-labile/heat-stable toxins raise cAMP/cGMP producing a mild, self-limited watery (non-inflammatory) diarrhea.

stem: A 60-year-old man abruptly develops a temperature of 40.1°C (104.2°F), shakes, a severe headache, and muscle pain. He initially had a dry, insignificant cough, but over the next few days, he developed marked shortness of breath that necessitated assisted ventilation. Culture of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid on buffered charcoal yeast extract (CYE) show growth of a predominant organism. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has a severe, potentially fatal atypical pneumonia with prominent systemic symptoms. Culture on charcoal yeast extract (CYE) is the specific clue that the organism is Legionella pneumophila. The disease is respiratory legionellosis, also known as Legionnaires' disease because the disease was first described when it occurred in epidemic form following an American Legion convention at a Philadelphia hotel. Exposure to this bacteria is usually associated with aerosol-producing devices such as air-conditioners, mist machines, etc. Patients tend to be older (age 40-70 years) and may have risk factors including cigarette use, alcoholism, diabetes, chronic illness, or immunosuppressive therapy. Additional manifestations of patients with legionellosis includes hyponatremia.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (choice A) is an agent of atypical pneumonia, but would require tissue culture for growth since it is an intracellular organism.

Haemophilus influenzae type b (choice B) is an agent of pneumonia and meningitis in unvaccinated children between 3 months and 2 years of age. It must be grown on chocolate agar, since it requires NAD and hematin.

Listeria monocytogenes (choice D) causes listeriosis and is not a notable cause of pneumonia. In the adult, listeriosis is often a bacterial meningitis. When the organism crosses the placenta, the result is granulomatosis infantiseptica, which has a high fatality rate in neonates. If the organism is acquired by the child passing through the birth canal, it is an agent of neonatal meningitis.

Staphylococcus aureus (choice E) can cause typical pneumonia and is easily cultured on blood agar.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (choice F) causes typical pneumonia and is easily cultured on blood agar.

choice_explanations.A: Chlamydia pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia but requires tissue culture, as it is an intracellular organism.
choice_explanations.B: Haemophilus influenzae type b causes pneumonia/meningitis in unvaccinated children and must be grown on chocolate agar (requires NAD and hematin).
choice_explanations.C: Legionella pneumophila grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract (CYE) with iron and cysteine; it causes severe atypical pneumonia with systemic symptoms and hyponatremia.
choice_explanations.D: Listeria monocytogenes causes listeriosis/meningitis and is not a notable cause of pneumonia.
choice_explanations.E: Staphylococcus aureus causes typical pneumonia and is easily cultured on blood agar.
choice_explanations.F: Streptococcus pneumoniae causes typical pneumonia and is easily cultured on blood agar.

fa_summary: Legionella pneumophila: gram-negative rod that grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract (CYE) with iron and cysteine; severe atypical pneumonia, often with hyponatremia.

stem: A 33-year-old primigravid woman at 24 weeks' gestation develops axillary lymphadenopathy and a low-grade fever 7 days after returning from Arizona. Physical examination shows a small papule and a healing excoriation on the left arm. Examination of tissue obtained on biopsy of a lymph node shows stellate granulomas with small, gram-negative bacilli. Which of the following is most likely to be present in this patient's history?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Bartonella henselae is a gram-negative bacillus that is the causative agent of cat-scratch disease. Cats, especially kittens, harbor the organism. It is usually inoculated through an easily forgotten scratch. A pustule forms at the site within days to weeks, accompanied by tender regional adenopathy. Microscopically, stellate granulomas with central necrosis and organisms are observed. Normally, treatment is not required because this disease is benign and self-limited, but immunosuppressed and pregnant patients are more susceptible to dissemination. Treatment is with ciprofloxacin or doxycycline. Pregnant patients should be treated with macrolides (azithromycin).

Camping (choice A) can be a point of exposure for a multitude of infectious agents. The mention of Arizona in the question stem could suggest coccidioidomycosis, which is a fungal infection; it is not caused by a gram-negative bacillus and it would not produce a stellate granuloma. Spores of the organism are inhaled, usually from the soil. These spores enlarge to sporangia, which burst and spread. The disease is characterized by pulmonary symptoms in the immunocompromised, and skin bumps (erythema nodosum) in the normal patient. Infection with Yersinia pestis, the causative agent of bubonic plague, is also possible after camping in Arizona, but it would present rather differently. True bubonic plague (incubation period 2-6 days) presents with sudden onset high fever, chills, and headaches, and tender, swollen lymph nodes (buboes). Cutaneous plague causes papules, but also pustules, a cutaneous eschar, and/or purpura, which may become necrotic.

Consumption of unpasteurized goat's milk (choice B) could lead to brucellosis. Brucella melitensis is associated with consumption of unpasteurized milk or soft cheese from infected animals. Brucella are small, gram-negative coccobacilli, but brucellosis typically produces a chronic, relapsing fever (undulant fever), chills, sweating, but few specific physical findings.

choice_explanations.A: Camping could expose to coccidioidomycosis (fungal, no stellate granuloma) or bubonic plague (Yersinia pestis), neither of which matches a gram-negative bacillus with stellate granulomas.
choice_explanations.B: Unpasteurized goat's milk causes brucellosis (Brucella, small gram-negative coccobacilli), which presents as undulant fever with few specific findings.
choice_explanations.E: Bartonella henselae, carried by cats/kittens and inoculated by scratch, causes cat-scratch disease with stellate granulomas; pregnant patients require macrolide (azithromycin) treatment.

fa_summary: Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease): contact with a cat/kitten, scratch, papule/pustule, regional lymphadenopathy, stellate granulomas; pregnancy requires macrolides.

stem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of progressive joint pain in her ankles, knees, and wrists. She has had three similar episodes within the past several years. She is sexually active, has multiple partners, and occasionally uses protection. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a diffuse petechial rash over the trunk and extensor surfaces. The ankles and knees are swollen, red, and tender with decreased range of motion, and there is tenderness over the tendon sheaths of the hands and forearms. Blood cultures are positive. ESR is 40 mm/hr. Examination of joint fluid shows a white cell count of 22,000/mm3. Which of the following best explains why this patient has had recurrent episodes of this infection?

options.text: It is resistant to complement-mediated lysis
Its pili undergo antigenic and phase variation

explanation:
The correct answer is E. This is a classic presentation of Neisseria gonorrhoeae (septic) arthritis, where there is a direct bacterial invasion of the joint space. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative, oxidase positive diplococcus that is transmitted sexually. It can be cultured on chocolate agar and the chocolate agar variant Thayer-Martin agar, which contain an assortment of antibiotics that select for Neisseria species.

There are 2 entities of gonococcal arthritis that you should be familiar with: localized septic gonococcal monoarticular arthritis (40% of patients), and disseminated gonococcal dermatitis-arthritis syndrome (60% of patients), as seen in this vignette.

Gonococcal dermatitis-arthritis syndrome has a triad of dermatitis, tenosynovitis, and polyarthritis, as seen in our patient. Patients with gonococcal septic arthritis commonly present with fever. The ankles and knees are the most commonly involved joints and are typically swollen, red, and tender, with decreased range of motion due to pain. These symptoms may develop over a few days to a few weeks. Patients are continuously susceptible to reinfection because of antigenic variation and phase variation of the pili. These pili are also protective against phagocytosis and mediate attachment to the mucosal surfaces. Even in patients with negative blood cultures, the high numbers of leukocytes in the joint fluid and the signs of endotoxin rash should suggest the diagnosis of gonococcal arthritis in a sexually active age group.

N. gonorrhoeae is not an intracellular pathogen (choice A), although it may be found intracellularly in neutrophils after it has been phagocytized.

Ceftriaxone (choice B) is the drug of choice for N. gonorrhoeae.
