Gonococci are especially susceptible to complement-mediated lysis, not resistant to it (choice C).

N. gonorrhoeae has an insignificant capsule that does not play a major role in its pathogenesis, but the capsule is immunogenic (compare with choice D). Streptococcus pyogenes and Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B are the best known examples of nonimmunogenic capsules, made of hyaluronic acid or sialic acid, respectively, but virtually all other capsules are known.

choice_explanations.A: N gonorrhoeae is not an intracellular pathogen, although it may be found intracellularly in neutrophils after phagocytosis.
choice_explanations.B: Ceftriaxone is the drug of choice for N gonorrhoeae; the organism is not resistant to it.
choice_explanations.C: Gonococci are especially susceptible to complement-mediated lysis, not resistant.
choice_explanations.D: N gonorrhoeae has an insignificant capsule that does not play a major role in pathogenesis, but the capsule is immunogenic; S pyogenes and N meningitidis serogroup B have nonimmunogenic capsules.
choice_explanations.E: Antigenic and phase variation of the pili make patients continuously susceptible to reinfection; the pili also protect against phagocytosis and mediate mucosal attachment.

fa_summary: Neisseria gonorrhoeae septic arthritis: disseminated gonococcal dermatitis-arthritis syndrome; recurrent infection due to antigenic and phase variation of the pili.

stem: A 19-year-old man comes to the physician because of a seven day history of weakness, malaise, and a dry cough. His temperature is 38.0°C (100.0°F). A bronchoalveolar lavage is performed and the washings show "slow-growing" organisms on sterol-containing media. Laboratory studies of serum show the presence of cold agglutinins. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
explanation: The correct answer is C. This patient has primary atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae. This is the most common atypical pneumonia in young adults and occurs in crowded living situations. This organism is fastidious and difficult to culture in the laboratory; however, serodiagnosis can be most helpful. It is an extracellular prokaryote with no cell wall, but with sterols in the membrane. When the bacteria is cultured it generally shows mulberry-shaped colonies on media containing sterols. Patients typically produce one or two heterophile antibodies during the course of the infection; one agglutinates human O+ red blood cells in the cold (the cold hemagglutinin), while the other causes the agglutination of a strain of Streptococcus salivarius termed strain MG (the Strep MG agglutinins). The treatment is with macrolides (i.e., erythromycin, azithromycin, or clarithromycin). Beta-lactams, such as the penicillins and cephalosporins, are ineffective in the treatment of this condition.

choice_explanations.C: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a fastidious extracellular prokaryote with no cell wall but sterols in its membrane; it grows as mulberry-shaped colonies on sterol media and can be suggested by cold agglutinins (IgM).

fa_summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae: atypical "walking pneumonia" with dry cough; no cell wall, needs sterols; cold agglutinins (IgM) and Strep MG agglutinins; treat with macrolides.

stem: Serology for hepatitis viruses is performed and shows the presence of HBsAg and HBc IgM antibody. Antibody tests for HBs IgG Ab and HAV are negative. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these results?

options.text: A dual infection of HBV and HAV

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The biology of HBV includes the expression of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) on the exterior of all viral particles (i.e., viral and subviral). The nucleocapsid or core is composed of hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg). Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) is secreted from infected cells and marks ongoing viral infection.

This patient has acute hepatitis B virus infection. This is based on the presence of HBsAg and HBcAb-IgM in addition to the absence of HBsAb as well as that of HBcAb-IgG. Additional laboratory tests would likely also reveal HBV DNA. Serology for HBsAg, HBeAg, and anti-HBc-IgM antibody, but absence of HBsAb and HBeAb.

Note: In contrast, the window period is the timeframe in which HBsAg disappears and before HBsAb IgG is detected. The resolution period would demonstrate and detect IgG antibodies for HBsAb, HBcAb, and HBeAb, and lack both HBsAg and HBcA IgM. Liver enzymes would not be elevated in both conditions. Persistence of HBsAg beyond 6 months indicates chronic hepatitis.

A dual infection of HBV and hepatitis A virus (HAV) (choice B) is not plausible since the IgM anti-HAV serology is negative. Chronic HBV infection (choice C) is unlikely because the patient has HBcIgM Ab, which is characteristic of an acute infection rather than a chronic infection. Persistence of HBsAg beyond 6 months indicates chronic hepatitis. In chronic infection, the profile would have absence of HBsAb IgG and presence of HBsAg, HBeAg, HBcAb IgG and IgM, and HBeAb IgG.

If the patient were making an excess of HBsAb (choice E), there would be a rising titer of HBsAb. Thus the patient would be positive for HBsAb and negative for HBsAg.

choice_explanations.A: HBsAg plus anti-HBc IgM (with negative anti-HBs IgG and anti-HAV) indicates acute hepatitis B virus infection.
choice_explanations.B: A dual HBV/HAV infection is not plausible because the IgM anti-HAV serology is negative.
choice_explanations.C: Chronic HBV is unlikely because HBc IgM indicates acute infection; chronic infection would show HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months with HBcAb IgG.
choice_explanations.E: Excess HBsAb would produce a rising anti-HBs titer with a positive anti-HBs and negative HBsAg, which is not the case here.

fa_summary: Acute hepatitis B: HBsAg positive with anti-HBc IgM and negative anti-HBs (and negative anti-HAV); chronic infection requires HBsAg persistence beyond 6 months.

stem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of diffuse muscle weakness, difficulty speaking and swallowing, and palpitations. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 127/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mydriasis. Which of the following agents is the most likely cause of the findings seen in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Botulism is caused by the systemic manifestations of a protein toxin produced by the gram-positive, spore-forming, obligate anaerobe Clostridium botulinum. Botulinum toxin type A is also available commercially as the compound OnabotulinumtoxinA, which is used for the treatment of overactive bladder, migraine headache prophylaxis, upper limb spasticity, and cervical dystonia.

Botulism is a serious neuroparalytic syndrome caused by the action of the toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum. Botulinum toxin acts by selectively cleaving the docking proteins for acetylcholine (ACh) exocytosis. As a result, there is decreased ACh transmission in all parasympathetic neuroeffector junctions and decreased sympathetic cholinergic transmission in sweat glands and neuromuscular junctions. Mydriasis is a result of decreased ACh activity on muscarinic receptors in parasympathetic neuroeffector junctions. Skeletal muscle weakness results from decreased ACh stimulation of nicotinic receptors in neuromuscular junctions. Skeletal muscle weakness is the differentiating feature between anticholinergic agents (e.g., atropine) and botulinum toxin. Serious adverse effects of botulinum toxin type A include respiratory compromise, development or worsening of acute angle-closure glaucoma, brachial plexopathy, dysphonia, muscle weakness, and anticholinergic side effects. Treatment of botulism is symptomatic; however, equine serum botulism antitoxin can be used if severe adverse effects are seen.

Atropine (choice A), a muscarinic receptor antagonist, causes tachycardia, mydriasis, and elevated body temperature but does not cause muscle weakness. You can remember these side effects with the following mnemonic "Blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, red as a beet, hot as a stone and dry as a bone."

Methylphenidate (choice C) is an indirect sympathomimetic and causes tachycardia, mydriasis, and possibly elevated body temperature.

choice_explanations.A: Atropine, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, causes tachycardia, mydriasis, and elevated body temperature but does not cause muscle weakness.
choice_explanations.B: Botulinum toxin cleaves ACh-exocytosis docking proteins, decreasing ACh release at parasympathetic and neuromuscular junctions, producing mydriasis and flaccid skeletal muscle weakness.
choice_explanations.C: Methylphenidate is an indirect sympathomimetic that causes tachycardia, mydriasis, and possibly elevated body temperature.

fa_summary: Botulism (Clostridium botulinum toxin) impairs ACh exocytosis, causing mydriasis and descending flaccid muscle weakness; unlike atropine, it weakens skeletal muscle.

stem: A 34-year-old man who recently emigrated from Brazil comes to the physician for a pre-employment physical examination. A chest x-ray shows a patchy, bilateral pneumonia and a lung mass. Examination of tissue obtained on biopsy of the mass shows spherical yeast cells with multiple peripheral buds encircling the central cell. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Latin America and multiply-budding ("pilot's wheel or mariner's wheel") yeasts are clues for paracoccidioidomycosis. The typical pathognomonic features for Paracoccidioides brasiliensis are large, thick-walled, spherical yeast cells with multiple peripheral buds encircling the central cell. In skin and mucous membrane lesions, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with intraepidermal abscesses may also be seen.

The adult (chronic) form of paracoccidioidomycosis accounts for the majority of cases and represents endogenous reactivation years after initial contact with the fungus. The lungs are the primary sites of infection with the oral mucosa involved in many cases also. Chronic pulmonary sequelae develop in approximately one third of patients and include pulmonary fibrosis, bullae, and emphysematous changes that can lead to the development of pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. Additionally, adrenal insufficiency is an associated manifestation in endemic countries. Antifungal medications are the mainstay of treatment for paracoccidioidomycosis and include itraconazole (drug of choice), ketoconazole, and fluconazole. Amphotericin B is used in patients with severe disease.

Blastomycosis (choice A), caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis, results in large budding yeasts in the sputum. It is found in the great riverbeds of the eastern half of the United States, with North and South Carolina being especially highly endemic. It causes acute and chronic lung infections as well as disseminated disease and is a special problem in the immunocompromised person. Itraconazole is the treatment of choice for mild blastomycosis and amphotericin B is used for more severe cases.

Coccidioidomycosis (choice B), caused by Coccidioides immitis, is a fungus of the U.S. desert southwest. It also causes acute and chronic pulmonary infections, disseminated infections, and cutaneous lesions.

choice_explanations.A: Blastomycosis (Blastomyces dermatitidis) shows large budding yeasts in sputum; it occurs in the great riverbeds of the eastern US.
choice_explanations.B: Coccidioidomycosis (Coccidioides immitis) is a fungus of the US desert southwest causing acute/chronic pulmonary and disseminated infection.
choice_explanations.D: Paracoccidioidomycosis (Paracoccidioides brasiliensis), seen in Latin America, shows thick-walled spherical yeast cells with multiple peripheral buds ("pilot's wheel"); it causes chronic pneumonia with oral mucosal involvement.

fa_summary: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (Latin America): thick-walled spherical yeasts budding in multiples ("pilot's wheel"), causing chronic pneumonia with oral mucosal lesions; treat with itraconazole.

stem: A 20-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressive vaginal itching for the past 3 days. She recently had a urinary tract infection and was treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for mild erythema of the vulvar area and a white vaginal discharge. A swab of the vaginal discharge is taken and inoculated into animal serum. Which of the following is most likely to be seen in this medium after 2-3 hours?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The vaginal pruritus and white discharge (often described as "cottage cheese-like"), especially after antibiotic use, strongly suggest vaginal candidiasis, which is definitively diagnosed by performing the germ tube test (inoculation of a sample into animal serum). Like many other pathogenic fungi, Candida albicans is dimorphic. Budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae can be seen in culture at 25°C, but at body temperature, and in the presence of animal serum (mimicking the tissue environment), characteristic germ tubes are formed, which are short, germinating nonseptate true hyphae. Candida is the only medically important organism that will grow germ tubes under these conditions.

Arthroconidia (choice A) would be characteristic of the diagnostic stages of agents of dermatophytes, which cause ringworm or tinea. These are cutaneous infections that cause itching and scaly skin but are not typically mucosal pathogens. They would not be likely to cause a white vaginal discharge.

Encapsulated yeasts (choice B) would be found in clinical specimens of Cryptococcus neoformans, which causes meningitis in patients with Hodgkin lymphoma and AIDS. It would not cause vaginal pruritus or discharge.

Hyphae with rosettes of microconidia (choice C) would be the environmental form for Sporothrix schenckii. This fungus causes rose-gardener's disease, which is a cutaneous mycetoma associated with traumatic implantation while gardening. It does not cause vaginitis.

Macroconidia (choice D) are the environmental form of Histoplasma capsulatum. This fungus causes atypical pneumonia in immunocompromised patients living in the Mississippi, Missouri, or Ohio river valleys. It is not a cause of vaginitis.

choice_explanations.A: Arthroconidia are the diagnostic stages of dermatophytes (ringworm/tinea), cutaneous infections that do not cause a white vaginal discharge.
choice_explanations.B: Encapsulated yeasts are found with Cryptococcus neoformans, which causes meningitis, not vaginitis.
choice_explanations.C: Hyphae with rosettes of microconidia are the environmental form of Sporothrix schenckii (rose-gardener's disease), which does not cause vaginitis.
choice_explanations.D: Macroconidia are the environmental form of Histoplasma capsulatum, which causes atypical pneumonia, not vaginitis.
choice_explanations.E: Candida albicans forms short, germinating nonseptate true hyphae (germ tubes) when inoculated into animal serum at body temperature; it is the only medically important organism to do so.

fa_summary: Candida albicans germ tube test: vaginal pruritus with "cottage cheese" discharge after antibiotics; inoculation into serum at body temperature yields short germinating true hyphae (germ tubes).

stem: A 1-month-old girl of northern European descent is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination because of productive cough, shortness of breath, and impaired growth. Her parents also report that she has been producing greasy, foul-smelling stools. The physician orders a sweat chloride test, which is positive. Which of the following best describes the mutation most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has the classic symptoms of cystic fibrosis, including productive cough due to excess mucus, shortness of breath, and greasy, foul-smelling stools. Blockage of pancreatic ducts prevents the secretion of pancreatic enzymes necessary for the breakdown of fats in the diet, resulting in greasy, foul-smelling stools. This condition is termed pancreatic insufficiency, and is common in severe cases of cystic fibrosis. The positive sweat chloride test is considered as the "gold standard" for diagnosing cystic fibrosis.

The most common mutation in individuals of northern European descent is the ΔF508 mutation. This mutation arises as a result of a deletion of three nucleotides in the coding region of the CFTR gene, comprising the codon encoding phenylalanine (F) at position 508 of the amino acid sequence. The loss of this single amino acid prevents the proper folding of the protein, resulting in its degradation. Individuals who have this mutation in both of their CFTR alleles typically have a severe form of the disease.

Frameshift mutations (choice A) typically result from insertion or deletion of one or two base pairs in the coding region of a gene. As a result, codons downstream from the mutation are "frame-shifted." Because three base pairs comprise a codon, insertions or deletions result in incorrect translation of all downstream codons. Insertions and deletions have been reported in the CFTR gene that result in frameshift mutations, but these types of mutations are not common.

An insertion mutation (choice C) is created when one or more extra nucleotides are inserted into a gene. Depending on the number of nucleotides inserted, this can result in a frameshift mutation or, if three nucleotides are inserted, the addition of a new amino acid to the protein encoded by the gene. Insertion mutations in cystic fibrosis patients have been identified, but they are not common.

Nonsense mutations (choice D) are mutations in which a stop codon is introduced upon the replacement of one nucleotide of a coding region with a different nucleotide. Some nonsense mutations, including G542X, cause cystic fibrosis, but they are not the most common mutation for this disease.

Substitution mutations (choice E) may occur as transversions or transitions. A transversion is the replacement of a purine with a pyrimidine. A transition occurs when a purine is replaced by a different purine. These types of mutations affect only one nucleotide and can result in either a missense or nonsense mutation if it occurs in the coding region of a gene. Some substitution mutations have been identified in cystic fibrosis patients, but these types of mutations are not as common as the ΔF508 deletion mutation.

choice_explanations.A: Frameshift mutations result from insertion or deletion of one or two base pairs that shift the downstream reading frame; such mutations occur in the CFTR gene but are not common.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: the most common cystic fibrosis mutation in northern Europeans is ΔF508, a deletion of three nucleotides (the phenylalanine-508 codon) in the CFTR gene.
choice_explanations.C: Insertion mutations (of one or more nucleotides) occur in cystic fibrosis but are not common.
choice_explanations.D: Nonsense mutations (e.g., G542X) introduce a premature stop codon and can cause cystic fibrosis, but they are not the most common mutation.
choice_explanations.E: Substitution mutations (transitions/transversions) occur in cystic fibrosis but are less common than the ΔF508 deletion.

fa_summary: Cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive; CFTR gene on chromosome 7) is most commonly caused by the ΔF508 deletion of three nucleotides, which removes phenylalanine-508 and causes protein misfolding/trafficking defects; a positive sweat chloride test is diagnostic.

stem: A 46-year-old man is brought to the physician by his wife because of a 6-month history of progressive memory loss and personality changes. His wife says that his father developed similar symptoms at the age of 60. Physical examination shows involuntary twitching movements of the limbs and poor coordination. Which of the following genetic mechanisms is most likely involved in this disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Several disorders, including Huntington disease, are caused by the expansion of a three-base sequence within a specific gene on chromosome 4. The majority of trinucleotide expansion disorders share certain common features. Normal individuals possess a range of copy numbers for the pathogenic trinucleotide. These normal copy numbers are relatively stable over meiosis, so that individuals in the next generation inherit the trinucleotide copy number as a simple, stable, Mendelian trait. However, some individuals display premutation, a characteristic in which the copy number of the trinucleotide is increased and unstable but their phenotype is normal. Individuals with premutations may pass on further expanded trinucleotide tracts to their offspring. The presence of more trinucleotide repeats in the offspring, resulting in an earlier age of onset and a more severe phenotype, is a phenomenon known as anticipation. Because this patient is presenting with symptoms much earlier in life than his father, this is most likely a case of anticipation. The mechanism by which trinucleotide repeats cause disease varies. In Huntington disease, the expansion of CAG repeats is thought to produce a toxic "gain of function." This means that the disease develops because the mutant form of the protein gains a new or greater function. Other genetic diseases caused by trinucleotide expansion include fragile X syndrome, myotonic dystrophy, and Friedreich's ataxia.

Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes are frequently cited examples of genetic diseases involving genomic imprinting (choice B). On the maternal chromosome, the genes responsible for Prader-Willi syndrome are normally silenced by an epigenetic mechanism. Similarly, on the paternal chromosome, the Angelman syndrome genes are epigenetically silenced. This produces a situation in which an individual is functionally heterozygous for these alleles. If a deletion occurs in the Prader-Willi genes on the paternal chromosome, then the individual has lost his only active copies of those genes, and he will have Prader-Willi. If a deletion occurs in the Angelman syndrome genes on the maternal chromosome, then that individual will no longer have any active Angelman genes, and he will have Angelman syndrome.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disease due to a large deletion (choice C) in the gene that encodes dystrophin. This deletion creates a frameshift in the coding region of the gene, preventing the formation of functional dystrophin protein. Large deletions occur in 60-70% of cases and small point mutations occur in 15-30% of cases.

Single amino acid substitutions (choice D) are common in recessive diseases. An example is sickle cell anemia, in which glutamic acid is replaced with valine in position 6 of the protein's amino acid sequence.

Translocations (choice E) of chromosomes give rise to several disorders, including chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML; Philadelphia chromosome), in which a translocation occurs between chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9,22), producing the oncogenic fusion protein BCR-ABL.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: Huntington disease is caused by expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat (on chromosome 4), producing a toxic gain-of-function protein; increasing repeat length in successive generations (anticipation) causes earlier, more severe disease.
choice_explanations.B: Genomic imprinting (e.g., Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes) depends on the parent of origin and is a different mechanism.
choice_explanations.C: Large gene deletions (e.g., dystrophin in Duchenne muscular dystrophy) cause a frameshift; they are not the mechanism in Huntington disease.
choice_explanations.D: Single amino acid substitutions (e.g., sickle cell anemia) are common in recessive diseases, not the mechanism here.
choice_explanations.E: Translocations (e.g., t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome in CML) are not the mechanism in Huntington disease.

fa_summary: Huntington disease is a trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion disorder on chromosome 4; expansions produce a toxic gain-of-function and can increase in successive generations, causing earlier onset (anticipation).

stem: A 4-month-old boy who appeared healthy at birth is brought to the physician because of poor growth and little interest in feeding. He has failed to achieve major developmental milestones, and is now in the 5th percentile for length. Physical examination shows listlessness, and distinct appearing hair that is kinky, matted, sparse, and pale in color. Laboratory studies show decreased serum ceruloplasmin and copper levels. An arteriogram shows elongation and tortuosity of major arteries. The activity of which of the following enzymes is most likely decreased in this child?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The disease described is the X-linked recessive disorder, Menkes disease (also known as Kinky hair disease), which is characterized by kinky, depigmented, lusterless hair as well as a number of vascular, neurologic, facial, and ocular manifestations. The disease occurs due to mutations in the gene ATP7A, which encodes an ATP-dependent copper efflux protein in the intestine. Copper can be absorbed into the mucosal cell, but it cannot be transported into the bloodstream. This leads to a severe copper deficiency and all copper-requiring enzymes will be adversely affected. One of these enzymes, lysyl oxidase, is involved in crosslinking collagen fibers, which accounts for the connective tissue involvement and vascular abnormalities seen in this disorder. Additional copper-dependent enzymes affected include cytochrome C oxidase (likely leading to neurologic symptoms) and tyrosinase (likely leading to the hypopigmentation of the hair and skin).

Abnormally low activity of cytochrome b5 reductase (choice A), an iron-dependent enzyme, would result in cyanosis and methemoglobinemia.

Low levels of glutathione peroxidase activity (choice B) can result from selenium deficiency. The clinical presentation includes myopathy and cardiomyopathy.

Deficiency of N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase (choice D) results in I-cell disease, characterized by mental retardation, skeletal abnormalities, a high, narrow forehead, and coarse facies. Inclusion bodies of undigested substrates occur in cells of many tissues as well as secretion of several lysosomal enzymes into the blood and extracellular fluid. "Kinky" hair, a hallmark feature of Menkes disease, is not seen in I-cell disease.

Abnormally low phenylalanine hydroxylase activity (choice E) would result in phenylketonuria (PKU). Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin as a coenzyme. Untreated individuals with PKU develop mental retardation after birth, but have none of the other symptoms described in this child (especially the distinct features of the patient's hair), although both Menkes patients and untreated PKU patients show hypopigmentation of the skin.

choice_explanations.A: Cytochrome b5 reductase is an iron-dependent enzyme; low activity causes cyanosis and methemoglobinemia, not the kinky hair and vascular findings here.
choice_explanations.B: Low glutathione peroxidase activity (from selenium deficiency) causes myopathy and cardiomyopathy, not these features.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: Menkes disease (ATP7A mutation) causes copper deficiency; decreased lysyl oxidase impairs collagen crosslinking, producing connective tissue and vascular abnormalities.
choice_explanations.D: N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase deficiency causes I-cell disease, which does not have kinky hair as a hallmark.
choice_explanations.E: Low phenylalanine hydroxylase activity causes phenylketonuria (PKU), which lacks the distinctive hair findings of Menkes disease.

fa_summary: Menkes disease (X-linked recessive, ATP7A mutation) causes severe copper deficiency; decreased lysyl oxidase impairs collagen crosslinking, causing connective tissue and vascular abnormalities along with kinky, depigmented hair.

stem: A healthy 48-year-old man with a family history of colon cancer undergoes his first colonoscopy, which reveals numerous adenomatous polyps. Examination of tissue obtained on biopsy of the colon shows carcinoma. Cells in this tumor are found to have mutations in both the KRAS and APC genes. Which of the following types of genetic changes has most likely affected the APC gene in this tumor?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Tumor suppressor genes block tumors by regulating cell growth. Some are directly involved in regulation of the cell cycle or growth inhibition by cell-to-cell contact (gatekeepers). Others are involved in repairing DNA damage and maintaining genomic integrity (caretakers). Tumor suppressor genes must be eliminated by some mechanism such as deletion, or a loss-of-function mutation in order to contribute to cancer. Familial colon cancer (familial adenomatous polyposis) can be due to mutations in APC, a tumor suppressor gene that regulates the bifunctional protein catenin. Catenin is important for cell adhesion and transcription of genes important for proliferation. APC promotes degradation of catenin by phosphorylation via GSK3β. Loss of APC would therefore promote cellular proliferation and contribute to the development of cancer.

There are several ways in which proto-oncogenes (normal, non-mutated) can be mutated to produce constitutively active oncogenes (also known as gain-of-function mutations). First, the gene can be amplified (choice A), resulting in abnormal amounts of the protein. The gene locus can also be hyperactive due to insertion of a retrovirus (choice D) or increased activity of the promoter (choice C).

A silent mutation (choice E) would not have any effect on the gene since silent mutations do not result in a change in a codon. Therefore, the resulting protein's amino acid sequence will be unchanged.

choice_explanations.A: Gene amplification produces abnormal amounts of the protein and is a mechanism of oncogene (gain-of-function) activation, not of tumor suppressor (APC) inactivation.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: APC is a tumor suppressor gene; tumor suppressors must be eliminated by deletion or loss-of-function mutation (two-hit hypothesis) to contribute to cancer, as occurs in familial adenomatous polyposis.
choice_explanations.C: Promoter hyperactivity increases gene expression and activates oncogenes, which is the opposite of what happens to a tumor suppressor such as APC.
choice_explanations.D: Retroviral insertion can hyperactivate a gene locus (an oncogenic mechanism), not inactivate a tumor suppressor.
choice_explanations.E: A silent mutation does not change the amino acid sequence and would have no effect, so it cannot inactivate APC.

fa_summary: Tumor suppressor genes (e.g., APC) require loss of function—such as deletion or a loss-of-function mutation of both alleles (two-hit hypothesis)—to promote cancer; APC is a negative regulator of the β-catenin/WNT pathway and its loss causes familial adenomatous polyposis/colorectal cancer.

stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a mole on her left forearm that seems to have increased in size over the past six months. She reports that it recently started to itch, and it bleeds when scratched. She has no family history of cancer. She works as a lifeguard during the summers and likes to sun since she was 12 years. Her temperature is 37 degrees C (98.6 degrees F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows an asymmetric mole measuring 10 mm in diameter with irregular borders and variegation. A loss of function mutation has most likely occurred in which of the following genes?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient's lesion has all of the clinical signs of melanoma as assessed by the "ABCDE rule." It is Asymmetrical, its Borders are irregular, there are variations in Color, its Diameter is greater than 6 mm, and it is Evolving. Mutation of CDKN2A is one of the most common types of mutations found in melanoma. This locus encodes two very important tumor suppressors: p16INK4a and p14ARF. The p16INK4a protein is an inhibitor of cyclin D-Cdk4/6 complexes, causing the cell to arrest in the G1 phase of the cell cycle. The p14ARF protein allows for the accumulation of p53, another tumor suppressor, by inhibiting MDM2, which normally targets p53 for degradation. Mutation of CDKN2A results in the loss of these important tumor-suppressive activities, leading to uncontrolled proliferation of the cell. Because the question refers to a loss of function mutation (loss of function mutation of tumor suppressor gene), CDKN2A is the correct answer.

The APC gene (choice A) encodes the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) protein. In healthy cells, APC is a tumor suppressor that is involved in the degradation of beta-catenin, preventing over proliferation of the cell. Mutation of this gene allows for the accumulation of beta-catenin and abnormal cellular proliferation. Mutations in APC are associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), a hereditary form of colon cancer.

BRAF (choice B) is a proto-oncogene encoding for a form of Raf kinase, which functions in a signaling cascade to induce cell proliferation. Mutations in this gene create an oncogene (gain of function mutation) resulting in constitutive activation of this mitogenic signaling cascade. Although mutations in this gene are common in the development of melanoma, the question refers to a loss of function mutation, so this would not be an appropriate answer choice.

PTCH1 (choice D) is a gene that encodes for a cell surface receptor that binds to the signaling molecule SHH and determines polarity during embryonic development. It is also involved in the regulation of hair follicle formation and hair growth. It is mutated in nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (NBCCS), also known as Gorlin syndrome.

SMAD4 (choice E) is a member of the TGF-beta signaling pathway. It functions to regulate gene expression as a downstream component of this pathway. Mutations or deletions in this gene are important contributors to some forms of cancer, such as pancreatic adenocarcinoma, in which more than half (55%) of all cases have lost SMAD activity.

choice_explanations.A: APC is a tumor suppressor (beta-catenin degradation); mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis/colon cancer, not melanoma with a loss-of-function mutation as asked.
choice_explanations.B: BRAF is a proto-oncogene (Raf kinase); its mutations in melanoma are gain-of-function (oncogenic) rather than the loss-of-function mutation asked about.
choice_explanations.C: CDKN2A encodes the tumor suppressors p16INK4a (inhibits cyclin D-Cdk4/6, arrests G1) and p14ARF (stabilizes p53); loss-of-function mutation of CDKN2A is a common finding in melanoma.
choice_explanations.D: PTCH1 encodes a SHH receptor; it is mutated in nevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome.
choice_explanations.E: SMAD4 is a downstream TGF-beta signaling component; its loss contributes to pancreatic adenocarcinoma and colorectal cancer.

fa_summary: CDKN2A encodes the tumor suppressors p16INK4a and p14ARF; a loss-of-function mutation is a common cause of melanoma.

stem: A 48-year-old man has been recently diagnosed with colon cancer. His maternal uncle died at the age of 50 from colorectal carcinoma. Further studies show no evidence of familial polyposis but genetic testing shows a mutation in his MLH1 gene. Which of the following is most likely associated with this mutation?

options.text: Active transcription of the telomerase gene

explanation:
The correct answer is B. This man most likely has hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer. Microsatellite instability is characteristic of individuals with loss-of-function mutations in the mismatch repair genes (hMLH1, hMSH2). These are associated with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), hereditary endometrial cancer, and microsatellite instability in the tumor cells. Areas of DNA with dinucleotide repeats (an example of microsatellites) are often associated with strand slippage during DNA replication, allowing change in the number of repeats on the newly synthesized strand (microsatellite instability). The mismatch repair enzymes normally correct this replication error.

Active transcription of the telomerase gene (choice A) and increase in euchromatin (choice D) are both characteristics of many tumor cells, but are not known to be specifically related to loss of mismatch repair and HNPCC.

Highly methylated CG sequences (choice C) are typically associated with silencing certain gene regions; such methylation is not a prominent mechanism related to tumorigenesis.

Large segment deletions (choice E) are associated with unequal crossovers during meiosis. A large segment deletion might result in a genetic deficiency or loss of a tumor suppressor gene, and a hereditary form of cancer. The mechanism is not strongly associated with a defective mismatch repair system.

choice_explanations.A: Active transcription of the telomerase gene is a feature of many tumor cells but is not specifically related to loss of mismatch repair and HNPCC.
choice_explanations.B: Loss-of-function mutations in mismatch repair genes (hMLH1, hMSH2) cause dinucleotide (microsatellite) repeat instability, characteristic of HNPCC/Lynch syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: Highly methylated CG sequences silence gene regions and are not a prominent mechanism related to this defective mismatch repair.
choice_explanations.D: Increased euchromatin is a feature of many tumor cells but is not specifically related to loss of mismatch repair and HNPCC.
choice_explanations.E: Large segment deletions arise from unequal crossover during meiosis and are not strongly associated with a defective mismatch repair system.

fa_summary: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is an autosomal dominant mutation of mismatch repair genes (eg, MLH1, MSH2) with microsatellite instability; it is associated with proximal colon, endometrial, ovarian, stomach, and skin cancers.

stem: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the physician because the family noticed that in certain light, the pupil of her left eye appears white. Ophthalmologic examination shows a tumor in her left eye. She is diagnosed with retinoblastoma. Which of the following tests could be used to determine whether this is a heritable or sporadic tumor?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. One of the first signs of retinoblastoma is leukocoria, which means "white pupil." It is most often initially noticed by close family members or on flash photography and is often the primary reason for consultation. Forty percent of retinoblastomas are heritable; the child inherits one mutant allele through the germline and a somatic mutation in the other allele occurs at some point during retinal development, resulting in the loss of function of that gene. This leads to tumor development, often with multiple tumors in both eyes. Children with heritable retinoblastoma usually are diagnosed within the first 5 years of life. Penetrance, however, is not complete because the second mutation is a chance event. Sixty percent of retinoblastomas are sporadic; both alleles are inactivated by somatic mutation within the same cell. Because this is a rare event, sporadic tumors usually are in only one eye and present at a later age.

To detect a mutation in the Rb gene and differentiate between heritable and sporadic cases of retinoblastoma, PCR is the most appropriate technique of the choices given. Using the appropriate primers, a deletion can be detected as a change in size of the DNA band amplified. In heritable cases, one chromosome will show the altered length from the deletion in any cell in the body. In sporadic retinoblastoma, samples isolated from anywhere other than the tumor should have two normal alleles. Not all mutations in retinoblastoma are deletions. In these cases, PCR would be followed by testing the PCR products for other alleles known to cause retinoblastoma.

ELISA (choice A) is a highly sensitive assay that can be used to identify the presence of an antibody against a specific antigen or protein. An example would be the ELISA HIV test. In this test, antigens representing HIV viral proteins are fixed to the bottom of a plate, and a blood sample from an individual is added to this plate. If there are antibodies in the patient's blood, indicating an infection with the virus, a color change will indicate a positive result. ELISA cannot be used to distinguish between a sporadic or heritable form of cancer.

FACS (choice B) uses antibodies coupled to fluorescent markers to determine cell surface molecules on whole cells. It is very useful for determining the stage of development or activation of cells (eg, detection of CD antigens on cells in the immune system), but does not give you any insight into the DNA. This technique also allows isolation of cells with specific markers such as CD34+ stem cells.

Northern blotting (choice C), the RNA counterpart to Southern blotting, will determine the size and abundance of mRNA transcribed from a specific gene in a given sample of RNA. RNA is not able to be cleaved by restriction enzymes the way DNA can; however, RNA molecules for different proteins are of different lengths and already short enough to be separated by gel electrophoresis. The sample is separated by agarose gel electrophoresis, transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane, and probed with a specific, labeled probe. This will be exposed to film and bands will appear, revealing the size and the abundance of specific mRNAs.

Western blotting (choice E) is the protein counterpart of Southern and Northern blotting. Proteins are isolated from the cell type of interest and separated by size on a polyacrylamide gel, then transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane. The filter is then incubated with antibodies that specifically react with the protein of interest, then it is incubated with a labeled antibody (eg, radioactive) that reacts with the first antibody. After this has been washed off, the membrane is exposed to film and bands characteristic of the protein being studied will appear. This is useful to determine whether a protein is present or absent in a patient or if it is the wrong size, suggesting an error in the DNA for this protein.

choice_explanations.A: ELISA detects antibodies against an antigen (eg, HIV) and cannot distinguish a sporadic from a heritable form of cancer.
choice_explanations.B: FACS uses fluorescent antibody markers to characterize cell surface molecules and does not give insight into the DNA.
choice_explanations.C: Northern blotting determines the size and abundance of mRNA and does not detect the DNA-level Rb deletion needed here.
choice_explanations.D: PCR is the test of choice: with appropriate primers, a deletion (germline) in the Rb gene can be detected as a change in the size of the amplified DNA band, distinguishing heritable from sporadic retinoblastoma.
choice_explanations.E: Western blotting detects protein presence/size using antibodies and is not used to detect the DNA deletion here.

fa_summary: Retinoblastoma involves the RB1 tumor suppressor (inhibits E2F, blocks G1-to-S); heritable cases carry a germline mutation detectable by PCR, whereas sporadic cases have both alleles inactivated only in the tumor.

stem: During an investigational study, cortisol is noted to increase gluconeogenesis in cultured hepatocytes. Which of the following processes is most directly involved in the observed cortisol-mediated stimulation of glucose production?

options.text: Activation of a transmembrane tyrosine kinase
Increased calcium influx from the extracellular fluid
Increased transcription of gluconeogenic enzyme genes

explanation:
The correct answer is D. Steroid hormones diffuse across the plasma membrane and enter the cytoplasm, where they bind to an intracellular protein receptor. When a glucocorticoid, such as cortisol, interacts with the cellular receptor, it undergoes a conformational change exposing a nuclear localization sequence. The hormone/receptor complex enters the nucleus and binds specific enhancer DNA sequences associated with certain genes, increasing mRNA transcription and thereby increasing protein synthesis. Cortisol increases gluconeogenic enzyme activity by increasing gene expression, not by initiating intracellular signal transduction cascades.

Most peptide/protein hormones and paracrine factors bind to and activate specific plasma membrane receptors. The activated receptor initiates an intracellular transduction cascade that modifies the action of existing proteins and regulates the transcription of certain genes. Membrane receptors coupled through the heterotrimeric Gs to adenylate cyclase (choice A) or to phosphodiesterase (choice E) regulate intracellular levels of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). The receptors for insulin and for several other growth factors have tyrosine kinase activity that is activated by hormone binding (choice B). The NMDA receptor for the neurotransmitter glutamate includes a calcium channel activated by glutamate binding (choice C).

choice_explanations.A: Gs-coupled membrane receptors activate adenylate cyclase to regulate cAMP; cortisol acts through a nuclear receptor, not this pathway.
choice_explanations.B: Insulin and growth factor receptors have transmembrane tyrosine kinase activity, which is not how cortisol acts.
choice_explanations.C: Increased calcium influx occurs via the NMDA receptor calcium channel and is unrelated to cortisol's action.
choice_explanations.D: Cortisol is a steroid that binds an intracellular receptor and increases transcription of gluconeogenic enzyme genes, raising enzyme activity by increasing gene expression.
choice_explanations.E: Phosphodiesterase terminates cAMP signaling for Gs/Gi-coupled receptors, not cortisol's genomic effect.

fa_summary: Cortisol (adrenal zona fasciculata) increases gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and proteolysis; as a steroid it acts through an intracellular receptor to increase transcription of gluconeogenic enzyme genes.

stem: A 7-year-old boy comes to the physician because of ptosis and drooping on the left side of his face for 2 days. He also has a 1-week history of pain and swelling in his right knee. His mother recalls that he had a tick bite several weeks ago that produced a ring-shaped rash. Which of the following techniques would most likely be appropriate for identifying seroconversion in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient demonstrates a late-phase presentation of Lyme disease, which is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi and is spread by the bite of infected Ixodes ticks. B. burgdorferi is a large spirochete that is gram-negative and difficult to culture. Infected ticks are found on reservoirs such as white-tailed deer or white-footed mice; the spirochete is transferred to humans by the bite of the tick. B. burgdorferi invades through the skin and into the bloodstream, and affects the heart, joints, and the central nervous system (CNS).

Lyme disease initially presents as a rash, erythema migrans, which is red and circular with a central clearing. The rash resembles a bull's-eye. Patients may also present with headache and general malaise during this phase. Weeks later, neurologic or cardiac symptoms may develop. Neurologically, patients may complain of a severe headache or Bell palsy (seen in the present case). Cardiac manifestations include arrhythmias and pericarditis. Months to years later, patients are likely to develop migratory arthritis.

Upon infection, the individual's body will produce antibodies that specifically recognize the pathogen, and these antibodies will be present in the patient's blood. This process is known as seroconversion. The presence of these reactive antibodies can be detected by Western blotting. This technique allows for the identification of multiple antibodies made against the spirochete.

Northern blotting (choice A), PCR (choice B), RFLP (choice C), and Southern blotting (choice D) are all methods that detect nucleic acids, not proteins. Therefore, these would not be appropriate techniques for detecting the presence of antibodies in the patient's blood.

choice_explanations.A: Northern blotting detects RNA (nucleic acids), not antibodies, and is therefore inappropriate for identifying seroconversion.
choice_explanations.B: PCR detects nucleic acids, not antibodies, and is therefore inappropriate here.
choice_explanations.C: RFLP analysis detects changes in DNA sequence, not antibodies.
choice_explanations.D: Southern blotting detects DNA, not antibodies.
choice_explanations.E: Western blotting detects proteins/antibodies; it can identify multiple antibodies made against B. burgdorferi in the patient's blood, confirming seroconversion and the diagnosis of Lyme disease.

fa_summary: Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi transmitted by Ixodes deer ticks; it presents with erythema migrans and later neurologic (eg, Bell palsy), cardiac, and joint manifestations, and seroconversion is detected by Western blot.

stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the physician because she found a lump in her right breast during self-examination. She is unaware of any family history of cancer because she was adopted. She has been otherwise healthy, and has not had a mammogram. Her temperature is 37.2 degrees C (99 degrees F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 130/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 2-cm mass in the right breast as well as firm, non-tender axillary lymph nodes. The left breast is normal. A mammogram reveals a stellate dense lesion with focal calcifications. Histological examination of a biopsy sample identifies the tumor as an invasive ductal carcinoma with positive HER-2 immunohistochemical staining. This tumor is most likely to have high activity of which of the following proteins?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. HER-2, also known as ERBB2, is a growth factor receptor found on the surface of cells. It is a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) and is a member of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) family. Amplification of HER-2 is found in up to 30% of sporadic breast cancers and is, thus, an important marker for these tumors. In healthy tissue, the activity of these receptors is necessary for ductal development in the mammary glands. Growth factor receptors such as HER-2 become activated by binding of their ligand. This results in dimerization of the receptor, followed by autophosphorylation of its intracellular tails. The activated receptor leads to activation of Ras, which in turn activates members of the MAPKKK family, ultimately leading to the expression of genes necessary to induce proliferation of the cell. Therefore, amplification of HER-2 would lead to high activity of the downstream signaling component Ras.

G-alpha-s (choice A) is a component of some forms of the heterotrimeric G protein complex. Other members of this complex include the beta and gamma subunits. The G protein complex associates with G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs). For some GPCR family members, binding of ligand to the receptor leads to the activation of the G-alpha-s subunit. G-alpha-s, in turn, activates adenylyl cyclase, resulting in production of cAMP. Mutations in GPCRs are not associated with breast cancer.

GLI (choice B) activity is important in normal embryonic development. It is induced by binding of the signaling molecule SHH to the PTCH1 receptor. GLI is an example of an oncogene, as mutations resulting in increased activity of the protein are found in many types of tumors, including glioblastoma. Mutations in PTCH1, resulting in high levels of GLI-1 activity, are associated with basal cell carcinoma.

SMAD (choice D) functions to regulate gene expression as a downstream component of the TGF-beta signaling pathway. Mutations or deletions in this gene are important contributors to some forms of cancer, such as pancreatic adenocarcinoma, in which more than half (55%) of all cases have lost SMAD activity.

High levels of STAT protein (choice E) activity give rise to some forms of myeloproliferative neoplasms. In these diseases JAK, a tyrosine kinase upstream of STAT, is mutated to a constitutively active form, resulting in high levels of STAT activity downstream and increased proliferation of the cell.

choice_explanations.A: G-alpha-s is a heterotrimeric G protein subunit that activates adenylyl cyclase and cAMP; GPCR mutations are not associated with breast cancer.
choice_explanations.B: GLI is a SHH/PTCH1 pathway oncogene associated with basal cell carcinoma and glioblastoma, not HER-2 breast cancers.
choice_explanations.C: HER-2 (ERBB2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase; its activation leads to Ras activation and downstream MAPK signaling, so HER-2-amplified tumors have high Ras activity.
choice_explanations.D: SMAD is a downstream TGF-beta signaling component; its loss contributes to pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
choice_explanations.E: High STAT activity results from constitutively active JAK in myeloproliferative neoplasms.

fa_summary: HER2 (ERBB2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase oncogene amplified in breast and gastric carcinomas; its signaling proceeds through Ras and the MAPK pathway.

stem: During an investigational study, cloning of a new eukaryotic gene is followed by insertion and ligation of the gene into an expression vector. The protein translated from this gene is then studied on a protein blot under non-denaturing conditions, and probed with 32P-DNA. Which of the following techniques was most likely used in this study?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The technique described is a Southwestern blot, which is used to identify a DNA-protein interaction. In this procedure, proteins in a sample are first separated by electrophoresis. These separated proteins are then transferred to a membrane and exposed to a 32P-labeled probe composed of a specific DNA sequence. If a protein on the membrane is able to bind to that specific sequence, there will be a positive signal for that protein. Note that although both Northern blots and Southwestern blots use 32P-DNA probes, only Southwestern blot can identify an interaction between a protein and DNA.

Northern blotting (choice A) is helpful in determining which tissues express the gene for a specific protein. mRNAs isolated from samples of tissue separated by electrophoresis, blotted and probed with a 32P-cDNA probe from the gene of interest. Results can reveal level of expression in different tissues or variability in length of the mRNAs, which may be result of alternative splicing. Northern blots are useful for analyzing abundance or size of mRNAs.

RNA interference (choice B), also known as RNAi technology, can be used to reduce the expression of a specific gene, which allows for the study of gene function in either cell culture or whole model organisms. The nucleotide sequence of the interfering RNA molecule is complimentary to the sequence of the mRNA of interest. Once the RNAi molecule binds to the target mRNA, the mRNA becomes degraded, resulting in loss of the protein encoded by that mRNA. Any cellular effect due to loss of that protein can be identified. RNAi technology is useful for analyzing function(s) of specific gene(s) of interest.

Western blotting (choice D), also called immunoblotting, refers to transfer of proteins from a gel to a membrane and their detection using antibodies that specifically bind to the protein of interest. The antigen (protein)-antibody interaction enables the identification of a target protein, as well as an estimation of its size.

Yeast two hybrid (choice E) is a technique to detect protein-protein interactions that take place in cells. In this technique, two molecules are introduced into a yeast cell: a protein of interest that is fused to one half of a transcription factor, and a protein that is predicted to interact with the protein of interest, fused to the other half of a transcription factor. If the two proteins interact, a functional transcription factor is made, which results in the expression of genes that allows for growth under specific conditions. Following this process, the presence of colonies on selective media indicates an interaction between the protein of interest and the test protein.

choice_explanations.A: Northern blotting separates and probes mRNA with a 32P-cDNA probe to assess expression/abundance, not DNA-protein binding.
choice_explanations.B: RNA interference reduces expression of a specific gene by degrading its mRNA to study gene function, not a blotting technique.
choice_explanations.C: Southwestern blotting separates proteins by electrophoresis, transfers them to a membrane, and probes with a 32P-DNA probe to identify DNA-protein interactions.
choice_explanations.D: Western blotting (immunoblotting) detects proteins using specific antibodies, not DNA probes.
choice_explanations.E: Yeast two hybrid detects protein-protein interactions using split transcription factors and reporter growth on selective media.

fa_summary: Blotting procedures: Southern (DNA), Northern (RNA), Western (protein/immunoblot), and Southwestern blotting identifies protein-DNA interactions using a labeled DNA probe.

stem: A 47-year-old man with a history of epilepsy is brought to the emergency department because of a grand mal seizure. He has a history of seizure disorder and is noncompliant with his medications. His current medications include carbamazepine. He appears confused, but responds slowly to commands. Pulse is 66/min and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. The cardiac and pulmonary examinations are noncontributory. Laboratory studies show a blood pH of 7.14, PCO2 of 43 mm Hg, and HCO3- of 14 mEq/L. Hemoglobin is 15 g/dL and hematocrit is 44%. Serum creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be present in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Tonic-clonic seizure activity produces lactic acid from skeletal muscle metabolism. This acid produces a condition of metabolic acidosis, which can be diagnosed by a severe reduction in HCO3-. Three values must be considered in acid/base diagnosis: pH, PCO2, and bicarbonate.

Respiratory acidosis will produce increased PCO2, decreased pH, and increased bicarbonate. Increasing CO2 increases production of carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and bicarbonate, so respiratory acidosis causes low pH and high bicarbonate. This patient has normal PCO2 (33-45 mm Hg), severe acidosis (normal: 7.35-7.45), and very low bicarbonate (normal: 22-28 mEq/L). Low bicarbonate with acidosis demonstrates metabolic acidosis. The patient should be compensating by increasing ventilation, but this has not occurred yet. The respiratory system normally compensates for metabolic acidosis by increasing ventilation to decrease PCO2 and raise pH. Because this patient has high normal PCO2, respiratory compensation has not yet occurred. Therefore, choice A is incorrect.

Metabolic alkalosis without compensation (choice C) is incorrect because the pH would be elevated, rather than decreased. Also, metabolic alkalosis would be accompanied by an increase in HCO3-, rather than a decrease.

Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation (choice D) and respiratory acidosis without compensation (choice E) are incorrect because although PCO2 is elevated, the reduction in HCO3- is more severe. Also, respiratory acidosis causes increased bicarbonate level due to production of carbonic acid; metabolic compensation would result in further elevation in HCO3- rather than a decrease.

choice_explanations.A: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation is incorrect: the high-normal PCO2 shows ventilation has not yet increased, so compensation has not occurred.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: low bicarbonate with acidemia indicates metabolic acidosis, and the absence of a compensatory fall in PCO2 indicates no respiratory compensation yet.
choice_explanations.C: Metabolic alkalosis without compensation is incorrect: it would raise, not lower, pH and would increase, not decrease, HCO3-.
choice_explanations.D: Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation is incorrect: the PCO2 is normal and the HCO3- reduction is more severe than expected for respiratory acidosis.
choice_explanations.E: Respiratory acidosis without compensation is incorrect: respiratory acidosis increases bicarbonate (via carbonic acid), whereas this patient's bicarbonate is markedly decreased.

fa_summary: Stepwise acid-base reading: low HCO3- with acidemia = metabolic acidosis; a high-normal PCO2 means respiratory compensation has not yet occurred.

stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of severe cramping abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. She is pregnant with her first child and is 21 weeks' gestational age. She has had prenatal care and a first trimester ultrasound had revealed delayed intrauterine growth, microcephaly, cleft palate, and polydactyly. On admission, she delivers a stillborn fetus. The placenta appears normal without infarcts, hemorrhage, or infection. The umbilical cord shows a single umbilical artery. Autopsy examination of the fetus reveals low-set ears, omphalocele, cardiac ventricular septal defect, and a horseshoe kidney. Polydactyly is noted; hands are not clenched and do not have overlapping fingers. A chromosomal abnormality is suspected. Which of the following features would most likely also be present in this fetus?

options.text: Absent cerebellar vermis and enlarged fourth ventricle
Corpus callosum agenesis and smooth philtrum

explanation:
The correct answer is C. The morphologic features described suggest Patau syndrome (trisomy 13). Patau syndrome has similar features to Edward syndrome (trisomy 18), but would not have clenched hands or overlapping fingers. When the forebrain does not divide to form the cerebral hemispheres (holoprosencephaly), there is also structural maldevelopment of the brain and face (eyes, nose, palate, and lips). Holoprosencephaly, cyclopia (single eye), cleft palate/lip, and proboscis (tubular nose appendage) can be seen in Patau syndrome. Gene mutations in the sonic hedgehog (SHH) protein can cause loss of ventral midline development, resulting in holoprosencephaly. SHH gene plays a critical role as a morphogen, forming the pattern for midline structures of the brain, spinal cord, and limbs.

Chromosomal abnormality is a common cause of miscarriage and stillbirth. Other causes include placental infarction, intrauterine infection, or placental abruption or previa (ruled out in our case vignette). The presence of a single umbilical artery is associated with genital-urinary structural anomalies. Increased maternal age is associated with Patau syndrome. Children with Patau syndrome who survive past birth would have intellectual disability, developmental delay, and congenital heart defects. Many children die within the first year of life.

Absent cerebellar vermis and enlarged fourth ventricle (choice A) is seen in Dandy-Walker syndrome, a rare congenital malformation that is not associated with a distinct chromosomal abnormality. It is characterized by enlargement of the posterior fossa, agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle, and supratentorial hydrocephalus.

Corpus callosum agenesis and smooth philtrum (choice B) is seen with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder. Exposure of the fetus to high levels of blood alcohol in utero can cause growth deficiency (small height and weight), craniofacial abnormalities (small palpebral fissures, thin vermillion, and smooth philtrum), and brain malformations (microcephaly, corpus callosum agenesis, cerebellar hypoplasia). It is usually not associated with stillbirth. Children would have neurologic and developmental disabilities.

Hypertelorism and micrognathia (choice D) can be seen with Cri du chat syndrome (chromosome 5p deletion). It is usually not associated with stillbirth. Neonates have a distinct cry (meowing). Clinically, microcephaly, growth retardation, hypertelorism (wide-set eyes), epicanthal folds, down-slanting palpebral fissures, low-set ears, micrognathia (small jaw), single palmar crease, congenital heart defects (ASD, VSD, PDA, Tetralogy of Fallot) are commonly present. Cleft lip/palate, intestinal malrotation, horseshoe kidney, and syndactyly, although not as common, can also be present.

Lissencephaly (choice E) is a rare maldevelopment of the brain in which there is lack of gyri and sulci formation. Neuronal migration occurs between the 12th to 24th weeks of gestation. Causes include viral infection of the fetus or uterus in the first trimester, insufficient blood flow to the fetal brain, or chromosomal abnormality (chromosome 7, 17, or X). Diagnosis is usually after birth, but ultrasound identification and visualization of the brain after 20 weeks gestation can be obtained. Microcephaly can be present. The syndrome associated with lissencephaly can have associated cranio-facial dysmorphology, but would not overlap with the structural malformations seen with Patau syndrome.

choice_explanations.A: Absent cerebellar vermis and enlarged fourth ventricle is seen in Dandy-Walker syndrome, a rare congenital malformation not associated with a distinct chromosomal abnormality.
choice_explanations.B: Corpus callosum agenesis and smooth philtrum is seen with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, which is not usually associated with stillbirth.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: holoprosencephaly and cyclopia (with cleft palate/lip and proboscis) are features of Patau syndrome (trisomy 13); SHH mutation causes loss of ventral midline development.
choice_explanations.D: Hypertelorism and micrognathia can be seen with Cri du chat syndrome (chromosome 5p deletion).
choice_explanations.E: Lissencephaly is a rare maldevelopment with lack of gyri/sulci formation and does not overlap with the malformations of Patau syndrome.

fa_summary: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) features holoprosencephaly/cyclopia, cleft palate/lip, polydactyly, and congenital heart defects; distinguish from Edwards (trisomy 18).

stem: A 3-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital for elective atrial septal defect repair. She has a history of mental retardation. Physical examination shows microcephaly, short palpebral fissures, small teeth, and ear deformities. There is decreased range of motion in all joints. Maternal use of which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient most likely has fetal alcohol syndrome, which is a combination of multiple abnormalities that are caused by maternal intake of alcohol during pregnancy. The craniofacial defects include epicanthal folds, short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum, a thin upper lip, small teeth, and a small head circumference.

Additional abnormalities include: atrial and ventricular septal defects; conotruncal heart defects (e.g., Tetralogy of Fallot); CNS and neurobehavioral abnormalities (e.g., microcephaly, intellectual impairment, cognitive impairment, developmental delay); skeletal abnormalities (e.g., flexion contractures, scoliosis, dislocated joints, aberrant palmar crease); renal anomalies; growth retardation; and hearing loss. Pregnant women should not drink alcohol, because it is not known exactly when and how much alcohol causes this syndrome.

Diethylstilbestrol (choice A) is associated with clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina in female offspring of women taking this drug.

Maternal lithium (choice C) intake is associated with Ebstein anomaly and tricuspid atresia. Other noncardiac teratogenic manifestations are rare.

Maternal thalidomide (choice D) intake is associated with variable cardiac manifestations and phocomelia. It is rarely associated with the craniofacial findings in this patient.

Valproic acid (choice E) inhibits maternal folic acid absorption, leading to neural tube defects, especially spina bifida.

choice_explanations.A: Diethylstilbestrol is associated with clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina in female offspring of women taking this drug.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: the craniofacial features (epicanthal folds, short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, small teeth) plus cardiac septal defects and joint contractures are due to maternal ethanol intake (fetal alcohol syndrome).
choice_explanations.C: Maternal lithium intake is associated with Ebstein anomaly and tricuspid atresia; other teratogenic manifestations are rare.
choice_explanations.D: Maternal thalidomide intake causes phocomelia and variable cardiac defects, but rarely the craniofacial findings seen here.
choice_explanations.E: Valproic acid inhibits maternal folic acid absorption and causes neural tube defects, especially spina bifida.

fa_summary: Fetal alcohol syndrome: maternal ethanol causes craniofacial defects (epicanthal folds, short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, small teeth), septal/conotruncal heart defects, and neurobehavioral and skeletal abnormalities.

stem: A clinical study is evaluating sensitivity of oral glucose intake versus intravenous glucose administration in testing for metabolic syndrome. One group of subjects is given 25 g of glucose intravenously and another group is given 25 g of glucose orally. Venous blood samples collected at 15 minute intervals showed that the oral glucose load is cleared from plasma more rapidly than the intravenous load. Which of the following factors best explains why the oral glucose load is cleared from plasma at a faster rate than the intravenous glucose load?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) is released by the presence of fat, carbohydrate, or protein in the gastrointestinal tract. GIP is a strong stimulator of insulin release and is responsible for the observation that an oral glucose load releases more insulin and is metabolized more rapidly than an equal amount of glucose administered intravenously. Intravenously administered glucose does not stimulate the release of GIP. GIP is sometimes called glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide. This is also the reason that testing for insulin and glucose response is typically by an oral glucose tolerance test rather than glucose infusion, because it better reflects the natural intake of nutrients.

CCK stimulates insulin release; however, since CCK secretion is not significantly secreted with a pure glucose load, it does not contribute to the response to OGTT; thus choice A is incorrect.

CCK does not stimulate the release of VIP (choice B), and VIP does not affect insulin release.

GIP does not stimulate glucagon release (choice C), and glucagon has the opposite effect of insulin, i.e., it would decrease the rate of glucose clearance from the blood.

VIP does not stimulate GIP release (choice E).

choice_explanations.A: CCK stimulates insulin release, but CCK is not significantly secreted with a pure glucose load, so it does not contribute to the OGTT response.
choice_explanations.B: CCK does not stimulate VIP release, and VIP does not affect insulin release.
choice_explanations.C: GIP does not stimulate glucagon release; glucagon has the opposite effect of insulin and would decrease the rate of glucose clearance.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: oral glucose stimulates GIP release, which strongly stimulates insulin release, giving a faster glucose clearance than intravenous glucose (which does not stimulate GIP).
choice_explanations.E: VIP does not stimulate GIP release.

fa_summary: GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) is released by oral nutrients and strongly stimulates insulin release, explaining why oral glucose is cleared faster than an equal intravenous glucose load.

stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of worsening watery diarrhea, cramping abdominal pain, and weight loss. He also tells the doctor he has had episodes of facial and neck flushing that occur with stress or alcohol ingestion. His pulse is 102/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 85/58 mm Hg. Physical examination shows erythema of the neck, shoulders, hands, and mild hepatomegaly. Hepatic ultrasound shows multiple lesions consistent with metastases. Elevated levels of which of the following substances is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has the cardinal features of the carcinoid syndrome: diarrhea, flushing, and abdominal pain. Patients are typically in their 50s, but the range of presentation spans adulthood to old age. Carcinoid tumors most commonly arise from the appendix, distal ileum, rectum, stomach and bronchi and may secrete a variety of bioactive substances, including gastrointestinal (GI) peptides (gastrin, insulin, vasoactive intestinal peptide [VIP], glucagon), other peptides (adrenocorticotropic hormone [ACTH], calcitonin), and biogenic amines (5-HT).

Cardiac involvement is present in up to 40% of cases during the course of the disease. Manifestations of carcinoid syndrome occurs in the setting of liver metastasis. The liver is overwhelmed and is unable to inactivate bioactive amines. Increased 5-HT levels enters the systemic circulation. Cardiac involvement occurs in 40% of cases (right atrium, tricuspid valve, and right ventricle fibrosis). Note: only the right heart is involved because the lungs are capable of inactivating vasoactive amines. Increased amounts of the serotonin metabolite 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) are excreted in the urine. Therefore, urinary 5-HIAA is the most frequently used diagnostic test.

Serotonin is derived from the amino acid tryptophan, which also serves as a precursor to niacin and several proteins. Increased metabolism of tryptophan by the tumor has been linked to symptoms in patients with carcinoid tumors. Patients may also present with signs and symptoms of pellagra (dermatitis, dementia, and diarrhea), and dermatitis is seen in our patient. Thus, niacin (choice C) and tryptophan (choice E) levels would be decreased, rather than increased. Note: In contrast, a side effect of niacin therapy for treating dyslipidemia causes flushing through dermal Langerhans cell activation, which increases arachidonic acid and prostaglandins, and causes cutaneous vasodilatation.

Increased estradiol (choice A) in men can be seen with liver damage, e.g., cirrhosis, liver metastasis. Hyperestrogen effects cause spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and gynecomastia, but not flushing or diarrhea.

Serum metanephrine (choice B) is a metabolite of epinephrine that would be elevated in pheochromocytoma (adults) and neuroblastoma (children), but would not cause symptoms of diarrhea and flushing.

choice_explanations.A: Increased estradiol in men (e.g., with cirrhosis or liver metastasis) causes spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and gynecomastia, but not flushing or diarrhea.
choice_explanations.B: Serum metanephrine is a metabolite of epinephrine elevated in pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma; it does not cause diarrhea and flushing.
choice_explanations.C: Niacin levels would be decreased (not increased), because tumor metabolism diverts tryptophan away from niacin production, producing pellagra-like findings.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: serotonin (5-HT), a biogenic amine secreted by the carcinoid tumor, causes the diarrhea, flushing, and abdominal pain; urinary 5-HIAA confirms the diagnosis.
choice_explanations.E: Tryptophan levels would be decreased, not increased, because the tumor consumes tryptophan to make serotonin.

fa_summary: Carcinoid syndrome: a serotonin-secreting tumor (usually metastatic to liver) causes diarrhea, flushing, and abdominal pain; diagnose with urinary 5-HIAA. Tryptophan diversion to serotonin lowers niacin and can cause pellagra.

stem: A 67-year-old man with COPD comes to the physician for a routine follow-up examination. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 22/min, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a barrel chested man in no acute distress. Auscultation reveals no wheezes but a prolonged expiratory phase is present. He has a plasma bicarbonate concentration of 32 mEq/L and an arterial pCO2 of 58 mm Hg. Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base status?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The patient has fully compensated for the respiratory acidosis associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because the pH of the blood is normal. pH is calculated using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation as follows: pH = pK + log (HCO3-/H2CO3). The pK is 6.1 for the bicarbonate buffer system. The concentration of carbonic acid (H2CO3) is estimated as 0.03 x pCO2. Therefore, pH = 6.1 + log (32/1.74) = 7.36. The normal range of pH for arterial blood is 7.35 to 7.45. Patients with COPD have chronic respiratory acidosis due to alveolar hypoventilation, which leads to production of carbon dioxide. The normal range for carbon dioxide is 35 to 45 mm Hg. The renal system compensates for the respiratory acidosis caused by carbon dioxide retention by retaining bicarbonate to restore acid-base balance.

Bicarbonate is depressed with metabolic acidosis (choice A). Normal bicarbonate is close to 24 mEq/L.

CO2 will not rise this high in order to compensate for a metabolic alkalosis (choice B); the pH has actually become less than 7.40. Compensated metabolic alkalosis would still have a pH greater than 7.40, though within or closer to the normal range; the bicarbonate will be higher, e.g., 32 mEq/L.

Respiratory alkalosis (choice D) is inconsistent with elevated arterial pCO2.

Uncompensated metabolic alkalosis (choice E) would not present with increased pCO2.

Uncompensated respiratory acidosis (choice F) with a pCO2 of 58 mm Hg would have a bicarbonate level of about 26-27 mEq/L; the bicarbonate level in the patient reflects metabolic compensation.

choice_explanations.A: Metabolic acidosis depresses bicarbonate; the patient's bicarbonate is elevated, so this is not metabolic acidosis.
choice_explanations.B: CO2 will not rise this high to compensate for metabolic alkalosis, and the pH here is less than 7.40; a compensated metabolic alkalosis would keep the pH above 7.40.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: chronic COPD causes respiratory acidosis (elevated pCO2) with renal bicarbonate retention (bicarbonate ~32 mEq/L) that fully compensates the pH to normal.
choice_explanations.D: Respiratory alkalosis is inconsistent with an elevated arterial pCO2.
choice_explanations.E: Uncompensated metabolic alkalosis would not present with increased pCO2.
choice_explanations.F: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis with a pCO2 of 58 mm Hg would have a bicarbonate of about 26-27 mEq/L; the higher bicarbonate here reflects metabolic compensation.

fa_summary: Chronic COPD causes respiratory acidosis (high pCO2); the kidney compensates by retaining bicarbonate, so a pCO2 of 58 mm Hg with bicarbonate of 32 mEq/L and a normal pH indicates compensated respiratory acidosis.

stem: A 60-year-old woman develops progressive lightening of the skin on her arms, hands, and face. She now has trouble cooking and cleaning at home because of limited movement in her hands. She also says she has some difficulty swallowing, initially with solid foods but now occasionally with liquids. Physical examination shows decreased breath sounds and focal, dry, inspiratory crackles in the lung bases bilaterally.
