Laboratory findings demonstrate elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), elevated anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) titer, elevated serum anti-topoisomerase antibody (anti-SCL 70) titer, and absent serum anti-centromere antibody titer. If she is untreated, which of the following will most likely occur?

options.text: Progression to potentially fatal diffuse organ involvement

explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has scleroderma (or more specifically, systemic sclerosis), an autoimmune connective tissue disorder more commonly found in women. The skin is most frequently involved in this disease and is characterized by excessive fibrosis and collagen deposition. This manifests on physical examination as taut, thickened skin without wrinkles. There are two main variants of this disease: limited systemic sclerosis and diffuse systemic sclerosis.

Our patient most likely presents with diffuse systemic sclerosis. Though symptoms may begin with skin fibrosis, the disease rapidly progresses to visceral involvement. Early evidence of this can be seen in our patient's symptoms of esophageal dysmotility, although some forms of limited systemic sclerosis (e.g., CREST syndrome) can present with isolated esophageal involvement. The most specific finding implicating diffuse systemic sclerosis is the positive anti-topoisomerase antibody (anti-SCL 70). The positive anti-nuclear antibody is non-specific and seen in a number of autoimmune conditions. The progression of diffuse systemic sclerosis is rapid, and patients usually succumb to visceral fibrosis, including pulmonary fibrosis (early signs demonstrated in this case), malignant hypertension, and constrictive pericarditis.

Scleroderma does not predispose to dermatologic malignancies (choice A). Common risk factors for skin cancers include sun exposure, fair skin, albinism, and an immunocompromised state.

Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (choice B) is a serious form of glomerulonephritis seen with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), which would have elevated titers of ANA, double-stranded DNA, and anti-Smith, but not elevated anti-topoisomerase antibody titer.

Scleroderma is a slowly progressive disease that will not stop or spontaneously reverse on its own (choices D and E).

choice_explanations.A: Scleroderma does not predispose to dermatologic malignancies; skin cancer risk factors are sun exposure, fair skin, albinism, and immunosuppression.
choice_explanations.B: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis is seen with SLE (anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith), not with elevated anti-topoisomerase antibody.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: diffuse systemic sclerosis (anti-topoisomerase/anti-SCL 70 positive) rapidly progresses to visceral fibrosis (pulmonary fibrosis, malignant hypertension, constrictive pericarditis), which can be fatal.
choice_explanations.D: Scleroderma is progressive and does not spontaneously remit.
choice_explanations.E: Scleroderma will not spontaneously stabilize; it progresses without treatment.

fa_summary: Diffuse systemic sclerosis (anti-topoisomerase/anti-SCL 70 positive) progresses rapidly to visceral fibrosis (lung, heart, kidney, GI), which can be fatal; limited disease (anti-centromere, CREST) is milder.

stem: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of a reddish, scaly plaque on his trunk and thigh that has increased in size over the last three months. The physician had previously prescribed an antifungal ointment, which did not eradicate the lesion. A tentative diagnosis of mycosis fungoides is made. The presence of which of the following on biopsy would best confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in which the malignant lymphocytes show tropism for the epidermis. The malignant CD4 T cells densely infiltrate the superficial dermis and epidermis (Pautrier abscess), producing the itchy, erythematous plaques and nodules. The lesions may be clinically mistaken for fungal infections, hence the deceptive term. NOTE: This condition should be distinguished from another T cell lymphoma associated with human T-cell lymphotropic virus (HTLV).

Intracellular inclusions are seen in viral infections, and cytoplasmic inclusions in the epidermal cells (choice A) are pathognomonic for molluscum contagiosum, a poxvirus that produces wartlike skin lesions.

Parakeratosis, hyperkeratosis, and acanthosis (choice C) are seen with psoriasis. Clinically, the lesions range from salmon-colored to silvery, scaly plaques. The scales can be scraped off, revealing underlying pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign). Additional histologic findings include Munro abscesses (inflammatory cells in the epidermis and dermis) and elongation of rete pegs and dermal papillae.

Hyphae (choice D) and yeasts are the hallmarks of superficial fungal infections. The tinea infections are caused by dermatophytic fungi and can cause erythematous plaques with central pallor. Fungi are usually appreciated in PAS stains. Treat with antifungal creams. Our patient was treated with anti-fungal medication, which did not rid the lesion.

Vascular proliferation (choice E) is the characteristic finding in hemangiomas, Kaposi sarcoma, and bacillary angiomatosis, which can present as red to dark-red plaques and papules on the skin.

choice_explanations.A: Cytoplasmic inclusions in epidermal cells are pathognomonic for molluscum contagiosum (a poxvirus), not mycosis fungoides.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: malignant-appearing (CD4) lymphocytes with epidermotropism densely infiltrate the dermis and epidermis (Pautrier abscess) in mycosis fungoides.
choice_explanations.C: Parakeratosis, hyperkeratosis, and acanthosis (with Munro abscesses and Auspitz sign) are seen in psoriasis.
choice_explanations.D: Septate hyphae and yeasts are hallmarks of superficial fungal (dermatophyte) infections, which did not respond to antifungal therapy here.
choice_explanations.E: Vascular proliferation is characteristic of hemangiomas, Kaposi sarcoma, and bacillary angiomatosis.

fa_summary: Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with epidermotropic malignant CD4 T cells forming Pautrier microabscesses; it mimics a fungal infection clinically but does not respond to antifungals.

stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine examination. Pelvic examination shows a 10-cm adnexal mass. The mass is resected. Gross examination of the mass shows a multiloculated cystic tumor. The cysts have thickened, nodular walls and are filled with yellow-tan fluid. Microscopic examination shows malignant cells admixed with occasional small, laminated, concentric, calcific spherules. These microscopic structures can also be found in tumors arising from which of the following organs?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The structures are psammoma bodies, which are thought to form from single clusters of necrotic cells that serve as a nidus for crystallization of calcium salts. While psammoma bodies are commonly discussed in pathology courses and tests because of their distinctive appearance, they are actually relatively uncommon. They are found most commonly in the four tumors listed in the mnemonic PSaMMoma:

Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid (choice E)
Serous papillary cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary (seen in this patient)
Meningioma
Malignant mesothelioma

Neoplasms of the colon (choice A), seminal vesicles (choice B), spleen (choice C), and stomach (choice D) do not typically contain psammoma bodies.

choice_explanations.A: Colon neoplasms do not typically contain psammoma bodies.
choice_explanations.B: Seminal vesicle neoplasms do not typically contain psammoma bodies.
choice_explanations.C: Splenic neoplasms do not typically contain psammoma bodies.
choice_explanations.D: Stomach neoplasms do not typically contain psammoma bodies.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is one of the four PSaMMoma tumors (papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous papillary cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary, meningioma, malignant mesothelioma) that contain psammoma bodies.

fa_summary: Psammoma bodies are dystrophic calcifications characteristic of the PSaMMoma tumors: papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous papillary cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary, meningioma, and malignant mesothelioma.

stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the emergency department in labor with her second child. She is 36 weeks' gestation and has not seen a physician since early trimester. A review of her records shows the normal vaginal birth of a child 2 years ago at home and that she is Rh-negative. Physical examination of the newborn shows severe jaundice and widespread edema. Laboratory studies show that the newborn is Rh-positive and has marked anemia, and direct Coombs test is positive. Which of the following structures is most likely to be permanently damaged as a result of this newborn's illness?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The infant has erythroblastosis fetalis, caused by Rh incompatibility, an immune attack by the Rh-negative mother's antibodies on the infant's Rh-positive antigen-bearing red cells (see figure). It is important to note that the first Rh-positive pregnancy results in sensitization of the Rh-negative maternal immune system, thus the first baby is normal. However, after sensitization, all subsequent Rh-positive fetuses will experience immune attack by anti-Rh maternal antibodies, resulting in pathology.

Infants with erythroblastosis fetalis can experience severe anemia with cardiac decompensation (high-output failure due to decreased blood volume and hypoxia) leading to profound edema and high serum unconjugated bilirubin levels. Direct Coombs test is positive and reflects coating of red cells by maternal antibodies. Conversely, the mother would have a positive indirect Coombs test and a negative direct Coombs test since only circulating anti-Rh antibodies are present. Skin and scleral pigmentation (jaundice) is the most obvious effect of the elevated unconjugated bilirubin. The most dangerous effect is toxic damage to the immature central nervous system (notably the basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum, cerebral gray matter, and spinal cord), known as kernicterus, which leads to neurologic abnormalities.

Lung tissue (choice B), pancreas (choice C), renal tissue (choice D), and retina (choice E) are not particularly vulnerable to damage by bilirubin. Note: At 36 weeks' gestation age, the neonate's lungs are mature enough for delivery, so hyaline membrane disease would not be considered in this neonate.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: the elevated unconjugated bilirubin in erythroblastosis fetalis can deposit in and permanently damage the immature CNS (basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum, cerebral gray matter, spinal cord), a process known as kernicterus.
choice_explanations.B: Lung tissue is not particularly vulnerable to bilirubin damage; at 36 weeks the lungs are mature.
choice_explanations.C: The pancreas is not vulnerable to bilirubin damage.
choice_explanations.D: Renal tissue is not vulnerable to bilirubin damage.
choice_explanations.E: The retina is not particularly vulnerable to bilirubin damage.

fa_summary: Rh incompatibility (Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive second fetus) causes erythroblastosis fetalis; unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia can deposit in the basal ganglia and cause kernicterus.

stem: A 28-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He has a history of progressive end-stage hereditary emphysema. Several first-degree relatives have emphysema and also have hepatic disease. Serum alpha-1-antitrypsin enzyme levels are low. Increased activity of which of the following serine proteases best accounts for lung tissue destruction in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The patient has α-1-antitrypsin deficiency, an autosomal codominant hereditary disorder in which an abnormal form of α-1-antitrypsin are produced, but not released from liver cells. This enzyme functions as an inhibitor protease trypsin. However, it actually inactivates a wide variety of enzymes with protease activity that have an essential serine residue in the catalytic centers. Examples of these serine proteases include all of the answer choices, and additionally, cathepsin G and plasminogen. The condition is common among northern European population. Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency is characterized by the following: α-1-antitrypsin specifically targets only the liver and the lungs and protects tissues from neutrophil elastase. The liver disease, which can be mild to life-threatening, is related to retained α-1-antitrypsin with residual enzymatic activity. In the lung, neutrophil elastase is one of the few enzymes that can successfully destroy the heavily crosslinked, insoluble elastin that is presented in the lung interstitium and contributes to its elasticity. With destruction of the lattice-like elastic tissue support structure, a pan-lobular emphysema can develop in the lungs (in contrast to the centrilobular type emphysema seen with active tobacco smoking).

Chymotrypsin (choice A) is a pancreatic enzyme formed in the intestinal lumen that cleaves aromatic aminoacyl bonds.

Plasmin (choice C) is an enzyme involved in fibrinolysis and breakdown of clots.

Thrombin (choice D) is an enzyme involved in coagulation.

Trypsin (choice E) is a pancreatic enzyme found in the intestinal lumen that cleaves arginyl and lysyl bonds.

choice_explanations.A: Chymotrypsin is a pancreatic enzyme formed in the intestinal lumen that cleaves aromatic aminoacyl bonds.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: in α-1-antitrypsin deficiency, unopposed neutrophil elastase destroys the crosslinked insoluble elastin of the lung interstitium, producing pan-lobular emphysema.
choice_explanations.C: Plasmin is involved in fibrinolysis and breakdown of clots.
choice_explanations.D: Thrombin is involved in coagulation.
choice_explanations.E: Trypsin is a pancreatic enzyme found in the intestinal lumen that cleaves arginyl and lysyl bonds.

fa_summary: α1-antitrypsin deficiency (autosomal codominant) causes pan-lobular emphysema from unopposed neutrophil elastase and liver disease from retained α1-antitrypsin.

stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless 10-cm soft tissue mass on her right thigh. During excision of the mass, the surgeon notices that it is adherent to the surrounding tissues without a well-demarcated capsule. Histologic analysis reveals a neoplasm composed of pleomorphic clear cells with vacuolated cytoplasm. The nuclei of many cells are indented by the cytoplasmic vacuoles. A frozen section of the lesion stains positive for Oil Red O by cytochemical methods. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Liposarcoma is a rare soft tissue tumor, affecting middle-aged and elderly persons. The thigh and retroperitoneum are the most frequent sites. The tumor is composed of pleomorphic lipocytes that resemble embryonic lipoblasts. The cytoplasm of neoplastic cells is filled with lipid vacuoles (positive for fat stains), which characteristically indent the nuclear membrane. Note: frozen sections are used to stain fat since fat is dissolved during the histologic process. Like other solid malignancies, these tumors are not well-encapsulated and invade surrounding tissue. They also have a propensity for hematogenous metastasis.

Chondrosarcoma (choice A) is a malignant, cartilaginous tumor, arising from the medullary cavities of bones, primarily in the pelvic region. This tumor consists of anaplastic chondrocytes that produce a basophilic intercellular substance known as the chondroid. Chondrosarcomas are mainly found in middle-aged to older men and can metastasize to the lungs.

Unlike liposarcomas, lipomas (choice B) are microscopically identical to mature fat tissue, with no pleomorphic characteristics. They are composed of adipocytes with a single large cytoplasmic droplet that displaces the nucleus to the periphery. Lipomas are well encapsulated and do not invade surrounding structures. They can become quite large, but are slow-growing.

Metastatic adenocarcinoma (choice D) would be composed of glandular structures containing cytoplasmic mucin. Special stains for mucin would be positive, but stains for fat would be negative. Additionally, metastases to soft tissues of the thigh would be highly unusual. Colonic adenocarcinoma, for example, classically metastasizes to the liver and lungs.

Rhabdomyosarcoma (choice E) is a malignant tumor originating from skeletal muscle. It is most common in children, although some variants do occur in adults. The tumor is composed of pleomorphic undifferentiated spindle-shaped cells admixed with "strap cells" containing myofilaments. It would not stain positive for lipids, but would stain positive for desmin.

choice_explanations.A: Chondrosarcoma is a malignant cartilaginous tumor of the medullary cavities of bone (pelvic region) that produces a basophilic chondroid matrix; it does not stain for fat.
choice_explanations.B: Lipomas are microscopically identical to mature fat (adipocytes with a single large lipid droplet), are well encapsulated, and do not invade or metastasize.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: liposarcoma is a malignant fat tumor (thigh/retroperitoneum) of pleomorphic lipoblasts whose lipid vacuoles indent the nucleus and stain positive for fat (Oil Red O); it lacks a capsule and metastasizes hematogenously.
choice_explanations.D: Metastatic adenocarcinoma forms glandular structures with cytoplasmic mucin (mucin-positive, fat-negative) and rarely metastasizes to soft tissue of the thigh.
choice_explanations.E: Rhabdomyosarcoma arises from skeletal muscle, is composed of spindle-shaped/strap cells with myofilaments, and stains positive for desmin but not lipid.

fa_summary: Liposarcoma (thigh/retroperitoneum, middle-aged/elderly) consists of pleomorphic lipoblasts with lipid vacuoles that indent the nucleus and stain for fat; distinguish from lipoma (benign, encapsulated, mature adipocytes).

stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital for a procedure. Prior to the procedure, she exhibited no signs of musculoskeletal abnormalities. After the procedure, she develops muscle aches and cramps in her back and both legs, which become progressively worse over the next several days. She also develops paresthesias of her lips, tongue, fingers, and feet. The nurses also note intermittent carpopedal spasms, which are aggravated when they try to measure her blood pressure. Two weeks later, the patient's symptoms subside. Which of the following procedures was most likely performed?

options.text: Excisional biopsy of a primary breast cancer

explanation:
The correct answer is E. The symptoms described are characteristic of a transient hypocalcemia that often occurs following a subtotal thyroidectomy. These findings are a result of accidental removal or damage to the parathyroid glands during the thyroidectomy procedure. The parathyroid glands are located on the posterior aspect of the thyroid lobes and produce parathyroid hormone (PTH). Reduced PTH excretion leads to reduced resorption of calcium from the bones and kidneys and decreased absorption from the gut (via vitamin D), resulting in lower serum calcium levels.

Hypocalcemia classically produces muscle cramps, paresthesias, tetany, and in some cases, Trousseau's sign (precipitation of carpopedal spasms by occluding blood supply to the hand with a blood pressure cuff or tourniquet). Another sign of hypocalcemia-induced tetany is Chvostek's sign (an involuntary twitching of facial muscles elicited by a gentle tapping of the facial nerve just anterior to the ear), although this sign is present in about 10% of healthy people. Both Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs result from neuromuscular excitability, induced by hypocalcemia. Additional sequelae of hypocalcemia include diarrhea and long QT interval.

Other causes of transient hypocalcemia include respiratory alkalosis (high pH potentiates albumin binding of calcium), use of loop diuretics, and hypomagnesemia (reduces PTH secretion).

Excision of a primary breast cancer (choice A) would not be expected to alter calcium metabolism. Metastatic breast carcinoma often leads to bone metastasis, though this is mostly associated with hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia. Hypercalcemia produces constipation, polyuria (inhibition of antidiuretic hormone), short QT interval, and rarely, acute pancreatitis.

Osteoporosis is a disease of old age, which is the major cause of hip replacement (choice B) surgery in elderly women. It is, however, not associated with disturbances in serum calcium levels.

Renal failure often results in reduced formation of 1,25(OH)2D3 (activated vitamin D), which can lead to decreased calcium uptake from the intestine. Additionally, retained phosphate can complex with calcium, decreasing serum levels even further. However, decreased calcium in renal failure is chronic and would not cause the acute symptoms seen in our patient. Renal dialysis (choice C) attempts to normalize metabolic abnormalities in renal failure patients and would be unlikely to produce hypocalcemia.

Resection of a pheochromocytoma (choice D) would not produce hypocalcemia. However, disturbing the tumor during surgery can cause release of stored catecholamines into the blood stream, which results in an intra-operative hypertensive crisis. To avoid this, patients often receive alpha and beta blocking drugs in the perioperative period to ensure adequate blood pressure control.

choice_explanations.A: Excision of a primary breast cancer does not alter calcium metabolism; metastatic breast carcinoma causes bone metastasis mostly associated with hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia.
choice_explanations.B: Osteoporosis is the major cause of hip replacement in elderly women, but it is not associated with disturbances in serum calcium levels.
choice_explanations.C: Renal failure decreases activated vitamin D and causes chronic hypocalcemia, but the decreased calcium is chronic, not the acute presentation seen here; dialysis would not produce this.
choice_explanations.D: Resection of a pheochromocytoma does not cause hypocalcemia; manipulating the tumor can instead release catecholamines and cause an intraoperative hypertensive crisis.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: accidental removal or damage of the parathyroid glands during subtotal thyroidectomy reduces PTH, lowering serum calcium and causing muscle cramps, paresthesias, carpopedal spasms (Trousseau's sign), and Chvostek's sign.

fa_summary: Transient hypocalcemia commonly follows subtotal thyroidectomy when the parathyroid glands are accidentally removed/damaged; reduced PTH lowers serum calcium and produces muscle cramps, paresthesias, tetany, and Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs.

stem: A 43-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of weight gain and irregular menstrual cycles. She states that she has had intermittent headaches, weakness, and tingling sensations in her hands and feet. She also has urinary frequency, voiding of 12/day and 3/night. Her urinary stream is normal but she thinks that the voided volumes are significant with each void. She reports feeling depressed and weak. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 168/105 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), normal free thyroxine, and elevated cortisol secretion. Which of the following is most likely to be present in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient likely has primary adrenal hyperfunction, whereby excessive adrenal gland activity or an adrenal tumor has caused hypersecretion of one or more adrenal hormones. Clinical manifestations of adrenal hyperfunction may thus reflect hypersecretion of mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), glucocorticoids (cortisol, corticosterone), adrenal androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, androstenedione) and/or catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine).

Hypersecretion of aldosterone (primary aldosteronism) produces symptoms reflecting increased renal Na+ reabsorption, including hypernatremia, hypervolemia, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hypertension. Aldosterone targets principal cells in the distal segments (i.e., the late distal convoluted tubule, connecting tubule, initial collecting tubule, and the cortical collecting tubule/duct), causing epithelial Na+ channels (ENaC) to be inserted into the apical membrane and increasing basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase expression. This provides a pathway for increased Na+ reabsorption and causes hypernatremia. Water is retained also to maintain ECF osmolarity at optimal levels, causing hypervolemia and hypertension.

After a few days (usually when patients gain ~3 kg in weight), the hypernatremia and hypervolemia are largely corrected during a phenomenon known as "aldosterone escape". Aldosterone escape is believed to be mediated in part by hypervolemia-induced release of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) from the cardiac atria and decreased Na+ reabsorption by the proximal tubule. For reasons that are not completely understood, hypertension persists, along with mild hypervolemia.

Hypokalemia occurs as a direct consequence of aldosterone-stimulated K+ secretion. This causes upregulation of apical H+/K+ ATPase expression in alpha-intercalated cells in the distal segments, which promotes H+ excretion and results in a metabolic alkalosis. Typical symptoms of hypokalemic alkalosis include episodic weakness, paresthesias, transient paralysis, and tetany. Diastolic hypertension and hypokalemic nephropathy with polyuria and polydipsia are common as well. In many cases, the only manifestation is mild to moderate hypertension, but edema is not present.

Hypercortisolism can also result from adrenal hypersecretion. These symptoms are somewhat different than those due to hyperaldosteronism. Prolonged exposure to glucocorticoids causes Cushing syndrome. Common symptoms of Cushing syndrome include upper body obesity, severe fatigue and muscle weakness, high blood pressure, backache, elevated blood sugar, easy bruising, and bluish-red stretch marks on the skin. In women, there may be increased growth of facial and body hair, and menstrual periods may become irregular or stop completely.

Hyperkalemia (choice A) is very unlikely to occur because excessive aldosterone increases secretion of potassium into the tubular fluid, increasing potassium excretion. High levels of aldosterone also tend to produce metabolic alkalosis, which causes hypokalemia.

Cortisol acts to increase bone breakdown and may result in osteopenia and osteoporosis. As a result, hypercalcemia may develop in these patients, leading to hypercalciuria rather than hypocalciuria (choice C). Chronic hypercalciuria can lead to renal calculi.

The excessive secretion of cortisol decreases glucose uptake rather than increasing it. Cortisol accelerates gluconeogenesis and increases the breakdown of peripheral tissue proteins. It acts to mobilize fatty acids and reduces the uptake of glucose into peripheral tissues. Therefore, excess cortisol leads to hyperglycemia rather than hypoglycemia (choice D).

Patients with adrenal hyperfunction release excessive aldosterone and frequently have hypernatremia rather than hyponatremia (choice E). The elevation in aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption, conserving salt and fluid volume; by itself, this does not produce hypernatremia because the salt and water are isoosmotically reabsorbed. Hypernatremia usually develops because the volume expansion suppresses secretion of ADH; the reduction of ADH promotes development of hypernatremia.

choice_explanations.A: Hyperkalemia is very unlikely: excess aldosterone increases potassium secretion into the tubular fluid (and the accompanying metabolic alkalosis causes hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia).
choice_explanations.B: Correct: aldosterone-induced renal Na+ and water retention causes hypervolemia (with hypernatremia, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hypertension).
choice_explanations.C: Cortisol increases bone breakdown, which can cause hypercalcemia and therefore hypercalciuria (not hypocalciuria).
choice_explanations.D: Cortisol accelerates gluconeogenesis and reduces peripheral glucose uptake, so excess cortisol causes hyperglycemia (not hypoglycemia).
choice_explanations.E: Excess aldosterone and ADH suppression cause hypernatremia, not hyponatremia.

fa_summary: Primary adrenal hyperfunction with aldosterone excess (hyperaldosteronism) causes renal Na+/water retention with hypernatremia, hypervolemia, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hypertension; cortisol excess instead causes hyperglycemia, hypercalciuria, and Cushing features.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because she has become completely paralyzed. By the time she is examined, the paralysis has begun to clear, and it completely resolves an hour later. She says that she has had previous episodes of severe transient weakness, but that this was the first time that she felt unable to move. She has also been experiencing paresthesias. Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show serum sodium is 156 mEq/L, potassium is 2.8 mEq/L, and serum renin is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Primary aldosteronism, or Conn syndrome, is a syndrome of aldosterone hypersecretion originating in the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex. The causes include an aldosterone-secreting adrenocortical adenoma, hyperplasia of the zona glomerulosa, and, very rarely, an adrenal carcinoma. Aldosterone activates the basolateral Na+/K+ pumps to drive sodium out of the principal cell of the distal tubule into the interstitium while exchanging it for potassium from the interstitium into the principal cell. The result is a concentration gradient, which is responsible for the increased reabsorption of sodium and the secretion of potassium. It is characterized by hypertension secondary to sodium retention, hypokalemia, and decreased serum renin due to negative feedback of increased blood pressure on renin secretion. Clinical manifestations can include episodic weakness, paresthesias, and transient paralysis due to hypokalemia.

Hypercortisolism (choice A), or Cushing syndrome, is the result of increased glucocorticoid production. Physical signs typically include "moon facies," truncal obesity, "buffalo hump," and purple abdominal striae. Primary causes arise from the adrenal cortex, whereas secondary cause arises from the pituitary gland (ACTH secretion), and ectopic cause is usually due to small cell carcinoma of the lung (ectopic ACTH secretion).

McCune-Albright syndrome (choice B), a hereditary disorder also known as polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, is characterized by autonomous stimulation of aromatase enzyme production of estrogen by the ovaries. This syndrome includes multiple cystic bone lesions and cafe-au-lait skin spots. This accounts for 5% of precocious puberty.

Pheochromocytoma (choice C) is a rare catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla or extra-adrenal origins (sympathetic paraganglia). It may precipitate life-threatening hypertension or cardiac arrhythmias. The classic history of a patient with a pheochromocytoma includes spells characterized by headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis associated with severe hypertension.

Renal artery stenosis (RAS; choice E) is a major cause of renovascular hypertension in older individuals. Atherosclerosis is by far the most common etiology of RAS. Younger patients, less than 40 years old, may have fibrodysplasia of the renal artery, which is a smooth muscle hyperplasia. RAS, on physical examination, would reveal an abdominal bruit in the vicinity of the renal artery. RAS could not account for this patient's weakness, and plasma renin levels would be raised, not lowered.

choice_explanations.A: Hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome) causes moon facies, truncal obesity, buffalo hump, and striae; it does not produce the hypertension with hypokalemia and low renin seen here.
choice_explanations.B: McCune-Albright syndrome (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia) causes cystic bone lesions and cafe-au-lait spots with precocious puberty, not hypokalemic paralysis.
choice_explanations.C: Pheochromocytoma causes paroxysmal headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis with severe hypertension, but not hypokalemia with low renin.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome) from an aldosterone-secreting adenoma causes hypertension, hypokalemia, and decreased renin, with episodic weakness and transient paralysis from hypokalemia.
choice_explanations.E: Renal artery stenosis raises (not lowers) plasma renin, and would not account for this patient's weakness.

fa_summary: Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome): aldosterone-secreting adrenocortical adenoma causes hypertension, hypokalemia, and decreased serum renin, with episodic weakness, paresthesias, and transient paralysis from hypokalemia.

stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of persistent headaches. Funduscopic examination shows papilledema and the left retina also shows a hypervascular abnormality. CT of the head shows a 2.5 cm hypervascular mass in the cerebellum. For which of the following complications is this patient most at risk?

options.text: Serum cholesterol of greater than 700 mg/dL

explanation:
The correct answer is B. The disease is von Hippel-Lindau disease, a rare genetic disorder characterized by a variety of benign and malignant tumors. It is an autosomal dominant syndrome associated with a mutation of the VHL gene on chromosome 3 (3p). Affected individuals develop vascular tumors (hemangioblastomas) of the retina, cerebellum, and/or medulla. Roughly half of the affected individuals later develop multiple bilateral renal cell carcinomas. There is also increased risk for pheochromocytoma.

Berry aneurysms (choice A) are a weakening of the vessel wall and are unrelated to hemangioblastomas, but are instead associated with adult type polycystic kidney disease and connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Berry aneurysm rupture can lead to subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Choreiform movements (choice C) are a feature of Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant disease, which is characterized by a degeneration of GABAergic neurons in the striatum (especially the caudate nucleus). The condition is due to CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion and affects the brain (striatum and later, cortex), but not the eye. Age of onset of symptoms occurs in middle age (~60 years).

Peripheral nerve tumors (choice D) are a feature of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1).

Extremely high serum cholesterol (choice E) suggests the homozygous form of familial hypercholesterolemia. High cholesterol levels can cause xanthomas of the skin and tendons, retinal ischemia, and coronary artery disease. Symptoms would not present this early.

choice_explanations.A: Berry aneurysms are associated with adult polycystic kidney disease and connective tissue disorders such as Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, not with von Hippel-Lindau disease.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL gene on chromosome 3p) causes retinal/cerebellar hemangioblastomas; roughly half of patients develop multiple bilateral renal cell carcinomas.
choice_explanations.C: Choreiform movements occur in Huntington disease (CAG repeat expansion), which affects the striatum but not the eye.
choice_explanations.D: Peripheral nerve tumors are a feature of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), not von Hippel-Lindau disease.
choice_explanations.E: Extremely high serum cholesterol suggests homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, which would not present this early.

fa_summary: Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL gene, chromosome 3p, autosomal dominant) causes hemangioblastomas of the retina, cerebellum, and/or medulla, and roughly half of patients develop multiple bilateral renal cell carcinomas (plus increased pheochromocytoma risk).

stem: A 75-year-old woman with chronic bronchitis comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. The following data are obtained from an arterial blood sample: pH 7.39, pCO2 55 mm Hg, plasma bicarbonate concentration 32 mEq/L. Which of the following is the major compensatory response to this patient's acid-base disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Hypercapnia (high arterial CO2 tension) is relatively common in patients with chronic bronchitis, which is a type of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Hypercapnia causes increased carbonic acid production, which results in respiratory acidosis. Patients with COPD may have stable hypercapnia for years.

The kidneys compensate for chronic respiratory acidosis by increasing renal excretion of acid and adding newly formed bicarbonate to the blood. The main form in which acid is excreted by the kidneys is ammonium ion. The kidney produces bicarbonate ion and H+ to compensate for acidosis; the H+ is secreted into the tubular fluid and excreted as ammonium ion or bound to titratable acid. The bicarbonate is transported across the basolateral surface and added to the blood.

The renal compensation (increased ammonium excretion and addition of bicarbonate to blood) for chronic hypercapnia in this patient has had plenty of time to compensate so the acidemia is mild and the pH is actually within a normal range in this particular case. (Normal values for arterial blood are as follows: pH 7.35-7.45; plasma bicarbonate concentration 22-28 mEq/L or carbon dioxide tension PCO2, 33-45 mm Hg.)

Increased renal excretion of ammonium ions rather than a decrease (choice A) contributes to the renal compensation for acidosis. The main renal compensations are to increase excretion of acid, predominantly as ammonium ion, and to add new bicarbonate to the blood.

Hyperventilation (choice B) is not an option for a patient with COPD because the primary problem is hypoventilation (choice C).

Excretion of free H+ in the urine (choice D) is quantitatively trivial to acid excretion. The only significant excretion of acid is as ammonium ion.

choice_explanations.A: Renal ammonium ion excretion increases (not decreases) as part of the renal compensation for chronic acidosis.
choice_explanations.B: Hyperventilation is not an option for a patient with COPD, whose primary problem is hypoventilation.
choice_explanations.C: Hypoventilation is the primary problem causing the CO2 retention, not the compensatory response.
choice_explanations.D: Excretion of free H+ in the urine is quantitatively trivial; acid is excreted mainly as ammonium ion.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: the kidneys compensate for chronic respiratory acidosis by increasing acid excretion (as ammonium ion) and adding newly formed bicarbonate to the blood.

fa_summary: Chronic respiratory acidosis (COPD/chronic bronchitis, high pCO2) is compensated by the kidneys: increased acid excretion (mainly as ammonium ion) and renal production/addition of new bicarbonate to the blood, restoring pH toward normal.

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of diarrhea; a red, scaly rash; and mild unsteady gait. His mother says that his diet is not deficient in protein or any other caloric foods or nutrients. She says that his sister has a similar condition. Urinalysis shows large amounts of free amino acids. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This child has Hartnup disease, an autosomal recessive condition resulting from defective amino acid transporters in intestinal and renal epithelial cells. Despite normal dietary intake, these patients present with poor absorption of dietary amino acids and excess amino acid secretion in urine.

Specifically, in Hartnup disease, there is impaired transport of neutral amino acids, including tryptophan, which is the precursor for niacin (requires B6 cofactor). This condition clinically resembles pellagra ("diarrhea, dementia, and dermatitis") and may be misdiagnosed as this nutritional (niacin) deficiency. Niacin supplementation may be helpful in controlling the symptoms.

Alkaptonuria (choice A) is an autosomal recessive condition characterized by urine that turns black on standing and, in later life, a debilitating arthritis. Cartilage also accumulates the dark brown/black pigmentation (ochronosis). Other features include pigmented sclera and kidney stones. Alkaptonuria results from deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase, an important enzyme in the tyrosine degradation pathway. Dysfunction results in accumulation of homogentisic acid.

Carcinoid syndrome (choice B) can also produce niacin deficiency. The syndrome occurs when serotonin-producing gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors metastasize to the liver. By spreading to the liver, the secreted serotonin can bypass hepatic metabolism, causing diarrhea, flushing, heart murmurs, and wheezing. Importantly, production of serotonin by the tumor requires tryptophan precursor, making it unavailable for niacin production. Niacin deficiency and symptoms of pellagra, including diarrhea, photosensitive dermatitis, and dementia, then ensue. The age of our patient and urinalysis findings make carcinoid tumor an unlikely diagnosis.

Cystinuria (choice C) is an autosomal recessive defect in renal epithelial transport of cysteine and the basic amino acids lysine, arginine, and ornithine. Absorption of these amino acids normally occurs in the proximal convoluted tubule. Defective absorption means cysteine accumulates in renal tubules and forms cystine (two cysteine molecules attached by disulfide bond), which can precipitate as cystine kidney stones. This process relies on an acidic tubular environment, thus alkalization of the urine (acetazolamide) can treat this issue. The other amino acids listed are much more soluble than cystine and do not cause nephrolithiasis.

Homocystinuria (choice E) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of various enzymes in the cysteine synthesis pathway. Affected enzymes include cystathionine synthase and homocysteine methyltransferase. The net result is excess serum homocysteine (and decreased cysteine), which disrupts connective tissue, blood vessels, and the coagulation cascade. Patient findings include mental retardation, Marfanoid habitus, osteoporosis, hypercoagulability (deep vein thrombosis, etc.) and increased risk for cardiovascular disease. As a caveat, on the USMLE, be careful to distinguish between Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria, since both present with similar connective tissue findings. Symptoms inconsistent with Marfan syndrome include mental retardation, hypercoagulability, limited joint mobility, downward lens subluxation (Marfan is upwards), and seizures. There are also no amino acid abnormalities in Marfan syndrome.

choice_explanations.A: Alkaptonuria (homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency) causes urine that turns black on standing, ochronosis, and later arthritis, not the pellagra-like findings and neutral aminoaciduria seen here.
choice_explanations.B: Carcinoid syndrome can also cause niacin deficiency/pellagra, but the young age and the pattern of free aminoaciduria make it unlikely here.
choice_explanations.C: Cystinuria is a renal transport defect for cysteine and basic amino acids and causes cystine kidney stones, not the pellagra-like rash and ataxia described.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive defect of neutral amino acid transport in intestinal and renal epithelia; impaired tryptophan absorption causes niacin deficiency resembling pellagra (diarrhea, dermatitis, ataxia) with excess amino acids in the urine.
choice_explanations.E: Homocystinuria causes Marfanoid habitus, mental retardation, hypercoagulability, and downward lens subluxation, without neutral aminoaciduria or pellagra.

fa_summary: Hartnup disease (autosomal recessive) is a defect of neutral amino acid transport in intestinal and renal epithelial cells; impaired tryptophan absorption leads to niacin deficiency resembling pellagra (diarrhea, dermatitis, ataxia), with large amounts of free amino acids in the urine.

He reports that earlier in the day during a football game, he suffered a blow to the shin from another player's helmet. stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of hearing loss. Physical examination shows a large amount of wax blocking the patient's right ear canal. The patient faints as a water-filled syringe is used to expel wax from the ear canal. This event can be explained by the fact that the posterior half of the external ear canal receives sensory innervation from which of the following?

options.text: Auricular branch of the vagus nerve
Auriculotemporal branch of the mandibular nerve

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The vagus nerve, through its auricular branch, supplies the posterior half of the external auditory meatus. Since the vagus also supplies many chest and abdominal organs, reflex symptoms may occur, including fainting (vasovagal syncope), coughing, and gagging. Vasovagal syncope is the most common cause of syncope and accounts for approximately 20-25% of all cases, particularly in patients without neurologic or cardiac disease. Reflex syncope is also the most common cause of syncope in heart disease patients and should be considered as a possible cause in these patients.

The auriculotemporal nerve (choice B) is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and supplies the anterior half of the external auditory meatus and the facial surface of the upper part of the auricle.

The greater auricular nerve (choice C), a branch of the cervical plexus, supplies both surfaces of the lower part of the auricle.

The lesser occipital nerve (choice D), a branch of the cervical plexus, supplies the cranial surface of the upper part of the auricle.

The vestibulocochlear nerve (choice E, CN VIII) supplies hearing and vestibular sense through innervation to the cochlear hair cells and the vestibular hair cells in the inner ear. It provides no innervation to the external ear.

choice_explanations.A: The auricular branch of the vagus nerve supplies the posterior half of the external auditory meatus. Because the vagus also supplies many chest and abdominal organs, stimulation can produce reflex symptoms such as fainting (vasovagal syncope), coughing, and gagging.
choice_explanations.B: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and supplies the anterior half of the external auditory meatus and the facial surface of the upper part of the auricle.

choice_explanations.D: The lesser occipital nerve, a branch of the cervical plexus, supplies the cranial surface of the upper part of the auricle.
choice_explanations.E: The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) supplies hearing and vestibular sense via the cochlear and vestibular hair cells; it provides no innervation to the external ear.

stem: A newborn born at 26 weeks' gestation undergoes a transcranial ultrasound that shows a grade II intraventricular hemorrhage. The newborn's head circumference enlarges more than expected over the following month. A follow-up ultrasound of the head shows increased ventricular dilatation. The lateral ventricles are symmetrically enlarged, but the third and fourth ventricles are normal-sized. At which of the following sites is the obstruction most likely located?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) represents the most significant long-term morbidity for the extremely preterm infant. It results from bleeding from the very vascular germinal matrix. Blood may be present in the lateral ventricles, and if the amount of blood is large, it generally clots before it can be reabsorbed. This leads to obstruction in the outflow tract of the lateral ventricles, i.e., the bilateral foramina of Monro. Therefore, bilateral large lateral ventricles with normal-sized third and fourth ventricles would be seen. Placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is typically performed to alleviate the hydrocephalus.

There are four interconnected ventricles in the brain. A lateral ventricle is located deep within each cerebral hemisphere. Each lateral ventricle communicates with the third ventricle by the interventricular foramen of Monro. CSF from the lateral ventricles exits via the interventricular foramina of Monro into the third ventricle, then via the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius into the fourth ventricle, which exits through the two lateral foramina of Luschka and the median foramen of Magendie into the subarachnoid space, and is ultimately returned by arachnoid granulation into the superior sagittal sinus (venous blood). Blockade of the interventricular foramina of Monro will cause enlargement of the lateral ventricles.

Obstruction of the aqueduct of Sylvius (choice A) would enlarge the lateral and third ventricles while leaving the fourth ventricle small. Obstruction at the level of the arachnoid granulations (choice B) or within the subarachnoid space (choice E) causes communicating hydrocephalus with enlargement of all ventricles. Obstruction of the foramen of Magendie (choice C) would selectively enlarge the fourth ventricle. Only blockade of the interventricular foramina of Monro (choice D) produces symmetric enlargement of the lateral ventricles with normal third and fourth ventricles.

choice_explanations.A: Obstruction of the aqueduct of Sylvius would enlarge the lateral and third ventricles while the fourth ventricle remains small.
choice_explanations.B: Obstruction at the arachnoid granulations produces communicating hydrocephalus with enlargement of all ventricles.
choice_explanations.C: Obstruction of the foramen of Magendie would selectively enlarge the fourth ventricle.
choice_explanations.D: Blockade of the interventricular foramina of Monro causes symmetric enlargement of the lateral ventricles with normal third and fourth ventricles, as seen here.
choice_explanations.E: Obstruction within the subarachnoid space produces communicating hydrocephalus with enlargement of all ventricles.

stem: A 42-year-old woman develops a painful blister over the vermilion of her upper lip. She has had several episodes of similar symptoms since age 12. The causal agent has most likely established a latency on a nerve that exits the skull through which of the following?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Herpes simplex is an enveloped, linear DNA virus that causes painful skin vesicles, often called "cold sores" or "fever blisters" to denote the precipitating event that preceded the appearance of the lesions. Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) belongs to the herpesvirus family; herpesviruses multiply in the nucleus and surround themselves with nuclear membrane envelopes. HSV-1 can remain latent in the trigeminal root ganglion. The treatment in immunocompromised patients or patients with severe infections is acyclovir. HSV-1 belongs to the herpesvirus family, which multiply in the nucleus and surround themselves with nuclear membrane envelopes.

Because the patient's lesions are on the upper lip, the nerve that transported HSV-1 to the site of recurrence had to be a branch of the maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve. The maxillary nerve exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.

A useful mnemonic for the foramina through which the branches of the trigeminal nerve leave the skull is "SRO"—or "Standing Room Only"—for V1 to V3:
- Superior orbital fissure—V1
- Foramen Rotundum—V2
- Foramen Ovale—V3

The mandibular branch (V3) of the trigeminal nerve exits the skull via the foramen ovale (choice A).

The glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), and spinal accessory (XI) nerves exit the skull via the jugular foramen (choice C).

The facial nerve (VII) enters the skull via the internal auditory meatus (where the greater petrosal nerve branches off), continues in the facial canal (where the chorda tympani branches off), and exits the skull via the stylomastoid foramen (choice D).

Nerves that exit the skull through the superior orbital fissure (choice E) include the ophthalmic branch (V1) of the trigeminal nerve, the oculomotor (III) nerve, the trochlear nerve (IV), and the abducens nerve (VI).

choice_explanations.A: The mandibular branch (V3) of the trigeminal nerve exits the skull via the foramen ovale.
choice_explanations.B: The maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve, which supplies the upper lip, exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.
choice_explanations.C: The glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), and spinal accessory (XI) nerves exit the skull via the jugular foramen.
choice_explanations.D: The facial nerve (VII) exits the skull via the stylomastoid foramen.
choice_explanations.E: The superior orbital fissure transmits V1, the oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), and abducens (VI) nerves.

stem: A 47-year-old man with a history of diabetes comes to the physician because of recent onset of double vision. He says his symptoms are particularly bad when looking to the right. He also describes polyuria, polyphagia, and tingling in his extremities. His last HbA1c was 8.6%. Which of the following nerves most likely has a lesion in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has dysfunction of the right lateral rectus muscle, which is innervated by CN VI (abducens nerve). The patient is unable to abduct his right eye when looking to the right, but can adduct it normally. (Abduct: look away from the nose; adduct: look toward the nose.) Note that when he is looking straight ahead, his right eye is deviated slightly toward the nose due to the unopposed action of the medial rectus muscle, innervated by CN III (oculomotor nerve). CN III is the nerve responsible for adducting the eye. Abducens nerve palsy can result from small vessel disease, particularly in diabetics. Other potential causes include trauma, tumor, and increased intracranial pressure.

The abducens nerve is CN VI, which innervates the lateral rectus muscle. Lesion of this nerve will cause an inability to abduct the ipsilateral eye and can lead to a persistent medial deviation.

A lesion of CN III (choice A, oculomotor) impairs adduction (and also causes ptosis, mydriasis, and loss of up/down gaze). CN IV (choice B, trochlear) innervates the superior oblique and normally causes vertical/torsional diplopia. CN V (choice C, trigeminal) provides facial sensation and motor supply to the muscles of mastication. CN VII (choice E, facial) supplies the muscles of facial expression.

stem: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a knife fight. A knife blade is found embedded in the patient's gluteal region and imaging reveals that the tip is located against the upper border of the greater sciatic foramen in the right hip. Physical examination reveals significant swelling and bleeding at the site of injury. The patient demonstrates some weakness in the leg. Which of the following physical findings is most likely in this patient?

options.text: Sensory deficit in the perianal and posterior scrotal region
Sensory deficit on the posterior right thigh
Weakness of abduction at the right hip
Weakness of adduction at the right hip
Weakness of extension and lateral rotation at the right hip

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Most of the greater sciatic foramen is occupied by the piriformis muscle. The superior gluteal nerve, artery, and vein exit through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis and lie against the upper border of the foramen. This nerve innervates the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae muscles. The gluteus medius and gluteus minimus are the major abductors at the hip.

The pudendal nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis and lies against the lower border of the foramen. After entering the gluteal region briefly, the nerve passes through the lesser sciatic foramen to enter the perineum. It provides sensory and motor innervation to structures in the perineum (choice A).

The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle. This nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the posterior thigh (choice B).

The obturator nerve exits through the obturator canal, an opening in the obturator membrane. This nerve innervates the muscles of the medial compartment of the thigh, the adductor longus, adductor brevis, part of the adductor magnus, gracilis, and part of the pectineus muscle. These are the adductors at the hip (choice D).

The inferior gluteal nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle and lies against the inferior border of the foramen. This nerve innervates the gluteus maximus muscle, which is an extensor and lateral rotator at the hip (choice E).

choice_explanations.A: The pudendal nerve exits below the piriformis and supplies sensory and motor innervation to the perineum (perianal and posterior scrotal region).
choice_explanations.B: The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve exits below the piriformis and supplies sensory innervation to the skin of the posterior thigh.
choice_explanations.C: The superior gluteal nerve exits above the piriformis and innervates the gluteus medius and minimus, the major abductors at the hip; injury causes weakness of hip abduction (Trendelenburg sign).
choice_explanations.D: The obturator nerve exits through the obturator canal and innervates the adductors of the thigh.
choice_explanations.E: The inferior gluteal nerve exits below the piriformis and innervates the gluteus maximus, an extensor and lateral rotator at the hip.

stem: A 61-year-old man with a longstanding history of cigarette smoking and alcohol use is diagnosed with oral squamous cell carcinoma. He undergoes surgical resection of the lateral tongue and several right-sided anterior cervical lymph nodes are also evaluated for the presence of cancerous cells. Two days later, he returns to the physician because he is unable to raise his right arm above the horizontal position and is also unable to shrug his right shoulder. Which of the following nerves is most likely to have been injured?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck immediately deep to the investing fascia of the neck and is placed at risk of injury in a cervical lymph node dissection. This nerve innervates the trapezius muscle, which is responsible for upward rotation of the scapula. A lesion of this nerve in the posterior triangle leads to paralysis of the trapezius. Because upward rotation of the scapula is necessary to abduct or flex at the shoulder beyond 90 degrees, paralysis of the trapezius prevents these movements above the horizontal. Although the deltoid is the primary abductor at the shoulder, without upward rotation of the scapula, this movement is limited to about 90 degrees. The trapezius is also responsible for shrugging of the shoulder and therefore this movement is impaired with paralysis of the trapezius muscle. The spinal accessory nerve also innervates the sternocleidomastoid, which rotates the head. However, this muscle is innervated before the spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle and therefore would not be affected by this injury.

Paralysis of the trapezius muscle, caused by spinal accessory nerve damage, can lead to shoulder droop, an inability to shrug the shoulder, and an inability to raise the arm above the horizontal.

The axillary nerve (choice A) supplies the deltoid and teres minor and is injured in fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus. The great auricular (choice B) and transverse cervical (choice E) nerves are branches of the cervical plexus supplying sensation to the ear and neck skin. The greater occipital nerve (choice C) arises from the posterior ramus of C2 and supplies sensation to the posterior scalp.

choice_explanations.A: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor and is injured in fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus.
choice_explanations.B: The great auricular nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus supplying sensation to the skin over the parotid gland and ear.
choice_explanations.C: The greater occipital nerve arises from the posterior ramus of C2 and supplies sensation to the posterior scalp.
choice_explanations.D: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the posterior triangle and innervates the trapezius (shoulder shrug, arm elevation above the horizontal) and the sternocleidomastoid; it is at risk during cervical lymph node dissection.
choice_explanations.E: The transverse cervical nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus supplying sensation to the anterior neck.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of pain and swelling of the left eyelid. His mother attributes his symptoms to a recent spider bite. Physical examination shows periorbital redness, tenderness, conjunctival injection, and edema that prevents him from voluntarily opening his eye. Visual acuity and extraocular eye movements are normal. Culture of the bite site reveals gram-positive cocci in clusters. Treatment with antibiotics is begun immediately to prevent spread of infection to which of the following areas?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient likely has preseptal cellulitis (in soft tissues anterior to the orbital septum), which can progress to orbital cellulitis if untreated. In preseptal cellulitis, the eye itself is not involved. If a preseptal infection progresses into the orbit, proptosis can develop and extraocular motility can become compromised. Visual acuity changes can occur with involvement of the optic nerve. Potential complications of orbital cellulitis include cavernous sinus thrombosis, blindness, intracranial abscess, and death.

The anterior continuation of the cavernous sinus, the superior ophthalmic vein, passes through the superior orbital fissure to enter the orbit. Veins of the face communicate with the superior ophthalmic vein. Because of the absence of valves in emissary veins, venous flow may occur in either direction. Cutaneous infections may be carried into the cavernous sinus and result in cavernous sinus infection, which may lead to septic cavernous sinus thrombosis. The cavernous sinus is located on either side of the sella turcica, is lateral to the pituitary gland, and contains portions of cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, and the internal carotid artery.

The occipital sinus (choice B), sigmoid sinus (choice C), straight sinus (choice D), and superior petrosal sinus (choice E) are dural venous sinuses that do not receive venous drainage from the face and are not the route by which a periorbital infection spreads.

choice_explanations.A: Facial and periorbital infection can spread via the valveless superior ophthalmic vein into the cavernous sinus, causing septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.
choice_explanations.B: The occipital sinus is a dural venous sinus at the posterior cranial fossa and does not drain the face.
choice_explanations.C: The sigmoid sinus drains into the internal jugular vein and is unrelated to periorbital venous spread.
choice_explanations.D: The straight sinus is a dural venous sinus in the posterior fossa and is not a route of periorbital infection.
choice_explanations.E: The superior petrosal sinus is a dural venous sinus and is not the site of venous spread from a periorbital infection.

stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to her physician because of anxiety and irritability. She reports that she recently has had a significant weight loss despite normal eating habits. Her menstrual cycle has become irregular, she has been having frequent bowel movements, and she has been having difficulty sleeping. Physical examination shows a fine tremor of her hands and a rapid and irregular heartbeat. There is a noticeable bulge in her anterior neck just below her larynx. She initially undergoes medical management, but it is not successful. Surgical treatment of her underlying disease is scheduled. Three days after surgery, the patient develops hoarseness and can barely speak above a whisper. Damage to a branch of which of the following nerves is the most likely cause of the hoarseness in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient had hyperthyroidism, likely a result of Graves' disease. The surgical treatment for this is subtotal or total thyroidectomy. The recurrent laryngeal nerves are at risk during this surgery because of their close relationship to the inferior thyroid arteries. The recurrent laryngeal nerves are branches of the vagus (CN X), and supply all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid (which is innervated by the external laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal branch of CN X). The recurrent laryngeal nerves:
- Are branches of the vagus (CN X)
- Supply all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid
- Are vulnerable during thyroid surgery, and damage may cause extreme hoarseness

The right recurrent laryngeal nerve recurs around the right subclavian artery. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve recurs in the thorax around the arch of the aorta and ligamentum arteriosum. Both nerves ascend to the larynx by passing in the tracheoesophageal groove, in close proximity to the thyroid gland. The recurrent laryngeal nerves are therefore particularly vulnerable during thyroid surgery, and damage may cause extreme hoarseness. Injury to both nerves can compromise the airway because of adduction of the vocal folds. Injury to one nerve will lead to hoarseness.

The facial nerve (choice A) supplies the muscles of facial expression. The glossopharyngeal nerve (choice B) supplies the stylopharyngeus and provides sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and pharynx. The hypoglossal nerve (choice C) supplies the muscles of the tongue. The trigeminal nerve (choice D) supplies the muscles of mastication and facial sensation.

choice_explanations.A: The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression.
choice_explanations.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the stylopharyngeus and sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and pharynx.
choice_explanations.C: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the muscles of the tongue.
choice_explanations.D: The trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication and facial sensation.
choice_explanations.E: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus (CN X) and supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid; it is at risk during thyroidectomy because of its relationship to the inferior thyroid artery, and injury causes hoarseness.

fa_summary: 甲状腺手术易损伤喉返神经（迷走神经 CN X 的分支，与甲状腺下动脉关系密切），致声音嘶哑。

stem: A 61-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She also says she has redness and dryness of her left eye. Which of the following additional findings is most likely present in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has unilateral (left) facial paralysis due to a lesion of the facial nerve (CN VII; Bell's palsy). Lower motor neuron lesions of CN VII affect the entire ipsilateral half of the face and upper motor neuron lesions cause contralateral symptoms that spare the forehead. Bell's palsy results in a complete ipsilateral paralysis of muscles of facial expression (causing an inability to wrinkle the forehead and shut the eye, and a drooping of the mouth) (facial nerve [CN VII] lesion).

A lower motor lesion of the facial nerve results in the inability to close the ipsilateral eye because of damaged motor fibers to the orbicularis oculi. As a result, she may need to protect her eye with a patch and use protective eyedrops to prevent damage to the eye. She would also lose her corneal reflex on that side because of an inability to blink. Other findings of a CN VII lesion include:
- Paralysis of muscles of facial expression (including the orbicularis oculi)
- Hyperacusis (caused by paralysis of the stapedius muscle)
- Loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
- Loss of corneal reflex (efferent limb)
- Lacrimal gland dysfunction

Hyperacusis (choice B) is caused by paralysis of the stapedius muscle, which is innervated by CN VII. Diplopia (choice A) results from dysfunction of the extraocular muscles (CN III, IV, or VI). Impairment of facial sensation (choice C) and inability to chew (choice D) are features of trigeminal (CN V) dysfunction. Inability to shrug the shoulder (choice E) results from spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) injury.

choice_explanations.A: Diplopia results from dysfunction of the extraocular muscles innervated by CN III, IV, or VI.
choice_explanations.B: Hyperacusis is caused by paralysis of the stapedius muscle, which is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).
choice_explanations.C: Impairment of facial sensation is a feature of trigeminal (CN V) dysfunction.
choice_explanations.D: Inability to chew is a feature of trigeminal (CN V) dysfunction (muscles of mastication).
choice_explanations.E: Inability to shrug the shoulder results from spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) injury.

fa_summary: 面神经（CN VII）下运动神经元损伤（Bell 麻痹）：同侧全部表情肌瘫痪、眼干红、听觉过敏（镫骨肌瘫痪）等。

stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a badly damaged nail on his index finger. He states that he accidentally crushed the finger while closing a door. In preparation for excision of the nail, a branch of which of the following nerves will most likely be anesthetized?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The median nerve supplies sensation to the lateral 3 1/2 digits on the palmar side, the adjacent area of the lateral palm, the distal dorsal surface of the lateral 3 1/2 digits (including nailbeds), and thenar eminence. Therefore, prior to performing surgery in this area, it is essential to anesthetize a branch of this nerve (possibly a proper digital branch) to eliminate pain sensation around the nail bed of the index finger.

The median nerve supplies the:
- Palmar surface of the lateral 3 1/2 digits and adjacent palm
- Distal dorsal surface of the lateral 3 1/2 digits (including nailbeds)

Note: Palm sensation is not affected by carpal tunnel syndrome; the superficial palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the carpal tunnel.

The anterior interosseus nerve (choice A) is a branch of the median nerve supplying the deep muscles of the anterior forearm. The musculocutaneous nerve (choice C) supplies the anterior compartment of the arm and sensation to the lateral forearm. The radial nerve (choice D) supplies the posterior compartments and sensation to the dorsum of the hand (except the median- and ulnar-innervated areas). The ulnar nerve (choice E) supplies sensation to the medial 1 1/2 digits.

choice_explanations.A: The anterior interosseus nerve is a branch of the median nerve supplying the deep muscles of the anterior forearm.
choice_explanations.B: The median nerve supplies the palmar surface of the lateral 3 1/2 digits and adjacent palm, and the distal dorsal surface of the lateral 3 1/2 digits (including nailbeds), including the index finger nail bed.
choice_explanations.C: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior compartment of the arm and sensation to the lateral forearm.
choice_explanations.D: The radial nerve supplies the posterior compartments and sensation to the dorsum of the hand.
choice_explanations.E: The ulnar nerve supplies sensation to the medial 1 1/2 digits.

fa_summary: 示指（外侧 3 1/2 指）掌侧及远端背侧（含甲床）感觉由正中神经支配；甲床手术需麻醉其分支。

stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of neck pain, dizziness, hoarseness, and facial numbness following chiropractic neck manipulation. Neurologic examination produces a gag reflex with deviation of the uvula to the right when the right side of the pharyngeal mucosa is stimulated. When the left side of the pharyngeal mucosa is stimulated, the patient does not gag. These findings are most likely caused by a lesion in which of the following structures?

options.text: Left glossopharyngeal nerve and left vagus nerve
Left glossopharyngeal nerve and right vagus nerve
Right glossopharyngeal nerve and left vagus nerve
Right glossopharyngeal nerve and right vagus nerve

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The number of options may at first appear overwhelming, but with a little basic knowledge and using the process of elimination, the correct answer can be easily identified.

The gag reflex requires the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) for the sensory limb of the reflex (unilateral) and the vagus nerve (X) for the motor limb of the reflex (bilateral). A lesion of the left glossopharyngeal nerve will denervate the sensory receptors on the left side of the pharynx. Thus, when the left side is touched, the patient does not feel it and does not gag. Therefore, you can immediately rule out any option with right glossopharyngeal (choices E and F) because the left CN IX must be involved.

The gag reflex requires the vagus nerve for the motor limb of the reflex. If the left vagus nerve is lesioned, the left side of the soft palate will not elevate during a gag and the uvula will deviate to the right. In this case, the patient feels only the touch on the right side and elevates only the right side of the palate. Therefore, you can rule out any answer with the right CN X (choices B and F) because the right CN X is working, but the left CN X is not. Additionally, because there are clearly problems in both the afferent (sensory) and efferent (motor) arcs of the reflex, single nerve lesions can also be eliminated (choices C and D).

The gag reflex requires an ipsilateral glossopharyngeal nerve (afferent) and a bilateral vagus nerve (efferent).

choice_explanations.A: Correct: the left glossopharyngeal nerve (afferent, sensory) and left vagus nerve (efferent, motor) account for the absent left gag and the rightward uvular deviation.
choice_explanations.B: The right vagus is working (the palate elevates on the right), so a right vagus lesion is excluded.
choice_explanations.C: A single glossopharyngeal lesion cannot explain the motor (uvular deviation) deficit.
choice_explanations.D: A single vagus lesion cannot explain the absent sensory (afferent) limb on the left.
choice_explanations.E: The left, not the right, glossopharyngeal nerve must be involved.
choice_explanations.F: Both the right glossopharyngeal and right vagus nerves are functioning, so this is incorrect.

fa_summary: 呕吐反射：传入为同侧舌咽神经（IX），传出为双侧迷走神经（X）；左侧 IX+X 受损 → 左咽无感觉不 gag、软腭右侧上提、悬雍垂偏右。

stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of uncontrolled hypertension is brought to the emergency department because of right-sided hemiplegia. His wife states that he has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the past 35 years and he consumes 3-4 beers daily. He appears to be in some distress and has difficulty speaking. Physical examination shows paralysis of the right side of the mouth, and the right upper and lower extremities. There is no loss of sensation noted on any of his extremities and he is able to wrinkle his forehead on both sides. The lesion responsible for this patient's symptoms is most likely located in which of the following?

options.text: Corticospinal tract in the upper cervical spinal cord
Medial portion of the left frontal lobe
Medial portion of the right frontal lobe

explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has sustained a hemorrhage of the left internal capsule secondary to uncontrolled hypertension. The internal capsule is an area of white matter in the brain that separates the caudate nucleus and the thalamus from the lenticular nucleus. The internal capsule receives its blood supply from the lenticulostriate arteries which, in uncontrolled hypertension, are prone to develop a lipo-hyaline arteriosclerosis (Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms) resulting in ischemic changes of the surrounding tissue (lacunar infarcts) and corresponding neurologic deficits of the affected area. Weakening of the affected blood vessel wall can occur and cause hemorrhage, resulting in a hemorrhagic stroke and increased mortality risk. Lacunar infarcts account for approximately 20-25% of ischemic strokes, while 35-45% of intracerebral hemorrhages involve the basal ganglia. Moreover, hypertension is associated with a majority of all intracerebral hemorrhages and lacunar infarcts. The internal capsule is supplied by arteries arising from the middle cerebral artery (lenticulostriate arteries). Ischemia of the internal capsule can be a result of uncontrolled hypertension, manifesting as contralateral hemiplegia.

There are 3 parts of the internal capsule:
- The anterior limb of the internal capsule conveys frontopontine fibers.
- The genu conducts corticobulbar fibers.
- The posterior limb of the internal capsule conveys corticospinal fibers to the contralateral arm and leg.

Hemorrhage of the left internal capsule can result in a right-sided dense hemiplegia in which paralysis of the arm and leg are of the same intensity. The lower facial paralysis is the result of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, which is also consistent with a stroke of the left internal capsule. (This is because the facial nucleus for the upper part of the face receives bilateral UMN innervation, whereas the facial nucleus for the lower part only receives contralateral UMN innervation.)

A lesion of the corticospinal tract in the upper cervical spinal cord (choice A) or of the right internal capsule (choice E) would cause left-sided (contralateral) deficits. A lesion of the medial portion of the left or right frontal lobe (choices C and D) involves the anterior cerebral artery territory and primarily affects the contralateral lower limb, not the face and upper limb.

choice_explanations.A: A lesion of the corticospinal tract in the upper cervical cord would produce ipsilateral or contralateral deficits depending on the level but would not cause a contralateral lower facial palsy.
choice_explanations.B: The left internal capsule carries corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers; its involvement produces right-sided hemiplegia with right lower facial paralysis sparing the forehead, as described.
choice_explanations.C: A medial left frontal lobe lesion (anterior cerebral artery) primarily affects the contralateral lower limb.
choice_explanations.D: A medial right frontal lobe lesion (anterior cerebral artery) primarily affects the contralateral lower limb.
choice_explanations.E: A right internal capsule lesion would produce left-sided deficits, opposite to those seen here.

fa_summary: 左侧内囊（豆纹动脉供血）病变：右侧偏身瘫痪，含右侧下半面部上运动神经元瘫（额纹保留），无感觉障碍。

stem: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after falling down a flight of stairs. She says that she has had increasingly blurry vision and was planning to make an appointment with the eye doctor. She has a 9-month history of pulmonary Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (MAI). She was initially treated with azithromycin, rifampin, and ethambutol. Rifampin was discontinued during the first month after the patient developed a rash. She has a 12-year history of diabetes mellitus, a 5-year history of Addison disease, and a 3-year history of hypothyroidism. Recent HIV and PPD testing was negative. Visual field testing shows bilateral central scotomas. A lesion involving which of the following structures is the most likely cause of this defect?

options.text: Optic radiations in the parietal lobe
