Optic radiations in the temporal lobe

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The most likely locations of lesions that produce visual defects are a favorite USMLE topic. Lesions of the retina that include destruction of the macula produce a central scotoma. The macula is an oval region approximately 3 by 5 mm that contains the fovea and is near the center of the retina. It is responsible for central, high-resolution vision. The macula is quite sensitive to intense light, trauma, aging, and neurotoxins. This patient was on ethambutol, a bacteriostatic antimycobacterial drug used to treat tuberculosis. Ethambutol is known to cause optic neuropathy and patients are advised to report any changes of visual acuity to their doctor. Recovery of visual acuity generally occurs over a period of weeks to months after discontinuation of the drug. Other causes of central scotoma include macular degeneration and multiple sclerosis.

A central scotoma can be caused by damage to the macula (e.g., neurotoxins such as ethambutol, optic neuritis, macular degeneration).

A lesion of the optic chiasm (choice C) results in bitemporal hemianopsia. Lesions distal to the chiasm, such as the optic tract (choice F) or optic radiations (choices D and E), produce contralateral defects that differ according to the structure affected. A lesion of the occipital lobe (choice B) produces a contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing.

choice_explanations.A: The macula is responsible for central, high-resolution vision; its damage (e.g., ethambutol-induced optic neuropathy) produces a central scotoma.
choice_explanations.B: An occipital lobe lesion produces a contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing, not a central scotoma.
choice_explanations.C: An optic chiasm lesion produces bitemporal hemianopsia.
choice_explanations.D: A lesion of the parietal optic radiations produces a contralateral inferior quadrantanopia.
choice_explanations.E: A lesion of the temporal optic radiations produces a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
choice_explanations.F: An optic tract lesion produces a contralateral homonymous hemianopsia without macular sparing.

fa_summary: 乙胺丁醇可致视神经病变（红绿色盲/视力下降/中心暗点）；双侧中心暗点提示黄斑（乳头黄斑束）受损。

stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the physician because of headache, nausea, and vomiting. She does not drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes. She does not take any medications. Neurologic examination shows that her pupils have a minimal reaction to light, but do constrict during accommodation. She is unable to look upward past the horizontal plane, but has full conjugate eye movements in other directions; she is unable to converge. Visual field testing shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Based on the neurological examination, this patient has a lesion of the vertical gaze center in the dorsal midbrain. Of the answer choices, a tumor of the pineal gland (eg, germinoma) is most likely, because of the close proximity of the pineal gland to the midbrain tectum. Tumors of the pineal gland (pinealoma) compress the vertical gaze center in the tectum of the midbrain. This can lead to Parinaud syndrome, characterized by eye movement and pupil dysfunction, such as a vertical gaze palsy and light near dissociation. Parinaud syndrome, which is a condition resulting from compression of the tectum, is the most important clinical presentation of pineal germinomas. This syndrome consists of a palsy of upward gaze, a dissociation of light and accommodation (light-near dissociation due to damage to the pretectal area), and a failure of convergence. It is also possible to have hydrocephalus because of compression of the cerebral aqueduct. An acoustic neuroma (choice A) is a schwannoma of the eighth cranial nerve. It results in deafness, ataxia, and dysarthria. Nystagmus may be present. The facial nerve is often also affected. The gaze centers are not affected. Astrocytomas of the cerebellum (choice B) are usually seen in children. These tumors present with headache, nausea, vomiting, papilledema, and cerebellar signs such as ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus, and intention tremor. The gaze centers are not affected. Craniopharyngiomas (choice C) are usually seen in children. There are headaches, bitemporal hemianopia, and a failure of growth. Parasagittal meningiomas (choice D) usually result in headache, spastic paresis, and urinary incontinence. Tabes dorsalis (choice F), which is associated with late-stage syphilis, can produce light-near dissociation, also called Argyll Robertson pupil (a mnemonic is "prostitute's pupil", because the pupil will accommodate, but does not react). However, many other symptoms (that this patient does not have) also occur because of degeneration of the dorsal roots and dorsal columns. These patients can have impaired vibration and position sense, astereognosis, paroxysmal pains, ataxia, diminished stretch reflexes, and incontinence.

choice_explanations.A: Acoustic neuroma is a schwannoma of the eighth cranial nerve; it causes deafness, ataxia, dysarthria, and sometimes nystagmus/facial nerve involvement, but not gaze center dysfunction.
choice_explanations.B: Astrocytomas of the cerebellum (usually children) present with headache, nausea, vomiting, papilledema, and cerebellar signs; gaze centers are not affected.
choice_explanations.C: Craniopharyngiomas (usually children) cause headaches, bitemporal hemianopia, and failure of growth.
choice_explanations.D: Parasagittal meningiomas usually result in headache, spastic paresis, and urinary incontinence.
choice_explanations.F: Tabes dorsalis (late-stage syphilis) can produce light-near dissociation (Argyll Robertson pupil), but also causes degeneration of dorsal roots/columns with impaired vibration and position sense, astereognosis, paroxysmal pains, ataxia, diminished stretch reflexes, and incontinence.

fa_summary: Parinaud syndrome (upward gaze palsy, light-near dissociation) results from a pineal gland tumor compressing the dorsal midbrain tectum.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with progressive myopia develops sudden patchy loss of vision in her right eye. Funduscopic examination shows large retinal detachment in the right eye. The retina in the left eye is normal. The physician tests the pupillary light reflex by swinging a light source from the left eye to the right eye. Which of the following will most likely occur after the light source reaches the right eye?

options.text: Constriction of the right pupil and constriction of the left
Constriction of the right pupil and dilation of the left
Dilation of the right pupil and constriction of the left
Dilation of the right pupil and dilation of the left
No reaction of the right pupil and constriction of the left

explanation: The correct answer is D. This patient is exhibiting a Marcus-Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect). This defect is caused by decreased sensitivity of the affected eye to light, which results from lesions of the retina, optic nerve, or the eye. A useful way to detect this defect is a swinging flashlight test, in which a flashlight is moved back and forth between both eyes every 2 to 3 seconds. The afferent pupil becomes obvious when the flashlight is moved from the normal to the affected eye, and the eyes dilate in response to light. Shine light in Marcus Gunn pupil = pupils do not constrict fully. Shine light in normal eye = pupils constrict fully. Shine light in affected pupil again = apparent dilation of both pupils because the stimulus carried by the optic nerve (CN II) of the affected eye is weaker than the normal eye. In other words, the pupils appear to dilate when the light is swung from the healthy to the affected eye. In actuality, they are not "dilating", but are constricting to a lesser degree as compared to when light is directed to the normal eye. The pupillary light reflex is diminished in the affected eye.
fa_summary: Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect): the swinging flashlight test shows apparent dilation of the affected eye due to a weaker afferent light stimulus.

stem: A 28-year-old man comes to the physician because of ptosis, muscle weakness, and facial muscle atrophy. The physician notices that the patient had a stiff and delayed relaxation after shaking hands upon greeting. The patient states that his father and brother have similar problems, but his symptoms appear more severe. His birth and childhood were normal. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 125/78 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals bilateral ptosis and distal limb muscle weakness. Gait, cranial nerves, and funduscopic examination are normal. Which of the following would most likely be associated with this patient's condition?

options.text: Demyelination in the central nervous system
Ring fibers seen on muscle biopsy

explanation: The correct answer is E. The patient has adult onset myotonic muscular dystrophy (DM1), an autosomal dominant disorder with CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion (>50 CTG repeats). Alleles >80 repeats tend to expand in maternal transmissions. Symptoms start in the second decade. Clinical features include frontal balding, eyelid and facial muscle atrophy, cataracts, distal muscle weakness, infertility, and insulin resistance. Proximal muscle weakness occurs later. Cardiac involvement with delayed conduction can also occur. Myotonia (delayed muscle relaxation) involves the tongue, forearm, and hand (delayed relaxation after hand shake). Histologically, ring fibers and central nuclei are present. Necrosis, regeneration, and increased collagen are not as severe as in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. In contrast, congenital myotonic dystrophy presents with neonatal hypotonia, facial diplegia, and motor and intellectual disabilities. Respiratory complications can occur. Those who survive, by age 10, develop myotonia and additional complications as seen in the adult-onset type. Antibodies to acetylcholine receptors (choice A) would be seen in myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disorder affecting the nicotinic postsynaptic receptor at the neuromuscular junction of the skeletal muscle. Patients present with ptosis, weakness of head flexion and extension, and proximal muscle weakness (as opposed to the distal muscle weakness seen in our patient). Repetitive or sustained use augments weakness. There is usually no abnormal handshake grip, as seen in our patient. Administration of pyridostigmine or edrophonium (Tensilon test) improves symptoms. Treat with plasmapheresis and/or immunosuppression. In contrast, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) affects the voltage-gated calcium channels of the presynaptic motor nerve terminal. Presynaptic acetylcholine stores are intact, so repetitive stimulation decreases the weakness (raises the endplate potential, which permits generation of muscle action potential). In 40% of patients with LEMS, paraneoplastic syndrome is present and commonly associated with small cell carcinoma of the lung. Antibodies to Hu antigen (choice B) is associated with an immune-mediated paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy seen more commonly with small cell carcinoma of the lung. The antibodies are directed against neurons in the central and peripheral nervous system. Patients present with asymmetrical weakness and autonomic neuropathy, orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary incontinence, pain and sensory loss ("stocking and glove" distribution), and ataxia, which are not seen in our patient. Treatment is to treat the underlying carcinoma and immunosuppression. Decreased dystrophin production (choice C) is seen in Becker muscular dystrophy, a less severe version of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (absent dystrophin). Onset of symptoms in Becker muscular dystrophy occurs later, with mean age of onset 11 years. Our patient had a normal, asymptomatic childhood, and onset of symptoms suggest a late presentation, which is not typical of Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophies. Both conditions are X-linked recessive inherited disorders. Dystrophin is responsible for connecting cytoskeleton of the muscle fiber to the extracellular matrix. Patients have proximal muscle weakness affecting the muscles of the hips and legs (distal limb muscle weakness is seen in our patient). Death usually results from respiratory or cardiac failure. Demyelination in the central nervous system (choice D) is seen with multiple sclerosis (MS), an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder characterized by destruction of oligodendrocytes and demyelinated plaques in the brain and spinal cord. The brain and spinal MRI does not show any lesions in our patient. The mechanism of demyelination involves activation of myelin-reactive T cells in the periphery, which can enter the blood brain barrier. Perivascular T cells in the brain can also activate cytokines (TNF alpha and interferon gamma), while B cells secrete antibodies against myelin. In addition, activated microglia release free radicals and protease, which contribute to tissue damage. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) shows elevated Ig levels in an oligoclonal pattern on electrophoresis.

choice_explanations.A: Antibodies to acetylcholine receptors occur in myasthenia gravis (autoimmune attack on the postsynaptic nicotinic receptor); it causes proximal weakness and abnormal fatigability, not the distal weakness and myotonia seen here.
choice_explanations.B: Antibodies to Hu antigen occur in an immune-mediated paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy (often small cell lung cancer), causing asymmetrical weakness and autonomic neuropathy.
choice_explanations.C: Decreased dystrophin production occurs in Becker muscular dystrophy (X-linked), which causes proximal muscle weakness, not distal weakness with myotonia.
choice_explanations.D: Demyelination of the CNS occurs in multiple sclerosis; no CNS lesions are present in this patient.

fa_summary: Adult-onset myotonic muscular dystrophy (DM1) is autosomal dominant (CTG repeat) with myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, and ring fibers on muscle biopsy.

stem: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressive weakness of his legs and arms. He mentioned that he had minor weakness of these muscles since childhood, but his symptoms have recently worsened. The patient reports no loss of sensation in his extremities. His vaccination history is unavailable. Vital signs are normal. To view part of the examination, click the "Play Media" button. Which of the following structures in the spinal cord is most likely to be affected in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is F. The disease presented in this question is post-polio syndrome, which is a long-term sequelae of acute poliomyelitis. This patient likely had an acute childhood infection by the poliovirus, a member of a family of positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses known as picornavirus. The virus is spread via the fecal-oral route and can then cause paralysis by infecting the alpha motor neurons of the ventral horn of the spinal cord. This can result in lower motor neuron disease including flaccid paralysis, muscle atrophy, fasciculations (as seen in the media clip), and areflexia. Early prodromal symptoms include malaise, headache, fever, abdominal pain, sore throat, and nausea. Typically, sensory neurons are unaffected. Fortunately, poliovirus has been mostly eradicated due to vaccination efforts in the 20th century. Unfortunately, many of its sequelae are still being felt in patients with post-polio syndrome. Usually, symptoms begin several decades after the initial polio infection and are characterized by progressive weakness and motor atrophy due to continuing damage to motor units in the ventral horn. Dysphagia and respiratory insufficiency may also result. The cause is unknown, although latent poliovirus, motor unit degeneration, and autoimmunity are common theories. Differential diagnoses include West Nile Virus, Guillain-Barre syndrome, autoimmune polymyositis, and non-polio enteroviruses. The central canal (choice A) contains no nerve fibers, but rather is filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and is continuous with the ventricles of the brain. Dilation of the central canal is known as syringomyelia, which affects decussating fibers of the spinothalamic tract (anterior white commissure) that surround the central canal. This produces a cape-like bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the upper extremities but preservation of touch sensation (no involvement of dorsal columns), typically at C8-T1. This condition is associated with Arnold-Chiari malformation and trauma. The corticospinal tract (choice B) contains the fibers from upper motor neurons. A lesion of this tract in the spinal cord would lead to upper motor neuron symptoms, such as ipsilateral spastic paresis and hyperreflexia. Our patient presents with fasciculations which, along with hyporeflexia and muscle atrophy, are caused by lower motor neuron disease, not upper motor neuron disease. The dorsal columns (choice C) can be affected in tertiary syphilis, in a condition known as tabes dorsalis. Lesions of the dorsal columns cause ipsilateral loss of conscious proprioception and vibration sensation, along with areflexia (due to loss of sensory afferents). Pain and temperature sensation and muscle strength are preserved. Dorsal root ganglia (choice D) contain the neuronal cell bodies of sensory neurons, not motor neurons. Lesions of dorsal root ganglia cause ipsilateral sensory deficits in associated dermatomes. The spinothalamic tract (choice E) contains sensory nerve fibers responsible for pain and temperature. A lesion of this tract in the spinal cord leads to contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation beginning 1-2 segments below the level of the lesion (due to decussation of axons below the lesion).

choice_explanations.A: The central canal contains CSF, not nerve fibers; its dilation (syringomyelia) causes a cape-like bilateral loss of pain/temperature sensation.
choice_explanations.B: The corticospinal tract carries upper motor neurons; a lesion causes ipsilateral spastic paresis and hyperreflexia, not the lower motor neuron findings here.
choice_explanations.C: The dorsal columns (affected in tabes dorsalis) cause ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sense with areflexia, while strength is preserved.
choice_explanations.D: Dorsal root ganglia contain sensory neuron cell bodies; their lesions cause ipsilateral sensory deficits.
choice_explanations.E: The spinothalamic tract carries pain/temperature fibers; its lesion causes contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning 1-2 segments below the lesion.

fa_summary: Post-polio syndrome results from continuing damage to motor units in the anterior (ventral) horn, which was destroyed by poliovirus.

stem: A 33-year-old man comes to the physician because of severe lower back pain, muscle weakness that began in his legs but now involves the arms as well, and tingling in his extremities. He had a diarrheal illness two weeks ago, but has otherwise been healthy. Physical examination shows generalized weakness, but there is no appreciable sensory loss. Over the next 2 months, the patient recovers, with minimal residual sequelae. The mechanism underlying this patient's disease is most similar to the mechanism associated with which of the following diseases?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The patient has Guillain-Barré syndrome, also known as acute idiopathic inflammatory polyneuropathy. Characteristically, this produces an ascending paralysis, which can eventually involve the diaphragm, leading to respiratory compromise and necessitating intubation. Most cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome resolve spontaneously. A few patients have recurrences, and rarely, patients can die because of respiratory muscle failure (artificial ventilation may be required, so vital capacity should be monitored). This condition, which typically follows an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (eg, by Campylobacter jejuni) by several days to a month, is due to an autoimmune attack on the myelin of peripheral nerves (Schwann cells). In this respect, it is most similar to multiple sclerosis, which is an autoimmune attack on the myelin in the brain and spinal cord (oligodendrocytes). One finding that is characteristic of Guillain-Barré is albuminocytologic dissociation in the CSF — the presence of increased protein without accompanying increases in cells. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, Lou Gehrig disease) (choice A) is a neurodegenerative disorder of unknown cause involving upper and lower motor neurons. It would not spontaneously resolve. Botulism (choice B) produces muscle weakness resulting from the paralyzing toxin of Clostridium botulinum, which blocks the release of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions. Diabetes mellitus (choice C) can lead to a diabetic neuropathy that affects neuronal axons, and to an extent, their myelin sheaths, but this is not the best choice since the damage to neurons in diabetes is not autoimmune in nature. Syringomyelia (choice E) is a disorder in which a cavity (syrinx) forms within the spinal cord. It classically leads to a cape-like loss of pain and temperature sensation due to damage to decussating spinothalamic fibers (not simply demyelination) in the anterior white commissure.

choice_explanations.A: ALS is a neurodegenerative disorder of upper and lower motor neurons that does not spontaneously resolve.
choice_explanations.B: Botulism causes weakness by blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction.
choice_explanations.C: Diabetic neuropathy damages axons and myelin sheaths, but the damage is not autoimmune in nature.
choice_explanations.E: Syringomyelia forms a cavity within the spinal cord and causes a cape-like loss of pain and temperature sensation, not demyelinating weakness.

fa_summary: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy) is an autoimmune demyelination of peripheral nerves after infection, analogous to the CNS demyelination of multiple sclerosis.

stem: A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of sudden onset severe headache and significant nausea and vomiting. His past medical history is remarkable for recurrent epistaxis during childhood, episodic seizures, melena, and iron deficiency anemia. He denies history of headaches. Physical examination shows multiple red lesions across the patient's face and palate. Since arriving at the emergency department, the patient has also developed significant neck stiffness. Laboratory studies show leukocyte count 5000/mm3, erythrocyte count 6 million/mm3, hematocrit 65%, platelets 475 x 10^3/mm3, prothrombin time 12 seconds, and activated partial thromboplastin time 35 seconds. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's most recent symptoms?
explanation: The correct answer is A. This HHT patient presents to the emergency department with the classic symptoms of a subarachnoid hemorrhage. These include sudden onset severe headache ("worst headache of my life"), nausea, vomiting, and meningeal signs such as neck stiffness (due to irritation of meninges from blood in the subarachnoid space). CT scan may or may not show blood in the intraventricular space. There are several potential causes of subarachnoid hemorrhage including saccular (berry) aneurysm rupture, and in the case of this patient, bleeding from arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in the brain. To distinguish between berry aneurysm and arteriovenous malformation, it is important that you look at other elements of this patient's history. His history points towards a diagnosis of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome. Key findings include a history of recurrent epistaxis (due to telangiectasias in nasal mucosa), melena (due to GI telangiectasias), and multiple cutaneous and mucosal vascular lesions. These patients also have a propensity to develop large AVMs in the brain, lungs, and liver, and cerebral AVMs can produce seizures. Patients may also develop high-output heart failure due to the presence of AVMs. This patient has a secondary polycythemia due to erythropoietin secretion from chronic hypoxemia from a right-to-left shunt. In addition, patients may also have iron deficiency anemia secondary to the patient's numerous bleeding episodes. HHT is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Treatment for AVMs usually involve surgical resection or embolization. Berry aneurysms (choice B) can produce both subarachnoid and parenchymal hemorrhage. They are typically located at the junction of the anterior cerebral artery and the anterior communicating artery in the Circle of Willis. Major risk factors for berry aneurysms include hypertension, connective tissue disorders (Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos), and adult polycystic kidney disease. An AVM is more likely in an HHT patient. Bridging veins (choice C) are located in the subdural space and result in subdural hematoma. Typically subdural hematomas result from trauma and can result in gradual onset headache and eventually transtentorial herniation due to elevated intracranial pressures. The elderly, alcoholics, and those with atrophic brains are at risk for subdural hemorrhages. CT scans show a crescent-shaped hemorrhage. Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms (choice D) are small intraparenchymal aneurysms that are related to hypertension (most common), diabetes, and amyloid angiopathy. They usually occur at the sites of small vessels in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and internal capsule. These patients usually present with intraparenchymal bleeds and focal neurologic signs. The middle meningeal artery (choice E) is the source of epidural hematomas, which classically have an initial loss of consciousness, followed by a lucid interval (a brief period of consciousness and alertness), which then proceeds to an altered mental state, coma, or death. This is due to rapid expansion of the hemorrhage (arterial bleed) and subsequent transtentorial herniation. CT scans show a lens-shaped hemorrhage.

choice_explanations.B: Berry aneurysms can cause subarachnoid/parenchymal hemorrhage and are associated with hypertension, connective tissue disorders, and adult polycystic kidney disease, but an AVM is more likely in an HHT patient.
choice_explanations.C: Bridging veins are in the subdural space and produce subdural hematoma (crescent-shaped on CT), typically after trauma in the elderly/alcoholics.
choice_explanations.D: Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms are small intraparenchymal aneurysms related to hypertension/diabetes/amyloid angiopathy, causing intraparenchymal bleeds.
choice_explanations.E: The middle meningeal artery is the source of epidural hematoma, which classically shows a lucid interval and a lens-shaped hemorrhage on CT.

fa_summary: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an autosomal dominant vascular disorder with epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and cerebral arteriovenous malformations that can cause subarachnoid hemorrhage.

stem: A 66-year-old man with a history of hypertension is brought to the emergency department by his family after he is noticed to have behavioral changes. To view the examination, click the "Play Media" button. Neurologic examination shows that he is unable to repeat phrases spoken to him. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?

options.text: Preserved ability to read and write

explanation: The correct answer is E. The first challenge of this question is to recognize that the patient has Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia. The patient produces speech that is fluent but nonsensical, with word sequences haphazardly strung together. The phenomenon of "word salad" arises from an impairment in language comprehension, leading to production of meaningless language, due to damage to Wernicke's area. These patients are usually unaware of their disability. Repetition is also impaired. Reading and writing are impaired in a similar fashion as the speech deficits in this condition. The second task is to realize that Wernicke's area is located in the temporal lobe, in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere. The third piece to the puzzle is to know what else is in the temporal lobe that could be damaged along with Wernicke's area. Since Wernicke's area is near the optic radiation fibers from the left lateral geniculate nucleus projecting to the left primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe, Wernicke aphasics commonly present with a right upper visual field cut (right upper quadrantanopia). A lesion of the optic radiations in the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) causes a right homonymous superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"). Wernicke's area is located in the left (dominant) hemisphere, so the visual field defect is on the right. Broca's aphasia (expressive aphasia) is characterized by decreased fluency of spontaneous speech. Speech is generated slowly and with effort, with the length of a phrase generally less than five words. Patients have intact comprehension and are aware of and generally very frustrated by their speech. Repetition is impaired. Patients who read and write aloud have similar deficits as with their spontaneous speech. Because Broca's area is in the frontal lobe (close to the motor area in the frontal lobe), commonly associated symptoms include a right hemiparesis affecting the face and arm (because of upper motor neuron damage) and dysarthria. Left facial hemiparesis (choice A) is incorrect for two reasons. First, this patient has Wernicke's, not Broca's aphasia. Secondly, in the vast majority of individuals, the language centers are on the left, which would more typically produce deficits on the right. Left hemineglect (choice B) is generally the result of damage to the right parietal (or frontal) cortex. Patients with this syndrome neglect the left side of their external world and often do not acknowledge the existence of the left side of their own body. This would not be likely to occur with a temporal lobe lesion. Patients with Wernicke's aphasia have impairment in their ability to read and write (choice C) in parallel with their speech deficit. A right Babinski sign (choice D) would be the result of left-sided upper motor neuron damage. This is more likely to occur in a patient with Broca's aphasia because Broca's area is close to the motor areas in the frontal lobe.

choice_explanations.A: Left facial hemiparesis would occur with Broca's (not Wernicke's) aphasia; moreover the language/ motor centers are on the left, producing right-sided deficits.
choice_explanations.B: Left hemineglect results from right parietal/frontal damage, not a temporal lobe lesion.
choice_explanations.C: Reading and writing are impaired in Wernicke's aphasia, in parallel with the speech deficit.
choice_explanations.D: A right Babinski sign would reflect left upper motor neuron damage, more likely with Broca's aphasia (near the frontal motor areas).

fa_summary: Wernicke (receptive) aphasia from a temporal lobe lesion of the dominant hemisphere is associated with a right superior (upper) quadrantanopia.

stem: A 65-year-old woman comes to the physician because of difficulty reading and blurred vision over the past 9 months. She says that when she rides in a car at night, the oncoming headlights cause more glare than they did previously. Ophthalmologic examination shows bilateral white opacifications. Which of the following is the most likely location of the disease process?
explanation: The correct answer is C. This patient has classic signs and symptoms of cataracts (lens opacifications). It is not known whether senile cataracts represent disease or normal opacification with age. Cataracts may occur as a consequence of diabetes mellitus, long-term steroid use, or congenital infections. Currently, they are successfully treated with lens extractions and implantation of prosthetic lenses. Cataracts are opacifications of the lens. Cataracts are slowly progressive, with blurring of vision occurring over months to years. Glare from automobile headlights is particularly troublesome, and color perception is reduced in general. The main sign on physical examination is the presence of white opacifications of the lens. Aqueous humor (choice A) is continually replaced due to active secretion by the ciliary body. It does not undergo opacification; it is in constant flux. Corneal opacification (choice B) is generally a consequence of squamous metaplasia, in which the transparent, nonkeratinized squamous cells are replaced by opaque, keratinized squamous cells. Squamous metaplasia is a reparative process, usually due to friction injury to the cornea or vitamin A deficiency. The optic nerve (choice D) is not transparent and it does not undergo opacification injury. It may, however atrophy due to ischemic, traumatic, infective, or metabolic insult. The retina (choice E) consists of multiple layers of neural cells. It is transparent, but is not the site of cataract formation.

choice_explanations.A: Aqueous humor is continually replaced by ciliary body secretion and does not undergo opacification.
choice_explanations.B: Corneal opacification is generally due to squamous metaplasia (eg, friction injury, vitamin A deficiency).
choice_explanations.D: The optic nerve is not transparent and does not opacify, though it may atrophy.
choice_explanations.E: The retina is transparent and is not the site of cataract formation.

fa_summary: Cataract is a painless, often bilateral opacification of the lens that causes glare and progressive blurring of vision.

stem: A 60-year-old woman is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of difficulty walking and memory loss. According to her husband, her symptoms are worsening. She has trouble remembering people's names and becomes confused easily. She has had trouble walking, and has been unable to walk without assistance for the past week. She also reports occasional involuntary jerking of her limbs, which has increased in frequency. She has no family history of neurologic disorders or history of major medical illness. She works as an executive and travels frequently. On neurologic examination, she is alert and oriented and follows simple commands. However, she remembers only one out of three items after 5 minutes. She also has trouble walking in a straight line and shows subtle dysmetria when asked to point from finger to nose. Muscle strength and reflexes are normal throughout. Which of the following is most likely associated with this woman's condition?
explanation: The correct answer is A. The presentation of rapidly progressive ataxia and dementia is suggestive of a prion-related disease. While the clinical symptoms and findings on neurologic exam might yield a broad differential, the acute nature of this woman's presentation suggests an infectious or prion-based etiology. Human prion-related diseases include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), kuru, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker syndrome, and fatal familial insomnia. Animal-related prion disease includes bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease) and scrapie (sheep). This patient most likely has the sporadic form of CJD, the most common form of human prion-related diseases. In the US, approximately 1 in 1,000,000 people develop CJD. The normal prion protein, PrP, is water-soluble and proteinase sensitive. Abnormal prion protein changes shape to become PrP^sc or PrP^res, which are proteinase resistant and form insoluble beta-pleated sheets (amyloid). The prion proteins accumulate within neuronal cells and produce spongiform encephalopathy with axonal degeneration, neuronal loss, gliosis, and astrocytic proliferation. CJD is characterized by a rapidly progressive dementia complicated by pyramidal signs (upper motor neuron dysfunction including paresis, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign), startle myoclonus (involuntary jerking of muscle groups induced by loud stimuli), and cerebellar (ataxia, nystagmus) or extrapyramidal signs (hypokinesia). The syndrome typically evolves over weeks to months, and death usually occurs within 1 year. The classic EEG finding is synchronous bi- or triphasic sharp wave complexes. CSF tests showing elevated 14-3-3 proteins are also suggestive of prion disease. Autopsy is the only method to confirm the diagnosis. Lewy bodies (choice B) are a prominent feature in Parkinson disease and in Lewy body dementia. Both conditions progress more slowly (over years rather than months). Parkinson disease is characterized by resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and postural instability. Lewy body dementia is characterized by cognitive decline associated with prominent visual hallucinations and delusions. Both conditions present with lesions in the substantia nigra of the midbrain, and have characteristic round eosinophilic inclusions comprised of alpha-synuclein (Lewy body). Multiple cerebral infarcts (choice C) underlie vascular dementia. After Alzheimer disease, vascular dementia is the second most common cause of dementia and is a common complication of patients with cerebrovascular disease and a history of stroke. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, age, atherosclerosis, and cardioembolic events. Our patient does not appear to have any of these risk factors. This type of dementia is characterized by step-wise cognitive decline with each new cerebrovascular event. Trinucleotide expansion (choice D) can lead to a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, including Huntington disease, which is caused by CAG repeats in the huntingtin (HTT) gene. This autosomal dominant disorder often presents with the triad of chorea (unlike myoclonus, these brief, involuntary movements are semi-directed and "dance-like"), behavioral changes or personality disorders, and dementia. These symptoms present in middle age and have a more gradual process than prion-based disease. Vertical gaze is impaired (choice E) in progressive supranuclear palsy, an atypical version of Parkinson disease. This disease is associated with dysarthria, dysphagia, dementia, gait ataxia, and extrapyramidal symptoms. However, the course is progressive over a longer period of time.

choice_explanations.B: Lewy bodies occur in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia, which progress over years and feature tremor/rigidity or visual hallucinations.
choice_explanations.C: Multiple cerebral infarcts cause vascular dementia, characterized by step-wise decline in patients with cerebrovascular risk factors (absent here).
choice_explanations.D: Trinucleotide expansion (eg, Huntington disease, CAG repeats) causes a more gradual neurodegenerative course, not the rapid progression seen here.
choice_explanations.E: Vertical gaze impairment occurs in progressive supranuclear palsy, which progresses over a longer period of time.

fa_summary: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion-induced spongiform encephalopathy causing rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus and ataxia.

stem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician for an ultrasound at 13 weeks' gestation. She found out that she was pregnant 4 weeks ago. She works as an executive in a business firm and admits to smoking and alcohol consumption up until news of her pregnancy. Ultrasound reveals a large defect in the occipital bone with an intact, sac-like protrusion containing tissue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is A. The central nervous system and its overlying bones are subject to a variety of malformations and developmental diseases. The defect described in the question stem is a cranial encephalocele, in which brain herniates through a defect in the skull bones, and is covered by skin. The most common site is the occipital bone. Neural tube defects include anencephaly, encephalocele (choice A), meningocele (choice B), meningomyelocele (choice C), and spina bifida (choice D). Elevated levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) may be present. Anencephaly is a malformation of the anterior aspect of the neural tube. There is absence of the calvarium and brain. Meningocele (choice B) is the term used when the meninges, but not the brain or spinal cord, herniate through a defect in the bony cranium or spinal column. Meningomyelocele (choice C) is the term used when the spinal cord and surrounding meninges herniate through a defect in the spinal column. Spina bifida (choice D) refers to vertebral defects through which the spinal cord or meninges may herniate. Spina bifida occulta is a milder form where only a small dimple and overlying tuft of hair are present. Folate deficiency (nutritional or use of folate-depleting medications such as methotrexate or phenytoin) during the initial prenatal period is the contributory factor. Meningocele, meningomyelocele, and spina bifida tend to occur in the lumbosacral region and can produce lower extremity paralysis, sensory dysfunction, and incontinence of bowel and bladder due to the affected region of the spinal cord. Small defects in the occipital bone can be treated surgically, but large defects are very problematic, particularly if there is significant herniation. The brain and spinal cord may be vulnerable to trauma and infection (myelitis, meningitis). Syringomyelia (choice E) is a tubular, fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord. Usually, the syringomyelia runs parallel to the central canal. Symptoms include loss of pain and temperature and weakness of the upper extremities. It is typically associated with Arnold-Chiari malformation.

choice_explanations.B: Meningocele is herniation of the meninges (but not brain or spinal cord) through a bony defect of the cranium or spinal column.
choice_explanations.C: Meningomyelocele is herniation of the spinal cord and surrounding meninges through a defect in the spinal column.
choice_explanations.D: Spina bifida refers to vertebral defects through which the spinal cord or meninges may herniate (spina bifida occulta is the mild form).
choice_explanations.E: Syringomyelia is a fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord, causing loss of pain/temperature and upper extremity weakness, often with Arnold-Chiari malformation.

fa_summary: Cranial encephalocele is a neural tube defect in which brain herniates through a skull defect and is covered by skin, most commonly at the occipital bone.

stem: A 34-year-old primigravid woman at 42 weeks' gestation is in the second stage of labor. To provide anesthesia to this patient, an obstetrician plans a transvaginal pudendal nerve block. Which of the following landmarks will most likely be used?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The pudendal nerve can be anesthetized to provide obstetric anesthesia (although epidural blocks are now more commonly used in preparation for delivery). The pudendal nerve arises from sacral segments 2, 3, and 4. It exits the pelvis by way of the greater sciatic foramen and then courses around the ischial spine (and sacrospinous ligament) to pass through the lesser sciatic foramen. The ischial spine is the boundary between the greater and lesser sciatic foramina. After entering the lesser sciatic foramen, the pudendal nerve enters the pudendal canal to supply the muscles and skin of the perineal area. The major branches of the pudendal nerve are the inferior rectal nerve, the posterior labial (or scrotal) nerve, and the dorsal nerve of the clitoris (or penis). A pudendal nerve block consists of administration of local anesthetic near the ischial spine. The anterior inferior iliac spine (choice A) is the point of attachment of the straight head of the rectus femoris and of the iliofemoral ligament. It is not related to the pudendal nerve and is not palpable through the vaginal wall. The anterior superior iliac spine (choice B) is the lateral attachment of the inguinal ligament. It is not related to the pudendal nerve and is not palpable through the vaginal wall. The ischial tuberosity (choice D) is the attachment point of the hamstring muscles: the semimembranosus, semitendinosus, and the long head of the biceps femoris. The ischial tuberosity forms the lower border of the lesser sciatic foramen. The pubic tubercle (choice E) is the medial attachment of the inguinal ligament. The superficial inguinal ring is immediately superolateral to the pubic tubercle. It is not related to the pudendal nerve.

choice_explanations.A: The anterior inferior iliac spine is the point of attachment of the straight head of the rectus femoris and of the iliofemoral ligament. It is not related to the pudendal nerve and is not palpable through the vaginal wall.
choice_explanations.B: The anterior superior iliac spine is the lateral attachment of the inguinal ligament. It is not related to the pudendal nerve and is not palpable through the vaginal wall.
choice_explanations.C: The ischial spine is the boundary between the greater and lesser sciatic foramina; the pudendal nerve courses around it, making it the landmark for a pudendal nerve block.
choice_explanations.D: The ischial tuberosity is the attachment point of the hamstring muscles and forms the lower border of the lesser sciatic foramen. It is not related to the pudendal nerve.
choice_explanations.E: The pubic tubercle is the medial attachment of the inguinal ligament; the superficial inguinal ring is immediately superolateral to it. It is not related to the pudendal nerve.

fa_summary: The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) can be blocked with local anesthetic during childbirth using the ischial spine as a landmark for injection to anesthetize the perineum.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after injuring her shoulder while playing soccer. Physical examination reveals an anterior dislocation of the glenohumeral joint. The dislocation is reduced without complication. The patient returns because of significant, ongoing pain in the right arm and some weakness. She denies any sensory loss. Physical examination shows weakness of internal rotation of her right arm at the shoulder. An injury in which of the following muscles is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The subscapularis muscle arises from the anterior surface of the scapula and inserts onto the lesser tubercle of the humerus. It is one of the rotator cuff muscles. Its tendon passes on the anterior side of the shoulder joint capsule, where it reinforces the capsule. Contraction of this muscle causes internal rotation of the arm at the shoulder. The subscapularis is innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves. The infraspinatus muscle (choice A) arises from the posterior surface of the scapula in the infraspinous fossa and inserts on the greater tubercle of the humerus. It is one of the rotator cuff muscles. Its tendon passes along the posterior surface of the shoulder joint capsule, where it reinforces the capsule. Contraction of the infraspinatus causes external rotation of the arm at the shoulder. The infraspinatus is innervated by the suprascapular nerve. The pectoralis minor muscle (choice B) arises from the chest wall and inserts onto the coracoid process of the scapula. The pectoralis minor does not attach to the humerus and therefore does not cause movement of the humerus at the shoulder. It is not part of the rotator cuff. The pectoralis minor is innervated by the medial pectoral nerve. The supraspinatus muscle (choice D) arises from the posterior surface of the scapula in the supraspinous fossa and inserts onto the greater tubercle. It is one of the rotator cuff muscles. Its tendon passes along the superior surface of the shoulder joint capsule, where it reinforces the capsule. Contraction of the supraspinatus causes abduction of the arm at the shoulder. It is most important in this function during the first 15-30 degrees of abduction. The supraspinatus is innervated by the suprascapular nerve. The teres minor muscle (choice E) arises from the axillary border of the scapula and inserts onto the greater tubercle. The teres minor is innervated by the axillary nerve.

choice_explanations.A: Infraspinatus arises from the infraspinous fossa and inserts on the greater tubercle; it causes external rotation and is innervated by the suprascapular nerve.
choice_explanations.B: Pectoralis minor arises from the chest wall and inserts on the coracoid process; it does not move the humerus and is not part of the rotator cuff.
choice_explanations.C: Subscapularis arises from the anterior scapula and inserts on the lesser tubercle; it causes internal rotation of the arm at the shoulder and is innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.
choice_explanations.D: Supraspinatus arises from the supraspinous fossa and inserts on the greater tubercle; it initiates abduction and is innervated by the suprascapular nerve.
choice_explanations.E: Teres minor arises from the axillary border of the scapula and inserts on the greater tubercle; it is innervated by the axillary nerve.

fa_summary: The subscapularis is a rotator cuff muscle that causes internal rotation of the arm at the shoulder; it is innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.

stem: A 43-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain in his groin. The patient reports previously noticing a bulge in the groin but only recently has it become painful. Physical examination reveals that the Valsalva maneuver produces a bulge palpable in the superficial inguinal ring. Compression of the abdominal wall at the deep inguinal ring does not prevent the appearance of the bulge at the superficial ring. The physician recommends surgery to alleviate the patient's symptoms. Which of the following best describes the hernial sac seen in this patient?

options.text: It is associated with failed closure of the processus vaginalis
It is covered by all three layers of the spermatic fascia
It passes medial to the inferior epigastric artery
It passes lateral and inferior to the pubic tubercle
It passes through the femoral canal

explanation: The correct answer is C. Direct inguinal hernias enter the inguinal canal by tearing through the posterior wall of the canal formed by the transversalis fascia. The typical location for this type of hernia is through the inguinal triangle, bounded laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. Direct inguinal hernias pass medial to the inferior epigastric artery. Though these hernias are typically asymptomatic, new onset pain at the site of these hernias may be indicative of bowel strangulation within the herniated pouch. Surgical intervention is indicated when bowel ischemia is suspected. Because the distinction between direct and indirect inguinal hernias is whether they pass through the deep inguinal ring (indirect) or do not pass through the deep inguinal ring (direct), these hernias can be differentiated during physical examination by compression of the deep inguinal ring while palpating at the superficial inguinal ring. After it has been determined that a patient has an inguinal hernia by having the patient cough while palpating at the superficial inguinal ring, the patient is asked to cough a second time while the deep inguinal ring is compressed. If this compression prevents the hernia from descending, that means that it is passing through the deep ring and therefore it is an indirect hernia. If compression of the deep ring does not prevent the hernia from descending (as in this patient), then it is a direct inguinal hernia. Indirect inguinal hernias are associated with failed closure of the processus vaginalis (choice A), which results in a persistent connection between the abdominal cavity and the inguinal canal, allowing bowel herniation to occur. These hernias typically occur in younger patients, and are more frequently associated with strangulation than direct hernias. They are also associated with hydroceles. In terms of location, as mentioned previously, indirect inguinal hernias pass lateral to the inferior epigastric artery. Both inguinal hernias pass through the superficial inguinal ring, while only the indirect hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring. Indirect inguinal hernias are covered by all three layers of the spermatic fascia (choice B). Direct inguinal hernias are typically covered by only the external spermatic fascia because the herniating sac tears through the other layers of fascia as it emerges through the abdominal wall. Indirect inguinal hernias pass lateral to the inferior epigastric artery because the deep inguinal ring is lateral to the artery. The femoral canal (choice E) is the site for femoral hernias, which pass posterior to the inguinal ligament and emerge lateral and inferior (choice D) to the pubic tubercle. In contrast, both types of inguinal hernias pass anterior to the inguinal ligament. The femoral canal is located medial to the femoral vessels in the femoral triangle. This type of hernia is more likely than inguinal hernias to produce strangulation and more commonly occurs in females than males.

choice_explanations.A: Failed closure of the processus vaginalis is associated with indirect inguinal hernias, not direct hernias.
choice_explanations.B: Being covered by all three layers of the spermatic fascia describes an indirect inguinal hernia. A direct hernia is typically covered by only the external spermatic fascia.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: direct inguinal hernias emerge through the posterior wall (transversalis fascia) of the inguinal canal and pass medial to the inferior epigastric artery through the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle.
choice_explanations.D: Passing lateral and inferior to the pubic tubercle describes a femoral hernia, not an inguinal hernia.
choice_explanations.E: Passing through the femoral canal describes a femoral hernia, which passes posterior to the inguinal ligament and is more likely to strangulate.

fa_summary: Direct inguinal hernias emerge through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (transversalis fascia) and pass medial to the inferior epigastric artery through the inguinal triangle.

stem: A 40-year-old man with a history of alcoholism is brought to the emergency department because of recent onset coffee ground emesis. The patient also reports that his stools have recently become darker with a "tarry" consistency. He appears pale and his skin is cool and clammy; his pulse is 105/min and his blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. Gastric lavage shows bright-red blood. Follow-up endoscopy reveals an ulcer with a visibly bleeding vessel located on the distal end of the lesser curvature of the stomach. The bleeding vessels are most likely direct branches of which of the following arteries?
explanation: The correct answer is C. There are several etiologies of upper GI bleeding in an alcoholic. Peptic ulcers from alcohol itself are a common cause of bleeding. Usually, patients will have epigastric tenderness and evidence of GI bleeding (anemia if chronic, hypotension and tachycardia if acute). The arterial supply of the stomach is complex and is consequently a target on the USMLE. In this instance, the patient is bleeding from the right gastric artery, which supplies the distal portion of the lesser curvature of the stomach. The right gastric artery is usually a branch of the proper hepatic artery. The right gastric artery anastomoses with the left gastric artery, which also supplies the lesser curvature and is a direct branch of the celiac trunk. The gastroduodenal artery (choice A) gives rise to the right gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery and the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery. Because this artery passes immediately behind the first part of the duodenum, it is often the source of bleeding from a duodenal ulcer. The left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery (choice B) supplies the proximal portion of the greater curvature of the stomach. It is a branch of the splenic artery. The right gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery (choice D) supplies the distal portion of the greater curvature of the stomach. It is a branch of the gastroduodenal artery. The right and left gastroepiploic arteries anastomose along the greater curvature of the stomach. The short gastric arteries (choice E) supply the fundus of the stomach. They are branches of the splenic artery.

choice_explanations.A: The gastroduodenal artery gives rise to the right gastroepiploic and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries; it lies behind the first part of the duodenum and is a source of bleeding from duodenal ulcer.
choice_explanations.B: The left gastroepiploic artery supplies the proximal greater curvature and is a branch of the splenic artery.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: the right gastric artery supplies the distal portion of the lesser curvature of the stomach and is usually a branch of the proper hepatic artery.
choice_explanations.D: The right gastroepiploic artery supplies the distal greater curvature and is a branch of the gastroduodenal artery.
choice_explanations.E: The short gastric arteries supply the fundus and arise from the splenic artery.

fa_summary: The right gastric artery supplies the distal portion of the lesser curvature of the stomach and is usually a branch of the proper hepatic artery.

stem: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of difficulty swallowing. He denies any history of acid reflux disease. He reports some recent episodes of palpitations. Auscultation of his chest reveals a systolic murmur in the left fourth and fifth intercostal spaces that radiates to the left axilla. A barium swallow with fluoroscopy and an esophagogram show that the anterior wall of the esophagus in the midthorax is being compressed. Enlargement of which of the following is most likely responsible for the development of this symptom in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is A. The left atrium forms the posterior wall of the heart (see figures below). The esophagus passes immediately posterior to the heart with only the pericardium separating them (see figures below). Enlargement of the left atrium may compress the anterior wall of the esophagus and cause dysphagia. The auscultatory finding is suggestive of mitral regurgitation, which is a cause of left atrial enlargement. Mitral regurgitation can cause atrial fibrillation, the cause of the palpitations that the patient reports. The left ventricle (choice B) forms most of the left border of the heart and most of the diaphragmatic surface of the heart. The left ventricle is not related to the esophagus. The pulmonary trunk (choice C) emerges from the right ventricle on the anterior surface of the heart. The pulmonary trunk is not related to the esophagus. The right atrium (choice D) forms the right border of the heart. It is not related to the esophagus. The right ventricle (choice E) forms most of the anterior wall of the heart and a small portion of the diaphragmatic surface of the heart. It is not related to the esophagus.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: the left atrium is the most posterior part of the heart; its enlargement (eg, from mitral regurgitation) compresses the esophagus and causes dysphagia.
choice_explanations.B: The left ventricle forms most of the left border and the diaphragmatic surface; it is not related to the esophagus.
choice_explanations.C: The pulmonary trunk emerges from the right ventricle on the anterior surface; it is not related to the esophagus.
choice_explanations.D: The right atrium forms the right border of the heart; it is not related to the esophagus.
choice_explanations.E: The right ventricle forms most of the anterior wall of the heart; it is not related to the esophagus.

fa_summary: The left atrium is the most posterior chamber; left atrial enlargement compresses the esophagus, causing dysphagia.

stem: A 52-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia comes to his physician for a follow-up visit 3 months after having had a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). He reports that he has significant improvement in his urinary flow rate. He now gets up only 2 times/night. He has no complaints of urine leakage. However, he reports a concern about his sexual function. He says that he is able to achieve arousal, and is able to have a normal erection and orgasm, however, upon ejaculation he notes that very little seminal fluid is released from his urethra. He also reports that when he urinates after sexual activity, his urine appears cloudy. Which of the following structures was most likely injured during the TURP procedure?
explanation: The correct answer is A. This patient is suffering from retrograde ejaculation as a result of damage to the internal urethral sphincter during the TURP procedure. This procedure resects the bladder neck and obstructing prostate tissue, including the internal sphincter. While improvement in urinary symptoms results from this procedure, nearly all patients suffer from retrograde ejaculation. The reason for this is because the internal urethral sphincter is the smooth muscle at the neck of the bladder, at the junction of the bladder and the urethra. This smooth muscle is sympathetically innervated, in contrast to the remaining smooth muscle of the bladder (detrusor muscle), which is parasympathetically innervated. The internal urethral sphincter is normally closed to retain urine and also is closed during ejaculation to prevent retrograde passage of seminal fluid from the urethra, retrograde into the bladder. The prostate surrounds the urethra and the neck of the bladder and during TURP, the internal urethral sphincter (bladder neck) is resected so it cannot fully close during ejaculation. Because the external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae) is still functional, urinary continence is maintained. Because of the retrograde ejaculation, the seminal fluid does not come out through the penis and it goes into the bladder where it mixes with urine. The urine during subsequent urination is cloudy due to the presence of seminal fluid. In the figure below, note that the ejaculatory duct enters the prostatic urethra between the internal urethral sphincter and the external urethral sphincter. Lumbar splanchnic nerves (choice B) are preganglionic sympathetic nerves arising from spinal cord levels L1-L2. These nerves innervate the smooth muscle of the prostate, seminal vesicles, ductus deferens, urethra, as well as the internal urethral sphincter. These are all muscles that normally contract during orgasm and ejaculation. If these nerves were damaged, the patient would not have a normal orgasm. Pelvic splanchnic nerves (choice C) are preganglionic parasympathetic nerves arising from spinal cord levels S2-S4. These are nerves that are responsible for erection. If damaged, the patient would not have normal erection. The pudendal nerves (choice D) are somatic nerves that arise from sacral levels S2-S4. The pudendal nerves in the male provide sensory innervation to the penis and posterior scrotum, as well as the perianal region. They also provide motor innervation to the muscles of the pelvic diaphragm and urogenital diaphragm, including the sphincter urethrae muscle. If these nerves were damaged, the patient would likely have sensory loss in the perineum as well as urinary incontinence. The sphincter urethrae muscle (choice E) is a skeletal muscle within the urogenital diaphragm. The urogenital diaphragm surrounds the membranous urethra below the prostate. The sphincter urethrae (also called the external urethral sphincter) is innervated by the pudendal nerve. This muscle is not likely to be damaged during a TURP procedure, and if it were damaged, it would not lead to retrograde ejaculation.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: the internal urethral sphincter (bladder neck) is resected during TURP; it normally closes during ejaculation, so its loss causes retrograde ejaculation.
choice_explanations.B: Lumbar splanchnic nerves (L1-L2) are sympathetic and innervate the prostate, seminal vesicles, ductus deferens, and internal urethral sphincter; damage would impair normal orgasm.
choice_explanations.C: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) are parasympathetic and responsible for erection; damage would impair erection.
choice_explanations.D: The pudendal nerves (S2-S4) provide sensory innervation to the penis, posterior scrotum, and perianal region and motor innervation to the sphincter urethrae; damage would cause perineal sensory loss and incontinence.
choice_explanations.E: The sphincter urethrae (external urethral sphincter) is skeletal muscle innervated by the pudendal nerve; it is not typically damaged during TURP and would not cause retrograde ejaculation.

fa_summary: TURP resects the bladder neck including the internal urethral sphincter, which normally closes during ejaculation; its loss causes retrograde ejaculation.

stem: A newborn is brought to the physician because of a palpable mass in the scrotum above the testis. Physical examination reveals a cystic structure in the scrotum, which transilluminates the entire scrotum when a penlight is held against the skin of the scrotum. The newborn has no discomfort during the examination. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this finding?

options.text: Communication between the epididymis and the tunica vaginalis
Complete failure of the processus vaginalis to fuse
Failure of the processus vaginalis to form
Incomplete fusion of the processus vaginalis

explanation: The correct answer is D. This newborn has a hydrocele. These masses are common in the newborn period and are usually asymptomatic. Physical examination findings include a scrotal mass that transilluminates when a penlight is shined upon it. The processus vaginalis is an evagination of the parietal peritoneum of the abdomen that descends through the inguinal canal before the descent of the testis. Normally the distal end of this evagination remains patent as the tunica vaginalis and the remainder of the processus vaginalis fuses and becomes fibrous. If a part of the processus vaginalis does not fuse (incomplete fusion), the resulting cystic structure is a hydrocele of the spermatic cord. Further, these lesions are small in size, typically 1 cm or less in diameter. The lesions are also nontender. Complete failure of the processus vaginalis to fuse (choice B) predisposes a patient to indirect inguinal hernia and may result in congenital inguinal hernia. Failure of the processus vaginalis to form (choice C) would result in an absence of the tunica vaginalis. Varicosities of the spermatic cord (choice E) or the pampiniform plexus is termed a varicocele. On physical examination this often feels like a "bag of worms." Varicocele may lead to infertility because of interference in the thermoregulatory function that keeps the testis below body temperature. Varicoceles do not transilluminate when light is shined upon the scrotum.

choice_explanations.A: Communication between the epididymis and the tunica vaginalis is not the mechanism of a hydrocele.
choice_explanations.B: Complete failure of the processus vaginalis to fuse predisposes to an indirect (congenital) inguinal hernia, not a hydrocele.
choice_explanations.C: Failure of the processus vaginalis to form would result in an absence of the tunica vaginalis.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: incomplete fusion of the processus vaginalis produces a hydrocele (accumulation of serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis) that transilluminates.
choice_explanations.E: Varicosities of the spermatic vein (varicocele) feel like a "bag of worms" and do not transilluminate; they may cause infertility.

fa_summary: A congenital (communicating) hydrocele results from incomplete obliteration (fusion) of the processus vaginalis and transilluminates.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of alcoholism is admitted to the hospital because of hematemesis. Physical examination shows jaundice and a distended abdomen with large, tortuous, distended anterior abdominal wall veins radiating from the umbilicus. The liver cannot be palpated secondary to the abdominal girth. An ultrasound of the abdomen reveals more than 1,500 mL of peritoneal fluid. Bleeding at which of the following anastomoses is the most likely cause of this patient's hematemesis?

options.text: Left gastric vein - right gastric vein
Left gastro-omental vein - right gastro-omental vein
Paraumbilical veins - superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall

explanation: The correct answer is B. This patient has hematemesis as a result of esophageal varices. These varices are secondary to portal hypertension resulting from alcoholic liver disease. The portal vein is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins posterior to the neck of the pancreas. The portal vein receives gastric veins from the stomach. The portal vein drains into liver sinusoids, which drain into the hepatic vein, which flow into the inferior vena cava. If there is an obstruction to flow through the portal system (portal hypertension), blood in the portal system will flow in a retrograde direction and pass through anastomoses to reach the vena cava. Because the left gastric vein is part of the portal system and esophageal veins drain into the azygos vein, which flows into the superior vena cava, anastomosis between these veins in the wall of the esophagus provides a pathway for blood to get from the portal system into the caval system. With increased flow through these anastomosing veins in the wall of the esophagus, esophageal varices develop. Rupture of these varices leads to profuse bleeding into the esophagus, which then leads to hematemesis. Other important sites for portacaval anastomoses include the rectum, where internal hemorrhoids can develop, and the anterior abdominal wall, where caput medusae can develop, as seen in this patient. Inferior phrenic and esophageal veins (choice A) are both parts of the caval system. Any anastomoses between these veins would be a cava-cava anastomosis and would not be useful in relieving portal hypertension. Left gastric and right gastric veins (choice C) are both parts of the portal venous system. While they do anastomose with one another, they do not form a portacaval anastomosis. The left and right gastro-omental veins (choice D) are both parts of the portal venous system. While they do anastomose, they form a porta-portal anastomosis, which would not relieve portal hypertension. The paraumbilical veins (part of the portal system) do anastomose with the superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall (part of the caval system) (choice E), and do form a portacaval anastomosis. Enlargement of these veins results in caput medusae, which is seen in this patient. However, this does not lead to hematemesis.

choice_explanations.A: The inferior phrenic and esophageal veins are both caval-system veins; their anastomosis is cava-cava and does not relieve portal hypertension.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: the left gastric (portal) and esophageal (draining into the azygos, caval) veins form a portacaval anastomosis; increased flow produces esophageal varices that can bleed.
choice_explanations.C: The left and right gastric veins are both portal; their anastomosis is not portacaval and does not relieve portal hypertension.
choice_explanations.D: The left and right gastro-omental veins are both portal; their anastomosis is porta-portal and does not relieve portal hypertension.
choice_explanations.E: Paraumbilical (portal) and superficial anterior abdominal wall (caval) veins form a portacaval anastomosis, but enlargement causes caput medusae, not hematemesis.

fa_summary: Esophageal varices arise from the portosystemic anastomosis between the left gastric (portal) vein and esophageal veins (which drain into the azygos/caval system).

stem: A 35-year-old man who is a construction worker comes to the physician because of a bulge in his groin. He reports that he first noticed this bulge several years ago, however only recently has he had some discomfort in the region. He says that the bulge is larger when standing. Physical examination shows a fluctuant mass lateral to the right symphysis pubis that becomes more prominent with the Valsalva maneuver. During surgical repair, the mass is noted to be medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Which of the following is most likely located along the inferior border of this mass?

options.text: Posterior wall of the inguinal canal

explanation: The correct answer is B. This man has a direct inguinal hernia. It can be identified as a direct inguinal hernia because the hernia sac passes medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. In contrast, indirect inguinal hernias pass lateral to these vessels. Both direct and indirect inguinal hernias pass through the superficial inguinal ring. However, direct inguinal hernias emerge through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal known as the fascia transversalis, which protrudes medial to the inferior epigastric vessels and passes through the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle, made up of: the inferior epigastric vessels (lateral border); the rectus abdominis (medial border; choice E); and the inguinal ligament (inferior border, choice B). Indirect inguinal hernias enter the inguinal canal by passing through the deep inguinal ring, which is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Inguinal hernias pass above the inguinal ligament and femoral hernias pass below it. Most femoral hernias occur in women. A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal, which is medial to the femoral artery (choice A). The internal abdominal oblique muscle (choice C), along with the transversus abdominis muscle, forms the roof of the inguinal canal; the internal oblique also forms the anterior wall of the lateral portion of the canal, along with the aponeurosis of the external oblique. The inguinal canal contains the round ligament in females, and the spermatic cord in males. The roof of the inguinal canal is the internal abdominal oblique and the transversus abdominis muscles; the anterior wall is formed by the aponeurosis of the external abdominal oblique and the internal abdominal oblique; the floor is formed by the inguinal ligament; and the posterior wall (choice D) is formed by the transversalis fascia laterally and the conjoined tendon medially. The conjoined tendon is formed by the aponeurosis of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles.

choice_explanations.A: The femoral artery is medial to the femoral canal, through which femoral hernias pass; it is not a border of the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: the inguinal ligament forms the inferior border of the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle, the typical location of a direct inguinal hernia.
choice_explanations.C: The internal abdominal oblique forms the roof of the inguinal canal (with the transversus abdominis) and the anterior wall of its lateral portion.
choice_explanations.D: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed by the transversalis fascia laterally and the conjoined tendon medially.
choice_explanations.E: The rectus abdominis forms the medial border of the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle.

fa_summary: The inguinal ligament forms the inferior border (floor) of the inguinal canal and the inferior border of the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle.

stem: A 54-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia is brought to the emergency department with acute onset abdominal pain. The pain began at about 6/10 and has been increasing in severity. He reports that for the past few months he has noted abdominal pain about an hour after eating, but not at other times. As a result, he has limited his food intake and lost about 15 pounds over the last 3 months. However, the current pain is much more severe and he reports not having eaten yet. Physical examination is significant for rebound tenderness in the abdomen. The physician decides to pursue mesenteric angiography, which shows significant infarction of the small bowel after thrombotic occlusion of jejunal branches of the superior mesenteric artery. The study also shows occlusion of the celiac trunk; however, there is no evidence of infarction in organs supplied by that artery. Anastomoses between which of the following pairs of arteries best explains the lack of infarction in these organs?

options.text: Left gastric artery and right gastric artery
Left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery and right gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery
Proper hepatic artery and gastroduodenal artery
Right colic artery and middle colic artery
Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery and inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery

explanation: The correct answer is E. The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery is a branch of the gastroduodenal artery, which is a branch of the common hepatic artery, itself a branch of the celiac trunk. The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. These two arteries have extensive anastomoses within the head of the pancreas. With occlusion of the celiac trunk, blood from the superior mesenteric artery would reach the branches of the celiac trunk via these anastomoses.

choice_explanations.A: The left and right gastric arteries are both branches of the celiac system; their anastomosis does not connect the celiac and superior mesenteric circulations.
choice_explanations.B: The left and right gastro-omental arteries are both branches of the celiac system and do not provide a celiac-to-SMA collateral.
choice_explanations.C: The proper hepatic and gastroduodenal arteries are both celiac-system branches and do not connect to the superior mesenteric artery.
choice_explanations.D: The right and middle colic arteries are both superior mesenteric artery branches and do not supply celiac organs.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: the superior pancreaticoduodenal (celiac/gastroduodenal) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal (SMA) arteries anastomose extensively, providing collateral flow to celiac-supplied organs when the celiac trunk is occluded.

fa_summary: The superior (celiac) and inferior (SMA) pancreaticoduodenal arteries anastomose extensively, providing collateral flow that protects celiac-supplied organs when the celiac trunk is occluded.

stem: During an exploratory laparotomy, a surgeon encounters significant bleeding in the region of the duodenum. In an effort to control the bleeding, the gastroduodenal artery is ligated. In the absence of other arterial pathology, which of the following is the most likely outcome?

options.text: Ischemia of the distal stomach along the greater curvature
Ischemia of the distal stomach along the lesser curvature
Ischemia of the proximal stomach along the greater curvature
Ischemia of the proximal stomach along the lesser curvature

explanation: The correct answer is E. The stomach has a very rich anastomotic arterial supply and can tolerate occlusion of the gastroduodenal artery. The right gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery, which supplies the distal greater curvature (choice A), is a branch of the gastroduodenal artery, which anastomoses with the left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery. The right gastric artery, which supplies the distal lesser curvature (choice B), usually arises from the proper hepatic artery, not from the gastroduodenal artery. The short gastric arteries, which supply the proximal greater curvature (choice C), arise from the splenic artery.
