The left gastric artery, which supplies the proximal lesser curvature (choice D), arises directly from the celiac artery.

choice_explanations.A: The right gastro-omental artery supplies the distal greater curvature and is a branch of the gastroduodenal artery, but it anastomoses with the left gastro-omental artery so flow is maintained.
choice_explanations.B: The right gastric artery supplies the distal lesser curvature and usually arises from the proper hepatic artery, not the gastroduodenal artery.
choice_explanations.C: The short gastric arteries supply the proximal greater curvature and arise from the splenic artery.
choice_explanations.D: The left gastric artery supplies the proximal lesser curvature and arises directly from the celiac artery.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: the stomach has a rich anastomotic arterial supply, so ligation of the gastroduodenal artery does not cause gastric ischemia.

fa_summary: The stomach has a rich anastomotic arterial supply (celiac branches and collaterals) and tolerates ligation of the gastroduodenal artery without ischemia.

stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of scrotal swelling. He also says that he has occasional urinary urgency and difficulty completely emptying his bladder. The patient is a former weightlifter, and acknowledges previous steroid use and occasional binge-drinking. Physical examination shows an enlarged prostate and a reducible scrotal mass. A few days later, he develops severe nausea, vomiting, and severe abdominal pain and is brought to the emergency department. His temperature is 37.7°C (99.8°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals a distended abdomen and decreased bowel sounds in all four quadrants. The right scrotum is enlarged and edematous. A firm 6 cm mass is palpable with significant tenderness. Abdominal paracentesis is performed and fluid analysis reveals an elevated ammonia level. Gram stain shows gram-negative rods and cocci. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The initial physical examination revealed a reducible mass in the scrotum. It is evident from the second examination in the emergency department that the mass is now firm and tender to palpation. This is an inguinal hernia, and as indicated by the fact that it was reducible, it was not incarcerated initially. It is, however, at risk for subsequent incarceration and/or strangulation. The term "incarcerated" is used to define a hernia that is no longer reducible but the vascular supply of the bowel is not compromised, whereas a strangulated hernia occurs when the vascular supply of the bowel is compromised. You must recognize that although a hernia is reducible, it is at risk for incarceration and strangulation, which occurred in this patient. Early identification of the incarcerated hernia is essential to prevent complications of bowel necrosis, sepsis and even death. An incarcerated or strangulated hernia would present as painful to palpation. The patient may also be febrile and manifest with symptoms of bowel obstruction including abdominal pain, decreased bowel sounds, vomiting, and hypotension. Peritoneal aspiration (paracentesis) will show increased ammonia levels (produced by the bacterial proliferation in the effusion of damaged intestine) without an increase in creatinine. Gram stain of the peritoneal fluid will demonstrate presence of enteric flora. Acute bacterial prostatitis (choice A) is hypothesized to be caused by reflux of infected urine into the ejaculatory and prostatic ducts. This usually occurs following sexual intercourse, instrumentation, and prolonged catheterization. This would not cause abdominal pain, fever, and hypotension as seen in our patient. Acute pancreatitis (choice B) is due to impacted gallstones and alcoholism. Recurrent acute pancreatitis is associated with alcoholism and would not present with these findings. Scrotal abscess (choice D) is typically superficial. These abscesses can be due to infected hair follicles, lacerations or other local causes and would not be associated with peritoneal effusion. Varicocele (choice E) is a dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus and the testicular vein. Patients can present with infertility, but not the clinical signs and symptoms presented in the case. Varicoceles are typically painful only along the course of the spermatic cord and along the inguinal ligament.

choice_explanations.A: Acute bacterial prostatitis results from reflux of infected urine into the ejaculatory and prostatic ducts and would not cause abdominal pain, fever, and hypotension.
choice_explanations.B: Acute pancreatitis is due to impacted gallstones and alcoholism and does not match the peritoneal and scrotal findings.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: a previously reducible inguinal hernia that becomes firm, tender, and edematous with bowel-obstruction signs and an elevated peritoneal ammonia level indicates strangulation.
choice_explanations.D: A scrotal abscess is typically superficial and would not be associated with peritoneal effusion.
choice_explanations.E: A varicocele is a dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus/testicular vein that presents with infertility, not the acute findings seen here.

fa_summary: A reducible inguinal hernia at risk for incarceration/strangulation: when the bowel's vascular supply is compromised, it produces obstruction signs and an elevated peritoneal ammonia level.

stem: A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after being involved in a gang fight. His blood pressure is 95/60 mm Hg and his pulse is 118/min. Physical examination shows several penetrating stab wounds to the abdomen. Emergency ultrasound shows an intra-abdominal fluid collection. An exploratory laparotomy is performed and the celiac trunk is found to be lacerated. The blood supply to which of the following will be most severely affected by this injury?

options.text: Body and tail of the pancreas
Duodenum distal to the entrance of the common bile duct

explanation: The correct answer is A. The celiac trunk arises from the abdominal aorta. It very quickly divides into three branches: the splenic artery, the left gastric artery, and the common hepatic artery. The splenic artery courses along the superior border of the body and tail of the pancreas on its way to the spleen and provides the blood supply to these parts of the pancreas. The splenic artery also gives rise to the short gastric arteries, which supply the fundus of the stomach, and the left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery, which supplies the greater curvature of the stomach. The left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach. The common hepatic artery supplies the liver, gall bladder, lesser curvature of the stomach, greater curvature of the stomach, head and neck of the pancreas, and proximal part of the duodenum. Therefore, of the structures listed, the body and the tail of the pancreas will be affected by this injury. The distal duodenum (choice B) and the inferior part of the head of the pancreas, the ascending colon, cecum, appendix, and transverse colon are supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. The hemidiaphragm (choice E) is supplied by the inferior phrenic artery (which arises from the abdominal aorta immediately proximal to the celiac trunk) and branches of the thoracic aorta.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: the splenic artery (a celiac trunk branch) courses along the superior border of the body and tail of the pancreas and supplies them, so celiac trunk laceration most severely affects the body and tail of the pancreas.
choice_explanations.B: The duodenum distal to the entrance of the common bile duct is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
choice_explanations.C: The ileum is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
choice_explanations.D: The jejunum is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
choice_explanations.E: The hemidiaphragm is supplied by the inferior phrenic artery (arising proximal to the celiac trunk) and branches of the thoracic aorta.

fa_summary: The celiac trunk gives rise to the splenic artery, which supplies the body and tail of the pancreas; celiac obstruction most severely affects these regions.

stem: A 64-year-old man with a history of asthma and chronic joint pain comes to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of heavy bleeding from his nose. He recently underwent surgery for the removal of large nasal polyps. In the emergency department, more conservative measures such as nasal packing and desmopressin spray fail to improve the patient's symptoms. The patient's INR is 1.1 and his PTT is within normal limits. The decision is made to take the patient to surgery and ligate the primary arterial supply to the nasal mucosa. The ligated artery is a direct branch of which of the following arteries?
explanation: The correct answer is B. The major source of blood supply to the nasal mucosa is the sphenopalatine artery, the terminal branch of the maxillary artery, which itself is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery. The sphenopalatine artery enters the nasal cavity from the pterygopalatine fossa by passing through the sphenopalatine foramen in the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. The facial artery (choice A) is a direct branch of the external carotid artery. It provides most of the blood supply to the superficial face. The superficial temporal artery (choice C) is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery. The other terminal branch is the maxillary artery. The superficial temporal artery provides blood supply to the temporal region and the lateral portion of the scalp. The superior labial artery (choice D) is a branch of the facial artery. The superior labial artery provides blood supply to the upper lip. It has a septal branch that provides some of the blood supply to the anterior portion of the septal mucosa of the nasal cavity. However, this is not the major blood supply to the nasal cavity. The superior labial arteries are a major pathway for anastomosis between the two facial arteries. The transverse facial artery (choice E) is a branch of the superficial temporal artery. It provides blood supply to the parotid gland, the parotid duct, and the skin of the lateral face.

choice_explanations.A: The facial artery is a direct branch of the external carotid artery and supplies the superficial face, not the nasal mucosa.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: the sphenopalatine artery, the terminal branch of the maxillary artery, is the major blood supply to the nasal mucosa.
choice_explanations.C: The superficial temporal artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery supplying the temporal region and lateral scalp.
choice_explanations.D: The superior labial artery is a branch of the facial artery; its septal branch supplies only part of the anterior septal mucosa.
choice_explanations.E: The transverse facial artery is a branch of the superficial temporal artery supplying the parotid gland, duct, and lateral face skin.

fa_summary: The major blood supply to the nasal mucosa is the sphenopalatine artery, a branch of the maxillary artery (posterior epistaxis).

stem: A 44-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after having been in a severe motor vehicle accident. He says he has severe abdominal and pelvic pain. Physical examination of the heart and lungs are normal. The abdomen is tender to palpation in all four quadrants. Genitourinary examination shows severe ecchymosis in the perineum and fresh blood is seen at the urethral meatus. Digital rectal examination reveals that his prostate is in its normal position. Radiography reveals multiple fractures of his pelvic ring. A retrograde urethrogram is performed and leakage of the dye indicates that there is a urethral tear at the point where the urethra enters the bulb of the penis. Into which of the following spaces is the dye most likely leaking?
explanation: The correct answer is E. The rupture of the urethra in this patient is at the junction of the membranous urethra and the spongy urethra. The membranous urethra is the portion of the urethra that passes through the urogenital diaphragm. Because this diaphragm is tightly attached to the two ischiopubic rami of the pelvis, this part of the urethra is very tightly held in place. The spongy urethra is the portion of the urethra in the bulb of the penis and the corpus spongiosum and is the less stable portion. The bulb of the penis is in the superficial perineal space. This space is bounded by the urogenital diaphragm above and the superficial perineal (Colles') fascia below. Other structures in this space (in the male) include the crura of the penis, the ischiocavernosus muscles, which cover the crura of the penis, and the bulbospongiosus muscle, which covers the bulb of the penis. If urine escapes into this space, it can spread into the anterior abdominal wall, into the scrotum and along the shaft of the penis. The extraperitoneal space (choice A) is above the urogenital diaphragm. In the male, the prostate is within the extraperitoneal space. The prostate contains the prostatic portion of the urethra. If there was a tear of the urethra at the junction of the prostatic urethra and the membranous urethra, then the dye would escape into the retroperitoneal space. The deep perineal space (choice B) is the region within the urogenital diaphragm. In the male, the deep perineal space contains the sphincter urethrae muscle, the deep transverse perineal muscle, the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands, and is traversed by the membranous urethra. The rectovesical space (choice C) is the portion of the peritoneal cavity that is between the rectum, posteriorly, and the bladder, anteriorly. The rectovesical space is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in the male. Rupture of the urethra, which is an extraperitoneal structure, would not likely result in leakage into the peritoneal cavity. The retropubic space (choice D) is the portion of the extraperitoneal space that, in the male, is between the pubic symphysis, anteriorly, and the bladder and the prostate, posteriorly. It is above the urogenital and pelvic diaphragms.

choice_explanations.A: The extraperitoneal space is above the urogenital diaphragm; a tear of the prostatic urethra would leak into the retroperitoneal space, not here.
choice_explanations.B: The deep perineal space lies within the urogenital diaphragm and contains the sphincter urethrae, deep transverse perineal muscle, and bulbourethral glands; it is traversed by the membranous urethra.
choice_explanations.C: The rectovesical space is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in the male; the urethra is extraperitoneal, so rupture would not leak here.
choice_explanations.D: The retropubic space is between the pubic symphysis and the bladder/prostate, above the urogenital and pelvic diaphragms.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: the bulb of the penis lies in the superficial perineal space (bounded above by the urogenital diaphragm and below by Colles' fascia), so a tear at the bulbomembranous junction leaks here.

fa_summary: Urethral rupture at the bulbomembranous junction leaks into the superficial perineal space, bounded by the urogenital diaphragm above and Colles' fascia below.

stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of dizziness and a headache. Two years ago, she was diagnosed with essential hypertension. Laboratory studies show an increased plasma renin activity with normal aldosterone:renin ratio. Her increased plasma renin activity is most likely due to which of the following?

options.text: Increased Cl- delivery to the macula densa
Increased Na+ delivery to the macula densa

explanation:
The correct answer is D. Increased sympathetic nervous system activity is a contributing factor in many cases of essential hypertension. One of the renal effects of sympathetic activity is increased renin secretion mediated by beta-1 receptors. This leads to increased plasma renin activity, and angiotensin II (Ang II) and aldosterone levels. Ang II has been shown to increase norepinephrine release by renal sympathetic nerves, potentiating the renal effects of sympathetic activity.

Many, but not all, patients with essential hypertension exhibit elevated renin levels, which stimulates angiotensin II and aldosterone secretion. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that increases total peripheral resistance. Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption in the distal nephron, producing volume expansion. Both factors tend to elevate blood pressure. This patient has increased plasma renin activity with normal aldosterone:renin ratio; therefore aldosterone levels are also elevated.

Decreased sympathetic activation (choice A) is incorrect, as sympathetic activation increases renin release.

Renin secretion is stimulated when there is a decrease in Na+ and Cl- delivery to the macula densa. Therefore, increased Cl- delivery to the macula densa (choice B) and increased Na+ delivery to the macula densa (choice C) are incorrect.

Renin secretion is inhibited by aldosterone. Primary hyperaldosteronism (choice E) displays low plasma renin activity with increased aldosterone:renin ratio.

choice_explanations.A: Decreased sympathetic activation is incorrect, as sympathetic activation increases renin release.
choice_explanations.B: Renin secretion is stimulated when there is a decrease in Na+ and Cl- delivery to the macula densa, so increased Cl- delivery to the macula densa is incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Renin secretion is stimulated when there is a decrease in Na+ and Cl- delivery to the macula densa, so increased Na+ delivery to the macula densa is incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Increased sympathetic nervous system activity increases renin secretion from juxtaglomerular cells (via beta-1 receptors), raising plasma renin activity, angiotensin II, and aldosterone.
choice_explanations.E: Renin secretion is inhibited by aldosterone; primary hyperaldosteronism displays low plasma renin activity with an increased aldosterone:renin ratio.

fa_summary: Sympathetic activation (beta-1) increases renin release from juxtaglomerular cells; renin is also stimulated by decreased NaCl delivery to the macula densa.

stem: A 39-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination because of renal disease. Laboratory studies show: Sodium 138 mEq/L, Potassium 5.1 mEq/L, Chloride 100 mEq/L, Bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, BUN 24 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL. A biopsy of the kidney is performed and the patient is diagnosed with a rare autoimmune disorder that causes progressive kidney destruction. Which of the following conversions will most likely be abnormal as a result of the renal destruction?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (the biologically active form of vitamin D3) occurs in the kidney by the enzyme 1alpha-hydroxylase, located in the tubular cells. This reaction is regulated primarily by parathyroid hormone (PTH), which is secreted in response to reduced plasma Ca2+ levels. Also, reduced plasma phosphate levels increase 1alpha-hydroxylase activity. Vitamin D3 acts on the small intestine to increase Ca2+ absorption.

The conversion of 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (choice A) is incorrect, because this reaction is the opposite of what actually occurs. In the kidney, 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is converted to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, and this reaction is not bidirectional.

The cholesterol to 7-dehydrocholesterol (choice C) conversion would not be altered by kidney failure. This conversion is the first step in the formation of vitamin D and does not occur in the kidney.

The conversion of vitamin D3 to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (choice D) is an inaccurate answer because this conversion occurs in the liver and would not be altered by kidney failure. While this reaction is largely unregulated, some drugs and liver disease may alter normal conversion rates.

Vitamin D3 is not converted into vitamin D2 (choice E). Vitamin D2 is found principally in plants and yeasts and is commonly used as a dietary supplement. It undergoes the same conversions as vitamin D3, and has the same biologic activity as vitamin D3, but is less potent.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect: this reaction is the opposite of what actually occurs. In the kidney, 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is converted to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, and the reaction is not bidirectional.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: the kidney's 1alpha-hydroxylase converts 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to the biologically active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol; this enzyme is regulated by PTH and is impaired by renal destruction.
choice_explanations.C: Conversion of cholesterol to 7-dehydrocholesterol is the first step in vitamin D formation and does not occur in the kidney, so it would not be altered by kidney failure.
choice_explanations.D: Conversion of vitamin D3 to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol occurs in the liver and would not be altered by kidney failure.
choice_explanations.E: Vitamin D3 is not converted into vitamin D2; vitamin D2 comes principally from plants and yeasts and undergoes the same conversions as vitamin D3.

fa_summary: The kidney's 1alpha-hydroxylase converts 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to the active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol; this step is impaired in renal failure.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is given 160 mg inulin intravenously. One hour is allowed for equilibration between plasma and interstitial fluid. After this time, the plasma inulin concentration is 1 mg/100 mL. During the hour of equilibration, urine is collected; urinary excretion of inulin is 60 mg during this time. Which of the following is the extracellular fluid volume of this woman?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The volume of a fluid compartment can be measured by placing a substance into the compartment, allowing it to disperse evenly throughout the compartment, and then measuring the extent to which the indicator is diluted in the fluid. The volume of a compartment can be determined using the following formula: Volume of Compartment = amount of indicator substance administered / concentration of indicator in compartment.

The extracellular fluid volume consists of the plasma and the interstitial fluid. The extracellular fluid volume can be measured using inulin as the indicator because inulin freely distributes between plasma and the interstitial fluid, is not taken up by cells, and is not metabolized. When crystalloids (inulin, mannitol) or ionics (bromide, isotopes of SO4 or chloride) are injected intravenously they distribute throughout the extracellular fluid. Crystalloids are excreted in the urine and the ionics are slowly taken into cells, so calculations must take these factors into account.

In this patient, 160 mg inulin was administered intravenously and the concentration of inulin in the compartment was 1 mg/100 mL an hour later (when the inulin had dispersed evenly in the extracellular fluid compartment). During this hour, 60 mg had been excreted in the urine, leaving 100 mg in the body. Therefore, extracellular fluid volume = 100 mg / (1 mg/100 mL) = 10 L.

choice_explanations.B: Correct: extracellular fluid volume = amount of indicator remaining in the compartment / concentration = (160 mg - 60 mg excreted) / (1 mg/100 mL) = 100 mg / (1 mg/100 mL) = 10 L.

fa_summary: Inulin distributes throughout the extracellular fluid (plasma + interstitium) and is used to measure ECF volume: V = amount of indicator / concentration.

stem: An 18-year-old female comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of urgency, frequency, and dysuria. Her temperature is 37.4°C (99°F), pulse is 87/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 104/53 mm Hg. On physical examination, there is no costovertebral angle tenderness. There is suprapubic tenderness. Laboratory studies show white blood cell count 9,500/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The patient is presenting with a cystitis or urinary tract infection as demonstrated by the dysuria, urinary urgency, and urinary frequency. Bacterial causes of urinary tract infection include Escherichia coli in a majority of patients. Other bacterial causes include Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus. The presence of leukocyte esterase in the urine dipstick is associated with >10 leukocytes per high power field seen on microscopic examination, indicating inflammation. Therefore, the presence of leukocyte esterase is not specific to a urinary tract infection. The presence of nitrites in the urine is a result of gram-negative bacteria, which causes the conversion of nitrate to nitrite. In conjunction, the presence of leukocyte esterase and nitrites is highly sensitive for a urinary tract infection with gram-negative E. coli, Klebsiella, and Proteus species, which cause the conversion of nitrate to nitrite. Enterococci and S. saprophyticus are unable to reduce nitrate to nitrite.

Gram-positive bacteria (choice B) that cause urinary tract infection include Staphylococcus saprophyticus and Enterococcus faecalis. Urinary tract infection with gram-positive bacteria would cause positive leukocyte esterase but not positive nitrite.

Oxalate kidney stones (choice C) would cause severe abdominal pain and costovertebral angle tenderness. Laboratory studies would show positive blood and possibly positive leukocyte esterase due to inflammation, but would not be positive for nitrites. Calcium oxalate stones can be associated with ingestion of particular foods and a complication of ethylene glycol ingestion. This patient does not have CVA tenderness or severe colicky abdominal pain, making this diagnosis unlikely.

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) (choice D) is an infection of the female reproductive tract caused by sexually transmitted diseases such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Patients may present with lower abdominal pain, fever, and cervical purulent discharge. Our patient does not have fever or cervical discharge, making this diagnosis unlikely. In addition, PID typically does not have an abnormal urine dipstick unless there is cross contamination.

Vaginitis (choice E) is an infection of the vaginal canal, typically caused by Candida or bacterial vaginosis. Patients present with foul smelling vaginal discharge and vaginal pruritus. Urine dipstick is normal. This patient does not have these symptoms or a normal dipstick to prompt this diagnosis.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: cystitis is most commonly due to gram-negative bacteria (E. coli most commonly). Nitrites on dipstick reflect reduction of urinary nitrate by gram-negative organisms.
choice_explanations.B: Gram-positive causes of UTI (Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Enterococcus faecalis) produce positive leukocyte esterase but not positive nitrite, because they cannot reduce nitrate to nitrite.
choice_explanations.C: Oxalate kidney stones cause severe abdominal pain and costovertebral angle tenderness, with blood and possibly leukocyte esterase (but not nitrites) in the urine; this patient has neither CVA tenderness nor colicky pain.
choice_explanations.D: PID presents with lower abdominal pain, fever, and cervical purulent discharge; this patient has no fever or cervical discharge and urine dipstick is typically normal unless contaminated.
choice_explanations.E: Vaginitis (Candida or bacterial vaginosis) presents with foul-smelling vaginal discharge and pruritus with a normal urine dipstick; this patient lacks these features.

fa_summary: Cystitis is most commonly caused by gram-negative bacteria (E. coli); the nitrite dipstick test is positive only with nitrate-reducing gram-negative organisms.

stem: A previously healthy 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because he collapsed at an all-weekend concert event. The event consisted of 48 hours of continuous music. The weather was hot and humid and there were limited drinking stations. Upon arrival in the emergency department, his pulse is 110/min and blood pressure is 118/78 mm Hg. His lips appear parched. His arms and legs are dry to the touch. A urinary catheter is placed and 76 mL of urine is expressed via the catheter. Laboratory studies show his plasma antidiuretic hormone (ADH) concentration is five times higher than the upper limit of the normal range. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Despite the body's efforts to retain water in the dehydrated state, an obligatory loss of water from the body continues to occur even when a person is deprived of water. Even if urine flow becomes extremely low, substantial water is lost by evaporation, especially from the pulmonary system. Evaporative water loss from the lungs is solute-free; it increases plasma sodium because sodium is not lost with the water. This loss of water from the body tends to concentrate the extracellular fluid, causing it to become hypertonic.

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is a peptide hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary gland in response to increases in plasma osmolarity and/or decreases in extracellular fluid volume. One function of ADH is to increase water reabsorption from the collecting system within the nephron by increasing the number of membrane aquaporins. The decrease in extracellular fluid (compare with choice C) and the increase in osmolarity act as stimuli for increased thirst and increased secretion of ADH.

The decrease in extracellular fluid volume also tends to decrease arterial pressure, which increases plasma renin activity (compare with choice B) and aldosterone levels in the plasma (compare with choice A). ADH acts by increasing water reabsorption in the collecting system.

Water deprivation tends to decrease left atrial pressure (compare with choice D). Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released from the atrium in response to elevated left atrial pressure. ANP causes dilation of the renal afferent arterioles, resulting in increased plasma filtration and increased urine output. This would not be evident in severe dehydration.

choice_explanations.A: Decreased plasma aldosterone is inconsistent with dehydration: the decrease in extracellular fluid volume increases plasma renin activity and aldosterone levels.
choice_explanations.B: Decreased plasma renin activity is inconsistent with dehydration: the decrease in extracellular fluid volume increases, not decreases, plasma renin activity.
choice_explanations.C: Increased extracellular fluid volume is incorrect; water deprivation causes extracellular volume contraction.
choice_explanations.D: Increased left atrial pressure is incorrect; water deprivation tends to decrease left atrial pressure.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: evaporation of solute-free water during water deprivation concentrates the extracellular fluid, raising plasma osmolarity, which along with decreased ECF volume is the major stimulus for ADH secretion.

fa_summary: ADH (vasopressin) is secreted in response to increased plasma osmolarity and decreased blood volume, increasing aquaporin-mediated water reabsorption in principal cells.

stem: A 43-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue. He has not seen a physician for 10 years. His pulse is 89/min and blood pressure is 190/100 mm Hg. Laboratory examination shows: Urea nitrogen (blood) 34 mg/dL, Creatinine (serum) 1.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient is presenting with hypertension in the malignant hypertension range, anemia, and renal dysfunction. Of the possible choices, only adult (autosomal dominant) polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) would be likely to cause the malignant hypertension. ADPKD is characterized by kidneys that progressively enlarge as a consequence of multiple renal cysts. Presenting signs (typically beginning when patients are in their 40s) include hypertension (secondary to renin production), renal failure (with elevated BUN and creatinine), and anemia (secondary to a failure of renal erythropoietin production). Hematuria may be present due to cyst rupture. This condition also causes cysts in other organs (liver, pancreas, spleen, gonads), berry aneurysms (the rupture of which may cause death), and abnormalities of cardiac valves.

Lipoid nephrosis, or minimal change disease (choice B), is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, and is not usually associated with renal failure.

Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (choice C) usually presents with hematuria ("smoky urine") following a bout of streptococcal pharyngitis, and is commonly seen in children and young adults.

Renal tumors typically present either as a mass or with hematuria. Renal cell carcinoma (choice D) generally affects adults with tobacco smoking history or patients with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, while Wilms tumor (choice E) is an early childhood tumor. While renal cell carcinoma can be seen in the setting of chronic hypertension, it does not usually cause malignant hypertension.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: ADPKD presents in the 4th-5th decade with progressively enlarging cystic kidneys, hypertension (from renin), renal failure (elevated BUN/creatinine), and anemia; it can cause malignant hypertension and is autosomal dominant (PKD1/PKD2).
choice_explanations.B: Lipoid nephrosis (minimal change disease) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and is not usually associated with renal failure.
choice_explanations.C: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis usually presents with hematuria ("smoky urine") after streptococcal pharyngitis and is commonly seen in children and young adults.
choice_explanations.D: Renal cell carcinoma generally affects adults with tobacco smoking history or von Hippel-Lindau syndrome; it can be seen with chronic hypertension but does not usually cause malignant hypertension.
choice_explanations.E: Wilms tumor is an early childhood renal tumor and would not present as malignant hypertension in a 43-year-old adult.

fa_summary: ADPKD (autosomal dominant, PKD1/PKD2) causes bilaterally enlarged cystic kidneys presenting in adults with flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, and progressive renal failure.

stem: A 40-year-old man comes to the physician because of blood in his urine. He has a history of a chronic cough and has intermittent hemoptysis over the past 10 years. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Physical examination of the lungs reveals bilateral rhonchi without wheezes. Good breath sounds are noted bilaterally. Nasal swab and sputum culture rules out viral or bacterial respiratory infection. Urinalysis shows red cells, red cell casts, and proteinuria. Laboratory studies reveal a serum creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL. A renal biopsy is obtained and will most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Sickled cells in the vasa recta

explanation:
The correct answer is B. Goodpasture syndrome, a form of anti-glomerular basement antibody disease (anti-GBM antibody disease), is characterized by autoantibodies (usually IgG) that are directed against the basement membranes found in the renal glomeruli and pulmonary alveoli. The antigen is a component of a non-collagenous domain of one of the chains of type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane. The immunologic reaction against the basement membranes predisposes for both rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage. With immunofluorescent techniques, these antibodies can be detected as linear deposits following the basement membranes in both renal and pulmonary biopsies. Goodpasture syndrome formerly had a dismal prognosis, with deaths related to either renal failure or pulmonary hemorrhage; however the prognosis has improved with intensive use of plasma exchange.

Note that you could have eliminated several options without reaching the specific diagnosis. This patient had red cells, red cell casts, and excessive amounts of protein in his urine, all consistent with some form of glomerulonephritis. This helps you eliminate effacement of podocyte foot processes (choice D), which is associated with nephrotic disorders such as minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis), the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Red cells and red cell casts would not be present in a pure nephrotic syndrome. Similarly, sickled cells in the vasa recta (choice E) would be associated with sickle cell disease, not glomerulonephritis. Finally, neither of these disorders is likely to be associated with pulmonary hemorrhage and hemoptysis.

Electron-dense subepithelial humps (choice A) are associated with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis or membranous glomerulonephritis. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis can produce rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, but does not produce lung disease.

Mesangial IgA deposits (choice C) are associated with IgA nephropathy (Berger disease), which causes glomerulonephritis, but pulmonary involvement with disease is not typical for IgA nephropathy. Typically, children are more commonly affected. There can be either a preceding or concurrent respiratory or GI tract infection. In our patient, there is no evidence for a respiratory tract infection. Also, he has had chronic cough and intermittent hemoptysis, which rules out an acute respiratory infection.

choice_explanations.A: Electron-dense subepithelial humps are associated with poststreptococcal or membranous glomerulonephritis; poststreptococcal GN can produce RPGN but does not produce lung disease.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM antibody disease) produces antibodies (usually IgG) directed against the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, seen on immunofluorescence as linear deposits; it causes rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis plus pulmonary hemorrhage.
choice_explanations.C: Mesangial IgA deposits are seen in IgA nephropathy (Berger disease); pulmonary involvement is not typical, and this patient has no evidence of an acute respiratory infection.
choice_explanations.D: Podocyte foot process effacement is associated with nephrotic disorders such as minimal change disease; red cells and red cell casts would not be present in a pure nephrotic syndrome.
choice_explanations.E: Sickled cells in the vasa recta would be associated with sickle cell disease, not glomerulonephritis, and would not cause pulmonary hemorrhage.

fa_summary: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease) causes rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis plus pulmonary hemorrhage; immunofluorescence shows linear IgG along the basement membrane.

stem: A 59-year-old woman is hospitalized after a motor vehicle accident with suspected internal hemorrhage. On admission, she has severe hypotension, which persists despite intravenous fluids. At 12 hours after admission, her serum creatinine is 2.5 mg/dL, with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 20 mL/min/1.73 m2, about 30 L/day. She is diagnosed with acute renal failure due to ischemia. In order to prevent worsening azotemia, GFR must be increased. Which of the following will most likely decrease this patient's serum creatinine concentration?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The elevated serum creatinine is caused by reduced GFR; increasing GFR toward normal will lower the serum creatinine concentration. Dilating the afferent arteriole increases glomerular capillary pressure. The forces that dictate plasma movement in the systemic circulation also apply in the glomerulus. Thus, glomerular hydrostatic pressure and the oncotic pressure gradients across the membranes control GFR. Increasing the glomerular capillary pressure increases the forces that drive plasma from the capillary into the capsule, the net filtration force. GFR will rise toward normal and serum creatinine will fall toward normal.

Constricting the afferent arteriole (choice A) of the nephron decreases glomerular capillary pressure and thus decreases GFR.

Dilating the efferent arteriole (choice C) would decrease the glomerular hydrostatic pressure and thus decrease GFR.

Increasing the plasma oncotic pressure (choice D) will decrease net filtration pressure in Bowman's capsule. Thus, GFR would decrease.

Hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's space opposes filtration by decreasing net filtration force. Increasing the hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's capsule (choice E) would decrease GFR by decreasing net filtration pressure. This is seen in cases of post-renal failure.

choice_explanations.A: Constricting the afferent arteriole decreases glomerular capillary pressure and thus decreases GFR.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: dilating the afferent arteriole increases glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, increasing the net filtration force and raising GFR, which lowers serum creatinine.
choice_explanations.C: Dilating the efferent arteriole decreases glomerular hydrostatic pressure and thus decreases GFR.
choice_explanations.D: Increasing plasma oncotic pressure decreases the net filtration pressure and thus decreases GFR.
choice_explanations.E: Increasing hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's capsule opposes filtration, decreasing net filtration pressure and thus GFR (seen in post-renal failure).

fa_summary: GFR rises when glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure increases (e.g., afferent arteriolar dilation) and falls when oncotic pressure or Bowman's capsule pressure rises.

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after being burned over 25% of his body in a house fire. The burns are located on both arms and legs with sparing of the torso. He is stabilized with intravenous fluid hydration. The burns are first and second degree and are wrapped in silver sulfadiazine dressings. He is admitted to the hospital for observation and treatment. On hospital day #1, his blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg and pulse is 96/minute. The heart, lungs and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. The examination of the burns are unchanged from prior. Urine output is 1700 mL/24 hour (normal: 800-2,000 mL/24 hours). Laboratory studies show a serum BUN is 30 mg/dL, serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, urine osmolality is 750 mOsm/kg of water. FeNa is 0.9% (normal <1%), and urine sediment shows no cells or casts. Which of the following most likely accounts for his laboratory findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has elevated BUN and normal serum creatinine. Raised BUN levels with normal creatinine can be seen in prerenal causes of azotemia, which can be subclassified into those due to increased synthesis of urea and those due to decreased perfusion of the kidney.

In this case, the boy's blood pressure is stable and urine output is adequate at 70 mL/hour. Thus, inadequate renal perfusion is unlikely. The burns themselves can cause significant urea production, since urea is the major nitrogen-containing end product of protein catabolism, which increases markedly in burn victims.

In prerenal azotemia, there is increased BUN:Cr ratio (>15) due to intact tubular function, reabsorbing BUN along with other solutes in the setting of intravascular volume depletion. Creatinine on the other hand is not absorbed in the tubules. In contrast, intrinsic renal azotemia lacks appropriate tubular function, thus BUN is not reabsorbed, resulting in BUN:Cr <15.

Urinary tract obstruction (post-renal azotemia) can initially cause an increased BUN:Cr ratio of >15 due to back pressure, increasing the reabsorption time of BUN. However, as this progresses to tubular damage (late stage), the BUN:Cr ratio drops <15 since there is less reabsorption.

Decreased renal perfusion (choice A) also produces prerenal azotemia with increased BUN and normal serum creatinine (BUN:Cr ratio >15), but you would expect to see a decrease in urine output to <500 mL/24 hours as a consequence of the inadequate perfusion.

Distal urinary tract obstruction (choice B) due to processes such as stones, cancer, or benign prostatic hyperplasia, causes postrenal azotemia in which both BUN and serum creatinine rise, but the rise in serum urea is proportionally higher than that of serum creatinine.

In renal glomerular disease (choice D) of sufficient severity to cause acute or chronic renal failure, creatinine and urea usually rise in parallel.

In renal tubulointerstitial disease (choice E), a cause of intrinsic renal azotemia, notably in acute tubular necrosis, creatinine may rise disproportionately to urea.

choice_explanations.A: Decreased renal perfusion produces prerenal azotemia with an increased BUN:Cr ratio, but urine output would be expected to fall to <500 mL/24 hours; this boy's urine output is adequate.
choice_explanations.B: Distal urinary tract obstruction causes postrenal azotemia in which both BUN and creatinine rise, with urea rising proportionally more than creatinine; it is not supported here.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: elevated BUN with normal creatinine reflects prerenal azotemia from increased urea synthesis. Burns markedly increase protein catabolism, and urea is the major nitrogen-containing end product.
choice_explanations.D: In renal glomerular disease severe enough to cause renal failure, creatinine and urea usually rise in parallel.
choice_explanations.E: In renal tubulointerstitial disease (e.g., acute tubular necrosis), creatinine may rise disproportionately to urea.

fa_summary: An elevated BUN with normal creatinine indicates prerenal azotemia; in burn patients it reflects increased urea synthesis from protein catabolism rather than decreased renal perfusion.

stem: A 2-week-old male infant has failure to thrive, oliguria, and recurrent urinary tract infections. Ultrasound reveals a dilated left renal pelvis and a normal left ureter. The right ureter and renal pelvis are both normal. Urinalysis shows 2+ blood and scattered neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the obstruction?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is a relatively common congenital condition that occurs principally in male infants. The obstruction can be partial or complete and may be due to several processes occurring at the ureteropelvic junction, including compression by aberrant renal vessels, disorganized smooth muscle growth, and intramuscular collagen deposition. Because the kidney produces urine at a rate that exceeds the amount of urine able to drain out of the renal pelvis into the ureter, accumulation of urine occurs in the kidney (hydronephrosis). These obstructions develop prenatally and can be diagnosed with prenatal ultrasound screening. In the absence of prenatal screening, presentation may include palpable abdominal mass caused by the enlarged obstructed kidney, urinary tract infections, hematuria, and failure to thrive. Symptomatic patients generally require surgical intervention.

Both primary (choice A) and metastatic (choice D) tumors of the ureter are rare, and would not be expected in an infant.

Calculi (choice B) are also rare in infants. Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism which causes a defect in amino acid reabsorption in the proximal tubules, resulting in excess cystine in the urine. Cystine crystals have a hexagonal shape seen on urine microscopy. NOTE: Cystinuria should not be confused with cystinosis, an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder where cystine accumulates within cells of the body and damages them. Cystinosis is a common cause of Fanconi syndrome: renal acidosis, hypophosphatemic rickets, and cataracts.

Chronic ureteritis (choice C) is usually a complication of either a lower or upper urinary tract infection.

choice_explanations.A: Primary tumors of the ureter are rare and would not be expected in an infant.
choice_explanations.B: Calculi are also rare in infants; note that cystinuria (defective proximal tubular amino acid reabsorption) can cause cystine stones, and should not be confused with cystinosis (lysosomal storage disorder causing Fanconi syndrome).
choice_explanations.C: Chronic ureteritis is usually a complication of either a lower or upper urinary tract infection.
choice_explanations.D: Metastatic tumors of the ureter are rare and would not be expected in an infant.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: ureteropelvic junction obstruction is a common congenital condition in male infants; urine production exceeds drainage from the renal pelvis into the ureter, causing hydronephrosis with UTI, hematuria, and failure to thrive.

fa_summary: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is a common congenital cause of hydronephrosis, occurring mainly in male infants; it may present with abdominal mass, UTI, hematuria, and failure to thrive.

stem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a feeling of intense heat over her trunk and face with an accompanying flushing of the skin. She says that this has been occurring more frequently over the past 3 months. The episodes last a couple of minutes and then subside. She states that she also has reduced vaginal lubrication and dyspareunia that makes having sex very uncomfortable. Which of the following is most likely to be seen in this patient?

options.text: Decreased FSH, decreased LH, increased estrogen
Increased FSH, no change in LH, decreased estrogen
Increased hCG, increased estrogen, increased progesterone
Increased LH, increased FSH, increased GnRH
Increased LH, increased progesterone, increased estrogen

explanation:
The correct answer is D. Around the age of 45-50 (varies individually), the sexual cycle becomes irregular and anovulatory, and eventually the cycle ceases altogether. This is the menopause, which by definition begins 12 months after the final menses. The features include vasomotor symptoms and urogenital symptoms such as vaginal dryness and dyspareunia.

Approaching menopause, only a few primordial follicles remain to be stimulated by FSH and LH. This leads to the reduced production of estrogen by the ovaries ("ovarian burnout"). At the point when estrogen synthesis falls below a critical level, the hormone can no longer exert negative feedback effect on gonadotropin hormone releasing hormone (GnRH), and gonadotropin (FSH and LH) production. Instead, high levels of GnRH and gonadotropins are produced in large and continuous quantities (notice loss of cycling). FSH and LH are then produced in high amounts without the monthly cycling.

The high hormonal levels, particularly those of LH, may be related to occurrence of hot flashes in menopause. This makes it still unlikely that the events at the level of hypothalamus cause menopause. Hypothalamic GnRH continues to be produced by the arcuate nucleus, which lies close to neurons involved in thermoregulation. Without follicular production, the postmenopausal estrogen is derived from the aromatization of androgens in the ovarian stroma and adrenal secretion of androstenedione, which is aromatized to estrone, the major source of circulating estrogen in the postmenopausal female. Long-term exposure to estrone unopposed by progesterone production (corpus luteum) can lead to endometrial hyperplasia, a precursor of endometrial cancer.

Precocious puberty in McCune-Albright syndrome (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait skin pigmentation, autonomous endocrine changes) is gonadotropin-independent. Estradiol levels are increased and gonadotropins are suppressed (choice A). An LHRH-stimulation test can help to differentiate between gonadotropin-dependent and independent disorders.

In women treated with GnRH analogues for infertility, downregulation of LH production can cause increased FSH/LH ratio and prevent spontaneous LH surges. The suppression of LH secretion can be used to delay ovulation, thereby increasing yield of mature oocytes. Administration of GnRH analogue suppresses hypothalamic GnRH production, so GnRH level is low, FSH is increased and LH is low (choice B).

Choice C is typical of pregnancy. In early pregnancy, the syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin), which binds to LH receptors on the corpus luteum to rescue it and stimulates estrogen and progesterone production. The placenta takes over at 7 weeks gestation and secretes large quantities of sexual hormones.

In the pituitary ovarian cycle, increased estrogen at about mid cycle helps stimulate a large and sudden LH surge (positive feedback), which causes the follicle to rupture and expel the egg into the Fallopian tube (ovulation). Immediately after ovulation, the corpus luteum begins secreting large amounts of progesterone (choice E).

choice_explanations.A: McCune-Albright syndrome is gonadotropin-independent: estradiol levels are increased and gonadotropins are suppressed (choice A).
choice_explanations.B: With a GnRH analogue, hypothalamic GnRH production is suppressed, so GnRH is low, FSH is increased and LH is low (choice B); this describes therapy, not menopause.
choice_explanations.C: Increased hCG, estrogen, and progesterone (choice C) is typical of pregnancy: the syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG, which rescues the corpus luteum and stimulates estrogen and progesterone production.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Menopause is a hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: loss of ovarian follicular estrogen removes negative feedback, so GnRH, FSH, and LH are all increased without monthly cycling, causing vasomotor (hot flash) and urogenital symptoms.
choice_explanations.E: Immediately after ovulation the corpus luteum begins secreting large amounts of progesterone (choice E).

fa_summary: Menopause causes loss of ovarian estrogen, which removes negative feedback and produces high GnRH, FSH, and LH, with vasomotor and urogenital symptoms.

stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of heavy menstrual periods and repeated episodes of vaginal spotting between periods. She denies any medical history or use of medications, and indicates that she still has regular menstrual cycles. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 124/72 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows an enlarged nontender uterus but is otherwise normal. Pelvic ultrasound shows a large, round, well-circumscribed, 4-cm submucosal mass on the anterior portion of the uterus. Laboratory studies show erythrocyte count is 3.0 million/mm³, leukocyte count is 6,000/mm³, hemoglobin is 10.5 g/dL, and platelet count is 200 x 10³/mm³. Endometrial biopsy performed at day 14 of her menstrual cycle reveals normal secretory endometrium; no evidence of inflammation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The differential diagnosis for vaginal bleeding should include uterine leiomyoma, uterine hyperplasia or carcinoma, other malignancies involving the uterus, inflammation (acute or chronic endometritis), and dys-synchronous endometrium (hormonal imbalance).

The patient is most likely presenting with a uterine leiomyoma. Uterine leiomyomas are common, benign smooth muscle tumors of the myometrium. These tumors have a very low malignant potential. These tumors are generally well-circumscribed, round masses. They can be submucosal, intramural or subserosal. Clinical presentation may include anemia, heavy menstrual periods (menorrhagia), bleeding between menstrual periods (menometrorrhagia), pelvic pain, and/or a pelvic mass. Submucosal and intramural tumors can also cause infertility by prohibiting implantation.

Endometrial adenocarcinoma (choice A) most commonly affects postmenopausal women and generally presents with postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. It is less likely that the patient in this vignette has endometrial cancer since she is still having regular menstrual cycles and also has a normal endometrial biopsy.

Endometrial hyperplasia (choice B) generally presents clinically with irregular bleeding between menses. Causes of endometrial hyperplasia include unopposed estrogen effect (exogenous hormone therapy, obesity with extra fat depot) or estrogen-secreting ovarian granulosa cell tumor. Our patient has none of the aforementioned causes, and normal secretory endometrium with no histologic confirmation of hyperplasia. Endometrial hyperplasia, if left untreated, can progress towards endometrial carcinoma.

Uterine leiomyosarcoma (choice D) is a rare malignant smooth muscle tumor and commonly seen in older age groups (over 60 years). These tumors arise from the uterine myometrium and are generally aggressive. Imaging may reveal a large, irregular, hemorrhagic mass with necrotic foci. While leiomyosarcoma is certainly a possibility in this vignette, the fact that this patient has a well-circumscribed, round mass on ultrasound imaging makes this less likely.

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID, choice E) results from an ascending infection of the genital tract by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and/or Chlamydia trachomatis. Patients will generally present with vaginal discharge, vaginal spotting/bleeding, and abdominal/pelvic pain with or without fever. Patients with Chlamydia infection are usually asymptomatic. Neisseria gonorrhoeae would cause acute endometritis, whereas Chlamydia trachomatis would cause chronic endometritis, so these features would be present on the endometrial biopsy. PID may cause scarring of the fallopian tubes, infertility, and increased risk of ectopic pregnancy. It is unlikely that the irregular bleeding experienced by the patient in this vignette is caused by PID.

choice_explanations.A: Endometrial adenocarcinoma most commonly affects postmenopausal women and presents with postmenopausal bleeding; this patient still has regular cycles and a normal endometrial biopsy.
choice_explanations.B: Endometrial hyperplasia presents with irregular bleeding between menses and is caused by unopposed estrogen (e.g., exogenous hormones, obesity, or an estrogen-secreting granulosa cell tumor); this patient has normal secretory endometrium.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Uterine leiomyomas are common benign smooth muscle tumors of the myometrium that are well-circumscribed and round, and can cause menorrhagia, metrorrhagia, and anemia.
choice_explanations.D: Uterine leiomyosarcoma is a rare, aggressive malignant smooth muscle tumor seen in older patients, with large irregular hemorrhagic masses; the well-circumscribed round mass here makes it unlikely.
choice_explanations.E: PID results from ascending N. gonorrhoeae and/or C. trachomatis infection and would show endometritis on biopsy, cause tubal scarring, and increase ectopic pregnancy risk; it does not fit this presentation.

fa_summary: Uterine leiomyomas are well-circumscribed benign smooth muscle tumors of the myometrium that cause menorrhagia, metrorrhagia, pelvic mass, and anemia.

stem: A 20-year-old primigravid woman is brought to the emergency department because of headaches and dizziness. She is 34 weeks' gestation. Her prenatal care has been up to date. She has a prior medical history of seasonal allergic rhinitis. Blood pressure since 30 weeks has ranged from 140-170/90-105 mmHg. Urinalysis shows 3+ proteinuria. Physical examination shows a gravid uterus palpable towards the xiphoid process. The lower extremities have +2/+4 edema towards the calves. Laboratory studies show a serum aspartate aminotransferase of 40 U/L and alanine aminotransferase of 45 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive therapy?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The woman has preeclampsia, the features of which include proteinuria and sustained elevation of blood pressure in pregnancy after 20 weeks of gestation (usually in the third trimester) in the absence of preexisting hypertension. A wide variety of other features of preeclampsia can also be seen, including excessive weight gain, generalized edema, ascites, hyperuricemia, hypocalciuria, increased plasma concentration of von Willebrand factor and cellular fibronectin, reduced plasma concentration of anti-thrombin III, thrombocytopenia, increased hematocrit, increased liver enzymes (as seen in our patient), intrauterine growth retardation, and intrauterine hypoxia. Modern theories suggest that the true primary lesion may involve the endothelium, and that medical control of hypertension (choice A) actually only treats a small part of the syndrome. At present, the only definitive therapy is delivery of the baby, and obstetricians often play a delicate game trying to delay delivery for a premature baby's sake as long as possible while judging the severity of the preeclampsia and its immediate risks to mother and fetus.

Low dose aspirin (choice C) may have a modest effect in preventing preeclampsia, but this is not yet well established.

Oxygen supplementation (choice D) is used in some cases of cerebral hemorrhage secondary to preeclampsia, but does not constitute definitive therapy.

Renal dialysis (choice E) is usually not necessary in preeclampsia, although severe cortical necrosis and renal tubular necrosis can occasionally occur in this disorder.

choice_explanations.A: Medical control of hypertension only treats a small part of the syndrome and is not definitive therapy.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. The only definitive therapy for preeclampsia is delivery of the baby.
choice_explanations.C: Low dose aspirin may have a modest effect in preventing preeclampsia, but this is not well established.
choice_explanations.D: Oxygen supplementation is used in some cases of cerebral hemorrhage secondary to preeclampsia, but does not constitute definitive therapy.
choice_explanations.E: Renal dialysis is usually not necessary in preeclampsia, although severe cortical necrosis and renal tubular necrosis can occasionally occur.

fa_summary: Preeclampsia is new-onset hypertension with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks of gestation; the only definitive therapy is delivery.

stem: A 15-month-old boy develops a testicular mass. Physical examination shows a 5 cm nontender, firm mass in the left testicle, which does not illuminate when light is placed against the mass. He undergoes orchiectomy. On cut section, the mass shows a variety of appearances. Histologically, many different tissues are seen, including cartilage, thyroid, and neural tissue. A small focus of squamous cell carcinoma is seen. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This is teratoma with malignant transformation, as evidenced by the focus of squamous cell carcinoma. Mature teratomas with very well differentiated tissues should be completely excised because there is a possible chance for malignancy. There is a bimodal age distribution of testicular teratoma: 0-4 years and 20-40 years. Malignant transformation is more common in testicular than ovarian teratomas. Squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma are the most common malignancies. Types of teratomas:

Dermoid cyst (choice A) is a cystic form of mature teratoma, usually found in the ovaries.

Embryonal carcinoma (choice B) is a type of adenocarcinoma rather than squamous cell carcinoma.

Immature teratoma (choice C), while clinically malignant, shows immature embryonal tissues.

Solid mature teratoma (choice D) without the added descriptor "with malignant transformation" is by definition a benign tumor in females and prepubertal males (all teratomas are considered to have malignant potential in postpubertal males). Careful extensive sampling is required to exclude minute foci of cancerous transformation.

choice_explanations.A: Dermoid cyst is a cystic form of mature teratoma, usually found in the ovaries.
choice_explanations.B: Embryonal carcinoma is a type of adenocarcinoma rather than squamous cell carcinoma.
choice_explanations.C: Immature teratoma, while clinically malignant, shows immature embryonal tissues (no squamous cell carcinoma focus).
choice_explanations.D: Solid mature teratoma without the descriptor "with malignant transformation" is by definition benign in females and prepubertal males; careful sampling is needed to exclude minute foci of cancerous transformation.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. A teratoma containing a focus of squamous cell carcinoma (or other malignancy) is a teratoma with malignant transformation.

fa_summary: Testicular teratomas are benign in children but can undergo malignant transformation (most commonly to squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma).

stem: A 28-year-old woman is being treated with sequential doses of a hormone, which produces a progressive rise in the hormone's plasma level over several days. Initially, the patient's plasma levels of FSH and LH decline, but later FSH and LH suddenly and dramatically increase. Which of the following hormones is she most likely being treated with?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Low plasma levels of estrogen, such as during the normal follicular phase, inhibit the secretion of FSH and LH (negative feedback). Within this low range, any increase of estrogen causes decreased LH and FSH. However, once the plasma level of estrogen reaches a certain level (as occurs with the repeated doses described in this question), and that level is maintained for a significant period of time, the negative feedback loop changes to a positive feedback loop and a surge in FSH and LH secretion occurs. This natural sequence occurs at the end of the follicular phase, and the LH surge induces ovulation.

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (choice B) given at a constant rate would first increase, then decrease (downregulation of receptors), FSH and LH. A pulsatile infusion, which eliminates downregulation, would always increase FSH.

Inhibin (choice C) and progesterone (choice D) both would inhibit FSH secretion.

Testosterone (choice E) normally provides the negative feedback for LH and does not directly affect FSH, although very high nonphysiologic levels of testosterone will reduce plasma FSH due to suppression of GnRH.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Low estrogen levels inhibit FSH and LH (negative feedback), but a sustained high estrogen level switches to positive feedback and triggers the midcycle FSH/LH surge.
choice_explanations.B: GnRH given at a constant rate would first increase, then decrease (downregulation of receptors), FSH and LH; only pulsatile infusion would persistently increase FSH.
choice_explanations.C: Inhibin would inhibit FSH secretion.
choice_explanations.D: Progesterone would inhibit FSH secretion.
choice_explanations.E: Testosterone normally provides negative feedback for LH and does not directly affect FSH, although very high nonphysiologic levels reduce plasma FSH by suppressing GnRH.

fa_summary: Sustained high estrogen switches from negative to positive feedback, triggering the midcycle surge of FSH and LH that induces ovulation.

stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a blood-tinged serous discharge from one nipple. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 122/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a small, palpable, subareolar tumor. The tumor is surgically resected. Which of the following features on histologic examination is most helpful in establishing that this tumor is benign?

options.text: Presence of both epithelial and myoepithelial cells

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Intraductal papillomas are small (usually less than 3 cm), benign papillary tumors found within the larger ducts of the breast. They are typically located under the areola. They can be frightening to the patient because they may produce a serous or bloody nipple discharge. They have a malignant counterpart, papillary ductal carcinoma of the breast, so it is important to be able to distinguish the benign from the malignant lesion. Both of these conditions produce bloody nipple discharge, but intraductal papillomas are more likely seen in premenopausal women.

Intraductal papillomas have fibrovascular projections lined by epithelial (luminal) and myoepithelial cells. Myoepithelial cells (spindle cells between the ductal epithelial cells and the stroma) are absent in invasive ductal carcinoma. The presence of myoepithelial cells is key to the diagnosis of intraductal papilloma. Features favoring the diagnosis of ductal carcinoma, rather than benign intraductal papilloma, include severe cytologic atypia, abnormal mitoses, and a cribriform growth pattern.

High mitotic counts (choice A) are observed in high grade invasive ductal carcinomas.

Both benign and malignant papillary tumors can be located within ducts (choice B). Both benign and malignant papillary tumors can have papillary fronds (choice D). Both benign and malignant papillary tumors can be small (choice E).

choice_explanations.A: High mitotic counts are observed in high grade invasive ductal carcinomas.
choice_explanations.B: Both benign and malignant papillary tumors can be located within ducts, so location does not establish benignity.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. The presence of myoepithelial cells (spindle cells between the ductal epithelial cells and the stroma) is key to the diagnosis of intraductal papilloma; they are absent in invasive ductal carcinoma.
choice_explanations.D: Both benign and malignant papillary tumors can have papillary fronds.
choice_explanations.E: Both benign and malignant papillary tumors can be small.

fa_summary: Intraductal papilloma is a benign papillary tumor of the large breast ducts; the presence of a myoepithelial layer distinguishes it from papillary ductal carcinoma.

stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has not experienced menarche. She has been in ballet training since the age of 6 years. She has maintained a strict low calorie and low fat diet with high protein intake since age 11. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 46 kg (101 lb); BMI is 17.9 kg/m². Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?

options.text: Decreased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency and decreased estrogen
Decreased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency and increased estrogen
Increased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency and decreased estrogen
Increased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency and increased estrogen

explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient's presentation is typical of exercise-induced amenorrhea with delayed puberty. This is a form of hypothalamic amenorrhea. Her presentation of intense exercise and chronic dieting with low weight and primary amenorrhea are two parts of the so called "female athlete triad," which also includes a high risk of skeletal disorders, such as osteoporosis and the attendant stress fractures as well as ordinary fractures, due in part to low estrogen levels, which predispose to osteopenia. The incidence of delayed menarche is especially high among girls who avidly pursue ballet because of the intensity of exercise and frequent dieting. Exercise alone will not usually cause amenorrhea; the combination of intense exercise and dieting producing imbalance between energy intake and expenditure often does. The basic mechanism of amenorrhea and delayed puberty with exercise and chronic dieting is suppression of pulsatile release of GnRH; this is reflected in reduced pulsatility of the gonadotropins leading to low estrogen.

Decreased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency and increased estrogen (choice B) is incorrect because, first, increased estrogen is inconsistent with her physical development; and, second, reduced FSH and LH would lead to reduced estrogen levels. Primary excess of estrogen would suppress GnRH, LH, and FSH, but, as described previously, she lacks the characteristic signs of excessive estrogen.

Decreased TSH and increased thyroxine (choice C) reflects either primary hyperthyroidism or Graves disease; either condition can cause amenorrhea, so they must be considered, especially given her low weight. However, her moderately lower-than-normal weight is explained adequately by her exercise and dietary restriction. She also lacks the characteristic signs of hyperthyroidism such as tendencies toward hypertension, tachycardia, tremors, and muscle weakness.

Increased TSH could suppress hypothalamic-pituitary control of reproduction. There would also be an increase in thyroxine (choice F) expected with this example of secondary (pituitary) hyperthyroidism; therefore, this option also is unlikely because of the absence of other characteristic signs of excessive thyroid hormone.

Increased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency and decreased estrogen (choice D) is consistent with primary ovarian defects; it would likely also cause delayed puberty and amenorrhea, but given her history and the apparently normal, but immature, ovaries and uterus, this is less likely than hypothalamic amenorrhea.

Increased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency and increased estrogen (choice E) would cause symptoms of excessive estrogens; one would not expect delayed puberty, but premature menarche would be more likely.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Exercise-induced hypothalamic amenorrhea suppresses pulsatile GnRH release, reducing FSH/LH pulsatility and lowering estrogen.
choice_explanations.B: Increased estrogen is inconsistent with her physical development, and reduced FSH and LH would lower (not raise) estrogen.
choice_explanations.C: Decreased TSH with increased thyroxine reflects primary hyperthyroidism or Graves disease, which can cause amenorrhea, but she lacks the associated signs.
choice_explanations.D: Increased FSH/LH pulsatility with decreased estrogen is consistent with primary ovarian defects; her normal but immature ovaries/uterus make this less likely than hypothalamic amenorrhea.
choice_explanations.E: Increased FSH/LH pulsatility with increased estrogen would cause symptoms of estrogen excess and premature (not delayed) menarche.
choice_explanations.F: Increased TSH with increased thyroxine would reflect secondary (pituitary) hyperthyroidism, which is unlikely given the absence of other signs of thyroid hormone excess.

fa_summary: Functional (exercise-induced) hypothalamic amenorrhea suppresses pulsatile GnRH secretion, reducing FSH, LH, and estrogen, with delayed puberty and the female athlete triad.

stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the physician because of gynecomastia. He also reports low libido and erectile dysfunction although he is not sexually active. Physical examination shows abnormally small, firm testes. Testicular biopsy shows fibrosis and hyalinization of the seminiferous tubules. The Leydig cells are present in clumps and are hyperplastic. Chromosomal analysis shows the presence of an XXY genotype. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by an XXY genotype and is associated with seminiferous tubule dysgenesis. In this disorder, there are usually few symptoms before puberty, which may be delayed. At puberty, the seminiferous tubules fail to enlarge normally and instead undergo fibrosis and hyalinization. The result is an inability to produce sperm. (There are, however, some islands of normal spermatogenesis in affected patients. Therefore, patients who are azoospermic and desire fertility will require testicular biopsy to determine if sperm are present. If so, the female partner can undergo egg retrieval and assisted reproduction can take place.)

The Leydig cells are hyperplastic and clumped together, and do not function normally (secretion of testosterone is decreased). As a consequence, plasma levels of LH are increased (not decreased, choice C) due to the loss of feedback inhibition. The increased LH stimulates the Leydig cells to increase (not decrease, choice A) estrogen secretion. The increased estrogen/testosterone ratio is responsible for the gynecomastia, small penis, sparse body hair, and other feminized features of Klinefelter syndrome. Because of dysgenesis of the seminiferous tubules, the secretion of inhibin is reduced (not increased, choice E). Low plasma levels of inhibin result in increased plasma FSH (not decreased, choice B) due to loss of feedback inhibition at the pituitary.

choice_explanations.A: Estrogen is actually increased: the elevated LH stimulates the Leydig cells to increase estrogen secretion, giving an increased estrogen/testosterone ratio that causes gynecomastia.
choice_explanations.B: FSH is increased, not decreased: dysgenesis of the seminiferous tubules lowers inhibin, removing feedback inhibition at the pituitary.
choice_explanations.C: LH is increased, not decreased, due to loss of feedback inhibition from the reduced testosterone.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. The hyperplastic, clumped Leydig cells do not function normally, so testosterone secretion is decreased.
choice_explanations.E: Inhibin is reduced, not increased, because of dysgenesis of the seminiferous tubules.

fa_summary: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes seminiferous tubule dysgenesis with reduced inhibin and increased FSH, and abnormal Leydig cells with decreased testosterone and increased LH.

stem: A healthy 25-year-old man lives at the beach on the Pacific coast of the United States. His twin brother has been living in a mountain cabin for the past 2 years. Which of the following indices is likely to be greater in the man living at sea level?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. A number of physiologic changes occur in a person living at high altitude. The diminished barometric pressure at high altitude causes alveolar hypoxia and arterial hypoxia. Pulmonary vasoconstriction occurs in response to alveolar hypoxia; therefore, the diameter of the pulmonary vessels would be greater in the brother living at sea level. This is an important difference between pulmonary and systemic arterioles; systemic arterioles dilate in hypoxia, but pulmonary vessels constrict. Acute hypoxic vasoconstriction is a main mechanism of high altitude sickness; unlike many of the responses to chronic hypoxia, vasoconstriction persists. Although it becomes somewhat less powerful than the acute response, it tends to cause chronic pulmonary hypertension. Hypoxia in patients with chronic lung disease is well-known to pose the risk of secondary pulmonary hypertension.

All of the other choices describe physiologic processes that would be enhanced by living at high altitude:

Increased erythropoietin production (choice B), caused by arterial hypoxia, leads to increases in hematocrit in people living at high altitude.

Muscle capillary density increases (choice C) in people chronically exposed to the hypoxemia caused by living at high altitude.

At high altitudes, the ventilation rate increases, causing a respiratory alkalosis. The kidney then compensates by decreasing H+ excretion and increasing the excretion of HCO3− (choice D).

Increasing the rate of respiration (choice E) is a very useful adaptation to the hypoxic conditions of high altitude. The primary stimulus is the hypoxic stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors.

choice_explanations.A: At high altitude, alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, so the pulmonary vessels of the sea-level brother are of greater diameter.
choice_explanations.B: Erythropoietin production is increased at high altitude in response to arterial hypoxia, raising hematocrit.
