choice_explanations.C: Muscle capillary density increases in people chronically exposed to high-altitude hypoxemia.
choice_explanations.D: At high altitude, respiratory alkalosis is compensated by decreased H+ excretion and increased HCO3− excretion.
choice_explanations.E: Respiratory rate increases at high altitude, driven by hypoxic stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors.

fa_summary: High altitude causes alveolar/arterial hypoxia and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction; the person at sea level therefore has larger pulmonary vessels.

stem: A 37-year-old man sees a physician because of progressive shortness of breath and vague right upper quadrant pain. He is unable to walk up 2 flights of stairs without “losing his breath.” He has smoked a half a pack of cigarettes per day for the past 15 years. His temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 22/min. Physical examination shows clubbing of fingers, scleral icterus, generalized jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Lung auscultation reveals diminished breath, voice, and heart sounds. Laboratory studies show an alkaline phosphatase of 85 U/L, ALT activity of 225 U/L, AST activity of 200 U/L, total bilirubin of 3.3 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin of 3.0 mg/dL. He undergoes a liver biopsy. Histologic examination shows the presence in hepatocytes of large numbers of eosinophilic globular cytoplasmic inclusions that stain with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain. There is also mild-to-moderate fibrosis of the portal triads. Which of the following pulmonary findings would most likely be seen in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The patient has alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency. Alpha-1-antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor, which counterbalances substances such as elastase. The normal phenotype is considered PiMM. With alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, a protease-antiprotease imbalance occurs. Inflammation in the lungs releases neutrophils into the alveolar spaces. Stimulated neutrophils release elastase from their granules and create oxygen free radicals, both of which can inactivate alpha-1-antitrypsin. The combination of high elastase activity and increased oxygen free radicals from tobacco smoking in patients with low antiprotease activity causes destruction of lung tissue (alveolar walls/septa), which leads to emphysema. Homozygous (PiZZ) patients who smoke develop emphysema at an earlier age, as in the patient in this vignette. A panacinar emphysema develops, in which the entire acinus is enlarged, from the respiratory bronchiole to the distal alveoli. In our patient, emphysema is reflected in the diminished lung, breath, and cardiac sounds on auscultation. A chest x-ray would show hyperinflation. In contrast, centriacinar emphysema is characterized by enlargement of the central portions of the acinus (e.g., the respiratory bronchiole). Its pathogenesis is related to exposure to tobacco products and coal dust.

The eosinophilic globular cytoplasmic inclusions are collections of a nonfunctional form of alpha-1-antitrypsin. They can accumulate within hepatocytes and cause inflammation, hepatic dysfunction (as seen in our patient), fibrosis, and cirrhosis.

Bronchiectasis (choice B) can be seen in cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, and repeated bacterial infections and cause progressive bronchial dilation, persistent infection, and lung atelectasis.

Interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate (choice C) is associated with viral infections, Mycoplasma pneumonia, and autoimmune conditions. Lymphocytes would accumulate and expand the alveolar walls (lymphocytic pneumonia). There would be no alveolar wall destruction.

Lobar consolidation (choice D) is associated with bacterial pneumonia such as Streptococcus. Influx and accumulation of neutrophils in response to the bacterium would occur, along with exudative fluid into the alveolar space. This would involve a focal area of the lung (bronchopneumonia or lobar pneumonia), rather than a diffuse, multi-lobe involvement. Destruction of alveolar walls may be seen with abscess formation, but this would also be focal.

Malignant mucus-secreting epithelial cells (choice E) implies either lung adenocarcinoma or bronchioloalveolar carcinoma. These lesions would not have a diffuse involvement such as what is presented here.

choice_explanations.A: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency causes unopposed elastase activity and destruction of alveolar walls (panacinar emphysema).
choice_explanations.B: Bronchiectasis (dilated airways with mucus plugs) is seen in cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, and recurrent infections, not in alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency.
choice_explanations.C: Interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate is seen with viral infections, Mycoplasma pneumonia, and autoimmune conditions; there is no alveolar wall destruction.
choice_explanations.D: Lobar consolidation is seen with bacterial pneumonia (e.g., Streptococcus) and is focal rather than diffuse.
choice_explanations.E: Malignant mucus-secreting epithelial cells imply lung adenocarcinoma or bronchioloalveolar carcinoma, which would not be diffusely involved.

fa_summary: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency causes panacinar emphysema (destruction of alveolar walls) from unopposed elastase, plus PAS-positive globules and cirrhosis in the liver.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because he inhaled a peanut. Physical examination shows cyanotic extremities and lips. Bronchoscopy shows a peanut is lodged in the right mainstem bronchus, largely occluding it. Peripheral oxygen saturation is 65%. Which of the following best explains these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Children younger than 4 years of age are at risk for foreign-body aspiration because of the size of the trachea and also because they have a tendency to put things in their mouths. The trachea and bronchi are the most common sites for foreign-body aspiration in children, especially the right mainstem bronchus. A commonly aspirated food is the peanut.

Inequalities of ventilation and perfusion contribute to hypoxia in many settings. In this case, blood goes to both lungs (perfusion), but air is prevented from entering one of the lungs (ventilation). Because the right lung is being perfused but not ventilated, hypoxemia ensues when the deoxygenated blood from the right lung mixes with oxygenated blood from the left lung. The loss of aeration to the right lung is referred to clinically as atelectasis, and can be very striking when viewed radiographically. If the inadequate ventilation of the lung persists long enough, the lung tissue itself can be damaged, making the problem even worse.

None of the other choice options for this question are applicable for consideration:

Decreased PO2 in inspired air (choice A) is generally only seen at high altitudes; perhaps may be seen among victims in certain types of toxic fires or explosions; and may also potentially occur on rare occasions of ventilator malfunction for a patient receiving mechanical ventilation.

Decreased pulmonary diffusion capacity (choice B) can occur when the blood-gas barrier is thickened (e.g., diffuse infiltrative lung diseases such as interstitial fibrosis, sarcoidosis, asbestosis), when the surface area of the blood-gas barrier is reduced (e.g., pneumonectomy, emphysema), or when less hemoglobin is available to carry oxygen (e.g., anemia, pulmonary emboli).

Hypoventilation of central origin (choice C) suggests either a major neurologic illness such as a cerebrovascular accident (CVA) or, not uncommonly, a medication/substance overdose.

Hypoventilation of peripheral origin (choice D) may refer to certain types of upper airway obstructive lesions (e.g., goiters, pharyngeal tumors, etc.), severe chest wall deformities (e.g., kyphoscoliosis), and several neurologic or neuromuscular disorders (such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, poliomyelitis, myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy, etc.).

choice_explanations.A: Decreased PO2 in inspired air is generally only seen at high altitude or with toxic fires/explosions or ventilator malfunction.
choice_explanations.B: Decreased pulmonary diffusion capacity occurs with a thickened or reduced blood-gas barrier or reduced hemoglobin (e.g., fibrosis, emphysema, anemia, pulmonary emboli).
choice_explanations.C: Hypoventilation of central origin suggests a major neurologic illness (e.g., CVA) or medication/substance overdose.
choice_explanations.D: Hypoventilation of peripheral origin refers to upper airway obstruction, severe chest wall deformity, or neuromuscular disorders.
choice_explanations.E: Foreign-body obstruction of the right mainstem bronchus perfuses but does not ventilate the right lung, producing V/Q inequality and hypoxemia.

fa_summary: Foreign-body aspiration occludes the right mainstem bronchus, so the right lung is perfused but not ventilated — a ventilation/perfusion mismatch causing hypoxemia and atelectasis.

stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of an earache. He has a history of chronic sinusitis, bronchitis, and recurrent otitis media. Physical examination shows that the nasal mucosa is pale and swollen, with mucopurulent secretions. Otologic examination also shows a retracted tympanic membrane with absent mobility and a middle-ear effusion. A sweat chloride test is performed twice; the results both times are normal. Microscopic analysis of the boy's semen reveals immotile spermatozoa. A defect in which of the following types of protein is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Although this boy's presentation is reminiscent of cystic fibrosis (CF), the negative sweat chloride test suggests an alternative etiology. Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a congenital impairment of mucociliary clearance because of a defect of cilia in the airways. Cilia are immotile due to defects in cytoskeletal structure of the cilia, particularly the dynein “cellular motors” on the microtubular doublets at the periphery of the ciliary axoneme. As a result, defects in mucociliary clearance lead to chronic upper and lower respiratory tract disease. Males demonstrate infertility secondary to immotile spermatozoa (in which the defect affects the sperm flagella motion as well). When chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis occur with situs inversus totalis (complete reversal of the circulatory system and viscera), the syndrome is called Kartagener syndrome.

Chaperones (choice A) are involved in protein folding, and their mutations do not produce symptoms similar to those of Kartagener syndrome.

Mutations in membrane channels (choice C), such as the chloride channel protein for CF, can lead to a similar clinical presentation. However, in CF, the sweat chloride test would be positive.

Mutations in secreted hormones (choice D) can lead to a variety of other illnesses that are unlike the presentation described here.

Mutations in transcription factors (choice E) cause various diseases unrelated to the clinical symptoms presented here.

choice_explanations.A: Chaperones are involved in protein folding; their mutations do not produce a Kartagener-like presentation.
choice_explanations.B: Primary ciliary dyskinesia results from defects in the cytoskeletal dynein motors of cilia and flagella, causing immotile cilia and sperm.
choice_explanations.C: Membrane channel mutations (e.g., CFTR) can mimic this presentation, but CF would have a positive sweat chloride test.
choice_explanations.D: Mutations in secreted hormones cause illnesses unlike this presentation.
choice_explanations.E: Mutations in transcription factors cause diseases unrelated to these symptoms.

fa_summary: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) is caused by a dynein arm defect in the cytoskeletal structure of cilia, producing immotile cilia and sperm.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents to the physician because of a worsening productive cough. These symptoms are worse in the morning and have been present for 4 years but have worsened over the past 6 months. He has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for the past 30 years. An increase in the number of which of the following cell types best accounts for these symptoms?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient has chronic bronchitis, which has been clinically defined as chronic cough with copious sputum production that has been present for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years. Smoking and inhalation of other irritating substances (including smog) are contributory factors. Sputum production in chronic bronchitis is the result of hypertrophy of submucosal glands in larger bronchi and goblet cell metaplasia of bronchioles and small bronchi also contributes significantly to the mucus production. Reid index would be greater than 0.5, reflecting increased submucosal gland hyperplasia (normal: less than 0.4). Patients can have hypoxemia (low PO2, high PCO2), decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, compensatory polycythemia, peripheral cyanosis, digital clubbing, right ventricular hypertrophy, and recurrent pulmonary infections.

Smooth-muscle (choice B) hypertrophy can be seen in larger bronchi in chronic bronchitis, and is related to the increased effort needed to clear bronchi of copious amounts of mucus. This feature is also seen with asthma. However, it does not cause increased mucus production.

Squamous cell (choice C) metaplasia is seen as a reaction to chronic irritation (smoking or inhalation of irritating fumes) in the larger bronchi. It is related to increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma in smokers.

Type I pneumocytes (choice D) are the normal, flat, lining cells of alveoli which are not affected in chronic bronchitis.

Type II pneumocytes (choice E) produce surfactant, not mucus. They can be increased as a reaction to lung damage by processes such as pneumonia, which has an increased incidence in the setting of chronic mucus production with impaired clearance of bacteria.

choice_explanations.A: Goblet cell metaplasia of bronchioles and small bronchi (with submucosal gland hypertrophy) accounts for the increased mucus production in chronic bronchitis.
choice_explanations.B: Smooth-muscle hypertrophy is seen in larger bronchi in chronic bronchitis and asthma but does not cause increased mucus production.
choice_explanations.C: Squamous cell metaplasia follows chronic irritation and increases the risk of squamous cell carcinoma in smokers.
choice_explanations.D: Type I pneumocytes are the normal flat alveolar lining cells and are not affected in chronic bronchitis.
choice_explanations.E: Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant, not mucus, and can increase in response to lung damage such as pneumonia.

fa_summary: Chronic bronchitis causes sputum via goblet cell metaplasia of small bronchi/bronchioles and submucosal gland hypertrophy (increased Reid index).

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of growth failure and recurrent episodes of pneumonia. The parents say that the boy's stools are noticeably foul-smelling. Gene studies show that the boy is homozygous for an autosomal recessively inherited gene mutation. Which of the following is normally a characteristic of the gene product that is defective in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a common fatal autosomal recessive disease among whites/northern European ancestry. It results from a defect in the chloride channel, cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR). Although CFTR is an ion channel that allows chloride flow down its concentration gradient, it is gated by ATP hydrolysis and involves regulation by protein kinase A phosphorylation. Patients present with persistent pulmonary infection, pancreatic insufficiency (leading to foul-smelling fatty stools), and elevated sweat chloride levels. Previously, patients with CF usually died of malnutrition. The use of oral pancreatic enzyme supplements has markedly changed the course of this disease, however, and death in the first few years of life is now uncommon.

Receptors that enter the nucleus (choice C) are commonly steroid receptors.

In contrast to tyrosine kinase receptors (choice D) such as insulin and epidermal growth factor receptors, CFTR does not have intrinsic kinase activity.

CFTR carries chloride ions, which are anions. Cation channels (choice E) carry sodium, potassium, or calcium ions. Receptors with cation channels include nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR) and serotonin-3 (5-HT3) receptors.

choice_explanations.A: CFTR is an ion channel gated by ATP hydrolysis (and regulated by protein kinase A phosphorylation), so it binds ATP.
choice_explanations.C: Receptors that enter the nucleus are commonly steroid receptors, not CFTR, which is a membrane channel.
choice_explanations.D: In contrast to tyrosine kinase receptors (e.g., insulin, EGF), CFTR has no intrinsic kinase activity.
choice_explanations.E: CFTR carries chloride ions (anions); cation channels carry sodium, potassium, or calcium (e.g., nAChR, 5-HT3 receptors).

fa_summary: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a defect in CFTR, an ATP-gated chloride channel on chromosome 7.

stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination because of aplastic anemia. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for pallor. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin of 6.0 g/dL and hematocrit of 24%. Three months ago, her hemoglobin was 6.2 g/dL and hematocrit was 25%. Which of the following is most likely to be decreased in this patient during resting conditions?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The patient has anemia, which reduces the hemoglobin (Hb) content of blood and thereby reduces its O2-carrying capacity. This impairs the ability of blood to deliver O2 to tissues. (Oxygen delivery to the tissues is approximately equal to cardiac output × Hb concentration × the amount of oxygen extracted from the blood [oxygen extraction = arterial oxygen content − venous oxygen content].) In an anemic patient, because the arterial O2 content is decreased, the extraction of a normal amount of oxygen causes the venous PO2 to fall to lower-than-normal levels.

Some of the compensatory mechanisms that come into play in an anemic person with a low Hb content include the following: increased levels of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG; choice A), increased cardiac output (choice C), and increased red blood cell (RBC) H+ concentration (choice E). The increases in 2,3-DPG and RBC H+ concentrations cause the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to shift to the right, which facilitates unloading of available oxygen in the tissues (see figure: increased tissue temperature, such as occurs during exercise, also shifts the curve rightward).

Arterial PO2 (choice B) is independent of hemoglobin concentration because it represents the partial pressure of dissolved O2. Blood O2 is typically monitored clinically using pulse oximetry, which measures blood O2 saturation (SaO2). SaO2 is also completely independent of Hb content because it reflects how many of Hb's four O2 binding sites are occupied, not Hb concentration.

The O2-carrying capacity of blood is proportional to RBC numbers (hematocrit; Hct) and, more directly, their Hb content. Both Hct and Hb concentration are used clinically. In males, a Hct of <41 or a Hb of <13 g/dL is considered an indication of anemia. In women, the values are lower (Hct <36, Hb <12 g/dL; values given for both males and females are approximate).

By way of illustration, think of a glass beaker containing a solution of Hb. If a gas having a PO2 of 100 mm Hg is bubbled through the solution, the PO2 of the solution will be 100 mm Hg regardless of the Hb concentration. However, if the concentration of Hb in the beaker is doubled, the beaker will now contain twice as much oxygen. Because each gram of Hb can normally carry a total of 1.34 mL oxygen, the arterial oxygen content of this patient can be calculated as follows: 1.34 mL O2/g Hb × 6.0 g Hb/dL blood = 8.04 mL O2/dL blood (normal = 20 mL O2/dL blood). When the oxygen content of the arterial blood is decreased to only 8 mL O2/dL, the loss of oxygen to the tissues will cause the venous oxygen tension to fall to lower-than-normal levels during rest and to very low levels whenever exercise is attempted.

Anemia can be a result of decreased RBC production, blood loss, or increased RBC lysis. Common causes include iron, folate and/or vitamin B12 deficiency, aplastic anemia, bone marrow diseases, and hemolytic anemias (e.g., autoimmune, sickle cell disease). The patient has aplastic anemia, a form defined by reduced numbers of hemopoietic stem cells. Aplastic anemia is commonly caused by stem cell injury following exposure to a variety of chemicals and drugs, viral infection, and radiation.

choice_explanations.A: 2,3-DPG is increased in anemia (a compensatory rightward shift of the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve), not decreased.
choice_explanations.B: Arterial PO2 is independent of hemoglobin concentration because it reflects the partial pressure of dissolved O2.
choice_explanations.C: Cardiac output is increased as a compensatory mechanism in anemia, not decreased.
choice_explanations.D: Because arterial O2 content is low in anemia, a normal amount of O2 extraction lowers the mixed venous PO2 below normal during rest.
choice_explanations.E: Red blood cell H+ concentration is increased in anemia (shifting the dissociation curve rightward), not decreased.

fa_summary: In anemia, reduced O2-carrying capacity lowers mixed venous PO2 at rest; compensations include increased 2,3-DPG, cardiac output, and RBC H+.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit because of third-degree burns over 35% of her body. During her stay she develops a fever. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 108/64 mm Hg. She has progressive difficulty breathing, requiring mechanical ventilation. Blood cultures grow gram-negative rods. Bronchoscopy with biopsy shows hyaline membranes within the alveolar walls, alveolar septal thickening, and neutrophilic infiltrate, but no hemosiderin deposits. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of injury?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has diffuse alveolar damage, clinically referred to as adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) or acute lung injury (ALI). ARDS is a severe lung condition characterized by diffuse damage to the alveolar/capillary barrier, which may result from diverse acute conditions. In this vignette, the patient has severe burns and developed a gram-negative sepsis, both of which can contribute to development of ARDS/ALI. The most frequent causes are trauma, sepsis, shock, and gastric aspiration. Other causes of ARDS include pancreatitis, near-drowning, and multiple blood transfusions. If a chest x-ray is performed, diffuse white out of the lungs may be present.

The pathogenesis is not entirely clear, but influx of neutrophils and release of cytokines, eicosanoids, and free radicals seem to be crucial in promoting alveolar damage. The most characteristic histopathologic hallmark of diffuse alveolar damage is formation of hyaline membranes within the alveolar cavities. Hyaline membranes consist of proteinaceous material of plasma origin and necrotic debris from desquamated epithelium. The condition is life threatening, has a 60% mortality, manifests with acute respiratory failure, and requires mechanical ventilation. In premature infants, hyaline membrane disease occurs as a result of immature lung and inadequate surfactant production.

The pathologic features of asthma (choice A) are relatively nonspecific. They are similar to the features of chronic bronchitis, including chronic inflammatory infiltration, hyperplasia of mucous glands, and hypertrophy of smooth muscle. The presence of numerous eosinophils, however, is more characteristic of asthma. Since asthma is considered a reactive bronchial airway disorder, the lung tissue would not be involved.

Bacterial pneumonia (choice B) is characterized by intra-alveolar exudation of neutrophils, fibrin, and erythrocytes. Bacteria are also present within the alveolar cavities, confirmed with culture or Gram stain. Intra-alveolar hyaline membranes would not be present.

Desquamative interstitial pneumonitis (DIP) (choice C) is associated with tobacco smoking. DIP is more responsive to steroid treatment. Histopathologically, DIP leads to hyperplasia of pneumocytes and accumulation of histiocytes that fill the alveolar cavities. Acute inflammation and intra-alveolar hyaline membranes would not be present.

Hemodynamic pulmonary edema (choice E) is caused by increased hydrostatic pressure, as occurs in acute left ventricular failure (cardiogenic pulmonary edema), e.g., acute myocardial infarction and left-sided congestive heart failure. It is due to escape of fluid from the intravascular compartment into the alveoli. Hemosiderin-laden macrophages can be identified in this condition, but hyaline membranes would not be present.

choice_explanations.A: Asthma is a reactive bronchial airway disorder with eosinophils, mucous gland hyperplasia, and smooth muscle hypertrophy; the lung tissue is not involved.
choice_explanations.B: Bacterial pneumonia shows intra-alveolar exudation of neutrophils, fibrin, and erythrocytes; hyaline membranes would not be present.
choice_explanations.C: Desquamative interstitial pneumonitis is associated with smoking and shows pneumocyte hyperplasia and histiocytes filling alveoli, without hyaline membranes.
choice_explanations.D: Diffuse alveolar damage (ARDS) shows hyaline membranes, alveolar septal thickening, and neutrophilic infiltrate, and is caused here by burns and gram-negative sepsis.
choice_explanations.E: Hemodynamic pulmonary edema is due to increased hydrostatic pressure; it shows hemosiderin-laden macrophages but no hyaline membranes.

fa_summary: ARDS (diffuse alveolar damage) presents with acute respiratory failure and hyaline membranes; common causes include sepsis, burns, trauma, shock, and aspiration.

stem: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician after routine laboratory screening shows a total cholesterol of 320 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol of 35 mg/dL (normal > 40 mg/dL), LDL cholesterol of 220 mg/dL (normal < 189 mg/dL), and triglyceride 325 mg/dL (normal < 150 mg/dL). He denies shortness of breath and chest pain with exertion, but admits to occasional knee and wrist pain. He works in a manufacturing plant packaging goods. BMI is 35 kg/m². Physical examination shows raised, irregular, yellow papules in the skin below the eyes. He denies trauma to the eyes. His fingers, wrists, and knees are nontender to palpation. Except for some distal phalangeal knobby deformities, no other joint or skin lesions are identified. Which of the following histologic features would most likely be present in the skin lesions?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The lesions are xanthomas, which are tumor-like dermal collections of foamy macrophages (histiocytes) containing cholesterol and lipids. Specifically, due to their location under the eyelids, these lesions are known as xanthelasmas. Xanthomas are a broader term encompassing cholesterol collections under the skin, within tendons, or over joints. Minus aesthetic concerns, these lesions are typically asymptomatic.

Xanthomas and xanthelasmas may be idiopathic or may be related to hyperlipidemia, as seen in our patient, or lymphoproliferative malignancies (e.g. leukemias and lymphomas). They can also be a prominent feature of primary biliary cirrhosis, which often presents with hyperlipidemia due to impaired bile excretion. Moreover, this patient has osteoarthritis, which may be attributed to the patient's weight and manual labor work.

Calcium deposits (choice A) can occur due to trauma as a result of intracellular calcium release from cell injury and degeneration (dystrophic calcification). In addition, calcium deposits in skin can occur with hypercalcemia (metastatic calcification), such as hyperparathyroidism and CREST syndrome.

Fibrinoid necrosis with palisading macrophages (choice B) describes rheumatoid nodules, which are associated with rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis typically affects the knees, wrists, and elbows, and presents with joint swelling and deformities. Rheumatoid nodules tend to occur in the elbows, ulnar aspect of the forearms, and less commonly in organs (lungs, pericardium, myocardium, spleen), but not around the eyes.

Malignant nevus cells (choice D) reflect malignant melanoma and produce the brown pigment, melanin. These lesions classically present with much darker coloration compared to xanthomas.

Microabscesses in the stratum corneum (choice E) are small collections of neutrophils located in the stratum corneum (most superficial layer) of the epidermis and are classically associated with psoriasis. Psoriasis presents as raised, red plaques with silvery scaling, particularly on knees and elbows, but not around the eyes. Some patients also have an inflammatory arthritis.

choice_explanations.A: Calcium deposits occur with dystrophic calcification (trauma/cell injury) or metastatic calcification (hypercalcemia, e.g., hyperparathyroidism and CREST syndrome).
choice_explanations.B: Fibrinoid necrosis with palisading macrophages describes rheumatoid nodules, seen in rheumatoid arthritis, typically on the elbows and forearm rather than around the eyes.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Xanthomas (here xanthelasmas, under the eyelids) are dermal collections of lipid-laden foamy macrophages (histiocytes) containing cholesterol.
choice_explanations.D: Malignant nevus cells reflect malignant melanoma and produce melanin, presenting with much darker coloration than xanthomas.
choice_explanations.E: Microabscesses in the stratum corneum are collections of neutrophils associated with psoriasis, which appears on the knees and elbows with silvery scaling.

fa_summary: Xanthomas and xanthelasmas are dermal collections of lipid-laden foamy macrophages and are a sign of hyperlipidemia (or primary biliary cirrhosis).

stem: A 3-day-old newborn develops a localized, crusted infection near the umbilical stump. Twenty-four hours later, tender, reddened patches appear near the crusted area, progressing to painful and generalized skin erythema. By the next day, large, flaccid blisters appear that rupture easily. Large sheets of skin appear to have peeled off. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This infant has staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome, which is a severe skin condition with acute widespread erythema and epidermal peeling as a result of staphylococcal exotoxin. Note: Exotoxins are produced by bacteria and released, while endotoxins are intrinsic parts of the bacterial structure (e.g. lipopolysaccharide) and are usually found in gram-negative bacteria. The staphylococcal exotoxins released in scalded-skin syndrome target desmosomes between keratinocytes in the stratum granulosum. This produces fragile blisters that have a positive Nikolsky sign, which is also present in toxic epidermal necrolysis and pemphigus vulgaris.

Susceptible populations include infants, young children, and adults who are immunosuppressed or have renal failure. The history given here is typical for the presentation in babies, including involvement of the umbilicus. Skin biopsy (or examination of exfoliated skin) with frozen-section analysis can provide rapid diagnosis. Prompt therapy with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics will usually prevent death. These babies should be treated like burn patients and fluid resuscitation is paramount.

Impetigo (choice A) is a skin infection that is usually caused by either group A Streptococcus or Staphylococcus aureus. It is a superficial infection that initially presents as erythematous macules, eventually progressing to pustules that rupture and leave a crusting, yellow ("honey-crusted") discharge. Infection classically occurs on the face.

Scarlet fever (choice B) produces a maculopapular red rash that usually starts at the neck and chest and travels towards the extremities, sparing the palms and soles. The rash can often have a fine texture that resembles sandpaper. The disease is caused by group A streptococcus, and patients can present with a strawberry tongue, fever, and sore throat.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) (choice D) is a more severe version of Steven-Johnson syndrome (SJS), which can also produce diffuse erythema and blistering with a positive Nikolsky sign. Clinically, they appear fairly similar to patients with scalded-skin syndrome. However, usually these patients are older and present with involvement of mucous membranes. TEN and SJS are usually triggered by use of a new medication (anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, meloxicam, etc.) rather than an infectious agent.

Toxic shock syndrome (choice E) is also caused by Staphylococcus aureus and results from release of the exotoxin, TSST-1. Patients usually present acutely with significant fever, myalgias, hypotension, rash, and encephalopathy. TSST-1 is a superantigen, triggering many T-cells at once and generating massive cytokine release, causing the symptoms listed above. Patients die from shock and multi-organ failure. It is associated with prolonged tampon or nasal packing use. Patients are given clindamycin to stop toxin production and vancomycin to eradicate the bacteria.

choice_explanations.A: Impetigo is a superficial S. aureus/S. pyogenes infection presenting with erythematous macules and pustules with a honey-colored crust, classically on the face.
choice_explanations.B: Scarlet fever is caused by group A streptococcus and produces a sandpaper-like maculopapular rash sparing the palms and soles, with strawberry tongue, fever, and sore throat.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome is caused by a staphylococcal exotoxin that splits desmosomes between keratinocytes in the stratum granulosum, producing widespread erythema and flaccid bullae with a positive Nikolsky sign, often starting near the umbilicus in neonates.
choice_explanations.D: Toxic epidermal necrolysis is a severe drug-triggered (not infectious) mucocutaneous reaction, more common in older patients with mucous membrane involvement.
choice_explanations.E: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by the S. aureus superantigen TSST-1, presenting with fever, myalgias, hypotension, rash, and encephalopathy, associated with tampon or nasal packing use.

fa_summary: Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome is a staphylococcal exotoxin-mediated splitting at the stratum granulosum, causing widespread erythema and flaccid bullae with a positive Nikolsky sign, often beginning near the umbilicus in neonates.

stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of intense itching on her trunk and arms. She ate lobster last night and says that she usually has these symptoms after eating shellfish. Physical examination shows multiple erythematous areas with excoriations. The physician advises her to avoid shellfish to prevent these symptoms. A skin biopsy would most likely show which of the following abnormalities?

options.text: Accumulation of damaged elastin in the dermis
Granular complement and IgG at the dermal/epidermal junction
Intradermal edema and dilated superficial lymphatics

explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has a classic history of urticaria (hives), triggered by allergy to shellfish. Urticaria (hives) are pruritic wheals that form when mast cells degranulate and release histamine. Histamine increases microvascular permeability and triggers localized dermal edema with dilation of superficial lymphatic channels.

Allergy-induced urticaria typically occurs through IgE-antigen interaction. Briefly, sensitized IgE is already bound to mast cells located on the skin, conjunctiva, or mucosal surfaces. When IgE is exposed to the stimulating antigen (in this case, shellfish), cross-linking occurs and results in immediate mast cell degranulation. Mast cells subsequently release vasoactive compounds including histamine, leukotrienes, cytokines, and serotonin. Symptoms occur within minutes, and patients can present with urticaria, conjunctivitis, laryngeal edema, and/or hypotension.

Accumulation of damaged elastin in the dermis (choice A) is a feature of solar elastosis. It results from chronic, prolonged sun exposure and presents as thickened, dry, wrinkled skin. There is no association with an allergic reaction.

Granular complement and IgG deposition at the dermal/epidermal junction (choice B) is a characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). SLE is an autoimmune disease, which can produce a malar or discoid rash, among other systemic manifestations. Patients can occasionally present with a photosensitive rash as well.

Microscopic blisters (choice D) located at the tips of the dermal papillae, which are filled with neutrophils and varying numbers of eosinophils, are a characteristic of dermatitis herpetiformis. This occurs in patients with gluten intolerance and has a strong association with celiac disease. Look for a history of abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, anemia, and failure to thrive in these patients.

Microabscesses in the stratum corneum (choice E), also known as Munro abscesses, are a feature of psoriasis. Psoriasis presents as raised, red plaques with silvery scaling, particularly on knees and elbows. Pathologic features include acanthosis (stratum spinosum proliferation) and parakeratosis (retaining nuclei in stratum corneum). Patients may also present with an inflammatory arthritis.

choice_explanations.A: Accumulation of damaged elastin in the dermis is a feature of solar elastosis from chronic sun exposure, not an allergic reaction.
choice_explanations.B: Granular complement and IgG deposition at the dermal/epidermal junction is a characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Urticaria (hives) are pruritic wheals that form after mast cell degranulation and histamine release, producing localized (superficial) dermal edema with dilation of superficial lymphatic channels.
choice_explanations.D: Microscopic blisters at the tips of the dermal papillae filled with neutrophils and eosinophils are characteristic of dermatitis herpetiformis, associated with gluten intolerance and celiac disease.
choice_explanations.E: Microabscesses in the stratum corneum (Munro abscesses) are a feature of psoriasis, which presents with silvery scaling plaques on the knees and elbows.

fa_summary: Urticaria is a type I hypersensitivity reaction; mast cell degranulation with histamine release causes pruritic wheals with superficial dermal edema and dilation of superficial lymphatic channels.

stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of a non-healing sore on the vermilion of the middle of his lower lip. He has no history of major medical illness, and frequently goes bicycling. Physical examination shows a 1.5-cm raised lesion with an ulcerated surface and a pale edge. Biopsy reveals malignant epithelial cells with accumulations of keratin. Which of the following is the most likely precursor of this lesion?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient has squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip, which can present as an erythematous, non-healing ulcer. Major risk factors include heavy sun exposure, tobacco use (chewing tobacco, cigars, or pipes), alcohol, radiation, human papilloma virus (HPV), and arsenic exposure. While the diagnosis can be strongly suspected on clinical grounds, biopsy should be performed to establish the diagnosis. Microscopically, these tumors demonstrate the presence of malignant epithelial cells and keratin accumulations ("keratin pearls") with evidence of invasion past the basement membrane.

This question is a good exercise in understanding nomenclature. If sun exposure is the predisposing factor, which is likely in our bicyclist patient, the precursor lesion at the vermillion of the lip is usually an actinic cheilitis (actinic lesion of the lip mucosa). You can think of this lesion as a variant of actinic keratosis, which would be the correct name for the same lesion on the skin of the face and scalp. These actinic lesions are small, rough, erythematous papules which on the skin can present as "cutaneous horns." Pathologic examination of these lesions shows epithelial dysplasia and hyperkeratosis, without evidence of invasion past the basement membrane.

Rarely, chronic oral candidiasis (choice B) can cause squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity, but it would be unusual for the lesion to be on the lip. Typically, chronic candidiasis will occur in patients who are immunosuppressed.

Herpes simplex I ulcer (choice D) and canker sores (choice C) are not considered major risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma of the lip. Reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus may present as a painful ulcer on the lip, more commonly known as a "cold sore." These lesions self-resolve and would not present with pathologic findings consistent with malignancy.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Actinic cheilitis (actinic keratosis of the lip mucosa) is the typical precursor lesion of sun-exposed squamous cell carcinoma of the vermilion of the lip.
choice_explanations.B: Chronic oral candidiasis can rarely cause squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity, but this is unusual on the lip and typically occurs in immunosuppressed patients.
choice_explanations.C: Canker sores are not considered a major risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the lip.
choice_explanations.D: Herpes simplex I ulcer is not a major risk factor; herpes reactivation presents as a self-resolving cold sore, not a malignancy.
choice_explanations.E: Herpes simplex II ulcer is not considered a major risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the lip.

fa_summary: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip typically arises from actinic cheilitis in sun-exposed patients and shows malignant epithelial cells with keratin pearls.

stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine examination. She has a ten-year history of diffuse joint aches and fatigue, but has not seen a physician for it. She now has intermittent fevers and a photosensitive rash over her nose and cheeks. Serum anti-nuclear antibody and anti-double stranded DNA titers are elevated. Histologic examination of tissue from the skin lesion would most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Complement and IgG deposit at the dermal-epidermal junction

explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has a classic presentation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Symptoms include diffuse joint aches, fatigue, intermittent fevers, and rash. Other sequelae of this disease include hemolytic anemia, serositis, mucositis, and glomerulonephritis. Serum autoantibodies to double-stranded DNA is one of the most specific markers of SLE, though not particularly sensitive. Other markers for SLE include anti-nuclear antibody (ANA; sensitive, but not specific) and anti-Smith antibody (specific, not sensitive).

The skin is involved in the majority of the patients with SLE. Some patients present with a malar rash that has a butterfly distribution over the forehead, nose, and cheeks. Others may present with a discoid rash that have a disk-shape and can present anywhere on the body. Many of these lesions are photosensitive. The rashes result from deposition of autoreactive IgG and complement at the dermoepidermal junction, triggering inflammation. A similar phenomenon occurs in other autoimmune diseases including scleroderma and dermatomyositis. Deposition of immunoglobulin and complement is also the mechanism behind glomerulonephritis in SLE patients.

Accumulation of fibroblasts and collagen (choice A) are characteristic of scleroderma. Scleroderma can be either limited (CREST syndrome) or diffuse/systemic. Both conditions will have collagen deposition within the face and hands, and elevated ANA titer. Limited scleroderma is associated with elevated anti-centromere antibody titer, while systemic sclerosis is associated with elevated anti-Scl-70 (DNA topoisomerase I) antibody titer.

Microabscesses (choice C), also known as Munro microabscesses, are small collections of neutrophils located in the stratum corneum (most superficial layer) of the epidermis, and are classically associated with psoriasis. Psoriasis presents as raised, red plaques with silvery scaling, particularly on knees and elbows. Some patients also have an inflammatory arthritis.

Horn cysts (choice D) are collections of keratin that occur in seborrheic keratosis. These are flat, greasy, pigmented benign epithelial tumors of the skin. They are very common in older individuals; however, sudden appearance of multiple seborrheic keratoses may be a sign of underlying gastrointestinal malignancy (Leser-Trélat sign).

A sawtooth dermal/epidermal junction (choice E) is a feature of lichen planus, an inflammatory skin condition resulting from lymphocytic infiltrate. A good mnemonic for describing lichen planus is the 4Ps (Polygonal, Pruritic, Purple Papules). Lichen planus is associated with hepatitis C infection.

choice_explanations.A: Accumulation of fibroblasts and collagen is characteristic of scleroderma (limited/CREST or diffuse/systemic).
choice_explanations.B: Correct. In SLE the rash results from deposition of autoreactive IgG and complement at the dermoepidermal junction.
choice_explanations.C: Microabscesses (Munro microabscesses) are collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum seen in psoriasis.
choice_explanations.D: Horn cysts are collections of keratin seen in seborrheic keratosis.
choice_explanations.E: A sawtooth dermal/epidermal junction is a feature of lichen planus, associated with hepatitis C.

fa_summary: SLE skin lesions result from deposition of autoreactive IgG and complement at the dermoepidermal junction.

stem: A 53-year-old man comes to the physician because of a lesion on his nose that does not heal. He has had this lesion for the past year and noticed that it slowly grew and began to ulcerate. His past medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia, currently well-controlled on simvastatin and lisinopril. He does not have any other symptoms, though he does report a recent trip to Mexico with his wife. Physical examination shows a nontender, 1-cm, waxy, flesh-colored lesion with a rolled edge, telangiectasias, and central ulceration. Biopsy results are pending. The cells in this tumor are most closely related to cells in which of the following layers of the epidermis?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This is a typical description of basal cell carcinoma. It begins as a slow growing, pearly or waxy papule with telangiectasias and progresses to a larger lesion with rolled edges and central ulceration that does not heal. Histologically, the tumor is composed of small malignant basal cells that form dermal nests and strands with peripheral nuclear palisading.

Basal cell carcinoma typically occurs on sun-exposed areas of the head, face, neck, and upper trunk mostly because of UV skin damage. They rarely metastasize and can be disfiguring due to local destruction. Treatments include surgical excision and radiotherapy. If the lesion is not completely excised, it can recur. Basal cell carcinoma arises from basal cells in the deepest layer of the epidermis, the stratum basale. This layer of the epidermis undergoes the most cell division out of any layer.

The stratum corneum (choice B) is the layer of keratin composed of dead and dying cells on the surface of the epidermis.

The stratum granulosum (choice C) is at the top of recognizable keratinocytes in the epidermis, and contains multiple dense basophilic keratohyalin granules that contain lipids and help to form a waterproof barrier that helps prevent fluid loss from the body.

The stratum lucidum (choice D) is a layer of dead cells immediately above the stratum granulosum that is most easily seen in thick epidermis such as on the soles of the feet.

The stratum spinosum (choice E) is the layer of epidermal cells in the mid region of the epidermis that characteristically show intercellular bridges between adjacent cells due to the presence of many desmosomes. This layer is affected in pemphigus vulgaris, where there is autoimmune attack of these desmosomes resulting in blistering of the skin and oral mucosa.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Basal cell carcinoma arises from basal cells in the deepest layer of the epidermis, the stratum basale, which undergoes the most cell division of any layer.
choice_explanations.B: The stratum corneum is the layer of keratin composed of dead and dying cells on the surface of the epidermis.
choice_explanations.C: The stratum granulosum contains basophilic keratohyalin granules with lipids that help form a waterproof barrier.
choice_explanations.D: The stratum lucidum is a layer of dead cells immediately above the stratum granulosum, best seen in thick epidermis (soles of the feet).
choice_explanations.E: The stratum spinosum shows intercellular bridges from many desmosomes and is affected in pemphigus vulgaris.

fa_summary: Basal cell carcinoma arises from the stratum basale and presents as a waxy pearly nodule with telangiectasias, rolled borders, and central ulceration on sun-exposed skin.

stem: A 24-year-old woman gives birth at 40 weeks' gestation to a 3.3 kg (7 lb 4 oz) boy via spontaneous vaginal delivery. There were no noted complications with the pregnancy or delivery. Examination of the newborn shows a large right-sided birthmark on his face, extending into the scalp. The lesion is later diagnosed as a capillary malformation. The patient is also noted to have an absent red reflex in the right eye. Which of the following additional findings is most likely present in this newborn?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. A facial or scalp port-wine stain (a facial angioma, or nevus flammeus) should specifically suggest evaluation for Sturge-Weber disease, a slowly progressive neurocutaneous disorder. Port-wine nevi present as large flat, pink-red birth marks, usually located on the face and in the distribution of a cranial nerve (usually V1 (ophthalmic) and V2 (maxillary) distribution of the trigeminal nerve). The lesions persist throughout life and may darken as the child becomes older. When biopsied, these lesions appear to be capillary malformations.

The other clue pointing towards Sturge-Weber syndrome in our patient is the absent red-reflex on physical examination, known as leukocoria. Though such a finding should always prompt evaluation for retinoblastoma, leukocoria may also present in patients with glaucoma, a finding frequently associated with Sturge-Weber.

Other characteristics of Sturge-Weber include ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis (vascular malformations within the meninges), mental retardation, and focal or generalized seizures, sometimes with hemiparesis, sensory changes, or hemianopia. Patients may also develop pheochromocytomas.

As a caveat, Sturge-Weber is part of a family of neurocutaneous disorders known as phakomatoses. Other phakomatoses include neurofibromatosis, Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis. As the name would suggest, these patients usually have both cutaneous and neurologic findings, with increased incidence of certain tumors. Unlike most phakomatoses, Sturge-Weber is usually sporadic rather than genetic in origin.

Acoustic neuromas (choice A) are a feature of neurofibromatosis type II. This is an autosomal dominant condition due to mutation of a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 22. Other findings include glaucoma (like Sturge-Weber) and meningioma, although a port-wine stain would be unusual.

Cerebellar hemangioblastomas (choice B) are a feature of von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, which is an autosomal dominant condition resulting from mutation in the VHL gene on chromosome 3. Features of this disease also include bilateral renal cell carcinoma and retinal hemangioblastoma. There is also an association with pheochromocytoma.

Neurofibromas (choice D) are a feature of neurofibromatosis type I. This is also autosomal dominant and due to a mutation in chromosome 17. Findings can be summarized by the mnemonic CAFESPOT: Café-au-Lait spots (hyperpigmented macules), axillary freckling, eye findings (iris hamartoma AKA Lisch nodules), scoliosis, pheochromocytoma, and optic tumor (gliomas).

Subependymal and cortical tubers (choice E) are found in tuberous sclerosis. Other features include cardiac rhabdomyoma, retinal hamartoma, adenoma sebaceum (red papules on cheek), astrocytoma, ash leaf spots (hypopigmented macules), mental retardation, and renal angiomyolipoma.

choice_explanations.A: Acoustic neuromas are a feature of neurofibromatosis type II (chromosome 22), which can also cause glaucoma and meningioma, but not a port-wine stain.
choice_explanations.B: Cerebellar hemangioblastomas are a feature of von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL gene, chromosome 3), with bilateral renal cell carcinoma and retinal hemangioblastoma.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Sturge-Weber syndrome includes ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis along with the facial port-wine stain and glaucoma (leukocoria).
choice_explanations.D: Neurofibromas are a feature of neurofibromatosis type I (chromosome 17), with cafe-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, and optic gliomas.
choice_explanations.E: Subependymal and cortical tubers are found in tuberous sclerosis, along with cardiac rhabdomyoma, ash leaf spots, and renal angiomyolipoma.

fa_summary: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder with a facial port-wine stain (V1/V2 distribution) and ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis, seizures, and glaucoma.

stem: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of tender blisters on his arm and flank, worsening over the last few months. His past medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He is currently taking atorvastatin and hydrochlorothiazide for these conditions. Physical examination shows blisters and flaccid bullae; a few have ruptured, leaving red, sore, denuded areas. Pathologic examination reveals acantholysis and few lymphocytes. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?

options.text: IgA deposits in the dermal papillae

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is a rare and potentially fatal autoimmune condition seen in middle-aged to older adults. It is associated with painful, flaccid suprabasal/intraepidermal bullae formation on the skin and oral mucosa. It results from IgG against epithelial desmosome protein (desmoglein 3), resulting in intraepidermal keratinocyte separation (acantholysis) and bullae formation. The flaccid bullae in this disease reflect the poor cell to cell adhesion between keratinocytes due to desmosome dysfunction. The bullae also present with a positive Nikolsky sign, in which manual stroking of these blisters result in rupture. Ruptured bullae leave red, raw areas, which can mimic burns. If not treated with steroids, most will die within 1 year.

An important condition on the differential diagnosis for autoimmune blistering conditions is bullous pemphigoid (BP). Histologically, prominent eosinophils within blisters (choice A) would support bullous pemphigoid as the diagnosis. This condition presents with IgG autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes (choice C). Hemidesmosomes anchor basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane. As a result, the epithelial layer lifts off the basement membrane producing a non-flaccid, tense sub-epidermal/sub-basal blister. Unlike pemphigus vulgaris, bullous pemphigoid does not affect desmosome adhesion proteins. The associated antigens are bullous pemphigoid antigen 1 and 2 (BPAG1, BPAG2). Patients with BP usually present with pruritus in the skin surrounding the blister rather than pain. Bullous pemphigoid can affect various areas of the skin but almost never has mucosal involvement, unlike pemphigus. Pemphigoid also has a more favorable prognosis.

IgA deposits in the dermal papillae (choice B) is characteristic of dermatitis herpetiformis. Patients present with pruritic vesicles and papules at the dermal-epidermal junction, primarily on extensor surfaces. The disease is strongly associated with gluten sensitivity and celiac disease, and may result from cross-reactivity between gluten and reticulin in the epidermal basement membrane.

Blisters that are resistant to shear stress and do not readily rupture present with a negative Nikolsky sign (choice D). This negative sign is seen with subepidermal blisters such as bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis, and porphyria cutanea tarda. It is worth a brief mention of porphyria cutanea tarda, the most common form of porphyria. It has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and is characterized by a defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (part of heme synthesis). Patients present with painful, small, subepidermal photosensitive blisters on sun-exposed skin (face, hands, arms, and legs) due to buildup of porphyrin compounds close to the skin.

choice_explanations.A: Prominent eosinophils within blisters would support bullous pemphigoid, not pemphigus vulgaris.
choice_explanations.B: IgA deposits in the dermal papillae is characteristic of dermatitis herpetiformis, associated with gluten sensitivity and celiac disease.
choice_explanations.C: IgG autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes are seen in bullous pemphigoid, producing a tense subepidermal blister.
choice_explanations.D: A negative Nikolsky sign is seen with subepidermal blisters such as bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis, and porphyria cutanea tarda.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Pemphigus vulgaris produces painful flaccid intraepidermal bullae on the skin and oral mucosa (IgG against desmoglein 3), so oral mucosal lesions are expected.

fa_summary: Pemphigus vulgaris is an IgG-mediated (anti-desmoglein 3) acantholysis that produces flaccid intraepidermal bullae with a positive Nikolsky sign and oral mucosal involvement.

stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of multiple skin lesions on her hands and face. Some of the lesions have been present for years, while others only recently developed. She has a history of developing severe sunburns. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse is 92/min, blood pressure is 112/69 mm Hg, and respirations are 12/min. The patient has nearly white hair, pink irises, fair skin, and a history of burning easily when exposed to the sun. On physical examination, one lesion on her arm appears to be red and scaly, with ulceration and bleeding. Biopsy reveals invasive squamous cell carcinoma. This patient's condition is most likely caused by a disorder involving metabolism of which of the following substances?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient presents with a classic history of albinism, characterized by an absence of melanin production by skin melanocytes. The most common form of albinism is caused by a deficiency of tyrosinase, blocking the production of melanin from the aromatic (ring-shaped) amino acid tyrosine. This form of albinism is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Other congenital causes of albinism include defective tyrosine transporter (decreased tyrosine and hence melanin) and failed neural crest migration (melanocytes derive from the neural crest). Affected individuals lack melanin pigment in skin, hair, and eyes, and are prone to develop sun-induced skin cancers, including squamous cell carcinomas, basal cell carcinoma, and melanomas.

Maple syrup urine disease is an example of failed metabolism of the branched chain amino acids (choice B), which are leucine, isoleucine, and valine. This disease results from congenitally decreased alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase. Build up of the branched-chain amino acids (also known as alpha-ketoacids) in the blood causes life-threatening metabolic ketoacidosis, motor abnormalities, and seizures. Urine smells like maple syrup or burned sugar, giving the disease its name.

Tay-Sachs disease is an example of a disorder of glycolipids (choice C). In this autosomal recessive disorder, a deficiency of hexosaminidase A leads to accumulation of ganglioside GM2 in neurons leading to blindness, loss of developmental milestones, and death before 5 years of age. Patients may also present with a cherry red macula, due to glycolipid in the surrounding retina.

Hunter disease is an example of a disorder of glycoproteins (choice D). This mucopolysaccharidosis is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait caused by a mutation in the gene for iduronate 2-sulfatase. Affected children excrete dermatan and heparan sulfate in urine. Multiple phenotypic abnormalities including mental retardation, coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac defects, clear corneas (as opposed to Hurler disease that involves corneal opacities), short stature, and hearing loss. In the severe form, the condition is lethal by 5 years of age.

Homocystinuria disease is an abnormality in methionine metabolism, resulting in accumulation of homocysteine, a sulfur-containing amino acid (choice E). It has an autosomal recessive inheritance. Symptoms include a Marfan-like habitus, limited joint mobility, and mental retardation (absent in the mild form). Increased levels of serum homocysteine increases the risk for thrombosis (deep vein thrombosis and myocardial infarction, and stroke) by the third and fourth decade of life.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Albinism most commonly results from deficiency of tyrosinase, which blocks synthesis of melanin from the aromatic amino acid tyrosine.
choice_explanations.B: Branched chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) are affected in maple syrup urine disease, not albinism.
choice_explanations.C: Glycolipid metabolism is affected in Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency, ganglioside GM2 accumulation).
choice_explanations.D: Glycoprotein metabolism is affected in Hunter disease (iduronate 2-sulfatase deficiency, a mucopolysaccharidosis).
choice_explanations.E: Sulfur-containing amino acid (methionine/homocysteine) metabolism is affected in homocystinuria.

fa_summary: Albinism is most commonly caused by tyrosinase deficiency, preventing synthesis of melanin from the aromatic amino acid tyrosine and increasing the risk of sun-induced skin cancers.

stem: A 21-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine physical examination. He reports being previously healthy except for a heart murmur, which has not affected his daily life. He denies any bruising, bleeding, or visual abnormalities. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), pulse is 60/min, blood pressure is 121/76 mm Hg, and respirations are 12/min. His height is 195 cm (6'5") and weight is 61.2 kg (135 lb). On physical examination, the patient is noted to have indentation of his sternum. When he closes his fingers over his thumb, his thumb extends past the ulnar edge of his hand. Heart auscultation reveals a late systolic murmur with a mid-systolic click over the apex. Which of the following is most severely affected in this patient's disease?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The patient has Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a defect in the gene encoding the glycoprotein, fibrillin. Fibrillin is a major component of elastin-associated microfibrils, which are common in large blood vessels, ligaments, and the suspensory ligaments of the lens. Microfibrils, as a category, are ubiquitous matrix polymers that are thought to provide elastic properties to all extracellular matrix structures.

Abnormal fibrillin predisposes patients to cystic medial necrosis of the aorta, which may be complicated by aortic dissection. Other features of the syndrome are subluxation of the lens of the eye, mitral valve prolapse (which can be noted on our patient's heart exam), and a shortened life span (often due to aortic rupture). The patients are usually very tall, with long fingers, and sometimes hyperextensible joints. The positive thumb test described in the question is called a Steinberg sign.

Collagen (choice A) is a component of skin, joints and ligaments. Defects in collagen synthesis may cause Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which includes 10 variants. Ehlers-Danlos can be difficult to distinguish from Marfan syndrome as both can present with joint and skeletal abnormalities, mitral valve prolapse, and arterial rupture. However, only Ehlers-Danlos patients present with bruising or poor wound healing, and skin hyperextensibility, which are not seen in our patient. Another important collagen disease is osteogenesis imperfecta, an autosomal dominant disorder resulting from a defect in type 1 collagen. These patients present with blue sclera and frequent fractures starting in early childhood.

Desmosomes (choice B) are focal adhesions between cells consisting of intermediate filaments, and are not associated with fibrillin. The autoimmune disease pemphigus vulgaris results from dysfunctional desmosomes in the epidermis, producing fragile, intraepidermal blisters with a positive Nikolsky sign (rubbing results in skin exfoliation). These patients often also have mucosal involvement and can require burn-level care.

Microfilaments (choice D) consist of actin polymers, which are involved in the structural integrity of all cells. There are no known genetic conditions in humans associated with a defect in actin.

Microtubules (choice E) are comprised of tubulin molecules and are involved in intracellular transport, such as the transport of chromosomes during mitosis and meiosis as well as motility produced by cilia or flagella. Disorders of microtubule function are often involved in neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer disease.

choice_explanations.A: Collagen defects cause Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and osteogenesis imperfecta; Ehlers-Danlos may resemble Marfan but also shows bruising, poor wound healing, and skin hyperextensibility.
choice_explanations.B: Desmosomes are focal adhesions between cells (intermediate filaments); dysfunctional desmosomes occur in pemphigus vulgaris, not Marfan syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Marfan syndrome is caused by defective fibrillin, a major component of elastin-associated microfibrils found in large vessels, ligaments, and the suspensory ligaments of the lens.
choice_explanations.D: Microfilaments are actin polymers involved in structural integrity; no known human genetic condition results from an actin defect.
choice_explanations.E: Microtubules are tubulin polymers involved in intracellular transport and ciliary/flagellar motility; dysfunction is implicated in neurodegenerative diseases.

fa_summary: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by defective fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein component of elastin-associated microfibrils.

stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of severe asthma. The patient's mother states that he has tried several standard treatments that have not improved his symptoms. Treatment with a newer, more expensive drug (Drug A) is begun and the patient has no exacerbations and symptoms are improved. Six months later, the patient returns for a follow-up examination and still remains symptom free. However, the patient's mother states that she received a letter from her insurance company that says they will no longer cover the current, expensive medication (Drug A) and will only cover the full cost of a different, cheaper medication (Drug B) that is considered to be the "standard of care." The mother says that she cannot afford the cost of the newer medication (Drug A) without insurance. The physician contacts the insurance company and argues that the new medication (Drug A) should be fully covered, but he is told that the review process will take several months. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit the child to an inpatient setting and try to find an acceptable, covered, alternative medication
Attempt to make arrangements to provide the new medication (Drug A) for the child free of charge while the review process is taking place
File a complaint with the American Medical Association to pressure the insurance company to change their policy
Refer the parents to legal counsel to sue the company to force coverage of Drug A
Seek the advice of hospital legal counsel
Seek to exert pressure on the insurance company by notifying the local media of the child's case
Switch the child to the covered medication (Drug B), and monitor the child closely.

explanation:
The correct answer is B. If the physician truly believes that the current, expensive medication (Drug A) is the best for the child, then he must do all he can to see that the patient has access to this treatment. If cost is the barrier and the physician can find some way to waive the cost, then this is the obvious course of action. Remember that traditionally, doctors and hospitals provide a certain amount of care without charging a fee. The guiding goal must be care, not cost. Some additional avenues that the physician could explore include local charities, patient-assistance programs from the drug manufacturer, and suggesting that the mother contact the local public assistance office to see if her child qualifies for medical assistance. In summary, there are numerous options available for the physician to explore. The key point to remember for the USMLE (and in clinical practice) is that every effort must be made to ensure that the patient receives the appropriate care.

Admitting the child (choice A) is a costly alternative when the child is already taking an effective medication. Simply stated: If the child is maintained on the current medication, hospitalization is not warranted.

While it might be personally satisfying to pressure the insurance company (choices C and D) and might help children in the broader society eventually, it does nothing to help the present patient.

This question is decided not on the basis of legal opinion (choice E) but on the basis of clinical judgment. If the current medication is working and the alternative that is covered by the insurance company is unproven, then every effort must be made to maintain the proven treatment.

This option transforms a focus on a child's care to a media event (choice F). The child's confidentiality and the parent's privacy are at risk. The physician here has lost focus. The goal is to treat the child, not harness the media to change the world.

The child has already been placed on a variety of medications, none of which had the same efficacy as the one he is currently taking. Allowing the insurance company to override or even influence the physician's clinical judgment is ethically questionable and professionally unacceptable. The present history suggests that putting the child on the medication covered by the insurance company (choice G) places the child at an unacceptable risk.

choice_explanations.A: Admitting the child is a costly alternative when the child is already taking an effective medication; if the child is maintained on the current medication, hospitalization is not warranted.
choice_explanations.B: If the physician believes Drug A is best, he must do all he can to ensure access; if cost is the barrier and he can waive it, that is the obvious course of action (local charities, manufacturer patient-assistance programs, public assistance). The guiding goal must be care, not cost.
choice_explanations.C: Pressuring the insurance company might be personally satisfying and might help children in the broader society eventually, but it does nothing to help the present patient.
choice_explanations.D: Pressuring the insurance company might be personally satisfying and might help children in the broader society eventually, but it does nothing to help the present patient.
choice_explanations.E: This question is decided on the basis of clinical judgment, not legal opinion; if the current medication is working and the covered alternative is unproven, every effort must be made to maintain the proven treatment.
choice_explanations.F: Transforms a focus on the child's care into a media event; the child's confidentiality and the parent's privacy are at risk, and the physician has lost focus.
choice_explanations.G: The child has already failed a variety of other medications; allowing the insurance company to override the physician's clinical judgment places the child at an unacceptable risk.

fa_summary: When a needed treatment is not covered by insurance, discuss all options and inform the patient/family of financial assistance programs; the goal is care, not cost.

stem: A large university-based hospital starts a new policy where all incoming medical residents are required to spend 3 days covering various hospital policies. At one of these sessions, the head of the hospital's infection control team covers proper hand hygiene. Which of the following policies are most likely conveyed to the medical residents?

options.text: Alcohol-based hand rubs are used as the sole means of surgical antisepsis
Barehanded touching of patient secretions is acceptable provided the hands are thoroughly washed afterwards
Hands should be washed before glove placement and after glove removal
Hands should be washed only after treating a patient
Hands must be washed with antibacterial soap at the beginning of the day and only when coming in contact with patients believed to be infectious

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Proper handwashing is considered to be the single most important measure to prevent transmission of microorganisms between patients and caregivers as well as prevent nosocomial infections. However, numerous studies have shown that routine hospital practice compliance with this preventative measure remains unacceptably low. Improper hand hygiene practices is associated with health care-related infections, the spread of multi-resistant organisms, and has been a major contributor to microorganism outbreaks. Studies have shown that the prevalence of health care-associated infections decreased as hand hygiene measures improved. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), indications for hand hygiene include the following:
- Before and after treating each patient. In other words, before glove placement and after glove removal (choice C is correct and choices D and E are incorrect).
- After barehanded touching of inanimate objects likely to be contaminated by blood, saliva, or respiratory secretions.
- When hands are visibly soiled; before regloving, after removing gloves that are torn, cut, or punctured.
- For oral surgical procedures, perform surgical hand antisepsis before donning sterile surgical gloves.

For surgical antisepsis (choice A), the CDC recommends the use of water and antimicrobial soap (chlorhexidine, iodine and iodophors, chloroxylenol, or triclosan-containing products) or water and non-antimicrobial soap (plain soap) followed by an alcohol-based surgical hand rub product.

Barehanded touching of patient secretions is NEVER acceptable due to the risk of contracting numerous types of infection (choice B). Examination gloves are recommended for use when physically coming in contact with patients.

choice_explanations.A: For surgical antisepsis, the CDC recommends water and antimicrobial soap (chlorhexidine, iodine/iodophors, chloroxylenol, triclosan) or plain soap followed by an alcohol-based surgical hand rub, not alcohol-based rubs as the sole means.
choice_explanations.B: Barehanded touching of patient secretions is NEVER acceptable due to the risk of contracting numerous types of infection; examination gloves are recommended when contacting patients.
choice_explanations.C: Hand hygiene should be performed before and after treating each patient, i.e., before glove placement and after glove removal.
choice_explanations.D: Hands should be washed before and after treating each patient, not only after.
choice_explanations.E: Hand hygiene is indicated before and after each patient contact, not only at the beginning of the day or when a patient is believed to be infectious.

fa_summary: Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent transmission of microorganisms/nosocomial infection; wash before and after each patient contact (before gloving, after glove removal).

stem: A physician prescribes furosemide for one of the nurses in his office. The next day, the physician receives a call from the local pharmacy informing him that this medication is likely to cause an allergic reaction in the nurse because the pharmacy records indicate that she has a hypersensitivity to sulfa-containing drugs. Which of the following was most likely performed by the pharmacist prior to calling the physician?
explanation: The correct answer is B. Drug utilization review (DUR) is an authorized, organized, continual review of prescribing, dispensing, and use of medication. A DUR incorporates a drug review alongside a predetermined set of parameters that results in changes to both new and existing drug therapy when these criteria are not met. DUR involves comprehensive review of patients' prescription and medication information before, during, and after dispensing to ensure appropriate medication decision-making and positive patient outcomes. It attempts to identify inappropriate medication use, including therapeutic duplication, drug-drug interactions, drug-disease interactions, improper dosage, and improper treatment durations. Here, pharmacy personnel performed the DUR before dispensing, preventing a potential serious adverse event. AHA/JSA are workplace hazard/risk-assessment tools; FMEA is a prospective process-failure analysis; RCA is retrospective problem solving to identify root causes after a fault or adverse event has occurred.

choice_explanations.A: Activity hazard analysis (AHA) and job safety analysis (JSA) are workplace hazard/risk-assessment tools.
choice_explanations.B: DUR is an authorized, organized, continual review of prescribing, dispensing, and use of medication, applied here before dispensing to prevent a potential serious adverse event.
choice_explanations.C: Job safety analysis (JSA) and activity hazard analysis (AHA) are workplace hazard/risk-assessment tools.
choice_explanations.D: FMEA is a prospective process-failure analysis.
choice_explanations.E: RCA is retrospective problem solving to identify root causes after a fault or adverse event has occurred.

fa_summary: Drug utilization review (DUR) is a systematic review of prescribing/dispensing/use to prevent inappropriate medication use and adverse events (a medication-safety/error-prevention process).

stem: A 56-year-old man is brought to the physician by his daughter because of poor appetite and weight loss over the past 2 months. He states that his wife died 2 months ago from cancer and that he is experiencing a great deal of guilt about his wife's death and feels that he could have done more at the end. He also says he has trouble sleeping and is frequently fatigued. Which of the following is the most appropriate response for the physician?

options.text: "Have you ever thought about dying or killing yourself?"
"I think you have major depressive disorder and need an antidepressant. What are your thoughts about taking an antidepressant?"
"I'm sure you did everything you could. Nobody could have saved her."
