Laboratory tests show an erythrocyte count of 3.0 million/mm3, hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, hematocrit of 30%, and MCV of 125 um3. Serum folate level is normal and serum methylmalonic acid is elevated. Oral vitamin absorption studies demonstrate that the patient is unable to absorb vitamin B12 in adequate amounts without added intrinsic factor. This patient's condition is associated with an increased risk of developing cancer of which of the following organs?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Megaloblastic anemia with neuropathy suggests vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, which in this patient suggests pernicious anemia. Neurologic symptoms are the result of subacute combined degeneration, characterized by demyelination and degeneration of the dorsal and lateral white matter of the spinal cord. Symptoms include glove and stocking paresthesias (numbness and tingling), decreased sensation, and gait disturbances. Patients will also have glossitis and macrocytic RBCs with hypersegmented neutrophils. Pernicious anemia is associated with autoimmune chronic gastritis and seen in adults over age 30, with a peak age of 60. In this condition, an autoimmune attack on gastric parietal cells or intrinsic factor leads to atrophic gastritis (chronic gastritis type A) with deficient synthesis of the intrinsic factor (IF). Haptocorrin (R-protein) binds to vitamin B12 in the stomach and protects vitamin B12 from the acidic environment. In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases cleave this complex and release vitamin B12, where IF can bind to create the vitamin B12-IF complex. The complex is then absorbed in the ileum. Vitamin B12 is required for DNA synthesis in blood cell precursors; deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia. Chronic atrophic gastritis can predispose for gastric carcinoma. Causes of vitamin B12 deficiency include: Pernicious anemia: Autoimmune gastritis; Nutritional: Pure plant-based diet, diet lacking meats, dairy, eggs; Surgery: Removal of stomach or ileum (source of IF or absorption of IF) or ileal bypass; Crohn disease: Inflammation of the ileum; Fish tapeworm Diphyllobothrium latum infection; Medications: Purine and pyrimidine antagonists; Blind loop syndrome: bacterial overgrowth. Vitamin B12 deficiency is associated with elevated levels of methylmalonic acid (serum and urine) and serum homocysteine. Recall, methylmalonyl CoA is converted to succinyl CoA and homocysteine is converted to methionine. Without B12, these reactions cannot proceed, leading to their accumulation. In contrast, folate deficiency will only have an increase homocysteine level. Note: due to elevated levels of homocysteine, these patients have an increased risk for development of cardiovascular disease. Predisposing factors for colon cancer (choice A) include familial polyposis syndromes, inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis), isolated adenomatous polyps, and a diet high in animal fat. Duodenal (choice B) and ileal (choice D) cancers are uncommon. Predisposing factors for esophageal cancer (choice C) include chronic exposure to hot foods/liquids, tobacco smoking, Barrett esophagus (associated with adenocarcinoma of the lower esophagus) and Plummer-Vinson syndrome (associated with iron deficiency anemia, esophageal webs, difficulty with solid food, and squamous cell carcinoma of the upper third of the esophagus).

choice_explanations.A: Predisposing factors for colon cancer include familial polyposis syndromes, ulcerative colitis, adenomatous polyps, and a high-animal-fat diet.
choice_explanations.B: Duodenal cancer is uncommon.
choice_explanations.C: Esophageal cancer is predisposed by hot foods/liquids, smoking, Barrett esophagus, and Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
choice_explanations.D: Ileal cancer is uncommon.
choice_explanations.E: Chronic atrophic gastritis from pernicious anemia can predispose to gastric carcinoma.

fa_summary: Pernicious anemia (autoimmune chronic atrophic gastritis) causes vitamin B12 deficiency and predisposes to gastric adenocarcinoma.

stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of cough that is occasionally associated with blood. He has had similar episodes in the past. His temperature is 37.6°C (99.6°F), pulse is 74/min, blood pressure is 134/79 mm Hg, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 90%. Laboratory tests show: Leukocyte count 10,000/mm3, Neutrophils 62%, Bands 3%, Lymphocytes 25%, Monocytes 7%, Eosinophils 3%, Hemoglobin 18 g/dL, Hematocrit 35.4%, MCV 85 um3, ALT 15 U/L, AST 50 U/L, Serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, Serum urea nitrogen 23 mg/dL. Urinalysis 2+ blood, no protein. Urine microscopy shows numerous red blood cells and red blood cell casts. Which of the following antibodies is most likely present in this patient's serum?
explanation: The correct answer is E. This patient has Goodpasture syndrome, which results from autoantibodies to glomerular type IV collagen. This leads to antibodies binding to the basement membranes in the kidney, resulting in glomerulonephritis and hematuria. Antibodies also recognize and bind to lung basement membrane, causing pulmonary hemorrhage and hemoptysis. This is an example of a type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity reaction. Indirect fluorescent antibody test would show a linear pattern of IgG deposition within glomeruli. Goodpasture syndrome is a type II hypersensitivity reaction in which the antibodies also target the basement membranes in the lungs. Patients typically present with hemoptysis, pulmonary hemorrhage, and glomerulonephritis. Anti-double stranded DNA (choice A), anti-Smith (Anti-Sm), and anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) could be used as markers for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). ANA markers are the most sensitive markers for SLE, whereas anti-double stranded DNA and anti-Sm are more specific markers for SLE. Anti-double stranded DNA levels correlate with disease activity and kidney involvement in some patients who have SLE. This is a type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity that may cause vascular damage from complement-mediated lysis within small diameter blood vessels. SLE is more common in females than males and would be likely to have the additional manifestations of malar rash, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and arthritis. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (choice B) are associated with primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC). Clinical signs and symptoms include pruritus, jaundice, xanthomas, and xanthelasma. Anti-myeloperoxidase (choice C; also known as p-ANCA) is a marker for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA; also known as Churg-Strauss syndrome). This is a vasculitis involving small to medium-sized blood vessels, most commonly in the lungs and GI tract. Clinical signs and symptoms include asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, and pulmonary infiltrates. Anti-proteinase 3 antibodies (choice D; also known as c-ANCA) are seen in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis). There is involvement of the upper respiratory tract (sinusitis, nosebleeds, saddle-nose deformity, oral ulcerations), lower respiratory tract (hemoptysis and pulmonary infiltrates), and kidney (glomerulonephritis). Although our patient has lower respiratory tract (lung) involvement, he does not have upper respiratory tract involvement.

choice_explanations.A: Anti-double stranded DNA, anti-Smith (Anti-Sm), and anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) are markers for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), a type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity.
choice_explanations.B: Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are associated with primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC).
choice_explanations.C: Anti-myeloperoxidase (p-ANCA) is a marker for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA; Churg-Strauss syndrome).
choice_explanations.D: Anti-proteinase 3 antibodies (c-ANCA) are seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; Wegener granulomatosis), which also involves the upper respiratory tract.
choice_explanations.E: Anti-type IV collagen (anti-glomerular basement membrane) antibodies cause Goodpasture syndrome, a type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity with glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

fa_summary: Goodpasture syndrome is a type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-type IV collagen) antibodies.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is preparing for elective surgery. During his pre-operative work-up, it is discovered that he has had recurrent lung infections as well as otitis media and sinusitis periodically for most of his life. He is referred to a specialist for further evaluation. Laboratory studies show the following: Ig isotype (Patient's Value, mg/dL): IgM 160, IgG 770, IgA 4. Which of the following additional findings is most likely to be seen in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is D. This patient has selective IgA deficiency. The serum values quoted in this case are normal for all isotypes except IgA, which is significantly depressed. Selective IgA deficiency is the most common immunodeficiency disease in the United States. Patients with selective IgA deficiency have a tendency toward recurrent pulmonary and upper respiratory infections as well as atopic allergy. These patients can also present with infectious diarrheas. These patients may isotype switch to IgE more frequently, because of their inability to produce IgA. It is important to note that many patients with selective IgA deficiency have anti-IgA IgE antibodies. As such, they may have severe allergic reactions to blood products. Interestingly, these patients can receive blood products safely from other IgA deficient donors. Contact dermatitis (choice A) is a type of delayed-type hypersensitivity that depends on TH1 cells, macrophages, and lymphocytes. It is not increased in patients with selective IgA deficiency. Decreased phagocytic efficiency (choice B) is the hallmark of chronic granulomatous disease, but it is not often associated with changes in immunoglobulin. Immune complex disease (choice C) is more common in patients with complement deficiency. C3b plays an important role in the clearing of immune complexes (antigen-antibody) from the serum. It would not be associated with selective IgA deficiency. Partial albinism (choice E) is found in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, which is a defect in phagolysosome fusion within phagocytic cells.

choice_explanations.A: Contact dermatitis is a delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity and is not increased in selective IgA deficiency.
choice_explanations.B: Decreased phagocytic efficiency is the hallmark of chronic granulomatous disease and is not associated with changes in immunoglobulin.
choice_explanations.C: Immune complex disease is more common with complement deficiency (impaired C3b-mediated clearance of immune complexes).
choice_explanations.D: Selective IgA deficiency predisposes to recurrent sinopulmonary infections and atopic allergy (increased atopy).
choice_explanations.E: Partial albinism is found in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, a defect in phagolysosome fusion.

fa_summary: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency; it causes recurrent sinopulmonary infections and atopy with low IgA but normal IgG/IgM.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a large, painful boil on his left knee. He has a history of repeated infections with Candida, Staphylococcus, and Klebsiella since the age of 14 months. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 105/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 92/56 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 3 x 4 cm erythematous boil that is tender and warm to touch. Laboratory studies show WBC is 14,000/mm3, hemoglobin is 13.5 mg/dL, and platelets are 195,000/mm3. Laboratory studies show an abnormal result from the nitroblue tetrazolium reduction test. Cultures of the fluid from the boil grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following intracellular defense mechanisms is most likely absent in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is E. This child has chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), which is a genetic defect in one or more of the subunits of NADPH oxidase. Activation of this membrane-bound oxidase is the critical first step in the generation of toxic oxygen radicals within the phagolysosome. One of the products of this reaction, hydrogen peroxide, serves as the substrate for the second most important killing mechanism: myeloperoxidase acting to produce toxic halide radicals. Patients with CGD are prone to persistent infections with catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, because these organisms destroy the hydrogen peroxide that they produce metabolically, so neither of the oxygen-dependent mechanisms can function in intracellular killing during these infections. Typical catalase-positive microbes include Staphylococcus, Klebsiella, Serratia, and Aspergillus. Failure of phagocytic cells to generate oxygen radicals are easily detected by the nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) reduction test. Defensins (choice A), hydrolytic enzymes (choice B), and lysozymes (choice C) are part of the oxygen-independent killing mechanisms of phagocytic cells. These make up the least powerful of the intracellular killing mechanisms used by phagocytes, and there are no known disease states that result from such deficiencies. Myeloperoxidase (choice D) is an enzyme present in lysosomes that acts on hydrogen peroxide to produce toxic halide radicals such as hypochlorite.

choice_explanations.A: Defensins are part of the oxygen-independent killing mechanisms of phagocytes; no known disease results from their deficiency.
choice_explanations.B: Hydrolytic enzymes are oxygen-independent killing mechanisms; no known disease results from their deficiency.
choice_explanations.C: Lysozymes are oxygen-independent killing mechanisms; no known disease results from their deficiency.
choice_explanations.D: Myeloperoxidase is present in lysosomes and acts on hydrogen peroxide to produce toxic halide radicals such as hypochlorite.
choice_explanations.E: NADPH oxidase is defective in chronic granulomatous disease, causing susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms (abnormal NBT test).

fa_summary: Chronic granulomatous disease is a phagocyte NADPH oxidase defect causing recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms and an abnormal NBT test.

stem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician because of painful, swollen hands, fingers, and wrists that have been present and worsening for the last 6 weeks. She states that the pain is worse when she gets out of bed in the morning, and gradually improves throughout the day. Her pulse is 78/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows symmetric swelling of the proximal phalangeal joints and wrist joints. The joints are warm. Laboratory studies show a WBC of 5.6 x 10^3/mm3, hemoglobin of 10.1 g/dL, platelets of 499 x 10^3/mm3, ESR of 92 mm/h, and C-reactive protein of 54 mg/dL (Normal: < 10 mg/dL). Autoantibodies directed against which of the following antigens would most likely be associated with this patient's condition?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The disease is rheumatoid arthritis (RA), which is a chronic, systemic, inflammatory disorder of unknown etiology that primarily involves the synovial joints. This disease is typically symmetrical and can cause destruction of joints and joint deformities if uncontrolled. RA generally starts in the periphery and moves proximally over time. The symptoms include pain, stiffness (especially morning stiffness), and swelling of joints. Rheumatoid factors (RF) are autoantibodies, usually an IgM or IgG (or less commonly, IgA) that are directed against the Fc portion of immunoglobulin G (IgG). They are found in 75-80% of RA patients at some point during their disease course. Rheumatoid arthritis is a multi-factorial autoimmune hypersensitivity that involves the production of immune complexes (type III hypersensitivity) and cell-mediated destruction (type IV hypersensitivity). Type IV hypersensitivity is now thought to be the predominant cause of pathology in rheumatoid arthritis. Note: anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) can also be present in rheumatoid arthritis. Patients with RA can also have thrombocytosis (seen in our patient), which correlates with disease activity. Autoantibody directed against the cell nucleus, called anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) (choice A), are found in many disorders and in some healthy individuals as well. A positive ANA test is a sensitive marker for lupus, but can also be found in other rheumatologic diseases including rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, Sjögren syndrome, and many others. Lupus is characterized by a malar rash, photosensitivity, painful or swollen joints, oral ulcers, and/or anemia. Autoantibody directed against double-stranded DNA (choice B) is a feature of systemic lupus erythematosus, which is a type III immune complex hypersensitivity. Autoantibodies directed against histones (choice C) are a feature of drug-induced lupus, which is a type III immune complex hypersensitivity. Drugs that induce lupus include procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, and others. Autoantibodies directed against ribonucleoprotein (choice E) are a feature of mixed connective tissue disease and Sjögren syndrome, which are examples of type III immune complex hypersensitivities. Sjögren syndrome is characterized by xerostomia and xerophthalmia.

choice_explanations.A: Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) are a sensitive but nonspecific marker seen in lupus, scleroderma, Sjögren syndrome, and others.
choice_explanations.B: Anti-double-stranded DNA is a feature of systemic lupus erythematosus (type III immune complex hypersensitivity).
choice_explanations.C: Antihistone antibodies are a feature of drug-induced lupus (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid).
choice_explanations.D: Rheumatoid factor is an IgM (or IgG/IgA) autoantibody directed against the Fc portion of IgG, characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis; anti-CCP is more specific.
choice_explanations.E: Anti-ribonucleoprotein antibodies are a feature of mixed connective tissue disease and Sjögren syndrome.

fa_summary: Rheumatoid factor is an autoantibody against the IgG Fc region (with anti-CCP more specific) in rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 15-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of sore throat, rhinorrhea, fever, and productive cough. A review of his records shows that this is the seventh time over the last 8 months that the child has been brought to the emergency department because of an illness. Prior visits have been because of severe infections, including recurrent otitis media, and several episodes of pneumonia. His temperature is 37.6°C (100°F), pulse is 96/min (normal 70-110/min), respirations are 38/min (normal 20-30/min), and blood pressure is 96/70 mm Hg (normal 90-105/55-70 mm Hg). Physical examination reveals erythematous and edematous oral mucosa and posterior pharynx, scattered crackles and rales in the lower lung lobes, no palpable lymph nodes, no skin rashes or lesions. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 7,300/mm3, Segmented neutrophils 55%, Lymphocytes 38%, Monocytes 7%, Erythrocyte count 5.0 million/mm3, Hemoglobin 15 g/dL, Platelet count 400,000/mm3, Serum IgG 10 mg/dL, Serum IgM 5 mg/dL, Serum IgA 2 mg/dL. Flow cytometry reveals absence of CD19+ cells and presence of CD3, CD4, and CD8 cells. Which of the following genes is likely mutated or deficient in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is B. Bruton X-linked agammaglobulinemia is the only one of the humoral immune deficiencies in which there are no peripheral immature and mature B cells (no CD19+ cells). The mutation is in the Bruton tyrosine kinase gene (BTK), which is required for pre-B cells to develop to immature B cells in the bone marrow. The general B cell maturation order: precursor cell to pro B cell to pre B cell to immature B cell to mature B cell to plasma cell. Therefore, there will be no circulating CD19-positive immature and mature B cells, although cell-mediated immunity is basically intact. Lymph nodes will show decreased germinal follicles and B cell populations. Bruton agammaglobulinemia classically presents with increased susceptibility to encapsulated pyogenic bacteria, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Pseudomonas species, due to the lack of humoral immunity. Infants may develop recurrent otitis media, sinopulmonary infections, and pneumonia. Children from 1-12 years old show similar infections, with pneumonia, sinusitis, and otitis media caused by S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae type b. Adults are more likely to develop skin infections, often caused by Staphylococcus and group A Streptococcus organisms. Chronic sinusitis and recurrent pulmonary disease are common in adults. Treatment is with monthly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) and antibiotics as needed. Adenosine deaminase deficiency (choice A) is the deficiency underlying the autosomal recessive form of severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID). This disorder would affect both B and T cell maturation, not just B cells. Thus patients would be prone to acquiring bacterial, viral, fungal, and protozoan infections. CD18 (choice C) is deficient in leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD), leading to failure of diapedesis, in which neutrophils are unable to extravasate to an area of inflammation due to lack of the common beta chain of integrin molecules. Leukocytosis with neutrophilia would be present. It would not cause an absence of B cells. LAD type I is more common than type II and may present with delayed umbilical cord separation. The most common infectious agents include Staph species, Gram-negative bacteria and fungi (Candida). CD40L (choice D) is missing in hyper-IgM syndrome, in which IgM-producing B cells cannot receive the signal to isotype-switch to production of IgA, IgG, and IgE. The actual deficiency is in TH cells that are deficient in expression of CD40L. B cells would be present, but would not undergo class switching. Serum studies would reveal elevated levels of IgM, and low levels of IgG, IgA, IgE. Patients would present with recurrent bacterial, viral, fungal, and protozoal infections. NADPH oxidase (choice E) is the enzyme that is deficient in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), which will then result in an inability to generate toxic oxygen metabolites inside phagocytic cells. This would cause increased susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms, but would not result in diminished numbers of circulating B lymphocytes or reduced immunoglobulin levels. Leukocytosis with neutrophilia would be present. The nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) dye test is a useful diagnostic test. Neutrophils in patients with CGD are unable to reduce the oxidized NBT to insoluble blue formazan (reflects inability to promote an oxidative response).

choice_explanations.A: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes autosomal recessive SCID, affecting both B and T cell maturation.
choice_explanations.B: A BTK (Bruton tyrosine kinase) mutation blocks pre-B to immature B cell maturation, causing X-linked agammaglobulinemia with absent CD19+ B cells.
choice_explanations.C: CD18 deficiency causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency (failure of diapedesis) with leukocytosis but not absence of B cells.
choice_explanations.D: CD40L deficiency causes hyper-IgM syndrome in which B cells are present but cannot class switch (high IgM, low IgG/IgA/IgE).
choice_explanations.E: NADPH oxidase deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease (susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms), without loss of B cells.

fa_summary: X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia is a BTK mutation causing absent B cells and low immunoglobulins with recurrent sinopulmonary infections after maternal IgG wanes.

stem: A 35-year-old man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 90 cells/mm3 is admitted to a hospital in Mississippi because of headache, fever, worsening cough, weight loss, malaise, and dyspnea. Physical examination shows erythematous maculopapular lesions on the skin and in the oropharynx. The patient is also somewhat confused and has trouble walking. A chest x-ray shows hilar lymphadenopathy with diffuse nodular infiltrates. The hospital staff is concerned about the possible spread of the organism to other patients. The physician explains that the organism is not communicable from person to person. Which of the following best explains why the causal organism does not infect other patients?

options.text: It exists in a yeast form

explanation: The correct answer is E. Histoplasmosis is a systemic fungal infection that is acquired through inhalation of conidia or spores in soil or dust. Endemic regions include the Eastern Great Lakes, Ohio, Mississippi, and Missouri River beds. Histoplasma capsulatum causes a "fungus flu," which may present as an acute pneumonia with flu-like symptomatology. In humans, the organism is an intracellular yeast, which is therefore not communicable. Endemic region: Great Lakes to Gulf of Mexico. Disseminated infections are common in AIDS patients in endemic areas. Mucocutaneous lesions are common in disseminated infections. Within the body, Histoplasma capsulatum occurs as tiny, 2- to 4-micrometer yeast forms and is found intracellularly, particularly within cells of the reticuloendothelial system and in the lungs. This intracellular location is the principal reason why histoplasmosis is not usually communicable from person to person. Most immunocompetent persons who acquire histoplasmosis are asymptomatic; pulmonary disease can occur if the inoculum is very large. In immunocompromised patients (CD4 count < 150/uL), disseminated histoplasmosis may occur. Disseminated disease can produce constitutional symptoms (fever, malaise, weight loss), pulmonary symptoms, CNS involvement, cardiac involvement (including endocarditis), and skin and mucosal lesions. H. capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that forms yeasts (choice A) at body temperature; and at lower temperatures, forms hyphal forms (choice B) with macroconidia (choice C) and microconidia (choice D) reproductive structures. Infection is acquired by inhaling spores.

choice_explanations.A: H. capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that forms yeasts (choice A) at body temperature; this yeast form is the intracellular form and is not by itself the reason the organism is non-communicable.
choice_explanations.B: H. capsulatum forms hyphal forms (choice B) at lower temperatures (environmental phase).
choice_explanations.C: Macroconidia (choice C) are reproductive structures formed by the hyphal (environmental) phase of H. capsulatum.
choice_explanations.D: Microconidia (choice D) are reproductive structures formed by the hyphal (environmental) phase of H. capsulatum.
choice_explanations.E: The correct answer is E. Within the body, Histoplasma capsulatum resides as an intracellular yeast within cells of the reticuloendothelial system and lungs; this intracellular location is the principal reason histoplasmosis is not usually communicable from person to person.

fa_summary: Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that is an intracellular yeast in humans (in the reticuloendothelial system/lungs), which is why histoplasmosis is not communicable person-to-person; disseminated disease is common with CD4 < 150/uL.

stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of flank pain. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 62/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 150/120 mm Hg. An ultrasound of the kidneys shows enlarged kidneys with multiple round cortical cysts of varying sizes. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is A. The patient has adult polycystic kidney disease, an autosomal dominant disorder that causes an irreversible decline in kidney function. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is caused by mutations of either PKD1 (encodes for polycystin-1) on chromosome 16, or PKD2 (encodes for polycystin-2) on chromosome 4. Patients with PKD1 or PKD2 defects develop renal cysts and often present with hypertension (almost 100%), hematuria, proteinuria, or renal insufficiency. Other common symptoms include flank pain due to renal hemorrhage, calculi, and urinary tract infections. Polycystic kidney disease leads to increased renin secretion, thereby causing overproduction of angiotensin II. Since essentially all patients with ADPKD (due to PKD1 or PKD2) defects develop renal cysts, it is essential to have an understanding of the effect of these cysts on the RAAS. The renal cysts impair perfusion of glomeruli, which triggers the secretion of renin by the juxtaglomerular complexes. The renin secretion triggers the renin/angiotensin/aldosterone system. ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors, such as captopril, enalapril, and lisinopril, directly interrupt this system by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Furthermore, the ACE inhibitors increase renal blood flow and may provide renoprotective effects to hypertensive patients with this condition. The angiotensin receptor blockers, such as candesartan and losartan, are also considered to be first-line agents for the treatment of adult polycystic kidney disease. When treating hypertension, the drug of choice should be selected based on the underlying cause of the hypertension, the appearance of a concomitant disease state, drug-drug interactions, and whether or not one drug will help improve or treat another non-hypertensive condition. In this case, the ACE inhibitors will 1) treat the hypertension, 2) treat the underlying cause of the hypertension, 3) increase renal blood flow, and 4) potentially provide a renoprotective effect. None of the other answer choices that are antihypertensive medications will provide these same effects. Centrally acting sympatholytics, such as clonidine (choice B), lower blood pressure by stimulating adrenergic receptors (alpha2) in the brain, thus reducing sympathetic outflow. Calcium channel blockers, such as diltiazem (choice C), nifedipine, and verapamil control hypertension by blocking calcium entry into cells, thereby inhibiting vascular smooth muscle contraction. Epoetin alfa (choice D) stimulates erythropoiesis in anemic patients with chronic kidney disease. Although patients with polycystic kidney disease may progress to the point where they would need this type of treatment, there is no indication that this agent is currently indicated. Thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide (choice E) act on the early distal tubule, and might be appropriate if this patient had medullary sponge kidney due to abnormal calcium metabolism. However, in medullary sponge kidney, the renal ultrasound study would have more likely demonstrated cysts and stones in the renal pyramids rather than the cortex.

choice_explanations.A: The correct answer is A. In ADPKD, renal cysts impair glomerular perfusion and trigger renin release, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. ACE inhibitors such as captopril block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, treating the hypertension and its underlying cause while increasing renal blood flow and providing renoprotection.
choice_explanations.B: Centrally acting sympatholytics, such as clonidine (choice B), lower blood pressure by stimulating alpha2 adrenergic receptors in the brain, reducing sympathetic outflow; they do not address the RAAS activation of ADPKD.
choice_explanations.C: Calcium channel blockers, such as diltiazem (choice C), control hypertension by blocking calcium entry into vascular smooth muscle cells.
choice_explanations.D: Epoetin alfa (choice D) stimulates erythropoiesis in anemic patients with chronic kidney disease and is not currently indicated in this patient.
choice_explanations.E: Thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide (choice E) act on the early distal tubule and would be more appropriate for medullary sponge kidney rather than ADPKD.

fa_summary: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD1 on chromosome 16 or PKD2 on chromosome 4) causes bilateral cortical cysts, flank pain, and hypertension; ACE inhibitors/ARBs are first-line because they blunt the cyst-driven RAAS activation and provide renoprotection.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of enuresis that seems to occur 4 to 5 times a week and sometimes twice in the same night. The mother states that the problem began over the past few months, after she gave birth to a baby girl. She says that the boy is very embarrassed about his enuresis and is afraid that his friends will find out. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange to interview the boy about his condition
Direct the mother to have a serious discussion with her son about whether anything is bothering him
Prescribe a course of imipramine for the boy
Refer the mother to a seminar on enuresis and behavioral techniques to treat this condition
Send the boy to a child psychologist for counseling
Suggest that the mother block out some special time each day and give exclusive attention to her son
Tell the mother that the boy's problem is normal and temporary, and will soon pass if left alone

explanation: The correct answer is F. This type of enuresis, the result of the defense mechanism of regression, is very common when new siblings enter the household. Regression is characterized by returning to an earlier stage of development. This defense mechanism is also common when people are tired, ill, or uncomfortable. In this case, the boy feels neglected and returns to response patterns more typical of a younger child, either out of anxiety or as a direct attempt to gain more parental attention. Spending more individual time with the boy will help to reassure him of the mother's continued love and affection. With the motive removed, the symptom is likely to dissipate as well. Regression is an immature defense mechanism characterized by returning to an earlier stage of development. Regression can result from a sense of neglect following the birth of a sibling. Giving the child more attention will address the underlying issue and should resolve the problem. Arranging to interview the boy about his condition (choice A) is incorrect. Having to discuss a problem about which he is already embarrassed with the physician is likely to heighten, not reduce, the boy's discomfort and embarrassment. The issue here is between mother and child. The physician should encourage that direct relationship and not seek to form an indirect substitute. Directing the mother to have a serious discussion with her son about whether anything is bothering him (choice B) is incorrect. The capacity of a 6-year-old to articulate the abstract relationship issues that may be bothering him will be limited. More likely, the child will feel uncertain as to what to say, and may walk away with heightened embarrassment about his enuresis. Prescribing a course of imipramine for the boy (choice C) is incorrect. This is the correct pharmacology, but the treatment is premature. Imipramine will reduce the bed-wetting, but this merely addresses the symptom, not the root of the cause. Remember that one of the key mechanisms by which imipramine reduces bed-wetting is through the reduction of delta sleep, which is not a long-term solution for the child. Referring the mother to an enuresis seminar (choice D) is an example of "passing off" the treatment of the child. For the purposes of the USMLE, a physician should never "pass off" or transfer the care of a patient to another clinician (or in this case counselor). Furthermore, the underlying issue of regression first needs to be addressed by the physician. Sending the boy to a child psychologist for counseling (choice E) is incorrect. "Passing off" the child is wrong. This boy's problem can and should be dealt with by the physician. Telling the mother that the boy's problem is normal and temporary, and will soon pass if left alone (choice G) is incorrect. Enuresis after age 5 is diagnosable and therefore beyond the normal range. It is distressing to the mother and a cause of embarrassment to the child. The physician can and should provide guidance and help.

choice_explanations.A: Arranging to interview the boy about his condition (choice A) is incorrect. Discussing a problem about which he is already embarrassed is likely to heighten, not reduce, the boy's discomfort and embarrassment. The issue here is between mother and child.
choice_explanations.B: Directing the mother to have a serious discussion with her son (choice B) is incorrect; the capacity of a 6-year-old to articulate abstract relationship issues is limited, and the child may feel heightened embarrassment about his enuresis.
choice_explanations.C: Prescribing imipramine (choice C) is incorrect. It is premature: imipramine reduces bed-wetting by reducing delta sleep but only treats the symptom, not the root cause.
choice_explanations.D: Referring the mother to an enuresis seminar (choice D) is an example of "passing off" the treatment of the child; the physician should not transfer care, and the underlying regression must first be addressed.
choice_explanations.E: Sending the boy to a child psychologist (choice E) is incorrect. "Passing off" the child is wrong; this problem can and should be dealt with by the physician.
choice_explanations.F: The correct answer is F. The enuresis is regression triggered by the birth of a sibling; spending exclusive individual time with the boy reassures him of his mother's love, removes the motive, and allows the symptom to dissipate.
choice_explanations.G: Telling the mother the problem is normal and temporary (choice G) is incorrect. Enuresis after age 5 is diagnosable, distressing to the mother, and embarrassing to the child; the physician should provide guidance.

fa_summary: Regression is an immature defense mechanism in which a person returns to an earlier developmental stage; in a child it commonly presents as enuresis after the birth of a sibling and resolves with increased parental attention.

stem: A strain of knockout mice in which the gene encoding phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase (PNMT) has been deleted is used to study catecholamine synthesis. The mice are stressed and the adrenal glands are dissected and analyzed for catecholamine content. This analysis will most likely show the absence of which of the following in the adrenal glands?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The enzymatic reactions responsible for catecholamine synthesis begin with the conversion of tyrosine to L-dihydroxyphenylalanine (dopa) by tyrosine hydroxylase. This is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis. Dopa decarboxylase then converts dopa into dopamine. Dopamine beta-hydroxylase is an enzyme located within the vesicle membrane that acts on dopamine as it enters the vesicle to produce norepinephrine. Norepinephrine is stored in the vesicles and released via exocytosis upon demand. However, norepinephrine can diffuse into the cytoplasm, where it may be converted into epinephrine by the enzyme PNMT. Epinephrine may then return to the vesicle, diffuse from the cell, or undergo catabolism. In periods of stress, the release of cortisol stimulates expression of the PNMT gene, thus increasing epinephrine synthesis. The transfer of a methyl group to norepinephrine is catalyzed by PNMT and involves S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. The animals in this experiment were unable to produce PNMT; therefore, epinephrine production was inhibited. Because PNMT is involved only in epinephrine synthesis, choices A, B, D, and E are incorrect.

choice_explanations.A: Because PNMT is involved only in epinephrine synthesis, choices A, B, D, and E are incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Because PNMT is involved only in epinephrine synthesis, choices A, B, D, and E are incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: The correct answer is C. PNMT catalyzes the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine (using S-adenosylmethionine as the methyl donor). Knockout mice lacking PNMT therefore cannot produce epinephrine in the adrenal glands.
choice_explanations.D: Because PNMT is involved only in epinephrine synthesis, choices A, B, D, and E are incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Because PNMT is involved only in epinephrine synthesis, choices A, B, D, and E are incorrect.

fa_summary: Catecholamine synthesis: tyrosine → dopa (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting) → dopamine → norepinephrine (dopamine beta-hydroxylase) → epinephrine (PNMT, induced by cortisol).

stem: A 3-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination because of recurrent seizures. The pediatrician observes hypotonia, psychomotor retardation and developmental delay. Laboratory analyses show hypoglycemia and elevated plasma levels of lactate, alanine, pyruvate, and ketoacids. The infant is referred to a medical geneticist who suspects an inherited enzyme deficiency. This patient most likely has a deficiency of an enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of which of the following molecules?
explanation: The correct answer is D. Pyruvate carboxylase is a mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the formation of oxaloacetate: Pyruvate + CO2 + ATP -> oxaloacetate + ADP + Pi. This reaction serves to make the oxaloacetate used within the citric acid cycle. A deficiency of this enzyme has very broad metabolic consequences because the citric acid cycle is downregulated, with resultant downregulation of the energy-producing capacity of the cell. In addition to a general loss of energy in the cell, pyruvate levels rise because pyruvate is not converted into oxaloacetate; alanine levels rise because the normal conversion to pyruvate is feedback-inhibited. In hepatocytes, pyruvate carboxylase is also an essential enzyme in gluconeogenesis from the major gluconeogenic amino acid alanine. Thus, a defect in the enzyme results in hypoglycemia as observed in the patient. The enzyme is also involved in converting lactate to glucose. Clinically, pyruvate carboxylase deficiency shows variable expression due to allelic heterogeneity. The North American type, a moderate phenotype, is associated with mental retardation and lactic acidosis. Alanine levels and pyruvate levels are typically elevated. A more complex and life-threatening type is common in Great Britain and France. These children die before 3 months of age. Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by elevated levels of alanine, pyruvate, lactate, and ketoacids. Acetyl-CoA (choice A) is the product of pyruvate dehydrogenase. A deficiency of the enzyme would result in some of the clinical manifestations observed in the patient (elevated alanine, pyruvate, and lactate). However, hypoglycemia would not be a problem since the enzyme is not in gluconeogenesis. Acetyl-CoA acts as an activator for pyruvate carboxylase and would be derived from fatty acid oxidation. Acetyl-CoA is not a substrate or product of the pyruvate carboxylase reaction. Citrate (choice B), malate (choice C), and succinyl-CoA (choice E) are also citric acid cycle intermediates whose levels drop when pyruvate carboxylase activity is low, but this is a secondary effect that follows decreased levels of oxaloacetate. None of these metabolites are substrates or products of pyruvate carboxylase.

choice_explanations.A: Acetyl-CoA (choice A) is the product of pyruvate dehydrogenase. A deficiency of the enzyme would result in some of the clinical manifestations observed in the patient (elevated alanine, pyruvate, and lactate). However, hypoglycemia would not be a problem since the enzyme is not in gluconeogenesis. Acetyl-CoA is not a substrate or product of the pyruvate carboxylase reaction.
choice_explanations.B: Citrate (choice B), malate (choice C), and succinyl-CoA (choice E) are also citric acid cycle intermediates whose levels drop when pyruvate carboxylase activity is low, but this is a secondary effect that follows decreased levels of oxaloacetate. None of these metabolites are substrates or products of pyruvate carboxylase.
choice_explanations.C: Citrate (choice B), malate (choice C), and succinyl-CoA (choice E) are also citric acid cycle intermediates whose levels drop when pyruvate carboxylase activity is low, but this is a secondary effect that follows decreased levels of oxaloacetate. None of these metabolites are substrates or products of pyruvate carboxylase.
choice_explanations.D: The correct answer is D. Pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-requiring mitochondrial enzyme that converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate. It replenishes the citric acid cycle and is required for gluconeogenesis from alanine and lactate; its deficiency causes hypoglycemia with elevated alanine, pyruvate, lactate, and ketoacids.
choice_explanations.E: Citrate (choice B), malate (choice C), and succinyl-CoA (choice E) are also citric acid cycle intermediates whose levels drop when pyruvate carboxylase activity is low, but this is a secondary effect that follows decreased levels of oxaloacetate. None of these metabolites are substrates or products of pyruvate carboxylase.

fa_summary: Gluconeogenesis: pyruvate carboxylase (mitochondrial, biotin/ATP-dependent, activated by acetyl-CoA) converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate; its deficiency causes hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and elevated alanine/pyruvate/ketoacids.

stem: To protect blood supplies from contamination, screening of all donors for hepatitis C infection is required. This screening test has a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 90% and is used on a sample of donors in which 10% are known to have hepatitis C infection. Which of the following is the best estimate of the chance that a donor who tests negative is actually free of infection?
explanation:
The correct answer is F. To answer this question, construct a 2 x 2 table. Start with a sample of 1,000 because it is a nice round number. Screening tests are about ratios; it does not matter what sample size is used. The table is then completed by computing 10% of 1,000 for the total number of diseased in the sample (100), and taking 95% (the sensitivity) of this 100 and 90% (the specificity) of the remaining 900 non-diseased part of the sample. With the table complete, negative predictive value (NPV) can be computed using the given numbers.

Negative predictive value (NPV): probability that a person with a negative test is a true negative. Can be calculated as: True Negatives / All Negatives (or True Negatives / [True Negatives + False Negatives]).

NPV = TN/(TN + FN) = 810/(810 + 5) = 810/815, or just over 99%. (You can estimate that without actually completing the calculation.)

To complete the full set of calculations:
- Positive predictive value (PPV) = TP/(TP + FP) = 95/(95 + 90) = 95/185
- Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN) = 95/(95 + 5) = 95/100
- Specificity = TN/(TN + FP) = 810/(810 + 90) = 810/900
- Accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN) = (95 + 810)/(95 + 810 + 90 + 5) = 905/1000

The test has excellent NPV but a PPV that is only slightly better than chance (50%).

A review of terminology:
Negative predictive value: the probability of no disease in a person who receives a negative test result, or the probability that a person with a negative test is disease-free. It is also known as the "predictive value of a negative test." NPV = TN/(TN + FN).
Positive predictive value: the probability of disease in a person who receives a positive test result, or the probability that a person with a positive test does have the disease. This is also known as the "predictive value of a positive test." PPV = TP/(TP + FP).
Sensitivity: the probability of correctly identifying a case of disease, or the proportion of truly diseased persons in the screened population who are identified as diseased. It is also known as the "true positive rate." Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN). Sensitivity is best utilized in ruling out disease. (SN-OUT)
Specificity: the probability of correctly identifying disease-free persons, or the proportion of truly nondiseased persons who have a negative test result. It is also known as the "true negative rate." Specificity = TN/(TN + FP). Specificity is best utilized in ruling in a disease. (SP-IN)
Accuracy: the total percentage correctly selected; the degree to which a measurement, or an estimate based on measurements, represents the true value of the attribute being measured. Accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN) = (true positives + true negatives)/total screened patients.

choice_explanations.A: Choice A (45%) is not the NPV; the NPV is the probability that a person with a negative test is truly disease-free.
choice_explanations.B: Choice B (50%) corresponds to the PPV in this example (95/185), which is only slightly better than chance, not the NPV.
choice_explanations.C: Choice C (85%) is not obtained by the correct calculation.
choice_explanations.D: Choice D (90%) equals the specificity, not the NPV.
choice_explanations.E: Choice E (95%) equals the sensitivity, not the NPV.
choice_explanations.F: The correct answer is F. NPV = TN/(TN + FN) = 810/(810 + 5) = 810/815, or just over 99%.

fa_summary: The negative predictive value is the probability that a person with a negative test is truly disease-free (TN/[TN + FN]); it rises with high sensitivity and low disease prevalence.

stem:
At a local medical center, the incidence of nurse-related needlestick injuries in the first year of employment is 3 times higher than that of nurses working 3 years or more. Wishing to reduce the incidence of needlestick injuries, the hospital administration hires a consultant to determine if the hospital should hire only those nursing-school graduates whose training includes formal instruction in universal precautions. To test this idea, 40 nurses who reported needlestick injuries during their first year of employment are compared with 40 nurses who reported no needlestick injuries during their first year. The schools of all 80 nurses are contacted and asked about formal training programs for universal precautions. The results of the study are presented below:

                Needle stick    No needle stick    Totals
Training  No    21              6
          Yes   19              34
          Totals 40             40

Which of the following formulas would most likely be used to analyze data from this study?
explanation:
The correct answer is F. This question tests the student's capacity to recognize the type of study design that is described, and then the ability to know the proper method for analyzing the data. The study presented here classifies the nurses on the basis of reports of needlestick injuries, then looks back in their history for the absence (risk factor) or presence (no risk factor) of formal universal-precautions training. This retrospective study is best characterized as a case-control study: cases (needlestick) compared to controls (no needlesticks). Case-control studies are analyzed by means of an odds ratio. The most commonly used formula for an odds ratio is (a/c)/(b/d) or for computational purposes (ad)/(bc). The "a" cell in the 2 x 2 table is the cases with the risk factor and a needle stick (21). In this study, "21" represents the number of students without training, hence, this is a risk factor. The "d" cell is diagonal from that (34), which is no needle stick and with training. The two remaining cells are "b" and "c", which are no needle stick, no training AND needle stick with training, respectively. Therefore (ad)/(bc) = (21 x 34)/(6 x 19).

An odds ratio can be calculated from a 2x2 table using the following formula:
Odds Ratio = (A/C) / (B/D) = (AD) / (BC)

Please note that if you put disease on the left and exposure on the top, you will get (21/19)/(6/34), which is the same as (21 x 34)/(6 x 19). The only difference would be that the cells would be labeled differently.

We encourage you to explore both ways of setting up the table, and seeing that the basic idea is: (Ratio of diseased people with risk factor to diseased people without risk factor) divided by (Ratio of nondiseased people with risk factor to nondiseased without risk factor). This formulation will ALWAYS work.

Choice D is the formula for relative risk, which would be the correct answer if this study were a cohort study (a prospective study looking at disease incidence).

Choice G is the formula for absolute risk reduction, which is the difference in risk attributable to the intervention compared to a control group.

Choice H is the formula for attributable risk which is the incidence rate of exposed group minus the incidence rate of the unexposed.

RISK ANALYSIS
Odds Ratio: AD/BC
Relative risk: [A/(A+B)] / [C/(C+D)]
Attributable risk: [A/(A+B)] - [C/(C+D)]

choice_explanations.A: Choice A is not the odds ratio; a case-control study is analyzed with the odds ratio, not with ratios of row totals.
choice_explanations.B: Choice B is not the odds ratio for this 2 x 2 table.
choice_explanations.C: Choice C is not the correct odds-ratio formula; the odds ratio is (AD)/(BC) = (21 x 34)/(6 x 19).
choice_explanations.D: Choice D is the formula for relative risk, which would be the correct answer if this study were a cohort study (a prospective study looking at disease incidence).
choice_explanations.E: Choice E is not the odds ratio for this 2 x 2 table.
choice_explanations.F: The correct answer is F. Case-control studies are analyzed by the odds ratio, (a/c)/(b/d) = (AD)/(BC) = (21 x 34)/(6 x 19).
choice_explanations.G: Choice G is the formula for absolute risk reduction, which is the difference in risk attributable to the intervention compared to a control group.
choice_explanations.H: Choice H is the formula for attributable risk which is the incidence rate of exposed group minus the incidence rate of the unexposed.

fa_summary: Case-control studies (retrospective) are analyzed with the odds ratio, calculated from a 2 x 2 table as (AD)/(BC) = (a/c)/(b/d).

stem: A study is conducted to evaluate intelligence quotient (IQ) scores for patients with different types of schizophrenia. Results for the 100 patients who complete the test show an average IQ of 110 with a standard deviation of 20. Which of the following is the best estimate of the 95% confidence interval for the mean in this sample?
explanation:
The correct answer is F. A confidence interval uses sample data to calculate an estimated range of values that is likely to include an unknown population parameter, for example, the mean. The confidence level (in this case 95%) reflects the probability that the confidence interval will contain the true parameter. The formula for the confidence interval of the mean is
CI = sample mean +/- Z x (SD/square root of n); SD = standard deviation and n is the sample size.
Note that (SD/square root of n) is the standard error of the mean (SEM). If the SD is larger, the chance of error is greater; if the sample size is larger, the chance of error in the estimate is less.

The mean is given as 110. To achieve a 95% confidence interval, use a Z-score of 1.96 (or 2.0, to make the calculation easier). The standard deviation (SD) is given as 20 and the sample size is given as 100. Inserting these values into the formula: CI = 110 +/- 2 x (20/10); CI = 110 +/- 4, or a range of 106 to 114.

Choice A is incorrect. In the population as a whole, the IQ mean is 100 with a standard deviation of 15. 95% of the scores would fall between 70 and 130 (mean +/- 2SD). Asking for a 95% confidence interval is not the same thing as asking for 95% of the cases in a normal distribution. The 95% confidence interval is an inferential statistic, and can be used to try and decide what the true mean might be, while the range of scores that account for 95% of the sample is merely a descriptive statistic, and cannot be used to make any assumptions about the true mean.

Choice B provides the given mean of 110 +/- 2SD. But the question asks for the 95% confidence interval, not for the scores of 95% of the people who took the test.

Regarding choice C, see the discussion of choice A. Choice C is the result for 68% of the cases in a population with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15 (mean +/- 1SD).

For choice D, see the comments on choice B. In this case, the result is for a mean of 110 +/- 1SD.

Choice E is simply the given mean (110) +/- 5. If this appeared to be the right answer, then a calculation error was made.

choice_explanations.A: Choice A is incorrect. In the population as a whole, the IQ mean is 100 with a standard deviation of 15; 95% of the scores would fall between 70 and 130 (mean +/- 2SD), which is a descriptive statistic, not a confidence interval.
choice_explanations.B: Choice B provides the given mean of 110 +/- 2SD. But the question asks for the 95% confidence interval, not for the scores of 95% of the people who took the test.
choice_explanations.C: Regarding choice C, see the discussion of choice A. Choice C is the result for 68% of the cases in a population with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15 (mean +/- 1SD).
choice_explanations.D: For choice D, see the comments on choice B. In this case, the result is for a mean of 110 +/- 1SD.
choice_explanations.E: Choice E is simply the given mean (110) +/- 5. If this appeared to be the right answer, then a calculation error was made.
choice_explanations.F: The correct answer is F. CI = 110 +/- 2 x (20/10) = 110 +/- 4, or a range of 106 to 114.

fa_summary: The 95% confidence interval of the mean = sample mean +/- Z x (SD/square root of n), using a Z-score of 1.96.

stem: An 8-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of repeated episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia. Laboratory studies of serum show very low levels of IgM, IgG, and IgA. Flow cytometry of a peripheral blood smear shows a near absence of CD19+ cells, although levels of CD4+ and CD56+ cells are within normal limits. A bone marrow biopsy shows abnormally high numbers of cells with cytoplasmic mu chains, but none bearing surface IgM molecules. Which of the following proteins is most likely deficient in this patient?

options.text: Gamma chain of the IL-2 receptor

explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient has X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia, which is one of the more common forms of primary immunodeficiency. It is caused by a block in the B-cell maturational process due to mutations in a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase, called Bruton tyrosine kinase (btk), which is believed to be critical in transducing signals that drive pro-B cells to pre-B cells and pre-B cells to mature naive B cells. As a result, B-cell maturation stops at the point that the heavy chain genes have been rearranged, and cells will not develop beyond the point at which they can produce cytoplasmic mu heavy chains.

Adenosine deaminase (choice A) deficiency is a cause of severe combined immunodeficiency. It causes the buildup of toxic products in lymphocytes, which decreases their levels in the peripheral blood and elsewhere. In such a case, all lymphocyte categories would be depressed in the blood.

CD40 ligand (choice B) deficiency is the cause of hyper-IgM syndrome, in which there is an inability to switch immunoglobulin isotypes due to the absence of a stimulatory TH cell signal. The present patient has depressed, not elevated, levels of IgM.

Absence of MHC class II (choice C) is found in bare lymphocyte syndrome. In this case there would be depressed numbers of CD4+ cells but normal maturation of B cells.

Absence of the gamma chain of the IL-2 receptor (choice D) is a cause of severe combined immunodeficiency. Its absence causes the failure of proliferative responses in both B and T lymphocytes, so both would be present at depressed levels.

choice_explanations.A: Adenosine deaminase (choice A) deficiency is a cause of severe combined immunodeficiency. It causes the buildup of toxic products in lymphocytes, which decreases their levels in the peripheral blood and elsewhere. In such a case, all lymphocyte categories would be depressed in the blood.
choice_explanations.B: CD40 ligand (choice B) deficiency is the cause of hyper-IgM syndrome, in which there is an inability to switch immunoglobulin isotypes due to the absence of a stimulatory TH cell signal. The present patient has depressed, not elevated, levels of IgM.
choice_explanations.C: Absence of MHC class II (choice C) is found in bare lymphocyte syndrome. In this case there would be depressed numbers of CD4+ cells but normal maturation of B cells.
choice_explanations.D: Absence of the gamma chain of the IL-2 receptor (choice D) is a cause of severe combined immunodeficiency. Its absence causes the failure of proliferative responses in both B and T lymphocytes, so both would be present at depressed levels.
choice_explanations.E: The correct answer is E. X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia is caused by a mutation in a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase (Bruton tyrosine kinase, btk); B-cell maturation arrests after heavy-chain rearrangement, so B cells are absent (low CD19+) and immunoglobulins are very low.

fa_summary: X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia is a B-cell immunodeficiency caused by a mutation in Bruton tyrosine kinase (btk), causing absent B cells (low CD19+) and low immunoglobulin levels with recurrent sinopulmonary infections.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman returns to her physician for progressive fatigue and decreased amount of urine. She reports chronic joint stiffness, particularly in her hands and knees, worse in the morning and improving with activity. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.9°F), blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg, pulse is 78/min, and respirations are 13/min. Physical examination reveals mild periorbital and ankle edema. There is ulnar deviation of both wrists and significant deformation of her proximal interphalangeal joints. Laboratory studies show:

Hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL
Leukocyte count 5.0 x 103/mm3
Erythrocyte count 2.0 x 106/mm3
Reticulocyte count 3.0%
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 30 mm/h
Platelet count 250 x 103/mm3
Mean corpuscular volume 96 um3
2 hr postprandial glucose 115 mg/dL
Serum sodium 156 mEq/L
Potassium 5.2 mEq/L
Calcium 9.0 mg/dL
Blood urea nitrogen (elevated)
Creatinine (elevated)

Urinalysis shows:
Protein 3 g
No crystals or casts

Renal biopsy shows thickening of the mesangial matrix and deposition of amorphous eosinophilic proteinaceous material. The material exhibits apple-green birefringence on polarization with Congo Red stain. In which of the following locations is this material most likely synthesized?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient most likely presents with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), complicated by amyloidosis. RA is a chronic inflammatory joint disease characterized by morning stiffness improving with activity, ulnar deviation, subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules, constitutional symptoms, and inflammatory pannus formation. RA can involve a number of joints but in the hand it characteristically affects the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, while sparing the distal interphalangeal joints (DIP).

As with other systemic inflammatory conditions, RA can also result in amyloidosis. The liver produces serum amyloid-associated (SAA) protein in response to systemic inflammation (cytokine-mediated). SAA can degrade to form amyloid-associated (AA) protein, which can distribute in the kidneys, heart, and gastrointestinal tract. In our patient, deposition of amyloid in the kidneys results in glomerular disease. Amyloid stains red with Congo Red stain and exhibits apple-green birefringence upon polarization. Other chronic inflammatory conditions associated with AA amyloid deposition include chronic tuberculosis and SLE.

This patient has an elevated ESR and normocytic anemia (low RBC count and Hb, normal MCV) associated with chronic inflammation. An elevated reticulocyte count reflects normal bone marrow response to anemia. Elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen support renal dysfunction due to amyloid deposition within the kidney. Proteinuria is characteristic of amyloidosis. A normal calcium level rules out multiple myeloma-associated amyloid. A normal postprandial glucose rules out diabetes mellitus.

Bone marrow (choice A) and lymph nodes are the source of the amyloid light chain proteins, which cause amyloidosis in plasma cell proliferations (e.g., multiple myeloma). Symptoms include hypercalcemia, renal disease, anemia (hemolytic), and lytic bone lesions (CRAB mnemonic), which is mostly inconsistent with our patient's presentation. This is the most common form of amyloidosis in the United States today.

Beta amyloid proteins found in the brain (choice B) form the core of the plaques in Alzheimer disease.

The synovium (choice D) may be the site of chronic inflammation and pannus formation in RA, but is not the site of amyloid synthesis.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma; excess calcitonin production by neoplastic parafollicular (C) cells leads to heavy amyloid deposition within the thyroid gland (choice E). Symptoms of this disease include an enlarging neck mass and diarrhea, which are not consistent with our patient's presentation.

choice_explanations.A: Bone marrow (choice A) and lymph nodes are the source of the amyloid light chain (AL) proteins, which cause amyloidosis in plasma cell proliferations (e.g., multiple myeloma; hypercalcemia, renal disease, anemia, and lytic bone lesions). This is mostly inconsistent with our patient's presentation.
choice_explanations.B: Beta amyloid proteins found in the brain (choice B) form the core of the plaques in Alzheimer disease.
choice_explanations.C: The correct answer is C. The liver synthesizes serum amyloid-associated (SAA) protein in response to systemic inflammation; SAA degrades to AA amyloid, which deposits in the kidney (Congo red, apple-green birefringence) in secondary amyloidosis from chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis.
choice_explanations.D: The synovium (choice D) may be the site of chronic inflammation and pannus formation in RA, but is not the site of amyloid synthesis.
choice_explanations.E: Medullary thyroid carcinoma; excess calcitonin production by neoplastic parafollicular (C) cells leads to heavy amyloid deposition within the thyroid gland (choice E). Symptoms of this disease include an enlarging neck mass and diarrhea, which are not consistent with our patient's presentation.

fa_summary: Secondary (AA) amyloidosis results when chronic inflammation (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis) drives hepatic production of serum amyloid-associated (SAA) protein, which is degraded to AA amyloid that deposits in the kidney and other organs (Congo red with apple-green birefringence).

stem: A 31-year-old woman who is a physical education teacher comes to the physician for a routine examination. She has no history of major medical illness. For several months, she has had heavy menstrual periods lasting 8 days. There is no family history of easy bruising or bleeding conditions. She denies recent infections. She occasionally takes ibuprofen for minor muscle aches. Physical examination shows mucosal petechiae and several nonpalpable ecchymoses on both legs from sports-related trauma. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 5 x 10³/mm³, a platelet count of 31,000/mm³, and a serum creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL. Urinalysis is normal. A peripheral blood smear shows decreased numbers of platelets, but normal cell morphology. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Idiopathic (immune) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) has two distinct clinical forms: acute and chronic. The acute form is commonly seen in children, particularly after an infection and usually resolves spontaneously. The chronic form is usually seen in adults and persists for longer than 6 months. Both forms of ITP are considered an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies form against platelet glycoproteins. Antibodies present on the platelet surface will be recognized by the reticuloendothelial system and removed, via phagocytosis, from the circulation, thereby causing the thrombocytopenia. Secondary thrombocytopenia can be produced by lupus, viral infections, and drugs. Only when secondary thrombocytopenia has been ruled out can the diagnosis of ITP be made. The bone marrow would show megakaryocyte hyperplasia. Peripheral blood smear would show presence of large, immature platelets that are released earlier as a compensatory mechanism in response to increased platelet destruction. Treatment of chronic ITP includes steroids and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). Splenectomy may be considered.

Defective platelet aggregation (choice B) is seen with two conditions: 1) Glanzmann thrombasthenia, an autosomal recessive disease with defective or decreased levels of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa. Patients have prolonged bleeding time but normal platelet number and morphology. 2) Bernard-Soulier syndrome, an autosomal recessive disease with deficient glycoprotein Ib. Bernard-Soulier syndrome presents with prolonged bleeding time and thrombocytopenia. Bernard-Soulier syndrome, however, is characterized by the presence of giant platelets on peripheral smear.

Hypersplenism (choice C) causes thrombocytopenia when an enlarged spleen traps normal platelets (splenic sequestration) in the absence of other specific platelet disorders. This type of thrombocytopenia can be cured with splenectomy. Although the thrombocytopenia in ITP often improves with splenectomy, ITP does not cause splenomegaly.

Megakaryopoiesis (choice D) is disturbed in any disorder that causes bone marrow failure, including drug toxicity, leukemia, and infections. In this setting, thrombocytopenia is often part of a pancytopenia.

A medication effect (choice E) on platelet function is seen with aspirin and NSAIDs. Aspirin irreversibly inactivates cyclooxygenase (COX) enzyme and suppresses prostaglandin and thromboxane production. NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, are reversible inhibitors of cyclooxygenase. These medications would not cause thrombocytopenia.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: ITP is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies form against platelet glycoproteins; antibody-coated platelets are removed by the reticuloendothelial system, causing isolated thrombocytopenia.
choice_explanations.B: Defective platelet aggregation is seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia (defective glycoprotein IIb/IIIa) and Bernard-Soulier syndrome (deficient glycoprotein Ib); platelet counts are normal (Glanzmann) or thrombocytopenia with giant platelets (Bernard-Soulier).
choice_explanations.C: Hypersplenism traps normal platelets, causing thrombocytopenia, but is accompanied by splenomegaly; ITP does not cause splenomegaly.
choice_explanations.D: Ineffective megakaryopoiesis occurs in bone marrow failure (drug toxicity, leukemia, infection) and is usually part of a pancytopenia.
choice_explanations.E: Aspirin and NSAIDs impair platelet function without lowering the platelet count; they do not cause thrombocytopenia.

fa_summary: ITP: autoimmune antiplatelet (anti-glycoprotein) antibodies cause splenic platelet destruction → isolated thrombocytopenia with normal RBC/WBC and no splenomegaly.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of reddish urine. He recently had a sinus infection and received trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Laboratory studies show: Erythrocyte count 4.0 million/mm³, Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, Mean corpuscular volume 90 μm³, Total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, Direct bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, Lactate dehydrogenase 180 U/L, Haptoglobin is decreased. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 3+ urobilinogen, negative proteins, leukocyte esterase, and nitrite. Urine microscopy shows no red cells. Numerous red blood cells with distinct inclusions are seen on peripheral smear. Which of the following best describes the inclusions seen on peripheral blood smear?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The presence of increased unconjugated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and low haptoglobin in the serum is highly suggestive of acute intravascular hemolysis, likely related to sulfonamide ingestion. The reddish urine is most likely due to hemoglobinuria, rather than hematuria, as no red cells were found in the urine. Positive blood on urinalysis reflects presence of red blood cells, hemoglobin, or myoglobin. Urinary urobilinogen is increased. The peripheral smear showed characteristic red cells with inclusions of oxidized and denatured hemoglobin, known as Heinz bodies. Their presence is indicative of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, in which hemolysis occurs following exposure to oxidants or infections. Other conditions where Heinz bodies can occur are the thalassemias and other variants of unstable hemoglobins.

Hemoglobin crystals (choice B) may be seen in hemoglobin C or hemoglobin SC disease. The crystals are often hexagonal or rhomboid in shape.

Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing (choice C), dark-blue granules found in Wright-stained red cells in patients with hemolysis and are related to oxidative stress.

Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants within red cells (choice D) that are normally removed by the spleen. The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies indicates either absence of the spleen (i.e., surgical removal) or a nonfunctioning spleen.

Ring forms (choice E) can be present in red cells in patients with malaria or babesiosis. Additionally, Cabot rings are seen in megaloblastic anemia or lead poisoning. There is no indication of any of these diseases in this patient.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: Heinz bodies are inclusions of oxidized and denatured hemoglobin seen in G6PD deficiency (and unstable hemoglobins), precipitated after oxidative stress such as a sulfonamide.
choice_explanations.B: Hemoglobin crystals are seen in hemoglobin C or hemoglobin SC disease and are often hexagonal or rhomboid.
choice_explanations.C: Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing granules seen in hemolytic states; they are not the inclusions of G6PD deficiency.
choice_explanations.D: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants normally removed by the spleen; they indicate asplenia or hyposplenism.
choice_explanations.E: Ring forms occur in malaria or babesiosis (Cabot rings in megaloblastic anemia/lead poisoning), none of which fit this patient.

fa_summary: Heinz bodies are denatured/precipitated hemoglobin inclusions in RBCs, classically caused by G6PD deficiency after oxidative stress.

stem: A 54-year-old man who is a teacher comes to the physician because of headaches and fatigue. He does not smoke cigarettes but has a history of alcohol abuse. Physical examination shows a small, nodular liver. Oxygen saturation is 98%. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte count of 6.5 million/mm³, hematocrit of 62%, mean corpuscular volume of 85 μm³, and total bilirubin of 2.0 mg/dL. A peripheral blood smear shows increased reticulocytes and nucleated red cells. Erythropoietin level is elevated and carboxyhemoglobin level is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Erythrocytosis is an important finding that always warrants further investigation. This patient's past alcohol abuse, nodular cirrhosis on examination, and elevated bilirubin all suggest that liver pathology may exist. In fact, hepatocellular carcinoma is one of the five tumors most commonly associated with the overproduction of erythropoietin (i.e. a paraneoplastic erythrocytosis) with resultant polycythemia. The four other tumors associated with paraneoplastic syndromes that are themselves associated with increased erythropoietin include renal cell carcinoma, hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, and uterine myomata.

Carbon monoxide toxicity (choice A) can cause erythrocytosis with prolonged exposure. This is often suggested by occupational exposures, for example, in people who work in underground parking garages, taxi drivers with prolonged exposure to car pollution, and industrial workers. The oxygen saturation measurement of 98% (presumably by pulse oximetry) does not completely rule out CO poisoning because carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin can give a falsely high apparent oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry. The carboxyhemoglobin level was not increased, however, ruling out CO poisoning.

Cardiac malformations (choice B) resulting in Eisenmenger syndrome can cause a secondary polycythemia; however, physical examination of the present patient is not suggestive of this condition.

Polycythemia vera (choice D) is a bone marrow disorder with proliferation of hematopoietic cells, characteristically associated with erythropoiesis, increased viscosity, and low levels of erythropoietin.

Reactive polycythemia (choice E) occurs in cases of tissue hypoxia, commonly seen in patients who smoke or have chronic lung conditions (COPD). Decreased oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry and a history of smoking are suggestive of reactive polycythemia.

choice_explanations.A: Carbon monoxide toxicity can cause erythrocytosis with prolonged exposure, but this patient's carboxyhemoglobin level is decreased, ruling it out.
choice_explanations.B: Cardiac malformations causing Eisenmenger syndrome can produce secondary polycythemia, but the physical examination here is not suggestive.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: hepatocellular carcinoma is one of the tumors associated with paraneoplastic overproduction of erythropoietin (erythrocytosis); the nodular liver and elevated bilirubin point to liver pathology.
choice_explanations.D: Polycythemia vera is a primary bone marrow disorder with low erythropoietin; this patient has an elevated erythropoietin level.
choice_explanations.E: Reactive polycythemia results from tissue hypoxia (smoking, COPD) and would show decreased oxygen saturation; here oxygen saturation is 98% and EPO is elevated from a tumor.

fa_summary: Paraneoplastic polycythemia: tumors (renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, uterine leiomyoma) overproduce erythropoietin.

stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has been having menses that last 10-12 days for the past 6 months. She is concerned because her brother has a blood disease and needed a blood transfusion after an appendectomy. The patient is otherwise healthy and denies tobacco smoking or alcohol use. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 120/74 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals marked pallor under the mucous membranes and few small bruises on her arms and legs. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 8500/mm³, Hemoglobin 9 g/dL, Platelet count 100,000/mm³, Bleeding time 12 min, PT 12.6 seconds, PTT 30 sec, Platelet aggregation studies with ADP Normal, Platelet aggregation studies with Ristocetin Abnormal, Von Willebrand level Normal, Peripheral blood smear Few giant platelets. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the findings in this patient?

options.text: Antibodies against platelet glycoprotein Ib receptor
Deficiency of platelet glycoprotein Ib receptor
Deficiency of platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor

explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has Bernard-Soulier syndrome, an inherited autosomal recessive bleeding disorder with platelet glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) receptor deficiency/dysfunction. Platelet glycoprotein Ib (GPIb) receptor binds to von Willebrand factor for platelet adhesion to occur (see figure). Patients present with petechia, purpura, menorrhagia, and prolonged bleeding with trauma and surgery.
