Laboratory studies reveals decreased platelet count, presence of giant platelets, prolonged bleeding time, and normal PT and PTT. Platelet aggregation studies with ristocetin identifies the ability of von Willebrand factor to bind to platelet GPIb receptor. Thus, an abnormal result suggests either Bernard-Soulier syndrome or von Willebrand disease.

Antibodies against platelet glycoprotein Ib receptor (choice A) is seen with immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). The acute type can be seen in children who have had a prior viral respiratory tract infection (1-3 weeks), which is self limited. The chronic type can be seen in women and is associated with a persistent autoimmune response. In both types, antibodies are directed against the platelet glycoprotein Ib/IX or IIb/IIIa receptors, which are recognized by splenic macrophages and results in platelet removal from the circulation. Patients present with petechiae, easy bruisability, hemorrhage after minor trauma and, if severe, intracerebral hemorrhage. Bone marrow examination would show compensatory increase in megakaryocytes. Treatment is with intravenous immune globulin (IVIG), which binds to these antibodies and prevents the platelet recognition by the splenic macrophages. Other treatments include corticosteroids, thrombopoietin, platelet transfusion, and splenectomy may be considered if the condition is refractory to other treatments.

Deficiency of ADAMTS13 metalloprotease enzyme (choice B) is seen with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). The enzyme cleaves large von Willebrand multimers that is required for platelet adhesion. Patients present with a pentad- Fever, Thrombocytopenia, Neurologic alterations, Renal dysfunction, and Schistocytes, which, except for thrombocytopenia, is not present in our patient.

Deficiency of platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor (choice D) is seen with Glanzmann thrombasthenia, an inherited autosomal recessive bleeding disorder. Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor binds to fibrinogen and allows for platelet aggregation and stable platelet-fibrin clot to occur. Patients present with petechia, purpura, menorrhagia, and prolonged bleeding with trauma and surgery. Laboratory studies reveal normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time, normal PT, PTT. Platelet aggregation studies with ADP identifies platelet aggregation, and will be abnormal with Glanzmann thrombasthenia. In our case, it is normal.

Von Willebrand factor dysfunction (choice E) is a qualitative defect rather than a quantitative defect of von Willebrand disease. There are 3 types of von Willebrand disease (1, 2, 3) as well as acquired type. Type 1 is the most common, type 2 has multiple subtypes (quantitative and qualitative defects), and type 3 is complete absence of VWF. PTT is slightly prolonged in von Willebrand disease because VWF helps prolong the half-life of clotting factor VIII. With qualitative defects, von Willebrand factor levels are usually normal, but molecules are defective in binding to platelet gp Ib receptors and, thus, platelet adhesion cannot occur. Platelet aggregation studies with ristocetin would be abnormal. However, giant platelets would not be present in these patients.

choice_explanations.A: Antibodies against platelet glycoprotein Ib receptor occur in immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), not in this inherited disorder.
choice_explanations.B: ADAMTS13 metalloprotease deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), which presents with a pentad (fever, thrombocytopenia, neurologic changes, renal dysfunction, schistocytes).
choice_explanations.C: Correct: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an autosomal recessive deficiency/dysfunction of platelet glycoprotein Ib, which binds vWF for platelet adhesion, producing thrombocytopenia with giant platelets and abnormal ristocetin aggregation.
choice_explanations.D: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa deficiency is Glanzmann thrombasthenia; platelet aggregation with ADP is impaired, whereas here it is normal.
choice_explanations.E: Von Willebrand factor dysfunction (qualitative vWD) shows abnormal ristocetin aggregation but normal vWF levels and no giant platelets.

fa_summary: Bernard-Soulier syndrome: autosomal recessive GpIb deficiency → defective platelet-vWF adhesion with thrombocytopenia and giant platelets; ristocetin aggregation is abnormal.

stem: A 47-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of fever, headache, and increased confusion for the past week. Her temperature is 38.7°C (102°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. She is disoriented to time and place. Examination shows jaundiced sclerae and skin, purpura on the trunk, and bleeding gums. Bladder catheterization reveals dark-colored urine and decreased urine output. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 8000/mm³, Hemoglobin 8 mg/dL, Hematocrit 20%, Platelet count 25,000/mm³, Total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, Direct bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL, Lactate dehydrogenase 125 U/L, Creatinine 4.9 mg/dL. A peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes and helmet-shaped cells. Prothrombin time is 13 seconds, partial thromboplastin time is 36 seconds, and bleeding time is 10 minutes. Fibrin split products and Coombs test are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a rare disorder. It is frequently seen in women and is characterized by a pentad:
- Thrombocytopenia with purpura
- Fever
- Neurologic symptoms (altered mental status)
- Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
- Acute renal failure

Thrombocytopenia causes the bruising, purpura, and prolonged bleeding time. Elevated indirect bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and schistocytes in the blood smear are characteristic of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Microthrombi occur within organs causing renal dysfunction and neurologic symptoms. Treatment is with plasmapheresis (exchange of patient's plasma with normal plasma) to remove the ULVWF.

The pathophysiology of TTP is becoming increasingly well understood. Idiopathic cases are due to a defect/deficiency of a metalloprotease that cleaves ultralarge von Willebrand factor (ULVWF), ADAMTS13. In the vast majority of TTP cases, the functional deficiency in ADAMTS13 is due to antibodies directed against the enzyme. In 5 to 10% of cases, a genetic-based enzyme deficiency (known as Upshaw-Schulman syndrome) is present. Formation of thrombi composed of uncleaved ULVWF multimers combine with platelets from the circulation without stimulation of the clotting cascade, hence the normal PT and PTT. Secondary cases are due to underlying conditions such as HIV, immunosuppression, cancers, pregnancy, or medications (hormone replacement therapy, immunosuppressants, platelet aggregation inhibitors, antivirals, etc.). In secondary cases, ADAMTS13 is not depressed and it is thought that endothelial damage may be the underlying mechanism.

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (choice A) can cause anemia and an elevated indirect bilirubin, but generally produces only mild symptoms, is not associated with thrombocytopenia, and does not cause fragmentation of red blood cells on the peripheral smear. The negative Coombs test argues against an immune-mediated hemolytic anemia.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC; choice B) can be differentiated from TTP because of abnormal coagulation tests. In DIC, microangiopathic hemolysis (schistocytes) is present, but the prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) are prolonged, fibrinogen levels are reduced, and fibrin split products are elevated.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS; choice C) and TTP are considered manifestations of the same pathogenetic spectrum. However, the condition is mainly seen in children, associated with enterohemorrhagic E. coli 0157:H7 verotoxin or Shiga toxin. Children who eat contaminated foods (e.g., hamburgers) present subsequently (5-10 days) with HUS: thrombocytopenia, bruising, purpura, acute renal failure, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. The vascular bed of the central nervous system is not involved in HUS. Thus, mental status changes are not part of the clinical picture of HUS.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP; choice D) is an immune disorder caused by autoantibodies to platelet antigens. Systemic illness is not present in ITP, which is characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia without other hematologic abnormalities. There are 2 forms: acute and chronic. The acute form is commonly seen in children, is treated with IV immunoglobulin, and has little sequelae. The chronic form is seen in adults, has an autoimmune basis, and can be treated with splenectomy. Ten percent of cases will manifest in association with autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Evans syndrome).

choice_explanations.A: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia causes anemia and elevated indirect bilirubin but not thrombocytopenia or schistocyte fragmentation; a negative Coombs test argues against it.
choice_explanations.B: DIC also shows schistocytes but is distinguished by prolonged PT/PTT, decreased fibrinogen, and elevated fibrin split products (a consumptive coagulopathy).
choice_explanations.C: HUS shares the microangiopathic picture but occurs mainly in children after Shiga toxin-producing E. coli; CNS involvement (mental status changes) is not part of HUS.
choice_explanations.D: ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia without microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, schistocytes, or systemic illness.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: TTP presents with the pentad of thrombocytopenia, fever, neurologic symptoms, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes), and renal failure, with normal PT/PTT.

fa_summary: TTP: ADAMTS13 deficiency → impaired cleavage of vWF multimers → platelet microthrombi; triad/pentad of thrombocytopenia, MAHA (schistocytes), neurologic and renal findings with normal PT/PTT.

stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up examination because of easy bruising and petechiae. She has been otherwise healthy. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 76/min, blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg, and respirations are 12/min. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 10,200/mm³, Erythrocyte count 4.5 million/mm³, Hemoglobin 13 mg/dL, Platelet count 23,000/mm³, Serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, Urobilinogen 10 mg/dL. A peripheral blood smear shows a few large, young platelets. The other cell lines are normal. Bone marrow studies show an increased number of megakaryocytes. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This clinical scenario is most consistent with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), which is an immune-mediated destruction of platelets by the spleen. Antibodies to platelet receptors (GP Ib or GP IIb/IIIa) are formed. There are 2 types of ITP: acute and chronic. The acute form is seen in children and young adults, is preceded by a viral infection, and is self-limited. The chronic type is seen in female adults and may require intravenous immune globulin (IVIG; prevents the spleen from recognizing platelets and platelet destruction), corticosteroid, or splenectomy as therapy. The peripheral smear and bone marrow show the features described. Immature giant platelets and increased megakaryocytes are compensatory mechanism in the bone marrow in response to the increased platelet destruction. Decreased platelets and normal red blood cells on peripheral smear help establish this diagnosis.

In both Glanzmann thrombasthenia (choice A) and von Willebrand disease (choice F), the platelet count will be normal. Platelet aggregation will be impaired with Glanzmann thrombasthenia, while platelet adhesion will be impaired with von Willebrand disease.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (choice B; HUS) is usually associated with exposure to enterohemorrhagic, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli 0157:H7 infection. Shigella, Campylobacter, and viruses (HIV, Coxsackie virus, Echovirus) may also cause this condition. Patients (most commonly children) may have eaten contaminated foods (e.g., hamburgers). Patients present with fever, bloody diarrhea, and subsequent (2-7 days afterwards) thrombocytopenia, bruising, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and acute renal failure (oliguria, elevated renal function tests). Patients may also have irritability, lethargy and seizures. Histologic changes in the renal glomeruli show presence of microthrombi. Peripheral blood smear reveals decreased platelets and schistocytes.

Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura is distinguished from microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (choice D) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (choice E; TTP) by the absence of fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on peripheral blood smear. TTP is due to ADAMTS13 enzyme deficiency, microthrombi formation, and has a characteristic pentad: fever, thrombocytopenia, neurologic dysfunction (altered mental status), renal dysfunction, and schistocytes (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia).

choice_explanations.A: In Glanzmann thrombasthenia the platelet count is normal and platelet aggregation is impaired (defective GpIIb/IIIa).
choice_explanations.B: HUS shows thrombocytopenia and schistocytes (fragmented red cells) after Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, unlike the isolated thrombocytopenia here.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: ITP is immune-mediated splenic platelet destruction producing isolated thrombocytopenia with large young platelets and increased megakaryocytes; red cells are normal.
choice_explanations.D: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia causes schistocytes and red cell fragmentation, which are absent here.
choice_explanations.E: TTP has a pentad (fever, thrombocytopenia, neurologic dysfunction, renal dysfunction, schistocytes) due to ADAMTS13 deficiency.
choice_explanations.F: von Willebrand disease has a normal platelet count with impaired platelet adhesion, not thrombocytopenia.

fa_summary: ITP: immune-mediated splenic platelet destruction → isolated thrombocytopenia with large young platelets and increased bone marrow megakaryocytes; schistocytes are absent.

stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of increased fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor and mild splenomegaly. Lung sounds are clear. There is no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 50 x 10³/mm³, Hemoglobin 10 g/dL, Platelet count 100 x 10³/mm³. Genetic testing shows a t(9;22) translocation. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The t(9;22) translocation (Philadelphia chromosome), results in a BCR-ABL fusion gene that encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that is implicated in the development of CML. It is the hallmark of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Typically, the peripheral blood has markedly increased circulating mature neutrophils, immature neutrophils (metamyelocytes), and basophilia. There are also a small number of circulating blasts (less than 10%). The disease has an indolent course. After several years, some patients can progress to an accelerated phase with increased numbers of circulating blasts. Treatment includes imatinib (Gleevec), which is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that inhibits the abnormal bcr-abl tyrosine kinase.

An increased lymphocyte count (choice A) would be seen in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), another indolent leukemia that is seen in older adults.

Increased numbers of blasts (choices C and D) are seen in the late stages of CML and CLL or in the acute leukemias (lymphocytic - ALL, or myeloid - AML). The Philadelphia chromosome is occasionally associated with ALL presenting in older children and adults, and is associated with a poor prognosis.

Pancytopenia (choice E) is typical of the myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), in which pluripotent stem cells produce abnormal development of all cell types. Pancytopenia would also be seen in aplastic anemia and other conditions with bone marrow dysfunction.

choice_explanations.A: An increased lymphocyte count is characteristic of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).
choice_explanations.B: Correct: the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)/BCR-ABL hallmark of CML drives proliferation of the granulocytic lineage, giving a marked increase in mature (and immature) neutrophils with basophilia.
choice_explanations.C: Numerous lymphoblasts occur in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), not the chronic phase of CML.
choice_explanations.D: Numerous myeloblasts (>20%) indicate blast crisis/acute myeloid leukemia, not chronic-phase CML.
choice_explanations.E: Pancytopenia is typical of myelodysplastic syndromes and aplastic anemia, not CML.

fa_summary: CML: t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome → BCR-ABL constitutively active tyrosine kinase, with marked neutrophilic (granulocytic) leukocytosis, basophilia, and splenomegaly; treated with imatinib.

stem: A 42-year-old African-American man is admitted to the intensive care unit after a motor vehicle collision in which he sustained multiple rib fractures, a femoral fracture, and head trauma. In the emergency department, his pulse is 90/min, blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg, and has a ruptured spleen. Complete blood count on admission shows an erythrocyte count of 3.0 million/mm³, hemoglobin of 14 g/dL, hematocrit of 42%, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 90 μm³, and platelet count of 320,000/mm³. He undergoes an emergency surgery for removal of his spleen and receives 4 units of compatible blood type, cross-matched packed red cells in surgery. On the third day in the hospital, he develops decreased consciousness and scattered bruises on his trunk and legs. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte count of 4.5 million/mm³, hemoglobin of 15 g/dL, hematocrit of 45%, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 90 μm³, platelet count of 80,000/mm³, BUN of 19 mg/dL, and serum creatinine of 2.0 mg/dL. A peripheral blood smear shows fragmented and helmet-shaped red cells which were not present on admission. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's most recent hematologic findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The peripheral blood findings suggest disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which is a feared complication of many disorders, such as massive trauma, obstetric complications (i.e. abruptio placenta), malignancy (adenocarcinoma), pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome (loss of antithrombin III into urine), and gram-negative bacterial sepsis. The pathogenic mechanism of DIC is endothelial cell injury leading to a cyclical process involving a prothrombotic event with consumption of clotting factors and the breakdown of these clots by the fibrinolytic system.

DIC is characterized by bleeding from mucosal surfaces, thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and PTT, decreased fibrinogen level (due to consumption of fibrin from the coagulation cascade), and elevated fibrin split products (breakdown of circulating fibrinogen and fibrin from blood clots).

Fragmented red blood cells, helmet cells and schistocytes, are seen on peripheral blood smear in any condition that causes mechanical damage producing hemolysis (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia). Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), DIC, and trauma from mechanical heart valves are major causes of such RBC damage.
- HUS is usually seen in children and associated with infection enterohemorrhagic E. coli 0157: H7 strain, i.e. ingestion of contaminated burgers, which cause thrombi within glomerular capillaries and hematuria.
- TTP is usually seen in women age 20-40 years who present with the classic pentad: fever, neurologic signs, thrombocytopenia, kidney dysfunction, and presence of schistocytes. TTP is due to the lack of the metalloprotease, ADAMTS13, which cleaves large von Willebrand multimers.
- Patients with HUS and TTP will have normal PT and PTT levels.

Functional asplenia (choice B) is associated with conditions with increased extravascular hemolysis such as sickle cell disease, hemoglobin SC disease, sickle cell hemoglobin (HbS), and beta thalassemia. Of course, functional asplenia is also seen with iatrogenic asplenism when the spleen is surgically removed. Normally, red cells with Howell-Jolly bodies or other inclusions are removed from the circulation by the splenic macrophages. Without a functioning spleen, increased in cells with cytoplasmic inclusions will be present in the circulation. Howell-Jolly bodies characteristically are small, round, densely stained nuclear remnants in red blood cells.

Hereditary spherocytosis (choice C) would be characterized by spherocytes in the peripheral smear. It is an autosomal dominant inherited condition due to defect in the cytoskeletal protein spectrin or ankyrin. Patients would have splenomegaly (extravascular hemolysis) and persistent jaundice.

Immune hemolysis (choice D) would be characterized by microspherocytes in the peripheral smear. Immune hemolysis can occur with conditions such as incompatible red blood cell transfusion, autoimmune (SLE), and medications (methyldopa). Patients present with jaundice, acute onset anemia, decreased renal function, hemoglobinuria, decreased levels of haptoglobin, and a positive direct Coombs test. Platelet count would not be low.

Mechanical heart valves (choice E) can fragment red blood cells as they pass through. In this patient, there is no history provided to suggest that this patient has had a mechanical valve placed. Schistocytes were not present on the peripheral blood smear on admission. The clinical presentation in this patient is highly suggestive of DIC given the presence of schistocytes after his trauma, the new onset neurologic symptoms, thrombocytopenia, and renal dysfunction occurring 3 days after his trauma.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: massive trauma triggers DIC (endothelial injury → prothrombotic consumption of clotting factors → bleeding), with schistocytes/helmet cells, thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/PTT, and elevated fibrin split products.
choice_explanations.B: Functional asplenia causes increased RBC inclusions (Howell-Jolly bodies) after splenectomy but does not produce schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, or renal/neurologic deterioration.
choice_explanations.C: Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes, not schistocytes, and is a chronic, not acute, presentation.
choice_explanations.D: Immune hemolysis shows microspherocytes and a positive direct Coombs test; platelet count would be normal.
choice_explanations.E: Mechanical heart valves can fragment RBCs, but there is no history of valve replacement and no schistocytes were present on admission.

fa_summary: DIC: widespread clotting factor activation and consumption → thromboses and hemorrhage; ↓platelets, prolonged PT/PTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑fibrin split products, schistocytes.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a sore throat, worsening fatigue, and shortness of breath for the past 3 days. She has a history of migraines and has been taking carbamazepine to prevent migraines for many years. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows several bruises on her legs and arms, conjunctival and oral mucosal pallor, and lungs clear to auscultation. Rectal examination and stool guaiac test are negative. A complete blood count shows a erythrocyte count of 2.0 million/mm³, hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, hematocrit of 30%, and 1,500 white blood cells/mm³. Platelet count is 50,000/mm³. The corrected reticulocyte count is <1%. She undergoes a bone marrow biopsy. Which of the following is the most likely finding on bone marrow biopsy?

options.text: Hypercellularity with megaloblasts and giant metamyelocytes
Marrow hypocellularity, predominance of fat cells and marrow stroma
Ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Aplastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia: red blood cells, platelets and leukocytes are very low. Patients have increased infections, anemia, fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, dizziness, epistaxis, bleeding gums, and unexplained/easy bruising. Another differential diagnosis for this type of presentation is acute leukemia.

A corrected reticulocyte (retic) count < 1% in an anemic patient indicates a poor bone marrow response. Thus, a bone marrow biopsy is indicated to determine the bone marrow pathology (aplastic anemia, bone marrow infiltration by malignancy, osteopetrosis, or myelofibrosis). The corrected reticulocyte (retic) count (reticulocyte count x patient's hematocrit/45) is often < 1%. [A corrected retic count, as opposed to the regular retic count, is a more accurate calculation in the context of anemia. Normal retic count in the context of anemia is >3% (normal range 0.5-1.0%), which reflects a normal bone marrow response.]

A bone-marrow biopsy in aplastic anemia typically reveals hypocellularity of all cell lines to < 25% of normal, normal cell architecture, and a predominance of fat and marrow stroma. The proportion of fat and marrow cellularity corresponds with age. Typically, a 32-year-old should have a marrow cell of approximately 68% with a marrow fat and stroma of 32%. With increasing age, marrow cellularity decreases while fat and stroma increases.

Causes of aplastic anemia may be either hereditary (20% of cases; e.g., Fanconi anemia) or acquired (80% of cases). Certain pharmacologic agents cause severe marrow hypoplasia or aplasia, such as busulfan and vinblastine. Chloramphenicol, anticonvulsant drugs (such as carbamazepine and phenytoin), phenylbutazone, gold, and other agents may produce aplastic anemia in an idiosyncratic manner. Aplastic anemias have also been linked to exposure to environmental toxins, such as benzene, and insecticides. Aplastic anemia may often be preceded by viral infections from cytomegalovirus (CMV), parvovirus, and hepatitis. The fever and sore throat in the present patient are consistent with a viral infection, possibly CMV or parvovirus.

Treatment of aplastic anemia includes discontinuing the medications, giving immunosuppressive medications (corticosteroids, immune globulin, cyclosporine, or stem cell/bone marrow transplantation.

Giant early red-cell precursors (choice A) (pronormoblasts, also known as proerythroblasts) are seen in pure red-cell aplasia. Acquired pure red-cell aplasia is seen after infection with parvovirus B19 and produces a selective deficit of the erythrocytic lineage, not all three lineages. Patients who are prone to developing red cell aplasia include those who have sickle cell anemia.

Hypercellularity with megaloblasts and giant metamyelocytes (choice B) signifies megaloblastic changes of vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency. Megaloblastic changes are seen mainly in neutrophils and red cells, but would not affect platelets counts. Our patient has all 3 cell lines affected. Reticulocyte count may be increased in response to the anemia.

Ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain (choice D) are characteristic of sideroblastic anemia. Patients are usually older and have a microcytic anemia. Pyridoxine (B6) deficiency or medications that interfere with pyridoxine can also cause sideroblastic anemia. Our patient has involvement of all 3 hematopoietic cell lines; not only red cells.

Sheets of abnormal plasma cells (choice E) are seen in multiple myeloma. Patients are usually older and may present with recurrent infections, anemia, bone pain, and pathologic bone fractures from osteolytic lesions (not seen in our patient).

choice_explanations.A: Giant early red-cell precursors (pronormoblasts/proerythroblasts) are seen in pure red-cell aplasia (e.g., parvovirus B19), which affects only the erythroid lineage, not all three.
choice_explanations.B: Hypercellularity with megaloblasts and giant metamyelocytes indicates megaloblastic anemia (B12/folate deficiency); it does not spare the other lineages in the way seen here.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: aplastic anemia is stem cell failure producing pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow (<25% cellularity) and predominance of fat cells and marrow stroma.
choice_explanations.D: Ringed sideroblasts (Prussian blue stain) are characteristic of sideroblastic anemia, usually a microcytic anemia, not pancytopenia with a fatty marrow.
choice_explanations.E: Sheets of abnormal plasma cells occur in multiple myeloma, which is typically seen in older patients with osteolytic lesions and bone pain.

fa_summary: Aplastic anemia: hematopoietic stem cell failure → pancytopenia with a hypocellular, fatty bone marrow (<25% cellularity) and a low corrected reticulocyte count.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of recurrent epistaxis for the past 2 days. He recently recovered from a mild illness with sore throat and cough. Physical examination shows multiple mucosal petechiae and several ecchymoses on the arms and legs, but no other abnormalities. Laboratory tests show: Hemoglobin 11 g/dL, Prothrombin time 13 sec, Partial thromboplastin time 30 sec, Platelet count 18,000/mm³. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Thrombocytopenia is a finding in many disorders. It can occur due to impaired production (e.g., viral infections, various medications, marrow aplasia, leukemias, vitamin deficiency) or accelerated destruction of platelets (e.g., medications, autoimmune diseases, sepsis, hemolytic uremic syndrome, artificial heart valves, DIC).

This patient has acute immune thrombocytopenic purpura (acute ITP). In children, it commonly follows a recent viral infection or exanthem. The thrombocytopenia in this disorder appears to be secondary to splenic destruction of opsonized platelets. The acute form of ITP, commonly seen in children, is usually explosive but self-limited; a chronic form in adults may respond to splenic therapy or splenectomy.

Bernard-Soulier syndrome (choice A) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by the absence of platelet glycoprotein Ib, a receptor for von Willebrand factor. Although thrombocytopenia may be seen, giant platelets would also be present.

Glanzmann thrombasthenia (choice B) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency or abnormality of either glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors for fibrinogen. This results in a functional defect in platelets that prevents them from aggregating. Thrombocytopenia is not a feature of this disease.

In von Willebrand disease (choice D), an autosomal dominant disorder, deficient von Willebrand factor (a protein cofactor essential for normal platelet adhesion and for the transport of factor VIII) produces platelet dysfunction. However, thrombocytopenia is not a prominent component of this condition and PTT would be prolonged.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (choice E) is an X-linked recessive congenital disorder characterized by thrombocytopenia, frequent infections, and eczema ("TIE"). Although this child has thrombocytopenia, there is no information given to suggest recurrent infections, nor did the physical examination show any signs of eczema. The timing of the disorder after a recent viral infection strongly suggests ITP.

choice_explanations.A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome (absent platelet glycoprotein Ib) is a rare recessive disorder and would also show giant platelets.
choice_explanations.B: Glanzmann thrombasthenia (defective glycoprotein IIb/IIIa) causes a platelet function defect without thrombocytopenia.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: acute ITP in children commonly follows a viral infection and causes isolated thrombocytopenia (petechiae, ecchymoses) due to splenic destruction of opsonized platelets.
choice_explanations.D: von Willebrand disease produces platelet dysfunction with a normal platelet count and a prolonged PTT.
choice_explanations.E: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (X-linked) includes thrombocytopenia plus recurrent infections and eczema ("TIE"), which are absent here.

fa_summary: Childhood acute ITP: post-viral, self-limited immune splenic destruction of platelets causing isolated thrombocytopenia and mucosal bleeding.

stem:
A 53-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her sister because of confusion and disorientation. She has a 2-day history of fever, chills, severe headache, and vomiting. She has no history of major medical illness. Examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) shows:

Lymphocyte count 120/mm3
Erythrocyte count 80/mm3
Protein 120 mg/dL
Glucose 40 mg/dL

An MRI of the brain shows three hypodense lesions in the left temporal lobe. If the patient dies of her infection, which of the following would most likely be seen on microscopic examination of the brain?

options.text: Both distinct nuclear and ill-defined cytoplasmic inclusions
Greatly enlarged oligodendrocyte nuclei with glassy amphophilic viral inclusions
Microglial nodules containing multinucleated giant cells

explanation: The correct answer is B. This patient most likely has herpes simplex type 1 (HSV-1) encephalitis. HSV-1 is the most common cause of fatal sporadic encephalitis in the United States, accounting for approximately 10% to 20% of the 20,000 viral encephalitis cases that occur annually. Viral encephalitis is characterized by elevated protein, lymphocytes and erythrocytes in the CSF. CSF glucose levels are generally normal to mildly decreased. The table shows CSF parameters in different forms of meningitis. The diagnosis of viral encephalitis is aided by demonstrating elevated lymphocytes in the cerebrospinal fluid. HSV-1 encephalitis is specific to the temporal lobes of the brain. Cowdry type A inclusions can be seen in neurons and glia in HSV-1 encephalitis. HSV-1 encephalitis has a propensity for the temporal lobes of the brain. Unilateral temporal lobe abnormalities (hypodense lesions) on brain imaging (MRI or CT scan) are considered strong evidence for herpes simplex encephalitis. Other types of viral encephalitis typically affect older patients, occur in the summer months (because of mosquito transmission), and have no particular association to regions of the brain. Cowdry type A inclusions are intranuclear viral inclusion bodies that may be found in both neurons and glia and are characteristic of herpes simplex infection. Acyclovir is the treatment of choice for HSV-1 encephalitis. Empiric therapy with IV acyclovir should be initiated as soon as the diagnosis is suspected. The presence of both distinct nuclear and ill-defined cytoplasmic inclusions (choice A) specifically suggests cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. CMV infection of the brain characteristically occurs in severely immunosuppressed patients, in whom it tends to localize to the paraventricular subependymal regions of the brain. Extracellular spirochetes (choice C) can sometimes be demonstrated in patients with neuroborreliosis, the brain infection seen in Lyme disease, and in neurosyphilis. Neuroborreliosis can cause aseptic meningitis, facial nerve palsies, and encephalopathy. Neurosyphilis can occur in three basic forms: meningovascular syphilis (involving the base of the brain), general paresis (involving the frontal lobe and other areas of the neocortex), and tabes dorsalis (involving the dorsal roots and spinal cord). Greatly enlarged oligodendrocyte nuclei with glassy amphophilic viral inclusions (choice D) are a feature of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). This viral encephalitis usually occurs in immunosuppressed patients and is caused by the JC polyomavirus. PML is characterized by demyelination because it preferentially infects oligodendroglia. Microglial nodules containing multinucleated giant cells (choice E) are characteristic of chronic HIV encephalitis, which tends to involve in particular the subcortical white matter, diencephalon, and brainstem.

choice_explanations.A: The presence of both distinct nuclear and ill-defined cytoplasmic inclusions (choice A) specifically suggests cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. CMV infection of the brain characteristically occurs in severely immunosuppressed patients, in whom it tends to localize to the paraventricular subependymal regions of the brain.
choice_explanations.B: The correct answer is B. This patient has HSV-1 encephalitis, which has a propensity for the temporal lobes. Cowdry type A inclusions are intranuclear viral inclusion bodies found in both neurons and glia and are characteristic of herpes simplex infection.
choice_explanations.C: Extracellular spirochetes (choice C) can sometimes be demonstrated in patients with neuroborreliosis, the brain infection seen in Lyme disease, and in neurosyphilis.
choice_explanations.D: Greatly enlarged oligodendrocyte nuclei with glassy amphophilic viral inclusions (choice D) are a feature of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), caused by the JC polyomavirus.
choice_explanations.E: Microglial nodules containing multinucleated giant cells (choice E) are characteristic of chronic HIV encephalitis.

fa_summary: HSV-1 encephalitis is the most common cause of fatal sporadic viral encephalitis; it localizes to the temporal lobes and shows Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions in neurons and glia (treat with IV acyclovir).

stem: A novel infectious disease has become prevalent and increasingly widespread over the past 2 years. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) has just isolated the cause of the illness, which is a virus. The virus looks like a brick-shaped complex. It consists of double-stranded, enveloped DNA, which replicates in the cytoplasm via a virion-associated transcriptase. This new virus would be most likely classified in which of the following families?
explanation: The correct answer is F. Examples of viruses in the Poxvirus family are variola, vaccinia, and molluscum contagiosum. All DNA viruses are icosahedral, except for Poxviruses, which are described as brick-shaped complexes. Poxvirus DNA is enveloped. All DNA viruses replicate their DNA in the nucleus, except for Poxvirus, which replicates in the cytoplasm via a virion-associated transcriptase. All of the enzymes and factors necessary for viral replication are then made in the cytoplasm. Poxviruses are described as brick-shaped complexes. Poxvirus is an enveloped DNA virus. All DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus except for Poxvirus, which replicates in the cytoplasm via a virion-associated transcriptase. All of the enzymes and factors necessary for viral replication are then made in the cytoplasm. Adenoviruses (choice A), like the other DNA viruses (except Poxvirus), are icosahedral and have double-stranded linear DNA that replicates in the nucleus. The DNA is not enveloped, and there is no virion-associated polymerase. The main example of the Hepadnavirus (choice B) family is the hepatitis B virus. It is icosahedral and contains partially double-stranded circular DNA that is enveloped. Viruses carry a DNA polymerase with reverse transcriptase activity to synthesize an RNA intermediate that is then used to make genomic DNA. Herpesviruses (choice C) consist of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, Epstein-Barr, and cytomegalovirus. These are icosahedral and contain enveloped, double-stranded, linear DNA. The DNA replicates in the nucleus and the virus is assembled in the cytoplasm. Papillomaviruses (choice D) are icosahedral and contain naked, double-stranded, circular DNA that replicates in the nucleus. The most important of the Parvoviruses (choice E) is parvovirus B19. It is icosahedral and is the only DNA virus that contains single-stranded DNA, which is naked and replicates in the nucleus.

choice_explanations.A: Adenoviruses (choice A), like the other DNA viruses (except Poxvirus), are icosahedral and have double-stranded linear DNA that replicates in the nucleus. The DNA is not enveloped, and there is no virion-associated polymerase.
choice_explanations.B: The main example of the Hepadnavirus (choice B) family is the hepatitis B virus. It is icosahedral and contains partially double-stranded circular DNA that is enveloped.
choice_explanations.C: Herpesviruses (choice C) are icosahedral and contain enveloped, double-stranded, linear DNA. The DNA replicates in the nucleus.
choice_explanations.D: Papillomaviruses (choice D) are icosahedral and contain naked, double-stranded, circular DNA that replicates in the nucleus.
choice_explanations.E: The most important of the Parvoviruses (choice E) is parvovirus B19. It is the only DNA virus that contains single-stranded DNA, which is naked and replicates in the nucleus.
choice_explanations.F: The correct answer is F. Poxviruses are brick-shaped, enveloped DNA viruses and the only DNA viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm (via a virion-associated RNA transcriptase).

fa_summary: DNA viruses are icosahedral and replicate in the nucleus except Poxvirus, which is a brick-shaped, enveloped virus that replicates in the cytoplasm via a virion-associated transcriptase.

stem:
A 71-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of severe COPD. He is a former smoker. He works for a fire and water damage restoration company. His wife reports that his mental status has declined over the past few days and is found to be confused and unable to understand or retain simple information. He is not using oxygen and denies dyspnea, but is using accessory muscles to breathe. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 74/min, respirations are 19/min, blood pressure is 121/69 mm Hg, and SpO2 is 93% on 2L of oxygen. Laboratory studies show:

Na 142 mEq/L
K 4.4 mEq/L
Cl 89 mEq/L
HCO3- 43 mEq/L
Glucose 86 mg/dL
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
BUN 16 mg/dL
Ca2+ 9.2 mg/dL
pH 7.36

Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's altered mental status?
explanation: The correct answer is B. The patient has severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which has resulted in chronically elevated CO2 levels (hypercapnia). In recent days, he has suffered a COPD exacerbation and his PaCO2 has risen to levels that have caused neurologic symptoms. These may include restlessness, confusion, delirium, and tremors. CO2 is a potent cerebral vasodilator, so hypercapnia increases cerebral flow and intracranial pressure, typically causing headaches and papilledema. At very high levels (>100 mm Hg), CO2 causes coma, respiratory depression, and death (CO2 narcosis). The PaCO2 level at which neurologic symptoms appear in healthy individuals is around 75-80 mm Hg. Patients with underlying lung disease may adapt to slow rises in PaCO2 as their disease progresses, so symptoms may not manifest until levels rise acutely above ~80 mm Hg. Adaptation involves a resetting of central chemoreceptor sensitivity in the face of rising PaCO2 and renal bicarbonate retention to compensate for the respiratory acidosis. While arterial blood gas values are not provided in the case history above, PCO2 can be estimated by inserting the stated values for HCO3- and pH into the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK + log([HCO3-]/[CO2]); [CO2] = 0.03 x PCO2. Using patient data (6.1 is the pK for carbonic acid, 0.03 is the CO2 solubility constant): 7.36 = 6.1 + log (44/(0.03 x PCO2)). COPD exacerbations are usually triggered by respiratory infections. Patients with advanced pulmonary disease often have little or no respiratory reserve and present with tachypnea and using accessory respiratory muscles to breathe. Patients with advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease adapt to a chronic rise in PaCO2 as their disease progresses; adaptation involves a resetting of central chemoreceptor sensitivity and renal HCO3- retention. The patient's presentation is most consistent with a COPD exacerbation that has caused his PCO2 to rise acutely to levels that produce neurologic symptoms (> 80 mm Hg), including altered mental status and confusion. Bacterial meningitis (choice A) is an inflammatory condition resulting from infection of the pia mater and cerebrospinal fluid. Patients present with a classic triad of symptoms that include altered mental status, nuchal rigidity, and high fever. Although not all patients exhibit all three symptoms, almost all have fever. The patient is afebrile, suggesting that bacterial meningitis is unlikely to be the cause of his confusion. Hypovolemia (choice C) can cause confusion and other neurologic symptoms depending on the ionic composition of the lost fluid, but the patient has a normal blood pressure and heart rate and his creatinine and BUN both fall within reference ranges, all of which suggest that he is euvolemic. Blood pressure would be expected to fall and heart rate to rise with hypovolemia due to decreased left ventricular preloading. Creatinine and BUN both rise due to renal vasoconstriction and a decrease in glomerular filtration rate. Hypoxemia (choice D) can also cause confusion and other neurologic symptoms, but the patient has a normal SpO2 and, thus, is not hypoxemic. The patient works in environments that increase exposure to fungi, which raises the possibility of so called "toxic mold syndrome" (choice E). While some mycotoxins can have adverse health effects, there is little evidence supporting a link between commonly encountered mycotoxins and neurologic symptoms shown by the patient.

choice_explanations.A: Bacterial meningitis (choice A) presents with the classic triad of altered mental status, nuchal rigidity, and high fever; the patient is afebrile, making this unlikely.
choice_explanations.B: The correct answer is B. A COPD exacerbation acutely raises PaCO2 above ~80 mm Hg, and hypercapnia (a potent cerebral vasodilator) produces headache, papilledema, and neurologic symptoms such as confusion and altered mental status.
choice_explanations.C: Hypovolemia (choice C) would cause hypotension and tachycardia with elevated BUN/creatinine; this patient is euvolemic with normal blood pressure and heart rate.
choice_explanations.D: Hypoxemia (choice D) can cause confusion, but this patient has a normal SpO2 and is not hypoxemic.
choice_explanations.E: Mycotoxin exposure (choice E) has little evidence supporting a link between commonly encountered mycotoxins and the patient's neurologic symptoms.

fa_summary: COPD exacerbations cause acute CO2 retention (hypercapnia), which acts as a cerebral vasodilator and produces headache, papilledema, and altered mental status once PaCO2 exceeds ~80 mm Hg.

stem:
A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of episodes of abdominal pain and headaches. He also says that his urine sometimes seems darker in color. He has a history of hepatic vein thrombosis. Physical examination shows mild jaundice and no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

Leukocyte count 5,000/mm3
Erythrocyte count 3.8 million/mm3
Hematocrit 24%
Platelet count 120,000/mm3
Reticulocyte count 5%
Mean corpuscular volume 85 mm3
Total bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL
Direct bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL
Lactate dehydrogenase 115 U/L
Urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL
Direct Coombs test negative
Indirect Coombs test negative

Urinalysis shows:
Color Dark yellow
Dipstick 2+ blood
Microscopy 0-2 RBCs/hpf, some renal epithelial cells with golden-yellow pigment; no red cell casts or crystals

Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is F. This patient most likely has paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), which can cause a striking hemoglobinuria with red-brown to black urine. The condition usually presents in adulthood, peaking in middle age. The hemoglobinuria occurs due to intravascular hemolysis of red blood cells, causing the release of free hemoglobin. It is most commonly seen in the first morning urine. It is hypothesized that hemolysis occurs more often at night when patients develop a mild acidosis. Note: Hemoglobinuria occurs during an acute hemolytic episode, whereas hemosiderin (epithelial cells with golden-yellow pigment) is detected after an episode.

PNH is an acquired red cell defect caused by an acquired mutation of the phosphatidylinositol glycan A (PIG-A) gene, which is essential for the synthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchoring protein. GPI-linked proteins CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (a potent inhibitor of C3 convertase) are unable to anchor to GPI, which causes red blood cells to become more sensitive to lysis by complement. Any systemic stress (e.g. infection, surgery, acidosis) may trigger hemolysis. Complement-mediated lysis also occurs in white blood cells and platelets, resulting in pancytopenia. Patients may later develop aplastic anemia or acute myelogenous leukemia.

Blood studies are consistent with intravascular hemolysis including normocytic anemia, reticulocytosis, decreased haptoglobin, increased unconjugated bilirubin, and increased LDH. The Coombs test is negative due to this being a complement-mediated process, rather than an antibody-mediated hemolysis.

These patients are also prone to venous thrombosis, which along with pigmented (bilirubin) gallstones, may be the source of the abdominal pain frequently experienced by this group. Thrombosis (in hepatic, portal, cerebral veins), due to dysfunctional platelets, are the most frequent immediate causes of death in PNH patients.

Historically, the tests specific for PNH are the sucrose test and the Ham test, in which serum is acidified to activate the complement pathway, then added to PNH red cells, resulting in lysis. Currently, flow cytometry is used to identify leukocytes deficient in the GPI-linked proteins: CD55 and CD59.

In aplastic anemia (choice A), the bone marrow function is deficient and the reticulocyte count would be decreased; not elevated. This patient has evidence of hemolysis (elevated reticulocyte count) without marrow aplasia, which usually presents with profoundly decreased cell counts. Patients with PNH are at risk for venous thrombosis.

Crigler-Najjar syndrome (choice B) is a cause of severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Because of a defect in hepatic bilirubin conjugation, it is usually fatal in the first year of life due to accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin in the brain.

Dubin-Johnson syndrome (choice C) is a usually asymptomatic cause of jaundice, but is not associated with hemolytic anemia. It results in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a black liver.

Glomerulonephritis (choice D) can cause changes in urine color secondary to hematuria and elevated BUN and creatinine. Hypertension and urinary red cell casts are common.

Hereditary spherocytosis (choice E) causes extravascular hemolysis, in which abnormally shaped red blood cells are phagocytosed by macrophages in the spleen. The clinical presentation is normocytic anemia, splenomegaly, and jaundice. Since it is due to extravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria is an unlikely presentation.

This patient has evidence of hemolysis (elevated reticulocyte count) without marrow aplasia, which usually presents with profoundly decreased cell counts.

This patient has paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH): an acquired PIG-A mutation causes loss of the GPI-anchored complement inhibitors CD55 and CD59, producing intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria, a negative Coombs test, and a predisposition to venous thrombosis.

fa_summary: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is an acquired intrinsic hemolytic anemia (PIG-A mutation → loss of CD55/CD59) causing intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis.

stem: A 39-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision in which she fell asleep at the wheel. She appears to have no major injuries, but is admitted overnight for observation because of dyspnea, weakness and back pain. During the night she snores loudly, and has choking episodes that awaken her. Pulse is 75/min and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Physical examination is normal except for BMI of 38.1 kg/m2 and moderate contusions of the torso. Which of the following is most likely to occur in this patient during sleep cycles?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient most likely has obstructive sleep apnea, which is transient airway occlusion that causes apnea (periodic cessation of breathing), progressive asphyxia, and arousal from sleep. Obstructive sleep apnea is highly associated with obesity; it is associated with obesity hypoventilation syndrome, also known as Pickwickian syndrome. Repeated periods of apnea during the night lead to increased cardiac afterload due to pulmonary and systemic vasoconstriction, acute carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia), transient arterial hypoxia, cerebral dysfunction, sleep fragmentation, and excessive motor activity. Arterial oxygen and carbon dioxide return to normal between periods of apnea.

Choices A and B are incorrect. Obstructive sleep apnea does not alter the diffusion characteristics of the lungs. It also does not increase the thickness of the diffusion barrier or decrease the surface area.

Hyperpnea (choice C) is incorrect because ventilation decreases during apnea.

Shunt (choice E) occurs when blood passes through a region of the lung in which there is no ventilation or there is no diffusion. It refers specifically to a regional disorder. This is not the same as decreased ventilation throughout the lungs, which is called hypoventilation, which is what occurs during periods of apnea.

choice_explanations.B: Choices A and B are incorrect. Obstructive sleep apnea does not alter the diffusion characteristics of the lungs. It also does not increase the thickness of the diffusion barrier or decrease the surface area.
choice_explanations.C: Hyperpnea (choice C) is incorrect because ventilation decreases during apnea.
choice_explanations.D: The correct answer is D. Obstructive sleep apnea produces recurrent nocturnal hypoventilation, causing transient arterial hypoxemia with carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia).

This is not the same as decreased ventilation throughout the lungs, which is called hypoventilation, which is what occurs during periods of apnea.

fa_summary: Obstructive sleep apnea (obesity hypoventilation / Pickwickian syndrome) causes nocturnal airway collapse with hypoventilation, producing hypoxemia and hypercapnia during sleep.

stem: A 64-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of malaise, fever and bilateral flank pain. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 96/min, blood pressure is 134/85 mm Hg, and respirations are 22/min. Several painful, erythematous nodules are present on the pads of the fingers, palms, and toes, bilaterally. Funduscopic examination shows multiple small white spots surrounded by hemorrhage bilaterally. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 18 x 103/mm3, differential: 50% segmented neutrophils, 15% bands, 25% lymphocytes, and 7% monocytes. Hb is 11.2 g/dL and platelet count is 150,000/mm3. Dipstick urine analysis shows 2+ blood, 1+ protein; negative for glucose, leukocyte esterase, and nitrite. Urine microscopy shows 10 RBCs/hpf. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The funduscopic lesions described are called Roth's spots, which are areas of retinal ischemia most commonly due to septic emboli from acute bacterial (infective) endocarditis. Bacterial endocarditis should be suspected in a patient with fever, positive blood cultures, or new heart murmur. A vigorous search should be undertaken for the clinical signs of endocarditis, including evidence of Osler nodes (as seen here; immune complex deposits on the pads of fingers and toes), Roth's spots, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages and Janeway lesions. Renal involvement by infective endocarditis can result in acute glomerulonephritis and infarction due to septic emboli to the kidneys, which can result in flank pain and hematuria, as seen in our patient.

Crohn disease (choice B) can occasionally be associated with uveitis but not with retinal hemorrhages. Crohn disease is associated with erythema nodosum, inflammation of the subcutaneous fat (panniculitis) typically present on the anterior lower extremities. However, these lesions should not be confused with Osler nodes present on the pads of the palms, fingers, and toes (seen in our patient).

Diabetes mellitus (choice C) can cause a variety of ocular changes, including microaneurysms, flame hemorrhages, and "cotton wool" spots, but Roth's spots are not produced. Although patients with diabetes mellitus can have flank pain due either to renal infection or diabetic nephropathy, glucosuria, pyuria, and/or severe proteinuria were not present in the urine analysis.

Glaucoma (choice D) causes increased pressure in the anterior chamber but does not produce Roth's spots. Cupping of the optic nerve may occur as a result of the increased intraocular pressure, which should be distinguished from papilledema.

Urosepsis (choice E) is not reflected in the urine analysis, which emphasizes the hematuria rather than pyuria. It does not usually cause any obvious eye or hand findings.

Roth's spots (small white spots surrounded by hemorrhage on funduscopy) are areas of retinal ischemia most commonly due to septic emboli from acute bacterial (infective) endocarditis; the Osler nodes, fever, and embolic glomerulonephritis are all consistent.

Crohn disease is associated with erythema nodosum, inflammation of the subcutaneous fat (panniculitis) typically present on the anterior lower extremities. However, these lesions should not be confused with Osler nodes present on the pads of the palms, fingers, and toes.

stem:
A 9-year-old boy has a history of degenerative changes and pain in both shoulders and his left knee. Physical examination shows a decreased range of motion of the shoulders, back, hips, and knees. His nose and ears have a dark blue hue. Laboratory studies show:
Erythrocyte count 5 million/mm3
Leukocyte count 10,600/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 60%
Bands 3%
Lymphocytes 31%
Monocytes 5%
Hemoglobin 14 g/dL
Platelet count 250,000/mm3
Rheumatoid factor is not present in serum. A sample of urine collected for routine urinalysis turns black upon standing at room temperature. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This boy's presentation, including the negative rheumatoid factor, suggests osteoarthritis at a very early age. The urine turning black on standing is classically associated with alkaptonuria, an arthritic disease caused by a deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase (homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase). Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder in which the lack of homogentisic acid oxidase blocks the metabolism of phenylalanine-tyrosine at the level of homogentisic acid. Thus, homogentisic acid accumulates in the body. A large amount is excreted, imparting a black color to the urine if allowed to stand and undergo oxidation. The retained homogentisic acid selectively binds to collagen in connective tissues, tendons, and cartilage, imparting to these a blue-black pigmentation (ochronosis) most evident in the ears, nose, and cheeks.

The most serious consequences of the ochronosis stem from deposits of the pigment in the articular cartilages of the joints. In some obscure manner, the pigmentation causes the cartilage to lose its normal resiliency and become brittle and fibrillated. Wear and tear erosion of this abnormal cartilage leads to denudation of the subchondral bone, and often tiny fragments of the fibrillated cartilage are driven into the underlying bone, worsening the damage. The vertebral column, particularly the intervertebral disc, is the prime site of attack, but later the knees, shoulder, and hips may be affected. The small joints of the hand and feet are usually spared. The metabolic defect is present from birth, but the degenerative arthropathy usually develops slowly and becomes evident later.

Childhood polycystic kidney disease (choice A) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by cysts in the kidneys and the liver. Death often occurs in infancy.

Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (choice C) is associated with hemolytic anemia and reddish-brown urine that is seen most often in the morning.

Phenylketonuria (choice D) is classically associated with a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, with mental retardation, light colored hair and skin, and a distinct strong musty odor in the sweat and urine. There is no associated joint involvement.

Rhabdomyolysis (choice E) may occur with traumatic injury, muscle ischemia, seizures, excessive exercise, heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, alcoholism, and various infectious or metabolic disorders. It would be associated with reddish urine due to myoglobinuria.

choice_explanations.C: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (choice C) is associated with hemolytic anemia and reddish-brown urine that is seen most often in the morning.
choice_explanations.D: Phenylketonuria (choice D) is classically associated with a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, with mental retardation, light colored hair and skin, and a distinct strong musty odor in the sweat and urine. There is no associated joint involvement.
choice_explanations.E: Rhabdomyolysis (choice E) may occur with traumatic injury, muscle ischemia, seizures, excessive exercise, heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, alcoholism, and various infectious or metabolic disorders. It would be associated with reddish urine due to myoglobinuria.

fa_summary: Alkaptonuria (尿黑酸尿症)：尿黑酸氧化酶缺乏致尿黑酸蓄积，尿久置变黑、软骨蓝黑色素沉着(ochronosis)、早发退行性关节病。

stem: A 46-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain in his large toe. He was recently diagnosed with hairy cell leukemia. He denies any trauma, but says that he has been exercising between chemotherapy sessions. Examination shows small nodules on his ears. His right first toe is extremely tender, warm, and erythematous. Which of the following is most likely to be found on joint aspiration?

options.text: Large notched rectangular crystals with various birefringence
Mixed pleomorphic crystals with various birefringence
Rhomboid crystals with weakly positive birefringence

explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has gout, which is characterized by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joint spaces and soft tissues. Patients often present with pain in the first toe (podagra). Late in the disease, patients may also present with tophi, most commonly found on the external ears. Tophi are the accumulation of the crystals in the soft tissues. Hyperuricemia leads to the urate deposition. This can occur in several ways, secondary to enzyme deficiencies, lifestyle choice, or drug treatment, for example, chemotherapy drugs.

Our patient has a leukemia and is undergoing treatment. Joint aspiration analysis with microscopy and polarization reveals needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. In general, one needs to know two conditions that are associated with negative and positive birefringence (gout and pseudogout, respectively). "Negatively birefringent" refers to the crystals' yellow appearance when viewed parallel to the polarizer and blue when viewed perpendicular to the polarizer (as seen in gout). "Positively birefringent" refers to the crystals' blue appearance when viewed parallel to the polarizer and yellow when viewed perpendicular to the polarizer (as seen in pseudogout; calcium pyrophosphate).

Gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters (choice A) indicate a Staphylococcus arthritis and cellulitis. There is no history of trauma or open cut on the skin, and bacterial dissemination to the ear is less likely.

Large notched rectangular crystals with various birefringence (choice B) are seen with cholesterol crystals. Synovial fluid containing cholesterol crystals are not common, but can be seen sporadically with rheumatoid arthritis.

Mixed crystals with various birefringence (choice C) may be seen with corticosteroid injections. Our patient does not have a history of intra-articular injections.

Rhomboid crystals which are weakly positively birefringent (choice E) reflect calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition (pseudogout), which classically affects the knee or other large joints. Polarization microscopy reveals weakly positive birefringence of crystals.

choice_explanations.B: Large notched rectangular crystals with various birefringence (choice B) are seen with cholesterol crystals. Synovial fluid containing cholesterol crystals are not common, but can be seen sporadically with rheumatoid arthritis.
choice_explanations.C: Mixed crystals with various birefringence (choice C) may be seen with corticosteroid injections. Our patient does not have a history of intra-articular injections.
choice_explanations.E: Rhomboid crystals which are weakly positively birefringent (choice E) reflect calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition (pseudogout), which classically affects the knee or other large joints. Polarization microscopy reveals weakly positive birefringence of crystals.

stem: A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a several month history of severe joint pain. At first, she noticed stiffness, pain, and swelling in her wrists, hands, ankles, and feet. Recently she has noticed her knees, elbows, and shoulders have also become affected. The pain is usually worse in the morning when she wakes up, but gradually decreases during the day. Her temperature is 36.6°C (97.9°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 116/74 mm Hg. Her wrists, ankles, knees, and elbows are all erythematous and warm with mild swelling. Laboratory studies show a complete blood count with WBC of 6x10^3/mm3 and hemoglobin of 9.5 g/dL. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 30 mm/hr, c-reactive protein (CRP) is 160 mg/L (normal < 10 mg/L), and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody titer is elevated. Which of the following findings is most likely on microscopic examination of a synovial biopsy specimen?

options.text: A proliferative synovitis with caseous granulomas
A proliferative synovitis with many lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells
A non-proliferative synovitis with macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and crystal deposition
A non-proliferative synovitis with neutrophils and abscess formation

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a symmetric, inflammatory, peripheral polyarthritis that primarily involves the synovial membranes and articular structures of multiple joints. Severe rheumatoid arthritis causes a proliferative synovitis with extensive damage to the synovium of the joint. The synovial membrane becomes markedly thickened (pannus formation), with edematous villous projections that extend into the joint space, which causes the joint stiffness. The intense inflammatory infiltrate that is present is typically composed of plasma cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages, indicative of chronic inflammation. Recall that RA is considered type III and IV hypersensitivity reaction: immune complexes can be generated (rheumatoid factor) in the synovial tissue and activated CD4+ T cells in the synovium, respectively. Deformities of the hand include ulnar deviation, proximal phalanges boutonniere deformity or swan-neck deformity.

The diagnosis of RA can be made in a patient with inflammatory arthritis involving three or more joints, disease duration of more than six weeks, positive rheumatoid factor (RF) and/or anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide/protein (CCP) antibody, elevated c-reactive protein (CRP) or erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and presence of subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules located on the ear, fingers, or extensor surfaces of the forearm. Since RA is considered a chronic inflammatory condition, patients can also have normochromic, normocytic anemia (anemia of chronic disease).

Normal synovium (choice A) may be seen with osteoarthritis, a condition that affects the articular cartilage rather than the synovium. There is no synovial inflammation. Osteoarthritis occurs in weight-bearing joints (hips, knees) or joints with repetitive motion (fingers as seen among typists, manual laborers). Symptoms include worsening pain with repetitive movement, morning stiffness, crepitus, and limited range of motion. Osteophyte formation occurs within the joints, which can cause crepitus, nerve impingement, loose bodies ("joint mice"), and Bouchard and Heberden nodes.

A proliferative synovitis with caseous granulomas (choice B) is seen with tuberculous arthritis. It usually occurs as a complication of adjacent osteomyelitis or general hematogenous dissemination. The affected synovium can proliferate, cause pannus formation, and erode adjacent bone. The hips, knees, and ankles are usually involved (descending order of frequency). Our patient does not have any history or exam findings to suggest tuberculous arthritis.

A non-proliferative synovitis with macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and crystal deposition (choice D) is seen with crystal-induced arthritis. Endogenous crystals (gout or pseudogout) or exogenous crystals (talcum, corticosteroid ester crystals) can deposit into synovial tissue and cause an inflammatory foreign body giant cell reaction. Patients may be asymptomatic or symptomatic. Our patient does not have any history or exam findings to suggest crystal-induced arthritis.

A non-proliferative synovitis with neutrophils and abscess formation (choice E) is seen with acute bacterial (septic) arthritis. Common causative organisms include: Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, gonococcus, and gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Salmonella, Pseudomonas, and others). H. influenzae and Streptococcus arthritis predominantly occurs in children under 2 years of age, S. aureus and Streptococcus occur mainly in older children and adults, gonococcus is prevalent during late adolescence and young adulthood, and Salmonella can occur at any age among patients with sickle cell disease. Patients classically present with fever, sudden onset of joint swelling with limited range of motion, leukocytosis, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Our patient does not have any risk for bacterial exposure, such as trauma.
