stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes is brought to the emergency department because of dysarthria and the inability to move his left arm and leg. His wife states that he has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the past 35 years and he consumes 3-4 beers daily. He appears to be in some distress and has difficulty speaking. Physical examination shows an inability to move his left arm and leg, hyperreflexia on the left, and an upgoing plantar reflex on the left. He also has left facial weakness, sparing his forehead. Sensation in his face and extremities is intact. The lesion responsible for this patient's symptoms is most likely located in which of the following areas?

options.text: Corticospinal tract in left upper cervical cord
Corticospinal tract in right upper cervical cord

explanation:
The correct answer is G. Don't be taken aback by the number of options. The correct answer can be arrived at quickly with a combination of eliminating incorrect answers and narrowing down potentially correct answers.

First, let's note his symptoms:
- Left-sided hemiplegia
- Left Babinski sign
- Left lower facial paralysis

So, it's pure motor and all on the left. We need to think of something that can only cause left-sided motor symptoms. We also know that because he has a facial paralysis in addition to paralysis of the body, the lesion must be in the brain (eliminating choices A and B, which are in the spinal cord).

The tract that must be affected is the corticospinal tract because he is showing upper motor neuron signs (paralysis, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign). Because we know the lesion is in the brain, the lesion must be contralateral to his signs and symptoms. In the figure below, we can see that the lesion must be above the decussation (crossing) of the corticospinal tract—so it must be on the right side (because he has left-sided symptoms). We can now eliminate every option on the left (choices A, C, D, E, F).

The lateral frontal lobes (choices D and H) can also be eliminated. The primary motor cortex is in the frontal lobes, however, the lateral portion controls the arm and face, whereas the medial portion controls the legs. This patient has paralysis of both arms and legs. The motor homunculus located in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe is shown below. (Furthermore, because this patient has a left-sided hemiplegia, if cortex was involved, it would have to be the right cortex.)

The pons (choices E and I) can be eliminated for a couple of different reasons. A lesion of the left pons (choice E) could lead to a right-sided hemiplegia because of disruption of the corticospinal tracts that run through the base of the pons. However, a lesion of the left pons would also likely cause a complete facial paralysis because of damage to the facial nucleus and fibers (lower motor neuron type). Our patient has an upper motor neuron type of facial weakness because his forehead is spared. In addition, because there are many tracts and nuclei present in the pons, a pontine lesion would likely cause much more than a pure motor deficit. We are asked to find the most likely location and there is a more likely option available for us to choose.

We have eliminated choices A, B, C, D, E, F, H, I, and J. So, we know the correct answer is choice G, the right internal capsule.

Let's also discuss why this answer is right. Our patient most likely had a lacunar infarct, which commonly involves lenticulostriate vessels, leading to small cystic areas of infarction. Hypertension and diabetes (which our patient has) are risk factors. There are different kinds of lacunar syndromes (e.g., pure motor, pure sensory) depending on the location of the pathology. Because our patient has a pure motor deficit, his lesion is most likely in the posterior limb and genu of the internal capsule. Corticospinal fibers originate in the primary motor cortex of the frontal lobe and descend through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, continue to descend in the ventral brain stem, cross in the caudal medulla, and continue primarily as the corticospinal tract in the contralateral spinal cord. Corticobulbar fibers to the facial nucleus originate in the primary motor cortex of the lateral frontal lobe and descend through the genu of the internal capsule.

A lesion in the right internal capsule would result in left-sided hemiplegia. The lower left facial paralysis is the result of an upper motor neuron lesion, which is also consistent with a stroke of the right internal capsule.

choice_explanations.A: Choice A (corticospinal tract in left upper cervical cord) is in the spinal cord; because this patient has a facial paralysis in addition to body paralysis, the lesion must be in the brain.
choice_explanations.B: Choice B (corticospinal tract in right upper cervical cord) is in the spinal cord and is eliminated for the same reason as choice A.
choice_explanations.C: Choice C (left internal capsule) and the other left-sided options are eliminated because the lesion must be contralateral to his left-sided symptoms, i.e., on the right.
choice_explanations.D: Choice D (left lateral frontal lobe) is on the left and is further eliminated because the lateral frontal lobe motor cortex controls the arm and face, whereas this patient has paralysis of both arms and legs.
choice_explanations.E: Choice E (left pons) is on the left; a left pontine lesion would also cause a complete (lower motor neuron) facial paralysis, but this patient's forehead is spared (upper motor neuron pattern).
choice_explanations.F: Choice F (left thalamus) is on the left and is eliminated because the lesion must be contralateral (right-sided).
choice_explanations.G: The correct answer is G. A lacunar infarct of the right internal capsule (posterior limb and genu) from lenticulostriate vessel involvement produces a pure motor deficit of the contralateral (left) body with upper motor neuron signs and a lower left facial paralysis.
choice_explanations.H: Choice H (right lateral frontal lobe) is eliminated because the lateral motor cortex controls the arm and face, not both the arm and leg as seen in this patient.
choice_explanations.I: Choice I (right pons) is eliminated because a pontine lesion would cause more than a pure motor deficit and would likely give a complete lower motor neuron facial palsy.
choice_explanations.J: Choice J (right thalamus) is eliminated because a pure motor deficit with these features is most consistent with the internal capsule.

fa_summary: A lacunar stroke involving the posterior limb/genu of the internal capsule (lenticulostriate arteries) causes a pure motor contralateral deficit with upper motor neuron signs and lower facial weakness, sparing the forehead.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia is admitted to the hospital after suffering a stroke. He is unable to recognize his family, and he says that he has never seen his wife and son before, however his visual acuity is intact. He appears confused when they talk to him because their voices "sound just like those of his family members." A diffusion weighted-MRI performed later reveals ischemia in the distribution of the right posterior cerebral artery. Which of the following best characterizes this patient's deficit?
explanation:
The correct answer is F. Agnosia occurs when a patient has normal perception but the perception is devoid of meaning. Prosopagnosia literally means "the inability to recognize faces." Infarcts of the non-dominant (usually right) posterior cerebral artery (PCA) territory are often accompanied by this phenomenon. Patients with prosopagnosia can describe another person's face well and can identify that a face is a face, but they cannot recognize the face even if it belongs to someone that they know well. Patients may be able to recognize people based on other clues such as voice, clothing, or hairstyle. Prosopagnosia can also be the result of bilateral lesions of the fusiform gyri.

Alexia (choice A) is impairment in reading caused by deficits in central language processing. It can occur in isolation or in conjunction with agraphia (impairment in writing). Pure alexia can result from infarction of the dominant occipital cortex by occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery. Curiously, these patients often have a color anomia (inability to name colors), and they are able to write.

Asomatognosia (choice B) is a lack of knowledge about one's own body. For example, hemiasomatognosia can occur with hemineglect, and patients will deny that half of their body actually belongs to them. Hemineglect most commonly occurs with lesions of the nondominant right parietal lobe.

Confabulation (choice C) refers to the fabrication of stories and events that never happened in order to fill in memory gaps. It is seen mostly in dementia.

Gerstmann syndrome (choice D) occurs as a result of a lesion of the angular gyrus in the dominant (usually left) hemisphere. These patients cannot comprehend written language (alexia) nor can they write it (agraphia). They also have acalculia (loss of ability to perform simple math), finger agnosia (inability to recognize one's own fingers), and a right-left disorientation.

Ideomotor apraxia (choice E) is the inability to carry out an action after receiving a verbal command. For example, these patients cannot imitate hand gestures such as brushing their teeth. They may be able to spontaneously do the actions, but when asked to imitate these actions, they are unable to perform the movements. Apraxia is the inability to execute learned purposeful movements.

Receptive aphasia (choice G) is also known as Wernicke's aphasia, caused by a lesion of Wernicke's area in the dominant temporal lobe. These patients cannot comprehend spoken language, and their speech is fluent but lacks meaning ("word salad").

choice_explanations.A: Alexia (choice A) is impairment in reading caused by deficits in central language processing. It can occur in isolation or with agraphia, and pure alexia can result from infarction of the dominant occipital cortex (PCA).
choice_explanations.B: Asomatognosia (choice B) is a lack of knowledge about one's own body (e.g., hemiasomatognosia with hemineglect), most commonly due to lesions of the nondominant right parietal lobe.
choice_explanations.C: Confabulation (choice C) refers to the fabrication of stories and events that never happened in order to fill in memory gaps; it is seen mostly in dementia.
choice_explanations.D: Gerstmann syndrome (choice D) results from a lesion of the angular gyrus in the dominant hemisphere and includes alexia, agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and right-left disorientation.
choice_explanations.E: Ideomotor apraxia (choice E) is the inability to carry out an action after a verbal command (e.g., cannot imitate gestures such as brushing teeth); apraxia is the inability to execute learned purposeful movements.
choice_explanations.F: The correct answer is F. Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognize faces, caused by an infarct of the non-dominant (usually right) posterior cerebral artery territory or bilateral lesions of the fusiform gyri.
choice_explanations.G: Receptive aphasia (choice G, Wernicke's aphasia) is caused by a lesion of Wernicke's area in the dominant temporal lobe; speech is fluent but lacks meaning ("word salad").

fa_summary: Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognize faces, caused by a lesion of the non-dominant (usually right) occipital cortex / posterior cerebral artery territory or bilateral fusiform gyrus lesions; it is a form of agnosia.

stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a sudden-onset headache and mental status changes. He sustained a blow to the right lateral side of his head 8 hours ago on a construction site and was "knocked out." He recovered consciousness after several minutes and remained asymptomatic until 2 hours ago. In the emergency department, he experiences nausea and vomiting. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is B. All of answer choices can occur in head trauma, however the scenario described is classic for epidural hematoma. In this scenario, a severe blow to the lateral skull causes both skull fracture and laceration of the middle meningeal artery, leading to a momentary loss of consciousness that is followed by a lucid (asymptomatic) period of 1-48 hours before the patient's neurologic condition deteriorates. This scenario is frequently tested on examinations, but you should be aware that in the real clinical world there may be no initial loss of consciousness. A CT scan of the head will typically demonstrate a lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma. Epidural bleeds can occur much faster than subdural bleeds because the arterial pressure from the middle meningeal artery is much greater than the venous pressure of the bridging veins. Epidural hematomas are caused by direct trauma to the lateral aspect of the skull, resulting in the laceration of the middle meningeal artery. Soon after the trauma, patients have a brief period of loss of consciousness, which is followed by a lucid-asymptomatic phase before further neurologic deterioration. Look for the classic lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma on the head CT scan. Basilar skull fractures (choice A) are usually located in the vicinity of the petrous bone or along the sphenoid bone. Clinical signs of basilar skull fracture include hemotympanum (blood visible behind the tympanic membrane), delayed ecchymosis over the mastoid process (Battle sign), or periorbital ecchymosis ("raccoon sign"). Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage (sometimes from the nose) or pneumocephalus may also occur. Intracerebral hemorrhage (choice C) is most often due to hypertension, anticoagulant use, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, or cocaine and/or methamphetamine abuse. On CT, there will be intraparenchymal brightness rather than a bright signal outside of the dura. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (choice D) is most commonly caused by rupture of a berry aneurysm, but may also be associated with arteriovenous malformations or intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Whenever a patient complains of "the worst headache of my life," consider subarachnoid hemorrhage as a possible cause. Blood can also appear in the ventricles on CT. Subdural hematomas (choice E) are due to rupture of the bridging veins between the meningeal dura and the superficial cerebral veins. Blood accumulates below the dura, producing symptoms of increased intracranial pressure in minutes to hours (acute subdural hematomas), or after weeks or months (chronic subdural hematomas, often seen in the elderly). An acute subdural hematoma may present like an epidural hemorrhage (although patients generally do not have a lucid period, but rather a progressive decline in consciousness); but a forceful blow to the lateral skull producing skull fracture is generally associated with an epidural, rather than a subdural, bleed. On head CT, subdural hematomas classically present as crescent-shaped hematomas.

choice_explanations.A: Basilar skull fractures (choice A) are usually located in the vicinity of the petrous bone or along the sphenoid bone. Clinical signs include hemotympanum, Battle sign, "raccoon sign," and CSF leakage.
choice_explanations.B: The correct answer is B. A blow to the lateral skull lacerates the middle meningeal artery, causing an epidural hematoma with a brief loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval and then neurologic deterioration; head CT shows a lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma.
choice_explanations.C: Intracerebral hemorrhage (choice C) is most often due to hypertension, anticoagulant use, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, or cocaine/methamphetamine abuse, producing intraparenchymal brightness on CT.
choice_explanations.D: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (choice D) is most commonly caused by rupture of a berry aneurysm and typically presents with "the worst headache of my life."
choice_explanations.E: Subdural hematomas (choice E) are due to rupture of the bridging veins and classically appear as crescent-shaped hematomas on CT; patients generally lack a lucid interval.

fa_summary: Epidural hematoma results from laceration of the middle meningeal artery after lateral skull trauma, producing a lucid interval followed by deterioration and a lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma on CT.

stem: A 40-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. A review of her records shows 2 admissions with similar symptoms. She reports that the pain is more frequent after she has had a fatty meal. Her temperature is 39.2°C (102.5°F), and she is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 81.6 kg (180 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m2. Physical examination shows a tenderness and inspiratory pause during palpation of the RUQ. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 12,300/mm3. An ultrasound confirms the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis and two days after admission, she undergoes a cholecystectomy. During the procedure, the arterial supply to the gallbladder must be ligated. Within which of the following peritoneal structures is this arterial supply most likely to be found?
explanation: The correct answer is D. This patient most likely has acute cholecystitis, which is acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall and usually occurs because of an obstruction of the cystic duct from cholelithiasis (gallstones). Risk factors for cholelithiasis include the "F's": Female, Fat, Fertile, Forty. Acute cholecystitis signs and symptoms include RUQ pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, and leukocytosis. Patients may show a Murphy sign, which is tenderness and an inspiratory pause during RUQ palpation. Uncomplicated cases may be treated with antibiotics, but complicated cases may require surgery. The hepatoduodenal ligament is the portion of the lesser omentum that connects the liver to the first part of the duodenum. Within the hepatoduodenal ligament are the proper hepatic artery and its branches, the common bile duct and its branches, and the portal vein. The cystic artery is usually a branch of the right hepatic artery, which is a branch of the proper hepatic artery. The cystic artery is a branch of the right hepatic artery. The proper hepatic artery along with its branches, the portal vein, and the common bile duct travel within the hepatoduodenal ligament. Falciform ligament (contains ligamentum teres of liver).

choice_explanations.A: Falciform ligament contains the ligamentum teres of the liver and does not carry the arterial supply of the gallbladder.
choice_explanations.D: The correct answer is D. The cystic artery (supplying the gallbladder) is usually a branch of the right hepatic artery, and the proper hepatic artery, portal vein, and common bile duct all travel within the hepatoduodenal ligament.
choice_explanations.B: See choice explanations above; the arterial supply of the gallbladder is carried in the hepatoduodenal ligament.
choice_explanations.C: See choice explanations above; the arterial supply of the gallbladder is carried in the hepatoduodenal ligament.
choice_explanations.E: See choice explanations above; the arterial supply of the gallbladder is carried in the hepatoduodenal ligament.

fa_summary: The hepatoduodenal ligament (part of the lesser omentum) carries the portal triad: proper hepatic artery, portal vein, and common bile duct; the cystic artery is usually a branch of the right hepatic artery.

stem: A 28-year-old primigravid woman comes to the emergency department following spontaneous rupture of membranes. She reports that she is now having periodic contractions about 5 minutes apart and they are increasing in frequency and intensity. The decision is made to perform an episiotomy to allow the baby to descend more easily and prevent soft tissue trauma. Prior to the procedure, a local anesthetic is administered to block sensation in that region. Palpation of which of the following bony landmarks would be most appropriate to locate the nerve that innervates this region?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The pudendal nerve innervates the perineum. It originates from S2, S3, S4 and leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, then wraps around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament to enter the lesser sciatic foramen and eventually reach the perineum. The ischial spine separates the greater sciatic foramen from the lesser sciatic foramen. Palpation of the ischial spine allows the physician to locate the pudendal nerve in order to perform a pudendal nerve block through the transvaginal approach. The pudendal nerve innervates the perineum. In order to block sensation in this region with a transvaginal approach, the ischial spine is used as a landmark to locate the pudendal nerve. The anterior superior iliac spine (choice A) is the most anterior point on the iliac crest. The lateral attachment of the inguinal ligament is to the anterior superior iliac spine. The greater trochanter (choice B) is at the superior end of the femur. The gluteus medius and gluteus minimus attach to the greater trochanter. The sciatic nerve in the gluteal region may be located at the midpoint between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity. The posterior superior iliac spine (choice D) is along the posterior border of the ilium and serves for the attachment of the oblique portion of the posterior sacroiliac ligaments and the multifidus. The pubic tubercle (choice E) is at the lateral end of the pubic crest. The medial attachment of the inguinal ligament is to the pubic tubercle.

choice_explanations.A: The anterior superior iliac spine (choice A) is the most anterior point on the iliac crest. The lateral attachment of the inguinal ligament is to the anterior superior iliac spine.
choice_explanations.B: The greater trochanter (choice B) is at the superior end of the femur. The sciatic nerve in the gluteal region may be located at the midpoint between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity.
choice_explanations.C: The correct answer is C. The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) wraps around the ischial spine; palpating the ischial spine via the transvaginal approach is used as a landmark to locate the pudendal nerve for a pudendal nerve block of the perineum.
choice_explanations.D: The posterior superior iliac spine (choice D) is along the posterior border of the ilium and serves for the attachment of the posterior sacroiliac ligaments and the multifidus.
choice_explanations.E: The pubic tubercle (choice E) is at the lateral end of the pubic crest. The medial attachment of the inguinal ligament is to the pubic tubercle.

fa_summary: The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) innervates the perineum and wraps around the ischial spine; the ischial spine is the palpable landmark for a transvaginal pudendal nerve block.

A 65-year-old woman comes to the physician because of oliguria and peripheral edema, which developed over several weeks. She noticed that her urine has a dark color. She had episodes of dark urine in the past, but never thought to seek medical consultation. She denies headaches, dizziness, blurry vision, sore throat, cough, shortness of breath, weakness, rash, or weight loss. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.6°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/94 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals pale conjunctiva, slight puffiness around the eyes, lungs clear to auscultation, soft, nontender abdomen, and mild bilateral ankle swelling. Laboratory tests show:
Leukocyte count 12,750/mm3
Hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL
MCV 86 um3
Platelet count 490,000/mm3
ALT 20 U/L
Albumin 3.0 g/dL
Urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL
Creatinine 2.2 mg/dL
Na+ 140 mEq/L
HCO3- 18 mEq/L
Phosphorus 7.8 mg/dL
Glucose 125 mg/dL (2 hr postprandial)
Urinalysis shows 4+ blood and 3+ protein; urine microscopy reveals red cell casts. An x-ray of the abdomen and a renal ultrasound show no abnormalities. A renal biopsy shows atrophic and scarred glomeruli surrounded by a cellular proliferation within Bowman's space. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient most likely has rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN, or crescentic glomerulonephritis). There are three causes of RPGN:
• Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibody such as in Goodpasture syndrome and isolated anti-glomerular basement membrane disease.
• Primary systemic vasculitis associated vasculitis (pauci-immune type) such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis.
• Immune complex-related conditions such as post-infectious glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy, and Henoch-Schonlein purpura.

Given the presentation of only kidney involvement without lung involvement, this patient most likely has isolated anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (limited to the kidney only, rather than systemic as in Goodpasture syndrome: triad of glomerulonephritis (nephritic presentation), pulmonary hemorrhage, and anti-GBM antibodies), which developed into RPGN. The anti-GBM antibodies are directed against the alpha 3 chain of type IV GBM collagen. The incidence of anti-GBM is bimodal: 2nd to 3rd decade (M=F), then 6th to 7th decade (F>M). Most patients present with RPGN, which is characterized by nephritic syndrome (hematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts), rapid progression of renal failure, and oliguria. Histologically, crescents are comprised of proliferation of parietal epithelial cells lining Bowman's capsule and infiltration of monocytes. The crescents increase within the Bowman's space and encroach around the glomeruli, causing atrophy and scarring of the glomeruli.

Laboratory findings may show signs of nephritic syndrome (leukocytosis, anemia, low albumin) and signs of renal failure (elevated creatinine, urea nitrogen, phosphorus). Immunofluorescence studies reveals the presence of positive linear staining with IgG depositions to confirm anti-GBM disease, and positive staining with fibrinogen within crescents to confirm RPGN. Treatment is with immunosuppression (steroids, cyclophosphamide) and plasmapheresis, but mortality rate is high (death weeks to months).

Diabetic nephropathy (choice B) typically begins with microalbuminuria and hypertension and may progress to nephrotic syndrome and renal failure over a period of 10 to 20 years. It is not associated with hematuria. Histologically, there is thickening of the glomerular basement membrane by deposition of glycosylated proteins, presence of Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (proliferation of proteinaceous mesangial matrix) located within the glomerular tufts, and hyaline arteriolosclerosis. These structural changes cause glomerular ischemia, which can progress to glomerular scarring and atrophy, but not to RPGN. Although our patient has a slightly elevated glucose level, these histologic findings are not seen in our patient.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (choice C), formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis, is a systemic vasculitis that is commonly seen in older age males and is associated with upper respiratory, lower respiratory and renal involvement. Patients will have nasal mucosal ulcerations, "saddle nose" due to weakening of the nasal structure at the nasal bridge, cavitary lesions in the lung, and hematuria. Histologically, there is necrotizing and granulomatous inflammation/vasculitis in affected tissues. RPGN can occur. C-ANCA is positive. These clinical and histologic findings are not seen in our patient.

Membranous glomerulonephritis (choice D) is characterized by nephrotic syndrome. A smaller percent of patients can also present with hematuria and hypertension. Most cases are idiopathic and do not have an underlying associated condition. Secondary causes of membranous glomerulonephritis include 1) drugs: penicillamine, gold salts, NSAIDs, and captopril (Note: NSAIDs can also cause minimal change disease), 2) underlying malignant tumor: lung and colon carcinoma and melanoma, 3) SLE, 4) infections: chronic hepatitis B or C virus, syphilis, malaria, and schistosomal infections, and 4) autoimmune conditions, thyroiditis and secondary membranous glomerulopathy. Histologically, there is thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, but not RPGN. Electron microscopy would reveal subepithelial dense deposits. Immunofluorescence study would show granular IgG and C3 deposition. These clinical and histologic findings are not seen in our patient.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (choice E), a classic example of post-infectious glomerulonephritis, is seen more frequently in children who have not been treated for group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. Clinically it presents with nephritic syndrome (hematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts, edema, hypertension) and occurs 1-4 weeks after a streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo/cellulitis (skin infection). Histologically, there is proliferative glomerulonephritis with hypercellular glomeruli (endothelial and mesangial cell proliferation, neutrophilic and monocyte infiltrate). Electron microscopy reveals subepithelial dense deposits. Immunofluorescence study shows granular IgG and C3 deposits. This condition may progress to RPGN. Laboratory studies reveal positive anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titers, elevated serum urea nitrogen and creatinine levels, and low serum complement (C3). Our patient did not have signs or symptoms of a recent streptococcal infection (she denied sore throat and rash).

It is not associated with hematuria. Histologically, there is thickening of the glomerular basement membrane by deposition of glycosylated proteins, presence of Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (proliferation of proteinaceous mesangial matrix) located within the glomerular tufts, and hyaline arteriolosclerosis. stem: A 48-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She says she has occasional visual disturbances and is scheduled to see an optometrist. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 130/72 mm Hg. She is 162.5 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (181 lb); BMI is 31.1 kg/m2. She denies headaches, dizziness, change in weight, use of medications, tobacco smoking, or licit drugs. Physical examination shows soft tissue swelling around the eyes and mild ankle swelling. Funduscopic examination shows proliferative retinopathy with neovascularization. A recent HbA1c is 9.5%; 24-hour urinalysis shows a protein of 3.9 g/day, creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL, and BUN of 30 mg/dL. Which of the following would a renal biopsy most likely show?

options.text: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes in otherwise normal-appearing glomeruli
Linear IgG deposits along the basement membrane
Ovoid hyaline masses in the periphery of the glomerulus
Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive, electron-dense deposits distributed along the epithelial side of the capillary basement membrane

explanation:
The correct answer is D. A high BMI value increases a person's risk for diabetes type 2 and metabolic syndrome. Although diabetes and metabolic syndrome can also occur in lower BMI, the info provided in the question is pertinent and is not a "pertinent negative". The question is focused on the differential diagnosis for decreased renal function and proteinuria, given a middle-aged woman with increased BMI. Diabetes would be high on that differential as well as FSGS.

This woman most likely has type 2 diabetes, as evidenced by fundoscopic retinal changes (most likely proliferative retinopathy or ischemic changes), peri-orbital and ankle edema, proteinuria (nephrotic range; protein >3.5 g/day), and renal failure. 20-30% of diabetic patients will develop diabetic nephropathy. Diabetes is associated with a number of renal changes. Initial mesangial expansion is thought to be directly related to hyperglycemia, thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) occurs, and glomerular sclerosis can occur secondary to intraglomerular hypertension. Nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease) is the most distinctive glomerular lesion associated with diabetes mellitus. It is characterized by proteinuria (nephrotic syndrome), nodular (ovoid) PAS+ deposits of mesangial matrix (hyaline), and thickened basement membranes. Remember that diabetic nephropathy can also present as a diffuse glomerulosclerosis.

A photomicrograph of a glomerulus showing a characteristic Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodule (asterisk) is presented below. There is expansion of the mesangium and diffuse thickening of the capillary basement membrane with an amorphous PAS-positive material that also forms the nodules of Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease.

Control of blood glucose levels and blood pressure are the most important means to halt or prevent the progression of diabetic nephropathy. Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) monitors glycemic control within the past 3 months (recommended <6% to prevent microvascular damage). A high HbA1c level in our patient indicates poor glycemic control. ACE inhibitors (and angiotensin receptor blockers) have been shown to have a positive effect in slowing or preventing this disorder.

It is worth mentioning that focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is considered the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults (commonly African Americans and Hispanics). Most cases are idiopathic, however, and secondary causes include pre-existing glomerular disorders (IgA nephropathy), sickle cell anemia, HIV/AIDS, obesity, heroin use, and morbid obesity. Histologic examination shows select glomeruli; not all (focal) and only partial glomerular tufts; not entire (segmental) involvement. Our patient is obese with an increased BMI, however, the K-W nodules and glomerular involvement in diabetes mellitus is diffuse.

Minimal change disease, the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, is characterized by the podocyte changes described in choice A.

Hyperplastic arteriolitis (choice B) is associated with hypertensive damage (especially malignant hypertension) to the kidneys. Other features include fibrinoid necrosis and necrotizing glomerulitis. Hypertension can cause fundoscopic retinal ischemic changes (increased vessel wall thickening) and ankle swelling (increased hydrostatic pressure). Although hypertension contributes to diabetic glomerulosclerosis, there is no indication from the vignette that the patient is hypertensive.

Goodpasture syndrome is associated with linear deposits of IgG along the basement membrane (choice C). Goodpasture syndrome is a nephritic syndrome, and so could be eliminated quickly as an answer choice. It would be associated with hematuria and red cell casts, whereas nephrotic-level proteinuria is less common, although it may develop as the disease progresses.

Membranous glomerulonephritis is characterized by PAS-positive, electron-dense deposits distributed principally along the epithelial side of the capillary basement membrane (choice E). It is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in Caucasian adults. Causes include primary/idiopathic, chronic infections/inflammation (e.g., syphilis, viral hepatitis B or C), autoimmune (SLE), malignancy (lung, colon, CLL), and medications/toxins (e.g. NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold salts, mercury).

choice_explanations.A: Minimal change disease, the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, is characterized by the podocyte changes described in choice A.
choice_explanations.B: Hyperplastic arteriolitis (choice B) is associated with hypertensive damage (especially malignant hypertension) to the kidneys. Other features include fibrinoid necrosis and necrotizing glomerulitis. Hypertension can cause fundoscopic retinal ischemic changes (increased vessel wall thickening) and ankle swelling (increased hydrostatic pressure). Although hypertension contributes to diabetic glomerulosclerosis, there is no indication from the vignette that the patient is hypertensive.
choice_explanations.C: Goodpasture syndrome is associated with linear deposits of IgG along the basement membrane (choice C). Goodpasture syndrome is a nephritic syndrome, and so could be eliminated quickly as an answer choice. It would be associated with hematuria and red cell casts, whereas nephrotic-level proteinuria is less common, although it may develop as the disease progresses.
choice_explanations.E: Membranous glomerulonephritis is characterized by PAS-positive, electron-dense deposits distributed principally along the epithelial side of the capillary basement membrane (choice E). It is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in Caucasian adults. Causes include primary/idiopathic, chronic infections/inflammation (e.g., syphilis, viral hepatitis B or C), autoimmune (SLE), malignancy (lung, colon, CLL), and medications/toxins (e.g. NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold salts, mercury).

fa_summary: Diabetic nephropathy (糖尿病肾病)：Kimmelstiel-Wilson结节(PAS+系膜基质结节)、GBM增厚、弥漫/结节性肾小球硬化，表现为肾病综合征。

stem: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because of urinary urgency and pain on urination. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows 5 RBC/hpf, 10-15 WBC/hpf, and many bacteria. Treatment with amoxicillin is begun. Two days later, the patient calls the physician angrily and says, "The pharmacist said that taking this medication might decrease the effectiveness of my birth control pills! Why would you prescribe me this drug?" Which of the following is the most appropriate response for the physician?

options.text: I'm sorry. This is my fault because I should have discussed this issue with you when I prescribed the medication.
It's not the pharmacist's job to be tinkering with your medications. I will call the pharmacist and handle this personally.
It's really such a small chance that it's not worth worrying about.
Really, there is no problem here. Pharmacists just like to show what they know.
Really, there is nothing to worry about. I'll call the pharmacist and work it out.
The pharmacist is being overly cautious. As long as you take both medications as I prescribed them for you, you will have no problem.
Well, if you don't feel comfortable with the drug I prescribed, I would be happy to prescribe another medication for you.
You seem angry. Why don't you tell me why you are so upset by this?

explanation: The correct answer is A. Always admit a mistake. In this case, the physician erred in not discussing the interaction of the new prescription with other drugs the patient was taking. The right answer starts by admitting the mistake and apologizing, moves on to provide the necessary information to the patient, and closes by admitting the mistake again. Physicians are only human beings, and they do make mistakes. Within the context of a good relationship with the patient, most mistakes can be discussed openly and then corrected. With this discussion, the physician-patient relationship is strengthened. Choices B and E are defensive. Worse, they do not acknowledge the mistake and they miss the opportunity to educate the patient. Denigrating the pharmacist, who is correctly doing his job, seeks to hide the mistake rather than correcting it. Choice C provides an explanation without admitting that a mistake was made. If the physician wants honesty from the patient, he must provide it in turn. Admit the error and then correct it. Choice E suggests both that there is no problem, and that the physician will talk with the pharmacist and solve it. This response is deceitful. No mistake is admitted, and the chance to educate the patient is lost. In choice F, again, no mistake is admitted and the patient's anger with the physician is not addressed. Rather than educating the patient, the physician offers to prescribe a new medication, which in itself is irresponsible. In choice G, again, no mistake is admitted. Rather than educating the patient, the physician asks the patient to prescribe for herself. The physician is the one with the expertise, and must provide the options from which the patient can choose. Ideally, this should have been done before the amoxicillin was prescribed. Discussing the patient's feelings (choice H) is off the point, and it avoids dealing with the mistake. The error, not the patient's feelings about it, should be the first focus of the discussion.

choice_explanations.A: Start by admitting the mistake and apologizing, provide the necessary information, and close by admitting the mistake again.
choice_explanations.B: Defensive; does not acknowledge the mistake and misses the chance to educate the patient; denigrates the pharmacist.
choice_explanations.C: Provides an explanation without admitting that a mistake was made.
choice_explanations.E: Deceitful; states there is no problem and offers to handle it with the pharmacist, so no mistake is admitted.
choice_explanations.F: No mistake is admitted and the patient's anger is not addressed; offering a new medication is irresponsible.
choice_explanations.G: No mistake is admitted; asking the patient to choose undermines the physician's expert role.
choice_explanations.H: Off the point; avoids dealing with the mistake, which should be the first focus.

fa_summary: When a medical error occurs, the physician is ethically obligated to disclose the mistake to the patient (honesty).

stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of discomfort in his lower abdomen and difficulty with urination. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 30.7 kg/m2. Physical examination shows an enlarged prostate. The physician explains that a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test to detect the possibility of prostate cancer should be performed. The patient is anxious, visibly upset, and inconsolable about the possibility of having cancer. A few days later, the patient's lab results return and the PSA level is 3.5 ng/dL, which is within the normal range. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in patient care?

options.text: Arrange an appointment to talk with the patient in the next several days and review the results in person
Call the patient at once to deliver the news
Call the patient to deliver the news and congratulate him on the test results
Call the patient to deliver the news and schedule him for a follow-up appointment to review what he can do to improve his overall health
Have the practice's nurse call the patient to deliver the news and take time to answer any questions he may have
Schedule an appointment to talk to the patient about the results and offer him a referral for counseling
Send the patient an email or letter immediately detailing the test results and suggest the next course of action

explanation: The correct answer is D. All communication with a patient is best handled face-to-face. When this is not possible because of the need to deliver news in a timely manner, as in the present case, the phone conversation should be followed up by a visit. The follow-up visit is needed to discuss some of the patient's other health issues, including his weight. This patient's body mass index (weight/height2) is too high; his BMI is classified as obesity class I according to the National Institute of Health and World Health Organization (WHO). The patient is likely to have high anxiety over the next several days as he waits to hear the results (choice A). Alleviate the anxiety by telling him as soon as possible. The phone call (choice B) gets the good news to the patient quickly, but does nothing to either further the building of a good long-term relationship with the physician or address the patient's other health concerns. Choice C, while getting the patient the news quickly and in a cheery manner, does not address the patient's other health conditions, such as obesity. The physician, not a nurse (choice E) or other member of the office staff, should be the one to deliver the news. The practice of having the physician call with bad news and a staff member call with good news only heightens patients' anxiety any time the physician calls. The physician is in the best position to answer any questions the patient might have, and to talk about the next steps to improve the patient's health. Also, remember that the physician should not "pass off" their responsibilities to another clinician on the USMLE. The good and bad news should be delivered to the patient by the physician and not a third party. Waiting for days to hear the test results is understandably likely to cause anxiety in the patient. Also, the physician himself should do the counseling and not refer the patient to someone else (choice F). An email or letter from the physician (choice G) may take time to reach the patient and is a very informal and somewhat unprofessional way of handling this situation. The patient was initially in obvious distress and a timely phone call would be the most recommended course of action. Furthermore, an informal letter or email generally creates anxiety, and offers no one to discuss the meaning of the results. The patient's other health issues need to be addressed as well.

choice_explanations.A: Waiting several days for an in-person visit prolongs the patient's anxiety unnecessarily.
choice_explanations.B: A phone call delivers good news quickly but does not build the long-term relationship or address other health concerns.
choice_explanations.C: Congratulating by phone does not address the patient's other health conditions, such as obesity.
choice_explanations.D: Call to deliver the news in a timely manner, then schedule a follow-up visit to address other health issues (the best answer).
choice_explanations.E: The physician, not a third party such as a nurse, should deliver the news.
choice_explanations.F: The physician should do the counseling rather than refer the patient to someone else.
choice_explanations.G: An email or letter is informal and unprofessional and provides no opportunity for discussion.

fa_summary: Deliver news to patients in a timely, direct, empathetic manner (SPIKES); when possible follow a phone call with an in-person visit.

stem: A 24-year-old man is injured and sustains thoracic and closed-head trauma during a motor vehicle collision. A pedestrian, who is a resident physician coming home from a night on call and still wearing his hospital scrubs, seeing that a small fire has begun under the automobile, pulls the driver out of the vehicle, and attempts to maintain a patent airway. The driver dies at the scene of the collision despite appropriate lifesaving measures. At autopsy, it is determined that moving the patient from the car exacerbated a spinal injury and contributed to the patient's death. The patient's family sues the physician and the hospital at which she works, claiming negligence. They state that sleep deprivation contributed to the physician's poor decision-making. Which of the following is the most likely outcome?

options.text: Civil, but not criminal, penalties for both the physician and the hospital
Civil, but not criminal, penalties for the hospital and no penalties for the physician
Civil, but not criminal, penalties for the physician and no penalties for the hospital
Criminal and civil penalties for both the physician and the hospital
Criminal and civil penalties for the hospital but not for the physician
Criminal and civil penalties for the physician but not for the hospital
Neither civil nor criminal penalties for either the physician or the hospital

explanation: The correct answer is G. The Good Samaritan law says that physicians do not have to stop to help in a non-medical situation such as an automobile accident. However, to encourage them to stop, physicians are shielded from legal liability as long as they: Act within their area of competency; Perform standard procedures; Stay at the scene until relieved by competent medical personnel; Receive no compensation. The physician can still be sued, but is protected from any adverse judgment. In the present case, all four of these conditions are met. Moving the patient from a vehicle when there is threat of fire is perfectly reasonable as the car could explode if the fire reaches the gas tank. The physician is shielded from liability. The hospital is also shielded from liability. The resident is technically an employee, but was traveling home after a night on call and is therefore "off duty." The fact that the resident was wearing his hospital uniform/scrubs does not affect the hospital's or his personal liability in this situation. Finally, neither the physician nor the hospital is subject to any criminal charges. There was no malicious conduct, perverse neglect, or anything else that would rise to the level of criminal action.

choice_explanations.G: Under Good Samaritan law the physician (acting within competency, performing standard care, staying until relieved, and accepting no compensation) is shielded from liability, as is the off-duty employer hospital; there is no criminal conduct, so neither faces civil or criminal penalties.

fa_summary: Good Samaritan laws shield physicians who render aid at an emergency scene (acting within competency, without compensation) from liability.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is being discharged after she experienced a transient ischemic attack. Prior to her discharge, a nurse administers an influenza vaccine. It is later determined that the nurse administered the vaccine to the wrong patient. The patient who received the vaccine was notified and replied "Thank you! You saved me from having to get one within the next couple of weeks". She did not have any adverse effects from the vaccine. The nurse manager asked the nurse to fill out an incident report. Which of the following best characterizes this report?

options.text: Generally accepted as an admission of negligence
Generally filled out by hospital administrators
Useful for identifying latent errors only

explanation: The correct answer is E. Patient safety event reporting systems, such as incident reports, are considered universal patient safety tools in all hospitals. These reports are one of the primary measures to detect patient safety events and quality problems. These reports should be filled out whenever there is any type of discontinuity in patient care (choice G); however, these reports are not an admission of negligence (choice B). Incident reports are simply records of all events that are not part of routine medical care. Incident reports are: To document the exact detail of an accident or unusual incident that occurred in a health-care institution; A record that can be used in the future when dealing with liability issues stemming from the incident; A means to protect staff members against unjust accusations (choice E); A means to protect the patient in case of negligence on the part of the staff member; A way to evaluate overall patient care. Incident reporting is most frequently used to describe all voluntary patient safety event reporting systems (compare to choice D). These systems rely on those persons involved in the core event to provide detailed information. This voluntary event reporting tool is considered a passive form of surveillance for near misses or unsafe conditions. This is in contrast to more active methods (choice A) of surveillance, such as direct personnel observation or chart review. Incident reports are generally filled out by frontline personnel (physicians, pharmacists, nurses) directly involved in an event or the actions leading up this particular adverse event instead of management (choice C) or patient safety professionals. These incidence reports are necessary to help identify both active and latent (choice G) safety problems.

choice_explanations.A: Incident reporting is a passive, voluntary form of surveillance, not an active one (eg, direct observation or chart review).
choice_explanations.B: Incident reports are not an admission of negligence; they are records of events outside routine care.
choice_explanations.C: Incident reports are generally filled out by frontline personnel, not hospital administrators.
choice_explanations.D: Incident reporting is a voluntary, not involuntary, reporting system.
choice_explanations.E: Incident reports serve as a means to protect staff members against unjust accusations (the best characterization).
choice_explanations.G: Incident reports help identify both active and latent safety problems, not latent errors only.

fa_summary: Incident reports are voluntary patient-safety event reporting tools that detect active and latent errors and protect staff from unjust accusations.

stem: Strategies that help to reduce or prevent medication errors include the "5 Rs" of medication safety. In addition to right drug, right patient, right dose, and right route, which of the following best represents the remaining "R"?
explanation: The correct answer is E. All patients should receive safe and appropriate health care in and out of the hospital. It is the responsibility of each clinician to ensure that each patient receive the care they deserve each time. The 5 Rs of medication safety help to confirm several key points before the administration of each medication and are as follows: Right drug; Right patient; Right dose; Right route; Right time. Depending on the source, the list may include three other "Rs". The extended list includes: Right to know information about the drug; Right to refuse the drug; Right documentation.

choice_explanations.E: The fifth "R" of medication safety is right time (along with right drug, right patient, right dose, and right route).

fa_summary: The 5 Rs of medication safety are right drug, right patient, right dose, right route, and right time.

stem: An 80-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a right hip fracture after a fall at home. Her right hip is pinned and she is confined to bed rest. Her past medical history is significant only for hypertension. On the fifth day, she develops sudden-onset dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain that worsens during inspiration, and collapses. Her pulse is 150/min, blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg, respirations are 30/min and shallow, and O2 saturation is 72%. A left parasternal heave and a loud pulmonic component of S2 are noted. She is resuscitated, but dies 1 hour later. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her death?

options.text: Emboli from right common femoral vein thrombus
Release of vasoactive material from bone marrow space

explanation: The correct answer is A. Ninety percent of deep vein thrombi are formed in the lower extremities. These thrombi may dislodge and travel to distant sites; most importantly, to the lungs, forming pulmonary emboli. The most frequent cause of pulmonary thromboembolism is deep venous thrombosis of the legs. Pulmonary embolism is estimated to be responsible for 15% of all cases of sudden death. In this case, the patient's prolonged bed rest predisposed her to deep venous thrombosis. Other factors that predispose to clot formation include pregnancy, cancer, or other hypercoagulable states. Some emboli are clinically silent; others affect only those with preexisting cardiac compromise. However, if the clot is large enough, it will cause nearly instantaneous death. A postoperative patient is at risk of a myocardial infarction (choice B); however, in this case, this is not the most likely scenario. The physical examination and the character of the pain more strongly support pulmonary embolism. A pulmonary embolus can cause heart failure, but this is not the primary etiologic event. Fat emboli (choice C) can occur after a fracture of long bones that releases material from the bone marrow; this is also much less likely than a thromboembolus. The fat particles cause a systemic inflammatory response. Veins in the upper limbs (choice D) rarely develop thrombosis. This occurs only in disorders leading to a marked thrombotic propensity, such as carcinoma-associated migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome), antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, protein C deficiency, and inherited mutations of the factor V gene. An embolus to the pulmonary artery is the typical sequela of deep venous thrombosis, rather than clot formation in the pulmonary vein (choice E).

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Ninety percent of deep vein thrombi form in the lower extremities; they may dislodge and embolize to the lungs. The patient's prolonged bed rest predisposed her to a femoral deep venous thrombosis, the most frequent cause of pulmonary thromboembolism and of sudden death.
choice_explanations.B: A postoperative patient is at risk of a myocardial infarction (choice B); however, in this case, this is not the most likely scenario. The physical examination and the character of the pain more strongly support pulmonary embolism; heart failure from an embolus is not the primary etiologic event.
choice_explanations.C: Fat emboli (choice C) can occur after a fracture of long bones that releases material from the bone marrow; this is also much less likely than a thromboembolus. The fat particles cause a systemic inflammatory response.
choice_explanations.D: Veins in the upper limbs (choice D) rarely develop thrombosis. This occurs only in disorders leading to a marked thrombotic propensity, such as carcinoma-associated migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome), antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, protein C deficiency, and inherited mutations of the factor V gene.
choice_explanations.E: An embolus to the pulmonary artery is the typical sequela of deep venous thrombosis, rather than clot formation in the pulmonary vein (choice E).

fa_summary: Pulmonary thromboembolism is most often caused by deep venous thrombosis of the lower-extremity veins (femoral, iliac, popliteal); prolonged bed rest (stasis) is a major risk factor (Virchow triad).

stem: A 25-year-old man participates in a clinical study to determine the cardiovascular response to physical exercise. He is previously healthy and physical examination is unremarkable. Basal measurements are: respiratory rate 15/min; blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg; cardiac output 5 L/min; heart rate 50/min. Which of the following is this man's stroke volume during resting conditions?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The cardiac output (CO) is equal to the volume of blood ejected from the heart during each systole (i.e. the stroke volume; SV) multiplied by the number of times the heart beats each minute (heart rate; HR). In other words, CO = SV x HR. Therefore, SV = CO/HR, and since CO = 5,000 mL/min and HR = 50/min, SV = 5,000/50 = 100 mL.

choice_explanations.D: CO = SV x HR, so SV = CO/HR = 5,000 mL/min / 50/min = 100 mL.

fa_summary: Cardiac output CO = SV x HR; stroke volume SV = CO/HR (here 5,000 mL/min / 50/min = 100 mL).

stem: A 56-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and congestive heart failure comes to the physician for a health maintenance examination. His blood pressure is 172/92 mm Hg. A review of his records shows that his blood pressure during two previous visits were 176/90 and 188/91 mm Hg. Treatment is begun with an antihypertensive drug that is associated with the development of a dry cough and angioedema. Which of the following is an additional adverse effect of this drug?
explanation: The correct answer is C. Diabetics with hypertension are usually treated with an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor because these drugs are protective against diabetic nephropathy and will effectively manage their high blood pressure. Examples of ACE inhibitors include enalapril, captopril, ramipril, and lisinopril. The ACE inhibitors decrease the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II (AII), leading to reduced production of AII and an increase in bradykinin (ACE breaks down bradykinin). ACE-inhibitor hypersensitivity is usually a direct result of increases in bradykinin in sensitive individuals. These reactions can be life-threatening even if they are not true allergic reactions. Therefore, ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in patients with a history of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema, hereditary angioedema, or idiopathic angioedema. The excess bradykinin is also thought to be responsible for the ACE inhibitor-induced dry chronic cough. The ACE inhibitors decrease the production of AII, which is a major stimulus for aldosterone secretion. In this fashion, ACE inhibitors markedly reduce the secretion of aldosterone. Aldosterone potently stimulates urinary secretion of potassium; thus, an occasional undesirable side effect of ACE inhibitors is a potentially dangerous elevation of serum potassium. Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) such as losartan can be used in hypertensive patients with a past history of ACE inhibitor-induced cough. ARBs act by competitively inhibiting angiotensin II at the AT-1 receptor. Decreased secretion of aldosterone (choice A) is one of the major therapeutic benefits of the ACE inhibitors. Decreased secretion of renin (choice B) is incorrect, because a reflex increase in renin secretion is expected with ACE inhibitors. Aliskiren, a direct renin inhibitor, acts by decreasing plasma renin activity, thus interfering with the conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I. Aliskiren is indicated for the treatment of hypertension. Increased total peripheral resistance (choice D) is incorrect because reduction of circulating angiotensin II causes decreased total peripheral resistance, a major contribution to the therapeutic benefit. Increased urinary excretion of sodium (choice E) is expected to occur secondary to reduced aldosterone, but this is beneficial because it contributes to the diuretic effect of these drugs. Methemoglobinemia (choice F), cyanide toxicity, and severe hypotension are all side effects of the vasodilator nitroprusside, which is indicated for hypertensive emergency and acute heart failure.

choice_explanations.A: Decreased secretion of aldosterone (choice A) is one of the major therapeutic benefits of the ACE inhibitors.
choice_explanations.B: Decreased secretion of renin (choice B) is incorrect, because a reflex increase in renin secretion is expected with ACE inhibitors.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: Diabetics with hypertension are usually treated with an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor because these drugs are protective against diabetic nephropathy and will effectively manage their high blood pressure.
choice_explanations.D: Increased total peripheral resistance (choice D) is incorrect because reduction of circulating angiotensin II causes decreased total peripheral resistance, a major contribution to the therapeutic benefit.
choice_explanations.E: Increased urinary excretion of sodium (choice E) is expected to occur secondary to reduced aldosterone, but this is beneficial because it contributes to the diuretic effect of these drugs.
choice_explanations.F: Methemoglobinemia (choice F), cyanide toxicity, and severe hypotension are all side effects of the vasodilator nitroprusside, which is indicated for hypertensive emergency and acute heart failure.

fa_summary: ACE 抑制剂引起干咳与血管性水肿；因减少醛固酮分泌而导致高钾血症。

stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine examination following treatment with an antihypertensive medication. His blood pressure is 128/83 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: total cholesterol 210 mg/dL, HDL 29 mg/dL, LDL 168 mg/dL, and triglycerides 260 mg/dL. He states that his lipid panel was normal prior to the start of the antihypertensive medication. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for these findings in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The question states that the patient began antihypertensive therapy and now has elevated total cholesterol and triglyceride levels, as well as a low HDL level. Therefore, there is a strong possibility that the antihypertensive medication caused the dyslipidemia. Metoprolol is a beta-adrenergic antagonist that is known to cause dyslipidemias in patients. Although thiazides also cause hyperlipidemias, none of the other medications given as choices are associated with the development of dyslipidemias. Metoprolol is commonly used in the treatment of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias. This agent is also associated with the development of bradycardia, dizziness, sexual dysfunction, and potentially, heart failure and bronchospasm. The ACE inhibitor benazepril (choice A) is commonly used in the treatment of hypertension, heart failure and diabetic nephropathy. Common adverse effects include chronic cough, hyperkalemia, and angioedema. Clonidine (choice B), a centrally acting alpha2-receptor agonist, is generally used in patients unresponsive to other antihypertensive therapies. It has been shown to be efficacious in ameliorating symptoms of alcohol, tobacco, opiate, and benzodiazepine withdrawal. Clonidine is also used in the treatment of attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity. Clonidine causes severe hypotension, depression and syncope. The calcium-channel blocker diltiazem (choice C) is used to treat essential hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias. This agent is associated with the development of bradycardia, AV block, orthostatic hypotension, and sexual dysfunction. It is not associated with the development of dyslipidemias. Prazosin (choice E), a selective alpha-1 blocker, represents another class of antihypertensive agents that has a favorable effect on plasma lipids, lowering total cholesterol, reducing triglyceride levels, and mildly raising HDL-cholesterol.

choice_explanations.A: The ACE inhibitor benazepril (choice A) is commonly used in the treatment of hypertension, heart failure and diabetic nephropathy.
choice_explanations.B: Clonidine (choice B), a centrally acting alpha2-receptor agonist, is generally used in patients unresponsive to other antihypertensive therapies.
choice_explanations.C: The calcium-channel blocker diltiazem (choice C) is used to treat essential hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: The question states that the patient began antihypertensive therapy and now has elevated total cholesterol and triglyceride levels, as well as a low HDL level.
choice_explanations.E: Prazosin (choice E), a selective alpha-1 blocker, represents another class of antihypertensive agents that has a favorable effect on plasma lipids, lowering total cholesterol, reducing triglyceride levels, and mildly raising HDL-cholesterol.

fa_summary: β受体阻滞剂（美托洛尔）可引起血脂异常：升高甘油三酯、降低 HDL。

stem: A 65-year-old man develops a vesicular rash localized to a narrow circumferential band on one side of his chest. He says that he had a burning sensation in the same area starting several days before the rash appeared. Physical examination shows a painful rash with confluent vesicles and some ulceration. No other significant findings are demonstrated on physical examination. Which of the following would be the most appropriate course of therapy?
explanation: The correct answer is B. This patient has shingles, the recurrent form of herpes zoster infection, which is usually (except in the case of immunosuppressed patients) confined to a single dermatome. In otherwise healthy adults, the virus (which is usually introduced to the body as a childhood case of chickenpox) remains dormant sometimes for decades in a dorsal root ganglion only to reactivate in later life, causing a painful vesicular eruption that characteristically conforms to the distribution of a single dermatome, but can occasionally affect two or three neighboring dermatomes. Additionally, some patients may have a few scattered vesicles located at some distance away from the involved dermatome. The thoracic and lumbar dermatomes are the most commonly involved sites of herpes zoster. In patients with shingles, acyclovir, famciclovir, and valacyclovir are approved for use, but the improved pharmacodynamics of famciclovir and valacyclovir make them the preferred drugs for varicella zoster virus. It should also be noted that the zoster live-virus vaccine is indicated for the prevention of herpes zoster (shingles) in patients > 50 years old. It is not indicated for the treatment of herpes zoster. Foscarnet (choice C) is approved for use in immunosuppressed patients suffering from cytomegalovirus infections. It inhibits the viral DNA polymerase by mimicking the pyrophosphate portion of nucleoside triphosphates. The Oka strain live attenuated vaccine (choice D) for varicella zoster virus (VZV) is administered during childhood on the same schedule as the MMR vaccine. It is effective as prophylactic treatment even after exposure to VZV and may be used to limit the onset of shingles in the elderly, but would not be effective once the shingles outbreak has occurred. Pooled immune globulin (choice E) or varicella-zoster immunoglobulin can be given to immunosuppressed patients susceptible to severe disease, but would not be effective as a therapy for patients already suffering from active infections.

choice_explanations.B: Correct: This patient has shingles, the recurrent form of herpes zoster infection, which is usually (except in the case of immunosuppressed patients) confined to a single dermatome.
choice_explanations.C: Foscarnet (choice C) is approved for use in immunosuppressed patients suffering from cytomegalovirus infections.
choice_explanations.D: The Oka strain live attenuated vaccine (choice D) for varicella zoster virus (VZV) is administered during childhood on the same schedule as the MMR vaccine.
choice_explanations.E: Pooled immune globulin (choice E) or varicella-zoster immunoglobulin can be given to immunosuppressed patients susceptible to severe disease, but would not be effective as a therapy for patients already suffering from active infections.

fa_summary: 带状疱疹首选核苷类抗病毒药（泛昔洛韦/伐昔洛韦优于阿昔洛韦）；疫苗仅用于预防。

stem: A 41-year-old woman with a history of angle-closure glaucoma begins treatment with a first-line oral drug for this condition. Three weeks later, she returns to the physician for a follow-up examination. Laboratory studies show an arterial pH of 7.34, arterial PCO2 of 29 mm Hg, and plasma HCO3- of 15 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation: The correct answer is A. The laboratory results indicate that the arterial pH, arterial PCO2, and plasma HCO3- concentrations are all low. These changes clearly demonstrate metabolic acidosis, which occurs commonly when a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor is administered. In this case, the patient is likely receiving acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used to treat hypertension and glaucoma. The carbonic anhydrase enzyme attached to the brush border of the tubular epithelial cells normally catalyzes the dissociation of carbonic acid into water and carbon dioxide. Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase prevents the removal of bicarbonate ions from the tubular fluid, which initially increases urine pH. The result is heavy spillage of bicarbonate in the urine, which is the hallmark of type 2 RTA (renal tubular acidosis). However, once the plasma levels of bicarbonate have decreased sufficiently, the bicarbonaturia ceases and the plasma HCO3- levels stabilize at a lower than normal level. Consequently, the urine pH falls typically to 4.5-5.0. Winters formula applied in this case would be: PCO2 = (1.5 x [HCO3-]) + 8 +/- 2; PCO2 = (1.5 x 15) + 8 +/- 2 = 30.5 +/- 2. The PCO2 falls within this range and it is thus appropriate respiratory compensation. If it were below that range it would be mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, and above it would be respiratory and metabolic acidosis. Knowing how and when to apply Winters formula is a high-yield topic for Step 1 and 2. The following table shows the changes in plasma pH, plasma HCO3-, and arterial PCO2 characteristic of the various acid-base abnormalities: metabolic acidosis (choice A) - low pH, low PCO2, low HCO3-; metabolic alkalosis (choice B) - high pH, high PCO2, high HCO3-; mixed acidosis (choice C) - low pH, high PCO2, low HCO3-; mixed alkalosis (choice D) - high pH, low PCO2, high HCO3-; respiratory acidosis (choice E) - low pH, high PCO2, high HCO3-; respiratory alkalosis (choice F) - high pH, low PCO2, low HCO3-.

stem: A 64-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 36-hour history of progressively worsening hematuria. Physical examination shows multiple bruises on the lower legs and forearms. Laboratory studies show an INR of 5.8. He is currently being treated for chronic atrial fibrillation and for Haemophilus influenzae lower lobar pneumonia. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the antibiotic most likely used to treat his pneumonia?

options.text: Blocks attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site

explanation: The correct answer is A. This question involves both a drug-drug interaction and an indication for usage. The correct answer is therefore a drug that is both indicated for the treatment of Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia and capable of decreasing the metabolism of warfarin, resulting in the elevated INR, hematuria, and bleeding. Warfarin is a coumarin anticoagulant used for the prophylaxis and treatment of various thromboembolic complications associated with cardiac valve replacement and treatment and prophylaxis of embolism secondary to chronic atrial fibrillation. It acts by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor synthesis (II, VII, IX, X, proteins C and S). This agent has one of the most significant drug interactions related to increased or decreased warfarin effect. Warfarin is metabolized hepatically and is susceptible to cytochrome inducers and inhibitors. Inhibitors of CYP2C9, 1A2, and/or 3A4 have the potential to increase the effect of warfarin (increase INR) by decreasing drug metabolism. Likewise, inducers of these same enzymes will increase the metabolism of warfarin thereby decreasing the patient's INR. For example, the macrolides, such as clarithromycin and erythromycin, are common hepatic enzyme inhibitors that decrease the elimination of warfarin, resulting in an increased therapeutic effect. Increased levels of warfarin result in increased INR, hematuria, and bruising. Lower respiratory tract infections, such as those caused by H. influenzae, are commonly treated with clarithromycin and azithromycin. (Note that azithromycin is a macrolide that does not have the potent enzyme inhibitory effects seen with clarithromycin.) Macrolides act by binding to the P site of the 50S ribosomal subunit, thereby interfering with bacterial protein synthesis. Tetracyclines, such as tetracycline and doxycycline, bind to the 30S ribosomal subunit and prevent attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA (choice B). Tetracyclines are used for cholera, acne, Lyme disease, and Rickettsia. These agents may produce a mild interaction with warfarin; however, because they are not indicated for the treatment of H. influenzae pneumonia, choice B is incorrect. Aminoglycosides, such as gentamicin and tobramycin, inhibit protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, cause misreading of mRNA (choice C), and possibly inhibition of translocation. They are used for severe gram-negative rod infections and could be used as second-line therapy in the treatment of H. influenzae pneumonia, in combination with beta-lactams. The aminoglycosides are not associated with a severe drug-drug interaction with warfarin. Both trimethoprim and the sulfonamides can inhibit folate synthesis (choice D). Although these drugs are often used in combination (trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole or TMP/SMX) for treating urinary tract infections, they are not indicated for the treatment of lower respiratory tract infections. The sulfonamides would be expected to produce the same drug-drug interaction with warfarin, however, increasing its anticoagulant effects. Because these agents are not indicated for the treatment of H. influenzae pneumonia, choice D is incorrect. One very important point to remember is that trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole does not generally attain adequate drug concentrations in the lower lung. Therefore, it is not generally used for the treatment of a lower lobar pneumonia. Isoniazid (or INH) prevents the synthesis of mycolic acids (choice E) and is specifically used for the treatment of mycobacterial infections. Isoniazid may produce a mild-to-moderate drug-drug interaction with warfarin; however, because it is not indicated for the treatment of H. influenzae pneumonia, choice E is incorrect.
