stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of alcoholism, cigarette smoking, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the physician for a routine examination. Current medications include theophylline. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies of serum show lower than expected levels of theophylline. The patient says that he takes his medication daily and that he has not missed any of the doses. Which of the following best explains this laboratory finding?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The patient is an alcoholic and smoker, and alcohol and smoking normally induce the cytochrome P450 (CYP450) system in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) of the liver. Clinically, the most important polymorphic variations in the hepatic CYP450 system are the CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 genes. These genes code for enzymes that are responsible for the phase I metabolism of approximately 60% of all therapeutic medications. The cytochrome enzymes can be induced or inhibited by both medications and genetic polymorphisms. For the latter, genotypic CYP variations result in three primary metabolic phenotypes: ultra-rapid metabolizers, extensive (normal) metabolizers, and poor metabolizers. The ultra-rapid metabolizers and poor metabolizers can be compared to drugs that are inducers and inhibitors, respectively. Specifically, theophylline is primarily metabolized by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 isozymes; therefore, agents or pathologic processes altering these pathways will affect theophylline's metabolism. The hepatocyte SER undergoes hyperplasia as a response to alcohol ingestion and synthesizes the enzyme gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). An elevation of GGT in this particular patient would help confirm the likelihood of increased hepatic drug metabolism as the cause of low drug levels. It is also important to remember that cigarette smoking also has a hepatic enzyme-inducing effect as well. Chronic alcohol consumption and cigarette smoking are the most likely reasons for the lower than expected theophylline levels. Cirrhosis of the liver (choice A) would likely increase the serum levels of theophylline because of poor metabolism of the drug. Decreased absorption of the drug (choice B) in the gastrointestinal tract is a possible choice. However, the history of excess alcohol intake and lack of a history of malabsorption suggest increased hepatic metabolism. Increased clearance of theophylline in the urine (choice D) implies an increase in the glomerular filtration rate, which would not be expected in this patient. Acute alcohol ingestion (choice E) is associated with a decrease in theophylline's renal clearance for approximately 24 hours. Hence, one would expect to see the blood levels of theophylline increase. Conversely, chronic alcohol ingestion is associated with increased hepatic metabolism of theophylline leading to a decreased theophylline level.

choice_explanations.A: Cirrhosis of the liver (choice A) would likely increase the serum levels of theophylline because of poor metabolism of the drug.
choice_explanations.B: Decreased absorption of the drug (choice B) in the gastrointestinal tract is a possible choice.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: The patient is an alcoholic and smoker, and alcohol and smoking normally induce the cytochrome P450 (CYP450) system in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) of the liver.
choice_explanations.D: Increased clearance of theophylline in the urine (choice D) implies an increase in the glomerular filtration rate, which would not be expected in this patient.
choice_explanations.E: Acute alcohol ingestion (choice E) is associated with a decrease in theophylline's renal clearance for approximately 24 hours.

stem: A patient with coronary artery disease is scheduled to undergo coronary stent implantation. To reduce the risk of an adverse cardiovascular event after stent placement, a combination of aspirin and another drug with similar indications is administered. The patient is instructed to return in 2 weeks for a complete blood count because of the risk of neutropenia caused by this drug. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this additional drug?

options.text: Binds to and potentiates antithrombin III
Binds to the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors on activated platelets
Inhibits vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of clotting factors
Prevents adenosine diphosphate from binding to platelet receptors

explanation: The correct answer is E. This two-step question asks you to identify the mechanism of a drug commonly used in conjunction with aspirin to lower risk for a myocardial infarction after stent placement in a patient with coronary artery disease. The challenge is that you must match the indication with neutropenia, which is an important adverse effect of ticlopidine. Similar to clopidogrel, ticlopidine irreversibly blocks ADP from binding platelets. Subsequently, ADP-induced expression of glycoprotein receptors is reduced, resulting in less fibrinogen binding. Because aspirin and ticlopidine work through different mechanisms, they typically synergize. Ticlopidine may be used as a second-line agent to prevent thromboembolism or stroke. First-line therapy is typically clopidogrel in combination with aspirin because of the adverse side effects of ticlopidine. Roughly 2% of patients in clinical trials experienced neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count [ANC] < 1500/mm3) or even agranulocytosis (ANC < 100/mm3) with ticlopidine. The heparins, including the low molecular weight heparins (LMWH) such as enoxaparin and dalteparin, potentiate heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). HIT arises from antibodies generated by heparin usage that will activate platelets and cause increased clearance of the platelets, leading to thrombocytopenia. Adverse effects of LMWH are similar to those of heparin, however, they carry less risk for HIT and osteoporosis than unfractionated heparin. Three potent parenteral GpIIb/IIIa inhibitors (disintegrins) (choice B) are used in the settings of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), unstable angina, and non-Q-wave MI: abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban. These agents inhibit the binding of fibrinogen to the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors. The thrombolytic agent alteplase converts plasminogen to plasmin (choice C). Adverse effects of thrombolytics are related to their primary mechanism, and include intracranial hemorrhage/stroke and severe bleeding. Inhibition of vitamin K function (choice D) is descriptive of warfarin. Adverse effects of warfarin include hemorrhage, skin/tissue necrosis, and birth defects. Skin/tissue necrosis arises from a paradoxical hypercoagulable effect seen early on in the course of treatment because of warfarin's rapid inhibition of protein C's anticoagulating effects. If women use warfarin during pregnancy, birth defects in the child include skeletal abnormalities and developmental disability.

choice_explanations.B: Three potent parenteral GpIIb/IIIa inhibitors (disintegrins) (choice B) are used in the settings of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), unstable angina, and non-Q-wave MI: abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban.
choice_explanations.C: The thrombolytic agent alteplase converts plasminogen to plasmin (choice C).
choice_explanations.D: Inhibition of vitamin K function (choice D) is descriptive of warfarin.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: This two-step question asks you to identify the mechanism of a drug commonly used in conjunction with aspirin to lower risk for a myocardial infarction after stent placement in a patient with coronary artery disease.

stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious on the playground during school recess. An electrocardiogram shows ventricular tachycardia with a rate of 170/min, and a prolonged QT of approximately 0.5 seconds. When her parents arrive, the mother says that there is a family history of arrhythmias. Which of the following drugs is contraindicated for the treatment of this child?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The child is most likely suffering from long QT syndrome, a family condition associated with an increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias. This disease may result from a mutation in the gene that encodes cardiac potassium channels. Drugs known to prolong the QT interval (or cause hypokalemia and/or hypomagnesemia) are contraindicated for use in patients with long QT syndrome. These agents include quinidine, procainamide, sotalol, amiodarone, disopyramide, dofetilide, phenothiazines, and tricyclic antidepressants. Procainamide increases AP duration, increases effective refractory period, and increases the QT interval. Procainamide causes SLE, QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, hypotension, and flushing. Adenosine (choice A) is an unclassified antiarrhythmic medication with a half-life of < 10 seconds. It can slow both SA and AV nodal activity, as well as prolong the AV nodal refractory period. Its mechanism of action involves the activation of adenosine receptors and the reduction of the level of cAMP. It is not contraindicated in the treatment of patients with long QT syndrome. It is used for treatment of PSVT conversion and in cardiac stress testing. Lidocaine (choice B) is a class IB antiarrhythmic drug and is not contraindicated in the treatment of this patient. It acts by inhibiting Na+ ion channels and depresses action potential phase 0. Since lidocaine acts on Na+ channels it would not prolong the QT interval (which is repolarization). Lidocaine is used in treatment of ventricular arrhythmias, ventricular fibrillation and digitalis-induced arrhythmias. Metoprolol (choice C) is a selective beta-1 blocker that has negative inotropic and chronotropic effects on cardiac myocytes. It is a class II drug and is not contraindicated in long QT syndrome treatment. In fact, select beta-blockers such as nadolol are used in treatment of SVT, slowing of ventricular rate during atrial fibrillation, and atrial flutter. Verapamil (choice E) is a calcium channel blocker and class IV antiarrhythmic medication that acts by blocking nodal activity. It is used in the treatment of nodal arrhythmias, such as SVT, and rate control in atrial fibrillation.

choice_explanations.A: Adenosine (choice A) is an unclassified antiarrhythmic medication with a half-life of < 10 seconds.
choice_explanations.B: Lidocaine (choice B) is a class IB antiarrhythmic drug and is not contraindicated in the treatment of this patient.
choice_explanations.C: Metoprolol (choice C) is a selective beta-1 blocker that has negative inotropic and chronotropic effects on cardiac myocytes.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: The child is most likely suffering from long QT syndrome, a family condition associated with an increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias.
choice_explanations.E: Verapamil (choice E) is a calcium channel blocker and class IV antiarrhythmic medication that acts by blocking nodal activity.

stem: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressive fatigue, shortness of breath, and easy bruisability. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for pallor. Laboratory studies show: leukocyte count 14,000/mm3, hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, hematocrit 30%. A bone marrow biopsy is performed and shows myeloblasts containing few Auer rods as well as monoblasts and monocytes. Treatment is initiated with a drug that inhibits DNA polymerase and can cause leukopenia and anemia. Which of the following is the most likely therapeutic agent described?
explanation: The correct answer is B. In acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), myeloblasts may have intracytoplasmic rods (stain red) called Auer rods. Auer rods are composed of abnormal lysosomes (primary granules) that are pathognomonic of myeloblasts and not found in ALL. Auer rods also stain positive with myeloperoxidase (MPO) or Sudan-black B stain. Auer rods can be found in M2, M3, and M4 AML. The tissue form of AML is called granulocytic sarcoma (chloroma). Given the bone marrow finding, this patient most likely has myelomonocytic type AML (M4). Cytarabine is a pyrimidine analog that is commonly administered with idarubicin, daunorubicin or mitoxantrone, to induce remission of acute myelogenous leukemia (AML). This agent primarily acts via inhibition of DNA polymerase, and has also been shown to incorporate into both DNA and RNA as well. Cytarabine is known to be a “bone marrow suppressant”; hence, anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and megaloblastosis are well-documented toxic effects of this agent. Cytarabine is not used to treat acute promyelocytic leukemia (M3 AML) and all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) is the treatment of choice. Bleomycin (choice A) is an intercalating agent that complexes iron-forming reactive oxygen species and induces DNA strand breaks. This agent is commonly associated with the development of pulmonary fibrosis. Similar to daunorubicin, doxorubicin (choice C) is an antitumor antibiotic that inserts between DNA bases and induces DNA strand breaks. Cardiotoxicity, myelosuppression and extravasation necrosis are the most common adverse effects with this medication. Etoposide (choice D) is a topoisomerase inhibitor used in the treatment of testicular cancer, small cell lung carcinoma, and acute myelogenous leukemia. Myelosuppression is the dose-limiting toxicity associated with this agent. Paclitaxel (choice E) inhibits mitosis by binding tubulin and preventing degradation of microtubules. This agent is used in the treatment of ovarian cancer, breast cancer, and non-small cell lung cancer. Bone marrow suppression, alopecia, and hypersensitivity reactions are the most common toxic effects seen with paclitaxel.

choice_explanations.A: Bleomycin (choice A) is an intercalating agent that complexes iron-forming reactive oxygen species and induces DNA strand breaks.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: In acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), myeloblasts may have intracytoplasmic rods (stain red) called Auer rods.
choice_explanations.C: Similar to daunorubicin, doxorubicin (choice C) is an antitumor antibiotic that inserts between DNA bases and induces DNA strand breaks.
choice_explanations.D: Etoposide (choice D) is a topoisomerase inhibitor used in the treatment of testicular cancer, small cell lung carcinoma, and acute myelogenous leukemia.
choice_explanations.E: Paclitaxel (choice E) inhibits mitosis by binding tubulin and preventing degradation of microtubules.

stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of palpitations and fatigue. Further evaluation shows atrial fibrillation, and treatment is begun with a medication that acts by inhibiting sodium-potassium ATPase. Three weeks later he returns to the physician for a follow-up examination with a complaint of yellow/green visual halos, dizziness and abdominal pain. His serum drug levels are well above the therapeutic range. This patient is at highest risk for developing which of the following?
explanation: The correct answer is B. Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside that directly inhibits cardiac Na+/K+ ATPase, leading to indirect inhibition of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, which leads to increased intracellular Ca2+ and positive inotropy. It also inhibits neuronal Na+/K+ ATPase, resulting in increased vagal nerve activity and a decrease in heart rate. Digoxin is used for CHF (increases inotropy) and supraventricular tachycardias (decreases AV conduction and depresses the SA node). Digoxin has a low therapeutic index. Early toxic doses include anorexia, nausea, and ECG changes. Later signs include disorientation, visual effects (e.g., blurred vision, yellow-green halos; may have contributed to Van Gogh's “Yellow Period”). Toxic doses can cause a variety of cardiac arrhythmias. If a life-threatening complication of toxicity occurs, the patient can be treated with digoxin immune Fab, which binds to digoxin, making it unavailable to bind to the Na+/K+-ATPase and facilitating its removal from the body. Correction of electrolyte imbalances is also important. Digoxin toxicity is unlikely to result in the development of acute renal failure (choice A), hypokalemia (choice C), or hyponatremia (choice D). Tonic-clonic seizures may occur (choice E), but this is extremely rare. It is important to note that digoxin toxicity does NOT cause hypokalemia; however, hypokalemia can lead to the development of digoxin toxicity. When a patient is hypokalemic, digoxin toxicity can occur at any therapeutic concentration. This occurs because digoxin binds to the K+ site on the Na+/K+-ATPase, and binds more easily if there is less concentration of potassium.

choice_explanations.A: Digoxin toxicity is unlikely to result in the development of acute renal failure (choice A), hypokalemia (choice C), or hyponatremia (choice D).
choice_explanations.B: Correct: Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside that directly inhibits cardiac Na+/K+ ATPase, leading to indirect inhibition of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, which leads to increased intracellular Ca2+ and positive inotropy.
choice_explanations.C: Digoxin toxicity is unlikely to result in the development of acute renal failure (choice A), hypokalemia (choice C), or hyponatremia (choice D).
choice_explanations.D: Digoxin toxicity is unlikely to result in the development of acute renal failure (choice A), hypokalemia (choice C), or hyponatremia (choice D).
choice_explanations.E: Tonic-clonic seizures may occur (choice E), but this is extremely rare.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a history of osteoarthritis comes to the physician because of progressive pain in his knees despite treatment with aspirin. He states that the usual dose of the drug is no longer effective for treating his knee pain, and that he has increased the dose and frequency of aspirin without consulting his physician. Which of the following is the most likely earliest sign or symptom of salicylate intoxication this patient would experience?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Aspirin remains a commonly used analgesic despite the general preference for nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). It is also widely prescribed for antiplatelet therapy. Aspirin is present in a multitude of over-the-counter (OTC) medications and in many prescription drugs, making salicylate toxicity an important cause of morbidity and mortality. Early recognition is essential for successful management. Aspirin can cause toxic effects in a variety of ways. Salicylates are neurotoxic and initially cause tinnitus. Higher levels can result in hearing loss. Stimulation of the medullary chemoreceptor trigger zone can cause nausea and vomiting. Irreversible inhibition of cyclooxygenase leads to decreased synthesis of prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxanes. This has a role in gastric mucosal injury and platelet dysfunction. Stimulation of the medullary respiratory center leads to hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. Disruption of the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation later can lead to a metabolic acidosis. Early symptoms of acute aspirin toxicity include tinnitus, nausea and vomiting, hyperventilation, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and hyperactivity. Additional symptoms that indicate a more severe intoxication include altered mental status, hyperpyrexia, pulmonary edema, and coma. Doses that can cause fatality are 10 to 30 g in adults and as little as 3 g in children. Management includes supportive care and alkalinization of serum and urine with IV sodium bicarbonate to keep salicylates in the blood and away from tissues and enhance urinary excretion (ion trapping). Alkalinization with acetazolamide is contraindicated because the loss of bicarbonate promotes salicylate movement into the brain, potentially worsening the salicylate neurotoxicity. Acidosis (choice A) does not occur initially. Salicylates first stimulate the medullary respiratory center, causing hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. An anion-gap metabolic acidosis can follow as a result of accumulation of organic acids such as lactic acid and ketoacids. Salicylic acid itself has only a minor effect on pH because of the low serum concentration (even on overdose). Electrocardiogram (ECG) changes (choice B) may reflect hypokalemia and include sinus tachycardia, u waves, flattened T waves, and QT prolongation. These alterations generally do not occur until the patient has blood levels consistent with serious toxicity. Hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia (choice C), may occur as a result of aspirin toxicity. This is likely the result of increased cellular metabolism due to uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation. It is possible to have depletion of intracellular glucose with a normal serum glucose, producing symptoms of CNS hypoglycemia (e.g., altered mental status). Supplemental glucose should be administered to patients with alterations in mental status regardless of their serum glucose concentration. Hyperventilation, not hypoventilation (choice D), can occur as a result of stimulation of the medullary respiratory center. This can initially lead to respiratory alkalosis.

choice_explanations.A: Acidosis (choice A) does not occur initially.
choice_explanations.B: Electrocardiogram (ECG) changes (choice B) may reflect hypokalemia and include sinus tachycardia, u waves, flattened T waves, and QT prolongation.
choice_explanations.C: Hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia (choice C), may occur as a result of aspirin toxicity.

stem: A 57-year-old man with a 2-year history of hypertension managed by diet and exercise comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. His blood pressure is 166/97 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show plasma renin activity 3-4 times higher than normal. Treatment with losartan is begun. Following administration of losartan, which of the following is most likely to be increased in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Losartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) commonly used in the treatment of hypertension that competitively inhibits angiotensin II at the receptor. Angiotensin II is the most powerful sodium-retaining hormone of the body. The effects of angiotensin II can be attributed to: direct stimulation of sodium reabsorption in the proximal and distal tubules of the kidney; stimulation of aldosterone secretion, which is another sodium-retaining hormone; and constriction of the efferent arterioles, which increases peritubular capillary pressure, thereby enhancing reabsorption of salt and water from the proximal tubule. Therefore, when the effects of angiotensin II are blocked with losartan, the ability of the kidneys to excrete sodium increases greatly. Because angiotensin II normally stimulates aldosterone (choice A) secretion, losartan decreases plasma aldosterone levels. Overstretching of the two atria, usually as a result of increased blood volume, causes atrial natriuretic peptide (choice B) to be released into the blood. Because losartan increases the ability of the kidneys to excrete sodium (and therefore water), the blood volume should decrease, and the plasma levels of atrial natriuretic peptide should decrease. Bradykinin (choice C) levels are not affected by ARBs. However, bradykinin levels are increased in patients taking the ACE inhibitors because ACE is the enzyme responsible for the metabolism of bradykinin. Increased levels of bradykinin are thought to be the reason patients on ACEIs develop dry cough. These patients can be switched to an ARB if the dry cough is too aversive to the patient.

choice_explanations.A: Because angiotensin II normally stimulates aldosterone (choice A) secretion, losartan decreases plasma aldosterone levels.
choice_explanations.B: Overstretching of the two atria, usually as a result of increased blood volume, causes atrial natriuretic peptide (choice B) to be released into the blood.
choice_explanations.C: Bradykinin (choice C) levels are not affected by ARBs.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: Losartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) commonly used in the treatment of hypertension that competitively inhibits angiotensin II at the receptor.

stem: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. Treatment with a continuous infusion of morphine at a dose of 0.1 mg/min is begun. The half-life of morphine is 1.9 hours and its volume of distribution (Vd) is 230 L. The clearance (CL) for morphine is 60 L/h. Which of the following is the steady-state concentration that will most likely be attained?
explanation: The correct answer is D. In the calculation of an appropriate dosing rate, drug clearance is the most important pharmacokinetic value to consider when determining a rational steady-state drug dosage regimen. At steady-state, the dosing rate ("rate in") must equal the rate of elimination ("rate out"). Remember to keep all of the "time" and "volume" units the same. Hence, 60 L/h = 1 L/min. Dosing rate = Css x CL. The equation can be rearranged to solve for Css: Css = Dosing rate/CL = (0.1 mg/min)/(1 L/min) = 0.1 mg/L.

choice_explanations.D: Correct: In the calculation of an appropriate dosing rate, drug clearance is the most important pharmacokinetic value to consider when determining a rational steady-state drug dosage regimen.

stem: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of constant worrying, muscular tension, poor concentration, and restlessness. She also reports that although she is a generally happy person, her "constant worrying about work, the kids, and her house" sometimes makes it difficult to either fall asleep or stay asleep, causing her fatigue. She further states that these symptoms have been occurring for the past 8-9 months and cannot recall a specific event that makes them worse or could have caused them to begin. She does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. Which of the following mechanisms best describes the drug of choice for the short-term management of this patient's condition?

options.text: Increases the duration of GABAA channel opening
Increases the frequency of GABAA channel opening
Increases the release of norepinephrine from central noradrenergic neurons
Inhibits biogenic amine reuptake at the presynaptic neuron

explanation: The correct answer is C. Generalized anxiety disorder is associated with excessive worry and can lead to symptoms such as insomnia, muscle tension, impaired concentration, autonomic arousal, and restlessness. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for generalized anxiety disorder is outlined below. First-line medications for the treatment of generalized anxiety disorder are the selective-serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). However, since it takes several weeks for the full beneficial effects of these agents to be realized, the use of a benzodiazepine in the short-term may be initially indicated. GABA (gamma-aminobutyrate) reduces the firing rate of neurons and is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. The GABAA receptor is a chloride ion channel receptor. Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam, alprazolam, and diazepam potentiate the effects of GABA at the GABAA receptor by increasing the frequency of GABAA channel opening, leading to antianxiety, sedative, and anticonvulsant effects. In contrast, barbiturates such as phenobarbital potentiate GABA at the GABAA receptor by increasing the duration of channel opening (choice B). Note that benzodiazepines are much safer than barbiturates. Barbiturates are used less frequently because of the safety issues and are used primarily for seizures and sometimes for induction of anesthesia. Propranolol and metoprolol are beta-blockers, since they antagonize beta-adrenergic receptors (choice A). Beta-blockers are indicated for the treatment of hypertension, angina pectoris, and various other cardiovascular conditions. Amphetamines act, in part, by increasing the release of norepinephrine from central noradrenergic neurons (choice D). They are indicated for the treatment of narcolepsy, attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity, and exogenous obesity. Tricyclic antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, nortriptyline and doxepin, block the uptake of biogenic amines (norepinephrine and serotonin) at the presynaptic neuron (choice E). These agents are second-line drugs for the treatment of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. Like the SSRIs and SNRIs, the full beneficial effects of these drugs will not be apparent for several weeks, and would not be indicated for the short-term treatment of this patient's condition.

choice_explanations.A: Propranolol and metoprolol are beta-blockers, since they antagonize beta-adrenergic receptors (choice A).
choice_explanations.B: In contrast, barbiturates such as phenobarbital potentiate GABA at the GABAA receptor by increasing the duration of channel opening (choice B).
choice_explanations.C: Correct: Generalized anxiety disorder is associated with excessive worry and can lead to symptoms such as insomnia, muscle tension, impaired concentration, autonomic arousal, and restlessness.
choice_explanations.D: Amphetamines act, in part, by increasing the release of norepinephrine from central noradrenergic neurons (choice D).
choice_explanations.E: Tricyclic antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, nortriptyline and doxepin, block the uptake of biogenic amines (norepinephrine and serotonin) at the presynaptic neuron (choice E).

stem: A 54-year-old woman with a 3-year history of type 2 diabetes comes to the physician for a follow-up appointment. She is 162 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall, weighs 82 kg (181 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m2. Laboratory studies show: total cholesterol 190 mg/dL, triglycerides 940 mg/dL, HDL 24 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c 9.5%. She is currently taking metformin and glipizide. The physician then prescribes a drug that activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-alpha (PPAR-alpha). Which of the following symptoms will this patient most likely experience as a result of the latest drug added to her regimen?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Fibrates such as gemfibrozil, fenofibrate, and clofibrate activate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-alpha (PPAR-alpha) and increase the expression of lipoprotein lipases. PPARs are a group of nuclear receptor proteins that act as transcription factors. Fibrates act on PPAR-alpha, whereas the antidiabetic thiazolidinediones (e.g., pioglitazone) act on PPAR-gamma. Fibric acid derivatives lower triglycerides by approximately 35-50% and increase HDL-c by 5-20%. Fibrates increase the cholesterol content of bile, and therefore increase the risk of gallstones, which can manifest as right upper quadrant pain. The risk is greatest with clofibrate, and this agent is less frequently used. Fibrates also cause muscle toxicity, which is exacerbated when taken in combination with statins. Constipation (choice A) is a frequent complaint with bile acid sequestrants such as cholestyramine and colestipol. Gemfibrozil, for example, is commonly associated with diarrhea. Facial flushing (choice B) is an adverse effect of niacin. Niacin also causes flushing, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, and a chemical hepatitis. Niacin can cause hyperglycemia (choice C) and hyperuricemia. Rhabdomyolysis (choice D) is a rare, but potentially life-threatening side effect of statins. Statins act by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase; examples include simvastatin, pravastatin, lovastatin, and atorvastatin. Other adverse effects of statins include myopathy and hepatotoxicity. Fibrates can increase the risk of rhabdomyolysis when given with statins.

choice_explanations.A: Constipation (choice A) is a frequent complaint with bile acid sequestrants such as cholestyramine and colestipol.
choice_explanations.B: Facial flushing (choice B) is an adverse effect of niacin.
choice_explanations.C: Niacin can cause hyperglycemia (choice C) and hyperuricemia.
choice_explanations.D: Rhabdomyolysis (choice D) is a rare, but potentially life-threatening side effect of statins.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: Fibrates such as gemfibrozil, fenofibrate, and clofibrate activate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-alpha (PPAR-alpha) and increase the expression of lipoprotein lipases.

stem: A 22-year-old man who is a soldier in the Armed Forces comes to the physician because of a non-healing, ulcerated lesion on his left hand. He returned from a tour of duty in Afghanistan two months ago and says he was bitten on his hand by a bug shortly before he returned to the United States. If this infection is transmitted by the bite of female phlebotomine sandfly, which of the following drugs is most appropriate for this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is E. In this question, you must make the correct diagnosis, then determine the most optimal therapy. The patient is suffering from cutaneous leishmaniasis. Leishmaniasis is a vector-borne disease caused by a heterogeneous group of protozoa belonging to the genus Leishmania. Leishmaniasis is transmitted by sand fly vectors and can produce both cutaneous and visceral manifestations. Skin manifestations include erythematous macules or papules, and skin ulcers, which form at the site of original lesion and heal slowly (over a period of months). Cutaneous leishmaniasis can progress to mucosal or visceral leishmaniasis. Ulcers of the mouth, tongue, gums, lips, nose, and nasal septum may occur. Dysphagia with esophageal involvement and dyspnea can also occur. Visceral leishmaniasis is associated with fever, which can be persistent and can last for weeks, or may cycle irregularly. Night sweats, fatigue, weakness, anorexia, weight loss, thinning of the hair, and scaly gray, dark, ashen skin also occur. Death, often within 2 years in untreated individuals, usually results from complications (often infectious) rather than from the disease itself. Cases of leishmaniasis have been reported on all continents except Australia. In the Americas, Leishmania can be found in Mexico and south into the South American continent. Antimony-containing compounds are the principal medications used to treat localized cutaneous leishmaniasis, and include sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimonate. Paromomycin ointment can also be used for the topical treatment of milder forms of localized cutaneous leishmaniasis. Other medications that may be used for systemic therapy include azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole), pentamidine, and amphotericin B. The azoles can be used for moderate cases of cutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis. However, amphotericin B is the drug of choice for the treatment of severe diffuse cutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis. Albendazole (choice A) is a broad-spectrum antiparasitic indicated for the treatment of “worm” infections, such as Enterobius vermicularis, Trichuris trichiura, and Ascaris lumbricoides. Cefuroxime (choice B) is a second-generation cephalosporin indicated for a variety of gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria. Ganciclovir (choice C) is used in the treatment and prophylaxis of cytomegalovirus infections in both solid organ transplant and HIV-infected patients. Pyrazinamide (choice D) is a bactericidal agent typically used in short-course therapy for the treatment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections.

choice_explanations.A: Albendazole (choice A) is a broad-spectrum antiparasitic indicated for the treatment of “worm” infections, such as Enterobius vermicularis, Trichuris trichiura, and Ascaris lumbricoides.
choice_explanations.B: Cefuroxime (choice B) is a second-generation cephalosporin indicated for a variety of gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria.
choice_explanations.C: Ganciclovir (choice C) is used in the treatment and prophylaxis of cytomegalovirus infections in both solid organ transplant and HIV-infected patients.
choice_explanations.D: Pyrazinamide (choice D) is a bactericidal agent typically used in short-course therapy for the treatment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections.
choice_explanations.E: Correct: In this question, you must make the correct diagnosis, then determine the most optimal therapy.

stem: A 67-year-old African-American man comes to the physician because of fever, increased frequency of urination, and perineal pain. He has a history of type 2 diabetes and an X-linked recessive disorder, which causes red cell hemolysis. Digital rectal examination shows a boggy and tender prostate. Cultures of urine grow E coli. The physician then prescribes an antimicrobial agent used in the treatment of this condition. Which of the following would most likely be contraindicated for use in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is D. This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms suggestive of acute bacterial prostatitis, which is associated with fever, chills, perineal/prostatic pain, dysuria, obstructive urinary tract symptoms, and potentially lower back or abdominal pain. This condition is generally treated with a 14 to 28 day course of antibiotics, which include sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (SMX-TMP) or a fluoroquinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin). Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is part of the hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt (pentose phosphate pathway) and catalyzes the oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate and the reduction of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP+) to NADPH. NADPH maintains glutathione in its reduced form, which acts as a scavenger for dangerous reactive oxygen species (ROS). Because red blood cells (RBCs) contain a large amount of oxygen, they are prone to spontaneously generate ROS that damage protein and lipid in the cell. In the presence of ROS, hemoglobin may precipitate (Heinz bodies) and membrane lipids may undergo peroxidation, weakening the membrane and causing hemolysis. As peroxides form, they are normally rapidly destroyed by the glutathione peroxidase/glutathione reductase system in the RBC, thus avoiding these complications. Patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD or G6PDH) deficiency (an X-linked recessive disorder affecting 10-15% of African-American males) may develop hemolytic anemia as a result of oxidative stress (due to insufficient NADPH to reduce glutathione) in red blood cells (RBCs), generated either by infections or exposure to certain drugs (e.g., sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim), nitrofurantoin, fluoroquinolones, isoniazid, dapsone, primaquine, and quinine, or ingesting fava beans. Cefaclor (choice B) is a second-generation cephalosporin indicated for a variety of bacterial infections, including those of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts, and skin and soft-tissue infections, as well as several other types of bacterial infections. Nitrofurantoin (choice C) is an antibacterial commonly used in the treatment and prophylaxis of uncomplicated cystitis. Although this medication is contraindicated for use in patients with G6PD deficiency, it is not used in the treatment of acute bacterial prostatitis, and is an incorrect answer choice. Tetracycline (choice E) is most commonly used in the treatment of acne vulgaris and gonococcal infections.

choice_explanations.B: Cefaclor (choice B) is a second-generation cephalosporin indicated for a variety of bacterial infections, including those of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts, and skin and soft-tissue infections, as well as several other types of bacterial infections.
choice_explanations.C: Nitrofurantoin (choice C) is an antibacterial commonly used in the treatment and prophylaxis of uncomplicated cystitis.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms suggestive of acute bacterial prostatitis, which is associated with fever, chills, perineal/prostatic pain, dysuria, obstructive urinary tract symptoms, and potentially lower back or abdominal pain.
choice_explanations.E: Tetracycline (choice E) is most commonly used in the treatment of acne vulgaris and gonococcal infections.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who is an actress comes to a physician because she is concerned about facial wrinkles. The physician recommends botulinum toxin injections. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this medication?

options.text: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in neurons
Inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of muscle
Inhibits uptake of acetylcholine into the motor neurons
Prevents fusion of motor neuron secretory vesicles with the nerve membrane

explanation: The correct answer is E. Botulinum toxin is a protein toxin produced by the gram-positive, spore-forming, obligate anaerobe Clostridium botulinum. Botulinum toxin blocks neuromuscular conduction by binding to protein sites on motor nerve terminals, entering nerve terminals via endocytosis, and inhibiting the release of acetylcholine (ACh), thereby reducing local skeletal muscle activity. Different subtypes of the toxin cleave different SNARE proteins, which are essential to the successful docking and release of acetylcholine from vesicles located within nerve endings. Examples of SNARE proteins are SNAP-25 and synaptobrevin. The toxin causes flaccid paralysis of the muscle, resulting in a localized reduction in muscle activity. Additionally, the muscle may atrophy, axonal sprouting may occur and extra-junctional acetylcholine receptors may be expressed. Pharmacologically the botulinum toxin is sold as onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox). It is used to treat moderate-severe glabellar and lateral canthal lines as well as overactive bladder, migraine headache prophylaxis, upper limb spasticity and cervical dystonia.

choice_explanations.E: Correct: Botulinum toxin is a protein toxin produced by the gram-positive, spore-forming, obligate anaerobe Clostridium botulinum.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis comes to the physician because of frequent stomach aches for the past 8 months. She is currently taking aspirin daily for her joint pain. Treatment with an alternate drug is initiated that is relatively similar in overall effectiveness, but is less likely to cause gastric irritation. This alternate drug is most likely which of the following?
explanation: The correct answer is A. Celecoxib is a selective cyclooxygenase (COX)-2 inhibitor that is usually prescribed because it causes less gastrointestinal toxicity when compared with conventional nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) is known to be present throughout most tissues. In the gastrointestinal tract, COX-1 maintains the normal lining of the stomach. This enzyme is also involved in kidney and platelet function. Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) is primarily restricted to sites of inflammation. By targeting COX-2 specifically, celecoxib theoretically provides relief from inflammation, while sparing degradative effects on the stomach lining. Celecoxib has been approved for pain relief associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and osteoarthritis (OA), as well as for a variety of acute and chronic pain syndromes. Potential cardiotoxicity resulted in the withdrawal of rofecoxib, valdecoxib, and parecoxib from the market. Although the potential for cardiotoxicity exists with all of the NSAIDs and celecoxib, these agents remain on the market since it is believed that the potential for developing this side effect is much lower with these agents. Gabapentin (choice B) is an analgesic and antiepileptic used for epilepsy, postherpetic neuralgia, neuropathic pain, and restless legs syndrome (RLS). It does not have anti-inflammatory effects and is not used for rheumatoid arthritis. Hydrocodone (choice C) is an opioid analgesic indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe pain as well as cough suppression. It would not be indicated for use in this patient since it has no anti-inflammatory effects. Ibuprofen (choice D) and naproxen (choice E) are non-selective NSAIDs. These may help with the pain and inflammation, but they will also continue to cause gastric irritation.

stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of severe pain in his first metatarsophalangeal joint. He says that the pain was so bad that it woke him up from sleep. Physical examination shows a tender and erythematous metatarsophalangeal joint. Laboratory studies show leukocyte count is 12 x 10(9)/mm3, creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, calcium is 8.6 mg/dL, and uric acid is 9.5 mg/dL. A review of his records shows that the patient was started on a new drug 2 weeks ago. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: The correct answer is D. Acute gouty arthritis (AGA) is characterized by the rapid onset of pain, swelling, and inflammation. The attack is often monoarticular at first, affecting the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint; eventually, it may involve the insteps, ankles, heels, knees, wrists, fingers, and elbows. Note: >90% of all gouty patients experience attacks in the great toe. Uric acid levels are generally >7.5 mg/dL when an attack occurs. Acute gouty arthritis occurs in urate crystal deposition disease (gout), which occurs when uric acid or urate accumulates in blood or tissues. When the tissues become supersaturated, urate salts precipitate, forming crystals. Crystals are more likely to form in cool, peripheral joints. Phagocytosis of the urate crystals by leukocytes leads to rapid lysis of cells, which subsequently leads to an inflammatory reaction that causes intense joint pain, erythema, warmth, and swelling. Changes in urate levels, leading to gout flares, can result from acute alcohol intoxication, overindulgence of foods high in purines, rapid weight loss, dehydration, and trauma. Medications (e.g., thiazide or loop diuretics, allopurinol, uricosuric agents, low-dose aspirin) can also precipitate gout. Thiazides such as hydrochlorothiazide can increase serum urate concentrations by as much as 35% by decreasing the renal clearance of urate. Possible mechanisms include competition for the same organic anion transporter pathway and extracellular volume depletion. None of the other drugs affect uric acid elimination and are not associated with the development of AGA. Aripiprazole (choice A) is an atypical antipsychotic used for the treatment of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and adjunct treatment of major depression. It is not associated with AGA but can cause weight gain, extrapyramidal side effects (though less than the typical antipsychotics), and insomnia. Enalapril (choice B) is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor that is associated with anaphylactoid reactions, angioedema, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and cough. Felodipine (choice C) is a calcium channel blocking agent associated with hypotension, reflex tachycardia, peripheral edema, and dizziness. Pravastatin (choice E) is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor indicated for the treatment of hyperlipidemia. This drug is most commonly associated with the development of myopathy, myalgia, rhabdomyolysis, and hepatic enzyme elevation.

choice_explanations.A: Aripiprazole (choice A) is an atypical antipsychotic used for the treatment of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and adjunct treatment of major depression.
choice_explanations.B: Enalapril (choice B) is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor that is associated with anaphylactoid reactions, angioedema, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and cough.
choice_explanations.C: Felodipine (choice C) is a calcium channel blocking agent associated with hypotension, reflex tachycardia, peripheral edema, and dizziness.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: Acute gouty arthritis (AGA) is characterized by the rapid onset of pain, swelling, and inflammation.
choice_explanations.E: Pravastatin (choice E) is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor indicated for the treatment of hyperlipidemia.
