stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a mass on the side of his neck. Physical examination shows a small, mobile cyst along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. This cyst is the result of incomplete obliteration of which of the following developmental structures?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. In normal development of the neck, the second pharyngeal arch grows inferiorly, covers over the second, third and fourth pharyngeal clefts to fuse with the cardiac ridge, thereby obliterating clefts 2-4. The cervical sinus formed by the fusion of these tissue masses is normally a transient structure but may persist as a branchial or lateral cervical cyst, which is usually derived from the second, third, or fourth pharyngeal cleft.

Branchial cysts (lateral cervical cysts) result from incomplete obliteration of the second (or third or fourth) pharyngeal cleft. They are always laterally placed, and are usually situated along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

The first pharyngeal arch (choice A) gives rise to various bony, muscular, and ligamentous structures: the maxilla, the mandible, the malleus and incus; the muscles of mastication, plus the tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and anterior digastric; the sphenomandibular ligament; and the anterior malleolar ligament.

The first pharyngeal cleft (choice B) is retained as the external auditory meatus and canal.

The first pharyngeal pouch (choice C) gives rise to the tympanic cavity and auditory tube.

The second pharyngeal arch (choice D), like the first, gives rise to bones, muscles, and ligaments: the stapes and lesser horn and upper part of the body of the hyoid bone; the muscles of facial expression, plus the stapedius, stylohyoid and posterior digastric; and the stylohyoid ligament.

The second pharyngeal pouch (choice F) becomes the tonsillar fossa.

choice_explanations.A: First pharyngeal arch derivatives include the maxilla, mandible, malleus, incus, and muscles of mastication. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: The first pharyngeal cleft is retained as the external auditory meatus. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: The first pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the tympanic cavity and auditory tube. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Second pharyngeal arch derivatives include the stapes, styloid process, and muscles of facial expression. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. A branchial (lateral cervical) cyst results from incomplete obliteration of the second (or third or fourth) pharyngeal cleft, and lies along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
choice_explanations.F: The second pharyngeal pouch becomes the tonsillar fossa. Incorrect.

stem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman in the first trimester is exposed to a person with mumps. The patient states that she has never been immunized, nor has she had mumps previously. Seven months later, she delivers a newborn with macrocephaly. A CT scan of the head shows hydrocephaly with symmetric enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles. The fourth ventricle is of normal size. Which of the following embryonic structures contributes to the development of the obstructed structure in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This woman acquired a mumps infection in the first trimester as a result of being non-immune. A known teratogenic result of this is aqueductal stenosis, resulting in proximal ventricular enlargement and thus noncommunicating hydrocephalus. This is consistent with the description of enlarged lateral and third ventricles and a normal size fourth ventricle. The cerebral aqueduct connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle. The cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) is in the midbrain, or mesencephalon.

Aqueductal stenosis due to the teratogenic effects of mumps can result in proximal ventricular enlargement and a noncommunicating hydrocephalus.

CSF flows from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramen of Monro to the third ventricle, through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, out the foramen of Magendie and foramina of Luschka into the subarachnoid space, through the arachnoid granulations, and out via the venous sinuses and internal jugular vein.

The primitive central nervous system (CNS) is composed of the three primary neural tube vesicles: the hindbrain, the midbrain, and the forebrain. From these develop five secondary vesicles. The hindbrain develops into the myelencephalon and the metencephalon; the midbrain develops into the mesencephalon; the forebrain develops into the diencephalon and telencephalon. The rostrocaudal order of the vesicles is: telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, and myelencephalon.

The diencephalon (choice A) develops into the thalamus, pineal gland, neurohypophysis, hypothalamus, retina, and third ventricle.

The metencephalon (choice C) develops into the pons and cerebellum, and contributes to the fourth ventricle.

The myelencephalon (choice D) develops into the medulla, and also contributes to the fourth ventricle.

The telencephalon (choice E) develops into the cerebral hemispheres, most of the basal ganglia, and the lateral ventricles.

choice_explanations.A: The diencephalon develops into the thalamus, pineal gland, neurohypophysis, hypothalamus, retina, and third ventricle. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. The cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) lies in the midbrain (mesencephalon); stenosis of the aqueduct causes noncommunicating hydrocephalus with enlarged lateral and third ventricles.
choice_explanations.C: The metencephalon develops into the pons and cerebellum and contributes to the fourth ventricle. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: The myelencephalon develops into the medulla and contributes to the fourth ventricle. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: The telencephalon develops into the cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia, and lateral ventricles. Incorrect.

stem:
A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of trouble swallowing. Over the last few months, she has had difficulty with ingesting solid food, but only recently, she developed problems with thick liquids. She describes her condition as a "lump" in her throat. She expresses some concern because her father passed away from esophageal cancer.

Her temperature is 37.4°C (99.4°F), pulse is 77/min, blood pressure is 121/77 mm Hg, and respirations are 12/min. Physical examination shows several small clusters of dilated capillaries on the face and trunk, normal cardiac and lung auscultation, and several 1.5-3 cm firm, nontender nodules on the elbows, forearm, and knees. The patient receives a full complement of swallowing studies. Esophageal manometry shows decreased peristalsis and decreased lower esophageal sphincter tone. Serum antibody studies are shown.

Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Limited scleroderma, also known as CREST syndrome, is an autoimmune disease characterized by fibroblast stimulation and deposition of collagen in the skin and esophagus. Clinical features include involvement of the skin of the face and hands, late involvement of visceral organs, and a relatively benign course. Anti-centromere antibodies are a marker for the CREST variant of scleroderma. The name "CREST" highlights its most important findings: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias.

Esophageal dysfunction in CREST and diffuse scleroderma results from fibrotic disruption of esophageal musculature and innervation. Decreased peristalsis impairs swallowing of both liquids and solids, and lower esophageal sphincter tone can also be present, producing reflux.

Achalasia (choice A), like scleroderma, can also produce progressive dysphagia for solids and liquids. Though these patients have dysfunctional peristalsis, they typically present with elevated lower esophageal sphincter tone, due to destruction of nitrous-oxide producing neurons. This condition is not associated with serum auto-antibodies.

Diffuse scleroderma (choice C) is a more aggressive form of scleroderma which presents with more extensive skin involvement and early organ fibrosis (pulmonary fibrosis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, etc). The marker for diffuse scleroderma, anti-Scl-70 (antibodies against DNA topoisomerase I), is usually negative in patients with CREST syndrome.

Esophageal carcinoma (choice D) can present with progressive dysphagia, though positive anti-centromere antibodies would be unusual. Risk factors for esophageal cancer include chronic gastroesophageal reflux (GERD leading to Barrett esophagus), chronic alcoholism, achalasia, tobacco smoking, and Plummer-Vinson syndrome. This patient would be young for esophageal cancer.

Mixed connective tissue disease (choice E) is a combination of features from SLE, myositis, scleroderma, and rheumatoid arthritis. Serum markers for this condition include anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein and rheumatoid factor. This condition has a favorable prognosis, although some can evolve into a fatal autoimmune condition; pulmonary hypertension is the most common cause of death in these patients.

choice_explanations.A: Achalasia can cause progressive dysphagia for solids and liquids but is associated with increased (not decreased) lower esophageal sphincter tone and is not associated with serum autoantibodies. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome) explains the high-titer anti-centromere antibody, telangiectasias, calcinosis-like nodules, and esophageal dysmotility (decreased peristalsis and decreased LES tone).
choice_explanations.C: Diffuse scleroderma is associated with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) and earlier, more extensive skin and visceral involvement; anti-Scl-70 is not detected here. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Esophageal carcinoma can cause progressive dysphagia but does not account for the anti-centromere antibody or the cutaneous/systemic findings; the patient is young for this diagnosis. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Mixed connective tissue disease is associated with anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein, which is not detected here. Incorrect.

fa_summary: Limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is marked by anti-centromere antibodies; diffuse scleroderma is marked by anti-Scl-70/anti-DNA topoisomerase I.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of mild intellectual disability. The parents state that their other son has a similar condition, and their three daughters appear to be normal. A cytogenetic test shows a specific chromosomal breakage site. Which of the following chromosomes is most likely to have this breakage site?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The heritable mental retardation condition associated with chromosomal breakage is fragile X syndrome, which is X-linked dominant; therefore, the penetrance in males is 100%. The break point is in the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR-1) gene, which is at Xq27.3 on the X chromosome.

The chromosome testing (cytogenetic test) for this condition involves culturing lymphocytes either in folate-deficient medium or with chemical agents such as methotrexate, which inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and tends to break chromosomes. To make the diagnosis, at least 4% of metaphase chromosomes must show the specific break-point on the X chromosome. The percentage of defective X chromosomes above 4% does not correlate well with the degree of mental retardation. The breakage point is a site of CGG trinucleotide repeats, which tends to expand in successive generations, producing the clinical feature of worsening mental retardation in each generation. The actual number of CGG repeats can be determined by PCR analysis. Southern blotting can be used to determine if there is mosaicism of the gene in different tissues.

Y chromosome (choice B) damage is not part of fragile X syndrome, but loss of this chromosome is one mechanism of producing 45,X (Turner syndrome).

Trisomy 13 (choice C, Patau syndrome), trisomy 18 (choice D, Edwards syndrome), and trisomy 21 (choice E, Down syndrome) are all associated with mental retardation, but not chromosomal breakage syndromes. Children with trisomy 13 and 18 rarely survive their first year.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Fragile X syndrome is caused by a breakage/CGG-repeat expansion at the FMR-1 gene on the X chromosome (Xq27.3).
choice_explanations.B: Y-chromosome loss produces 45,X (Turner syndrome), not fragile X. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) is a trisomy, not a breakage syndrome. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) is a trisomy, not a breakage syndrome. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is a trisomy, not a breakage syndrome. Incorrect.

stem: A male newborn has a small head, small eyes, and six fingers on each hand. A two-dimensional echocardiogram shows multiple congenital heart defects. Which of the following genetic conditions is most likely responsible for the findings seen in this newborn?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This is Patau syndrome, or trisomy 13. This disorder is also associated with severe mental retardation, abnormal forebrain structures (holoprosencephaly), growth retardation, microphthalmia, cleft lip and cleft palate, polydactyly, and death within one year of birth. Patau syndrome has an incidence of 1:8000-1:12,000 births in the U.S., making it the least common form of viable autosomal trisomy.

Trisomy 18 (choice B) is Edwards syndrome, characterized by severe mental retardation, rocker bottom feet (also sometimes seen in Patau syndrome, so be careful), low-set ears, micrognathia, clenched hands, prominent occiput, and death within one year. Edwards syndrome has an incidence of about 1:5000, making it the second most common autosomal trisomy.

Trisomy 21 (choice C) is Down syndrome, and is characterized by mental retardation, flat facial profile, prominent epicanthal folds, simian crease, duodenal atresia, and congenital heart disease. Down syndrome is the most common autosomal trisomy, with an incidence of 1:1000.

XXY (choice D) is Klinefelter syndrome and is associated with male hypogonadism and infertility, eunuchoid body habitus, gynecomastia, and lack of male secondary sexual characteristics.

XYY (choice E) is double Y syndrome. Affected individuals often go undetected, but may be taller than average, and may be more likely to exhibit aggressive, antisocial behavior.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Microcephaly, microphthalmia, polydactyly, and congenital heart defects (with holoprosencephaly) indicate Patau syndrome, trisomy 13.
choice_explanations.B: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) features rocker-bottom feet, clenched hands, and micrognathia. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) features a flat facial profile, epicanthal folds, and a simian crease. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) causes male hypogonadism, not these malformations. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: XYY (double Y syndrome) is usually clinically subtle. Incorrect.

stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of concerns about frequent falls and apparent muscle weakness in his legs. She states that none of her five daughters have this condition. Physical examination shows that the patient displays toe walking and uses his hands and arms to "walk" up his legs to rise from a sitting position. A muscle biopsy shows defects in the connections between the cytoskeleton inside the muscle cell and the plasma membrane. Which of the following types of mutations is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a lethal, X-linked recessive disease affecting approximately 1 in 3300 live male births. The disease becomes symptomatic in early childhood. Typical features of the disease include progressive muscular weakness of shoulders and pelvic girdles, calf pseudohypertrophy, respiratory insufficiency, and pulmonary infections. Toe walking and positive Gowers' sign are common in the early stages of the disease. Inability to walk occurs by the end of the first decade, and death usually occurs by the second decade.

Nearly all patients show the complete absence of the protein dystrophin, which connects the cytoskeleton inside a muscle fiber to the plasma membrane. DMD results from a frameshift mutation in the dystrophin gene, which disrupts the entire downstream coding region of the mRNA. This leads to defective dystrophin protein production and loss of the cytoskeleton-plasma membrane connections that it mediates, ultimately leading to progressive muscular degeneration.

Rare cases of DMD in females have been caused by an X chromosome-autosome translocation (choice A) with the breakpoint on the X chromosome within the DMD gene. This gives rise to a female who is heterozygous for the DMD gene but phenotypically expresses the disease.

A missense mutation (choice C) is a type of point mutation in which a single nucleotide change results in a codon that codes for a different amino acid. DMD in a patient with no family history is not generally due to a point mutation in the dystrophin gene.

Trinucleotide repeat expansion (choice D) is characterized by the insertion of multiple copies of a three-nucleotide repeat in either the coding region of the gene or the promoter. This type of mutation gives rise to diseases such as fragile X syndrome and Huntington disease.

choice_explanations.A: An X-autosome translocation can rarely cause DMD in females, but not this classic male presentation. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Duchenne muscular dystrophy results from a frameshift mutation in the dystrophin gene, disrupting the downstream coding region and abolishing dystrophin.
choice_explanations.C: A missense mutation would produce an altered (not absent) protein; sporadic DMD is not generally due to a point mutation. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Trinucleotide repeat expansion causes fragile X syndrome and Huntington disease, not DMD. Incorrect.

stem:
A study is conducted to characterize the malignant cells from several patients with leukemia and lymphoma using cell surface markers and other identifying features. The table shows the results of this study. TdT = terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase.

Which of the following best identifies the malignancy with the largest proportion of primitive cells?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Of the cell markers listed, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is present only in extremely primitive cells of the lymphocyte lineages. It is the enzyme that is active when VDJ rearrangement of the heavy chain (or both chains of the T-cell receptor) variable domain genes is occurring, and it is responsible for mediating N-nucleotide addition to the junctions of the gene segments. Of the two cases that are TdT-positive (cases 3 and 4), one (case 4) has successfully completed VDJ rearrangement and is therefore less primitive than the cells of case 3. Most B cell ALLs are pro-B cell types, which would have the CD10 TdT markers, but would not exhibit the cytoplasmic mu marker yet (case 3). Pre-B cells would exhibit the cytoplasmic mu marker (case 4). CD34 is a sialomucin found on the surface of cells of hematopoietic origin.

Case 1 (choice A) contains cells that have successfully rearranged the genes in the variable domain of the heavy chain, and are producing cytoplasmic IgM heavy chains. TdT is no longer present, so this cell is more advanced than the cell in case 3.

Case 2 (choice B) is composed of cells that have switched the isotype of antibody to IgG. Isotype switching requires the interaction of CD40 and CD40L on T-helper cell, so this cell is quite mature. B7 is a costimulatory molecule that is induced on B cells during the activation process, and is likewise a mature B-cell marker.

Case 4 (choice D) includes cells that have successfully completed VDJ rearrangement but have not yet turned off TdT production. It is the next most primitive cell behind the cell described in case 3.

Case 5 (choice E) is comprised of cells that are probably of the same maturational stage as those of case 2. These cells have probably switched isotype to another class of antibody other than that of IgG.

choice_explanations.A: Case 1 cells have successfully rearranged the heavy-chain variable domain and produce cytoplasmic IgM; TdT is no longer present, so they are more advanced than case 3. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Case 2 cells have isotype-switched to IgG (requiring CD40/CD40L interaction) and express B7, making them quite mature. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Case 3 cells are TdT-positive pro-B cells that have not yet expressed cytoplasmic mu, making them the most primitive of the listed malignancies.
choice_explanations.D: Case 4 cells are TdT-positive but have completed VDJ rearrangement (pre-B cells with cytoplasmic mu), so they are less primitive than case 3. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Case 5 cells are at the same maturational stage as case 2 (isotype-switched, mature). Incorrect.

fa_summary: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) marks the most primitive cells of the lymphocyte lineages (pro-B/pro-T ALL); cells that have completed VDJ rearrangement and expressed cytoplasmic mu (or turned off TdT) are progressively more mature.
