stem: A 30-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever and night sweats for six weeks. A CT scan of the chest and abdomen shows enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, abdominal lymph nodes, and multiple liver lesions. A biopsy specimen of one of the lymph nodes confirms a nodular lymphoma showing follicle formation with predominantly small lymphocytes containing scanty cytoplasm and irregular, twisted, and indented nuclei. Which of the following cytogenetic translocations is most likely associated with this patient's disease?

options.text: Kappa immunoglobulin light chain and myc
Lambda immunoglobulin light chain and myc

explanation:
The correct answer is B. The lymphoma described in the question stem is the follicular B-cell lymphoma, and its characteristic reciprocal translocation is t(14;18)(q32;q21). The site on chromosome 14 involves the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus (IgH), while that on chromosome 18 involves the bcl-2 oncogene. The translocation produces a hybrid bcl-2/immunoglobulin heavy-chain transcript. Bcl-2 inhibits apoptosis, so this translocation promotes cell proliferation.

Translocations occur when chromosomes are broken and the broken elements reattach to other chromosomes. They can be classified into two major types: reciprocal and Robertsonian. Reciprocal translocations occur when genetic material is exchanged between nonhomologous chromosomes. Reciprocal translocations can occur in gametogenesis due to errors in meiosis, or they can occur during cellular division of somatic cells due to errors in mitosis. The latter type can lead to the formation of cancers by altering the genetic code controlling cellular proliferation. More than 100 different chromosome rearrangements involving nearly every chromosome have been observed in more than 40 types of cancer.

Robertsonian translocations only occur in the acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, and 22) and involve the loss of the short arms of two of the chromosomes and subsequent fusion of the long arms. An example is shown below, which is a cause of Down syndrome, in which the mother carries the Robertsonian translocation and can have more than 1 child with trisomy 21.

A t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation involving bcl-1 and Igk (choice A) is seen in mantle cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma. Burkitt lymphoma is usually associated with t(8;14) (myc and IgH; choice C), but sometimes with t(2;8) (kappa immunoglobulin light chain and myc; choice D) or t(8;22) (lambda immunoglobulin light chain and myc; choice E).

A list of some important translocations involving oncogenes is provided below:
• t(14;18), follicular lymphomas
• t(11;14), mantle cell lymphoma
• t(9;22), chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
• t(15;17), acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), promyelocytic type (APL)
• t(8;14), Burkitt lymphoma

choice_explanations.A: t(11;14) involving bcl-1 and Igk is seen in mantle cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Follicular B-cell lymphoma has the t(14;18)(q32;q21) translocation (IgH and bcl-2), producing a hybrid bcl-2/IgH transcript that inhibits apoptosis.
choice_explanations.C: IgH and myc (t(8;14)) is associated with Burkitt lymphoma. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Kappa immunoglobulin light chain and myc (t(2;8)) is a variant of Burkitt lymphoma. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Lambda immunoglobulin light chain and myc (t(8;22)) is a variant of Burkitt lymphoma. Incorrect.

fa_summary: Follicular B-cell lymphoma is characterized by the t(14;18) translocation juxtaposing the IgH locus (chromosome 14) with the bcl-2 oncogene (chromosome 18), causing bcl-2 overexpression and impaired apoptosis.

stem:
A 69-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after fracturing his left humerus by bumping into a door frame at his home. He has been hospitalized three times with pneumonia during the past year. Laboratory studies show:

Leukocyte count 10,200/mm3
Platelet count 130,000/mm3
Calcium 15 mg/dL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 65 mm/h
Prostate-specific antigen 25 ng/mL (normal < 4.0 ng/mL)

Immunofixation electrophoresis of urine shows free monoclonal kappa light chains. An x-ray shows several lytic bone lesions of the left humerus in addition to a midshaft fracture. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This man is suffering from multiple myeloma, a neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells (or their precursors) found within the bone marrow. These malignant cells are responsible for the production of excessive amounts of immunoglobulin (usually IgG or IgA) and increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Excess free kappa or lambda chains from the immunoglobulin may be filtered into urine (Bence-Jones proteins), where they can be detected with immunofixation electrophoresis.

The decreased platelet count probably reflects infiltration of the bone marrow by myeloma cells. It is not unusual for patients with malignant myeloma to have recurring bacterial infections, particularly pneumococcal pneumonia, because the overall production of normal immunoglobulins of all isotypes is decreased. Infiltration by myeloma cells causes lytic bone lesions and leads to pathologic fractures.

Amyloidosis (choice A) is the extracellular deposition of fibrillar protein. The amyloid may be deposited locally or distributed widely throughout the body. Most common deposits are in the kidneys, heart, and liver. While proteinuria is often a feature of amyloidosis, lytic bone lesions are not found in this disease.

Patients with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) (choice B) are generally asymptomatic, although they have a predisposition for subsequently developing myeloma, lymphoma, amyloidosis, or Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

Plasmacytoma (choice D) (solitary myeloma) is a rare, isolated plasma cell neoplasm in bone or soft tissues. If the primary cancer is in bone, it is likely to disseminate; extraosseous tumors tend to remain localized. Since this patient has multiple lytic bone lesions, multiple myeloma is the correct diagnosis.

Prostate carcinoma (choice E) may present with bone pain and pathologic fractures in an elderly male. However, bone lesions are characteristically osteoblastic in nature. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is not specific for prostate cancer (it may also be elevated in benign prostatic hypertrophy), but is often significantly elevated, along with elevated bone alkaline phosphatase levels, in patients with metastatic prostate disease. This patient's PSA is within the normal range.

choice_explanations.A: Amyloidosis can cause proteinuria but is not associated with lytic bone lesions. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: MGUS is generally asymptomatic and does not cause lytic bone lesions or pathologic fracture. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Multiple myeloma causes lytic bone lesions, pathologic fractures, hypercalcemia, monoclonal immunoglobulin (kappa light chains in urine), and increased infection risk.
choice_explanations.D: Plasmacytoma is a solitary plasma cell tumor; multiple lytic lesions indicate multiple myeloma. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Prostate carcinoma metastases are characteristically osteoblastic (blastic), not lytic. Incorrect.

fa_summary: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm causing lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, monoclonal immunoglobulin/Bence-Jones proteinuria, anemia, and increased infection risk (blastic lesions instead suggest prostate or breast carcinoma).

stem: A 7-month-old boy with failure to thrive is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination. He is the second child. He was born full-term with no complications. His hemoglobin is 4.4 g/dL. The peripheral smear shows very small red blood cells with marked central pallor. Further evaluation shows very low levels of hemoglobin A, with elevated fractions of hemoglobin A2 and hemoglobin F. Which of the following underlying mechanisms is most likely responsible for the findings seen in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Beta-globin is encoded by two genes, and mutations can result in minor (asymptomatic), intermedia (varies in presentation), and major disease types (Cooley's anemia; homozygous state; symptomatic microcytic hypochromic anemia). Decreased or absent beta-chain production leads to decreased or absent hemoglobin A and a compensatory increase in hemoglobin F and hemoglobin A2. The anemia of beta-thalassemia is microcytic and hypochromic with anisocytosis.

Amino acid substitutions in beta-globin (choice A) lead to hemoglobinopathies, of which sickle cell anemia (glutamic acid to valine substitution at position 6) is the archetype. Homozygotes with these hemoglobin variants do not produce any hemoglobin A but rather mutant types, such as hemoglobin S or hemoglobin C.

Antibodies against fetal blood cells (choice B) are generally produced by a mother who has been sensitized to fetal blood antigens by transfusion or a previous pregnancy. Such immune-mediated hemolysis (Rh incompatibility) leads to intrauterine anemia and hydrops fetalis.

Cytoskeletal protein defects (choice C), such as spectrin and ankyrin deficiency causing hereditary spherocytosis, produce anemia and jaundice that are apparent at birth. The red blood cells contain the normal types of hemoglobin.

Alpha-thalassemia is due to inadequate production of alpha-chains (choice D). The chains are coded for by four copies of the gene. Alpha thalassemia is associated with microcytic hypochromic anemia and varies in severity, from silent carrier (one dysfunctional gene; asymptomatic), to alpha-thalassemia trait (two dysfunctional genes; asymptomatic), to hemoglobin H disease (three dysfunctional genes; marked microcytic anemia), to alpha-thalassemia major (Hemoglobin Barts; fetal hydrops; four dysfunctional genes).

choice_explanations.A: Amino acid substitutions in beta-globin cause hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell anemia, not beta-thalassemia. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Antibodies against fetal blood cells cause immune-mediated hemolysis (Rh incompatibility), not thalassemia. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Cytoskeletal protein defects (spectrin/ankyrin) cause hereditary spherocytosis. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Insufficient alpha-globin production causes alpha-thalassemia. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Insufficient beta-globin production causes beta-thalassemia major, with decreased hemoglobin A and compensatory increases in hemoglobin A2 and F.

fa_summary: Beta-thalassemia results from decreased or absent beta-globin chain synthesis, causing microcytic hypochromic anemia with low hemoglobin A and compensatory elevations of hemoglobin A2 and F.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of concern about ovarian cancer. The patient is counseled on the risk of ovarian cancer and decides to undergo prophylactic oophorectomy because of a strong family history. Examination of ovarian tissue shows normal tissue. One section of the specimen shows large numbers of unusually large cells surrounded by a single layer of flat epithelial cells. Which of the following identifies the phase of the cell cycle at which these cells are arrested?

options.text: Diplotene stage of the 1st meiotic division
Diplotene stage of the 2nd meiotic division
Prophase stage of the 2nd meiotic division

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The cells described are the primary oocytes, which stay arrested in the diplotene stage of prophase I of the first meiotic division from before birth until the month in which they will be ovulated, a period that may be 40 or more years. Prior to ovulation, they complete the first meiotic division to give rise to secondary oocytes, which arrest in metaphase of the second meiotic division. The second meiotic division is completed shortly after fertilization. Primary oocytes are found in the ovary as single large cells surrounded by a layer of flat epithelial cells that is one cell thick.
Choices B and E are incorrect because the oocytes are stopped in the first, not second, meiotic division. Choices C and D are incorrect because the cells described are oocytes and divide by meiosis, not mitosis.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Primary oocytes remain arrested in the diplotene stage of prophase I of the first meiotic division until ovulation.
choice_explanations.B: Oocytes are not arrested in the second meiotic division at the diplotene stage.
choice_explanations.C: Oocytes divide by meiosis, not mitosis.
choice_explanations.D: Oocytes divide by meiosis, not mitosis.
choice_explanations.E: Secondary oocytes arrest at metaphase of the second meiotic division, not prophase.

stem: A 58-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a fever, shaking chills, and a productive cough. She has a history of alcohol abuse. Culture of the sputum grows gram-negative, lactose-fermenting rods. A chest x-ray will most likely show which of the following?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a well recognized cause of community-acquired lobar pneumonia associated with cavitation. It is a gram-negative, oxidase negative rod with a large polysaccharide capsule. It produces mucoid, lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar. It is found typically in alcoholics over 40 years of age with underlying diabetes or obstructive lung disease. Klebsiella pneumoniae mimics Streptococcus pneumoniae as a pulmonary pathogen, except that Klebsiella has a greater tendency to progress to lung abscess and empyema. Third-generation cephalosporins with or without an aminoglycoside can be used for the treatment of a Klebsiella pneumoniae infection. Fluoroquinolones may also be used. Aspergilloma (choice A) is also called a fungus ball and is usually observed in a cavitary lesion remaining after a case of tuberculosis, for example. Itraconazole and voriconazole are the drugs of choice for the treatment of chronic pulmonary aspergillosis with posaconazole being substituted for failure, toxicity, or emergence of resistance. Ghon complex (choice B) is the granulomatous lesions formed during an infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The initial drug regimen for tuberculosis is based on knowledge of the likely drug susceptibility. However, the most commonly used drugs are isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Interstitial pattern (choice C) is the pattern commonly seen in atypical pneumonia. The bacteria most commonly associated with atypical pneumonia are Legionella species, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia pneumoniae. The mainstays of therapy for atypical pneumonia are macrolides such as erythromycin and azithromycin or doxycycline. Mediastinal widening (choice D) is observed in chest x-rays of individuals with pulmonary or inhalation anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis. Ciprofloxacin is considered to be the drug of choice for treatment of inhalation anthrax. Other causes of mediastinal widening include aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, esophageal rupture, mediastinal mass, and pericardial effusion.

choice_explanations.A: Aspergilloma is a fungus ball in a pre-existing cavity (e.g., after tuberculosis).
choice_explanations.B: Ghon complex is the granulomatous lesion of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
choice_explanations.C: Interstitial pattern is seen in atypical pneumonia (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia pneumoniae).
choice_explanations.D: Mediastinal widening is seen with inhalation anthrax (Bacillus anthracis).
choice_explanations.E: Klebsiella pneumoniae causes lobar pneumonia with cavitation, especially in alcoholics.

fa_summary: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a gram-negative, lactose-fermenting rod that causes lobar pneumonia (with cavitation in heavy alcoholics) and has a tendency to form abscesses and empyema.

stem: A 23-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a two-week history of persistent pelvic pain and vaginal discharge. She is sexually active with a new partner. Her temperature is 37.8C (100.1F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no rashes or palpable lymphadenopathy. Lower abdominal tenderness is present. Pelvic examination reveals purulent yellow-white discharge present in the vaginal vault and cervical os. The cervix is erythematous and tender to palpation. Gram stain of the cervical discharge shows multiple polymorphonuclear leukocytes, but culture on Thayer-Martin medium is negative. Pap smear results demonstrate squamous cells with intracellular inclusions and numerous neutrophils and scattered lymphocytes, consistent with infection; no evidence of dysplasia. The patient is subsequently treated with doxycycline and ceftriaxone. Which of the following immunologic mechanisms serves as the primary host defense against the most likely causative agent in this case?
explanation: The correct answer is B. The first thing you need to determine is that the patient has pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). The second step is to recognize that Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular pathogen, is a common cause of STDs and is the most important cause of PID in the United States. It is not unusual to have PID in association with both Chlamydia and Gonorrhea infections, which is why the patient was treated for both (doxycycline for Chlamydia and ceftriaxone for Gonorrhea) even though culture on Thayer-Martin medium was negative. Thayer-Martin medium was referenced in the stem because it is used to culture and isolate pathogenic Neisseria species. Lastly, you need to determine the immunologic mechanism the body uses to defend against Chlamydia. Immune mechanisms capable of targeting intracellular pathogens will be of the most use to the host in this case. Of the choices, cell-mediated cytotoxicity (a Th1-dominant response) will be the primary defense against Chlamydia infection. Recall lymphocytes are seen on the Pap smear. Acute phase cytokines (choice A) include agents such as TNF-alpha and IL-1 beta, which are important in innate, first-line responses such as inflammation and fever. Although these cytokines are likely to be produced during a Chlamydia infection as a result of inflammation and tissue damage, they are not the primary and strongest response against this pathogen. Complement-mediated lysis (choice C) is an important defense mechanism against extracellular bacteria such as Streptococcus species and Staphylococcus species, which are less likely to cause PID. IgE-mediated activation of mast cells (choice D) is an important type I hypersensitivity reaction that is part of allergic responses, which is not present in this case. T-regulatory cell responses (choice E) are important for returning an immune response to homeostasis and preventing autoimmune diseases, which is not present in this case.

choice_explanations.A: Acute phase cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta) drive innate inflammation and fever but are not the primary defense against intracellular Chlamydia.
choice_explanations.B: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen, so cell-mediated immunity (a Th1-dominant response) is the primary host defense.
choice_explanations.C: Complement-mediated lysis targets extracellular bacteria (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus), which are less likely to cause PID.
choice_explanations.D: IgE-mediated mast cell activation is a type I hypersensitivity/allergic response, not relevant here.
choice_explanations.E: T-regulatory cells return immune responses to homeostasis and prevent autoimmunity; not the primary defense here.

fa_summary: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen and a leading cause of pelvic inflammatory disease; cell-mediated immunity is the primary host defense against it.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes comes to the physician because of left-sided hearing loss. She states that she also has pain and discharge from the left ear. Physical examination shows a tender pinna, swelling and erythema of the external auditory canal, as well as a purulent discharge. The tympanic membrane cannot be visualized. A CT scan of the head shows temporal bone erosions and new bone formation. Culture of the discharge will most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Gram-negative bacillus requiring factors X and V

explanation: The correct answer is C. This patient has malignant (necrotizing) external otitis, which is caused almost exclusively by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common cause of self-limited external otitis. It may, however, penetrate the epithelium and invade the underlying soft tissue, cartilage and bone. The presenting symptoms include severe ear pain, discharge and potential hearing loss. As the infection progresses, osteomyelitis of the temporomandibular joint and base of the skull can develop. Progression of the osteomyelitis can lead to cranial nerve palsies and facial nerve paralysis. A CT scan may reveal bony erosions and soft-tissue swelling. Cultures will isolate the organism. Malignant external otitis is most common in elderly diabetic patients and there have been increasing reports in immunocompromised patients. Pseudomonas is a genus of gram-negative bacilli that are oxidase-positive, aerobic, nonfermenting and produce blue-green pigments and a grape-like odor. Other diseases caused by Pseudomonas include septicemia, wound or burn infections, urinary tract infections in catheterized patients, and life-threatening pneumonias in cystic fibrosis patients. Antipseudomonal drugs, such as the fluoroquinolones, are the mainstay of therapy for malignant (necrotizing) external otitis. A gram-negative bacillus requiring factors X and V (choice A) describes the genus Haemophilus. This genus may cause otitis media but not malignant otitis externa; symptoms of otitis media include ear pain, fever, and a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane. A gram-negative, oxidase-negative, non-lactose fermenting bacillus (choice B) describes some members (Shigella, Yersinia, Proteus, and Salmonella) of the family Enterobacteriaceae. There are no agents of ear infections present in this group. Most of the Enterobacteriaceae are diarrhea-causing agents, or are causes of enteric fevers, neonatal meningitis, or urinary tract infections. A gram-positive, catalase-negative, alpha-hemolytic coccus (choice D) describes Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is the most common cause of otitis media but not of otitis externa, as in this case. A gram-positive, catalase-negative, beta-hemolytic coccus (choice E) describes Streptococcus pyogenes and Streptococcus agalactiae. S. pyogenes is a common cause of otitis media, and S. agalactiae is the most common cause of neonatal septicemia and meningitis in the United States.

choice_explanations.A: Haemophilus (requires factors X and V) causes otitis media, not malignant otitis externa.
choice_explanations.B: Oxidase-negative, non-lactose fermenters (Shigella, Yersinia, Proteus, Salmonella) cause enteric disease or UTIs, not ear infections.
choice_explanations.C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative, oxidase-positive, nonfermenting bacillus and the cause of malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa.
choice_explanations.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae (alpha-hemolytic) is the most common cause of otitis media, not otitis externa.
choice_explanations.E: Streptococcus pyogenes/agalactiae (beta-hemolytic) cause otitis media and neonatal sepsis/meningitis, not otitis externa.

fa_summary: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative, oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting rod that causes malignant (necrotizing) external otitis, especially in elderly diabetic patients.

stem: During an investigational study, 5-alpha reductase is shown to metabolize cortisol into an inactive metabolite. If insulin activates 5-alpha reductase, a significant increase of which of the following in plasma will most likely be seen in a patient with hyperinsulinemia?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Increased 5-alpha reductase activity would lead to decreased circulating cortisol due to increased metabolism. Therefore, anterior pituitary secretion of ACTH would increase as a result of decreased negative feedback (see figure). ACTH stimulates the secretion of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) from the zona reticularis in the adrenal cortex.

Cortisol is metabolized by 5-alpha reductase. Insulin increases 5-alpha reductase activity, resulting in decreased circulating cortisol, leading to increased ACTH secretion due to less negative feedback.

Although the scenario mentions that 5-alpha reductase metabolizes cortisol, this is only one of its effects. The increased degradation of cortisol does not prevent cortisol synthesis, so as ACTH stimulates pregnenolone and progesterone (choice D) production, these precursors are immediately consumed to replace the deficient cortisol and some also is shunted into secondary androgen release.

The most common associations of excessive activity of 5-alpha reductase are related to its effects on androgen pathways. Increased activity drives conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone. The precursors to testosterone, such as DHEA, are also increased. Consider the observation that increased 5-alpha reductase activity is strongly associated with cases of hirsutism in women and in increased DHEA due to increased hepatic 5-alpha reductase in hyperthyroidism.

Serum potassium (choice C) is controlled by aldosterone, an adrenal mineralocorticoid hormone produced by the zona glomerulosa (see figure). Aldosterone release is stimulated by hyperkalemia and by activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Aldosterone release is not stimulated by ACTH. Aldosterone regulates Na+ and K+ reabsorption by the renal tubule.

Adrenal cortex zones and their control: Zona glomerulosa — aldosterone — angiotensin II, [K+]; Zona fasciculata — cortisol — ACTH; Zona reticularis — androgens — ACTH (LH has no effect on the production of adrenal androgens); Medulla — epinephrine — autonomic nervous system.

Renin (choice E) is an enzyme released by glomerular afferent arterioles in response to a decrease in renal perfusion pressure. Renin catalyzes the formation of angiotensin I from angiotensinogen, initiating RAAS (see figure).
fa_subchapter: Adrenal steroids and congenital adrenal hyperplasias

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Decreased cortisol → increased ACTH → increased adrenal androgen (DHEA) production from the zona reticularis.
choice_explanations.B: Estradiol is not a product of the ACTH-driven adrenal zona reticularis pathway. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Potassium is regulated by aldosterone, not by ACTH. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Progesterone is a precursor consumed to replace cortisol, not increased in plasma. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Renin is released from the kidney in response to decreased renal perfusion, not by this mechanism. Incorrect.

stem: A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of difficulty breathing and swelling of the face and right arm for one week. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 103/min, and blood pressure is 130/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows facial erythema, facial and arm edema, with prominence of neck veins. On chest x-ray, there is a mass in the right superior mediastinum with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following conditions most likely contributed to the patient's symptoms?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx

explanation:
The correct answer is B. Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome is characterized by obstruction of venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Clinical presentation includes facial plethora (vascular congestion), facial and arm edema, and distended jugular veins. Over 85% of cases of SVC syndrome are related to malignancy. Bronchogenic carcinomas (most commonly small cell cancer and squamous cell cancer) account for over 80% of these cases. The tumor is arising in the right upper lobe, which is immediately lateral to the superior mediastinum. This can impinge on the SVC, which is in the right superior mediastinum. Recall that the superior mediastinum has the lower border located at the level of the sternal angle, at the level of T4 (see image below; black line). The superior mediastinum holds the superior vena cava (SVC) and the aortic arch and its branches.

SVC syndrome results from obstruction of the superior vena cava. The patient presents with facial plethora, facial and upper extremity swelling; dyspnea can be present. It is mainly associated with a lung malignancy, where small cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma are the most frequent types.

Lymphomas such as Hodgkin disease (choice A) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma are uncommon causes of SVC syndrome. Lymphoma can affect the hilar lymph nodes; however, it would not present as a mass in the right superior mediastinum, but rather can be present in the middle or anterior mediastinum.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx (choice C) may extend inferiorly and/or laterally, but would not be a cause of SVC syndrome since the larynx is located superiorly in the neck region.

Thrombosis (choice D) can be caused by hypercoagulable states (hereditary, hormones, malignancy, SLE, etc.), indwelling intravenous lines, or pacemaker wires. This patient does not have a history of any of these predispositions.

Infectious etiologies such as tuberculosis (choice E), syphilis, and histoplasmosis are less common causes of SVC syndrome.

choice_explanations.A: Hodgkin lymphoma is an uncommon cause of SVC syndrome and typically involves the middle/anterior mediastinum. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Small cell (and squamous cell) bronchogenic carcinoma arising in the right upper lobe is the most common cause of SVC syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is too superior to obstruct the SVC. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: No predisposing factors for thrombosis (lines, hypercoagulable state) are present. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Tuberculosis is a less common infectious cause of SVC syndrome. Incorrect.

stem: An 83-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her daughter. The patient had severe shortness of breath when walking from the car to the office, and her daughter said she looked ashen. A walk test in the office showed her to have severe desaturations and she was sent to the emergency department. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 127/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 142/92 mm Hg. An X-ray computed tomography scan showed a right lung embolus, deep vein thromboses, and masses consistent with ovarian neoplasms associated with peritoneal carcinomatosis. Which of the following structures is most likely responsible for initiating the cardiopulmonary response in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The patient has an embolus obstructing arterial blood flow in the right lung. Reflexive hypoxic vasoconstriction in affected lung regions shifts pulmonary flow to more well-perfused areas, but the V/Q mismatch leads to varying degrees of hypoxemia and hypercapnia. Arterial blood gas composition is monitored primarily by central chemoreceptors. These comprise pH-sensitive neurons located behind the blood-brain barrier (BBB) that are highly sensitive to changes in PCO2. CO2 crosses the BBB and dissolves in cerebrospinal fluid to form carbonic acid, facilitated by carbonic anhydrase. H+ then stimulates the central chemoreceptors; respiratory control centers respond to their input by increasing ventilation. Connectivity between the medullary respiratory and cardiovascular control centers allows for the observed cardiovascular response to chemoreceptor activation (i.e., increased heart rate, increased blood pressure).

Changes in lung function are sensed primarily by central chemoreceptors located in the medulla. The chemosensitive region is stimulated by arterial PCO2. CO2 diffuses across the blood-brain barrier and acidifies cerebrospinal fluid. The chemoreceptor neurons, which are pH-sensitive, drive compensatory increases in ventilation and cardiac output when stimulated appropriately.

The BBB is relatively impermeable to H+, so isolating the chemoreceptors from the circulation prevents them from being influenced by non-specific changes in blood pH.

Most pulmonary emboli originate from deep vein thromboses (DVT) located in the lower extremities. The patient probably mobilized a DVT when walking from the car to the physician's office.

Arterial blood gases are also monitored peripherally. The carotid bodies and aortic bodies located in the carotid sinus and aortic arch, respectively, contain chemoreceptors that sense arterial PCO2 and PO2 (choice A). These chemoreceptors are capable of responding to changes in arterial blood gases more quickly than the central chemoreceptors, but their contribution to overall ventilatory control is minor compared with those located in the CNS.

choice_explanations.A: Peripheral (carotid/aortic body) chemoreceptors respond to PO2/PCO2 but contribute only a minor fraction of ventilatory control. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are pulmonary C-fibers that sense interstitial congestion/edema. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Oxygen-sensitive sustentacular (type I/glomus) cells are components of the peripheral chemoreceptors, not the primary sensor. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. pH-sensitive neurons behind the blood-brain barrier (central chemoreceptors) are the primary sensors of arterial PCO2 and drive the ventilatory response.
choice_explanations.E: Stretch-sensitive nerve endings (pulmonary stretch receptors) mediate the Hering-Breuer reflex. Incorrect.

stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the physician because of new-onset seizures and a 13.6-kg (30-lb) weight loss over the past 3 months. Physical examination shows irregular-sized abdominal masses on deep palpation. A CT scan of the head reveals three hyperdense lesions in the temporal lobes bilaterally. A CT of the abdomen shows multiple masses up to 3 cm in diameter on the serosal aspect of the small intestine. Biopsy of one of the masses shows a uniform population of malignant cells that are positive with S-100 and HMB-45 immunohistochemical stains. Which of the following is the most likely primary malignancy?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The presence of multiple nodular tumor masses involving the serosa of the small intestine is an unusual metastatic pattern that should suggest the possibility of malignant melanoma. Malignant melanomas arise from melanocytes, which are the pigment (melanin) producing cells of the skin, embryologically derived from the neural crest. Brown or black melanin pigment can sometimes be seen within the tumor cells.

S-100 is a protein that is normally present in melanocytes. Melanocytes have their embryologic origin in the neural crest. S-100 and HMB-45 are used as markers for malignant melanoma.

Main risk factors for melanoma include sunlight exposure and immunocompromised status. Many times, the primary lesion may go unnoticed or regress until the cancer is at an advanced stage. Key features of the primary lesion can be summed up with the mnemonic ABCDE (asymmetry, border irregularity, color heterogeneity, diameter >0.6 mm, and enlarging). The metastatic pattern of melanoma is highly unusual and is infamous for spreading anywhere (brain, placenta, eyeball, small bowel serosa, etc.) and at any time (more than ten years after removal of primary tumor).

Key markers for melanoma are S-100 and HMB-45. S-100 protein is produced in cells derived from the neural crest. As a result, S-100 positivity can be found in melanomas, schwannomas, neurofibromas, astrocytomas, and other tumors with a neural crest association. HMB-45 (human melanoma black 45) is a melanocytic marker that is positive with melanoma and nevi. The other answer choices do not demonstrate S-100 or HMB-45 staining.

Useful markers for some gastric adenocarcinomas (choice A) are carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and bombesin immunohistochemical stains.

A useful marker for hepatocellular carcinoma (choice B) is the alpha-fetoprotein immunohistochemical stain.

Useful markers for prostatic carcinoma (choice D) are prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and prostatic acid phosphatase.

Some useful markers for testicular carcinoma (choice E) include alpha-fetoprotein (yolk sac tumors and embryonal carcinoma) and human chorionic gonadotropin (choriocarcinoma and embryonal carcinoma) depending upon the tumor type.

choice_explanations.A: Gastric adenocarcinoma markers are CEA and bombesin, not S-100/HMB-45. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma marker is alpha-fetoprotein. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. S-100 and HMB-45 positivity with an unusual serosal/brain metastatic pattern indicates malignant melanoma.
choice_explanations.D: Prostatic carcinoma markers are PSA and prostatic acid phosphatase. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Testicular carcinoma markers are alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin. Incorrect.

stem: A 62-year-old man who is an accountant comes to the physician because of worsening shortness of breath, which now occurs at rest. He has no history of cardiac disease and denies cough, hemoptysis, and tobacco use. Physical examination shows scattered small subcutaneous nodules on the arms and thighs. Bone tenderness is noted in the left humerus. A chest x-ray reveals foci of dense linear and nodular interstitial lesions. Bronchoscopy is performed and the biopsy specimen shows diffuse calcium deposition in the pulmonary interstitium without evidence of malignant cells. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient has metastatic calcification due to hypercalcemia. It is characterized by the pathologic deposition of calcium into normal, viable tissues. Hypercalcemia can arise from many conditions including hyperparathyroidism, breast cancer, squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, or osteolytic bone lesions caused by multiple myeloma or metastatic malignancies. Note: Hyperphosphatemia (chronic renal failure or extensive cell lysis) can also contribute to metastatic calcifications. This occurs when serum calcium x phosphorous product exceeds a critical value, where the calcium-phosphate becomes insoluble. It is also important to distinguish metastatic calcification from dystrophic calcification (associated with degenerative changes such as aortic stenosis, Monckeberg arteriosclerosis, and myositis ossificans).

Metastatic calcification is the pathologic deposition of calcium in normal tissues. Metastatic calcification occurs in states of hypercalcemia, e.g., in multiple myeloma, primary hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, and CREST syndrome.

Multiple myeloma, in particular, is one of the more common causes of hypercalcemia in older individuals. The disease results from monoclonal proliferation of plasma cells, resulting in over-production of specific immunoglobulins. The CRAB mnemonic summarizes the findings in multiple myeloma: hyperCalcemia, Renal disease, Anemia (hemolytic), and Bone lesions (osteolytic). Other conditions that have hypercalcemia include primary hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, and CREST syndrome.

Amyloidosis (choice A) is characterized by the pathologic deposition of abnormally folded proteins into tissues. Amyloidosis does not calcify, but instead appears as an amorphous, hyaline, eosinophilic material on histology. The amyloid deposits demonstrate apple-green birefringence when Congo Red stain is viewed under polarized light. Interestingly, in addition to metastatic calcifications, multiple myeloma can cause a light-chain (AL) amyloidosis. However, these light chains are not deposited into skin or lung, but more commonly deposit in the kidney and heart.

Goodpasture syndrome (choice B) presents as hemorrhagic interstitial pneumonitis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis; calcifications would not be expected and, if found, would be dystrophic, not metastatic.

Hypoparathyroidism (choice C) would result in low levels of parathyroid hormone and thus hypocalcemia, rather than the phosphate deposits and hypocalcemia because of calcium precipitating out of the blood. These patients present with secondary hyperparathyroidism rather than hypoparathyroidism.

Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (choice D) is a neoplastic disease of thyroid parafollicular cells (C-cell lineage) that produces calcitonin, a hormone that normally decreases serum calcium levels. Interestingly these patients rarely present with hypocalcemia, but instead present with diarrhea, flushing, and occasionally thyroid amyloid deposits. Calcifications would be uncommon.

choice_explanations.A: Amyloidosis deposits amorphous eosinophilic material (apple-green birefringence) and does not calcify. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Goodpasture syndrome causes hemorrhagic pneumonitis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia with metastatic calcification. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Medullary thyroid carcinoma produces calcitonin and causes diarrhea/flushing, not metastatic calcification. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Multiple myeloma causes hypercalcemia (CRAB) with metastatic calcification of normal tissues such as the pulmonary interstitium.

stem: A 68-year-old woman comes to her physician because of a 3-month history of headaches and weakness in her arms and legs. She has no history of migraine headaches or trauma. She has smoked a half pack of cigarettes for the past 48 years, she drinks occasional beer and wine at social gatherings, and has a family history of breast cancer (mother), colon cancer (brother). Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 136/80 mm Hg. Her weight is 67.5 kg (148 lb), which is a 10 kg (22 lb) decrease since her last check-up 4 months ago. Physical examination shows decreased strength in the proximal upper and lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ out of 4+. Repetitive testing results in increased strength of the deltoid and quadriceps muscles. An MRI of the brain shows a single well-demarcated 3 cm mass in the left frontal lobe. Biopsy of the lesion reveals malignant small blue cells that stain positive for cytokeratin and chromogranin. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and leukocyte common antigen (LCA) are negative. Which of the following tumors most likely contributed to this patient's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The patient has a Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) and metastatic brain tumor from small cell lung carcinoma. LEMS is a presynaptic disorder with impaired acetylcholine release, associated with antibodies directed against voltage-gated calcium channels. LEMS is usually associated with small cell lung carcinoma. However, other cancers can also contribute to LEMS (e.g., non-small cell lung carcinoma, breast, colon, kidney, and bladder). The brain biopsy histology of malignant, small, blue cells positive for cytokeratin (epithelial cell marker) and chromogranin (neuroendocrine marker) supports the diagnosis of small cell lung carcinoma. Clinically, there is decreased proximal muscle weakness/strength in the arms and legs. There is an increase in strength with repetitive movement. Reflexes are reduced or absent. Repetitive nerve stimulation studies would show increased amplitude of compound muscle action potentials (CMAP).

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with small cell carcinoma of the lung, a neuroendocrine tumor characterized by blue cells that are positive for cytokeratin and chromogranin. Clinically there is decreased proximal muscle strength that increases with repetitive movement, and reduced or absent reflexes.

CNS lymphoma (choice A) falls under the "small blue cell neoplasm" differential diagnosis. Primary CNS lymphomas are extra-nodal high grade non-Hodgkin B cell lymphoma, which can originate in the brain, meninges, and spinal cord. Lymphoma cells are positive for leukocyte common antigen (LCA). It can be seen in immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients, such as HIV/AIDS. Lymphoma presenting as a mass lesion in the brain may cause seizures rather than the muscle weakness seen in our patient.

Ductal carcinoma of the breast (choice B) can metastasize to the brain. Cells can vary from well- to poorly-differentiated features and are cytokeratin positive, but negative for synaptophysin. Metastasis to the brain can cause headaches and, if there is compression of the cortex, can potentially cause unilateral weakness, but not bilateral proximal muscle weakness in the arms and legs seen in our patient.

Ependymoma (choice C) is a glial tumor which generally presents as infratentorial tumors in children (mean age 6 years). Adults tend to have spinal ependymomas, although the anaplastic type can occur in the brain and rarely in the spine. Histologically, cells are arranged in pseudorosettes around blood vessels and are GFAP positive. Patients may present with headaches due to increased intracranial pressure, obstructive hydrocephalus (seen with ventricular lesions), and/or neurologic deficits.

choice_explanations.A: CNS lymphoma is LCA-positive and typically causes seizures, not proximal muscle weakness. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Ductal breast carcinoma is cytokeratin-positive but synaptophysin-negative and does not cause LEMS. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Ependymoma is a GFAP-positive glial tumor that does not cause LEMS. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Glioblastoma multiforme is a GFAP-positive glial tumor, not chromogranin-positive. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a paraneoplastic syndrome of small cell lung carcinoma (chromogranin/cytokeratin-positive small blue cells).
choice_explanations.F: Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis, not LEMS. Incorrect.

stem: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of dry mouth and dry, "scratchy" eyes. Eye drops and oral hydration have not improved her symptoms. She also has sore, aching joints that have limited her ability to ambulate. Which of the following findings is most likely on examination of a synovial biopsy specimen from one of the affected joints?

options.text: Excessive cartilage loss and reactive bone formation
Non-proliferative synovitis with many neutrophils and gram-negative diplococci
Proliferative synovitis with many lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Dry eyes and mouth in a late middle-aged woman are probably due to Sjogren syndrome, which is an autoimmune attack on the salivary and tear glands. Sjogren syndrome is associated, in some cases, with rheumatoid arthritis. Joint findings in rheumatoid arthritis are highlighted by a proliferative synovitis with many lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells.

Sjogren syndrome is a progressive inflammatory disorder that characteristically affects the lacrimal and salivary glands; it occurs either as a primary disorder or in association with other autoimmune disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis. Joint analysis typically reveals an autoimmune proliferative synovitis with many lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells.

Osteoarthritis (choice B) appears to be due to repetitive low-level trauma to joints and is marked by excessive cartilage loss and reactive bone formation.

Gout (choice C) and pseudogout (choice A) can cause arthritis secondary to crystal deposition in joints.

Gonococcal arthritis (choice D) is a systemic complication of gonorrhea, typically observed in young women who have had a recent sexual encounter.

choice_explanations.A: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals cause pseudogout, not the sicca/joint picture of Sjogren syndrome. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Excessive cartilage loss and reactive bone formation describe osteoarthritis. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Monosodium urate crystals cause gout. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Non-proliferative synovitis with neutrophils and gram-negative diplococci describes gonococcal arthritis. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Sjogren syndrome (often with rheumatoid arthritis) shows a proliferative synovitis with many lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells.

stem: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine examination with no complaints. Physical examination shows strong pulses at both wrists and weak pulses at both ankles. The blood pressure in his right arm is 152/90 mm Hg, and the blood pressure in both of his legs is 95/55 mm Hg. Chest x-ray shows a thinning of the bone on the lower edges of the ribs. Anterograde flow through which of the following is responsible for perfusion of the lower extremities in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The patient has a large difference in blood pressure between his upper and lower limbs. This suggests disease of the aorta distal to the arch, where the vessels supplying the upper limbs arise. In younger individuals (such as this patient), postductal coarctation of the aorta is the most probable diagnosis. In older individuals, severe atherosclerosis of the abdominal aorta, iliac system, and/or femoral system is the most probable diagnosis.
In patients with severe aortic coarctation, anterograde flow through the stenotic portion of the aorta is severely limited. Perfusion to the aorta distal to the coarctation is maintained by collateral flow originating from the internal thoracic (mammary) arteries, which are branches of the subclavian arteries. The internal thoracic arteries give rise to the anterior intercostal arteries. These anastomose with the posterior intercostal arteries that branch from the descending aorta. With increased flow through the internal thoracic-anterior intercostal arterial system, retrograde flow through the posterior intercostal arteries develops, providing oxygenated blood to the descending aorta distal to the coarctation. Rib notching occurs when increased flow through the intercostal arteries slowly enlarges these arteries, resulting in resorption of bone along the lower borders of the ribs.
The axillary arteries (choice A) are the continuations of the subclavian arteries. Although there is anterograde flow through these arteries, they supply the upper limbs and not the lower limbs.
The isthmus of the aorta (choice C) is the common site for postductal coarctation of the aorta. The isthmus is the region of the aorta between the ligamentum arteriosum and the descending aorta. Because of the narrowing of the aorta in this region, there is very limited blood flow through the aorta.
The ductus arteriosus (choice D) is an embryonic structure that connects the pulmonary arterial system to the aortic arch. During fetal development, the ductus arteriosus provides a conduit through which the umbilical blood can bypass the pulmonary circulation and reach the systemic circulation. In adults, a patent ductus arteriosus would allow flow from the systemic circulation to the pulmonary circulation and would not account for the perfusion of the lower limbs. Additionally, in postductal coarctation, the stenotic region is distal to the ductus arteriosus. Because the brachiocephalic trunk and the left subclavian artery both arise from the aortic arch proximal to the site of the coarctation, the blood pressure in both upper limbs is elevated. In contrast, the common iliac arteries are distal to the coarctation, resulting in decreased blood pressure in the lower limbs.
The posterior intercostal arteries (choice E) arise from the descending aorta. Since flow distal to the aortic coarctation would be severely limited, anterograde flow into the posterior intercostal arteries would also be decreased. In order to perfuse the lower limbs, retrograde flow through the posterior intercostal arteries develops.

choice_explanations.A: Axillary arteries supply the upper limbs, not the lower limbs.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Internal thoracic (mammary) arteries give anterior intercostal arteries that anastomose with posterior intercostal arteries, carrying blood to the aorta distal to the coarctation.
choice_explanations.C: The isthmus is the common site of postductal coarctation; flow through it is limited.
choice_explanations.D: A patent ductus arteriosus shunts systemic-to-pulmonary flow and does not perfuse the lower limbs.
choice_explanations.E: Posterior intercostal arteries carry retrograde (not anterograde) flow to reach the lower body.

stem: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a persistent cough and hemoptysis. She reports a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight gain over the past 3 weeks. She has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 43 years. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds at both lung bases and also in the left upper lobe. A chest x-ray shows a 4-cm nodule in the left upper lobe and a diagnosis of lung cancer is made. Further imaging studies show that the tumor has spread and is occluding the thoracic duct. This patient most likely has edema in which of the following sites?

options.text: Entire left side and right lower limb
Entire right side and left lower limb
Right upper limb and right half of head only

explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient has lung cancer. This neoplasm typically has hyper-metabolic and anorexic effects producing weight loss. However, there are scenarios where weight gain can occur in cancer, such as edema from lymphatic blockage or paraneoplastic endocrine syndromes (such as ectopic ACTH production from small cell lung cancer causing Cushing syndrome). Lymphatic obstruction will typically produce non-pitting edema (versus congestive heart failure or nephrotic syndrome related edema, which produce pitting edema).
Lymph flow returns to the venous system by 2 major lymphatic vessels: the thoracic duct drains lymph from the left side of the head, neck, and chest, the left upper limb, and the entire body below the diaphragm; the right lymphatic duct drains the right upper limb, the right side of the chest, and the right side of the head and neck. Both the right lymphatic duct and the thoracic duct flow into the large venous channels at the base of the neck. Occlusion of this drainage can produce intractable edema in sites feeding these ducts.
The left side and right lower limb would be affected, rather than the right side and left lower limb (choice B). The entire left side (rather than just the left upper limb, choice C) and the right lower limb drain into the thoracic duct. The right upper limb and the right half of the head and neck (choices D and E) drain to the right lymphatic duct.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. The thoracic duct drains the entire left side plus the right lower limb and the body below the diaphragm.
choice_explanations.B: Reversed drainage pattern.
choice_explanations.C: The thoracic duct drains more than just the left upper limb.
choice_explanations.D: The right upper limb and right half of the head and neck drain to the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.
choice_explanations.E: The right upper limb drains to the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with recent onset fever and chest pain. The symptoms began after a recent episode of aspiration 3 days ago while the patient was drinking water in bed. His mother reports he was lying supine at the time of the choking event. Chest x-ray reveals dense consolidation in one of the lobes of the lung. In which of the following bronchopulmonary segments did the aspiration event most likely occur?

options.text: Apical segment of the left upper lobe
Apical segment of the right upper lobe
Medial segment of the right middle lobe
Posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe
Superior segment of the right lower lobe

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Because the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical than the left, foreign objects are more likely to be aspirated into the right main bronchus. The superior segmental bronchus of the lower lobar bronchus is the only segmental bronchus that exits from the posterior wall of the lobar bronchi. Therefore, if a patient is supine at the time of aspiration, the object is most likely to enter the superior segmental bronchus of the lower lobe.
None of the segmental bronchi of the left lung (choices A and D) are likely to receive the object because the object is less likely to enter the left main bronchus.
The apical segment of the right upper lobe (choice B) is not likely to receive the foreign object because of the sharp angle that the upper lobar bronchus makes with the right main bronchus and the sharp angle that the apical segmental bronchus makes with the lobar bronchus.
The medial segmental bronchus of the right middle lobe (choice C) arises from the anterior wall of the right middle lobar bronchus. Therefore, when the patient is supine, the effects of gravity will tend to prevent the object from entering this segmental bronchus.

choice_explanations.A: Left lung; object is less likely to enter the left main bronchus.
choice_explanations.B: The apical segment of the right upper lobe is reached only through sharp angles.
choice_explanations.C: The medial segment of the right middle lobe arises from the anterior wall; gravity prevents entry when supine.
choice_explanations.D: Left lung; object is less likely to enter the left main bronchus.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. When supine, aspirated material enters the superior segment of the right lower lobe (only segment exiting the posterior wall).

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a fever and abdominal pain for the past 2 weeks. The patient recently had abdominal surgery. Physical examination shows abdominal and costovertebral tenderness. Blood cultures reveal gram-negative rods and antibiotics are started. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a retroperitoneal abscess. Which of the following is the most likely source of this patient's underlying condition?

options.text: Proximal portion of the first part of the duodenum

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The patient in this vignette has CT findings of a retroperitoneal abscess. Organs found in the retroperitoneum include both primary retroperitoneal organs and secondary retroperitoneal organs. The major primary retroperitoneal structures include the kidney, ureter, adrenal gland, aorta, inferior vena cava, and anal canal. The major secondary retroperitoneal organs include most of the duodenum (except the proximal portion of the first part), most of the pancreas (except for the tail), ascending colon, descending colon, and most of the rectum. Of the five choices that are listed, only the ascending colon is a retroperitoneal structure. The other options are all peritoneal organs.
The major intraperitoneal organs are the stomach (choice B), liver and gallbladder, spleen, proximal portion of the first part of the duodenum (choice D), tail of the pancreas, jejunum (choice C), ileum, appendix, transverse colon, sigmoid colon, and uterus (choice E).
Intraperitoneal organs are suspended by a mesentery and are almost completely enclosed in visceral peritoneum. These organs are mobile. Retroperitoneal organs are partially covered on one side with parietal peritoneum and are immobile or fixed organs. Many retroperitoneal organs were originally suspended by a mesentery in the embryo and become secondarily retroperitoneal during fetal development.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Of the listed organs, only the ascending colon is a (secondary) retroperitoneal structure.
choice_explanations.B: The stomach is an intraperitoneal organ.
choice_explanations.C: The jejunum is an intraperitoneal organ.
choice_explanations.D: The proximal first part of the duodenum is intraperitoneal.
choice_explanations.E: The uterus is an intraperitoneal organ.

stem: A 47-year-old Asian man comes to his physician because of a 3-month history of weight loss and abdominal pain. He says that he has recently experienced vomiting and an overall feeling of malaise. His stools have also become darker recently. Laboratory studies show mild anemia but no evidence of infection. An abdominal CT scan shows a large mass protruding into the lumen of the stomach. The patient is given an initial diagnosis of gastric carcinoma and decides to undergo a gastric resection. In order to access the mass, the surgeon must dissect through the lesser omentum. Which of the following structures is most likely at risk for damage during the dissection of the lesser omentum?
explanation: The correct answer is A. The free edge of the lesser omentum, which is also called the hepatoduodenal ligament, contains three important structures known as the portal triad: the common bile duct, the proper hepatic artery, and the portal vein. These structures could be at risk during the dissection of the lesser omentum. The common bile duct is formed from the union of the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct and travels to the duodenum in the free edge of the lesser omentum as part of the portal triad. The proper hepatic artery is a branch of the common hepatic artery. The portal vein is formed by the union of the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein. This union occurs behind the neck of the pancreas and from there the portal vein travels to the liver in the hepatoduodenal ligament as part of the portal triad. The lesser omentum is attached to the lesser curvature of the stomach.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. The common bile duct is part of the portal triad within the free edge (hepatoduodenal ligament) of the lesser omentum.
choice_explanations.B: The gastroduodenal artery is not part of the portal triad.
choice_explanations.C: The hepatic vein drains into the IVC and is not in the lesser omentum.
choice_explanations.D: The left gastro-omental artery runs along the greater curvature.
choice_explanations.E: The short gastric arteries supply the fundus along the greater curvature.

stem: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressively worsening early satiety after meals for the past 4 months. He states that he has lost 13.6 kg (30 lb) over this time period. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the past 30 years. He has no history of any major medical illness and takes no medications. Physical examination shows a thin man and the spleen is palpated 5 cm below the costal margin. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a large gastric tumor impinging on the splenic artery as it passes posterior to the greater curvature of the stomach. Blood supply to the tissue supplied by which of the following arteries will most likely be compromised?
explanation: The correct answer is E. The splenic artery passes behind the stomach and gives off the short gastric arteries and the left gastro-omental artery after passing the greater curvature but before reaching the spleen. The left gastro-omental artery has an excellent anastomotic connection with the right gastro-omental artery (a branch of the gastroduodenal artery). These two arteries supply the greater curvature of the stomach. The short gastric arteries, which supply the fundus of the stomach, do not have good anastomoses, so occlusion of the splenic artery would have a greater effect on these arteries, subjecting the fundus to a greater risk of ischemia.

choice_explanations.A: The left gastric artery arises directly from the celiac trunk and supplies the lesser curvature.
choice_explanations.B: The left gastro-omental artery anastomoses well with the right gastro-omental artery, so occlusion is compensated.
choice_explanations.C: The right gastric artery is a branch of the proper hepatic artery and supplies the lesser curvature.
choice_explanations.D: The right gastro-omental artery anastomoses with the left gastro-omental artery.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. The short gastric arteries supply the fundus and lack good anastomoses, so occlusion of the splenic artery risks fundal ischemia.

stem: A 20-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after acute onset abdominal pain. She claims the pain was originally diffuse and now has emerged as a tender point on her right side. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.8°F) and she is unable to keep down food. She has had several episodes of nausea and vomiting. CT scan shows a collection of fluid in the right lower quadrant with inflammatory tissue. If surgery is performed on this patient, which of the following is the sequence of structures that will be encountered, after the skin is incised?

options.text: Camper fascia, Scarpa fascia, internal oblique, transversalis fascia, parietal peritoneum
Camper fascia, transversus abdominis, internal oblique, transversalis fascia, parietal peritoneum
Scarpa fascia, Camper fascia, external oblique, transversalis fascia, transversus abdominis
Scarpa fascia, transversalis fascia, external oblique, internal oblique, parietal peritoneum
Transversalis fascia, Scarpa fascia, internal oblique, external oblique, parietal peritoneum

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The layers of the anterior abdominal wall are as follows: Camper fascia (fatty layer); Scarpa fascia (fibrous layer); external oblique muscle/aponeurosis; internal oblique muscle/aponeurosis; transversus abdominis muscle/aponeurosis; transversalis fascia; extraperitoneal fascia; and parietal peritoneum. The parietal peritoneum would then be the final layer of tissue before entering the peritoneal cavity.
Camper fascia and Scarpa fascia are superficial fascial layers composed of fatty and membranous tissue, respectively. The external oblique muscle fibers run inferomedially. Medially, the muscle is replaced by aponeurosis. The external oblique aponeurosis joins with the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to form the rectus sheath.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Superficial to deep: Camper fascia, Scarpa fascia, then the muscular layers, transversalis fascia, and finally parietal peritoneum.
choice_explanations.B: Transversus abdominis lies deep to the internal oblique, not superficial to it.
choice_explanations.C: Scarpa fascia lies deep to (after) Camper fascia.
choice_explanations.D: Transversalis fascia lies deep to the muscular layers, not superficial to the external oblique.
choice_explanations.E: Transversalis fascia is a deep layer and would not be encountered first.

stem: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after sustaining an injury while skiing. Physical examination shows a swollen right knee. The skin covering the right foot is pale, the dorsalis pedis pulse is not detectable, and no pulse is felt posterior to the medial malleolus. An x-ray of the right leg shows a fracture of the femur immediately proximal to the femoral condyles. Which of the following arteries is most likely compressed as a result of this fracture?
explanation: The correct answer is C. The patient has suffered a supracondylar fracture of the femur. The supracondylar surface of the femur forms the floor of the popliteal fossa. The popliteal fossa contains the popliteal artery in close proximity to the femur. Because of its proximity, the popliteal artery is subject to injury from a supracondylar fracture of the femur and from a posterior dislocation of the knee. Proximal to becoming the popliteal artery, the vessel is called the femoral artery and passes through the adductor hiatus (an opening in the tendon of the adductor magnus). After crossing the knee, this artery divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries, which supply the leg and foot.

choice_explanations.A: The anterior tibial artery is distal to the knee and not compressed by a supracondylar fracture.
choice_explanations.B: The femoral artery is proximal and passes through the adductor hiatus before becoming the popliteal artery.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. The popliteal artery lies on the supracondylar surface forming the floor of the popliteal fossa, so a supracondylar fracture risks its injury.
choice_explanations.D: The posterior tibial artery is distal to the knee.
choice_explanations.E: The profunda femoris is a deep branch of the femoral artery in the thigh.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after sustaining blunt trauma to her chest during a motor vehicle accident. Her pulse is 105/min and her blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. The blood pressure drops to 78/40 during inspiration. Physical examination shows elevated jugular venous pulse and cool, clammy extremities. Chest x-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Into which of the following potential spaces is this patient most likely hemorrhaging?

options.text: Between the epicardium (visceral pericardium) and the parietal pericardium
Between the fibrous pericardium and the parietal pleura
Between the myocardium and the epicardium (visceral pericardium)
Between the parietal pericardium and the fibrous pericardium
Between the parietal pleura and the visceral pleura

explanation:
The correct answer is A. With a dropping blood pressure and elevated heart rate, there are two possibilities for the cause of bleeding in this scenario: either blood loss in the thorax (thus hypovolemic shock) or tamponade (thus cardiogenic shock). The elevated jugular venous pulse points toward tamponade (since JVP would be low-normal in hypovolemic shock). This is further suggested by the enlarged cardiac silhouette, which is also seen in cardiac tamponade.
The pericardial space is located between the epicardium (also known as the visceral pericardium) and the parietal pericardium. A tear of a blood vessel immediately outside of the heart will cause bleeding into the pericardial space. This accumulation of blood in the pericardial space causes reduced heart sounds and increased pressure on the heart, which restricts filling of the heart during diastole (cardiac tamponade), resulting in jugular venous distension. This reduced filling results in reduced cardiac output and reduced blood pressure. This is a life-threatening condition. The blood in the pericardial space may be removed by pericardiocentesis, thus relieving the pressure on the heart.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. The pericardial cavity (between the visceral and parietal pericardium) is the potential space that fills with blood in cardiac tamponade.
choice_explanations.B: This is not the pericardial cavity.
choice_explanations.C: The myocardium and epicardium are contiguous layers of the heart wall.
choice_explanations.D: There is no potential space between the parietal and fibrous pericardium.
choice_explanations.E: This is the pleural cavity, not the pericardial space.

stem:
A 67-year-old man diagnosed with cancer begins treatment with an antineoplastic drug that causes less bone marrow suppression than other antineoplastic drugs. Three weeks later, he returns to the physician because of shortness of breath, a nonproductive cough, and fatigue. Pulmonary function tests show:

Test | Value (% predicted)
TLC | 60%
FVC | 65%
FEV1 | 60%
DLCO | 55%

(TLC, total lung capacity; FVC, forced vital capacity; FEV1, forced expiratory volume in 1 second; DLCO, diffusing capacity.) A chest x-ray shows peripheral linear and nodular opacities at bilateral lung bases. Which of the following is the most likely prescribed drug?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The pulmonary function tests and x-ray indicate restrictive lung disease. Restrictive lung diseases are characterized by an increase in elastic recoil (decrease in lung compliance), which is measured as a decrease in all lung volumes. A low DLCO in combination with reduced lung volumes suggests interstitial lung disease.
Bleomycin is an intercalating agent that complexes with iron (forming reactive oxygen species) and induces DNA strand breaks. Bleomycin can cause a chronic pneumonitis that can progress to pulmonary fibrosis. Because of the known effects on pulmonary function, patients should be monitored for cough, dyspnea, rales, and pulmonary infiltrates. Pulmonary fibrosis accompanying bleomycin therapy can be seen on x-ray as diffuse, ground-glass opacities at the mid-to-basal areas of the lungs and/or poorly defined pulmonary nodules. Bleomycin should be discontinued in patients suspected of bleomycin-induced lung injury. Up to 10% of patients receiving bleomycin can develop a life-threatening interstitial pulmonary fibrosis.
Cisplatin (choice B) is a platinum compound that forms metabolites that bind and crosslink DNA strands. While cisplatin is less likely to cause myelosuppression than many other anticancer drugs, it can cause both renal and neurologic toxicity.
Cyclophosphamide (choice C) is a DNA crosslinking agent used to treat non-Hodgkin lymphoma as well as ovarian and breast cancers. Cyclophosphamide is particularly myelosuppressive and hepatotoxic.
Doxorubicin (choice D) is an antibiotic that inserts between DNA bases and induces DNA strand breaks. Both myelosuppression and cardiac damage are dose-limiting for doxorubicin.
Vincristine (choice E) is a plant alkaloid that is used to treat lymphoma, Wilms tumor, and choriocarcinoma. This agent is associated with the development of neurotoxicity.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Bleomycin causes pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis with a restrictive pattern and reduced DLCO.
choice_explanations.B: Cisplatin causes renal and neurologic toxicity, not pulmonary fibrosis.
choice_explanations.C: Cyclophosphamide is markedly myelosuppressive and hepatotoxic.
choice_explanations.D: Doxorubicin causes myelosuppression and cardiotoxicity.
choice_explanations.E: Vincristine causes neurotoxicity.

stem: The table shows the relative concentrations of inulin and an unknown substance measured in the tubular fluid of an experimental animal's juxtamedullary nephron. Substance X (Sub X) is most likely to be which of the following?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. The data for inulin reveal how water is handled throughout the nephron, since it is not reabsorbed or secreted. The increase in the inulin concentration from 1 to 3 is a result of reabsorption of 2/3 of the volume in the proximal tubule. An increase in the tubular fluid concentration from 3 to 12 from the end of the proximal tubule to the end of the distal tubule is a result of reabsorbing an additional 3/4 of the volume. Since the thick ascending limb and distal tubule are impermeable to water, the water reabsorption occurred in the thin descending limb. A ten-fold increase in inulin concentration indicates that 9/10 of the remaining volume was reabsorbed in the collecting duct.

Since the concentration of substance X increased more than inulin, it must be secreted in the proximal tubule. The concentration of substance X increases by the same factor for the remaining segments compared to inulin, indicating it is not reabsorbed or secreted after the proximal tubule. The only substance listed here that is freely filtered and secreted in the proximal tubule is creatinine. The secretion of creatinine only adds about 10% to the filtered load, so creatinine clearance (or estimated clearance for serum creatinine level) is often used in clinical medicine to estimate GFR.

Bicarbonate (choice A) is freely filtered and 90% is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. Therefore, its relative concentration should be less than 3. The remainder is reabsorbed throughout the rest of the nephron and its concentration at the end of the collecting duct would be close to zero.

Glucose (choice C) is freely filtered and, under normal circumstances, 100% is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. So, its relative concentration should be zero by the end of the proximal tubule.

Sodium (choice D) is reabsorbed in the same proportion as the water and its relative concentration would remain around 1 at the end of the proximal tubule. It is also reabsorbed in the ascending limb of Henle's loop and the distal tubule. Therefore, its relative concentration would decrease.

About 50% of the urea (choice E) is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so the relative concentration would be less than 3 at the end of the proximal tubule. There is some secretion in the thin ascending limb, so its relative concentration should be higher than 12.

choice_explanations.A: Bicarbonate is freely filtered and 90% is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so its relative concentration should be less than 3 and near zero at the end of the collecting duct. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Creatinine is freely filtered and slightly secreted in the proximal tubule, so its concentration increases more than inulin; creatinine clearance is used clinically to estimate GFR.
choice_explanations.C: Glucose is 100% reabsorbed in the proximal tubule under normal circumstances, so its relative concentration should be zero by the end of the proximal tubule. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Sodium is reabsorbed in proportion to water, so its relative concentration would remain around 1 and then decrease. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: About 50% of urea is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so its relative concentration would be less than 3. Incorrect.

fa_summary: Inulin is neither reabsorbed nor secreted (clearance = GFR); creatinine is freely filtered and slightly secreted in the proximal tubule, so its relative concentration rises above inulin, which is why creatinine clearance estimates GFR.
