stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of severe colicky flank pain. Urinalysis shows yellow-brown hexagonal crystals. An abdominal x-ray shows radiopaque staghorn calculi of both renal pelvises. A nitroprusside cyanide test on urine produces a deep purple color. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This is cystinuria, which is an autosomal recessive defect of the renal tubules in which the amino acid cystine cannot be resorbed. The cystine often precipitates in the urine, forming radiopaque stones (because of enough coprecipitation with calcium) in the bladder or renal pelvis. The renal pelvis stones often take the form of staghorn calculi. The x-ray below shows a staghorn calculus on the left and multiple isolated stones on the right.

Isolated crystals of cystine have a characteristic yellow-brown, hexagonal morphology that can be identified in urine specimens. A positive nitroprusside cyanide test on urine will confirm the diagnosis. Cyanide converts cystine to cysteine; the sulfhydryl group then reacts with nitroprusside to produce a deep purple color if the urine contains significant amounts of cystine.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive renal tubular defect of cystine reabsorption causing radiopaque staghorn calculi, hexagonal crystals, and a positive nitroprusside cyanide test.
choice_explanations.B: Familial iminoglycinuria is a benign disorder of proline/hydroxyproline/glycine transport and does not cause cystine stones. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Fanconi syndrome is a generalized proximal tubular dysfunction, not the specific cause of cystine staghorn calculi. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Hartnup disease is a defect of neutral amino acid (including tryptophan) transport causing pellagra-like symptoms, not cystine stones. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Hypophosphatemic rickets is a phosphate-wasting disorder and is not associated with cystine stones. Incorrect.

fa_summary: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive proximal tubular reabsorption defect for cystine (and ornithine, lysine, arginine) that produces radiopaque staghorn calculi, yellow-brown hexagonal crystals, and a positive nitroprusside cyanide test; treat with hydration and alkalinization of urine.

stem:
A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. He appears confused and lethargic. Physical examination shows a morbidly obese male with contusions and a shallow laceration over the left shoulder and no signs of head trauma. Mucous membranes are dry, capillary refill time is prolonged, and skin turgor is slow. CT of the head and an x-ray of the left shoulder show no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:

Sodium 150 mEq/L
Potassium 3.4 mEq/L
Chloride 108 mEq/L
Bicarbonate 24 mEq/L
BUN 10 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL

His urine output is 145 mL/hr with urine osmolality of 800 mOsm/kg. An injection of ADH is given. Two hours later, his urine output is still 145 mL/hr and osmolality is unchanged. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the continued diuresis?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has clinical signs of moderate dehydration. He is confused, with no evidence of head trauma. It has only been 30 minutes since the accident, so dehydration is most likely unrelated to the accident. A patient who is morbidly obese with excessive urination suggests type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM). Hyperglycemia, as would occur with DM, can prevent the complete reabsorption of glucose in the proximal tubule. This would also cause a reduced reabsorption of water and electrolytes in the proximal tubule. The increased delivery of fluid and electrolytes to the loop of Henle overloads this segment of the nephron and reduces its ability to maintain the medullary osmolar gradient. This gradient is required for the antidiuretic hormone (ADH)-induced reabsorption of water from the collecting duct. ADH simply places water channels in membranes lining the collecting ducts, which then permits the passive reabsorption of water. Any failure at the level of the collecting duct or the loop of Henle reduces the ability of the kidney to form a concentrated urine. In the nephrogenic form of diabetes insipidus, the patient would also fail to respond to the ADH, but urine osmolality would be low, rather than elevated.

Why is type 2 diabetes mellitus the best choice from among the options given? This patient is hypernatremic with normal bicarbonate. Poorly managed type 2 DM is most likely to produce a hyperglycemic, hyperosmotic, non-ketotic state (HHNS). DKA can occur, but it is not the most common presentation. HHNS usually is associated with a prolonged period of osmotic diuresis; most often water loss exceeds sodium loss, so they have hypertonic dehydration. So, it is quite likely for a person to have undiagnosed type 2 DM. Hyperglycemia increases the filtered load of glucose. If the filtered load exceeds the glucose transport maximum, glucose will appear in the urine; this causes an osmotic diuresis. The patient becomes dehydrated despite compensatory increases of ADH and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAS). The dehydration usually will be associated with hypernatremia; the body is avidly reabsorbing sodium chloride to attempt to conserve fluid. The osmotic diuresis overwhelms this response.

None of the other choices would produce the described interference with ADH action.

Volume expansion tends to cause metabolic acidosis. It is difficult to consume enough sodium (choice A) to cause hypernatremia if the kidneys are healthy. Volume expansion and metabolic acidosis are likely so long as water is also available to be consumed.

Hypoaldosteronism (choice C) will not cause hypernatremia; it will cause hyponatremia and possibly also metabolic acidosis. In addition, the hyponatremia with deficient aldosterone is secondary to compensatorily increased ADH (ADH increased because of volume loss caused by low aldosterone). If a patient has hypernatremia, aldosterone deficiency is not likely to be responsible.

Hyperthyroidism (choice B) and vitamin D (choice E) deficiency have no direct connection to his condition.

choice_explanations.A: It is difficult to consume enough sodium to cause hypernatremia if the kidneys are healthy. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Hyperthyroidism has no direct connection to a hyperglycemic osmotic diuresis. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Hypoaldosteronism causes hyponatremia (not hypernatremia) with possible metabolic acidosis. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes exceeds the glucose transport maximum, causing an osmotic diuresis that overloads the loop of Henle and impairs the medullary osmolar gradient needed for ADH-induced water reabsorption.
choice_explanations.E: Vitamin D deficiency is unrelated to the described polyuria. Incorrect.

fa_summary: In type 2 diabetes, hyperglycemia exceeding the glucose transport maximum causes osmotic diuresis; the increased solute delivery to the loop of Henle impairs the medullary osmolar gradient, reducing collecting-duct water reabsorption and producing hypertonic (hypernatremic) dehydration.

stem:
A 41-year-old Puerto Rican-American man comes to the physician because of swollen ankles. He has a history of IV drug use, mainly injected heroin. His temperature is 37°C (99°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 138/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows 3+ lower extremity pitting edema and periorbital swelling. No cardiac murmur is heard. Peripheral pulses are strong and regular. Laboratory tests show:

Leukocyte count 3500/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 65%
Bands 5%
Lymphocytes 18%
Monocytes 10%
Eosinophils 2%
Serum urea nitrogen 27 mg/dL
Creatinine 2.6 mg/dL
Fasting serum glucose 105 mg/dL

Urine dipstick 4+ protein, negative for blood and glucose
24-hour urine protein of 6/24 hr

ELISA test positive for HIV; confirmed on Western blot analysis. He is scheduled for a kidney biopsy. Which of the following conditions would most likely be found on the kidney biopsy?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has nephrotic syndrome, as evidenced by the presence of edema and massive proteinuria. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is currently considered the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome. Other primary glomerulonephropathies that cause nephrotic syndrome include membranous glomerulonephritis, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Secondary causes of nephrotic syndrome include diabetes mellitus, SLE, and amyloidosis.

FSGS is common among adults of Hispanic and African American descent. Causes of FSGS include obesity, heroin use, sickle cell anemia, and HIV infection. Our patient has a history of heroin use and is HIV positive. Histologically, there is sclerosis and scarring of the glomerular tufts. Not all glomeruli are affected (focal) and only parts of the glomerular tuft are affected (segmental). FSGS has a poor prognosis. Treatment includes immunosuppressive therapy, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs. The disorder returns even with transplantation.

Diabetic nephropathy (choice A) can cause nephrotic syndrome but there would likely be elevated fasting serum glucose levels. Albumin and glucose would also be present in the urine. Our patient has a normal fasting blood glucose level and urine dipstick has absent glucose.

IgA nephropathy (choice C), also called Berger disease, presents as a nephritic syndrome. It is more common among children who had a nonspecific upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection 1-2 weeks prior to the nephritic syndrome presentation. IgA deposits are present within mesangial cells.

Membranous glomerulonephritis (choice D) used to be the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, but has been surpassed in recent years by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. It is common in Caucasians. Causes of membranous glomerulonephritis include chronic hepatitis B or C virus infection, rheumatoid arthritis, medications (penicillamine, gold salts), SLE, and malignancy (lung or breast cancer, or, rarely, lymphoma).

Minimal change disease (choice E) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Normal microscopy and flattened effacement of podocytes seen on electron microscopy are characteristic of this condition. Most of these cases are treatable with steroid therapy. It can also occur in adults and may have a poorer prognosis.

choice_explanations.A: Diabetic nephropathy would be accompanied by elevated fasting glucose and glycosuria; this patient's fasting glucose is normal and urine glucose is absent. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. HIV infection and heroin use are causes of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults; histology shows focal, segmental sclerosis of the glomerular tufts.
choice_explanations.C: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) presents as a nephritic syndrome following a URI/GI infection with mesangial IgA deposits. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Membranous glomerulonephritis is more common in Caucasians and is associated with hepatitis B/C, medications, SLE, and malignancy. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, with normal light microscopy and podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy. Incorrect.

fa_summary: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and is associated with obesity, heroin use, sickle cell disease, and HIV; histology shows sclerosis of only some glomeruli (focal) and only part of the tuft (segmental).

stem: An 83-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an erythematous, itchy, ulcerating lesion of her left nipple associated with an oozing, serosanguinous nipple discharge that has been present for the past month. She has tried over the counter topical creams, but they do not help. A biopsy specimen shows scattered large cells with clear, abundant cytoplasm located within the epidermis of the nipple. Immunohistochemical staining reveals these large cells are positive for cytokeratin. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Paget disease of the breast is associated with an underlying breast cancer that is either invasive or in situ in 97% of cases. A palpable breast mass would indicate the presence of an invasive ductal carcinoma. If there is no palpable mass, then consider the presence of an underlying ductal carcinoma in situ. Moreover, the ductal carcinoma cells can show amplification of Her2-neu (erb-B2).

Paget disease is one of the less common presentations of breast cancer, but it is important to know the pathology. Lesions that are scaly, vesicular, or oozing start in the nipple then spread to the areola. Sometimes a bloody discharge is also present. Patients may complain of pain, burning, or pruritus before the lesions appear. Histologically, malignant, mucin-containing cells (Paget cells) extend intraepidermally within the large ductal system into the nipple skin without crossing the basement membrane.

Acute mastitis (choice A) is a disease of nursing women in which bacteria (usually Staph. aureus) gain entry to the breast tissue via cracks in the traumatized nipple. It is characterized by acute inflammation, tissue necrosis, and abscess formation.

Intraductal papilloma (choice C) is a subareolar tumor in the ducts that may produce a bloody or serous nipple discharge. Most intraductal papillomas are benign and are cured with complete excision.

Invasive lobular carcinoma (choice D) is a tumor of the terminal ductules of the breast. It presents as poorly circumscribed, rubbery breast mass, comprised of invasive single-filing arrangement of tumor cells. In contrast, invasive ductal carcinoma tends to appear as a hard, stellate, and fibrous tumor. Lobular carcinoma does not produce Paget disease since it does not invade along large duct epithelium.

Phyllodes tumor (choice E) usually presents in older patients as a large, firm, circumscribed breast tumor. Microscopically, there is stromal and epithelial proliferation. The tumors tend to be benign, but a small number may have malignant transformation. There is no nipple involvement.

choice_explanations.A: Acute mastitis occurs in nursing women via bacterial entry through cracks in the traumatized nipple, causing acute inflammation, necrosis, and abscess. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Paget disease of the breast features intraepidermal malignant glandular (Paget) cells at the nipple and is associated with an underlying ductal carcinoma (in situ when no palpable mass is present).
choice_explanations.C: Intraductal papilloma is a benign subareolar ductal tumor causing bloody/serous discharge. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Invasive lobular carcinoma arises from terminal ductules and does not invade along large duct epithelium, so it does not cause Paget disease. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Phyllodes tumor is a stromal/epithelial breast tumor without nipple involvement. Incorrect.

fa_summary: Paget disease of the nipple presents as an erythematous, scaly, oozing, or ulcerated nipple lesion from intraepidermal malignant glandular (Paget) cells and is associated with an underlying breast carcinoma (ductal carcinoma in situ if no palpable mass).

stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressively worsening shortness of breath and a dry cough. A chest x-ray shows hilar lymphadenopathy and diffuse abnormalities of the lung parenchyma. A biopsy specimen of a segment of lung shows noncaseating granulomas. Acid-fast, silver, and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stains of the granulomas are negative. Which of the following is most likely to be increased in this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is B. This patient has sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis is a common granulomatous disease, the etiology of which remains unclear. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, and mycobacterial (acid-fast) and fungal (silver stain, PAS) stains are used to rule out infectious etiologies. The granulomas are characteristically small, noncaseating (hard) granulomas that may contain giant cells. Although sarcoidosis can affect all organs, the disease most frequently involves the lungs (cutaneous and ocular lesions are also common clinical manifestations, affecting ~25% of patients). The disease causes inflammation and fibrosis of the lung parenchyma, and the pleura may thicken. Fibrosis is a restrictive pulmonary disease. The lung becomes stiff and difficult to expand (ie, increased elasticity, decreased compliance), which decreases all lung volumes and capacities as measured by pulmonary function testing, increases elastic recoil, and increases the work of breathing. Fibrosis also impairs gas exchange. Patients who die typically do so from pulmonary fibrosis and cor pulmonale. Loss of lung compliance reduces all lung volumes, including FEV1 (choice C), FVC (choice D), and residual volume (choice F). Inspiration is typically more arduous, hence ventilation (choice E) tends to decrease, which, along with the negative effects of fibrosis on gas exchange, tends to decrease arterial PO2 (choice A) and cause hypoxemia.

choice_explanations.A: Arterial PO2 is decreased (hypoxemia), not increased.
choice_explanations.B: Elastic recoil is increased in restrictive lung disease.
choice_explanations.C: FEV1 is decreased in restrictive disease.
choice_explanations.D: FVC is decreased in restrictive disease.
choice_explanations.E: Minute alveolar ventilation decreases because inspiration is more arduous.
choice_explanations.F: Residual volume is decreased in restrictive disease.

fa_summary: Sarcoidosis causes a restrictive lung disease with increased elastic recoil and decreased lung volumes.

stem: A 49-year-old African-American woman comes to the physician because of shortness of breath, cough, and chest pain. Chest x-ray shows hilar lymphadenopathy and biopsy of one of the lymph nodes is consistent with a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Which of the following histologic findings in the biopsy specimen best confirms this diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is D. A granuloma is a collection of immune cells that form as an attempt to wall off a foreign substance such as infection, which the body cannot eliminate. The predominant cell type is the epithelioid macrophage (also known as histiocyte). Epithelioid macrophages are the cells that define a granuloma. They are transformed macrophages and can, but not invariably, fuse to form a multinucleated giant cell. Epithelioid histiocytes are recognized on standard H&E preparation by their pale pink cytoplasm and indistinct cell boundaries. Sarcoidosis is a disease that is characterized by non-necrotizing (e.g. noncaseating) granulomas in multiple organs including the lungs, lymph nodes, and skin. Asteroid bodies (stellate inclusions), Schaumann bodies, or multinucleated giant cell features may be present, but are not required for the diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Aschoff bodies (choice A) describe the granulomatous appearance and transformed macrophages seen in acute rheumatic myocarditis. Calcifications within a lymph node (choice B) may be seen with silicosis or tuberculosis. Caseous necrosis (choice C) has a characteristically amorphous and eosinophilic appearance on H&E microscopy and is suggestive of tuberculosis, not sarcoidosis. Over time, fibroblasts proliferate (choice E) within the core of old, inactive granulomas, eradicating the histiocytes and the stereotypical appearance and producing a dense collagenous scar; this feature is not required for the diagnosis of granulomas.

choice_explanations.A: Aschoff bodies are seen in acute rheumatic myocarditis.
choice_explanations.B: Calcifications are seen with silicosis or tuberculosis.
choice_explanations.C: Caseous necrosis suggests tuberculosis, not sarcoidosis.
choice_explanations.D: Epithelioid histiocytes (macrophages) are the cell type that defines a granuloma.
choice_explanations.E: Fibroblast proliferation occurs in old, inactive granulomas and is not diagnostic.

fa_summary: Sarcoidosis is defined by noncaseating granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up examination. She has had worsening dyspnea and fatigue for 2 months, and chest pain on exercise. She has a history of two documented episodes of pulmonary thromboemboli in the past year. Physical examination shows displacement of the cardiac apex to the right and jugular venous distention. There is mild hepatomegaly and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Chest x-ray shows a prominent right ventricle. Echocardiography shows an elevated pulmonary artery pressure and right ventricular hypertrophy. Lung biopsy shows pulmonary artery atherosclerosis and medial hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is characterized by elevated pulmonary arterial pressure and secondary right ventricular failure. Echocardiography shows high pulmonary artery pressure (>30 mm Hg) and hypertrophy of the right ventricular wall. Normally, the pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure system, eliciting very little endothelial or medial response. PH, however, leads to medial hypertrophy, arterial fibrosis, and marked narrowing of the arterial lumina, predisposing to arterial thrombosis. Tufts of endothelial proliferations (producing so-called plexogenic pulmonary arteriopathy) are prominent in severe cases. In this patient's case, pulmonary endarterectomy may be of significant benefit. This patient suffers from what was previously called secondary pulmonary hypertension caused by pulmonary embolism (now called Group 4, or chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension; CTEPH). Other causes for secondary pulmonary hypertension are chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), interstitial lung disease, and left heart failure. Primary PH, on the other hand, includes idiopathic pulmonary hypertension (now called Group 1) and is more common in women. Adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS; choice A) is a clinical term for rapid-onset respiratory insufficiency secondary to diffuse alveolar damage. The lungs show alveoli filled with proteinaceous debris and desquamated alveolar lining cells, and alveolar septa lined by hyaline membranes. The heart and pulmonary vasculature show no specific changes in ARDS; this patient does not have ARDS because her symptoms have been relatively chronic and there is no evidence of pulmonary edema. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (choice B) produces early-onset panacinar emphysema, with hyperlucency of the lungs and destruction of alveolar walls. Atopic asthma (choice C) is characterized by chronic airway inflammation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness, without cardiovascular changes. Goodpasture disease (choice D) is a necrotizing and hemorrhagic pneumonitis accompanied by rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Sarcoidosis (choice F) is an interstitial pneumonitis that produces noncaseating giant cell granulomas and would involve both ventricles if there is cardiac involvement.

choice_explanations.A: ARDS is acute diffuse alveolar damage without pulmonary vascular remodeling.
choice_explanations.B: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency causes early-onset panacinar emphysema.
choice_explanations.C: Atopic asthma causes airway inflammation without pulmonary vascular changes.
choice_explanations.D: Goodpasture disease causes pneumonitis plus rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
choice_explanations.E: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (Group 4) with right ventricular hypertrophy.
choice_explanations.F: Sarcoidosis causes noncaseating granulomas; cardiac involvement would affect both ventricles.

fa_summary: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (Group 4) causes elevated pulmonary artery pressure and right ventricular hypertrophy.

stem: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician with concerns of a chronic nonproductive cough. He has smoked 1.5 packs per day for the past 40 years and occasionally drinks beer and hard liquor. He says he has occasional blood-tinged sputum after coughing, increasing fatigue, and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss in the past 5 months. His temperature is 37.6C (99.6F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Chest auscultation reveals decreased breath sounds and occasional wheezing and crackles in the right mid to lower regions. The left side has decreased breath sounds, occasional wheezes, and hyperresonance. A chest x-ray shows a mass in the right middle lobe and hyperinflation in the remaining lung lobes. Bronchoscopy reveals a 3-cm grey-tan bronchial tumor. Biopsy shows a tumor composed of uniform cells with dark round blue nuclei, scant cytoplasm, and prominent crush artifact on H&E section. Immunohistochemical stains are positive for neuron specific enolase (NSE) and negative for lymphocyte common antigen (LCA). A mutation in which of the following oncogenes is most likely associated with this tumor?
explanation: The correct answer is D. The presence of a lung mass with hemoptysis and a hilar mass suggests bronchogenic carcinoma. The uniform size of the neoplastic cells with scant cytoplasm and prominent crush artifact suggests small cell carcinoma (oat cell carcinoma). Small cell carcinoma morphologically resembles lymphocytes and can exhibit cell crush artifact, so lymphoma should be excluded (negative LCA immunohistochemical stain). The oncogene associated with small cell carcinoma of the lung is myc. Small cell carcinoma has a strong association with smoking, grows rapidly, and disseminates early. Tumor cells are derived from bronchial neuroendocrine cells; tumors are centrally located along the bronchial airways (as opposed to peripheral adenocarcinoma), appearing as gray-tan-white masses, and tend to be high stage or disseminated at the time of diagnosis but can be treated with chemotherapy. Microscopically the tumor is composed of small round or polygonal blue cells with little cytoplasm. NOTE: L-myc, N-myc, and C-myc have been seen in small cell lung cancer, where they collectively are seen in 20-30% of cases. C-myc is also seen with Burkitt lymphoma, whereas N-myc is also seen with neuroblastoma. abl (choice A) is associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). cdk4 (choice B) and erb-2 (HER2; choice C) are associated with other malignancies such as breast cancer, and ret (choice E) is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma and MEN 2.

choice_explanations.A: abl is associated with CML and Ph-positive ALL.
choice_explanations.B: cdk4 is a cell-cycle kinase associated with several cancers, not small cell lung cancer.
choice_explanations.C: erb-2 (HER2) is associated with breast and other carcinomas.
choice_explanations.D: myc (L-myc/N-myc/C-myc) is amplified in 20-30% of small cell lung cancers.
choice_explanations.E: ret is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma and MEN 2.

fa_summary: Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma of the lung is strongly associated with myc oncogene amplification.

stem: A 49-year-old Chinese man comes to the physician because of sinus pain and difficulty breathing through his nose. He states that he had occasional episodes of bleeding from his nose. He denies tobacco smoking and he has not seen a physician in years. He migrated to the United States 12 years ago and works as a restaurant cook. His temperature is 37.3C (99.2F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows an ulcerated lesion in the left nostril, slight asymmetry of the posterior pharynx, normal intact tonsils. CT of the head shows a mass involving the nose, pharynx, and maxillary sinuses. A biopsy specimen shows a nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. The virus that is most likely associated with this patient's malignancy is also related to which of the following conditions?
explanation: The correct answer is B. This patient has nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which is associated with the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a member of the herpes virus family. This tumor is commonly seen in adults from Southern China and children from Africa. The tumors can arise in the nasopharynx, tonsil, posterior tongue, and sinuses. There are three morphologic patterns, all of which are associated with a non-neoplastic lymphocytic infiltrate: keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, and undifferentiated carcinoma. The EBV genome is identified in the tumor epithelial cells, not the lymphocytes. Treatment is with radiation therapy. Epstein-Barr virus is also associated with the African (endemic) form of Burkitt lymphoma, which characteristically is seen in children and young adults and involves the jaw. Other sites of involvement in endemic Burkitt lymphoma include GI tract (ileum, cecum), kidney, ovaries, breast, and adrenal glands. EBV is present in all endemic tumors, 25% of HIV-associated tumors, and <20% of sporadic cases. All forms of Burkitt lymphoma are associated with a translocation of c-myc on chromosome 8. Other neoplasms associated with EBV include some forms of Hodgkin lymphoma (mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, and lymphocyte-depleted types) and B cell lymphomas arising in HIV-positive and immunosuppressed patients. HTLV-1 is associated with adult T-cell leukemia (choice A). HPV is associated with genital warts (choice C), cervical carcinoma, penile carcinoma, and anal carcinoma. Hepatocellular carcinoma (choice D) can arise from chronic hepatitis C or hepatitis B virus infection. HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma (choice E).

choice_explanations.A: HTLV-1 is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
choice_explanations.B: EBV is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma and the African (endemic) form of Burkitt lymphoma.
choice_explanations.C: HPV is associated with genital warts and cervical carcinoma.
choice_explanations.D: HBV/HCV are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma.
choice_explanations.E: HHV-8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma.

fa_summary: EBV is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Burkitt lymphoma (and Hodgkin lymphoma).

stem: An 80-year-old woman from a nursing home is admitted to the hospital because of respiratory distress. She has a 4-day history of difficulty breathing and cough. Her pulse is 110/minute and blood pressure is 150/80 mmHg. Pulmonary auscultation reveals decreased breath sounds and crackles in the right middle lung field. Portable chest x-ray shows right middle and right lower lobe infiltrates. Arterial blood gases show a PO2 of 50 mm Hg. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 30 mm/h and serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains the patient's hypoxia?

options.text: Decreased surface area of alveolar capillary membranes
Decrease of PO2 in inspired air

explanation: The correct answer is E. This patient has pneumonia with lobar infiltrates and hypoxemia. The most common mechanism of hypoxia in pneumonia is ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch: regions of the lung that are poorly ventilated (consolidated alveoli) continue to be perfused, producing intrapulmonary shunting of blood and hypoxemia. Decreased surface area of alveolar capillary membranes (choice A) is the mechanism of diffusion impairment (e.g., emphysema, interstitial lung disease). A decrease of PO2 in inspired air (choice B) refers to a low fraction of inspired oxygen (e.g., high altitude). Hypoventilation of central (choice C) or peripheral (choice D) origin lowers alveolar PO2 through reduced minute ventilation and would typically be accompanied by an increased PaCO2.

choice_explanations.A: Decreased surface area is the mechanism in diffusion-impairment diseases such as emphysema.
choice_explanations.B: A decrease of inspired PO2 occurs at altitude.
choice_explanations.C: Central hypoventilation causes hypercapnia, not the classic mechanism in pneumonia.
choice_explanations.D: Peripheral hypoventilation (e.g., neuromuscular) also raises PaCO2.
choice_explanations.E: Pneumonia causes ventilation-perfusion mismatch with intrapulmonary shunting.

fa_summary: Pneumonia causes hypoxemia primarily through ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch.

stem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of dyspnea and a persistent, nonproductive cough for the past 6 weeks. She has smoked 1.5 packs of cigarettes daily for 20 years. Her blood pressure is 153/92 mm Hg. Physical examination shows central obesity, a rounded face, thin extremities, and abdominal striae. A chest x-ray shows a 3-cm mass involving the lung hilum and collapse of the right upper lobe of the lung. A CT-guided biopsy specimen of the mass shows sheets of uniform cells with a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and nuclear hyperchromasia. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation: The correct answer is D. This patient presents with small cell lung cancer complicated by paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome. Small cell carcinomas are of neuroendocrine origin and often retain the ability to secrete hormonal substances, including adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), as seen in this patient. On physical exam, the patient presents with a Cushingoid appearance, which is characterized by facial rounding, central adiposity, thin extremities, dorsocervical fat pad (buffalo hump), and abdominal striae. These findings suggest elevated serum cortisol, likely from tumor secretion of ACTH. Other effects of elevated cortisol include hypertension, thinning of the skin, muscle wasting, osteoporosis, menstrual irregularities, and increased susceptibility to infection. Importantly, ectopic release of ACTH also can produce hyperpigmentation from binding to melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) receptors. Other clues pointing to small cell lung carcinoma include the patient's history of smoking and the central location (hilum) of the tumor; the microscopic findings of hyperchromatic nuclei also suggest small cell lung cancer. Other examples of paraneoplastic syndromes from small cell lung cancer include syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) and Lambert-Eaton syndrome. Adenocarcinoma (choice A) is a malignant epithelial tumor characterized by glandular architecture and mucin secretion, most common in nonsmokers and usually peripheral. Poorly differentiated lymphoma (choice B) can present with hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm but would not produce paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome. Metastatic adrenal tumor (choice C) is a remote possibility; adrenal carcinomas are usually nonfunctioning. Squamous cell carcinoma (choice E) is characterized by squamous differentiation and its most frequent paraneoplastic syndrome is hypercalcemia due to ectopic PTH-related peptide.

choice_explanations.A: Adenocarcinoma is typically peripheral with glandular/mucin features.
choice_explanations.B: Lymphoma lacks neuroendocrine features and does not cause paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: Adrenal carcinomas are usually nonfunctioning and metastatic disease is unlikely.
choice_explanations.D: Small cell carcinoma secretes ACTH, producing paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome.
choice_explanations.E: Squamous cell carcinoma is associated with hypercalcemia (PTHrP), not Cushing syndrome.

fa_summary: Small cell lung cancer is a neuroendocrine tumor that can secrete ACTH, causing paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome.

stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of recurrent episodic non-bloody, watery diarrhea, which happens mostly after drinking alcohol. His wife says that when he drinks alcohol, his face turns red and he starts coughing and wheezing. A chest x-ray shows a left upper lobe lung mass. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?
explanation: The correct answer is A. This patient has carcinoid syndrome, in which vasoactive mediators secreted by carcinoid tumors produce recurrent diarrhea, flushing, wheezing, and carcinoid heart disease. Although many substances may be produced by these tumors, serotonin is one of the more important mediators produced, probably accounting for the observed diarrhea. Other substances include prostaglandins and histamine (which contributes to bronchospasm). Tumors arising from neuroendocrine cells are most often found in the lung, small bowel (commonly ileum), and appendix. Patients with bronchial or other extraintestinal carcinoid tumors present with classic symptoms of diarrhea, flushing, and bronchospasm (wheezing) since the vasoactive mediators cannot be readily cleared by the liver. In contrast, patients with intestinal carcinoid tumors rarely have symptoms in the absence of metastasis due to liver metabolism. Patients with carcinoid tumors should avoid alcohol, as this may be a trigger for the release of vasoactive substances. Treatment is usually surgery if the lesion is confined; chemotherapy if metastatic disease. Inflammatory bowel disease (choice B) is characterized by bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramping, fever, and weight loss. Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) use (choice C) in combination with alcohol can cause increased serotonergic activity, increased heart rate, sweating, dilated pupils, diarrhea, hypertension, tremors, and muscle twitching. Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) tumor (choice E) is a differential diagnosis for watery diarrhea and flushing; it is usually associated with pancreatic islet cell tumors and MEN type 1, and metastasis to lung is rare. Squamous cell carcinoma (choice D) does not produce carcinoid syndrome.

choice_explanations.A: Bronchial carcinoid releases serotonin and other vasoactive mediators, causing flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing.
choice_explanations.B: Inflammatory bowel disease causes bloody diarrhea and cramping, not flushing/wheezing.
choice_explanations.C: MAOI use with alcohol causes serotonergic symptoms, not the classic carcinoid picture.
choice_explanations.D: Squamous cell carcinoma does not secrete serotonin.
choice_explanations.E: VIPoma is usually pancreatic (MEN 1) and rarely metastasizes to lung.

fa_summary: Carcinoid tumors (commonly lung or intestine) secrete serotonin and other vasoactive substances, causing flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing.

stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination because of peripheral neuropathy. He has been taking 3 different drugs for his symptoms without improvement over the past 4 months. A pharmaceutical company is seeking subjects to be included in a phase 3 clinical trial of a drug that treats peripheral neuropathy and has shown promising phase 2 data. The pharmaceutical representative says that the company will pay a modest administrative fee to the physician for each patient referred to this study. The representative explains that the fee covers the physician's time spent to explain and subsequently refer the patient to the study. The physician believes this patient is an excellent candidate for the study. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in patient care?

options.text: Allow the pharmaceutical representative to meet with the patient and explain the details of the clinical trial, and decline to accept the administrative fee
Decline to enroll the patient to receive an untested treatment
Discuss the clinical trial with the patient and fully disclose the physician's financial arrangement with the pharmaceutical company
Discuss the clinical trial with the patient and offer to rebate the administrative fee to him as an incentive to participate
Discuss the clinical trial with the patient and disclose the offer of an administrative fee, but decline the fee and inform the patient of that decision
Refer the patient to the clinical trial, accept the administrative fee, and donate it to the scholarship fund at a local medical school
Refer the patient to the study and accept the administrative fee as offered because extra time and effort is required to get the patient enrolled in the study
Refer the patient to the study but decline the administrative fee offered

explanation: The correct answer is E. Payment for referrals, even for a study, even when the referral is appropriate, even when the payment is disclosed, is a breach of ethics, period. Professional judgment must not be clouded by other considerations, including financial incentives. The clinical trial is right for the patient, so he should be referred, but the "modest administrative fee" is a bribe in disguise and must be refused. In addition, the patient must be fully informed about the circumstances surrounding the referral, including the offer of the administrative fee. Furthermore, the receipt of any gift (beyond a small token) is also considered to be unethical. An example of a "token gift" would be homemade baked goods, a thank you card, or other nominal handcrafted items. The physician must deal directly with his or her own patient. Communication about the study must come from the physician and not be passed off to the pharmaceutical rep (choice A). Who knows what pressure the rep might place, however unwittingly, on the patient to consent to enroll in the clinical trial? Choice B is incorrect. All of the indications are that this treatment may be the patient's best hope. Remember that the treatment is not completely unknown. Phase 2 data are available and, although not definitive, certainly give an indication of this drug as a reasonable option. Choice C is incorrect. Disclosure is not enough. The fee must be refused. Bribing the patient to accept a presented treatment option (choice D) is also not appropriate. True, the physician does not benefit, so the money does not cloud his or her judgment. The problem is that it may cloud the patient's judgment when rendering consent. The administrative fee is tainted money. Laundering it by donating it to a scholarship fund (choice F) does not prevent it from influencing the physician's judgment. In the worst-case scenario, a medical school might pressure faculty to institute this procedure as a way to fund the medical school. Just say "No!" to the money. Choice G is wrong on three counts: First, the patient is not told about the fee. Second, the physician accepts the fee. Third, the patient is referred but is not given the chance to understand the circumstances and consent. Note: it does not matter that additional time and effort is made to enroll the patient in the study. Accepting any type of fee is unethical. Remember, the physician should only enroll a patient in a clinical trial if they feel that it is in the best interest of the patient. Choice H is incorrect. The referral and the decline of the fee are appropriate, but the physician must also explain all of the circumstances to the patient so the patient can make a fully informed decision.

choice_explanations.A: The physician must communicate directly with the patient; the study should not be explained by the pharmaceutical representative.
choice_explanations.B: The trial drug is not completely untested (phase 2 data exist) and may be the patient's best option, so declining enrollment is wrong.
choice_explanations.C: Disclosure alone is not enough; the referral fee must still be refused.
choice_explanations.D: Rebating the fee to the patient improperly clouds the patient's judgment when giving consent.
choice_explanations.E: Payment for referrals is unethical and must be refused, but the patient must be fully informed, including disclosure of the offered fee.
choice_explanations.F: Donating the tainted fee to a scholarship fund does not prevent it from influencing the physician's judgment.
choice_explanations.G: Accepting any referral fee is unethical, even with extra time and effort, and the patient must be informed.
choice_explanations.H: Declining the fee is appropriate, but the physician must also fully explain the circumstances to the patient.

fa_summary: Physicians must generally decline gifts and sponsorships from industry, including referral fees, to avoid any conflict of interest; payment for referrals is unethical and must be refused.

stem: A 67-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of progressive weakness, cough, abdominal pain, and a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss. Physical examination shows no abnormalities and an x-ray of the chest shows a 5-cm nodule in the left upper lobe. A biopsy specimen of the nodule shows adenocarcinoma. A CT scan of the abdomen shows metastasis to the liver and adrenal glands. As the physician approaches the patient's room to discuss the results of the tests, the patient's daughter asks to speak with the physician and says, "If it is cancer, please don't tell him." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: "I'd be happy to wait a little bit if you can tell me why I should."
"I do need to tell him what we know. Would you like to come in with me while I tell him?"
"I know you are concerned, but I have to ask you not to interfere."
"I'm sorry, but I am required to tell my patient everything, even the bad news."
"Talk to me about why you don't want me to tell him if it is cancer."
"Why don't we go into a quiet room over here and I can tell you about your father's condition."
"Would you have me lie to my patient?"
"You seem upset. Please try to compose yourself and then we can talk about it."

explanation: The correct answer is E. The patient needs to be told what the doctor knows, and told in a timely fashion; this is an essential component of informed consent. The patient needs to receive all of the medical information pertaining to his diagnosis so that informed decisions can be made. Full informed consent requires that the patient has received and understood five pieces of information: nature of the procedure/diagnosis, purpose of the procedure/diagnosis, risks, benefits, and availability of alternatives. Although it is essential for the patient to be told this information in a timely manner, something else has occurred that must be dealt with first by the physician. Confronted with the daughter's pleading, the correct response is to seek some information from the daughter to discover if she has any information the physician should know. The physician must be clear about the fact that there is nothing the daughter can say that will stop him from going into the room and telling the patient what he knows. Rather, she may have information that changes the way the physician approaches the patient or the method the physician uses to break this bad news. Notice that with this question, the physician is asking for but not giving information. Along with these specifics, there is a more general rule here. The physician should not be carried away by momentum. The doctor was on the way to talk to the patient. But when new events occur, the physician must change his tack in order to deal with them. The physician wants to know what the daughter thinks, but should not delay telling the patient (choice A). The patient has the right to know the results of the test. The physician has no right to tell the daughter he will delay the necessary conversation. It is also antagonistic, as "tell me why you are worth my time" is essentially what is being said, and this is not an appropriate way for a physician to handle conversations with patients or family members. The patient, not the physician, should be the one to decide if the daughter should be present. Confidentiality is absolute and should not be violated by inviting the daughter into the discussion (choice B). Choice C scolds the daughter. At best, it misses the chance to seek information from her. At worst, it sets up a confrontation that could escalate right outside the patient's door. The physician must tell the patient everything, but should take the opportunity to gain additional information about the patient from the daughter. Simply bypassing her (choice D) misses the opportunity. The physician must respect the patient's confidentiality. This means not discussing the patient's health, even with family members, without the patient's explicit permission. It is appropriate to ask the daughter what she knows, but not to tell her about her father (choice F). Choice G is very challenging and confrontational. It is more likely to lead to an emotional exchange than any useful information. Choice H also misses the opportunity to find out what the daughter knows. In addition, it could be perceived as condescending, that is, treating the daughter like a child rather than an adult.

choice_explanations.A: Antagonistic and delays disclosure; the patient has the right to know without delay.
choice_explanations.B: Violates confidentiality by inviting the daughter into the discussion; the patient must decide who is present.
choice_explanations.C: Scolds the daughter and misses the chance to gather information from her.
choice_explanations.D: Telling the patient everything is right, but simply bypassing the daughter misses the opportunity to learn what she knows.
choice_explanations.E: Correctly seeks information from the daughter while making clear the physician must still tell the patient the diagnosis.
choice_explanations.F: Breaches confidentiality by revealing the father's condition to the daughter without the patient's permission.
choice_explanations.G: Challenging and confrontational; more likely to provoke emotion than be useful.
choice_explanations.H: Misses the chance to learn what the daughter knows and can seem condescending.

fa_summary: Patients have the right to know their diagnosis; disclosure is an essential component of informed consent, while confidentiality must not be breached without the patient's permission.

stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to a new physician for a routine examination. Although the patient had been instructed by the nurse to remove her clothes, put on a gown, and have a seat on the examination table, she remains fully clothed. She glances up briefly when the physician enters the room, but returns her gaze to the floor. She says nothing. Which of the following is the most appropriate response for the physician?

options.text: "Didn't the nurse ask you to remove your clothes and put on a paper gown?"
"Hello, I'm Dr. Green. How are you feeling today?"
"I see that you are still dressed. Is there something you want to talk with me about?"
"OK. Hop up on the table and let's have a look at you."
"So, what brings you to see me today?"
"You seem a little depressed. Why don't you tell me about it?"
"You seem very quiet. I'll just sit here for a moment while you collect your thoughts."

explanation: The correct answer is B. Before discussing the patient's demeanor or problems, the simple ritual of introduction is required. The doctor has never met this patient, and needs to mark the meeting by identifying herself/himself. An introduction at this point also has the virtue of giving something to the patient (the doctor's name) before anything is asked of the patient. Asking the patient a short question at the end of the introduction invites, but does not force, her reply. "Didn't the nurse ask you to remove your clothes and put on a paper gown?" (choice A) is very confrontational. Beginning a relationship by suggesting that the patient has not followed instructions is unlikely to result in a positive response from the patient. Calling the patient's awareness to some aspect of her appearance (choice C) or demeanor (choice F) is confrontation. All confrontations can be perceived as hostile. Asking the patient to confide in the physician before even the rudiments of a relationship are in place is unlikely to be successful. The content must be set before confidence can be gained. "OK. Hop up on the table and let's have a look at you" (choice D) is too abrupt. This option focuses on task only, without recognizing who the patient is or even attempting to hear from her what issues she might have brought with her. "So, what brings you to see me today?" (choice E) is perfunctory and a bit abrupt. There is no attempt to establish rapport or to make the patient comfortable before asking the patient to say what is going on. However, if the physician said "Hello, I am Dr. Green. What brings you to see me today", then this would have been an appropriate opening response. Sitting quietly in the room with the patient without even an introduction (choice G) is likely to feel awkward. No responses are elicited from the patient, and the physician here makes no attempt to engage the patient or to facilitate interaction.

choice_explanations.A: Very confrontational; suggesting the patient did not follow instructions is unlikely to elicit a positive response.
choice_explanations.B: The physician should first introduce herself/himself; a brief question invites, but does not force, the patient's reply.
choice_explanations.C: Calling attention to the patient's appearance is confrontational and can be perceived as hostile.
choice_explanations.D: Too abrupt; focuses on the task without recognizing the patient or eliciting her concerns.
choice_explanations.E: Perfunctory and abrupt, with no introduction or attempt to establish rapport.
choice_explanations.F: Confrontational; asking the patient to confide before a relationship is established is unlikely to succeed.
choice_explanations.G: Sitting in silence without an introduction is awkward and fails to engage the patient.

fa_summary: Patient-centered interviewing begins with a formal introduction: introduce yourself and ask how the patient would like to be addressed; avoid confrontational or abrupt openings.

stem: A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician because of vague aches and pains for the past 1 year. A review of her records shows that she has had similar symptoms nine times over the past 1 year and extensive tests have shown no abnormalities. During the physical examination, the patient says, "What I want doesn't matter. Do what you want, I trust you. I'm afraid you won't have time to see me anymore." Which of the following personality disorders does this patient most likely have?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This scenario is classic for the Cluster C disorder, dependent personality disorder. These patients commonly have a strong reliance on others, there is a subordination of the patient's own needs to the needs of others, and fear of abandonment and rejection. They tend to get others to assume responsibility, cannot express disagreement, and have a great fear of having to care for his or herself. Note that in real life, patients may show symptoms of more than one personality disorder.

According to the DSM-5, the diagnostic criteria for a dependent personality disorder are as follows:
A pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of that leads to submissive and clinging behavior and fears of separation, beginning in early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts as indicated by five or more of the following:
• Has difficulty making everyday decisions without an excessive amount of advice and reassurance from others
• Needs others to assume responsibility for most major areas of his or her life
• Has difficulty expressing disagreement with others because of fear of loss of support or approval
• Goes to excessive lengths to obtain nurturance and support from others to the point of volunteering to do things that are unpleasant
• Has difficulty initiating projects or doing things on their own
• Feels uncomfortable or helpless when alone
• Urgently seeks another relationship as a source of care and support when a close relationship ends
• Often has an unrealistic preoccupation with fears of being left to take care of oneself

Histrionic personality disorder (choice B) is characterized by theatricality, suggestibility, a strong desire for attention, and shallowness.

Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (choice C), also called anancastic personality disorder, is characterized by obsessions, perfectionism, rigidity, and self-doubt. While there is some overlap in the names of OCPD and OCD (obsessive compulsive disorder), there are a couple of key differences to note: 1) Patients with OCD generally seek help for psychological stress and OCPD patients do not, 2) Obsessions and compulsions are not present in OCPD. Although both OCPD and OCD patients may engage in excessive tasks that require exquisite attention to detail such as list-making, individuals with OCD use these tasks to decrease anxiety caused by the obsessional thoughts. Conversely, OCPD patients justify list-making as a good strategy to improve efficiency. Also, OCD patients are usually distressed by having to carry out these tasks or rituals. However, OCPD patients view list making activities, for example, as necessary and even beneficial.

Paranoid personality disorder (choice D) is characterized by suspiciousness, oversensitivity, querulousness, and an unforgiving character.

Schizoid personality disorder (choice E) is characterized by emotional coldness, solitude, and social insensitivity.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Dependent personality disorder (Cluster C) features submissive, clinging behavior with an excessive need to be cared for, subordinating one's own needs, inability to express disagreement, and fear of abandonment/separation.
choice_explanations.B: Histrionic personality disorder features theatricality, suggestibility, attention seeking, and shallowness. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.C: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder features perfectionism, rigidity, and self-doubt (without true obsessions/compulsions). Incorrect.
choice_explanations.D: Paranoid personality disorder features suspiciousness, oversensitivity, and an unforgiving character. Incorrect.
choice_explanations.E: Schizoid personality disorder features emotional coldness, solitude, and social insensitivity. Incorrect.

fa_summary: Dependent personality disorder (Cluster C) is a pervasive, excessive need to be taken care of leading to submissive and clinging behavior and fears of separation; patients cannot express disagreement and subordinate their needs to others.

stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of pain in her left lower leg after a fall. An x-ray of the lower extremity shows a fracture of the left tibia, and the leg is placed in a cast. Several days later, she develops sensory loss of the dorsum of the left foot. Physical examination shows weakness in extension of the left great toe. Compression of a nerve by the cast at which of the following locations is most likely responsible for the development of this symptom in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The common fibular (peroneal) nerve passes around the neck of the fibula, where it is susceptible to injury. Just distal to the neck of the fibula, the common fibular nerve divides into two main branches, the superficial fibular nerve and the deep fibular nerve. The superficial fibular nerve supplies sensory innervation to most of the skin of the dorsum of the foot in addition to motor innervation to the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg that evert the foot. The deep fibular nerve supplies motor innervation to muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg that dorsiflex the foot, extend the toes, and assist in foot inversion. It also supplies sensory innervation to a small patch of skin in the dorsum of the first web space. Compression of the common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula would account for both symptoms seen in this patient. The sensory innervation of the lower leg and foot is shown below.

No major nerves pass over the anterior border of the tibia (choice A). Compression of nerve branches passing near the lateral malleolus (choice B) could cause some sensory loss from the skin of the lateral foot (secondary to compression of the lateral dorsal cutaneous nerve). The saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, passes near the medial femoral condyle (choice C). Compression of this nerve could result in loss of sensation from the skin of the medial leg and ankle. The tibial nerve passes posterior to the medial malleolus (choice D). This nerve divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves, which provide cutaneous innervation to the plantar surface of the foot. Therefore, compression in this location could cause sensory loss to the plantar foot, not to the dorsum of the foot.

choice_explanations.A: No major nerves pass over the anterior border of the tibia.
choice_explanations.B: Compression of nerve branches passing near the lateral malleolus could cause some sensory loss from the skin of the lateral foot (lateral dorsal cutaneous nerve).
choice_explanations.C: The saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, passes near the medial femoral condyle; compression could cause loss of sensation from the skin of the medial leg and ankle.
choice_explanations.D: The tibial nerve passes posterior to the medial malleolus and divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves, which innervate the plantar surface of the foot.
choice_explanations.E: The common fibular nerve passes around the neck of the fibula; compression here accounts for both the sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and the weakness of great toe extension.

fa_summary: Common fibular (peroneal) nerve injury at the neck of the fibula causes foot drop (weakness of dorsiflexion/toe extension) and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after sustaining a high impact injury to his arm during a baseball game. He reports being hit in the right shoulder with a batted ball, causing immediate pain and swelling in that region. Physical examination of the right upper extremity is limited by the patient's pain, and full motor and sensory examination are unable to be performed. X-ray of the shoulder shows a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. Which of the following additional findings will most likely be seen in this patient?

options.text: Laceration of the profunda brachii artery
Weakness in medial rotation of the arm
Weakness in the ability to abduct the arm at the shoulder
Weakness in the ability to elevate the scapula
Weakness in the ability to protract the scapula

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Injuries involving fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus place the axillary nerve at risk of injury. This nerve passes through the quadrangular space, the lateral border of which is the surgical neck of the humerus. This nerve innervates the deltoid muscle and the teres minor. The clinical features of injury to this nerve include weakness of shoulder abduction and a sensory loss in the lateral upper arm and shoulder.

Laceration of the profunda brachii artery (choice A) might occur if one suffers a midshaft fracture of the humerus. This artery accompanies the radial nerve in the musculospiral groove of the humerus. A surgical neck fracture may lacerate the posterior circumflex humeral artery, which accompanies the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space. Weakness in medial rotation of the arm (choice B) may result from a lesion to the posterior cord of the plexus and one or more of the subscapular nerves, or injury to the lateral or medial pectoral nerves. The major medial rotators of the arm at the shoulder are the subscapularis muscle, innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves, the latissimus dorsi muscle, innervated by the middle subscapular nerve, the teres major, innervated by the lower subscapular nerve, and the pectoralis major muscle, innervated by the lateral and medial pectoral nerves. Weakness in the ability to elevate the scapula (choice D) may result from a lesion of the accessory nerve; this nerve may be lacerated by a wound to the lateral neck, but not by a humeral fracture. This nerve innervates the trapezius muscle. Weakness in the ability to protract the scapula (choice E) results from an injury to the long thoracic nerve, which innervates the serratus anterior muscle, causing "winging" of the scapula. This presents as protrusion of the scapula when the patient pushes against a wall. There will be no sensory deficits. The nerve is subject to injury during axillary surgery, such as axillary node dissection for breast cancer.

choice_explanations.A: A midshaft humeral fracture may lacerate the profunda brachii artery, which accompanies the radial nerve in the musculospiral groove.
choice_explanations.B: Medial rotation weakness results from a lesion of the posterior cord/subscapular nerves or the pectoral nerves.
choice_explanations.C: The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space at the surgical neck of the humerus and innervates the deltoid and teres minor; injury causes weakness of shoulder abduction and sensory loss over the lateral upper arm.
choice_explanations.D: Scapular elevation weakness results from injury to the accessory nerve (trapezius), which is not injured by a humeral fracture.
choice_explanations.E: Scapular protraction weakness (winging) results from injury to the long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior).

fa_summary: Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus injures the axillary nerve, causing weakness of shoulder abduction and sensory loss over the lateral upper arm.

stem: A 66-year-old man is involved in a motor vehicle collision. Upon arrival, paramedics stabilize the patient's neck then transport him to the emergency department. He says that he has neck pain that radiates down the right arm. Physical examination shows a loss of sensation in a small region of the lateral upper right arm. An MRI of the spine shows a herniated intervertebral disc impinging on the right C5 nerve roots. Which of the following movements will most likely be affected?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Patients involved in high impact injuries, such as motor vehicle accidents, are prone to very serious spinal cord injury. Fortunately, this patient apparently sustained a comparatively mild injury with herniation of the intervertebral disc at C5. Disc herniation may occur as a result of sudden injury, as in the case of this patient, or from chronic stress to the back (from heavy lifting, etc.). In this condition, the tough, fibrous covering of the intervertebral disc is compromised, allowing the inner nucleus pulposus to bulge out and compress the spinal nerves. This characteristically produces the radiating symptoms that we see in this patient.

As shown in the figure of the brachial plexus below, the C5 nerve root significantly contributes to the upper trunk, which in turn innervates the lateral and posterior cords. Only certain nerves branching from these cords receive input directly from C5, and typically these nerves innervate more proximal muscles. Specifically, C5 makes contributions to the suprascapular nerve, musculocutaneous nerve, axillary nerve, lower subscapular nerve, upper subscapular nerve, lateral pectoral nerve, long thoracic nerve, and part of the phrenic nerve. For the purposes of this question, the important nerve in this list is the musculocutaneous nerve, which provides innervation to major flexors of the elbow (choice C) including the biceps brachii and brachialis. Also mentioned in the question is the loss of sensation in the lateral upper arm. This is the region of the C5 dermatome. C5 contributions to the axillary nerve are responsible for sensation in this region.

Adduction of the thumb (choice A) is mediated by the intrinsic hand muscle known as the adductor pollicis. This muscle is innervated by the ulnar nerve, which receives fibers from C8 and T1 via the medial cord. Because of the proximal-distal gradient of segmental motor innervation, we should anticipate that a C5 injury would affect proximal limb muscles. The distal limb muscles (in the hand) are innervated by C8 and T1 spinal cord segments.

choice_explanations.A: Thumb adduction is mediated by the adductor pollicis, innervated by the ulnar nerve (C8-T1) via the medial cord.
choice_explanations.C: C5 contributes to the musculocutaneous nerve, which innervates the major elbow flexors (biceps brachii and brachialis).
choice_explanations.E: Pronation of the forearm (pronator teres/quadratus) is innervated by the median nerve (C6-T1) and is not preferentially lost with a C5 lesion.

fa_summary: A C5 nerve root lesion preferentially affects proximal upper limb muscles; C5 contributes to the musculocutaneous nerve, so elbow flexion (biceps/brachialis) is affected.

stem: A 35-year-old man comes to his physician because of pain in the right groin and buttock region. He reports that the pain is exacerbated by weight bearing and is relieved by rest. His medical history is significant for alcohol abuse. Physical examination shows a limp with limitation of right hip flexion during ambulation and decreased abduction at the right hip. Passive range of motion of the right hip is limited and painful. An x-ray of the hip shows flattening of the femoral head and an irregular appearance of the capital femoral epiphysis compared to the left side. Avascular necrosis of the right femoral head is diagnosed. A disruption of blood supply from which of the following vessels is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head is sometimes traumatic in origin (e.g., femoral neck fracture, hip dislocation) but most often is nontraumatic. Chronic steroid use and alcohol abuse are frequently associated with this condition. Although the etiology is unclear, it is likely that intravascular coagulation plays a role. The clinical picture is usually a limp to avoid pain (antalgic gait) or a painless limp. If there is pain, it is often referred to the anterior thigh and groin region or the gluteal region. The diagnosis may be confirmed radiographically, which shows the findings indicated in the question. Passing deep to the inguinal ligament, the external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery. A major branch of the femoral artery in the anterior thigh is the deep (profunda) femoral artery, which has two major branches, the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries. Most of the blood supply to the head of the femur arises from the medial circumflex femoral artery. This artery ascends along the neck of the femur to reach the head of the femur. See figure below.

The deep femoral artery (choice A) is a branch of the femoral artery. Its major region of supply are the muscles of the thigh. The external iliac artery (choice B) is a branch of the common iliac artery at the pelvic brim. The external iliac artery does not cross over the pelvic brim to enter the pelvis. It gives rise to the inferior epigastric artery and then continues into the thigh by passing deep to the inguinal ligament. At this point, its name is changed to the femoral artery. The femoral artery (choice C) is a continuation of the external iliac artery. The deep (profunda) femoral artery is a branch of the femoral artery and one of its branches, the medial circumflex artery (choice E), is the primary blood supply to the head of the femur. The femoral artery is primarily responsible for the blood supply to the lower limb distal to the knee. The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus to enter the popliteal fossa, at which point its name is changed to the popliteal artery. The popliteal artery divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries. The lateral circumflex femoral artery (choice D) is also a branch of the deep femoral artery. It joins the medial circumflex artery to loop around the proximal femoral shaft, but its major blood supply is to the upper shaft of the femur and muscles of the anterior thigh muscles. A figure of the arterial supply to the lower limb is shown below.

choice_explanations.A: The deep femoral artery supplies the muscles of the thigh, not the femoral head.
choice_explanations.B: The external iliac artery does not supply the femoral head; it becomes the femoral artery deep to the inguinal ligament.
choice_explanations.C: The femoral artery is primarily responsible for blood supply to the lower limb distal to the knee.
choice_explanations.D: The lateral circumflex femoral artery supplies the upper femoral shaft and anterior thigh muscles.
choice_explanations.E: Most of the blood supply to the head of the femur arises from the medial circumflex femoral artery, which ascends along the neck of the femur; disruption causes avascular necrosis.

fa_summary: The femoral head is supplied mainly by the medial circumflex femoral artery (a branch of the deep femoral artery); disruption causes avascular necrosis, associated with alcohol abuse and chronic steroid use.
